How a GPU Works, and How to Optimize Its Performance

Using one H200 as the example, we zoom from a whole large model down to a single instruction and bit: how the GPU works, where the time goes, and how to make it faster.

A draft GPU tutorial, under review round by round. Every figure is interactive: press the buttons, drag the timeline.

1What Questions Does This Book Answer, and With Which Example?

In this book, we follow one sentence through a 62-layer large language model, derive the three inference regimes, and then open up one layer to see how the hardware runs it and how to push it as fast as it can go.

That comes down to three questions. First, once a sentence enters the model, what steps turn it into the next token? Second, the model has only one set of fixed parameters (called weights), so why does running it to generate output (called inference) split into three regimes? Those regimes are prefill (processing the whole known input at once), decode (token-by-token decoding, generating 1 new token at a time), and verify (speculative decoding verification: guessing a few tokens first and checking them all in one pass). Primer 1, Sections 5 to 7 cover all three. Third, when we open up one layer, what does each step compute, what does it hand to the next step, and how do we push it, step by step, close to the shortest time the hardware allows?

The whole book uses only one example: the 62-layer Muse Spark Open. It is an open-weight Mixture of Experts (MoE) large language model with about 816 billion total parameters, where each layer picks only a few small expert networks out of many to run (see Primer 1, Section 2). Our task comes from a public GPU performance optimization competition. Muse Spark Open runs across 8 NVIDIA H200s (a data-center GPU), and we write the GPU program for one layer on a single card. For each layer type, the task gives the shortest time that the nominal hardware peaks allow, called the lower bound. You can calculate the non-expert part of that bound directly from the full-layer rules in Primer 2, Section 3. The expert part is whatever is left after you subtract everything else from the given bound (see Primer 2, Section 4). We first take apart every step of that single layer on one H200. Then, at the end of Chapter 9, we add the 62 measured single-layer times back up into a full decode pass and state which parts are measured and which are not measured (for how the 8 GPUs split the work, see the opening of Primer 1).

We wrote this book for engineers and students who want to make large language model inference run fast or understand low-level GPU performance. By the end, you will be able to break down one layer's execution time across its stages and calculate whether each step is memory-bound or compute-bound, read GPU machine instructions to locate where time is going, and judge whether a code change pays off or is a net loss at the current token count.

2In What Order Does the Book Dissect the System?

We zoom in through the profiler's six levels, from coarse to fine. Each chapter opens up the part we saw in the previous chapter, and a single matrix-vector multiplication ties the evolution together from chapter to chapter.

The opening three chapters are Primers (Primer 1 to Primer 3), which look in turn at the full model, a single layer, and a minimal GPU program (kernel; see Primer 3). Then we enter Part I (Chapters 1–6), which maps to Level 1 through Level 6 of a profiler (a performance profiling tool that measures the latency and utilization of each hardware unit): Chapter 1 starts at the execution timeline, and each subsequent chapter zooms in one level deeper.

One worked example runs through all of Part I. It is the first matrix multiplication in a layer when the input has only 1 token, which makes it a matrix-vector multiplication, gemv (one matrix times one vector; see Primer 2, Section 1). Primer 3 writes its first version, and each of Chapters 1–6 uses that chapter's new mechanism to make it one step faster. Multi-token GEMM, at 8 to 256 tokens, needs mechanisms that are not all in place until Chapter 6, so we walk through its full evolution in one go in the final section of Chapter 6.

Part II (Chapters 7–9) returns to a layer's two main operators and the full-layer assembly. The two operators are attention, which looks across the context, and Mixture of Experts (MoE), which picks experts to compute for each token (see Primer 1, Section 2 for what they are). The two operators and the full-layer assembly each walk their own evolution chain from slow to fast, and the end of Chapter 9 adds the measured single-layer time back up into the full 62-layer decode pass. In Part III, Chapter 10 summarizes how to take a slow kernel and track down its bottleneck one level at a time. Finally, Appendix A explains what changes in hardware from H200 to the next-generation NVIDIA GPU (B200), Appendix B provides a quick-reference table of machine instructions (the low-level instructions the GPU actually executes), Appendix C provides the glossary and term index, and Appendix D summarizes single-GPU H200 inference hardware topology and extended modes for quick reference.

4What Prerequisites Do You Need, and What Can You Skip on a First Read?

You only need to know how to read C/C++, multiply matrices, and understand CPU caches and multithreading; we build every GPU concept from scratch.

Before starting this book, you need only four things:

  • Reading C/C++: pointers, arrays, loops, and functions;
  • Multiplying matrices and computing vector dot products;
  • Knowing what a CPU cache is: a small, fast copy of memory sitting close to the compute core;
  • Knowing that multiple threads can read and write the same memory at the same time, and that doing so can cause errors.

You do not need any prior GPU background. Primer 3 writes our first CUDA GPU program from scratch, and Chapters 1–6 open up the GPU hardware one level at a time. Chapter 2, Section 6 explains when data written by one GPU thread becomes visible to other threads, and compares that behavior with common desktop and server CPUs (x86). And you do not need an H200 on hand to read this book.

On a first read, you can skip three parts and come back to them when you need them:

  • The one-line cost breakdown under each step caption in the interactive figures;
  • Multi-token GEMM in the final section of Chapter 6 (Section 8), which draws on all the mechanisms from Chapters 1–6;
  • Chapter 10 and the four appendices, which are meant for reference.

5How Do You Use the Figures and Charts in This Book?

Every figure draws the real hardware units and data paths, and you step through them using the buttons and sliders outside the figure. We plot every measured result as a chart and state how it was measured.

Each interactive figure in this book opens right in the middle of an active execution step. You can use the buttons outside the figure to switch modes, or drag the slider to walk through execution one step at a time; each step's caption card lists the formula, the inputs (tensor shape, data type, and where they live), the outputs (where they are written), what gets handed to the next step, and a single line for the cost of that step.

We plot latencies, speedups, and before-and-after comparisons as charts right under the paragraph they belong to, without separate figure numbers. The main text states only the conclusion and at most one key number. Primer 3, Section 5 and Chapter 10 explain how we measure latencies in this book. Each chart's note states in only one sentence how that chart was measured, and we do not mix results from different measurement setups in the same chart. Finally, the lower-bound line in a chart shows the shortest time that the nominal hardware peaks allow; it is calculated, not measured (see Primer 2, Section 4).

This book works at two reading speeds: skim only the section headings, the bold sentences, and the figure readouts to catch the mechanism of each section, or read the full text to follow one causal chain through the entire derivation.

6How Are Units, Terms, and Formulas Written Throughout This Book?

  • Units: We use decimal units (MB, GB, TB/s) for device memory capacity, weight size, and bandwidth (bytes transferred per second), and binary units (KiB, MiB) for on-chip storage and tile sizes. Memory vendors quote bandwidth in decimal units, whereas on-chip storage is aligned to powers of 2.
  • Token: Throughout this book, we call the basic unit processed by the model a token, and do not shorten it to "word."
  • Operator and kernel: An "operator" is one computation step in the model (such as a single matrix multiplication); we call the function that implements it on the GPU a kernel throughout this book (not a "core"). One operator can be implemented by one or several kernels.
  • Single layer and full model: "single layer" means one decoder layer on a single GPU, with time measured in µs; "full model" means the complete 62-layer network, with time measured in ms.
  • Speedup notation: "~XX× faster" and "a ~XX× speedup" mean old time ÷\div new time (the ratio, without subtracting 1). "X%X\% faster" means old time ÷\div new time −1- 1, and a latency drop is written as "takes X%X\% less time."
  • Formulas and tensor shapes: We typeset formulas in math notation; a multidimensional array of numbers is called a tensor, and we write a tensor shape as W:[rows,columns]BF16\shape{W}{\text{rows},\;\text{columns}}{BF16}—the tensor name, the length of each dimension in square brackets, and the element data type in the subscript (for example, BF16 stands for 16-bit floating point, and we explain each data type the first time it appears).
  • Chinese and English terms: We explain each English technical term the first time it appears, and Appendix C at the end of the book provides the glossary and term index.

Takeaway: This book follows a single model on a single H200 from start to finish: first we trace how one sentence passes through the entire model, and then we open up one layer level by level down to instructions and bits.

Next chapter's question: Once a sentence enters this 62-layer model, what steps turn it into the next token? Why do we run the same set of weights in three regimes: prefill, decode, and verify?

When you feed a sentence into the 62-layer Muse Spark Open, what steps turn it into the next token? And if the weights are the exact same, why do we split inference into three regimes: prefill, decode, and verify? Let's answer the second question first, because the reason is simple: on every forward pass (when running only a few tokens), a single GPU must stream about 9.0 GB of fixed weights from device memory (HBM, the GPU's main memory; see Section 4). You pay that read cost per pass, not per token. How many known tokens you have in hand before the pass starts decides which regime you run.

The model runs across 8 H200 GPUs (an NVIDIA data-center GPU), and each GPU stores and computes only a slice of each layer's weights (Primer 2, Section 2 shows how we slice them)—that ~9.0 GB above is what one GPU reads per pass, not a total split across the 8 GPUs. Throughout this book, we look at only one of those GPUs. Whenever a pass processes at most 8 tokens (see the subsection at the end of Section 6 for what changes past 8), because each GPU holds only part of a result so all 8 GPUs must sum or concatenate their parts, a pass runs 188 cross-GPU data exchanges (marked with ◆ in the figures and tables; Section 4 names the 3 per-layer exchanges, and Primer 2, Section 2 shows where they sit), and every exchange waits for all 8 GPUs to arrive before execution moves on. Those 188 cross-GPU exchanges stay out of our single-GPU HBM ledger, and their end-to-end pass latency was not measured (Chapter 9, Section 9 benchmarks the three per-layer collectives in isolation on an 8-GPU node). Figure P1-1 lays out the whole model from input to output. This chapter and Primer 2 will unpack every block in turn; for now, let's trace the order they run in.

1Inbound: How Does One Sentence Become the Two Inputs to Layer 0?

We first split a sentence into integer token IDs and look up their vectors; after RMSNorm, we get Layer 0's two inputs: 32-bit stream_0 and 16-bit x_0.

A GPU only crunches arrays of numbers. Figure P1-2 brings together all 8 steps (Sections 1–3) across the three execution regimes (Sections 5–7); in Step 1, we split the input sentence into tokens and map each one to its integer ID in the 202,048-entry vocabulary. We call the full trip from embedding lookup all the way to scoring every candidate in the vocabulary one forward pass (or one pass for short), and we write T for the number of tokens processed together in that pass (our running example in this chapter uses a 5-token prompt, so T = 5). Those T IDs form a 1D array ids of shape [T][T].

The model represents every token with 8,192 numbers. That width is the hidden size, and every 8192 you see in the tensor shapes below is that same dimension. In Step 2, we use ids to look up the embedding table W𝑒𝑚𝑏𝑒𝑑:[202048,8192]BF16\shape{W_{embed}}{202048,\;8192}{BF16}, where BF16 is 16-bit floating point (2 bytes per number). Note that this lookup is not a matrix multiplication: it just grabs the T rows indexed by ids and writes them out as e:[T,8192]BF16\shape{e}{T,\;8192}{BF16}. Each GPU stores only about 1/8 of the embedding table's rows. Whenever an ID falls outside a GPU's local 1/8 slice, that GPU fills the row with zeros, and all 8 GPUs then sum their local ee tensors so every GPU has the complete ee. Because the lookup reads only these T rows, it does not count toward the fixed weights we have to read on every pass in Section 4.

Next, we turn ee into Layer 0's two inputs. RMSNorm (root mean square normalization) divides a vector vv by the square root of the mean of its squared elements, RMSNorm(v)=v/1n∑ivi2+ϵ (where ϵ\epsilon is a tiny constant to avoid dividing by zero), keeping the numerical range stable. Weighted RMSNorm does that same division and then multiplies elementwise by a learned scale vector of the same length, with a separate scale vector learned at each site that uses one. The RMSNorm right after embedding lookup does not multiply by a scale vector: it divides and immediately casts to FP32 (32-bit floating point, 4 bytes per number) to produce stream0:[T,8192]FP32\shape{\mathrm{stream}_0}{T,\;8192}{FP32}. Later layers never overwrite this tensor—they add their outputs onto it (Section 2 shows how), which is why we call it the residual stream, written stream. In the source code, this post-embedding normalization is called embed_norm. It runs only once at the very start, leaving each token's vector with an RMS of about 1, and while passing through all 62 layers, the residual stream itself is not normalized again.

Why keep two copies of the state at different precisions? A floating-point number consists of a sign, an exponent range, and significant digits: if we kept only a single 16-bit state, adding all 62 layers' outputs into the same stream would accumulate rounding drift, so we store the residual stream in 4-byte, 32-bit FP32, which keeps more significant digits than 16-bit formats. Inside each layer, though, the matrix multiplications take 2-byte, 16-bit BF16 inputs so they read half as many bytes and run faster. That is why at the end of Step 2 we copy stream_0, run a weighted RMSNorm on the copy, and cast it to BF16 to get Layer 0's matrix-multiplication input x0:[T,8192]BF16\shape{x_0}{T,\;8192}{BF16} (input_layernorm in the source code). Every layer prepares its input the exact same way—copy the residual stream and normalize the copy, leaving the residual stream itself untouched. Starting from Layer 1, Layer l−1 computes this input for Layer l at the end of its own final stage, using Layer l's scale vector (Primer 2, Section 2). So the two normalizations at the start are not doing duplicate work: the first sets the starting scale of the residual stream, and the second prepares the input to Layer 0. Throughout the book, we write stream_l and x_l for these two inputs to Layer l.

2Passing Through 62 Layers: What Goes to the Next Layer, and What Stays for Future Tokens?

Vertically, each layer hands the updated stream and x down to the next layer; horizontally, it writes each token's key and value into the layer's KV cache for future tokens to read.

Every layer splits into two halves—attention first, then an expert (MoE) block—and each half adds its result back into stream.

Each layer runs two merges on the GPU's compute units—one after attention and one after the experts—to fold each branch's result back into the residual stream stored in HBM (Primer 2, Section 2 gives the equation), keeping the residual stream's RMS near 1 so its scale does not drift across all 62 layers. Here is how: at each merge, we normalize the new term to an RMS of about 1 and multiply it elementwise by β\beta, while multiplying the existing residual stream elementwise by α\alpha. Both α\alpha and β\beta are 8,192-element vectors derived from a learned vector at that merge site (this book leaves out the exact formula). At every coordinate ii, they satisfy αi2+βi2=1.

Only when βi\beta_i gets extremely close to 1 does αi\alpha_i hit a floor of about 0.03, nudging the identity slightly off. Because the first normalization already set Layer 0's residual stream to an RMS of about 1, as long as the two terms being combined are roughly uncorrelated and each has a similar magnitude across all 8,192 coordinates, following this rule at every merge keeps their sum at an RMS of about 1 too (we did not measure those two statistical conditions).

In Step 3 of Figure P1-2, look at the handoff: each Layer l (l = 0..60) passes stream_{l+1} and x_{l+1} down to the next layer. Only the final layer (l = 61) is an exception—with no next layer after it, it outputs only stream_{62} and skips computing x.

Why does every layer stash its keys and values in memory? When a token enters Layer l, it first projects x_l into three vectors: a query Q, a key K, and a value V. It takes the dot product of its own Q against the K of itself and every earlier token to get a list of similarity scores sis_i, runs softmax (pi=esi/∑jesj) to turn those scores into weights that sum to 1, and computes a weighted sum of those tokens' V vectors—that step is attention. Because each token looks only at itself and earlier tokens, we call it causal attention. Here is the key observation: once an earlier token's K and V are computed, they never change, yet every future token will need to read them again. Accordingly, each layer stores the computed K and V in its own region of device memory—the KV cache, written K_cache[l] and V_cache[l].

K and V come from multiplying x by a narrower weight matrix, so they are much narrower than x. We slice them into chunks of 64 numbers, where each chunk is one key-value head (KV head). We slice Q into 64-wide query heads the same way, and several query heads share a single KV head as each one runs the attention step above (Primer 2, Section 2 shows how many query heads share each KV head and how they are grouped). Each layer has 16 KV heads in total, so across 8 GPUs each GPU handles 2 of them. Across the attention half of the layer, that makes two weight matrices in total: the input projection matrix that produces Q, K, V, and the gate values (a set of scaling coefficients) from x, and an output projection matrix afterward that maps the weighted sum of V back to 8,192 numbers (Primer 2, Section 2).

Every number in the KV cache is stored in FP8 (8-bit floating point, 1 byte per number—half the bytes of BF16 and saving three quarters compared with FP32). On a single GPU, the cache space that one token takes up in one layer is called one slot (KV cache slot), which comes to 2 (K, V)×2 (heads)×64×1 B=256 B.

The second half of every layer is a Mixture of Experts (MoE) block: each layer has 256 experts, and each GPU holds 32 of them (its local experts). Each expert is a feed-forward network (FFN) with 3 weight matrices: the first two each project the input into a vector, one passes through an elementwise nonlinearity to act as a gate that multiplies the other elementwise, and the third matrix projects that product back out. Before the experts run, a tiny scoring matrix scores all 256 experts; each token routes to only its top 8 experts and takes a score-weighted sum of their outputs (see Primer 2, Section 2). Framing the experts are two shared matrices that every token passes through: pooler squeezes the vector narrower before the experts, and unpooler widens it back to 8,192 dimensions afterward (Primer 2, Section 2 gives their shapes)—together with the two attention matrices and the expert scoring matrix above, these 5 weight matrices that every token passes through are called the dense weights (listed in Section 4).

Across all 62 layers, two things change from layer to layer. First is how far back attention looks: 46 sliding-window layers look only at the most recent 2,048 positions, while 16 full-attention layers (1 in every 4 layers—the layers with index l % 4 == 1, i.e., Layers 1, 5, …, 61) attend to the entire history from the very start—so while history stays within 2,048 positions both layer types read the exact same number of cache slots, and once history grows longer sliding-window layers cap their reads at 2,048 slots (sliding-window layers also apply rotary position embedding, whereas full-attention layers skip it; see Primer 2, Section 2). Second is how expert weights are stored: Layers 1–60 compress them into a 4-bit format, whereas Layers 0 and 61 keep them in BF16 (Section 4 gives the byte sizes; why Layers 0 and 61 keep their experts in BF16 was not determined in this book).

3Outbound and Loopback: How Do 8,192 Numbers Turn Back into a Token ID?

After the final RMSNorm, we pick out only the rows that need a prediction, score all 202,048 vocabulary candidates to get logits, and feed the chosen token ID back to Step 2 (embedding lookup).

In Step 4 of Figure P1-2, once all 62 layers finish, we cast all T rows of stream_{62} to BF16 and run them through a weighted final RMSNorm. Only then do we pick out the rows that actually need a next-token prediction; call that row count R (because RMSNorm works row by row, normalizing before or after picking rows gives the exact same result). During prefill, the prompt already tells us the next token for positions 1–4, so we take only the last row (R = 1); during decode, we only have 1 row to begin with (R = 1); and during verify, we check predictions across all 8 positions at once, so we keep all 8 rows (R = 8; see Section 7). Those R rows form h𝑓𝑖𝑛𝑎𝑙:[R,8192]BF16\shape{h_{final}}{R,\;8192}{BF16}.

Step 5 runs lm_head (vocabulary projection, the matrix that scores every candidate token in the vocabulary). We split the vocabulary evenly by rows across the 8 GPUs, so each GPU holds about one eighth—W𝑙𝑚:[≈25k,8192]BF16, or 0.414 GB. Each GPU multiplies h_final by its local shard to get its slice of logits z:[R,vocabulary/8]FP32\shape{z}{R,\;\text{vocabulary}/8}{FP32}, and the 8 GPUs concatenate their slices into the full 202,048-candidate scores. Notice the contrast with Step 2: inbound embedding lookup fetches only T rows by index, whereas outbound scoring has to take the dot product of every candidate with h_final. Regardless of R, every forward pass has to stream the entire 0.414 GB local shard.

Step 6 applies the logit softcap: we multiply each score by a fixed scale factor ss and pass it through c⋅tanh⁡(⋅/c) (where s=0.17678 and c=20 are model constants) to smoothly cap every score inside [−c, c][-c,\ c] so no single score blows up. Once capped, these RR rows of unnormalized candidate scores are called logits, with shape logits:[R,202048]FP32\shape{\mathrm{logits}}{R,\;202048}{FP32}.

In Step 7, we select the new token ID next_id from logits (this book leaves out the sampling rules). Step 8 feeds next_id right back into Step 2 (embedding lookup) as the row index for the next pass, so from this point on we never run the tokenizer again.

We call the number of valid slots in the KV cache the committed sequence length (written CC), and the next pass writes its first new token at position C+1. Prefill advances the committed sequence length by T (5 in our example, so the next pass starts at position 6), decode advances it by 1, and Section 7 shows how many slots verify advances it by. Putting all 8 steps from Sections 1–3 together for our T = 5, R = 1 (C=0→5) pass gives the step-by-step map below. Section 4 explains the Bytes column:

Step Reads (from) Writes (to) Bytes at T = 5 (R = 1) Execution unit & cross-GPU waits
1. Tokenize / fetch IDs Input text (later passes reuse next_id in HBM) HBM: ids [T][T] 0 B weights; writes 20 B ID array (4 B per ID) Tokenizer (where it runs and its latency were not measured)
2. Embedding lookup & two RMSNorms HBM: hit rows in this GPU's ~1/8 embedding shard HBM: stream_0 [T,8192][T, 8192] FP32 and x_0 [T,8192][T, 8192] BF16 Reads ≤80 KiB\le 80\ \mathrm{KiB} (at most 5 rows), writes 160+80=240 KiB HBM and GPU compute units; waits on ◆ #1 8-GPU sum (latency not measured)

6. Logit softcap HBM: scores z [R,202048][R, 202048] FP32 HBM: logits [R,202048][R, 202048] FP32 0 B weights; reads 808,192 B, writes 808,192 B HBM and GPU compute units (latency not measured)

4Forward-Pass Accounting: What Is the Minimum Number of Bytes One GPU Must Read per Pass, and How Long Does That Take?

When you run only a few tokens, every pass still streams ~9.0 GB of fixed weights plus 28.3 MB per active compressed expert, while the KV cache traffic for those few tokens is negligible.

A GPU's off-chip main device memory is HBM (High Bandwidth Memory); bandwidth is how many bytes it can move per second, and the H200 has a nominal peak HBM bandwidth of 4.8 TB/s. Because the shared on-chip cache across the entire chip totals only 60 MiB, the several gigabytes of weights on a single GPU cannot fit on the chip itself—so every forward pass has to stream them fresh from HBM.

Before we compare the three regimes, let's do the math on what a single forward pass has to read from HBM. The bill breaks into three parts, starting with the fixed weights you pay for on every pass. The 5 matrices read on every pass that every token passes through—without any token-dependent routing—are called dense matrices (the dense weights): the projection matrix for Q, K, V, and gating values (a set of scaling coefficients; see Primer 2, Section 2), the attention output matrix, the router scoring matrix for the experts, and the two matrices that squeeze the vector narrower before the experts and widen it back up afterward.

Here is everything that sits in a single GPU's HBM and the rule for how much of each item one pass reads (Primer 2, Section 2 gives the exact matrix shapes and splits):

Resident in HBM Breakdown & size stored per GPU Read rule per pass (T ≤ 8)
Embedding shard W_embed ~1/8 of vocabulary rows, ~0.414 GB Reads at most T rows by ID (≤16T KiB\le 16T\ \mathrm{KiB}); excluded from fixed weights
Dense weights (62 × 5) 197.1 MB stored per layer: Q/K/V/gate projection 37.75 MB, attention output projection 16.78 MB, FP32 router 8.39 MB, pre-expert squeeze pooler 67.11 MB, post-expert widening unpooler 67.11 MB Read every pass; at T ≤ 8, unpooler reads only this GPU's 1/8 slice (8.39 MB), so each layer reads 138.4 MB (8.58 GB across 62 layers)
Local experts (62 × 32) 28.3 MB/expert in Layers 1–60 (4-bit); ~100.7 MB/expert in Layers 0 & 61 (BF16) Read only when a token in this pass routes to that local expert
KV cache (62 layers, FP8) 2 KV heads on this GPU, 256 B per token per layer Writes T new slots first, then reads visible slots by history length (up to 2,048 in sliding-window layers; all visible history in full-attention layers)
lm_head shard W_lm ~1/8 of vocabulary rows, 0.414 GB Reads the entire 0.414 GB shard every pass, regardless of R

Add up the two "read every pass" items in the table: across the three T ≤ 8 regimes in this chapter, the 197.1 MB of dense weights stored per layer and the 138.4 MB read per layer differ only by the unread 7/8 slice of unpooler (197.1−58.7=138.4 MB), giving 8.58 GB across all 62 layers; add this GPU's 0.414 GB lm_head shard and the total comes to 8.995 GB (about 9.0 GB). Here is the catch: whether you feed 1 token in a pass or batch 5 or 8 tokens side by side, you still read that exact same 9.0 GB.

Even if the GPU did nothing else at all, just streaming those fixed weights into the chip takes at least 8.995 GB÷4.8 TB/s≈1.87 ms (before counting experts or cross-GPU communication).

The second part of the bill is the expert weights: each touched local expert adds one weight read, and every layer is paced by the busiest GPU (or straggler rank—the GPU whose local experts receive the most (token, expert) pairs in that layer) finishing its reads and compute. That wait comes straight from the cross-GPU exchanges noted at the start of the chapter: at T ≤ 8, each layer runs 3 cross-GPU exchanges (one sum after attention, one sum after the experts, and one concatenation after the post-expert widening projection; see Primer 2, Section 2), which together with 1 cross-GPU sum after embedding lookup and 1 cross-GPU concatenation after vocabulary scoring come to 1+62×3+1=188 per pass; every exchange synchronizes all 8 GPUs, so any GPU that finishes early sits waiting at the exchange for the slowest GPU. When a pass runs 1 token, the 8 chosen experts average 1 per GPU across the 8 GPUs, yet the busiest GPU touches more than 1 local expert (Primer 2, Sections 2 and 4 show how many local experts the busiest GPU touches on average).

As a baseline, across the middle 60 layers the 4-bit expert format also stores a 1-byte scale factor per 16 weights, so each touched 4-bit local expert adds 28.3 MB of reads rather than the ~25.2 MB of bare 4-bit weights; touching even 1 local expert per layer across those 60 layers adds 60×28.3 MB≈1.7 GB, or at least about 0.354 ms at 4.8 TB/s (Layers 0 and 61 leave their experts uncompressed in 2-byte BF16 at about 100.7 MB per expert—about 3.6× as many bytes per touched expert as the 4-bit format, with the exact formula in Primer 2, Section 2—which we set aside here so 1.7 GB counts only the middle 60 layers). As a pass processes more tokens together, it touches more experts overall, though different tokens often land on the same expert and share a single read of its weights.

The third part is the KV cache, at 256 B per visible historical token in each layer (Section 2). Even the largest pass in this chapter (verify in Section 7) reads only a dozen or so slots per layer. That is well inside Section 2's 2,048-token sliding window, so sliding-window layers and full-attention layers read the exact same number of slots here: less than 0.21 MB across all 62 layers, which is a rounding error next to 9.0 GB. That holds only while the history is short, though; once the history reaches tens of thousands of tokens, the picture changes (Primer 2, Section 4).

Once we stream all those weights into the chip, how much math do we actually do on them? We write FLOP for floating-point operations, counting one multiply-add as 2 FLOPs. A single BF16 weight takes up 2 bytes, and each of the T tokens in the pass does one multiply-add with it for a total of 2T2T FLOPs—which works out to about T FLOPs for every 1 byte of BF16 weight read. Meanwhile, in the time it takes an H200 to read 1 byte from HBM, its compute units can execute hundreds of FLOPs (Primer 2, Section 1 gives the exact number). So when T is small, the compute units spend almost all their time sitting idle waiting on HBM; Primer 2, Sections 1 and 4 show how large T has to grow to flip that balance.

5Prefill: Why Can Known Tokens Run in Parallel in a Single Pass?

Under causal attention, each token uses only its own and earlier tokens' keys and values—all computed in the same pass—so we can stack all 5 tokens into a matrix and run them together.

When a user first submits a prompt, the pass that processes it is called prefill. Because all 5 tokens at positions 1–5 are already in hand before computation starts (T = 5), there is no need to feed them one by one: we stack all 5 rows directly into xl:[5,8192]BF16\shape{x_l}{5,\;8192}{BF16} and push them through side by side, so each weight matrix multiplies a 5-row matrix at once instead of multiplying a single vector across 5 separate passes. Feeding those 5 tokens one by one across 5 passes would stream the 8.995 GB of fixed weights five times (44.98 GB in total, raising the single-GPU weight-read floor to 5×1.874 ms=9.37 ms at 4.8 TB/s) and run 5×188=940 cross-GPU exchanges.

On this pass, at each layer all 5 rows compute their K and V from x_l, the layer writes all 5 new KV slots (5×256 B) into its cache first, and then row i reads positions 1..i under the causal mask; because the cache starts empty (C=0), there is no prior history to read, and attention reads only the 5 slots written in this pass (79.4 KB across all 62 layers). Once all 5 rows finish Layer 61, we take only the last row (R = 1, Section 3) to predict token 6. Look at the bill for this pass: because all 5 tokens share the same fixed-weight read, each token pays an amortized cost of only about 1.80 GB, and we do about 5 FLOPs per byte of BF16 weight read (Section 4). When a prompt is very long, we slice it into chunks and run them across several passes (Primer 2, Section 4).

6Decode: Why Can Each Pass Process Only 1 Token, and What Is Its Bottleneck?

Token 7 does not exist until token 6 is generated, so decode can feed only 1 token per pass while still re-reading all the fixed weights—doing only ~1 FLOP per byte read.

Once prefill produces token 6 and we move on to generating token 7 and token 8, the picture changes completely. A large language model generates text autoregressively: producing each new token requires computing over all preceding tokens. Until we finish computing token 7, token 8 does not exist yet. So from this step on, we enter decode (token-by-token decoding), where the input to each pass shrinks to just the single token we just generated, token 6 (T = 1). Each layer writes 1 new slot into the KV cache and reads 6 slots in total—that new slot plus the 5 slots left behind by prefill—before finishing Layer 61 with R = 1 to produce token 7. Put decode next to prefill and the bottleneck jumps right out: to generate that 1 token, the fixed-weight read per token shoots up 5× (9.0 GB vs. 1.80 GB). As noted at the start of the chapter, we count only the bytes that a single GPU reads from HBM here, leaving cross-GPU communication out of the ledger. In words, at about 1 FLOP per byte, the GPU's compute units sit waiting on HBM rather than on math (see the end of Section 4).

Can Several Requests Share One Pass?

Yes: batching BB concurrent requests into one pass shares a single fixed-weight read across all BB requests, while each request still reads its own KV cache. When BB independent requests are active online at the same time, each contributes its 1 newly generated token so all BB rows run together in one pass (T=B).

Why do fixed weights step up once a pass exceeds 8 tokens? That limit comes from a threshold rule in the baseline inference code for the post-expert widening matrix unpooler (Section 2; Primer 2, Section 2), though why it is set to 8 was not determined in this book: at T ≤ 8 each GPU reads an 8.39 MB slice and concatenates across GPUs, whereas at T > 8 every GPU reads the full 67.11 MB matrix locally and skips that cross-GPU concatenation (dropping cross-GPU exchanges per pass from 188 to 126); by arithmetic, adding 58.72 MB per layer lifts the 62-layer plus lm_head fixed weights from ~9.0 GB to about 12.6 GB, after which they stop growing with token count.

Meanwhile, because every request has its own conversation history, KV cache reads cannot be shared: at an 80,000-token history (unlike the dozen-slot short example in Section 4), going from 1 to 16 requests caps sliding-window KV reads at the recent 2,048 slots per request so extra touched local experts lead the byte growth, whereas full-attention layers read tens of thousands of historical KV slots per request so KV cache traffic becomes the largest byte growth term and stretches single-layer time much further (Primer 2, Section 4 covers how multiple requests merge into one pass and how latency and bottlenecks shift).

7Verify: How Can One Request Yield More Than 1 Token in a Single Pass?

We first draft 7 candidate tokens, stack them with the known token 6 into an 8-row pass, and compare left to right up to the first mismatch—getting 1 to 8 tokens in a single pass.

If running 1 token for a single request streams 9.0 GB of fixed weights, and running 8 tokens side by side streams that exact same 9.0 GB, can we pack 8 tokens into a single pass for one request too? That is the idea behind verify (speculative decoding verification). It is not a step that runs after decode, but an alternative way to run decode: it starts from the exact same post-prefill state, with 5 slots in the KV cache and token 6 already known. A separate drafting mechanism (such as a small draft model, or drafter) first proposes 7 candidate tokens for positions 7 through 13, called draft tokens. 1 known token + 7 drafts = 8 matches the drafter's block size of 8 and stays within T ≤ 8, where fixed weights remain at ~9.0 GB (past 8 they jump to ~12.6 GB, as shown in the subsection at the end of Section 6; why this size was chosen was not determined in this book). Right or wrong, all 8 tokens are concrete numbers before the pass begins—so just like prefill (Section 5), we stack them into xl:[8,8192]BF16\shape{x_l}{8,\;8192}{BF16} (T = 8) and push them through all 62 layers in a single pass. Each layer writes 8 slots into the KV cache and reads 13 slots in total (including the existing 5 slots), and at the end we send all 8 rows into lm_head (R = 8) so we can check the prediction at every row.

Why can a single pass verify all 7 guesses at once? Look at the lower-triangular causal mask in Figure P1-3: under causal attention, row i looks only at the first i rows (Section 2). That means the output of row i (i = 1..8) in Figure P1-3 is the large model's prediction for position 6 + i, assuming the draft tokens at positions 7 through 5 + i are all correct. In particular, row 1 depends only on the known tokens 1–6 and on no draft tokens at all, so its prediction for position 7 is guaranteed to be valid.

To keep the accounting concrete, let's assume greedy decoding where we always pick the highest-scoring token (if serving uses probabilistic sampling, acceptance switches to a probabilistic rule as well, which this book leaves out). Walking from left to right, we compare the large model's predictions against the draft tokens one by one: we accept every draft token before the first mismatch, and at the first mismatch we reject that draft token and directly adopt the large model's own prediction for that position. That way, even if all 7 draft tokens miss, the pass is still guaranteed to yield token 7; if the first k draft tokens match, the pass yields k + 1 tokens in one shot (up to 8). Under greedy selection, each accepted token is the model's own top choice for that position given the same earlier tokens—the same selection rule that decode uses (though bitwise equality between a T = 8 pass and T = 1 passes was not measured).

What about the KV cache slots that the rejected draft tokens already wrote across all 62 layers? We just leave them where they are: the committed sequence length advances only by k + 1, and later passes read only up to the committed sequence length, so those rejected slots are never read and future passes simply overwrite them.

Look at the bill for this pass: we still stream the exact same 9.0 GB of fixed weights, doing about 8 FLOPs per byte of BF16 weight read (Section 4). Spread across the k + 1 tokens produced by the pass, each token's share drops to 9.0 GB÷(k+1)—falling from 9.0 GB when every draft token misses (k = 0) all the way down to 1.12 GB when all 7 hit (k = 7), as shown in the chart below.

Of course, verify comes with its own costs. Compared with decode, it pays three extra bills: the time to run the drafting mechanism itself, writing 7 extra KV slots and reading 7 extra KV slots per layer, and any extra local experts that 8 tokens may hit beyond a single token (adding 28.3 MB of reads per layer for each extra local expert hit). If the very first draft token misses, the pass yields only 1 token after paying all three extra bills, coming out slower than plain decode. Verify pays off only when the average number of tokens yielded per pass exceeds "(verify pass latency ++ drafting latency) ÷\div decode pass latency"; we did not measure drafting latency or how many extra experts 8 tokens touch.

Putting the three single-request regimes side by side for our short-context example (byte counts and per-token shares derived from model shapes, excluding experts, drafting, and the 188 cross-GPU exchanges):

Regime Tokens in pass T Rows into lm_head R Committed length CC step KV slots written / read per layer (62-layer total) Fixed weights per pass (1 GPU) Fixed weights per newly confirmed token
prefill (Section 5) 5 1 0→5 (+5+5) Write 5 first, read 5 (79,360 B each, ~79.4 KB) ~9.0 GB (8.995 GB) ~1.80 GB
decode (Section 6) 1 1 5→6 (+1+1) Write 1 first (15,872 B), read 6 (95,232 B, ~95.2 KB) ~9.0 GB (8.995 GB) ~9.00 GB
verify (Section 7) 8 8 5→6+k (k∈0..7 accepted drafts, +(k+1)) Write 8 first (126,976 B), read 13 (206,336 B, <0.21 MB) ~9.0 GB (8.995 GB) 9.0÷(k+1) GB (9.00–1.12 GB)

Once you see the full-model ledger across prefill, decode, and verify, it becomes clear why the next chapter can narrow its focus to just 1 layer. The three regimes differ only in how many tokens run side by side in a pass, and apart from the inbound embedding steps at the start and the outbound scoring steps at the end, the main body of every pass simply repeats the exact same single-layer structure 62 times: each layer takes (x_l, stream_l) from the layer before it, reads and writes its own KV cache, and hands the updated inputs to the next layer (Section 2). Yet a whole-GPU black-box ledger can see only "about T FLOPs per byte read" without distinguishing the parts inside a layer—and as token count grows or history stretches out, different parts inside a layer do not change speed the same way. Once we pry open 1 layer and understand what it computes and how many bytes it reads as T varies, we understand the main body of all 62 layers.

Takeaway: Every forward pass reads the fixed weights once, so how many tokens we can process in parallel in that pass defines the three regimes: prefill (batching known prompt tokens together), decode (generating 1 token at a time), and verify (drafting 7 candidate tokens and verifying them together).

Next chapter's question: If we open up any one of the 62 layers on a single H200, what steps does it break into and what does each step compute? What is the fastest that each step can run under decode and prefill—and when is it waiting on HBM versus turning to wait on Tensor Cores (the units inside the GPU dedicated to matrix multiplication)?

Primer 2

Dissecting One Model Layer — What It Computes, and Whether It Is HBM-Bound or Tensor Core-Bound

  • Primer 2
  • Primer 3
  • Chapter 1 [Level 1]
  • Chapter 2 [Level 2]

In Primer 1, we treated every layer as a black box that takes in (xl, streaml)(x_l,\ \mathrm{stream}_l) and hands back (xl+1, streaml+1)(x_{l+1},\ \mathrm{stream}_{l+1}). Now let's pry one layer open and answer the title question directly: at single-token decode (T=1), every weight- or KV-reading stage waits on HBM bandwidth; as the token count TT grows, the stages move to the Tensor Core (the dedicated on-chip unit for matrix multiply-accumulate; this chapter groups on-chip math into one "compute units / Tensor Core" block) one by one, ordered by how many tokens share each byte read. To derive that answer step by step, starting from the layer's first step, qkv_gate, this chapter follows four questions in order: (1) Testing the waters with Stage 1 qkv_gate: how fast can a matrix stage possibly run, and why does adding tokens flip it from waiting on HBM to waiting on the Tensor Core? (2) What do the 8 stages in a layer compute, and why do the matrices on a single GPU have these shapes? (3) Chained together across 8 stages, which memory reads must wait for the previous step to finish, and can reading expert weights early save time? (4) As the token count TT grows from 1 to 256 to 16,384, in what order do the 7 stages move to the Tensor Core?

1Testing Stage 1 qkv_gate: How Fast Can a Matrix Stage Run, and Why Do More Tokens Flip It from HBM to the Tensor Core?

Minimum execution time is the slower of byte transfer time and compute time; below 206 FLOP/B the stage is HBM-bound, and above 206 FLOP/B it is Tensor Core-bound: at T=1, qkv_gate does only ~1 FLOP/B and needs at least 7.86 µs waiting on HBM; once TT tokens share the same weights and push intensity past 206 FLOP/B, the bottleneck flips to the Tensor Core.

Rather than laying out every matrix in the layer at once, let's start with just the first step at the layer's entrance: Stage 1 (qkv_gate). This step's weight matrix W𝑞𝑘𝑣W_{qkv} on our GPU takes 37.75 MB (the size listed in Primer 1, Section 4) and has shape W𝑞𝑘𝑣:[2304,8192]BF16\shape{W_{qkv}}{2304,\;8192}{BF16} (Section 2 works out why it has 2,304 rows when we unpack the layer's sharding): it takes xl:[T,8192]BF16\shape{x_l}{T,\;8192}{BF16} (for the pass token count TT, see Primer 1, Section 1) and multiplies qkv=xlW𝑞𝑘𝑣⊤ to produce qkv:[T,2304]BF16\shape{\mathrm{qkv}}{T,\;2304}{BF16}. At single-token decode (T=1), this step simplifies to a matrix-vector multiplication y=Wx (gemv); when multiple tokens enter side by side (T>1), it becomes a matrix-matrix multiplication (GEMM).

In this chapter's accounting, a single H200 has two hard hardware ceilings: HBM read bandwidth tops out at 4.8 TB/s, and Tensor Core dense (non-sparse) BF16 matrix-multiplication throughput tops out at 989 TFLOP/s. Even if you overlap memory transfers and math perfectly, a stage can never finish faster than whichever of those two jobs takes longer:

tmin⁡=max⁡(bytes transferred4.8 TB/s, FLOP989 TFLOP/s)t_{\min} = \max\!\left(\frac{\text{bytes transferred}}{4.8\ \text{TB/s}},\ \frac{\text{FLOP}}{989\ \text{TFLOP/s}}\right)

That minimum time is the stage's lower bound (floor). Let's settle the 989 TFLOP/s convention right here: the NVIDIA datasheet's 1,979 TFLOP/s figure requires 2:4 structured sparsity (half of every 4 weights equal to zero), whereas our model uses dense weights, so dense BF16 matrix multiplication runs at half that rate, 989 TFLOP/s; switching the inputs to 1-byte dense FP8 matrix multiplication doubles dense peak throughput back to about 1,979 TFLOP/s (used for the FP8 attention floor in Chapter 7, Section 1).

Compare the two terms inside the maximum and you can tell right away which side is the bottleneck. We call the number of floating-point operations a stage performs per byte transferred its arithmetic intensity, written I=FLOP/byte (in FLOP/B). Divide the machine's peak compute throughput by its peak memory bandwidth and you get its ridge point—on an H200, 989/4.8≈206 FLOP/B. Plot achievable compute throughput against arithmetic intensity and you get the roofline model (Figure P2-4 in Section 4 plots every stage of the layer on it).

Whenever I<206, moving bytes takes longer than doing the math: the compute units sit waiting on memory, so the stage is memory-bound (HBM-bound). Whenever I>206, the math takes longer than moving the bytes: data already on chip waits on the matrix units, so the stage is compute-bound (Tensor Core-bound).

Now plug in the numbers for Stage 1's gemv at T=1. In Primer 1, Section 4, we saw that at T=1 we do only 1 floating-point operation per byte of BF16 weight read, putting the arithmetic intensity at I≈1 FLOP/B—just 1/2061 / 206 of the ridge point. Alongside the Tensor Cores built for matrix tiles, the chip also has general-purpose CUDA Cores that run elementwise multiply-adds: at T=1, a single vector row cannot fill a matrix tile, so Part I's gemv runs on CUDA Cores, yet even CUDA Core throughput sits far above 1 operation per byte (against the 989 TFLOP/s ceiling, at most 0.5% is tapped), leaving the lower bound set entirely by streaming weights from HBM:

37.75 MB4.8 TB/s=7.86 µs\frac{37.75\ \text{MB}}{4.8\ \text{TB/s}} = 7.86\ \text{µs}

That 7.86 µs lower bound is the finish line that every gemv version in Part I will try to close in on. Conversely, when TT tokens enter Stage 1 side by side (turning it into a matrix-matrix multiplication, GEMM), all TT tokens share the same 37.75 MB read of W𝑞𝑘𝑣W_{qkv}: the weights stream from HBM once while each 2-byte BF16 weight runs one multiply-add per token (2T2T FLOPs), raising arithmetic intensity to about TT FLOP/B (Primer 1, Section 4); once TT crosses two hundred or so (I>206; see Chapter 5, Section 3 for the exact crossover including activation bytes (activations: the intermediate results the previous stage just produced, detailed in Section 3)), matrix math takes longer than moving bytes, and Stage 1's bottleneck flips from waiting on HBM to waiting on the Tensor Core.

Because the exact same Stage 1 hits two different hardware ceilings at T=1 versus multiple tokens, Part I of this book (Chapters 1–6) forks right here into two optimization tracks (each chapter finishes Track 1 end to end first, then covers Track 2 in one block; the on-chip mechanisms previewed in the last column—registers, shared-memory ring buffers, and asynchronous pipelines—are introduced step by step in Primer 3 and Chapters 1–6):

Track Regime & Operator Weight Reuse & Bottleneck On-Chip Data Path & Part I Progression
Track 1 (main line) T=1 single-token gemv (y=Wx) Each weight multiplies 1 token (I≈1≪206), HBM-bound (floor 7.86 µs) Used once and discarded via thread-private registers: cut launch gaps and saturate in-flight reads (both real-hardware gaps are explained at the end of Section 4), then narrow weight bits (v0 → v10)
Track 2 (multi-token branch) T=8..256 multi-token qkv_gate GEMM One 37.75 MB weight read shared across TT tokens (I≈T, crossing 206 as TT grows), shifting to compute pipelines and the Tensor Core Staged into an on-chip shared-memory ring buffer to feed asynchronous Tensor Core pipelines repeatedly (g0 → g5, wrapped up in Chapter 6, Section 8)

2Expanding from Stage 1 to the Whole Layer: What Do the 8 Stages Compute, and Why Do Single-GPU Matrices Have These Shapes?

Stages 1–3 compute attention and add the result back into the residual stream, while Stages 4–8 split into two branches to select experts and project down the hidden dimension, merge at Stage 6, and add back into the residual stream; across 8 GPUs, attention splits by head (two matrices), experts split by index, and three unpartitioned dense matrices sit as full copies on every GPU—so when T≤8 (for TT, see Primer 1, Section 1), a single GPU must read all five dense weight matrices totaling 138.4 MB per layer plus the weights of whichever local experts get routed.

Following the activations forward from Stage 1 (just tested in Section 1), let's first see how the attention half of the layer is sliced across the 8 GPUs using TP8 (tensor parallelism: splitting the same matrix by head across 8 GPUs; top band of Figure P2-1). Across the layer, Q has 128 query heads of width 64 (Primer 1, Section 2); divided across 8 GPUs, our GPU handles 16 query heads and 2 key-value heads. On our GPU, every 8 query heads share 1 key-value head—an 8:1 grouping called GQA (grouped-query attention), which cuts both historical KV cache footprint and per-pass KV read traffic to one-eighth. Each query element also gets a gate value (used as a scaling factor in the next stage). Stack Q, K, V, and the gate together and our local projection matrix has 1,024+128+128+1,024=2,304 output rows, explaining the W𝑞𝑘𝑣:[2304,8192]BF16\shape{W_{qkv}}{2304,\;8192}{BF16} (37.75 MB) shape from Section 1; once Stage 1 (qkv_gate) computes qkv=xlW𝑞𝑘𝑣⊤, it slices qkv:[T,2304]BF16\shape{\mathrm{qkv}}{T,\;2304}{BF16} by column into q (1,024), k (128), v (128), and gate (1,024) and hands them to Stage 2. Once attention finishes, Stage 3's output matrix projects those 1,024 columns back to 8,192 dimensions with shape Wo:[8192,1024]BF16\shape{W_o}{8192,\;1024}{BF16}, taking 16.8 MB.

Continuing through Figure P2-2 (you can click any stage in the figure to see its full step card), Stage 2 (attention, gated attention; see Chapter 7, Section 1) starts by running per-head RMSNorm on q and k. In the 46 sliding-window layers, it then applies rotary position embedding (RoPE; the 16 full-attention layers skip RoPE—for both layer types, see Primer 1, Section 2): each pair of elements rotates by an angle set by the token position, so the position-dependent part of the q–k inner product depends only on how far apart the two tokens are. After that, it casts the freshly computed k and v down to 1-byte FP8 and writes them into the layer's KV cache.

Next, Stage 2 reads the visible historical KV cache—only the most recent 2,048 tokens in a sliding-window layer, or the entire history in a full-attention layer. Each query head takes its q, computes the inner product against every historical k in its shared key-value head, runs softmax (Primer 1, Section 2) to turn that row of scores into weights that sum to 1, and takes the weighted sum over the historical v vectors. One final per-head RMSNorm and an elementwise multiply by σ(gate)\sigma(\text{gate}) (where σ\sigma is the sigmoid function mapping values into 0..10..1) produces the attention output o𝑎𝑡𝑡𝑛:[T,1024]BF16\shape{o_{attn}}{T,\;1024}{BF16} for Stage 3.

Stage 3 (o projection and first gated residual) multiplies the local GPU's 1,024-column attention output by WoW_o to get a=o𝑎𝑡𝑡𝑛Wo⊤, and all 8 GPUs sum their partial aa tensors with an all-reduce to form the full a:[T,8192]BF16\shape{a}{T,\;8192}{BF16}. Next, we blend that summed aa into the layer's incoming residual stream stream_in\mathrm{stream\_in} (that is, streaml\mathrm{stream}_l): stream_mid=α1⊙stream_in+β1⊙RMSNorm(a). Here α1\alpha_1 and β1\beta_1 are two length-8,192 FP32 coefficient vectors—one value per coordinate—derived from a length-8,192 vector learned for Stage 3 (satisfying α12+β12=1 elementwise; see Primer 1, Section 2). Because they do not depend on the token, we read them only once per layer. Finally, Stage 3 runs the pre-FFN normalization h=RMSNorm(stream_mid)⊙(1+wpre_ffn) and hands h:[T,8192]BF16\shape{h}{T,\;8192}{BF16} to both Stage 4 and Stage 5. Because the learned length-8,192 vector wpre_ffnw_{\mathrm{pre\_ffn}} stores an offset relative to 1, the formula multiplies by 1+wpre_ffn—the weighted RMSNorm from Primer 1.

At hh, the dataflow forks into Stage 4 and Stage 5. Together with Stage 7's unpooler below, these steps use the three unpartitioned dense matrices stored as full copies on every GPU (with the two head-partitioned attention matrices above, that makes five dense matrices per layer; bottom band of Figure P2-1). Because neither branch depends on the other, they can run side by side (Chapter 9, Section 1 shows how we schedule them). One branch is Stage 4 (router), which handles routing (picking experts for each token) by scoring all 256 experts as s=σ(cr⋅hW𝑟𝑜𝑢𝑡𝑒𝑟⊤); stored in 4-byte FP32 with shape W𝑟𝑜𝑢𝑡𝑒𝑟:[256,8192]FP32\shape{W_{router}}{256,\;8192}{FP32}, its weights take 8.4 MB, and crc_r is a fixed scaling constant (for its T≤8 vs. T>8 precision switch and hh-copy read rule, see Row 4 of the summary table at the end of this section). To pick the winning experts, we add a bias (router_bias, stored in the checkpoint) to each expert's score and take the top 8. That bias is used only to pick the winners; the final routing weights still come from the unbiased scores. Stage 4 hands two outputs to Stage 6: the chosen expert indices topk_ids:[T,8]int32\shape{\mathrm{topk\_ids}}{T,\;8}{int32} (int32 is a 32-bit integer, 4 bytes each) and the normalized routing weights topk_weights:[T,8]FP32\shape{\mathrm{topk\_weights}}{T,\;8}{FP32} (the 8 selected unbiased scores divided by their sum).

The other branch is Stage 5 (pooler) before the experts, which narrows 8,192 dimensions down to 4,096 using W𝑝𝑜𝑜𝑙:[4096,8192]BF16\shape{W_{pool}}{4096,\;8192}{BF16} (67.1 MB): it computes p=RMSNorm(hW𝑝𝑜𝑜𝑙⊤)⊙(1+wpre_expert) and sends p:[T,4096]BF16\shape{p}{T,\;4096}{BF16} to Stage 6.

The two branches meet again at Stage 6 (expert stage; see Chapter 8, Section 1). We split the experts across GPUs using EP8 (expert parallelism: assigning different experts to different GPUs; middle band of Figure P2-1): dividing all 256 experts evenly across 8 GPUs puts 32 local experts on each GPU, and out of the 8 experts a token picks, we run only the ones that live on our GPU. In Primer 1 we saw that each expert has 3 matrices; in code, we pack the first two side by side into a single matrix w13w_{13} (projecting the narrowed 4,096-dimensional input to 8,192 dimensions, with the first 4,096 columns holding the gate gg and the last 4,096 columns holding uu), and the down projection w2w_2 maps 4,096 dimensions back to 4,096, so the two matrices together hold 3×40962 weights. Across the middle 60 layers, expert weights are stored in NVFP4 (4-bit floating-point format): each weight's own 4 bits (0.5 B) store its relative value while every 16 weights share a 1-byte scale factor (0.0625 B per weight), averaging 0.5625 B per weight and unpacking to BF16 on chip before multiplying; that puts 1 compressed expert at 28.3 MB, whereas the first and last layers (layers 0 and 61) keep their experts in uncompressed 2-byte BF16 at 100.7 MB per expert. For each local (token, expert ee) pair, we run four steps:

  1. Project gu=pW13,e⊤ to get the first 4,096 columns gg and the last 4,096 columns uu.
  2. Apply SwiGLU: inter=silu(g)⊙u, where silu(z)=z⋅σ(z).
  3. Run the down projection y=interW2,e⊤ back to 4,096 dimensions.
  4. Normalize each yy and accumulate it weighted by its routing weight: mtok+=wtok,e⋅RMSNorm(y⊙(1+wpost_expert)) (note that multiplying by 1+wpost_expert happens before the RMS division here—the opposite order from Stage 3), where wtok,ew_{\mathrm{tok},e} is the token's topk_weights entry for expert ee. Once every local (token, expert) pair finishes, Stage 6 hands m:[T,4096]BF16\shape{m}{T,\;4096}{BF16} to Stage 7.

Now look at how many local experts our GPU reads at T=1. A single token picks 8 out of 256 experts, so spread across 8 GPUs (32 local experts each), the per-GPU average is 8×32/256=𝟏.𝟎 local expert. Because all 8 GPUs sum expert outputs once per layer, though, any GPU that finishes early must wait for the slowest one; what paces the layer is not the per-GPU average, but the busiest GPU—the GPU whose local experts receive the most (token, expert) hit pairs in that layer (at T=1, hit pairs equal distinct local experts touched). Under a uniform-random statistical model (drawing 8 experts out of 256 without replacement and taking the expected maximum across the 8 GPUs), the busiest GPU touches about 2.56 local experts on average (Section 4 works out how the benchmark's single-layer floor budgets ~1.87 local experts, or ~53 MB, when we break down the T=1 full-layer ledger).

After the experts, Stage 7 (unpooler) computes f=mW𝑢𝑛𝑝𝑜𝑜𝑙⊤ to widen 4,096 dimensions back up to f:[T,8192]BF16\shape{f}{T,\;8192}{BF16} for Stage 8; the full weight matrix stored on each GPU has shape W𝑢𝑛𝑝𝑜𝑜𝑙:[8192,4096]BF16\shape{W_{unpool}}{8192,\;4096}{BF16}, also taking 67.1 MB. There is a twist in how unpooler runs, though. When T≤8, each GPU computes only 1/8 of the columns of output f (1,024 columns), reading only the corresponding 1,024 rows of W𝑢𝑛𝑝𝑜𝑜𝑙W_{unpool} (8.4 MB) before an 8-GPU all-gather stitches the full T×8,192 result together. Once T>8, each GPU simply reads the entire 67.1 MB matrix and computes all 8,192 columns locally, skipping that all-gather.

Putting the five dense matrices and the local experts on one GPU into a single table (all resident in single-GPU HBM):

Matrix Single-GPU Shape Dtype Single-GPU Bytes 8-GPU Split Rule
W𝑞𝑘𝑣W_{qkv} [2304, 8192][2304,\ 8192] BF16 37.75 MB By head (TP8: 16 query heads + 2 KV heads + 1,024 gate rows on this GPU)
WoW_o [8192, 1024][8192,\ 1024] BF16 16.8 MB By head (TP8: takes the 1,024 cols of this GPU's 16 query heads)
WrouterW_{\mathrm{router}} [256, 8192][256,\ 8192] FP32 8.4 MB One full copy per GPU
WpoolW_{\mathrm{pool}} [4096, 8192][4096,\ 8192] BF16 67.1 MB One full copy per GPU
WunpoolW_{\mathrm{unpool}} [8192, 4096][8192,\ 4096] BF16 67.1 MB stored (T≤8 reads 1,024 rows = 8.4 MB; T>8 reads all 67.1 MB) One full copy per GPU (T≤8 reads 1/8 by output column)
One local expert (w13+w2) [8192, 4096]+[4096, 4096] NVFP4 (layers 1–60) / BF16 (layers 0, 61) 28.3 MB (NVFP4) / 100.7 MB (BF16) By expert index (EP8: 256 experts split into 32 local experts per GPU)

Add up the exact byte counts of the five dense weight matrices in the table that a single GPU reads per layer at T≤8 and you get 138.4 MB—the exact number we used in Primer 1. For T>8, the five dense weight matrices read per layer jump to about 197.1 MB (197.132 MB exact), or about 12.22 GB across all 62 layers; adding this GPU's 0.414 GB shard of lm_head—the outbound vocabulary-projection matrix that scores every candidate token (Primer 1, Section 3)—brings the total to 62×197.132 MB+0.414 GB≈𝟏𝟐.𝟔 GB (12.636 GB exact). Why switch between the two? Each choice pays a clear cost: the T>8 path reads 197.1−138.4=𝟓𝟖.𝟕 MB more of W𝑢𝑛𝑝𝑜𝑜𝑙W_{unpool} per layer on every GPU to skip one 8-GPU all-gather, whereas the T≤8 path saves those 58.7 MB of HBM reads at the cost of running that all-gather. The all-gather latency is not measured in a full pass (isolated timing in Chapter 9, Section 9); the benchmark takes the T=8 threshold straight from the baseline inference code (the existing serving program for this model used as the timing baseline), so this book does not derive the T=8 break-even and the exact break-even point is unknown.

Finally, Stage 8 (second gated residual) blends the expert branch back into the residual stream: stream_out=α2⊙stream_mid+β2⊙RMSNorm(f⊙(1+wpost_ffn)), which becomes the streaml+1\mathrm{stream}_{l+1} handed to the next layer. Just like Stage 6, multiplication comes before division here, and α2,β2\alpha_2, \beta_2 are two length-8,192 FP32 coefficient vectors (32 KiB each, precomputed from one learned BF16 gate vector for Stage 8 and satisfying α22+β22=1 elementwise). To wrap up the layer, Stage 8 also computes the next layer's input xl+1=RMSNorm(stream_out)⊙(1+wnext) (the final layer skips xl+1x_{l+1}), where both wpost_ffnw_{\mathrm{post\_ffn}} and wnextw_{\mathrm{next}} are length-8,192 BF16 vectors (16 KiB each). Together, those 4 runtime vectors total 2×32+2×16=𝟗𝟔 KiB (98,304 B)—which happens by coincidence to match the 96 KiB of full-layer entry/exit activations counted in the T=1 benchmark floor (reading xlx_l 16 KiB + stream_in\mathrm{stream\_in} 32 KiB and writing stream_out\mathrm{stream\_out} 32 KiB + xl+1x_{l+1} 16 KiB, or ~0.02 µs), even though they are two separate sets of tensors.

Because Stage 8 reads no weight matrices, we list only Stages 1–7 separately when computing matrix and attention lower bounds below. Putting all 8 stages side by side at T=1 (sliding-window layer) shows what each stage reads and writes on one GPU, what it waits on, which cross-GPU exchanges follow it, which hardware units hold and run it, and its derived byte floor (bytes÷4.8 TB/s from Section 1, not measured):
