Residual 2 + next-layer norm 0 B weight matrix (reads 4 length-8,192 vectors = 96 KiB) Read concatenated ff 16 KiB + stream_mid\mathrm{stream\_mid} 32 KiB → write stream_out\mathrm{stream\_out} 32 KiB + xl+1x_{l+1} 16 KiB Concatenated ff after Stage 7 and Stage 3's stream_mid\mathrm{stream\_mid} (4 vectors ready at t=0) None HBM ↔ compute units Layer I/O 96 KiB ~0.02 (included in 40.0 µs)

Beyond the all-reduce inside Stage 3, the 8 GPUs run a second all-reduce sum on mm right after Stage 6; when T≤8, they also run an all-gather after Stage 7 to stitch each GPU's 1,024 columns into 8,192 columns. All three cross-GPU collectives sit on the main chain, so all 8 GPUs must wait for each one to finish before moving on (their communication time stays outside our single-GPU ledger—see Primer 1; for isolated 8-GPU timings, see Chapter 9, Section 9).

3Chained Across 8 Stages, Which Reads Must Wait, and Can Prefetching Expert Weights Save Time?

In single-request decode, inter-stage activations account for under 0.2% of total bytes read, the five dense weight matrices and historical KV cache can be read from the start, and expert weights can be prefetched right after Stage 4 selects the experts; at the idealized T=1 byte floor on a shared 4.8 TB/s bus, however, early reads save 0 µs, saving real wall-clock time only when a running stage leaves HBM bandwidth unused or is Tensor Core-bound.

If we draw these 8 stages by "who has to wait for whose output," we get a directed acyclic graph (DAG, where each solid arrow means "must wait for this result"; see Figure P2-3). The whole layer forms a single serial main chain that forks only at hh into Stage 4 and Stage 5 and merges back at Stage 6. Outside that main chain sit three extra edges: one carries incoming stream_in straight to Stage 3, one sends stream_mid straight from Stage 3 to Stage 8, and the third keeps the KV cache written by this layer horizontally for future tokens.

Every byte a stage reads from memory falls into one of two buckets. The first bucket is activations: the intermediate results that the previous stage just produced in the current forward pass, which do not exist until that previous step finishes. Summing every stage's single-GPU activation and residual reads and writes from the Section 2 table at T=1 gives 170,560 B read plus 156,480 B written, or 327,040 B in total (~0.33 MB derived from 170,560+156,480: 0.17% of a sliding-window layer's bytes and 0.15% of a full-attention layer's, both under 0.2%; the benchmark floor formula itself counts only the 96 KiB, or 98,304 B / ~0.1 MB, of full-layer entry/exit I/O). The second bucket is weights and historical KV cache, which already sit in HBM before the forward pass begins and make up over 99.8% of single-GPU bytes (the table below splits that second bucket into Rows 2a and 2b by whether the read addresses are known before the layer starts or only after Stage 4 picks the experts):

Bucket Data Included (Single-GPU HBM) When Readable T=1 Single-GPU Bytes (Share)
1. Activations (must wait) Inter-stage activation & residual reads + writes across Stages 1–8 (170,560 B read + 156,480 B written; layer entry/exit is 96 KiB) After the producer stage (and any collective) finishes writing 327,040 B (0.17% sliding, 0.15% full)
2a. Weights & historical KV (ready at t=0) Five dense matrices (138.4 MB) + Stage 8's 4 vectors (96 KiB = 0.098 MB) + historical FP8 KV (0.52 MB sliding or 20.48 MB full) At t=0 (already in HBM with known addresses) ~139.0 MB derived (138.4+0.52+0.098, sliding) / ~159.0 MB derived (138.4+20.48+0.098, full)
2b. Expert weights (Bucket 2; ready after Stage 4) Routed local expert weights (w13, w2w_{13},\ w_2) Resident in HBM at t=0; addresses known once Stage 4 emits topk_ids (no wait on Stage 5) ~53 MB in the floor (Section 4; > 99.8% together with row above)

The last row of the table settles the dependency question for Stage 6's expert weights: the expert weights themselves sit in HBM from t=0, and only their indices are unknown before the layer starts; as soon as Stage 4 (router) emits topk_ids, the addresses to fetch are known, with no causal need to wait for parallel Stage 5 (pooler) to finish computing pp. Does prefetching those expert weights while Stage 5 is still running actually save wall-clock time? Applying Section 1's lower-bound formula to the whole layer settles that question right away.

For the layer as a whole, the lower bound is likewise whichever is longer: total bytes moved across the layer divided by 4.8 TB/s, or total operations across the layer divided by 989 TFLOP/s. Under a consistent byte and FLOP accounting, the full-layer lower bound never exceeds the sum of the stage lower bounds: the full-layer bound equals the sum of the stage bounds whenever every stage waits on the same ceiling—as at T=1, where every stage waits on HBM (summing to 40.0 µs; see the Section 4 chart), or at large token counts where every stage waits on the Tensor Core—and it is smaller than the sum only when stages mix ceilings (Section 4 checks that gap once we compute the mixed regime), because the full-layer formula assumes that while a Tensor Core-bound stage is busy on the matrix units, free HBM bandwidth overlaps weight reads for other stages.

That directly answers whether prefetching Stage 6's expert weights while Stage 5 runs saves time: at the idealized T=1 byte floor, early expert reads save zero time; prefetching saves real wall-clock time only when a real kernel leaves part of the 4.8 TB/s HBM bandwidth unused (Chapter 1, Section 4; Chapter 9, Sections 4–5), or when the running stage is Tensor Core-bound and leaves HBM bandwidth free. Because the whole GPU shares one 4.8 TB/s HBM bus and Stage 5 already saturates it streaming 67.1 MB of WpoolW_{\mathrm{pool}} at the idealized T=1 floor, reordering reads on that shared bus cannot shrink total bytes÷4.8 TB/s; conversely, whenever Stage 5 leaves bandwidth unused on real hardware or becomes Tensor Core-bound at larger TT, waiting until Stage 5 finishes pp wastes that free HBM headroom.

4Pushing T from 1 to 256 to 16,384: In What Order Do the 7 Stages Move to the Tensor Core?

Dense weights are shared across all tokens in the forward pass, historical KV is shared only across new tokens of the same request, and expert weights are shared only across tokens routed to that expert; thus dense stages cross 206 FLOP/B first.

Let's write BB for the number of concurrent requests batched into a single pass and LL for the number of new tokens per request in that pass, so the total token count is T=B×L. In online serving, the exact same layer runs across three typical regimes:

  • Regime 1 (decode, T=1): A single request with 80,000 historical tokens generates tokens one by one, with B=1, L=1.
  • Regime 2 (verify, T=256): 32 concurrent online requests with varying history lengths (about 80,000 historical tokens on average) each verify 8 draft tokens at once, with B=32, L=8.
  • Regime 3 (chunked prefill, T=16,384): When a prompt is tens of thousands of tokens long, holding tens of thousands of activation rows in device memory all at once would use too much memory, so we break the prompt into 16,384-token chunks and run them one after another—a technique called chunked prefill. Here we look at chunk 5, where 65,536 tokens are already cached, with B=1, L=T=16,384.

As TT grows, why don't all 7 stages cross 206 FLOP/B at the same time? It comes down to how many tokens get to share each byte you pull from HBM:

Byte Class (Stages) Shared Across Whom Intensity Gain per Sharing Token Sharing Tokens Needed to Cross 206 FLOP/B
Five dense weight matrices (Stages 1, 3, 4, 5, 7) All TT tokens in the pass ~1 FLOP/B for BF16; ~0.5 FLOP/B for FP32 router Two to three hundred for the four BF16 matrices (Chapter 5, Section 3); much later for router
Historical KV cache (Stage 2) The LL new tokens of the same request 16 FLOP/B at L=1; 127.5 FLOP/B at L=8 Does not cross in verify (L=8); far above 206 in chunked prefill (L=16,384)
Local expert weights (Stage 6) The MeM_e tokens routed to that expert in this pass ~3.56 FLOP/B (NVFP4, 0.5625 B/weight) About 206/3.56≈58 tokens on the same expert
  • Weights of the five dense matrices (Stages 1, 3, 4, 5, and 7): When a matrix is narrower—o has only 1,024 input columns—each token's input and output activations take a larger share of the bytes and pull intensity down slightly, so at T=256 qkv_gate has crossed 206 while o sits just below it. For 256-row, 4-byte FP32 router, the benchmark floor books the logical matrix product as one pass at 989 TFLOP/s (for T>8, the baseline inference code splits it into two BF16 passes, doubling the math; at T=256 it remains HBM-bound so its floor is unchanged, and only above about T>360, once doubled math time exceeds byte-read time, does the single-pass floor become optimistic for router).
  • Historical KV cache (Stage 2): Separate requests do not share history. At L=1, for each 256 B KV slot read, our 16 query heads each run one 64-dimensional inner product and one 64-dimensional weighted sum (64 multiply-adds each at 2 FLOPs), giving 2×2×16×64=4,096 FLOPs and I=4096/256=16 FLOP/B; at L=8 in verify, intensity climbs to 127.5 FLOP/B, still below 206.
  • Expert weights (Stage 6): Because the expert activations (pp and inter\mathrm{inter}) are BF16 and H200 Tensor Cores have no native 4-bit floating-point matrix multiply, weights unpack to BF16 on chip before multiplying, keeping the compute ceiling at BF16's 989 TFLOP/s. Each routed token does 1 multiply-add (2 FLOPs) per 0.5625 B weight, giving 2/0.5625≈3.56 FLOP/B per token and needing 206/3.56≈58 tokens on the same expert to cross 206.

Start with Regime 1: decode (T=1). With only 1 token in flight, no bytes are shared across tokens at all: all 7 stages sit between 0.5 and 16 FLOP/B (Figure P2-4), every one of them waiting on HBM. Now we can close the T=1 expert budget deferred from Section 2: for a sliding-window layer at T=1, the benchmark specification sets a full-layer lower bound of 40.0 µs. Everything outside the experts adds up directly: 138.4 MB of dense weights, 2,048 sliding-window slots of historical KV cache (0.52 MB), and the layer's own inputs and outputs (reading and writing the FP32 stream and BF16 x, 96 KiB total or about 0.1 MB), totaling about 139 MB, or about 29 µs at 4.8 TB/s (28.84+0.11+0.02=28.97 µs exact). Subtracting that non-expert time from 40.0 µs leaves 11.03 µs (52.97 MB exact, about 53 MB) as the lower-bound budget for experts, which divided by 28.31 MB per expert equals about 1.87 local experts. Why does the lower bound count 1.87 instead of ~2.5? As documented in the benchmark source code, routing fluctuates around its mean from run to run, so to keep the bound a true lower bound the formula counts only 75% (ROUTING_SHARE = 0.75) of the mean number of distinct local experts touched on the busiest GPU. Divide 1.87 by 75% to back-solve (derived, as the raw count table is not shipped on disk), and the busiest GPU in the benchmark workload touches about 2.5 local experts on average—right next to the 2.56 from the uniform-random model in Section 2. Listing all four "local expert counts" side by side keeps them distinct:

  • 1.0: the 8-GPU mean when 8 chosen experts spread across 8 GPUs;
  • 2.56: the busiest-GPU mean under the uniform-random statistical model;
  • ~2.5: the busiest-GPU mean back-solved from the benchmark floor via 75%;
  • ~1.87 (=0.75×2.5, about 53 MB / 11.03 µs): the discounted count booked in the 40.0 µs floor.

The chart below shows the stage-by-stage breakdown, where the 7.86 µs bar for qkv_gate is the gemv lower bound from Section 1.

Next, look at Regime 2: verify (T=256, where B=32 requests each verify L=8 tokens). Here the three widest-input matrices among the four BF16 dense matrices (qkv_gate, pooler, and the fully read unpooler) cross 206 FLOP/B first and become Tensor Core-bound. Meanwhile, o sits right below 206, router stays low because its weights take 4 bytes each, and attention shares historical KV reads only across the L=8 tokens within each request, stopping at 127.5 FLOP/B.

What about the expert stage? Under uniform routing, the 256×8=2,048 hit pairs spread evenly across all 256 experts: our GPU gets 256 hit pairs, touches nearly all 32 local experts, and feeds each expert only 8 tokens on average.

The benchmark specification instead defines its lower bound under skewed routing (where popular experts attract more tokens; see Chapter 8, Section 1): skew concentrates hits onto fewer popular experts and lowers the count of distinct local experts on the busiest GPU, and because expert weights are read once per distinct expert rather than once per hit pair, skew pulls the full-layer byte floor down. Here is the arithmetic: subtracting non-expert reads from the full-layer floor (see the chart note below) leaves an expert budget of about 16.0 local experts; since the floor formula counts 75% of the busiest GPU's mean distinct local experts, back-solving gives 16.0÷0.75≈𝟐𝟏 local experts—fewer than the ~32 under uniform routing. Meanwhile, the busiest GPU receives at least the 8-GPU average of 256 hit pairs: 256÷16.0=𝟏𝟔 tokens per expert, still far short of the 58-token crossover, and multiplying by 3.563.56 FLOP/B per token gives an expert arithmetic intensity of 16×3.56≈𝟓𝟕 FLOP/B (Figure P2-4)—well below 206, so experts remain HBM-bound.

Putting the pieces together, the T=256 verdict is straightforward: stage by stage, 3 stages wait on the Tensor Core and 4 stages wait on HBM, while the full-layer lower bound is booked by total bytes divided by 4.8 TB/s (143.8 µs on a sliding-window layer and 267.2 µs on a full-attention layer; because the benchmark does not state how many hit pairs land on the busiest GPU, its actual hit-pair count and exact whole-layer compute share are unknown). That also illustrates Section 3's mixed-ceiling rule: summing the 7 stage bounds gives 149.43 µs (sliding) and 272.55 µs (full), exceeding the full-layer byte floor by 5.63 µs and 5.35 µs (Figure P2-2 Step 9)—by the model (derived, not measured), about 4.95 µs of that gap is the extra compute time of the 3 Tensor Core-bound stages over their own HBM read floors, hidden behind overlapped memory reads in the full-layer byte formula (plus about 0.41 µs from counting inter-stage activations per stage rather than layer entry/exit only, and about 0.28 µs on sliding layers from full 2,048-slot KV versus the 0.925-scaled KV in the chart note below). Compared with T=1, the lower bound of a sliding-window layer grows to only about 3.6× its T=1 value, while processing 255 additional tokens in the same pass (see the chart below).

When multiple concurrent requests batch into one decode pass (L=1; see Primer 1, Section 6), they share the five dense weight matrices while each still reads its own historical KV cache: derived from the competition benchmark's single-layer benchmark time floors (which assume 80,000 historical tokens per request, skewed routing, and 4-bit experts across all layers), if we define single-layer floor throughput as tokens processed in the layer divided by that single-layer benchmark time floor, batching 16 requests instead of 1 raises floor throughput by about 8× on sliding-window layers (derived from single-layer benchmark floors of 40.0 µs→76.7 µs, ~8.3×) and about 5× on full-attention layers (derived from single-layer benchmark floors of 44.2 µs→137.5 µs, ~5.1×).

Finally, look at Regime 3: chunked prefill (T=16,384, chunk 5 of a long prompt with 65,536 tokens already cached). Under uniform routing, each local expert now gets 16,384×8/256=512 tokens—well past the 58-token threshold—and attention's LL is 16,384 as well. At this point, all 7 stages cross 206 FLOP/B and become Tensor Core-bound. By the rule from Section 3, once every stage is Tensor Core-bound, the full-layer lower bound is simply the sum of the stage lower bounds; if we assume uniform routing and include causal attention within the current chunk, the stage bounds of a full-attention layer add up to about 9.87 ms, with attention alone taking about 5.00 ms at the Tensor Core rate. That 9.87 ms total differs by only about 0.2% from the benchmark's 9.85 ms—the benchmark formula adds extra expert work for skewed routing but leaves out in-chunk attention, and the two effects largely offset each other.

One final note: every lower bound above counts only the memory traffic and arithmetic on a single GPU, excluding launch overhead (Primer 3, Section 5) for a kernel (a function run in parallel by thousands of threads on the GPU; see Primer 3, Section 1) as well as cross-GPU communication time (Primer 1); likewise, the skewed routing distribution is the load assumption set by the benchmark.

Of course, the theoretical lower bound assumes perfect overlap between memory transfers and math at 100% of rated bandwidth, which real hardware does not hand you for free. Each kernel launch carries a fixed overhead that does not shrink when you read fewer bytes (Primer 3, Section 5 measures an empty kernel to size this up, and Chapter 10, Section 1 isolates the launch and event-recording portion). And to get anywhere near 4.8 TB/s, the chip has to keep enough unanswered read requests in the air at the same time (called in-flight reads; Chapter 2, Section 3 measures how much you need). As a result, measured runtime always sits above the lower bound—and squeezing out that gap is what the rest of this book is all about.

Once you know what a stage is waiting on, you know how to make it faster: HBM-bound stages speed up when you read fewer bytes and pack the available memory bandwidth more tightly (Chapters 2, 3, and 6), whereas Tensor Core-bound stages speed up when you keep the matrix units fed (Chapter 5). Part I starts with the cleanest HBM-bound stage in the layer—gemv at T=1—and pushes it step by step toward its 7.86 µs lower bound.

Takeaway: What a stage waits on comes down to how many tokens share each byte it reads. In single-request decode, no bytes are shared and all 7 stages are HBM-bound; as the token count and byte sharing grow, the stages become Tensor Core-bound one by one.

Next chapter's question: At T=1, Stage 1 is a single matrix-vector multiplication y=Wx, and reading the 37.75 MB of WW takes at least 7.86 µs. Written as a minimal CUDA program running on an H200, what does the code look like, what does each keyword do, and why assign a group of threads—rather than a single thread—to compute one output row?

What Does Stage 1's y=Wx Look Like as a Minimal CUDA Program, and Why Assign One Thread Block per Row?

Primer 2 left off at a hard lower bound: at T=1, Stage 1 needs at least 7.86 µs just to stream WW out of HBM. Before we can try to approach that line, we need working code on the GPU. What does a minimal CUDA program look like, and how does it coordinate thousands of threads to compute y=Wx together?

1How Does CUDA Turn the Row Loop of y=Wx into Parallelism?

The outer row loop disappears: each of the 2,304 rows goes to a thread block (CTA) scheduled onto the 132 SMs in batches, while the 128 threads inside each CTA split up the 8,192 columns and accumulate them in parallel.

Our job is to compute y=Wx from Stage 1 of Primer 2, where W:[2304,8192]BF16\shape{W}{2304,\;8192}{BF16} and x:[8192]BF16\shape{x}{8192}{BF16} both sit in HBM and each output row is yr=∑k=08191Wr,kxk. Let's write M=2,304 for the number of rows and K=8,192 for the number of columns. To keep the code short, the listing below writes the output yy in FP32; the real Stage 1 writes BF16 and slices it into q, k, v, and gate for Stage 2. The arrows at the end of the lines point to the chapters that unpack the hardware mechanism behind each line.

// #include <cuda_bf16.h> and device memory allocation omitted; stream is a pre-created CUDA stream
__global__ void gemv_kernel(const __nv_bfloat16* W, const __nv_bfloat16* x,
                            float* y, int K) {
    __shared__ float smem[128];                                // → Chapter 3
    int row = blockIdx.x;                                      // → Chapter 2
    int tid = threadIdx.x;                                     // → Chapter 3
    float acc = 0.0f;                                          // → Chapter 3
    for (int k = tid; k < K; k += blockDim.x) {
        acc += __bfloat162float(W[row * K + k])                // → Chapter 3 (load), Chapter 6 (conversion)
             * __bfloat162float(x[k]);                         // → Chapter 5 (multiply-add)
    }
    smem[tid] = acc;
    __syncthreads();                                           // → Chapter 4
    if (tid == 0) {                                            // → Chapter 4
        float sum = 0.0f;
        for (int i = 0; i < blockDim.x; ++i) sum += smem[i];
        y[row] = sum;
    }
}
gemv_kernel<<<M, 128, 0, stream>>>(W, x, y, K);                // → Chapter 1, Chapter 2

Let's read through the code from top to bottom. At the top, __global__ marks the function as a kernel—a function launched once by the CPU and executed in parallel by thousands of threads on the GPU. CUDA calls a group of threads that team up on a piece of work a thread block (CTA) (short for cooperative thread array, and called block in code), and all the CTAs from a single launch make up a grid. The launch statement on the last line spins up M=2,304 CTAs at once, with 128 threads in each CTA running this function from start to finish (128 threads per CTA is the starting choice here—why 128 was chosen is not determined in this chapter, and we do not tune it here; Chapter 3, Section 1 shows how CTA size sets per-SM residency). Inside the loop, __bfloat162float widens 2-byte BF16 values to 4-byte FP32 values before multiply-adding them into the thread's own acc, preventing precision loss across 8,192 additions.

Notice what happened to the outer loop: on a CPU you would loop over the rows one after another in time, but in CUDA we flatten that outer loop into 2,304 CTAs—one per row—and let the on-chip hardware dispatcher dispatch them in batches across its SM (Streaming Multiprocessor) units. An SM is the hardware core that actually executes instructions; an H200 has 132 of them, and any given CTA stays on a single SM from start to finish. Each SM can hold only so many resident CTAs at once, so whichever CTAs do not fit in the first batch wait in line until slots free up (Chapter 2, Section 1 and Chapter 3, Section 1 explain how many fit and why; Section 7 counts the CTAs that are left over).

2How Does Each Thread Know Which Segment to Compute?

Via built-in hardware thread coordinates: blockIdx.x identifies the CTA index, threadIdx.x identifies the thread index within the CTA, and blockDim.x gives the CTA size used as the loop stride.

If thousands of threads all run the exact same function, how does each thread know which numbers to read? Hardware supplies every thread's coordinates in built-in special registers. Start with row = blockIdx.x: the CTA index runs from 00 to 2,3032{,}303, mapping straight to the row of WW that this CTA claims. Next, tid = threadIdx.x (0..1270..127) and blockDim.x (128) split the columns of that row across the 128 threads: on loop iteration rr (r=1..64), thread tid reads column k=tid+128(r−1).

With 8,192 columns per row split across 128 threads, each thread runs 8,192/128=64 iterations, and across all 64 iterations the 128 threads together read one full 16 KiB row of WW and 16 KiB of xx. Better yet, on any single iteration, adjacent threads read adjacent addresses in that row, covering a contiguous 256 B span across the CTA. Hardware groups every 32 adjacent threads into a warp that issues load instructions together, and device memory transfers at least a 32 B minimum segment per request (Chapter 3, Sections 1–2 show how a warp issues loads and how hardware coalesces adjacent addresses into fewer requests): here the 32 adjacent threads of 1 warp read a contiguous 32×2 B=64 B on the same iteration, landing cleanly on two 32 B segments. Conversely (derived from the loop stride and the 32 B minimum segment), if each thread took its own block of 64 adjacent columns, adjacent threads on the same iteration would read addresses 64 columns (128 B) apart, so one warp load would touch separate 32 B segments—the same scattered access pattern that Section 6 describes for v0.

You can check this formula yourself in Figure P3-1 by dragging the sliders to row = 2, tid = 5, and iteration 24 (r=24): on that step, the thread reads column k=5+128×23=2,949, fetching W[2 * 8192 + 2949] = W[19333] and x[2949].

3How Are 128 Partial Sums Safely Reduced into One Value?

Each thread writes its partial sum to CTA-shared smem, __syncthreads() waits until all 128 threads finish writing, and thread 0 sums the values and writes back yry_r.

The three kinds of variables in this kernel live in three different storage tiers. First, row, tid, and acc reside in registers, with each thread holding its own private instance. Second, the array __shared__ float smem[128] (128×4 B=512 B) sits in on-chip shared memory, where all 128 threads in this CTA can read and write it, while other CTAs cannot see it (Chapter 3, Section 1 covers these two levels of on-chip storage). Third, W, x, and y sit in global memory in HBM, where every CTA can read and write them.

Summing many partial results into one total is called a reduction. Since each thread holds acc in its own private register, this code gathers the 128 partial sums via shared memory smem, starting with every thread executing smem[tid] = acc.

Right after that store comes __syncthreads() (a CTA barrier). It holds all 128 threads in this CTA at that line until every last one of them has arrived; once past the barrier, every thread in the CTA is guaranteed to see the values that all 128 threads just wrote into smem. Keep in mind that this guarantee applies only inside a single CTA—exchanging data across different CTAs takes a different set of rules (Chapter 2, Section 6). If you omit __syncthreads(), thread 0 may read smem[i] before thread i has finished writing its partial sum into that slot.

Once past the barrier, thread 0 sums smem[0..127] one by one and writes y[row], while the other 127 threads exit right away—yet the CTA still holds its SM residency slot and 512 B of shared memory until thread 0 finishes. Because the CTAs of a batch (whether the first batch or the queued tail batch) start together and finish their 64 load iterations to reach this epilogue at roughly the same time, there may be no other CTA on that SM still issuing memory reads—so the SM may have no other in-flight reads (unanswered memory read requests still in transit; see Primer 2, Section 4) left to overlap and hide that serial addition chain behind, letting it land on total runtime.

Putting the software concepts and hardware units from Sections 1–3 side by side shows how gemv_kernel (v1) maps onto the chip:

Software unit / variable Hardware unit Count or size in gemv_kernel (v1) Visibility & residency rule
CTA (block) Residency slot on one SM 1 CTA per row (full grid: 2,304 CTAs, 294,912 threads total) Stays on one SM from start to finish; each SM holds a bounded number of CTAs at once (exact cap in Chapter 2, Section 1 and Chapter 3, Section 1)
Warp Group of adjacent threads issuing loads together on an SM 32 adjacent threads per warp, 4 warps per CTA Reads a contiguous 64 B of WW and 64 B of xx per iteration (Chapter 3, Sections 1–2)
Thread & locals (row, tid, acc, k, sum) Thread-private registers 128 threads per CTA; 22 registers/thread measured in compiled machine code (including compiler-allocated addresses and temporaries; see Chapter 3, Section 1) Private to that single thread
__shared__ float smem[128] On-chip shared memory 512 B per CTA (128 FP32 values; driver-reserved overhead in Chapter 3, Section 1) Read/write across all 128 threads of this CTA, invisible to other CTAs; paired with 1 __syncthreads() CTA barrier
W, x, y Off-chip global memory in HBM WW: 37.75 MB (16 KiB/row); xx: 16 KiB; yy: 9,216 B (4 B/row) Read/write across all CTAs on all 132 SMs

Having thread 0 finish the reduction serially produces the exact right yry_r, and its three costs (512 B of shared memory per CTA, 1 CTA barrier, and 128 dependent serial additions) are small in v1—a stall-field walk of the compiled machine code estimates ~970 cycles (one cycle is one tick of the SM clock, see Chapter 2, Section 2; ~0.54 µs per CTA at ~1.8 GHz; an estimate from machine-code stall counts rather than a timing run, and we did not measure this epilogue cost separately). Chapter 4, Sections 5–6 show how to parallelize the reduction across threads.

4What Does the Launch Statement Do, and When Is yy Ready?

A kernel launch statement just enqueues a command into a CUDA stream and returns right away before yy is computed; by default, the next kernel in the same CUDA stream is guaranteed to see the data written by the previous one.

Look closely at the triple angle brackets on the last line: gemv_kernel<<<M, 128, 0, stream>>>. The first argument sets the number of CTAs for this launch (M=2,304), and the second sets the number of threads per CTA (128). The third argument asks for extra dynamically allocated shared-memory bytes per CTA; we don't need any here, so we pass 0. The fourth argument picks the target CUDA stream—a queue of GPU commands that execute in the order you enqueue them, stored in the variable stream. When the CPU runs this launch line, it simply drops a command into the queue and immediately moves on without waiting for the GPU to finish—a mechanism called asynchronous launch.

By default, commands in the same CUDA stream run strictly in enqueue order, so an earlier kernel happens-before the next one: without a single line of extra synchronization, the next kernel is guaranteed to see everything the earlier kernel wrote to memory. When the CPU itself needs the result in hand, it calls cudaStreamSynchronize(stream) to block until the stream finishes. Adding this launch layer completes Section 3's mapping table:

Software unit / variable Hardware unit Count or size in gemv_kernel (v1) Visibility & residency rule
Launch command & grid CUDA stream → full GPU (132 SMs) 1 launch command creating 2,304 CTAs (294,912 threads total) CPU enqueues and returns immediately; commands in one stream run in enqueue order by default

5How Do We Measure Latency Here, and What Part Lies Outside the Kernel?

Each run flushes the on-chip cache first, brackets a single kernel launch with GPU events, and takes the median of 500 runs—including ~4.6 µs of fixed overhead incurred even by an empty kernel.

We time every gemv version in Part I with the exact same setup. Before each timed launch, we read a 512 MiB buffer of unrelated data to flush the chip's fast small storage (the on-chip cache), forcing the GPU to stream WW fresh from HBM. We then bracket a single launch with two GPU events—timestamps that the GPU records directly inside the CUDA stream—run 20 warmup iterations, and take the median across 500 timed runs. Flushing the cache before each run mirrors what happens in single-request decode from Primer 2 (Chapter 2, Section 2 explains why).

If we time an empty kernel that does nothing at all (1 CTA of 32 threads) with the exact same method, it still measures ~4.6 µs—the baseline cost we call fixed overhead. Because the benchmark pre-fills the CUDA stream before recording the start event, host-side CPU enqueue latency is excluded from this 4.6 µs: it is purely the GPU-side floor of recording the start/stop events and having the GPU front end—which receives the command stream and issues grids—handle and finish one empty launch (its internal split between GPU event recording and GPU front-end empty-grid handling was not measured; Chapter 10, Section 1 compares event timing against profiler kernel duration). Every measured latency we report in Part I includes that 4.6 µs without subtracting it out, whereas the 7.86 µs bandwidth lower bound from Primer 2 does not include it. Back-to-back kernels also pay handoff overhead between launches, which we will meet in Chapter 1, Section 1.

6Why Assign a Thread Block per Row Instead of a Single Thread? (gemv v0 → v1)

Assigning one row per thread launches only 18 CTAs, leaving most of the 132 SMs idle, and adjacent threads read addresses separated by an entire row; switching to one CTA per row speeds up execution by ~12.5×.

We number each gemv version in Part I starting from v0. If you bring your CPU loop habits straight to CUDA, the most obvious first try is v0, where each thread computes one entire row on its own: row = blockIdx.x * 128 + threadIdx.x, launched with <<<18, 128, 0, stream>>> (2,304/128=18 CTAs), so each thread loops across all 8,192 columns of its row from start to finish. v1 is the kernel from Section 1, launched with <<<2304, 128, 0, stream>>>, which assigns a full 128-thread CTA to each row:

// v0: each thread computes 1 full row on its own(int row = blockIdx.x * 128 + threadIdx.x;)
for (int k = 0; k < K; ++k) acc += __bfloat162float(W[row * K + k]) * __bfloat162float(x[k]);
// v1: the 128 adjacent threads of 1 CTA cooperate to read one row in segments (full code in Section 1)
for (int k = tid; k < K; k += 128) acc += __bfloat162float(W[row * K + k]) * __bfloat162float(x[k]);

Here is what happens when we time both versions on the H200 using the method from Section 5:

That 12.5× gap comes from two places. First, almost the entire chip is sitting idle: hardware dispatches work to SMs one CTA at a time (Chapter 2, Section 1), and 18 CTAs can occupy at most 18 of the 132 SMs while the other 114 SMs do nothing.

Second, look at the memory access stride. As introduced in Section 2, the 32 adjacent threads of a warp issue one load instruction together, and device memory transfers at least a 32 B minimum segment per request (Chapter 3, Section 2 covers coalesced access). In v0, those 32 threads ask for 32 addresses that sit a full row (16 KiB) apart from one another: a single load instruction requests 32×32=1,024 B on chip even though the current iteration uses only 64 B of it. Each 32 B segment holds the next 16 BF16 elements of that row, and the current iteration uses just 1 of them; the other 15 sit untouched until the next 15 iterations, when they may still be in the on-chip cache (checked right after the next paragraph with profiler counters; Chapter 3, Section 2 covers L1 details).

In v1, those same 32 adjacent threads read a contiguous 64 B span on every iteration: each load requests just two 32 B segments, and every byte gets used right away.

Does the chip pay for those extra requests at off-chip HBM? No. Start with WW: v0's 16× segment fan-out does not make off-chip HBM transfer WW 16 times. In a cold single-launch profiler pass with clocks locked to base (locking SM clocks to base makes the profiler's 862.05 µs and v1's 56.54 µs below longer than Section 5's unlocked-clock event times), v0 ran in 862.05 µs at dram = 0.9%, matching the 37.75 MB÷862.05 μs=43.8 GB/s (0.91% of 4.8 TB/s, derived from measured counters) needed to read WW once—so the on-chip caches as a whole absorbed the remaining 15 elements per segment, keeping off-chip HBM traffic at roughly 1×W.

Now look at xx: in v0, all 32 threads in a warp read the same x[k] on a given iteration, sharing one read across 32 rows, whereas in v1 each CTA requests all 16 KiB of xx on its own—2,304×16 KiB=37.75 MB of on-chip xx requests in total, equal in volume to WW—yet the on-chip caches absorb those repeated requests too, so off-chip HBM still transfers roughly 1×W (derived the same way from the base-clock profiler pass: v1 ran in 56.54 µs at dram = 14.2%, matching 1×W at 13.9%; Chapter 2, Section 2 covers why).

One more coupled compiler change comes along with that switch: compiled machine code shows that the compiler unrolled v0's loop 16×—issuing 13 alternating 2 B loads of WW and xx, ~7 of them for WW, before the first use (keeping ~7×2 B=14 B of WW reads in flight per thread)—while leaving v1 un-unrolled (1×2 B per thread; why the compiler unrolls v0's loop and not v1's loop is not determined in this chapter). Hardware measures a cap of 16 concurrent resident CTAs per SM for v1 (why the cap is 16 is unpacked in Chapter 3, Section 1): across 132 SMs, v0's 18 CTAs average an estimated 18×128×14 B÷132≈ 0.2 KiB/SM of WW in flight, whereas v1's first batch fills all 132 SMs at 16 CTAs/SM (128×2 B=256 B per CTA), raising in-flight WW bytes per SM to 16×256 B= 4.0 KiB/SM.

Putting both versions side by side reconciles all the numbers (because switching from 1 thread per row to 1 CTA per row simultaneously changes active SMs, access stride, compiler unrolling, and intra-CTA reduction, the sub-split of the 12.5× speedup between populating 132 SMs and coalescing WW loads was not measured in isolation):

Metric gemv v0 (1 thread / row) gemv v1 (1 CTA = 128 threads / row) Basis & notes
Launch grid (CTAs × threads/CTA) 18 × 128 (2,304 threads total) 2,304 × 128 (294,912 threads total) From kernel launch
Active SMs used (out of 132) At most 18 (114 SMs idle) All 132 (in batches) Hardware dispatches whole CTAs
Per warp WW load: segments / bytes requested vs. used now 32 segments = 1,024 B requested / 64 B used now 2 segments = 64 B requested / 64 B all used now Derived from 32 B minimum segment (Chapter 3, Section 2)
Total on-chip xx (16 KiB) read requests across grid 18×16 KiB=288 KiB (32 rows share x[k]) 2,304×16 KiB= 37.75 MB (re-read per CTA) Derived from code; absorbed by on-chip cache (Chapter 2, Section 2)
Chip-average WW bytes in flight per SM ~0.2 KiB/SM (16× compiler unroll, 7×2 B/thread: 18×128×14 B÷132) ~4.0 KiB/SM (unroll 1×, 1×2 B/thread: 16×256 B at full residency) Measured machine-code unroll + estimated in-flight volume
Actual off-chip HBM traffic ~1×W (37.75 MB) ~1×W (37.75 MB) Derived from base-clock profiler dram = 0.9% / 14.2%
Intra-CTA reduction cost None (each thread writes y[row]) 512 B smem + 1 barrier + 128 serial adds on thread 0 (~2% estimate, not measured alone) Section 3
Measured latency (includes ~4.6 µs fixed overhead) 674.58 µs 54.08 µs (~12.5× faster; factor split not measured) Clean GPU-event timing (Section 5)

What if a matrix has fewer than 132 rows to begin with? Then even 1 CTA per row cannot fill all 132 SMs, and we have to split each row across multiple CTAs (Chapter 2, Section 5).

7Why Is v1 Still ~7× Above the 7.86 µs Floor?

Four costs unpacked from the outside in across the next four chapters stand in the way: ~4.6 µs of fixed single-launch overhead, 192 left-over CTAs running a second 64-iteration wave, too few WW bytes in flight per SM, and a short serial reduction tail.

Look back at the chart in Section 6: even after a 12.5× speedup, v1 (54.08 µs) still takes ~7× (6.88×) the 7.86 µs lower bound; even after subtracting the 4.6 µs fixed overhead, its estimated effective bandwidth for reading WW is ~0.76 TB/s, only about one-sixth of 4.8 TB/s. Why is a kernel that fills all 132 SMs and reads contiguous bytes still so far from the floor? The next four chapters unpack these four pieces from the outside in:

  • ~4.6 µs of fixed single-launch overhead (measured; Chapter 1, Sections 1–3): Already 8.5% of v1's runtime, and a growing share as the kernel body shrinks.
  • A second-wave tail of 192 CTAs running another full 64-iteration chain (Chapter 2, Sections 1 and 7): As noted in Section 6, hardware measures a cap of 16 concurrent resident CTAs per SM for this kernel (why the cap is 16 is unpacked in Chapter 3, Section 1), so the first batch fits 132×16=2,112 CTAs and leaves 2,304−2,112= 192 CTAs queued (derived from the measured per-SM CTA residency cap), which must walk a second 64-iteration dependent load chain once slots free up.
  • Too few WW bytes in flight per SM (Chapter 2, Section 3; Chapter 3, Section 3; Chapter 4, Section 3): Within a single thread, each iteration's multiply-add acc += ... must wait until both loads (W[...] and x[k]) return to registers; and as verified in compiled machine code, the compiler does not unroll v1's stride-128 loop to issue later iterations' loads early, so each thread keeps only 1×2 B of WW reads in flight at a time (matching Step 4's card in Figure P3-1; Chapter 4, Section 2 covers in-order issue)—about 4.0 KiB/SM at full SM residency (16×256 B, estimated from machine code), far below the tens of KiB/SM needed to saturate HBM (24–40 KiB/SM for 95% of the measured 16 B load plateau, and >98% by 64 KiB/SM; see Chapter 2, Section 3)—so nearly every one of the 64 iterations waits on a memory round trip.
  • Thread 0's 128-add serial reduction tail (~2% estimate, not measured in isolation; Chapter 4, Sections 5–6): Estimated at ~0.54 µs per CTA from machine-code stall counts, or ~1.1 µs (~2% of v1's 54.08 µs) if exposed in both CTA batches, a minor piece here.

As a rough order-of-magnitude check against the total runtime: Chapter 2, Section 2's unloaded HBM round-trip model (~0.33 µs per round trip) puts one 64-iteration serial chain at ~64×0.33≈21 μs and both waves plus fixed overhead at ~2×64×0.33+4.6≈47 μs (estimated, ~7 µs shy of the measured 54.08 µs; neither per-wave duration nor the exact four-term sum was measured directly with timestamps, and Chapter 2, Section 7 bounds both waves from the measured gap between v1 and v3).

Takeaway: CUDA flattens the outer loop into 2,304 CTAs that go onto the SMs in batches; having a group of adjacent threads work together on a single row is what fills all 132 SMs and lets them read contiguous bytes.

Next chapter's question: A single v1 launch takes 54.08 µs (including fixed overhead that does not depend on byte count); yet before we zoom inside one kernel, a real model layer does not run this kernel in isolation—Stage 1 is immediately preceded by an input normalization kernel and followed by a post-processing kernel. When we launch a sequence of kernels back to back along the same CUDA stream, where does the time between two adjacent kernels go, and how do we squeeze it out?

In Primer 3, every timing run of gemv_kernel (v1) carried ~4.6 µs of fixed overhead (see Primer 3, Section 5). When you actually run a single model layer, though, the GPU doesn't run just that one kernel—it launches a whole chain of kernels back to back along a CUDA stream (see Primer 3, Section 4). Where does the time between two adjacent kernels go, and how can we eliminate it?

Figure I-1 lays out the six zoom levels of Part I, going step by step from the outermost timeline all the way down to instructions and bits. In this chapter, we start at the outermost level—Level 1: Timeline.

To see what happens on the timeline, let's put gemv_kernel from Primer 3 (the T=1 matrix-vector multiplication for Stage 1 qkv_gate of a single layer; see Primer 2, Section 1) back where it sits inside a single layer: right after a normalization kernel and right before a post-processing kernel, forming a three-kernel chain. We'll use this one example from start to finish in this chapter:

  1. ① Normalization kernel: reads x:[8192]BF16\shape{x}{8192}{BF16} (16 KiB; see Preface, Section 6 for tensor shape notation, and Primer 1, Section 1 for 16-bit float BF16, 32-bit float FP32, and the RMSNorm definition), writes xn:[8192]BF16\shape{x_n}{8192}{BF16} (16 KiB), and computes xn=x⋅r, where r=1/1K∑kxk2+ϵ (K=8,192; we skip multiplying a weight vector here). This step launches just 1 CTA of 1,024 threads (see Primer 3, Section 1 for CTAs and threads; 1,024 is the per-CTA thread limit).
  2. ② gemv_kernel (v1): multiplies weight W:[2304,8192]BF16\shape{W}{2304,\;8192}{BF16} (37.75 MB; see Primer 2, Section 1) by xnx_n (16 KiB) to compute y=Wxn and writes y:[2304]FP32\shape{y}{2304}{FP32} (9,216 B), launching 2,304 CTAs of 128 threads each.
  3. ③ Post-processing kernel: runs elementwise operations in place on y:[2304]FP32\shape{y}{2304}{FP32} (9,216 B) (standing in for the actual per-head normalization and rotary position embedding (RoPE): real per-head normalization has to reduce the 64 elements of one head sitting across 64 separate 1-row CTAs, whereas this stand-in omits that cross-CTA reduction, and Section 3 brings the real per-head normalization back for comparison; see Primer 2, Section 2), with 256 threads per CTA across ⌈2304/256⌉=9 CTAs in total.

Most of the building blocks used in these three steps already appeared in the three Primers: off-chip main memory HBM (see Primer 1, Section 4); thread blocks (CTAs), threads, SMs (132 in total), and the on-chip hardware dispatcher that pulls commands from the stream and assigns CTAs onto SMs (see Primer 3, Section 1); registers, shared memory, and global memory (see Primer 3, Section 3); a CUDA stream (see Primer 3, Section 4); and the on-chip cache (see Primer 3, Section 5). On top of those, this chapter introduces two new mechanisms: the chip-wide shared on-chip second-level cache that provides cross-SM write visibility in Section 1, and PDL, which lets the hardware dispatcher dispatch a successor kernel early in Section 4.

Here are the launch shapes, SM occupancy, and byte counts of the three steps side by side:

Step Launch shape (CTAs × threads) SMs occupied (out of 132) Reads (from, bytes) Writes (to, bytes)
① Normalization 1×1,024 1 SM (131 SMs idle; exact SM not measured) Global memory HBM: xx (16 KiB) Global memory HBM: xnx_n (16 KiB)
② gemv_kernel (v1) 2,304×128 All 132 SMs Global memory HBM: WW (37.75 MB); each CTA reads all of xnx_n (16 KiB, inferred by capacity to stay in on-chip cache; hit rate not measured) Global memory HBM: yy (9,216 B)
③ Post-processing 9×256 At most 9 SMs (2–9 SMs, leaving 123–130 idle; exact placement not measured) Global memory HBM: yy (9,216 B) Global memory HBM: updates yy in place (9,216 B)

Direct answer to the chapter question first: along a single CUDA stream, the dead time between kernels comes from two places—the larger one is the CPU launch gap when the stream queue runs dry and the GPU waits on the CPU (~41 µs measured in total under empty-queue one-by-one launch on this chain), and the smaller one is the hardware handoff gap while waiting for all CTAs of the previous kernel to exit and make their writes visible to all SMs (not measured directly on this chain; ~1.13 µs per seam derived by the additive estimate in Section 3). The table below summarizes the tools that remove or overlap each gap:

Gap Why the GPU stalls Where it lands on this chain (scale) Tool that removes or overlaps it Section
CPU launch gap Stream queue runs dry; GPU waits for CPU to issue the next command Empty-queue start (before ①) and ①→② (~41 µs measured combined, split not measured; none at ②→③) Pre-filled command queue (while CPU stays ahead); CUDA Graph (single submission removes inter-node gaps; empty-queue replay not measured) Sections 1, 2, 5
Hardware handoff gap Hardware dispatcher waits until all CTAs of the previous kernel exit and writes are visible to all SMs ①→② and ②→③ (not measured directly; ~1.13 µs per seam derived in Section 3) Kernel fusion (merges into one kernel, deleting the boundary); PDL (spec permits early weight reads overlapping epilogue and handoff; chain latency change not measured) Sections 1, 3, 4

1Why Does the GPU Stall Between Two Kernels?

Along a CUDA stream, the idle gaps that stall the GPU come from two places: first, when the CPU issues commands slower than the GPU finishes them, the stream queue runs dry and the GPU sits waiting on the CPU (both before the first kernel when starting from an empty queue and after a short kernel finishes before the next command arrives); second, even when commands are already waiting in the queue, the next kernel still cannot land on SMs until every CTA of the previous kernel has exited and its writes are visible to all SMs. We call the first one the CPU launch gap and the second one the hardware handoff gap.

Let's do the math for the first gap. A kernel launch statement just drops a command into the CUDA stream and returns right away (see Primer 3, Section 4), so the CPU is the producer, the GPU is the consumer, and the CUDA stream is the command queue between them. When starting from an empty queue, the GPU first has to wait for the CPU to put command ① into the stream (~t𝑐𝑝𝑢t_{cpu}) before it can run anything. Once running, suppose the current kernel runs on the GPU for t𝑔𝑝𝑢t_{gpu}, while the CPU takes t𝑐𝑝𝑢t_{cpu} to issue one launch command. Whenever t𝑐𝑝𝑢>t𝑔𝑝𝑢, the GPU finishes the current kernel before the next command reaches the queue. The queue runs dry, the start-to-start spacing between back-to-back kernels stretches out to t𝑐𝑝𝑢t_{cpu}, and the GPU sits idle for ~t𝑐𝑝𝑢−t𝑔𝑝𝑢 every time. Conversely, whenever commands are already queued before timing starts—or t𝑐𝑝𝑢≤t𝑔𝑝𝑢 while running—the CPU stays ahead of the GPU, the queue never runs dry, and that wait on the CPU vanishes.

Small kernels are where this gap hurts most, because their t𝑔𝑝𝑢t_{gpu} is only a few microseconds. In our three-kernel chain, both the 1-CTA normalization kernel and the 9-CTA post-processing kernel are that small. Our benchmark script fires off the three launches in sequence from Python, and the first two rows of Figure 1-1 compare two ways of running them: in Row 1 ("CPU one-by-one launch"), the stream queue is empty when timing starts, and Python issues the three launches one by one; in Row 2 ("Pre-filled command queue"), we first enqueue a kernel that keeps the GPU busy for a short window before timing starts, and the CPU uses that window to queue up all three launch commands ahead of time.

In our measurements (two-machine means; see the chart in Section 5), launching the kernels one by one from the CPU (102.6 µs) is ~41 µs slower than starting from a pre-filled command queue (61.6 µs). By the queue rule we just walked through, those 41 µs land at the two spots where the queue is empty: the first launch (when timing starts with an empty queue) and the ①→② boundary (because ① runs for only a few microseconds). While ② runs on the GPU for ~50 µs (its 54 µs standalone timing includes ~4.6 µs of fixed overhead), the CPU uses that time to queue up ③, so the ②→③ boundary no longer waits on the CPU. How large t𝑐𝑝𝑢t_{cpu} is on its own and how the 41 µs split between those two places were not measured.

Now look at the second row of Figure 1-1, "Pre-filled command queue". Even when all three commands are already waiting in the queue, a gap still separates adjacent bars. The CPU has nothing to do with this second gap: the global-memory read/write path does not order visibility on its own, so a single CUDA stream enforces its ordering guarantee (happens-before; see Primer 3, Section 4) by waiting until the previous kernel has completely finished and all of its writes are visible before starting the next one.

Here all writes are visible means the previous kernel's outputs (xnx_n from ①, yy from ②) are visible to all SMs across the chip so no successor CTA on any SM can read stale data. The handoff waits only for that visibility across SMs, without waiting for write-back to off-chip HBM: a chip-wide on-chip second-level cache shared by all SMs catches those writes, so pushing the previous kernel's outputs to that shared on-chip cache makes them visible across every SM (Chapter 2, Section 2 measures the round-trip latencies across this cache and HBM).

While the last few CTAs of a multi-CTA kernel are still wrapping up, SMs that finished early are already sitting idle. Once the very last CTA exits too, during the handoff all 132 SMs across the chip sit completely empty before the on-chip hardware dispatcher places the next kernel's CTAs onto SMs (see Primer 3, Section 1 for dispatch). We define the hardware handoff gap as that interval from the exit of the previous kernel's last CTA, across write visibility to all SMs, until the hardware dispatcher places the next kernel's CTAs onto SMs. Next to the measured ~41 µs CPU launch gap, an individual hardware handoff on this chain was not measured separately—from the difference between the standalone runs and the chain total, it is only derived at ~1.13 µs per seam (a derived estimate only; see Section 3 for the derivation). Here is who holds what across the timeline handoff on this chain:

Unit What it holds Role at the chain handoffs
CPU Launch commands (t𝑐𝑝𝑢t_{cpu} per launch; standalone value not measured) Issues the launch commands for ①, ②, and ③ into the CUDA stream in order
CUDA stream Queue of pending launch commands (FIFO; command byte size and queue capacity not covered here) Running dry creates a CPU launch gap; when pre-filled, ①, ②, and ③ are already waiting in line
On-chip hardware dispatcher & 132 SMs Resident CTAs of the running kernel Waits until all CTAs of the previous kernel exit and its writes are visible to all SMs before placing the next kernel's CTAs onto SMs; all 132 SMs sit empty during the handoff
Shared on-chip second-level cache & global memory HBM xnx_n from ① (16 KiB), yy from ② (9,216 B), and static weights WW (37.75 MB) The shared on-chip second-level cache catches writes to xnx_n and yy, making them visible across all SMs without waiting for write-back to off-chip HBM

2Which Gap Does CUDA Graph Eliminate, and Which Does It Leave Behind?

A CUDA Graph pre-records the entire chain and submits it in one call, structurally eliminating any CPU launch gap between nodes inside the graph; when launched from an empty queue, one host submission wait before Node ① still remains (not measured), and the hardware handoff gaps between nodes stay.

A CUDA Graph records a sequence of GPU commands and their dependencies ahead of time, with each kernel in the graph represented as a graph node. Using one takes two steps. First comes recording and instantiation: during warm-up before formal timing, we record the three kernel launches in order into a single graph, and at instantiation time the driver (the CPU-side software that manages the GPU) validates the whole graph and does most of the launch setup up front. Second comes replay: at runtime, the CPU makes a single cudaGraphLaunch call to submit the whole graph at once, without redoing that setup on later runs. Because the CPU submits the chain once instead of once per kernel, no CPU launch gap can ever open up between nodes inside the graph (①→② or ②→③). Here is the v1 → v2 launch comparison from Section 5 (the GPU machine code of all three kernels is byte-for-byte identical):

// v1: the CPU puts [normalization, gemv_kernel, post-processing] into the CUDA stream one by one
gemv_kernel<<<2304, 128, 0, stream>>>(W, xn, y, K);
// v2: during warm-up, record these three steps on stream and instantiate them into graph_exec; at runtime, submit once
cudaGraphLaunch(graph_exec, stream);

Each graph node is still a separate kernel, though, and back-to-back nodes still obey the ordering rule of a single CUDA stream: the next node cannot start until every CTA of the previous node has exited and all of its writes are visible to all SMs. So the hardware handoff gaps stay right inside the graph. On this three-kernel chain, how long each handoff takes was not measured (the additive estimate on the pre-filled stream run in Section 3 derives ~1.13 µs per seam as a schematic figure only). To give you two reference points from other tests: across 93 per-node replay calibrations on real inference graphs from another serving framework (SGLang; see Chapter 7, Section 1), the calibrated launch overhead per node has a median of ~1.0 µs (not measured on this chapter's chain). In a separate synthetic test that only adds empty kernels to a graph, each extra empty kernel adds 0.37–1.19 µs to the full-graph time.

Compare that with "Pre-filled command queue" from Section 1: pre-filling the queue hides all ~41 µs of CPU queue wait too, but only as long as the CPU stays ahead of the GPU, whereas full-graph replay submits once and never relies on the CPU keeping pace between nodes. When both are timed pre-queued in the stream before t=0, full-graph replay (60.0 µs) on our three-kernel chain also runs ~1.6 µs faster than the pre-filled command queue (61.6 µs; where that ~1.6 µs comes from was not measured; see Section 5). The four ~1 µs numbers across the last two paragraphs measure different things; the table below keeps them straight:

Value What it measures Which test setup Epistemic status
~1.13 µs Schematic width of one hardware handoff gap This chapter's three-kernel chain (pre-filled standard stream; standalone runs minus 4.6 µs vs. chain total, split across two seams) Derived / schematic (individual seam not measured; see Section 3)
~1.0 µs Median per-node launch overhead during graph replay 93 per-node replay calibrations on real SGLang inference graphs (not this chapter's chain; Chapter 7, Section 1 introduces SGLang only) Measured
0.37–1.19 µs Extra full-graph time per added empty kernel Synthetic graph-slope test adding only empty kernels (not this chapter's chain) Measured
~1.6 µs Full-chain speedup of full-graph replay (60.0 µs) over pre-filled standard stream (61.6 µs) This chapter's three-kernel chain (both pre-queued at t<0; difference of two-machine means) Measured delta (exact source and timeline location not determined; see Section 5)

Here is how the CUDA Graph trade-off works out:

  • What you gain: one submission covers the whole graph, structurally removing any CPU launch gap between nodes inside the graph; when both are pre-queued in the stream, it runs ~1.6 µs faster than standard stream launch on this three-kernel chain (~42.6 µs faster than empty-queue one-by-one launch when combined with the ~41 µs from pre-filling the queue; if the stream queue starts empty, Node ① still waits for that single host graph submission to reach the stream, and Section 5's full-graph replay was likewise timed pre-queued before t=0 while empty-queue replay was not measured—see Row 3 of Figure 1-1 and Section 5).
  • What it costs: you do an extra recording and instantiation pass during warm-up. Once the graph is instantiated, every kernel's arguments, launch configuration, and device memory addresses are locked into it. To change them, you have to call a graph update API (such as cudaGraphExecUpdate or cudaGraphExecKernelNodeSetParams) or record the graph again. When the input token count TT varies, the common approach is to record a separate graph for each value of TT (or pad the input up to a recorded TT).
  • When it loses: on this three-kernel chain, full-graph replay beats both standard stream-launch modes; the extra cost of recording multiple graphs or padding shapes, and whether it loses in other scenarios, were not measured.

3What Do You Save and What Do You Pay When Fusing Two Kernels into One?

Fusing two kernels into one saves a boundary, a launch, and a global-memory round trip; you pay with one extra step in the main kernel, and it works only when the next step does not force all CTAs to stop and wait for each other.

Putting the work of two adjacent kernels into a single kernel—so the intermediate result stays in registers or on-chip memory instead of taking a round trip through global memory—is called kernel fusion. Every extra standalone kernel costs you more than a hardware handoff: it also writes its intermediate result out to global memory, only for the next kernel to read it right back in. Whether two steps can be fused boils down to one question: can the second step get the data it needs without forcing every CTA across the GPU to stop and wait for one another? You can fuse in two cases: either the data is already inside the same CTA (as in our elementwise post-processing stand-in and normalization reading all of xx), or the results from multiple CTAs only need to come together in one place so the last CTA to finish writing can wrap them up (as in the real per-head normalization flow covered below in this section; see Chapter 2, Section 6 for how to write the counter safely). Normalization fits the first case because every CTA already reads all of xx (the vector is only 16 KiB, so by capacity it is inferred to stay in the on-chip cache; see Chapter 2, Section 2—we did not measure the hit rate).

So how do we actually fuse them? Walk through Figure 1-2. First, let's name one part of a kernel: the wrap-up work that runs after the main loop finishes and right before the final result is written out is called the epilogue.

Folding this chapter's elementwise post-processing into the epilogue is straightforward. In gemv_kernel, right after thread 0 of each CTA finishes the intra-CTA reduction (see Primer 3, Section 3) for its row's dot product, that result is already sitting in its register. Because elementwise post-processing doesn't need results from any other CTA, thread 0 can finish that math in place before writing out y[row]. (Keep in mind that Step ③ in our chain is an elementwise stand-in; real Stage 2 begins with per-head normalization across the 64 elements of a head, which live across 64 separate 1-row CTAs rather than inside 1 CTA—putting it in the second fusible case above, right below Figure 1-2.)

Folding normalization in takes one more step of thought. In xn=x⋅r, the scale factor r=1/1K∑kxk2+ϵ depends on the sum of squares across the entire vector xx. At first glance, it looks as if you have to finish reading all of xx to get rr before the matrix multiply can even start. But look back at the v1 loop in Primer 3: to compute its own row's dot product, every CTA already reads the entire vector xx (8,192 elements) from start to finish. Since every CTA reads all of xx anyway, it can accumulate the sum of squares ∑kxk2\sum_k x_k^2 right alongside the dot product in that same loop; after the intra-CTA reduction in the epilogue, thread 0 computes rr and multiplies it into the dot product to write out y[row]=r⋅acc=r⋅∑kW[row,k]xk, while the other threads never need rr. That works because:

y=W(x⋅r)=r(Wx)y = W(x \cdot r) = r\,(Wx)

Without a normalization weight vector, those two expressions are algebraically identical; even with a weight vector, the expression just becomes rW(wnorm⊙x), which still uses only the data read by the current CTA. Numerically, only two things change: you skip one BF16 rounding step from writing xnx_n out to global memory (rounding a 32-bit float to the nearest 16-bit value), and you change the rounding order of the multiply-adds. Tracing the middle hardware box of Figure 1-2 puts every piece of data inside one fused 128-thread CTA into a small table (eliminating the global-memory write-and-read round trips of intermediate xnx_n 16 KiB and intermediate yy 9,216 B):

Storage What lives here (size) Who reads or writes it, and for what
Registers Per-thread acc and ss (4 B FP32 each); epilogue r and y[row] All 128 threads accumulate dot-product partials acc and sum-of-squares partials ss; after reduction, thread 0 alone computes rr, y[row]=r⋅acc, and elementwise post-processing (the other threads do not need rr)
Shared memory 512 B → 1 KiB (two 128×4 B arrays) All 128 threads stage both partial-sum arrays across __syncthreads() (the CTA barrier; see Primer 3, Section 3), then thread 0 sums them in registers
On-chip cache Full input vector xx (16 KiB, inferred by capacity; hit rate not measured) Reused across all 2,304 CTAs during the main loop
Global memory HBM Weight WW (16 KiB per row, 37.75 MB total); final output yy (4 B per row, 9,216 B total) All 128 threads read this row of WW from HBM; thread 0 writes final y[row]y[\text{row}] to HBM once in the epilogue

Now let's bring back the real per-head normalization that Step ③ and our elementwise epilogue stand-in left out (see Primer 2, Section 2). As long as each CTA in gemv still computes 1 row, the 64 elements of one Q or K head sit across 64 separate CTAs, so no single CTA can finish the head on its own as in the elementwise stand-in; instead, it falls into the second fusible case we stated earlier: after writing its BF16 value, each of the 64 CTAs increments that head's global counter by 1; the first 63 CTAs to arrive exit right away, while the 64th (last-arriving) CTA reloads the head's 64 values, runs per-head normalization, and writes out FP8 (Chapter 2, Section 6 covers how to write that counter safely). The V CTAs do no per-head normalization and each write the FP8 V cache directly without a counter.

Keep in mind that fusion cuts out only the kernel boundaries and global-memory round trips; the computation you fold in still has to run. We measured this on v9n (14.91 µs without epilogue, the faster BF16-output gemv kernel taught in Chapter 6, Section 3): folding that per-head normalization and the FP8 Q and KV cache writes into its epilogue to build v9e (16.02 µs) still adds ~1.1 µs inside the kernel itself (see the chart below). How that extra 1.1 µs splits across those steps was not measured.

Now that we see how fusion works, how many microseconds can it save at most on our three-kernel chain? On a single H200 (one machine, whereas the 61.6 and 60.0 µs chain values in Section 5 are two-H200 means and the 54.08 and 54.19 µs values in the single-kernel evolution ladder are two-H200 pooled medians, which is why the last digits differ slightly), we measured each of the three kernels standalone and the full chain back to back, all launched on a standard stream with the command queue pre-filled (see the chart below): the full chain (61.63 µs) takes only about 7.5 µs (exact difference 7.45 µs) longer than gemv_kernel standalone (54.18 µs).

At first glance, one thing in that chart looks backwards: adding the three standalone medians (9.02, 54.18, and 5.34 µs) gives a total longer than the 61.63 µs full chain (61.6 µs two-machine mean)! The reason is the ~4.6 µs fixed event-timing overhead from Primer 3, Section 5: timing the three kernels separately brackets three runs and includes ~4.6 µs in each standalone median (paid 3 times across the three standalone runs), so Row 1 subtracts 4.6 µs from each run first to get the sum of the three net widths without event brackets (54.74 µs); timing the pre-filled chain brackets the whole sequence once, following the additive model pre-filled chain total = 1 × 4.6 µs (the chain's single event pair) + sum of the three net widths (54.74 µs) + 2 hardware handoffs. Rows 1–4 solve that equation for the 2 handoffs (which is why Row 4 subtracts the chain's own single 4.6 µs once; Row 2 of Figure 1-1 draws this schematic width):

Step Arithmetic & result Machine source Epistemic status
1. Sum of schematic net widths after subtracting fixed overhead (9.02−4.6)+(54.18−4.6)+(5.34−4.6)=4.42+49.58+0.74=54.74 µs Single-H200 cold-cache standalone medians minus two-machine mean 4.6 µs fixed overhead Derived / schematic (xnx_n and yy inside the chain were just written by the prior step; in-chain per-kernel times not measured)
2. Pre-filled chain total 61.6 µs61.6\ \text{µs} (61.63 µs61.63\ \text{µs} on the matched single H200) Two-H200 pre-filled stream mean Measured
3. Non-kernel residual on the chain 61.6−54.74=6.86 µs Row 2 minus Row 1 (two-machine mean minus single-machine standalone sum) Derived
4. Subtract the chain's 1× fixed overhead and split across two seams (6.86−4.6)/2=2.26/2=𝟏.𝟏𝟑 µs per seam Remaining 2.26 µs split equally across ①→② and ②→③ Derived / schematic (individual hardware handoff not measured directly)

Moreover, the ~7.5 µs (61.63−54.18=7.45 µs) by which the chain exceeds gemv_kernel standalone still includes the arithmetic of normalization and post-processing themselves—merging kernels does not make that math vanish, so ~7.5 µs is only an upper bound on what fusion can save (a fused v1 kernel was not built or measured). Here is how the fusion trade-off works out:

  • What you gain: you cut out 2 hardware handoffs and 2 launches, and the intermediate results xnx_n (16 KiB, which is small at T=1) and intermediate yy (9,216 B) no longer go out to global memory only to be read right back in.
  • What it costs: the main kernel takes on an extra step in its loop or epilogue, the code gets more complex, shared memory per CTA grows from 512 B to 1 KiB, and all 2,304 CTAs redundantly compute the exact same rr (each CTA does 8,192 extra multiply-adds and one extra intra-CTA reduction)—computing rr once for all CTAs would require either keeping the separate normalization kernel ① (bringing a hardware handoff back) or a device-wide barrier inside one kernel (next bullet).
  • When it loses:
    • When every CTA of the second step needs results produced by many CTAs of the first step, forcing both steps into one kernel requires a device-wide barrier where all CTAs across the GPU stop mid-flight and wait for the slowest CTA to finish writing. Device-wide synchronization also requires every CTA to be co-resident on the chip at once: as we saw in Primer 3, Sections 1, 3, and 7, each SM holds only a bounded number of CTA residency slots at once (for instance, v1 fits at most 16 CTAs per SM, so all 132 SMs hold 2,112 CTAs in the first batch while the remaining 192 wait in line outside); if SM residency slots cannot fit all CTAs simultaneously, queued CTAs outside cannot enter while resident CTAs on-chip wait forever for them to arrive, deadlocking both sides (see Chapter 2, Section 6 for deadlock-free cross-SM handoffs). In that case, keeping two separate kernels is usually better—and the next section shows how to overlap them partially.
    • Even the second fusible pattern above (letting the last finishing CTA do the work) can lose when the small wrap-up step could otherwise overlap early via the method in the next section (we weigh that case right after introducing it at the end of Section 4; see also Chapter 9, Section 6).

4Can the Next Kernel Start Before the Previous Kernel Finishes?

Yes. PDL permits the next kernel to land on SMs early to start reading weights, and wait until the previous kernel's writes are all visible before reading its output.

As we saw in Primer 2, Section 3, static weights don't depend on the activations from the previous step, so nothing stops you from reading them early. And in our three-kernel chain, the normalization kernel has only 1 CTA—while it runs, it occupies just 1 SM and leaves the other 131 SMs sitting idle (this chapter shows PDL only at the "normalization → gemv" boundary; its effect at the second boundary, "gemv → post-processing", and on the whole chain was not measured, so any gain there is unknown). In a standard CUDA stream, though, the hardware ties two things together: the next kernel (which we'll call the dependent kernel (successor)) can start dispatching only after the previous kernel (the primary kernel (predecessor)) has completely exited. Hopper (the H200 architecture) provides PDL (Programmatic Dependent Launch) to uncouple those two events in four steps (Figure 1-3):

  1. When launching the successor kernel, the CPU passes an extra launch attribute telling the GPU that the successor may dispatch before the predecessor finishes.
  2. Inside the predecessor, each CTA issues a trigger call after finishing its main loop and before writing back its output; once every predecessor CTA has triggered (or exited), the hardware may dispatch CTAs of the successor onto SMs with free resources (the specification permits early dispatch, though it does not guarantee it).
  3. Once a successor CTA lands on an SM, it starts with work that does not depend on the predecessor's output—at the "normalization → gemv" boundary, it fires off the first batch of weight reads for WW from HBM. Any bytes read before the wait call returns must sit in on-chip storage until xnx_n is ready (see Chapter 9, Section 4 for how a single layer prefetches weights), so how much you can prefetch is bounded by on-chip capacity.
  4. Right before reading the predecessor's output, the successor issues a wait call; once that call returns, the entire predecessor grid has finished executing and all of its global-memory writes are visible to the successor.

Here is who holds what—and what the trigger permits versus what the wait blocks—at the "normalization → gemv" boundary:

Unit What it holds What the trigger permits vs. what the wait blocks
Predecessor CTA (① normalization, 1 CTA) Main-loop reduction state and xnx_n (16 KiB) to write back Issues the trigger call after the main loop: only permits early dispatch of the successor while continuing to write xnx_n and exit
On-chip hardware dispatcher & 132 SMs Predecessor's 1 CTA (1 SM occupied, 131 SMs idle) and pending successor CTAs Once all predecessor CTAs have triggered (or exited), may place successor CTAs early onto SMs with free resources (permitted by spec, not guaranteed)
Successor CTAs (② gemv, 2,304 CTAs) Early-fetched initial weight chunks WpreW_{\text{pre}} staged on-chip (bounded by on-chip space) Once on an SM, issue xnx_n-independent reads of WW from HBM; blocked at the wait call before reading xnx_n, and read xnx_n plus remaining WW after it returns
Shared on-chip second-level cache & global memory HBM Static weights WW (37.75 MB) and predecessor output xnx_n (16 KiB) Serves pre-wait WW reads; when the wait call returns, the predecessor has fully exited and xnx_n is visible across all SMs in the shared on-chip cache 
// Predecessor: issue the trigger (placement: see below)
cudaTriggerProgrammaticLaunchCompletion();
// Successor: the CPU launches the successor through the launch API with the PDL launch attribute; the successor first issues reads that do not depend on the predecessor, then waits
cudaGridDependencySynchronize();   // read the predecessor's output only after this call returns

There is one hard rule here: in this chapter's pattern, code that reads the predecessor's output must be placed after the wait call. If you put a read before the wait call, the successor can silently read stale values left over from the previous replay with no runtime error at all. Likewise, until the wait call returns, the successor must not write into any buffer the predecessor might still be reading (our three-kernel chain does not run into this). Where you place the trigger call inside the predecessor only controls how early the successor can land on SMs; it does not change visibility (Chapter 9, Section 5 reproduces both the stale-read and write-conflict bugs in measured runs).

Why place the trigger call after the main loop (as in step 2 above) rather than right at function entry? If you place it right at function entry, successor CTAs may land on SMs while the predecessor's main loop is still running. On the attention-to-merge chains measured in Chapter 7, Section 11, triggering at function entry rather than after the main loop slowed the predecessor attention kernel by 0.07–1.65 µs—likely because successor CTAs co-scheduled onto the same SM sit blocked at the wait call and contend with the still-running predecessor CTAs (exact mechanism not verified). For a 1-CTA predecessor like the one in this chapter (whose single SM likewise has free resources where successor CTAs may co-reside), the difference between triggering at function entry and after the main loop was not measured.

Triggering early only slows you down, though—it can never deadlock. The hardware starts dispatching the successor only after every predecessor CTA has either triggered or exited. By that point, no predecessor CTA is still waiting in line outside for an SM slot, and every unfinished predecessor CTA is already resident on an SM running. Because no predecessor CTA is waiting for an SM, successor CTAs taking free slots can never starve the predecessor from finishing, so deadlock is impossible. Accordingly, both this chapter (step 2 above) and Chapter 7 place the trigger call after the predecessor's main loop finishes and right before its epilogue writeback.

On the timeline, PDL can save at most two pieces of time: the overlap between the successor's independent reads and the full window before visibility completes—the predecessor's epilogue plus the handoff gap—bounded by whichever of the two is shorter, plus any shortening of the handoff gap itself. We timed that handoff in a small test program built to measure just this one step (which we'll call a microbenchmark): in a 1-CTA test setup, we link two kernels with PDL and have the successor call wait right at entry, measuring ~0.64 µs per handoff. Take 0.64 µs only as the size of one PDL handoff in this minimal 1-CTA case, not as a time saving—a non-PDL baseline in that same microbenchmark is not in our data (unknown), and the 1.0 µs in Section 2 is a median per-node replay launch overhead on real SGLang inference graphs, so the two measure different quantities in separate tests and cannot be subtracted directly; how much PDL saves on this chapter's gemv chain was not measured.

Here is how the PDL trade-off works out:

  • What you gain: you allow the successor's predecessor-independent reads (such as prefetching static weights) to overlap with the predecessor's epilogue and handoff gap (early dispatch is permitted by the specification, not guaranteed; the latency change from enabling PDL on this gemv chain was not measured).
  • What it costs: in this chapter's pattern, the successor has to insert a wait call before its first read of the predecessor's data; if you accidentally put a read before the wait call, it can intermittently read stale values left over from the previous replay without any runtime error (see Chapter 9, Section 5 for measured reproductions of this bug).
  • When it loses: triggering too early at function entry while the predecessor's main loop is still running slowed the predecessor by 0.07–1.65 µs on our measured attention-to-merge chains (likely due to same-SM contention, mechanism not verified; see above and Chapter 7, Section 11).

With PDL in hand, the fusion loss case we deferred from Section 3 is clear too: even in Section 3's second fusible pattern (letting the last finishing CTA wrap up), if that small wrap-up kernel could otherwise enter early onto idle SMs via PDL when kept separate, folding it into the predecessor's epilogue forces it to wait behind the very last CTA of the predecessor, forfeiting its PDL early entry and running slower in measured runs (see Chapter 9, Section 6).

5gemv Evolution v1 → v2: Recording the Three-Kernel Chain into a Single CUDA Graph

When both are timed with commands pre-queued in the stream, full-graph replay (v2, 60.0 µs) runs about 1.6 µs faster than standard stream launch of the exact same v1 code (61.6 µs); compared against CPU one-by-one launch of v1 from an empty queue (102.6 µs), the two steps together save about 42.6 µs (about 1.7× faster, including about 41 µs from eliminating CPU queue wait), while each individual kernel's runtime is unchanged.

In this step we make only the launch change shown in Section 2's snippet—replacing the three standard stream launches with a single cudaGraphLaunch(graph_exec, stream)—while the machine code of the three kernels running on the GPU is byte-for-byte identical to v1. We use the same timing setup as in Primer 3, Section 5, except now the GPU events bracket the entire three-kernel chain (Row 3 of Figure 1-1 is v2). To keep straight which part comes from v1 → v2 itself, the table below lines up all three runs shown in the first chart—notice that Rows 1 and 2 run the exact same v1 three-launch stream code and differ only in whether the stream queue starts empty at t=0; only the step from Row 2 to Row 3 is the isolated v1 → v2 change:
