1. CPU one-by-one launch v1 (3 standard stream launches) Empty (synchronized before timer) 102.6 µs — Baseline: includes initial + ①→② CPU launch waits + two hardware handoffs
2. Pre-filled command queue v1 (same 3 standard stream launches) All 3 commands pre-queued at t<0 61.6 µs (61.63 µs single-machine) −41.0 µs-41.0\ \text{µs} (~1.67×1.67\times faster) Removes both empty-queue CPU launch waits; both hardware handoffs stay

Look at the first chart below: stepping from Bar 1 to Bar 2 saves ~41 µs by pre-filling the queue, while stepping from Bar 2 to Bar 3 saves the additional ~1.6 µs isolated to v1 → v2 full-graph replay when both are pre-queued. Section 2 covered what you pay to use CUDA Graph.

Now look at the second evolution-chain chart below: when we time gemv_kernel by itself (two-H200 pooled medians, differing slightly from the single-machine 54.18 µs in Section 3), the 0.11 µs difference between v2 (54.19 µs) and v1 (54.08 µs) sits well inside measurement noise—the single-kernel runtime hasn't budged at all. That is our starting point for the next chapter.

Takeaway: The dead time between adjacent kernels comes from two places—the CPU falling behind on launches, and the hardware waiting for every CTA of the previous kernel to exit and make its writes visible to all SMs; CUDA Graph eliminates the first between nodes inside the graph, while when both runs are timed pre-queued in the stream full-graph replay on this chain is also ~1.6 µs faster (source not determined), kernel fusion cuts down how often you pay the second, and PDL allows the second to overlap in time with useful static-weight reads (latency change on this chain not measured).

Next chapter's question: Even after we strip away every gap between kernels, gemv_kernel by itself still takes 54.08 µs—nearly 7× slower than the 7.86 µs bandwidth lower bound. Its 2,304 CTAs already fill all 132 SMs, so where is all that time going?

In Chapter 1, we squeezed out the gaps between kernels, yet the runtime of a single gemv_kernel itself did not budge. Now let's open up that kernel and zoom in to Level 2: the full H200 chip.

The 2,304 CTAs of v1 already fill all 132 SMs, yet gemv takes 54.08 µs while the lower bound for reading WW once is only 7.86 µs—looking at the full chip, where does all that extra time go?

Throughout this chapter, we'll trace gemv_kernel from v1 / v2: weights W:[2304,8192]BF16\shape{W}{2304,\;8192}{BF16}, input x:[8192]BF16\shape{x}{8192}{BF16}, output y:[2304]FP32\shape{y}{2304}{FP32}, launched with <<<2304, 128>>>.

1How Are CTAs Distributed Across 132 SMs, and Why Does the Final Batch Hold Back the Entire Kernel?

The whole GPU can hold at most 2,112 resident CTAs at once; the remaining 192 CTAs have to wait for slots to free up and then walk all 64 serial load iterations from scratch.

The GPU hardware dispatches work to the 132 SMs in units of CTAs (see Primer 3, Section 1). Each SM has a cap on how many CTAs it can keep resident at once, and for v1 that cap is 16 (we'll work out why in Chapter 3, Section 1). Across all 132 SMs, the whole GPU can hold at most 132×16=2,112 resident CTAs at the same time.

We call that device-wide concurrent CTA capacity (wave size) 1 wave. Keep in mind that a wave is the on-chip capacity at any moment, not a batch that has to finish in lockstep before the next batch starts: as soon as one CTA finishes and exits, the next pending CTA immediately takes the slot it freed.

Now pack v1's 2,304 CTAs into a chip capacity of 2,112: 2,304=2,112+192. The first batch of 2,112 CTAs starts together, and because every CTA in v1 does the exact same amount of work, all 2,112 finish and exit at almost the same moment. Only then do the remaining 192 CTAs step into the freed slots and start computing. This final partial batch of less than 1 wave is the tail (tail wave), with remainder r=192 (Figure 2-1).

From the whole-chip view, v1's total runtime looks like two 64-iteration serial load chains laid end to end: the 2,112 CTAs of wave 1 walk the first 64-iteration chain, and the 192 tail-wave CTAs immediately walk a second 64-iteration chain of the exact same length from scratch. Throughout the tail wave, only 192 of the 2,112 device-wide slots are active (~9%) while the other ~90% sit empty, yet the entire kernel cannot finish until those last 192 CTAs complete all 64 iterations. Why not change the CTA shape so all 2,304 rows fit into a single wave right away (v6 in Chapter 3, Section 4 shrinks each CTA to 1 warp to eliminate the tail wave, and ends up slower)? Answering that needs the per-SM residency and bytes-in-flight budget, which we work out in Chapter 3, Section 4.

Why does each CTA have to walk all 64 iterations serially? Look inside a single CTA's loop: in iteration jj (j=0..63), its 128 consecutive threads read consecutive 2 B elements along the row—1 element W[row,k]W[\text{row}, k] and 1 element x[k]x[k] per thread (128×2 B=256 B of WW across the CTA per iteration)—and multiply-add into each thread's private FP32 register accumulator acc; sweeping across one row of 8,192 columns takes 8,192/128=64 iterations, after which the 128 threads write their acc values into shared memory (__shared__ float smem[128], 512 B), synchronize with __syncthreads(), and have thread 0 sum all 128 partial sums and write one 4 B output y[row] (see Primer 3, Sections 1 and 3 for the full code and intra-CTA reduction). The catch is that every iteration has to wait for its loaded data to return before the next iteration can start, because a thread issues its instructions in order (in-order issue). In v1's compiled loop, the next iteration's load sits behind the current iteration's multiply-add, and that multiply-add stalls until the current iteration's data comes back from global memory. As a result, each thread has only 1 read of WW (2 B) in flight at any moment (see Chapter 4, Section 2 for how in-order issue works).

A CPU core hides that wait with out-of-order execution and hardware prefetching, whereas each GPU warp issues strictly in order and the SM switches to other warps while one waits (whether the H200 has hardware prefetching was not measured); each thread keeps only 1 read of 2 B of WW in flight per iteration, and Section 3 works out why that is far too little to keep memory busy.

Which 192 CTAs end up in the tail wave? Direct answer: placing the highest-numbered CTAs in the tail wave is an extrapolated inference, not a direct measurement on this kernel—the CUDA specification makes no guarantee about CTA dispatch order, and v1 was not timestamped directly. The ascending direction comes solely from an observation on another kernel: on the H200, when we instrumented a 132-CTA PDL-chained kernel (see Chapter 1, Section 4) in Chapter 8 with the chip-wide global nanosecond timer %globaltimer (whose readings across SMs carry no strict synchronization guarantee; see Chapter 10, Section 5 for usage and caveats), CTA 131 began about 2.0–3.2 µs after CTAs numbered below 100 in measurement—consistent with ascending blockIdx.x dispatch. Section 7 tests this direction against the measured runtime after tail splitting (ruling out mixed dispatch orders, while correctness never depends on dispatch order—order affects only how much time is saved).

2How Long Does One Read Take to Return from HBM to an SM, and Why Does xx Not Need to Be Read 2,304 Times from HBM?

An unloaded HBM read round trip takes about 0.33 µs, whereas hitting the device-wide L2 cache takes about 0.18 µs; WW streams from HBM while xx stays in cache for reuse.

Figure 2-2 traces the memory path from off-chip memory into the compute units. On the outside sits off-chip HBM (High Bandwidth Memory, rated bandwidth 4.8 TB/s; see Primer 1, Section 4), one step onto the die sits the on-chip L2 cache (shared across all 132 SMs, 60 MiB total capacity), and inside each SM sit the L1 cache (each SM's private level-1 cache), shared memory, and registers (we'll unpack their capacities and details in Chapter 3, Section 1).

A default global memory read checks the local SM's L1 first; if the data isn't there, it checks the device-wide L2. If the data is sitting in L2 (a cache hit), L2 hands it straight back to the SM; if it isn't in L2 either (a cache miss), the request goes off-chip to HBM, pulls the data back through L2, and delivers it to the SM. In this section we focus on those outer two levels, L2 and HBM; keep in mind that L2 is the only cache level shared across all SMs, a fact we'll rely on again in Section 6 for cross-SM merging.

To measure the round-trip latency from issuing a read to getting the data back in a register, we first set a hardware time unit: the clock cycle, one tick of the local SM clock (in code, clock64() reads a per-SM counter that increments on every tick of that SM's clock, corresponding to PTX %clock64; see Appendix B). Tracing one read from off-chip memory all the way into a register, the table below maps what each hardware unit along the path holds or does in v1 (and in later steps), its unloaded round-trip latency where measured, and the basis of each fact (see Appendix D, Section 1 for the topology summary):

Path unit What it holds or does in v1 and later steps Unloaded round-trip latency (at ~1.8 GHz) Epistemic label
Off-chip HBM (4.8 TB/s rated) Holds weights WW (37.75 MB, read once per launch, ~0% L2 hit) and input xx (16 KiB, read once on the initial chip-wide cold fill; final output y is written to global memory via L2) 600.2 clock cycles (~600 cycles, 0.334 µs ≈ 0.33 µs) Rated peak documented; unloaded cycles measured on H200
HBM partitions (FBPA in the profiler) Multiple memory controllers between L2 and DRAM across which physical addresses spread to aggregate device-wide HBM bandwidth (Chapter 10, Section 5 returns here when buffer-address shifts perturb runtime) Included in the 600.2-cycle HBM round trip above (not isolated) Controller role documented; address mapping rule unpublished, and active count on H200 and address mapping not measured
Two L2 partitions & LTC Fabric (60 MiB shared total) Only cache shared across all 132 SMs, split into two L2 partitions joined by the L2 interconnect (LTC Fabric in the profiler) and preferentially serving SMs connected to each partition: serves the ~6% of xx reads that miss L1 in v1 (~100% hit after cold fill), and holds partial sums part and atomic counters cnt during the v3 cross-SM merge in Sections 6 and 7 327.8 clock cycles (~328 cycles, 0.182 µs ≈ 0.18 µs; serving partition unrecorded) Two-partition + LTC Fabric topology documented; 327.8 cycles measured on H200; near-vs.-far partition split on H200 not measured
Partitioned crossbar (XBAR in the profiler) On-chip packet switch connecting all 132 SMs to the two L2 partitions, carrying L1-miss requests, global writes, and Section 6 cross-SM atomics from source units to target L2 partitions and returning data to SMs (the profiler reports separate utilization rows for the L1-to-XBAR request interface and the XBAR-to-L1 return path) Included in the L2 / HBM round trips (not isolated) Packet routing and two interface rows documented; per-stage latency and arbitration order not measured
Per-SM private L1 cache & shared memory (L1TEX together in the profiler) Private to each SM and not hardware-coherent across SMs: directly serves ~94% of xx reads (measured by the profiler on v3, which reads xx in the same pattern as v1), while shared memory holds the 512 B smem reduction buffer; the cross-SM handoff in Section 6 invalidates the local SM's L1 (empirically observed, not a spec guarantee) Deferred to Chapter 3, Section 1 (measured cycle count given there) Per-SM privacy documented; ~94% xx hit rate measured on v3 (v1 not profiled separately); local-SM L1 invalidation in Section 6's cross-SM handoff empirically observed (not a spec guarantee)
Per-SM registers Hold each thread's loaded 2 B elements and private FP32 accumulator acc (4 B) right beside the execution units for multiply-add 0 cache round trips (capacity and allocation granularity in Chapter 3, Section 1) Documented

Converting unloaded clock cycles to time at about 1.8 GHz (about 0.56 ns per cycle; 1.7964 GHz in the recorded constants table) puts a cold HBM read and an L2 hit at about 0.33 µs and 0.18 µs (see the chart below).

With those numbers in hand, we can answer both questions left open in Primer 3. First, during a single kernel execution, every element of the weight matrix WW (37.75 MB) is read only once by one CTA, so it gets no L2 cache hits. In real inference, that same WW is not read again until the next forward pass; between the two passes, about 9.0 GB of fixed weights (see Primer 1, Section 4) stream through the 60 MiB L2 and evict the previous pass's WW well beforehand, which is why flushing the on-chip cache before timing matches real execution (see Primer 3, Section 5).

Second, the input vector xx is only 16 KiB—a tiny fraction of the 60 MiB L2 cache. From capacity alone, we can infer that once the first batch of CTAs reads xx for the first time and pulls it from HBM into L2, later reads of xx by CTAs on the same SM mostly hit in that SM's L1, and the rest hit in L2 (in profiler measurements on v3, which reads xx in the exact same pattern as v1, about 94% of xx reads hit directly in the local SM's L1, and the remaining about 6% that reach L2 hit nearly 100% of the time apart from the initial cold fill; v1 was not profiled separately).

Now plug those latencies back into the serial load chain from Section 1. In each loop iteration of v1, every thread issues one read of WW (from HBM) and one read of xx (hitting in L1 or L2) at the same time, so the wait per iteration is roughly one HBM round trip. Multiplying by the 0.33 µs unloaded round-trip latency puts a 64-iteration serial chain at about 64×0.33≈21 μs, which Section 7 will use as the reference for estimating tail-wave duration. Two serial chains back to back come to about 42 µs, and adding 4.6 µs of fixed overhead gives about 47 µs, about 7 µs shy of v1's measured 54.08 µs. This rough model is only meant to capture the order of magnitude: the actual durations of the two waves were not measured directly with timestamps (Section 7 bounds both waves from the runtime difference between v1 and v3, while why each iteration runs slower than unloaded was not measured).

3How Many Bytes Must Each SM Keep in Flight Simultaneously to Saturate HBM?

When all SMs read concurrently, round-trip time grows with bytes in flight (an upper bound estimated via Little's Law); keeping about 24–40 KiB in flight per SM (with 16 B wide loads, varying with how many loads each thread issues back to back) reaches 95% of the bandwidth plateau, and 64 KiB exceeds 98% (enough, not the minimum), whereas v1 keeps only 4.0 KiB in flight.

The bytes that an SM has requested from memory but has not yet received are called bytes in flight. Little's Law ties bytes in flight, bandwidth, and round-trip latency together:

bytes in flight=bandwidth×round-trip latency\text{bytes in flight} = \text{bandwidth} \times \text{round-trip latency}

In plain terms, for an SM to claim its full share of memory bandwidth, the bytes it keeps in flight at once have to cover an entire round trip.

Let's work out how high that target is. When all 132 SMs stream continuously from HBM, they reach a measured bandwidth plateau (the flat region where adding more bytes in flight no longer raises bandwidth) of about 4.50–4.55 TB/s (highest median 4.548 TB/s), or about 34 GB/s per SM. If we plugged the unloaded 0.33 µs round trip from Section 2 straight into Little's Law, it would look as if each SM needed only 34 GB/s×0.33 μs≈11 KiB in flight.

When the whole chip reads together, though, the story changes. We ran a dedicated bandwidth-sweep microbenchmark streaming 4 GiB from HBM across all 132 SMs (not gemv), verified in compiled machine code so that every resident thread issues all KK wide 16 B loads (see Chapter 3, Section 3) before consuming the first returned value; counted in machine code, peak bytes in flight per SM therefore equal "resident threads × KK × 16 B" (whether the memory subsystem accepts all KK loads at once is unknown). Under a very light load (1 warp per SM at K=1, or 0.5 KiB/SM), dividing peak bytes in flight by measured bandwidth gives an estimated upper bound on mean round-trip time of about 0.39 µs, close to the 0.33 µs unloaded round trip. At 16 KiB per SM, however, device-wide bandwidth spans 2.85–3.89 TB/s across K=1..16 (3.89 TB/s at K=1, about 86% of the plateau, and 3.41 TB/s at K=4, or 75.1%; see the chart below), pushing the peak-count Little's Law upper bound on mean round-trip time up to about 0.56–0.76 µs (about 1.7–2.3× the 0.33 µs unloaded round trip). Where along the memory path that extra time is spent was not measured.

Follow the chart to the right: reaching 95% of the bandwidth plateau takes 24 KiB per SM at 1 wide 16 B load per thread (K=1, where the peak-count upper bound on mean round-trip time is about 0.75 µs), and 28–40 KiB per SM when each thread issues 2–16 wide loads back to back (see Chapter 4, Section 3; reaching 98% takes 36–56 KiB/SM for K=2..16; why the knee rises with KK and what the time-averaged bytes in flight are were not measured). By 64 KiB per SM, every tested series reaches at least 98.3% of its plateau—so 64 KiB is enough, not the minimum. Pushing beyond 64 KiB adds less than 2% bandwidth while the bytes in flight÷bandwidth ratio (an estimated upper bound on mean round-trip time computed from peak bytes in flight, not a directly measured latency) grows in proportion: about 1.9 µs at 64 KiB/SM (about 6× the unloaded 0.33 µs) and about 3.8 µs at 128 KiB/SM. Which segment of Section 2's memory path (L1TEX → XBAR → L2 partition & LTC Fabric → HBM partition FBPA → HBM) accounts for that extra wait was not measured; queueing along that path is the common explanation.

Put that curve next to v1 and the second reason v1 is slow jumps right out. Keeping more bytes in flight per SM comes down to the product "resident threads × loads in flight per thread × bytes per load": wave 1 of v1 already fills all 2,048 resident threads that a single SM can hold (see Chapter 3, Section 1; resident threads stay below that cap only when an SM is under-filled, as in the tail wave or in v6 in Chapter 3, Section 4), so you cannot add more threads—pushing v1 higher relies on widening each load from 2 B to 16 B (see Chapter 3, Section 3) and having each thread issue multiple loads at once (see Chapter 4, Section 3). In v1, each thread keeps only one 2 B read of WW in flight per iteration, so 1 CTA (128 threads) has just 128×2 B=256 B in flight, and all 16 CTAs on 1 SM add up to only 4.0 KiB (Figure 2-3)—falling short of even the leftmost 8 KiB bar on the chart and sitting about 6× below the smallest measured 95% knee (24 KiB/SM at one 16 B load per thread; the bandwidth curve for 2 B loads per thread was not measured):

Configuration Resident threads Loads in flight / thread Bytes / load Bytes in flight (per SM or chip-wide)
16 B sweep K=1 95% knee (microbenchmark) 12×128 / SM (12 CTAs) 1 16 B 24 KiB/SM (4.34 TB/s chip-wide, 95.4% of plateau)
v1 wave 1 (2,112 full-row CTAs) 16×128=2,048 / SM (at cap) 1 2 B (reading WW) 4.0 KiB/SM (~1/6 of 24 KiB knee; 2 B curve not measured)
v1 tail wave (192 full-row CTAs) 192×128 chip-wide (~9% of 2,112 slots) 1 2 B (reading WW) 48 KiB chip-wide

Put Section 1 and this section side by side: Section 1 counted how many steps are in the serial load chain, while this section measures how busy each step keeps HBM. Because v1 keeps only 4.0 KiB in flight per SM—nowhere near the bandwidth plateau—the device-wide read load is light, which is why the rough model in Section 2 could estimate using near-unloaded round-trip latency (v1's per-iteration round-trip latency was not measured directly). Pushing concurrent loads per SM from 4.0 KiB up into the tens-of-KiB range needed to saturate HBM (Chapter 3 first widens each load to reach 32 KiB, and Chapter 4 then has each thread issue multiple loads at once), along with budgeting the registers and on-chip memory needed to hold those bytes, waits until Chapter 3 opens a single SM. At this chapter's whole-chip level, what we can change is the chip-wide grid partitioning and the shared L2 cache, so Sections 5–7 first cut the 192 tail-wave CTAs' 64-iteration chain in half; right before that, Section 4 closes the cache question from Section 2: can we tell L2 to keep the reused xx and evict the single-use WW first?

4Can We Tell L2 Which Data to Keep?

Yes. With a clean L2, tagging single-use streaming data as evict-first and reused data as evict-last preserves reused data when streaming traffic would otherwise evict it, whereas it only adds overhead when that data would not be evicted anyway (see Chapter 10, Section 2 for behavior under a dirty L2).

In Section 2, we inferred from capacity that the 16 KiB vector xx stays inside the 60 MiB L2 cache. While gemv runs, though, 37.75 MB of single-use weights WW also stream through L2—could that stream evict the data we want to reuse? Left to itself, the L2 hardware has no way of knowing which data will be read again shortly and which data is use-once-and-discard. When a large stream of single-use data pours through L2, it can evict data that later CTAs still need to re-read.

To override that default behavior, we construct a 64-bit L2 residency hint (cache policy) descriptor with PTX createpolicy (see Appendix B for the full syntax) and attach it to each load instruction: tag single-use streaming data with evict_first (telling L2 to evict it first when space runs tight), and tag data re-read repeatedly across CTAs with evict_last (telling L2 to keep it until last if possible); PTX loads and stores can also carry lightweight cache operators directly—default .ca caches in both L1 and L2, streaming .cs (or explicit L1::evict_first) marks both L1 and L2 evict-first, and .cg bypasses the local SM's private L1 to go straight to L2 (all of these are performance hints only, so cross-SM synchronization still requires the memory-ordering rules in Section 6; see Appendix B for remaining operators such as .lu and .cv).

When does this actually pay off? Look at a standalone microbenchmark (Figure 2-4): first read in 8–32 MB of data to be reused (Figure 2-4 uses 32 MB as the example), then stream through 64 MB of single-use data—more than the 60 MiB L2 can hold—and finally re-read the reused data from the first step. When we tag the two reads evict_last and evict_first, the re-read runs at 5.70–7.33 TB/s, matching 98.8%–100% of the interference-free rate (which implies, from the bandwidth ratio, that nearly all of the reused data remained in L2), or 1.7–1.9× cold HBM. Note that 5.70–7.33 TB/s here is only the re-read rate inside this launch-overhead-inclusive microbenchmark—used to compare retention against the interference-free baseline—and not the hardware bandwidth ceiling of L2 (L2 peak bandwidth is unpublished and was not measured separately in this book). Without those hints (leaving both reads at default eviction priority), re-read bandwidth falls to 3.36–4.19 TB/s—only 5%–7% above cold HBM (3.16–3.91 TB/s), indicating that most of the reused data was evicted from L2.

Here is how the L2 residency hint (cache policy) trade-off works out:

  • What you gain: keeps reused data in L2 when heavy streaming traffic would otherwise evict it (see the microbenchmark numbers above).
  • What it costs: you build the two residency-hint descriptors with PTX createpolicy (the compiler hoists descriptor construction out of the loop; the syntax and this hoisting come from the hinted gemv variant v4 in Section 7, while the retention microbenchmark's source is not archived) and pass one on every load, adding extra hint-passing instructions in the loop and making the code more verbose.
  • When it loses: under a clean L2, when the reused data would not be evicted anyway, the extra hints only add descriptor and hint-passing cost without saving time (Section 7 verifies this on gemv; see Chapter 10, Section 2 for the contrasting speedup when tagging WW as evict_first under a dirty L2 write flush).

Beyond per-instruction createpolicy hints, CUDA also provides host-configured L2 residency control (CUDA Programming Guide Section 4.15; not measured on H200 in this book)—conclusion first: just like instruction-level hints, a host set-aside window cannot hold about 9.0 GB of model weights per forward pass (about 143× the 60 MiB L2 cache) either. To use it, host code first calls cudaDeviceSetLimit(cudaLimitPersistingL2CacheSize, ...) to carve out an L2 set-aside region up to persistingL2CacheMaxSize (disabled in MIG mode), then attaches a cudaAccessPolicyWindow to a stream or CUDA Graph kernel node—specifying a contiguous global-memory range smaller than accessPolicyMaxWindowSize, a target hitRatio, a persisting hit property, and a streaming miss property—to keep up to tens of MiB of hot data in the set-aside region across kernels; because persisting lines can remain in L2 long after a kernel exits, call cudaCtxResetPersistingL2Cache() afterward or before benchmarking to reset them to normal priority (under that section's rule that normal or streaming accesses use the set-aside region only while persisting accesses leave it unused, we infer that a normal read flush may leave persisting lines behind).

5When Only a Few CTAs Remain in the Tail Wave, How Can More SMs Compute the Same Row Together?

Partitioning a row along the reduction dimension KK across multiple CTAs and merging is called Split-K; splitting only the tail-wave rows in half is called K-halves, where each half-row runs only 32 iterations.

Back in Section 1, we saw the bottleneck: the tail wave has only 192 CTAs, yet each one still has to grind through all 64 serial load iterations while ~90% of the chip's slots sit idle. Since one row's inner product is just a sum of 8,192 terms, we can slice it straight in half along KK:

y[row]=∑k=04095W[row,k]xk⏟first half+∑k=40968191W[row,k]xk⏟second halfy[\text{row}] = \underbrace{\sum_{k=0}^{4095} W[\text{row},k]\,x_k}_{\text{first half}} + \underbrace{\sum_{k=4096}^{8191} W[\text{row},k]\,x_k}_{\text{second half}}

Those two halves don't depend on each other at all: we can hand them to two CTAs on two different SMs to compute in parallel, each producing one partial sum, and then add the two partial sums together.

When does splitting only the tail wave in half fit without spilling into another wave? The no-overflow condition for S=2 is straightforward: the tail-wave remainder rr must be at most half of 1 wave capacity (r≤2,112/2=1,056). As long as that condition holds, splitting rr rows into 2r2r half-row CTAs packs all 2r2r CTAs into the slots that were sitting empty during the tail wave, without overflowing into an extra wave. We call splitting only the tail-wave rows in half K-halves (tail-wave half splitting). In v1, r=192, so splitting in half gives 2r=384≤1,056, well within the 1-wave capacity. With that cut, each half-row CTA's serial load chain drops from 64 iterations to 32 iterations, and device-wide bytes in flight during the tail wave double at the same time (384 CTAs instead of 192; Mode 2 in Figure 2-5).

Mapping that cut onto gemv's grid indices (placing the half-row CTAs at the end under the ascending dispatch order inferred in Section 1; the full source for the exact blockIdx.x-to-(i, half) expression is not included) splits all 2,496 CTAs across two roles:

CTA index range Assigned rows & columns Serial iterations Where output is written
0..2111 (2,112 full-row CTAs) Rows 0..2111, full row of 8,192 columns (16 KiB of WW) 64 iterations Directly writes y[row] (FP32, 4 B)
2112..2495 (384 half-row CTAs) Rows 2112..2303 (i = 0..191), half ∈ {0, 1} sweeping 4,096 columns each (8 KiB of WW) 32 iterations Writes part[2 * i + half] (FP32, 4 B), then merges into y[row] (Section 6)

Generalize that idea to the whole grid and you get Split-K: whenever you have too few output rows or output tiles to fill even 1 wave capacity, slice the reduction dimension KK into SS pieces so SS CTAs team up on the same output, multiplying the total CTA count by SS (see Chapter 5, Sections 7–8 for Split-K on multi-token GEMM, and Chapter 6, Section 8 for measured results along the evolution chain).

Why split only the 192 tail-wave rows on gemv instead of halving all 2,304 rows? Splitting every row forces every row to pay for partial-sum writes and a cross-SM merge, while any half-row CTAs beyond 1 wave capacity (2,112 CTAs) still have to wait in the queue for freed slots (Section 1); a full-grid S=2 split was not measured on gemv.

Here is how the Split-K and K-halves trade-off works out:

  • What you gain: K-halves cuts each tail-wave CTA's serial load chain in half (from 64 iterations to 32) and doubles device-wide bytes in flight during the tail wave (see Section 7 for the measured speedup).
  • What it costs: each split row writes two 4 B partial sums (8 B total) and needs one extra cross-SM merge, and the grid's block-index mapping gets more complex. In the Section 6 microbenchmark, one cross-SM handoff takes ~0.67 µs; we did not measure the wait-free merge in v3 on its own.
  • When it loses: if the tail remainder rr exceeds half a wave, splitting in half spills into another wave; more generally, crossing the 1-wave capacity boundary 192×S>2,112 (for example, S=12 with 2,304 slice-CTAs spills into an extra wave of ⌈64/S⌉\lceil 64 / S \rceil iterations compared with S=11 at 2,112 slice-CTAs in a single wave), or splitting so finely that extra partial-sum writes and merge overhead outweigh the shorter load chain, erodes the gain. Splitting beyond S=2 was not measured on gemv; separately, on a multi-token expert kernel in Chapter 8, Section 3 (distinct from single-wave overflow here), splitting into 4 slices measured slower than splitting into 2 (the specific cause was not measured separately).

6When Two SMs Each Compute Half a Row, How Do They Add Them Together Safely?

After writing its partial sum, each half-row CTA performs an atomic add on an L2 counter, and the last arriver (receiving old value 1) sums both halves; the two CTAs need not be co-resident on the chip.

First, why does the handoff have to go through L2? Because each SM's L1 cache is private to that SM, and the hardware does not automatically keep L1 caches coherent across different SMs. As we saw in Section 2, L2 is the only cache level shared by all SMs. With the global memory accesses we use in this chapter, cross-SM data exchange can only meet in the central L2 cache.

Second, how do the two CTAs decide who does the addition? That is the job of an atomic add: hardware fuses "read the old value, add the new value, and write back to memory" into a single indivisible operation so no other thread can slip in between, and hands back the old value from before the add. As soon as each half-row CTA finishes its partial sum, it does an atomic add of 1 on the same zero-initialized counter (int32, 4 B): the first one there (the first arriver) gets old value 0 and exits on the spot; the second one to reach the counter (the last arriver) receives old value 1, sees that its partner has already checked in, and adds the two halves together.

An atomic add by itself, though, is still not enough. Even though the first arriver writes its partial sum part before adding 1 to the counter in the source code, without memory-ordering constraints the CUDA memory model does not guarantee that another SM will see the new value of part before it sees the new value of the counter. On the hardware, the counter update can beat part to L2, or the last arriver can hit a stale line sitting in its own SM's L1 cache.

Before we look at the code, let's put the three memory orderings in plain language:

  • relaxed: guarantees only that the atomic operation itself is indivisible, without constraining the order of other reads and writes before or after it.
  • release: orders all prior reads and writes by this thread before this write; as long as the memory scope (see below) covers both threads, those prior writes become visible to any thread that observes this write via an acquire read.
  • acquire: keeps any subsequent reads and writes by this thread from being reordered ahead of this read.

Combining release and acquire gives acq_rel. You might wonder: the first arriver only needs release and the last arriver only needs acquire, so why do both write acq_rel? Because both half-row CTAs execute the exact same fetch_add instruction and learn whether they arrived first or last only from the returned old value (0 or 1), that single instruction must provide release for the first arriver and acquire for the last arriver. Every synchronization on a GPU also carries a memory scope (scope)—such as within a CTA, across the whole GPU (device), or across the whole system. Smaller scopes are cheaper in hardware, so you normally specify the smallest scope that covers the communicating threads (if omitted, CUDA C++ atomic types default to system scope). Here the two half-row CTAs can be dispatched to any two SMs on the GPU, so the scope must be at least device (device-wide scope, written thread_scope_device in CUDA C++; Figure 2-6 compares the cross-SM handoff path under both memory orderings).

Unlike common CPUs that keep per-core caches coherent in hardware, per-SM private L1 caches on a GPU are not automatically coherent, and unsynchronized normal (weak) reads and writes can reorder all four pairs—read-read, read-write, write-write, and write-read (unlike relaxed atomics, which still guarantee a single modification order on the same address).

#include <cuda/atomic>
// tail_store (last-arriver merge): thread 0 runs this after the intra-CTA reduction (a __syncthreads() precedes it)
// i = row index within the tail wave (0..191); half = 0 for the first half, 1 for the second half
part[2 * i + half] = sum;                                   // write this half-row's partial sum
cuda::atomic_ref<int, cuda::thread_scope_device> c(cnt[i]);
if (c.fetch_add(1, cuda::memory_order_acq_rel) == 1) {      // got old value 1: I am the last arriver
    y[row] = part[2 * i] + part[2 * i + 1];
    c.store(0, cuda::memory_order_relaxed);                 // used again only by the next launch
}

Four connected rules tie every step of tail_store together:

  1. Cumulativity: When a thread executes a release, it publishes not only its own writes, but also any writes from other threads that it already observed before that release through an acquire or an intra-CTA barrier. That lets a synchronization chain pass the baton hop by hop, and each hop only needs a scope wide enough to cover the two threads at that hop. Say thread A writes data and hands it to thread B in the same CTA across an intra-CTA barrier; when B then does a device-scope release and thread C on another SM does a paired device-scope acquire, C is guaranteed to see A's write. If the B→C hop used only CTA scope, the chain would snap right at that hop.
  2. Intra-CTA merge to thread 0: In tail_store, only thread 0 writes the single scalar part and does the atomic add. Even when many threads in a CTA each write their own partial sums (as in Section 8), we still don't need every thread to do an atomic add: run one __syncthreads() first (see Primer 3, Section 3) and let thread 0 do a single release; by cumulativity from step 1, that publishes every prior write from the entire CTA at once.
  3. Cross-SM pairing: The first arriver's release and the last arriver's acquire act on the exact same counter cnt[i]. The atomic read-modify-write chain on that counter passes the first arriver's release straight to the last arriver's acquire, so the two take effect by paired synchronization and guarantee under the memory-model specification that the part written by the first arriver is visible to the last arriver (its hardware behavior and cycle cost on this GPU are covered in the hardware cost ledger below).
  4. Counter reset: Once the last arriver adds the two halves and writes y[row], resetting cnt[i] back to 0 only needs relaxed—the counter won't be touched again until the next kernel launch, and kernel completion in between already provides a stream-order boundary (see Chapter 1, Section 1).

Matching Figure 2-6, the table below then maps out every step of tail_store—which SM runs it, where the data sits, the memory order and scope, the cycle count, and the basis of each claim (say the first-half CTA runs on SM A and arrives first, while the second-half CTA runs on SM B and arrives second; how cnt[] is zeroed before the very first launch is not included in the code snippet):

Step SM & actor Operation Where the data sits Order tag & scope Clock cycles / latency Basis label
Intra-CTA reduction precondition SM A, SM B (all 128 threads → thread 0) All 128 threads write acc into smem[128], synchronize via __syncthreads(), and thread 0 sums them into sum Register acc → per-SM shared memory (512 B) → thread 0 register sum (FP32, 4 B) CTA-scope barrier Not measured separately in v1 / v3 Normative rule (Primer 3, Section 3)
Step 1: write partial sum SM A thread 0 (part[2i]); SM B thread 0 (part[2i+1]) part[2 * i + half] = sum Thread 0 register → global memory (via shared central L2; 4 B FP32 each, 8 B total) Normal weak store (published by Step 2 release) 1 global store instruction (counted as the pending write ahead of Step 2) Normative rule (published via Rule 1 cumulativity above in Step 2)
Step 2: first arriver checks in & exits SM A thread 0 (first arriver) c.fetch_add(1, acq_rel) routes across the on-chip crossbar XBAR to the L2 partition holding cnt[i], increments cnt[i] from 0 to 1, gets old value 0, and exits immediately without waiting cnt[i] (int32, 4 B, round trip via XBAR) in shared central L2 partition acq_rel, device (thread_scope_device) See hardware cost ledger below (not measured inside v3) Cross-SM paired visibility normative rule; release wait for prior write to reach L2 inferred from the memory model
Step 3: last arriver checks in & sees partner done SM B thread 0 (last arriver) c.fetch_add(1, acq_rel) increments cnt[i] from 1 to 2 and gets old value 1 cnt[i] (4 B) in shared central L2; whole private L1 on SM B invalidated upon return acq_rel, device (thread_scope_device) See hardware cost ledger below (reload after atomic add not measured) Pairing with first arriver's release normative rule; local-SM private L1 invalidation empirically observed on this GPU (not a spec guarantee)
Step 4: read back, sum, & write output SM B thread 0 (last arriver) Bypasses invalidated L1 on SM B to read part[2i] and part[2i+1] from central L2, sums them, and writes y[row] Shared L2 (two part slots, 8 B) → SM B registers → global memory y[row] (FP32, 4 B, via L2) Normal loads and store (ordered after Step 3 acquire) Unloaded L2 hit 327.8 cycles (~328 cycles, ~0.18 µs; Section 7 models total merge m≈0.60+0.18=0.78 μs, not measured inside v3) Ordering after acquire normative rule; unloaded L2 hit cycles measured (Section 2); mm derived in model
Step 5: reset counter SM B thread 0 (last arriver) c.store(0, relaxed) resets cnt[i] back to 0 for the next kernel launch cnt[i] (4 B) in shared central L2 relaxed, device Not measured separately Normative rule (kernel completion provides a stream-order boundary between launches; Chapter 1, Section 1)

Notice a crucial property of this "last arriver merges" pattern: it never requires the two CTAs to be co-resident on the chip. The first arriver exits right after its atomic add without waiting on anyone, and the last arriver simply reads and sums both halves when it gets there. No matter how far apart in time the two half-row CTAs are dispatched, they can never deadlock.

Compare that with the alternative where one CTA sits in a loop repeatedly polling a flag written by another CTA until a condition holds—a spin-wait. Unlike operating-system threads on a CPU, GPU hardware does not preempt a resident CTA off its SM to make room for an undispatched CTA from the same launch. Whenever you use spin-wait, you must guarantee that the waiting and signaling CTAs are on the chip at the same time: because the CUDA specification guarantees neither dispatch order nor co-residency for a standard launch, if spinning CTAs fill every on-chip slot without exiting, the CTA that is supposed to write the flag can never get an SM, and the GPU deadlocks.

If you genuinely need one CTA to wait on another, there are three specification-sanctioned ways to avoid deadlock. First, put the flag-writing producer in a separate preceding kernel. Second, use cooperative launch, where the driver guarantees that all CTAs of the entire grid are co-resident on the chip at once and refuses to launch if they do not fit (see Chapter 3, Section 1 for how many CTAs fit per SM). Third, when only a few neighboring CTAs wait on each other, Hopper lets you group them into a co-resident small cluster, where the specification not only guarantees concurrent execution on SMs, but also lets CTAs in the cluster access one another's shared memory directly (we unpack this in practice in Chapter 7, Section 12; across arbitrary SMs in this chapter, handoffs always go through the central L2). Under a standard launch, putting the producer at the lowest block indices by counting on the ascending dispatch order observed in Section 1 can also run to completion—but if the driver or hardware ever changes dispatch order, it can deadlock silently without reporting an error.

Finally, let's tally the hardware cost of device-wide synchronization—takeaway first: the single number our model carries into Section 7 is the modeled last-arriver merge cost m≈0.60+0.18=0.78 μs, while all remaining cycle counts below serve only as evidence for how L1 and L2 behave on this GPU. On this GPU (neither mechanism below is a specification guarantee), to order accesses across addresses on a GPU without an atomic, you can also insert a standalone memory fence: an acq_rel fence (fence.acq_rel) keeps prior reads and writes before subsequent writes and subsequent reads and writes after prior reads (it does not forbid store-load reordering, and our algorithms do not depend on that). In compiled machine code, this acq_rel atomic add carries the same local-SM L1 invalidation instruction as a standalone device-wide memory fence fence.acq_rel.gpu (where .gpu denotes device scope): re-reading 16 KiB of xx across 1 CTA (128 threads) slows from 319.8 clock cycles with a valid L1 to 596.6 clock cycles after the fence (the last two bars in the first chart below; reload cost after the atomic add was not measured), empirically observing that acquire invalidates the local SM's L1 so subsequent reads fetch fresh data from L2, whereas a device-wide release waiting for prior writes from this thread to reach the central L2 is inferred from the memory model. Splitting the single-thread atomic-add measurements into "no prior pending write" versus "1 prior write in flight" puts all the numbers on one footing:

  • acq_rel atomic add (device scope): 1,047.2 / 1,050.8 clock cycles (across two runs) with no prior pending write, rising to 1,078.3 clock cycles (~1,078 cycles, ~0.60 µs at ~1.8 GHz; second bar below) with 1 prior write in flight—an extra 27.5–31.1 cycles.
  • relaxed atomic add: 500.9 / 502.8 clock cycles with no prior pending write, rising to 506.0 clock cycles (first bar below) with 1 prior write in flight—an extra 3.2–5.1 cycles of its own.
  • Gap between the two (acq_rel minus relaxed): already 546.3–548.0 clock cycles with no prior pending write (1,047.2−500.9=546.3, 1,050.8−502.8=548.0), widening to 572.3 clock cycles (1,078.3−506.0=572.3) with 1 prior write in flight, so that pending write adds 24.3–26.0 cycles to the gap (27.5−3.2=24.3, 31.1−5.1=26.0). How those baseline 546.3–548.0 cycles split internally inside the hardware was not measured (and was not determined).

Separately, when we time that standalone device-wide acq_rel memory fence (fence.acq_rel.gpu) by itself (the second chart), the fence waits about 206 extra clock cycles when 1 prior write is still in flight (about 200 cycles, rising from 269 cycles to about 475 cycles; those about +206 cycles belong to the standalone fence, whereas the acq_rel atomic add above waits only 27.5–31.1 extra cycles for the same 1 pending write, and why the two differ so much was not determined). From the memory model, we infer that this extra time goes to waiting until the write is visible across the GPU (reaching L2); this is not verified with hardware counters.

We also ran a separate cross-SM handoff microbenchmark: one CTA writes 256 values and hands them off via __syncthreads() and a release atomic add to a CTA on another SM that repeatedly polls with acquire loads (sleeping briefly between polls). The median time for one complete cross-SM handoff is ~0.67 µs.

Here is how the last-arriver merge via L2 works out:

  • What you gain: safely merges across SMs without launching a second reduction kernel and without requiring the two CTAs to be co-resident on the chip.
  • What it costs: each merge pays for one device-wide acq_rel atomic add (~1,078 clock cycles on a single thread) plus the last arriver's reads. We did not measure that cost separately in v3; for reference, the spinning cross-SM handoff microbenchmark above takes ~0.67 µs. Invalidating the local SM's L1 also slows down later re-reads, and you have to allocate an extra counter array and a partial-sum workspace buffer.
  • When it loses: when the partial sums to be merged are large or numerous, making that single last-arriver CTA serially read back and sum all of them by itself turns that CTA into a brand-new tail bottleneck.

7gemv Evolution v2 → v3: Splitting the 192 Tail-Wave Rows in Half with K-halves

v3 splits the last 192 rows into 384 half-row CTAs, cutting the tail-wave load chain from 64 iterations to 32 and achieving a ~1.25× measured speedup.

In code, v3 expands the grid to 2,496 CTAs following the role table in Section 5: the first 2,112 full-row CTAs (0..2111) still walk 64 iterations and write y[row] directly, while the trailing 384 half-row CTAs (2112..2495 for the last 192 rows, landing in the tail wave under Section 1's ascending-dispatch inference; the full v3 source and how cnt[] is zeroed before the first launch are not included) walk 32 iterations each and call tail_store from Section 6 to merge via the central L2 and write y[row]:

// v3: the first 2,112 rows use 1 CTA per row; the last 192 rows use 2 half-row CTAs per row (grid = 2,496)
gemv_v3<<<2112 + 2 * 192, 128, 0, stream>>>(W, x, y, M, K, part, cnt);

With that change in place, each SM still keeps 16 CTAs resident at once (see Chapter 3, Section 1 for why that limit doesn't change). Under the unloaded round-trip plus merge model, one split row drops from 64×0.334≈21.4 μs to 32×0.334+0.78≈11.5 μs, saving an estimated ~9.9 µs, or ~10 µs (matching Figure 2-7's readout).

On the hardware, v3 (43.34 µs) saves 10.85 µs over v2 (54.19 µs)—and 10.74 µs over v1 (54.08 µs), which runs the exact same kernel code—for about a 1.25× speedup. In the unloaded model, one split row takes 32 round trips (32×0.334≈10.7 μs) plus one last-arriver merge mm (mm inside v3 was not measured; converting the single-thread acq_rel atomic add of about 1,078 cycles to about 0.60 µs at about 1.8 GHz and adding about 328 cycles, or about 0.18 µs, for the last arriver's L2 read of part gives m≈0.78 μs), dropping from about 21.4 µs to about 11.5 µs and saving about 9.9 µs (about 10 µs); why the measured 10.74 µs saving slightly exceeds that unloaded estimate was not determined. The trade-off is one cross-SM handoff on each of the 192 tail-wave rows, plus an extra partial-sum workspace buffer and counter array (192×12 B≈2.3 KB in all; Section 5 covers when this loses).

That 10.74 µs measured speedup also tests the dispatch-order inference from Section 1: cutting only the highest-numbered batch (2112..2495, 384 half-row CTAs) to 32 iterations saves 10.74 µs (10.85 µs over v2, about 10.8 µs; v3 was not timestamped directly), proving in measurement that no 64-iteration full-row CTA (0..2111) entered after iteration 32 and ruling out mixed or interleaved dispatch orders; because freed slots refill immediately, however, pure ascending (64 + 32 = 96 iterations) and pure descending (32 + 64 = 96 iterations) both compress the device-wide critical path from 128 iterations to 96 iterations with the same time saving, so v3's runtime alone cannot tell ascending from descending, and which end forms the tail wave stays an inference extrapolated from Section 1's cross-kernel observation.

Following up on Section 4, we also tested adding residency hints for WW and xx on top of v3 (a rejected step v4; v4 also tags L1 as evict-first / evict-last, and an L2-only variant slows down too). Profiler measurements (where the profiler invalidates caches itself, leaving no dirty lines in L2) on both v3 and v4 show that the 16 KiB vector xx already hits nearly 100% in L2 apart from its initial cold fill, while the 37.75 MB matrix WW hits nearly 0% in both; v4 adds extra hint-passing instructions in the loop and regresses under a clean L2 from 43.34 µs to 44.29 µs (+0.95 µs, or about 1 µs slower; the exact cause of this slowdown was not determined), so we do not count it as a step of its own (under a dirty L2 write flush, by contrast, tagging WW as evict_first runs about 5 µs faster—see Chapter 10, Section 2; v5 in Chapter 3, Section 3 still carries these hints forward, and their isolated effect in v5 was not measured).

Closing our opening question for the chapter: v1's 54.08 µs (54.19 µs in v2) breaks down into non-CTA fixed overhead FF + wave 1 duration Tw1T_{\mathrm{w1}} + 64-iteration tail duration T1T_1 (using the bounds in the table below at F=4.6 μs and m≈0.78 μs: 4.6 μs4.6\ \mu\text{s} fixed overhead + 21.4–26.4 μs21.4\text{–}26.4\ \mu\text{s} wave 1 + 23.0–28.1 μs23.0\text{–}28.1\ \mu\text{s} tail).

Why fix the smaller tail wave first when wave 1 is the larger share? Because splitting the tail wave is a pure grid-level CTA partitioning lever available at the whole-chip view, whereas shrinking wave 1 (and the 32-iteration per-thread serial load chain that remains in wave 2) requires opening a single SM to widen loads from 2 B to 16 B (Chapter 3, Section 3) and issue multiple loads per thread (Chapter 4, Section 3).

Direct answer after v3: even at 43.34 µs (still ~5.5× the 7.86 µs bandwidth lower bound, which is 18.1% of total runtime), wave 1 duration Tw1T_{\mathrm{w1}} takes 21.4–26.4 µs—55%–68% of the 38.74 µs net time at the book's F=4.6 μs and modeled m≈0.78 μs (up to 72% if m≈0, or up to ~28.5 µs, ~70% of 40.84 µs, if F≈2.5 μs)—making wave 1 the primary bottleneck.

Subtracting v1−v3=54.08−43.34=10.74 μs under three explicit assumptions—(1) wave 1 (2,112 full-row CTAs) takes equal wall time Tw1T_{\mathrm{w1}} in v1 and v3, (2) doubling chip-wide tail bytes in flight in v3 (96 KiB vs. 48 KiB) leaves per-iteration tail time L3≥L1≥0.334 μs (assumptions 1 and 2 alone cancel FF), and (3) non-CTA launch/event overhead inside a long kernel equals FF—puts every piece of the budget in one table:

8When There Are Many Partial Sums, How Do We Avoid Making the Last CTA Read Them All Alone?

Two alternatives: either have each of the SS CTAs reduce 1/S1/S of the rows, or have all CTAs issue non-fetching atomic adds directly into a pre-zeroed output buffer.

That wraps up our single-token gemv (T=1) evolution at the full-chip level; before moving to the next chapter, let's also prepare how to merge large partial sums across SMs for multi-token tiled matrix multiplication (T>1; see Primer 2, Section 1). In Sections 6–7, gemv only split each tail-wave row in half: one counter tracked 1 row, and the last arriver only had to read back two 4 B scalars. Now suppose we pack many output rows of gemv into a single tile, split that tile into SS slices along KK, and have a group of SS CTAs share one counter—the partial sums that the last arriver has to read back on its own multiply right along with it. When we compute multiple tokens at once, that volume grows much larger still: for instance, when a tile of 64 tokens by 256 output columns is split along KK across S=4 CTAs (see Chapter 5, Sections 7–8 for tiled matrix multiplication), the 4 FP32 partial sums add up to 4×64×256×4 B=256 KiB. If we stuck with Section 6 and made that lone last-arriver CTA serially read back and sum the other 3 slices (192 KiB), its load chain would turn into a brand-new long tail (Figure 2-8, Mode 1).

The first fix is parallel slice reduction (Figure 2-8, Mode 2): instead of letting the first S−1 arriving CTAs exit right away, keep all SS CTAs around to split the merge work evenly across four steps:

  1. Each CTA writes its partial sums into the global workspace buffer and synchronizes within the CTA.
  2. Thread 0 of each CTA does an acq_rel atomic add on the counter to claim a ticket number tt (the old value returned by the atomic add, counting up from 0; the paired synchronization rule is the same as in Section 6). Notice that this counter is never reset. The reason is simple: no CTA knows whether the other S−1 CTAs have all seen the ticket count reach the target and exited their spin loops; if any CTA reset the counter to 0 right then, a CTA still spinning would never see the count reach the target. Instead, each subsequent call just keeps adding SS more tickets on top.
  3. Once every ticket in this group has been claimed, the counter reaches (⌊t/S⌋+1)⋅S. Thread 0 repeatedly reads the counter with acquire until it is at least that target (the last ticket holder does not need to wait), confirming that all SS partial sums are in place; once thread 0 finishes waiting, it runs another __syncthreads() before the rest of the threads in the CTA start reading (the counter here is a 32-bit signed integer that only increases, so a continuously running service must reset it before wraparound, or switch to a 64-bit counter to remove that requirement; see Chapter 5, Section 8).
  4. Using its own slice index along KK, each CTA reads back only its assigned 1/S1/S row slice from all SS partial sums (16 rows each when S=4), sums them, and writes out the result.

Because earlier-arriving CTAs now spin-wait for later-arriving CTAs, the co-residency rule from Section 6 applies in full force: all SS CTAs must be resident on the chip at the same time. Use cooperative launch from Section 6 (or the co-resident small cluster noted in Section 6); relying on the observed ascending dispatch order also runs to completion, but the specification does not guarantee that. Here is how parallel slice reduction trades off:

  • What you gain: spreads the merge reads evenly across SS CTAs, cutting off the long tail of a single CTA serially reading back all partial sums (see Chapter 6, Section 8 for measured results).
  • What it costs: still needs a partial-sum workspace buffer, one ticket claim with spin-wait, extra merge code in every CTA, and co-residency across all SS CTAs.
  • When it loses: when there are very few partial sums to merge (such as just 2 scalars in Section 6), the time saved by splitting the reads may not pay back the spin-wait overhead; we did not measure where that crossover point lies.

The second fix is even more direct—direct atomic add (Figure 2-8, Mode 3): as soon as each CTA finishes its slice of the inner product, all threads fire non-fetching atomic adds (the PTX reduction instruction red; see Appendix B) straight at the output array in global memory, adding without reading back the old value and without waiting for a return. That gets rid of the partial-sum workspace buffer, the ticket claim, and the counter all at once.

To use it safely, though, you have to satisfy three prerequisites:

  1. The output buffer must be zeroed before the first addition: the specification-safe way is to zero the output in a separate preceding kernel. If you use dedicated CTAs inside the same kernel to zero the output and publish a completion flag, you have to use the paired release / acquire synchronization from Section 6 and satisfy the co-residency requirement (see Section 6).
  2. The final result is visible only to the next kernel: inside the current kernel, no CTA has any way of knowing when the other CTAs have finished adding. The final sum across all partial sums becomes visible to the next kernel only after the current kernel finishes (or after the dependent kernel (successor) crosses the wait call in Chapter 1, Section 4).
  3. The output is no longer bitwise deterministic: because floating-point addition is not associative and the order in which CTAs reach L2 can shift from run to run, the accumulated floating-point values can differ in their last few bits.

Here is how the direct atomic add trade-off works out:

  • What you gain: eliminates both the partial-sum workspace buffer and the counter array.
  • What it costs: the output buffer must be zeroed ahead of time, the result is no longer bitwise deterministic, and when many CTAs atomically add to the same output address at once, requests queue up at L2 (see Chapter 7, Section 12 for measurements and analysis on single-request attention).
  • When it loses:
    • In this chapter's gemv, the output yy is FP32, which hardware supports with native atomic adds; if the output is BF16 and you write scalar BF16 atomic adds as in the kernel in Chapter 6, Section 8, however, two adjacent BF16 columns share a single 32-bit (4 B) word and the compiler lowers each add into a compare-and-swap (CAS) retry loop: fetch the 4 B word, compute the updated value, and store it only if neither the neighbor column nor another CTA modified that word in the meantime—otherwise start over and retry, which on the 12-bit-weight qkv_gate kernel (T=16/32) in Chapter 6, Section 8 makes the whole kernel about 2–3× slower in measurement than using block reduction (see Chapter 6, Section 8; Mode 3 and this counterexample were not compared directly).

Takeaway: A kernel finishes only when its last CTA exits, and whether HBM reaches saturation depends on how many bytes each SM keeps in flight at once. Splitting the tail-wave rows in half and merging them through L2 brings gemv down from 54.19 µs (v2) to 43.34 µs (v3).

Next chapter's question: Reaching 95% of the HBM bandwidth plateau takes at least about 24–40 KiB of 16 B loads in flight per SM (64 KiB already exceeds 98%; see Section 3), yet v3 keeps only 4.0 KiB of 2 B loads in flight per SM. Now let's open up a single SM: what limits how many bytes it can keep in flight, and once data enters the SM, how does it reach registers and shared memory quickly and safely?

Single SM — Once Data Enters the SM, How Does It Reach Registers and Shared Memory Quickly and Safely?

  • Preface
