In Chapter 2, Section 3, we saw that reaching 95% of the HBM bandwidth plateau takes about 24–40 KiB of 16 B loads in flight per SM (and 64 KiB exceeds 98%), yet v3 keeps only 4.0 KiB of 2 B loads in flight per SM. Now let's open up a single SM: what limits how many bytes it can keep in flight, and once data enters the SM, how does it reach registers and shared memory quickly and safely?

Once data enters an SM from L2, it takes one of two paths to the execution units. The first is the register path (Sections 1–4): when the pass token count is T=1 (Primer 2, Section 1), a single thread uses each byte of WW only once, so loading it straight into registers is enough, and we first follow Chapter 2's open question straight through gemv from v3 to v6. The second is the shared memory (SMEM) path (Sections 5–9): when TT tokens share the same block of WW, many threads in a CTA read that block over and over, so we stage a 16 KiB tile of WW in SMEM first and unpack on-chip staging, ring buffering, paired-barrier handoff against overwrites, role-based register reallocation, and XOR swizzle against bank conflicts one by one.

1How Many CTAs Can Reside on One SM Simultaneously?

Look at which of the SM's four fixed resource pools runs out first; gemv v1 fills all 64 warp slots first, so each SM holds 16 CTAs.

As long as the 32 threads in a warp (Primer 3, Section 2) do not branch apart, they issue the same instruction together (Chapter 4, Section 1 shows how the scheduler picks a warp each cycle, and Chapter 4, Section 4 covers branches). Each SM has four fixed-size resource pools, and whichever pool runs out first decides how many CTAs can reside on that SM at once:

  • warp slot: 64 slots per SM (2,048 threads; at most 1,024 threads, or 32 warps, in a single CTA).
  • CTA slot (thread block slot): 32 slots per SM.
  • SMEM (shared memory): Each SM has 256 KiB of on-chip storage, of which at most 228 KiB can go to SMEM, and the driver reserves an extra 1 KiB for each resident CTA (Section 6 covers the ten carveout steps and the dynamic-SMEM rule above 48 KiB); whatever is left serves as that SM's L1 data cache (L1 caches are not coherent across SMs; see Chapter 2, Section 6).
  • register: 65,536 32-bit registers per SM, with a cap of 255 per thread. Hardware allocates registers in chunks of 256 per warp, which means each thread's register count gets rounded up to a multiple of 8. (Note: the number of hardware barriers a kernel uses (such as the CTA barrier behind __syncthreads(), see Primer 3, Section 3) can also limit residency; the per-SM hardware-barrier total is not disclosed, and whether any kernel in this book is limited by it was not measured.)

Now let's plug gemv v1 (<<<2304, 128>>>) from Primer 3 into these four pools and see how many CTAs each one allows:

  • warp slot: Each CTA has 128 threads, or 4 warps, which gives 64÷4=16 CTAs.
  • CTA slot (thread block slot): 32 CTAs.
  • SMEM (shared memory): smem[128] takes 512 B, plus the reserved 1 KiB for 1.5 KiB in total, which fits ⌊228÷1.5⌋=152 CTAs.
  • register: The compiled kernel uses 22 registers per thread, which rounds up to 24 (the next multiple of 8). Each CTA takes 24×128=3,072 registers, fitting ⌊65,536÷3,072⌋=21 CTAs.

Take the minimum of those four numbers and you get 16 CTAs, or 16×4=64 resident warps per SM—filling all 64 warp slots. That is where "16 CTAs per SM" in Chapter 2, Section 1 comes from. The number of resident warps on an SM divided by 64 is called occupancy. Calculating it from the resource pools like this gives the theoretical occupancy, which is 100% for v1. At runtime, actual occupancy fluctuates from cycle to cycle, which we did not measure.

Wave 1 of both v1 and v3 (Chapter 2, Section 7) already fills all 64 warp slots, so residency is not why v3 keeps only 4.0 KiB in flight per SM; the other factor setting bytes in flight is bytes per load instruction (Section 2).

Look closely at the cutoff for the register pool. As long as each thread uses at most 65,536÷(64×32)=32 registers, all 64 warps fit on the SM. Once a thread goes past 32 registers, the register pool runs out before the warp slots do (drag the slider in Figure 3-1 to see this exact cutoff). What if a thread needs to keep more live variables on hand than the registers it gets? Then the compiler has to spill (register spilling) the extra variables into local memory—memory that is private to each thread, but physically lives in device memory and goes through L1 and L2 cache. Registers sit right next to the execution units and bypass the memory hierarchy completely. A spilled variable, on the other hand, has to travel through the memory hierarchy on every single access: about 54 clock cycles if it hits in L1, and about 600 clock cycles if it goes all the way to HBM; stack frames of uninlined functions and dynamically indexed local arrays also live in local memory (for compile-time checks, see Chapter 10, Section 6 and Appendix B, row 26).

At compile time, you can use __launch_bounds__ to tell the compiler the maximum number of threads per CTA and the minimum number of CTAs to keep on each SM. The compiler then caps how many registers each thread can use—trading per-thread register cap for higher occupancy. Suppose a 128-thread CTA needs to hold 40 live values per thread. At 40 registers per thread, each SM fits ⌊65,536÷(40×128)⌋=12 CTAs (48 warps). If you cap each thread at 32 registers, you fit 16 CTAs (64 warps) onto the SM, but now 8 values per thread spill to local memory and pay a memory round trip on every access.

So the four resource pools squeeze your kernel from both ends. Residency matters for speed because it directly sets how many bytes each SM keeps in flight: if each CTA takes more registers or SMEM, fewer CTAs and warps fit on each SM, and bytes in flight drop in proportion (dropping from 16 to 12 CTAs above cuts resident warps and bytes in flight by 25%). Go the other way and force the register cap down to pack more CTAs, and you trigger register spilling (spill). Whether the extra warps make up for those spill round trips is something you have to measure. Chapter 8, Section 4 shows a real case where it backfires: at T=256, forcing the register cap down to 72 spills 12 registers, and Stage 6 ends up running about 26 µs slower.

Note: Local memory interleaves 32-bit words across adjacent threads so accesses at the same relative offset across a warp coalesce.

Can CTAs Stay Resident on the SM and Loop Over Work Items?

Since each SM can hold only a fixed number of CTAs at once, another common way to launch work is a persistent kernel. The grid launches just enough CTAs to fill a single wave (one full-GPU batch of simultaneously resident CTAs; see Chapter 2, Section 1), and each CTA stays on its SM, looping to take the next piece of work until the job is finished. Writing Primer 3's gemv v1 (2,304 rows) as a single full wave (132×16=2,112 resident CTAs) wraps each CTA's body in a loop striding by gridDim.x (the total CTA count of the launch, here 2,112):

for (int row = blockIdx.x; row < 2304; row += gridDim.x) { /* dot product for row */ }

Each resident CTA therefore starts up once and claims its next row immediately, so later rows do not wait for new CTAs to schedule onto SMs (we did not measure how much time this saves). Resident CTAs can also hold intermediate state on the SM, claim work from a counter to slice the job more finely, and—when 1 heavy tiled CTA occupies an SM as in Section 8—overlap fetching the next tile with the current tile's epilogue (we did not measure the one-time-init and epilogue-overlap savings separately).

Keep in mind, though, that making a kernel persistent does not make the tail wave disappear. Spreading gemv's 2,304 rows across those 2,112 persistent CTAs still leaves the 192 CTAs with blockIdx.x < 192 running a second row while the other 1,920 CTAs finish their single row, leave the loop, and exit, leaving their 1,920 SM slots empty with no new CTAs to fill them—the exact same tail-wave shape as v1 in Chapter 2, Section 1 and v5's about 1.18-wave tail in Section 3 below (2,496 CTAs against 2,112 capacity, leaving 384 half-row CTAs). To shorten the tail wave, you still need to split the work more finely (Chapter 2, Section 5) or make the total work items an exact multiple of one wave's capacity.

The cost of a persistent kernel is one extra loop inside every CTA. When the total work cannot even fill a single wave, that loop is pure overhead; nor is a persistent kernel an automatic win—Chapter 9, Section 6 shows a measured case where the exact same load work runs slower as a persistent kernel than with a normal launch (for reasons not determined). And when two back-to-back steps have an all-to-all dependency, a persistent kernel can synchronize across the whole GPU inside the kernel, but it still requires cooperative launch (Chapter 2, Section 6) and still has to wait for the slowest CTA every single time (Chapter 1, Section 3).

2How Many Sector Requests Does One Warp Load Instruction Generate?

Hardware requests memory in 32-byte sectors, sending one request for every sector a warp load instruction touches; the more contiguous the addresses and the wider each thread reads, the fewer requests go out and the more useful bytes come back.

First, let's separate two hardware sizes: a sector is 32 B, which is the smallest unit the memory system requests, while a cache line is 128 B, or 4 sectors. When a warp issues a load instruction, the LSU (Load/Store Unit) inside the SM collects all 32 thread addresses and merges any addresses that fall into the same 32 B sector into a single request. The tighter those addresses pack into sectors, the fewer requests go out—and that is coalesced access (coalescing).

Let's compare one load instruction for WW across three versions of gemv (the three modes in Figure 3-2):

  • v0 and v1: As we saw in Primer 3, Section 6, one load instruction in v0 scatters across 32 sectors, while in v1 it lands in just 2. In the terms of this section, v0 sends 32 requests and v1 sends only 2 requests. What about the other 30 B in each sector that v0 does not use right away? Those happen to be the exact elements the same thread will read over the next 15 iterations, so they may stay in L1 and hit later—though we did not measure the L1 hit rate.
  • v5 (Section 3 of this chapter): Each thread switches to uint4 (a 16-byte vector load) to read 16 B (8 BF16 elements) in one go. Now a single warp instruction reads 32×16=512 B—4 full cache lines, or 16 sectors—and uses 100% of the 512 B it fetches on the spot.

Put them side by side and the payoff is obvious: one instruction in v5 brings back 8× as many useful bytes as v1. So to keep the same number of bytes in flight, v5 needs only one-eighth as many load instructions for WW as v1 (note that this is the count of load instructions for WW, not the total instructions in the kernel).

Wide coalesced loads require contiguous data and 16 B address alignment. Watch what they do to your register budget, too: a 16 B load ties up its 4 destination 32-bit registers from the moment it issues until the data comes back. If a single thread keeps kk such loads in flight at once, those pending loads alone take 4k4k registers (we will use this exact math in Chapter 4, Section 3).

The measured v3 → v5 result and the mechanism by which 16 B wide loads raise bytes in flight per SM by 8× are worked out and measured right in the next section.

3Why Is gemv v5 2.5× Faster Than v3? (v3 → v5)

Direct answer: v3 keeps only about 4.0 KiB/SM in flight and is starved of bytes in flight; v5 widens each per-thread load from 2 B to 16 B (while keeping the two residency hints from Chapter 2, Section 4), raising bytes in flight 8× to about 32 KiB/SM and cutting measured runtime from 43.34 µs to 17.49 µs (derived 2.48×, or about 2.5×).

Our starting point is v3 from Chapter 2, Section 7, with inputs W:[2304,8192]BF16\shape{W}{2304,\;8192}{BF16} and x:[8192]BF16\shape{x}{8192}{BF16} and output [2304][2304]. That kernel launches 2,496 CTAs of 128 threads each, and because each thread keeps just 1 2 B load of WW in flight before waiting on it for multiply-add, each SM keeps only about 16×128×2 B=4 KiB (4.0 KiB) in flight—6× below the 24 KiB/SM 95% knee for 1 16 B load per thread in Chapter 2, Section 3.

Why does widening each load to 16 B break that bottleneck? Tie together Section 1's residency and Section 2's wide coalesced loads: in the compiled machine code of both v3 and v5, each thread keeps 1 load of WW in flight before waiting for its data. Because in-flight loads per thread stay fixed at 1, "8× bytes per instruction and one-eighth as many WW load instructions" (cutting a full row's serial loop from 64 round trips to 8; Section 2) and "8× bytes in flight per SM" (64 resident warps ×\times 512 B per warp load = about 32 KiB/SM, jumping from 4.0 KiB past the 24 KiB/SM 95% knee for 1 wide load per thread) are one and the same fact—and that 8× jump in bytes in flight is what drives the v3 → v5 speedup (measured 43.34 → 17.49 µs, derived 2.48× faster, lifting net WW bandwidth after the 4.6 µs fixed overhead (Primer 3, Section 5) to about 2.93 TB/s).

In v5, we switch both WW and xx to uint4 loads so each thread reads 16 B at a time (8 consecutive BF16 elements, matching Mode v5 in Figure 3-2) while keeping the two residency hints from Chapter 2, Section 4. Adding those two hints alone on top of v3 (tagged at both L1 and L2, called v4) measures 44.29 µs under a clean flush (0.95 µs slower than v3's 43.34 µs, with no gain across two profiler re-tests; see Chapter 2, Section 4 and Chapter 10, Section 2); on top of that, v4 (44.29 µs) → v5 (17.49 µs) changes only to 16 B wide loads and is derived 2.53× faster (44.29÷17.49=2.53), while 16 B loads without the hints were not measured. That requires each row to start on a 16 B boundary, which rows of 8,192×2 B naturally satisfy. On each iteration, the thread converts those 8 BF16 elements to FP32 and accumulates their products:

𝑎𝑐𝑐+=∑i=07FP32(W[𝑟𝑜𝑤,8k+i])⋅FP32(x[8k+i])\mathit{acc} \mathrel{+}= \sum_{i=0}^{7} \mathrm{FP32}(W[\mathit{row}, 8k+i]) \cdot \mathrm{FP32}(x[8k+i])

The three lines of C++ below sketch how one iteration issues the 16 B loads and converts the first two BF16 elements. uint4 is a 16-byte vector of four 32-bit integers whose .x/.y/.z/.w fields each pack 2 BF16 values, and __bfloat1622float2 converts a pair of BF16 values (__nv_bfloat162) into a pair of FP32 values (float2) in one call. The full kernel converts all four fields of w_vec—8 BF16 values in all—to FP32 for multiply-add:

// v5 sketch: each uint4 load reads 16 bytes of W and x (8 consecutive BF16)
uint4 w_vec = reinterpret_cast<const uint4*>(&W[row * K])[k];
uint4 x_vec = reinterpret_cast<const uint4*>(x)[k];
float2 wf0 = __bfloat1622float2(*reinterpret_cast<const __nv_bfloat162*>(&w_vec.x));

Let's first work out residency using Section 1's rules (Figure 3-1): each thread in v5 takes 30 registers (v3 uses 23, and hints-only v4 uses 27). Rounded up to a multiple of 8, that lands at 32 registers—right on the 32-register cutoff from Section 1—so each SM still holds all 16 CTAs and 64 warps. If each thread used just 3 more registers (33 registers) and stepped past that cutoff, rounding up to a multiple of 8 would allocate 40 registers per thread and drop residency to ⌊65,536÷(40×128)⌋=12 CTAs per SM (we did not measure that variant).

With the cause of the speedup settled, look separately at what explains the remaining gap: on the 4 GiB plain-16 B-load streaming sweep, v5's shape—1 load per thread at a 32 KiB/SM machine-code peak—already reaches 97.6% of the bandwidth plateau (4.438 ≈ 4.44 TB/s; a 4-load-per-thread stream also reaches about 95%–98% at 32 KiB/SM, whereas issuing more loads per thread gives slightly less at equal bytes in flight; see the Section 6 note for another peak point from the same sweep), so v5's first wave is not shown to be short of bytes in flight. Estimating from that measured streaming rate plus 4.6 µs of fixed overhead gives about 13.1 µs (about 13.1–13.3 µs from the 4-load stream), about 4.4 µs faster than v5's measured 17.49 µs (see the chart note below). That remaining about 4.4 µs gap is not a first-wave bytes-in-flight shortage; it comes from the startup and drain of the short 37.75 MB launch, xx loads, intra-CTA SMEM reduction, and the about 1.18-wave tail (individual shares not measured): the first wave holds 2,112 CTAs at once, leaving 384 extra CTAs (corresponding to the 384 half-row CTAs under the ascending-ID extrapolation from the 132-CTA measurement in Chapter 2, Section 1; dispatch order on v5 was not measured) waiting for slots to open up.

4v5 → v6: Why Does Eliminating the Tail Wave Make Execution Slower?

v6 shrinks each CTA to a single warp; although all 2,304 CTAs now fit in a single wave, each SM gets only about 17 resident warps on average, dropping bytes in flight to ~8.7 KiB and pulling bandwidth down with it.

To get rid of v5's remaining tail wave, v6 shrinks each CTA from 128 threads down to 32 so that a single warp computes one full row:

gemv_v6<<<2304, 32, 0, stream>>>(W, x, y, K);

Each thread still issues 16 B loads per iteration just as in v5, and a row's 32 partial sums still reduce through 128 B of SMEM (in Chapter 4, Section 5, we will replace that SMEM reduction by exchanging values directly across registers within the warp).

First let's check the pool limits from Section 1 (preset v6 in Figure 3-1): per-thread registers match v5, and each CTA uses 128 B of SMEM plus the 1 KiB reserved by the driver. Because each CTA now has only 1 warp, warp slots would allow 64 CTAs, but CTA slots cap each SM at 32 CTAs, giving the full GPU a single-wave capacity of 132×32=4,224≥2,304. All 2,304 CTAs fit in a single wave, so we no longer need v3's KK-halves split or L2 merge.

Here is the catch: how many CTAs a resource pool allows is not how many CTAs your grid actually puts on the SM. The entire grid has only 2,304 CTAs. Spread across 132 SMs, each SM gets an average of just 2,304÷132≈17.45 CTAs—or about 17 warps, down from 64 in v5—leaving nearly three-quarters of the warp slots empty. Counting 1 in-flight 16 B load of WW per thread (the same iteration's 16 B load of xx mostly hits in L1 or L2 and is not counted toward HBM bytes in flight), each SM keeps only 17.45×512 B≈8.7 KiB/SM of WW in flight, about a quarter of what v5 had.

The table and chart below show the measured result: v6 runs slower than v5, regressing from 17.49 µs to 21.63 µs (+4.14 µs slower) in the exact direction predicted by the drop in bytes in flight. In v6, each thread issues only one 16 B load of WW before using the result (about 8.7 KiB/SM in flight). After subtracting 4.6 µs of fixed overhead, achieved bandwidth is about 2.2 TB/s. On the 4 GiB plain-16 B-load streaming sweep with 1 load per thread, 8–10 KiB/SM sustains 2.49–2.98 TB/s, or about 2.67 TB/s interpolated at 8.73 KiB/SM (giving an estimated about 18.8 µs for 37.75 MB plus 4.6 µs fixed overhead; see the chart note below for the round-trip and bandwidth bounds); v6 sits about 0.45 TB/s (about 2.9 µs) below that long-stream rate due to the startup and drain of the short 37.75 MB launch, per-round dependent unpack and multiply-add work between load return and the next load issue, xx loads, and intra-CTA SMEM reduction, whose individual shares were not measured.

So v6 gives us a clear measured counterexample: shrinking CTAs to eliminate a tail wave pays off only if it does not gut your bytes in flight, and when you do residency math, you have to count the warps actually placed on each SM, not just the ceiling allowed by the resource pools. Even so, the structure of v6 is well worth keeping: one warp computes one row, and the whole grid fits in a single wave. That gets rid of the tail-wave split and cross-CTA merge, and because all 32 partial sums for a row now live inside the same warp, we will soon be able to sum them directly in registers without touching SMEM at all (Chapter 4, Section 5). How a single thread keeps multiple independent loads in flight to lift bytes in flight back to the plateau—without adding resident warps to this single-warp skeleton—waits for Chapter 4 when we open the SM's sub-partitions; the table below summarizes bytes in flight, streaming models, and measured gaps across v3, v5, and v6 to wrap up the T=1 register path, before Sections 5–9 turn to the multi-token shared-memory path:

Version KiB/SM in flight Stream TB/s at that depth Model µs (incl. 4.6 µs fixed overhead) Measured µs Gap µs (internal shares not measured)
v3 (2 B loads, 64 resident warps) ~4.0 KiB 2 B stream curve not measured — 43.34 Starved at 4.0 KiB/SM in flight
v5 (16 B loads, 64 resident warps) ~32 KiB 4.44 (measured, 97.6% of plateau) ~13.1 (estimated) 17.49 ~4.4 (short launch, xx loads, SMEM reduce, 1.18-wave tail)
v6 (16 B loads, ~17.45 resident warps) ~8.7 KiB ~2.67 (estimated by 8–10 KiB interpolation) ~18.8 (estimated) 21.63 (+4.14 slower than v5) ~2.9 (short launch, dependent unpack/FMA gap, xx loads, SMEM reduce)

5How Does a Repeatedly Read Data Block Move into SMEM Without Passing Through Registers?

Hand regular rectangular tiles to TMA (Tensor Memory Accelerator, the SM's dedicated block-copy hardware unit) to move them into SMEM with a single instruction; use per-thread asynchronous copy cp.async when gathering scattered rows by index.

Sections 1–4 completed the T=1 register path, where one thread uses each byte of WW once; starting here, we switch to the shared memory (SMEM) path: when TT tokens share the same block of weights WW, many warps inside a CTA need to read that block over and over. Rather than having every warp fetch it from device memory on its own, we read it from HBM once into on-chip SMEM as a tile so one 16 KiB tile fetch serves all TT token rows of multiply-add work (Chapter 5, Section 7 shows how Tensor Core consumes it). Let's do the math on one 16 KiB tile of WW from qkv_gate, W𝑡𝑖𝑙𝑒:[128,64]BF16\shape{W_{tile}}{128,\;64}{BF16}: it has 128 rows of 64 BF16 elements (128 B) each. In device memory, those 128 row segments are each 128 B long, separated from one another by a full row stride of 16,384 B.

To move this 16 KiB tile into SMEM, the hardware gives us four paths (Figure 3-3; for Paths 1 and 2, we count a CTA of 128 threads, or 4 warps):

  • Path 1: Normal load into registers, then store to SMEM. Each thread issues 16,384÷(128×16)=8 loads of 16 B. Across the CTA, that takes 32 warp load instructions plus 32 warp store instructions, or 64 instructions in total. If you keep all 8 loads in flight at once, each thread ties up 8×4=32 staging registers; if you issue them one at a time, you need only 4 registers, but you pay for 8 serial round trips. Take this path only when you have to reformat the data in registers before writing it to SMEM.
  • Path 2: Per-thread asynchronous copy (cp.async). Each thread still computes its own addresses and together the warps issue 32 instructions, but the bytes go straight from L2 into SMEM without passing through registers (0 staging registers). On Hopper, TMA (Tensor Memory Accelerator) cannot gather rows through an index table in one command, so when we gather scattered rows by index (each full 128 B-aligned row still coalesces into 4 sectors; see below the table and Chapter 7, Section 5), we either take this path or issue one Path 3 1D bulk copy per row.
  • Path 3: TMA 1D bulk copy (cp.async.bulk). Give a start address and a byte count, and TMA copies one contiguous span of bytes; a single thread issues the instruction using 0 data registers. Because our tile of WW is not one contiguous span in memory but 128 separate row segments, taking Path 3 means issuing one copy per row, or 128 instructions in total.
  • Path 4: TMA multidimensional tensor bulk copy (cp.async.bulk.tensor). We typically build a descriptor on the CPU ahead of time recording the tensor's dimensions, row stride, and tiling rules; inside the kernel, a single thread passes the tile coordinates and issues 1 instruction. TMA computes all 128 segment addresses in hardware, fills out-of-bounds elements with 0 automatically, and can even reorder the bytes as they land in SMEM using the XOR swizzle rule from Section 9—all while using 0 data registers.

Before comparing the four paths in a table, let's see how each asynchronous path confirms its bytes have landed in SMEM (embedding these instructions in C++ uses inline PTX—NVIDIA's virtual assembly, translated at compile time into SASS, the machine instructions executed by the GPU): for Path 3 and Path 4 TMA reads, a hardware counter in SMEM tracks how many bytes remain unwritten, subtracting each batch TMA writes from 16,384 B until the count hits 0, at which point consumers see the completion signal and read SMEM directly (Section 7 completes the issuer-side condition and visibility rule). Plain cp.async on Path 2 does not decrement that byte counter automatically: under per-thread group waiting, a thread issues a batch of cp.async copies and calls cp.async.commit_group (compiled to SASS LDGDEPBAR) to seal the batch into a group; groups complete in commit order (individual copies within a group are unordered), and cp.async.wait_group N (SASS DEPBAR.LE SB0, N) waits until at most NN of that thread's most recent groups remain pending (followed by an intra-CTA barrier if other threads also read that SMEM; Section 7 adds a second waiting form). The table below compares all four paths on the same 16 KiB tile (128 rows × 128 B):

Path Instructions across the CTA Data-staging registers / thread Who computes addresses How completion is signalled (full handoff in Section 7)
Path 1: Normal wide loads to registers, then stores to SMEM 64 warp instructions (32 loads + 32 stores) 32 (or 4 across 8 serial trips) All 128 threads Each warp waits for its loads to reach registers, stores to SMEM, then crosses an intra-CTA barrier
Path 2: Per-thread async copy (cp.async) 32 warp instructions 0 All 128 threads Per-thread commit_group + wait_group N (plus an intra-CTA barrier if other threads read; second form in Section 7)
Path 3: TMA 1D bulk copy (cp.async.bulk) 128 issued by 1 thread (1 per row) 0 Thread gives each row start; TMA copies contiguous row bytes In-SMEM hardware byte counter decrements from 16,384 B to 0
Path 4: TMA multidimensional tensor bulk copy (cp.async.bulk.tensor) 1 issued by 1 thread 0 Thread gives tile coordinates; TMA hardware computes all 128 row addresses from descriptor Same as Path 3: hardware byte counter decrements from 16,384 B to 0, and consumers read SMEM directly

Now check the sector math when Path 2 gathers scattered rows through an index table: as long as each selected row is contiguous, 128 B-aligned, and used in full, 8 threads each issuing one 16 B load or copy for a 128 B row still coalesce into 4 sectors (1 cache line) just like contiguous data, so one warp gathering 4 scattered rows touches 16 sectors and uses 100% of all 512 B (any latency gap against contiguous rows at equal sector count is not measured here). What indexed gather actually loses is two things. Loss 1 is narrow scattered reads: if 32 threads jump to 32 distinct rows and read only a narrow slice (say 2 B each), the access scatters across up to 32 sectors. Loss 2 is no TMA gather on Hopper: Path 4's TMA multidimensional tensor copy cannot gather indexed rows in one command, so threads must compute row addresses and issue copies themselves, relying on enough resident warps or multiple in-flight loads per thread to keep bytes in flight high (see Chapter 4, Section 3, and Chapter 7, Section 5 for the KV-cache gather microbenchmark).

Picking one path over another does not change the HBM bandwidth ceiling: once enough bytes are in flight, both normal loads and TMA reach about 4.5 TB/s (see Chapter 2, Figure 2-3, and the chart in Section 6 of this chapter). Where Path 4 pays off is instruction and register overhead: 1 instruction takes the place of 32 to 64 instructions, consumes 0 data registers, and hands address calculation and bounds checking over to hardware.

What does Path 4 cost? First, each TMA transfer pays a fixed startup overhead (measured at about 43 cycles per multidimensional tensor copy; 1D bulk copy was not measured). Second, the descriptor usually has to be built on the CPU ahead of time (you can also patch one from a template on the GPU, but that needs an extra fence; see Appendix D, Section 4), and the tile shape has a cap: at most 256 elements along each dimension. On Hopper, TMA also cannot gather several rows through an index table in one command (issuing one 1D bulk copy per row still works; Appendix A, Section 4 covers the next-generation change). Finally, when a tile is very small, the fixed startup overhead outweighs the instructions you save, though we did not measure the exact size where that flips.

Note: CUtensorMap descriptor fields and inline PTX shared-memory addressing. Path 4's host-built descriptor is a 128 B CUtensorMap (usually passed to the device as a const __grid_constant__ kernel parameter) that records the full tensor's dimensions, row stride, tile box size, per-dimension traversal stride (elementStrides, set to 1 for dense tiles), on-chip swizzle mode (which permutes SMEM banks, distinct from interleave across memory-channel slices; interleave and .alloc_class are in Appendix D, Section 4), L2 promotion (l2Promotion, set to 128 B in most kernels in this book; NVIDIA documents only that it widens a cache policy's effect across a wider set of L2 cache lines, and its effect on fetch width was not measured), and out-of-bounds fill mode. When writing inline PTX, the shared-memory destination operand of cp.async and TMA takes a .shared state-space address converted from a generic pointer via cvta.to.shared / __cvta_generic_to_shared; this book's code uses a 32-bit offset (see Appendix B, Section 6).

6How Many Slots Does a Ring Buffer Need to Overlap Data Movement and Compute?

Direct rule first: when all 132 SMs are active with 1 resident CTA per SM and fixed 16 KiB slots, keep 3 slots (3×16=48 KiB) in flight plus 1 slot being computed on, for 3+1=4 slots in all (with fewer active SMs, each active SM needs proportionally more bytes in flight).

If SMEM has only 1 slot, moving data and computing on it have to take turns, so every tile waits out a full memory round trip. To overlap the two, we cut SMEM into NN buffer slots and cycle through them in order—0,1,…,N−1,0,1,…—forming a ring buffer (Figure 3-4; drag the slider N=1..6 in Figure 3-4 to watch consumers go from waiting on every tile to having data continuously ready). To match, we split the warps in the CTA into two roles: one producer warp does nothing but issue TMA loads to fill empty slots with upcoming tiles, while the remaining consumer warps do nothing but read each arrived slot's WW tile and run the multiply-add across all TT tokens. Splitting warps by role like this is called warp specialization.

Why split the CTA into 1 producer warp and many consumer warps instead of letting every warp copy a tile and then compute on it? If all warps ran the same copy-then-compute loop, every step would stop all warps together at __syncthreads() until the next tile finished arriving, so no warp could ever copy ahead; splitting warps by role lets copying and computing overlap across steps, at the cost of 1 producer warp that does no math.

When counting slots, remember that the 1 slot consumers are actively computing on has already landed in SMEM, so it does not count as in flight (call the time consumers take to compute one slot tct_c). So the number of slots you need in the ring is:

N=⌈bytes in flight needed per SMbytes per slot⌉+1N = \left\lceil \frac{\text{bytes in flight needed per SM}}{\text{bytes per slot}} \right\rceil + 1

When all 132 SMs are active with 1 resident CTA per SM (matching the chart below, and Section 8's register split also pins each SM to 1 CTA), the TMA bytes in flight needed per SM follow Little's Law from Chapter 2, Section 3 and are set by measurement: our reviewed 4 GiB 1D streaming sweep crosses the 95% plateau knee at about 36–40 KiB per SM (40 KiB at 1 CTA/SM; down to 32 KiB with 2 KiB copies at 4 CTAs/SM). Plug in 16 KiB per slot: whether you use the 36–40 KiB 95% knee (⌈40÷16⌉+1=4) or the 48 KiB plateau step (⌈48÷16⌉+1=4), for a single CTA N=4 is the count that is safe for every tc≤0.48 µs, taking 64 KiB of SMEM in total.

Sizing the ring in this chapter uses one rule: in a 16 KiB-slot ring, 2 slots in flight (32 KiB) fall just short, and 3 slots in flight (48 KiB) is the first whole-slot step solidly on the bandwidth plateau (about 98%–99%), giving N=3+1=4 slots.

This N=4 formula rests on one speed condition: consumers must finish computing one slot (tct_c) no slower than memory bandwidth can deliver one slot (derived at about 34 GB/s per SM, delivering 16 KiB takes about 0.48 µs; TMA ring bandwidth with consumer warps and tct_c of individual real kernels were not measured in this chapter). When that holds, consumers still wait on data, but they are waiting on the bandwidth ceiling rather than round-trip latency. If consumers take longer than that to compute a slot, the bottleneck is on the consumer side: adding more slots will never reach the bandwidth plateau, and you have to size the ring by measuring on the actual kernel.

The table below reconciles the measured streaming bandwidths, plateau shares, and Section 1 SMEM-pool capacity math across ring depths at 1 resident CTA per SM and 16 KiB per slot (corresponding to N=2..5 in Figure 3-4, where N−1=1..4 slots stay in flight while 1 slot is in compute; note the two denominators in column 5: before the parenthesis, 100% is the chart's own 64 KiB bar—4.589 TB/s for 2D and 4.599 TB/s for 1D—whereas the parenthetical "reviewed" share uses the separate 4 GiB reviewed sweep's full-family 4.597 TB/s plateau, where 64 KiB itself measured 4.569 TB/s = 99.4%):

In-flight slots (ring size NN) KiB/SM in flight 2D TMA TB/s 1D TMA TB/s % of this chart's 64 KiB bar (2D / 1D; reviewed 1D % of 4.597 TB/s plateau) SMEM per CTA (incl. 1 KiB reserve, excl. barriers) Max CTAs/SM by SMEM pool
1 (N=2) 16 KiB 2.835 3.087 ~62% / ~67% (reviewed ~68%) 32+1=33 KiB ⌊228÷33⌋=6
2 (N=3) 32 KiB 4.233 4.371 ~92% / 95.0% (reviewed 92.8%, below 95% knee) 48+1=49 KiB ⌊228÷49⌋=4

Note: Reconciling the two sweeps' percentages and comparing with Chapters 2–3's ordinary-load knees. At 32 KiB, 95.0% and 92.8% appear side by side because the chart's microbenchmark carries about 2% systematic bias: its 32 KiB 1D bar of 4.371 TB/s is 95.0% of its own 4.599 TB/s 64 KiB bar (2D is about 92%), sitting 2.4% higher in relative bandwidth—or 2.2 percentage points higher in plateau share—than the reviewed 4 GiB 1D sweep's 4.268 TB/s (92.8% of its 4.597 TB/s plateau, where the 1 CTA/SM 95% knee is 40 KiB, or 36–40 KiB overall). In Section 3's 4 GiB ordinary-16 B-load sweep, v5 (128×16=2,048 threads = 32 KiB/SM) reached 97.6%, while that sweep's 1-load-per-thread peak of about 97.9% sat at another thread count (1,984 threads = 31 KiB/SM) from the same sweep. Overall, TMA's 36–40 KiB 95% knee sits in the same range as the 24–40 KiB that ordinary 16 B loads need for 95% of the plateau in Chapter 2, Section 3 (36–56 KiB for 98% at 2–16 loads per thread): up to 32 KiB, ordinary loads with 1–2 loads per thread outpace TMA at equal bytes in flight, whereas 16 loads per thread fall behind TMA up to 48 KiB, so ordinary loads do not always have the longer round trip.

That N=4 count assumes all 132 SMs are active with 1 resident CTA per SM; when either count changes, the bytes needed per CTA move accordingly: first, when the grid is too small to fill all 132 SMs, fewer active SMs must pull the whole chip's bandwidth, so each active SM needs proportionally more bytes in flight—if only half the SMs are running, each active SM needs roughly twice as many bytes in flight; second, conversely, if CC resident CTAs on one SM share that SM's bytes in flight, each CTA needs only ⌈Btarget÷(16C)⌉+1 slots.

The upside of a ring buffer is clear: data movement overlaps with compute, and keeping N−1 slots in flight pushes read bandwidth onto the plateau (first chart). The price you pay is 16 KiB of SMEM for each extra slot, plus one dedicated producer warp for the ring. Here are the SMEM carveout and dynamic-cap rules deferred from Section 1: inside each SM's 256 KiB of on-chip storage, the driver picks one of ten steps per kernel—0, 8, 16, 32, 64, 100, 132, 164, 196, or 228 KiB—for SMEM (leaving at most 227 KiB requestable by a single CTA after the driver's 1 KiB per-CTA reserve), while static SMEM per CTA is capped at 48 KiB; our 4-slot ring alone takes 64 KiB (plus barrier bytes), exceeding 48 KiB, so it must use dynamic SMEM after the host opts in via cudaFuncSetAttribute(..., cudaFuncAttributeMaxDynamicSharedMemorySize, bytes) (omitting this causes launch to fail). Counting residency from the SMEM pool alone, each CTA takes 64+1=65 KiB including the 1 KiB reserve (excluding barrier bytes), so each SM fits at most ⌊228÷65⌋=3 such CTAs (195 KiB total, requiring at least the 196 KiB carveout step; which step the driver actually selects and how much L1 remains are undocumented and were not measured in this book; expanding to 5 or 6 slots drops the cap to at most 2 CTAs). Furthermore, the deeper you make the ring, the longer each step's data takes from issue until it is ready to read (see the second chart below). That follows directly from Little's Law in Chapter 2, Section 3: round-trip latency = bytes in flight ÷ bandwidth, so once bytes in flight grow faster than bandwidth, each round trip takes longer. Still, that longer round trip makes consumers wait extra time only when the ring is first filling up or when the next step's address becomes known late (we did not measure this effect separately).

As the chart shows, with only 1 slot in flight, read bandwidth reaches just 60%–70% of the plateau. Going from 3 in-flight slots to 4, however, gains less than 1% in bandwidth while costing another 16 KiB of SMEM. In practice, the sweet spot has to be measured on the real kernel: multi-token qkv_gate in this book uses 4–10 slots across its settings (Chapter 6, Section 8), the expert kernel in Chapter 8 slows down when cut to 2 slots (Chapter 8, Section 9), and expanding the T=32 projection kernel in Chapter 9 from 6 slots to 7 speeds it up by about 0.55 µs (Chapter 9, Section 7).

7How Do Producers and Consumers Hand Off a Slot Without Overwriting Data Before It Is Read?

Pair each buffer slot with two mbarrier objects—one for full, one for empty; consumers must not signal empty until the data read from the slot has returned to registers.

If you hand off buffer slots with __syncthreads(), the entire CTA has to stop together at every step: the producer warp cannot run ahead on its own, and consumers have to wait on each other. An mbarrier (a hardware-counted barrier) makes only the two sides using a given slot wait on each other, leaving every other warp free to keep running. Physically, an mbarrier is an 8-byte hardware object in SMEM that tracks two counts: how many threads still need to arrive (arrive), and how many bytes still need to be written (transaction bytes). Only when both counts hit zero does the current round finish and the barrier's phase flip. Hardware uses a single parity bit that alternates between 0 and 1 to tell adjacent rounds apart, so the same barrier object can be reused round after round.

We pair each slot ss with two barriers: full[s] (ready to read) and empty[s] (ready to write). Figure 3-5 walks through the handoff across round rr and round r+1 in time order:

  • producer: First waits for empty[s] to finish the previous round's phase (round rr waits on parity (r−1) mod 2), confirming the slot is free. Next, 1 leader thread chosen from the producer warp with elect.sync (SASS machine instruction ELECT) arrives on full[s], registers the 16,384 bytes expected for this transfer, and issues the TMA load. Each time TMA finishes writing a batch of bytes, it subtracts them from full[s]; once both the arrival count and the byte count hit zero, full[s] flips phase.
  • consumer: Waits on full[s] until round rr's phase flips, at which point the bytes written by TMA are already visible to it (TMA read completion carries a built-in cross-proxy fence, explained right after the next paragraph). It then issues shared-memory loads from the slot, uses the loaded values in multiply-adds, and finally arrives on empty[s] to hand the empty slot back.

A warp waiting on full[s] or empty[s] issues no instructions while stalled, so its wait does not take issue slots away from other eligible warps (see Chapter 4, Section 1 for how schedulers pick eligible warps each cycle); as for whether every consumer thread, one thread per warp, or a single representative thread arrives on empty[s], Figure 3-5 illustrates expected = 1, while the arrival-count convention across this book's real kernels is not cataloged here (unknown).

Before lining up the completion-handoff paths and unpacking the overwrite hazard below, look at the two hardware paths touching one slot in Figure 3-5: consumer warps read slot ss into registers with ordinary shared-memory loads, while the next round's TMA unit writes new bytes into that very same slot ss. The GPU memory model calls such distinct memory-access paths different proxies (proxy, a distinction that extends beyond SMEM): normal thread shared/global reads and writes, as well as Section 5's Path 2 cp.async, go through the generic proxy, whereas Section 5's Path 3 and Path 4 TMA reads and writes go through the async proxy (in a later chapter, Chapter 5, Section 4's wgmma Tensor Core instruction reading matrices from SMEM is another async-proxy case). When two proxies access the same address, nothing orders them automatically; handing data from one proxy to the other requires crossing a cross-proxy fence (by the specification, a completed TMA read carries a built-in cross-proxy fence, so once full[s] flips, consumers read slot ss directly through the generic proxy).

Putting Section 5 and this section side by side, there are three completion-handoff paths into SMEM:

Copy kind Proxy Who issues What counts completion Who waits, and on what Extra barrier / fence
TMA (cp.async.bulk / .tensor) Async proxy 1 leader thread elected via elect.sync in the producer warp full[s] expected transaction-byte count hits 0 + producer arrival count hits 0 Consumer warps wait on full[s] phase flip Built-in cross-proxy fence on TMA load completion; none added by consumers
cp.async + commit_group / wait_group N Generic proxy Each copying thread issues its own copies Per-thread async-group queue (groups complete in commit order; unordered within a group) That same issuing thread calls wait_group N (SASS DEPBAR.LE SB0, N) Needs an intra-CTA barrier if other threads read that SMEM
cp.async + cp.async.mbarrier.arrive Generic proxy Each copying thread issues copies and posts a linked mbarrier arrival System triggers an arrival on the mbarrier once all prior cp.async copies from that thread complete Consumer warps wait on that mbarrier phase flip Same generic proxy needs no cross-proxy fence; add one if feeding async-proxy wgmma (Chapter 5, Section 4)

Two instruction details behind that table are worth noting. First, when a Path 2 cp.async ring uses the third row's cp.async.mbarrier.arrive to tie completion to an mbarrier, Chapter 7's verify kernels and Chapter 8, Section 15's prefill gather warps use this form, whereas Chapter 6, Chapter 7's decode kernels, and Chapter 8, Section 3's weight rings use the second row's wait_group; when writing inline PTX, just as in Section 5, the barrier operand of mbarrier instructions takes a .shared state-space address from cvta.to.shared (32-bit offset in this book's code). Second, the first row elects the producer's single issuing thread with elect.sync rather than if (threadIdx.x == 0) because with if (threadIdx.x == 0) the compiler cannot verify that only 1 thread initiates the copy and may insert a peeling loop over active threads (its effect on uniform registers (registers that hold one value shared by the whole warp, see Chapter 4, Section 5) or branch instructions and its standalone timing delta were not measured).

Here is a trap that is easy to fall into: issuing a shared-memory load only hands off a request to hardware; the actual bytes do not land in the destination register until tens of cycles later. That gives us one iron rule: Consumers must not arrive on empty[s] before the shared-memory loads from slot ss have returned to registers. If a consumer arrives too early, the producer sees empty[s] flip, assumes the slot is free, and kicks off the next round's TMA into that same slot. If the new TMA bytes overwrite the slot before those earlier shared-memory loads finish reading, the consumer ends up loading data from the next tile. Breaking read-before-write order like this is a write-after-read hazard (WAR). Worst of all, it raises no error—the output just comes out silently wrong. Chapter 8's expert kernel ran into this very issue, and stress testing (repeatedly replaying the kernel and checking its outputs) caught the overwrite.

You might ask: arriving on empty[s] carries a CTA-scope release by default (Chapter 2, Section 6), so why didn't it stop this overwrite? Two separate things are going on here:

  • First, the specification itself makes no such promise. That default release orders earlier shared-memory loads before the arrival only inside the generic proxy. The next round's TMA write into this slot goes through the async proxy, and PTX requires a cross-proxy fence whenever two proxies access the same address (above).
  • Second, the compiled arrival instruction did not actually wait for those loads. When the arrival went out, the earlier shared-memory loads had not yet returned to registers. Adding an intra-CTA fence (fence.acq_rel.cta) before the arrival made it wait for the loads; the reason is not determined (see Chapter 8, Section 11).

Both safe engineering patterns aim for the exact same state—making sure the loads from slot ss are already sitting in private registers when the arrival goes out:

  • The first pattern is to use the loaded values in compute instructions before arriving. Because the compiler can still move those compute instructions past the arrival, you also put the intra-CTA fence from above right before the arrival so it waits for the shared-memory loads to return (Chapter 8, Section 11). Once the data is sitting in registers, no later write to SMEM through either proxy can touch it.
  • The second pattern is to issue the loads from slot ss, hold off on arriving, and wait on another signal first (in Chapter 8, that signal is the same step's full barrier on the activation ring buffer), then arrive on slot ss afterward. That intervening wait gives the loads from slot ss time to return to registers, though the specification does not guarantee it is long enough. You have to check the compiled instructions to verify that no load is still pending when the arrival goes out.

Mapping those two causes against Pattern 1 and Pattern 2 shows why each pattern is safe:

Cause of the WAR overwrite Safe Pattern 1 (consume loaded values + fence.acq_rel.cta before arrive) Safe Pattern 2 (issue loads, wait on another barrier first, then arrive on empty[s]) Specification guarantee
Cause 1: empty[s]'s default CTA release orders only the generic proxy, not next-round async-proxy TMA writes Data is already in private registers, so next-round TMA writes to SMEM cannot reach it (no cross-proxy fence needed) Data is likewise already in private registers, so next-round TMA writes to SMEM cannot reach it (no cross-proxy fence needed) PTX specification gives no cross-proxy ordering guarantee
Cause 2: compiled arrival instruction did not wait for prior shared-memory loads to return to registers Closed: fence.acq_rel.cta makes the arrival wait for shared-memory loads to return (underlying reason not determined) Closed: the intervening barrier wait gives loads time to return, verified by checking compiled machine instructions for zero pending loads Specification does not guarantee the wait is long enough; must verify compiled SASS

The final expert kernel in Chapter 8 uses the second pattern. After issuing the weight loads from slot ss, it waits on the same step's full barrier of the activation ring buffer, arrives on empty[s], and only then computes with those weights. Only on compiler versions whose compiled output we have checked does it omit the intra-CTA fence; every other compiler version retains the fence. In the standalone Stage 6 expert-kernel paired benchmark, comparing the delayed-arrival fix (moving arrival after the activation-ring full wait, with no intra-CTA fence) against the racy early-arrival baseline cut observed overwrites from 551 in about 4.58 million calls to 0 in about 4.40 million calls, slowing Stage 6 alone by about 0.4–1.6 µs (the racy baseline's per-shape microsecond totals were not retained, so the percentage share of Stage 6 was not measured; see Chapter 8, Section 11).

The upside of paired mbarrier handoffs is that only the producer and consumers touching that slot wait on each other, while other warps keep moving. Even though a single thread's unloaded arrive-plus-wait round trip takes about 200 cycles, in the steady state of a warp-specialized loop each step's handshake adds only about 27 cycles. The cost is two 8 B counters per slot—and whenever consumers arrive a little later, the producer refills that slot a little later, which makes the ring slightly shallower in practice.

8What If Data-Movement Warps Have Excess Registers While Compute Warps Do Not Have Enough?

Reallocate registers per warpgroup at kernel entry using setmaxnreg: the producer warpgroup lowers its quota and returns registers to the CTA pool, and the consumer warpgroups raise their quota to claim them, keeping the CTA's total registers within the amount allocated at launch.

Four consecutive warps whose starting warp index is a multiple of 4 (128 threads in all) form a warpgroup. The setmaxnreg instruction (per-warpgroup register reallocation) operates on whole warpgroups, and all 128 threads in a warpgroup must execute it together.

Picture a CTA with 1 producer warpgroup and 2 consumer warpgroups. Because setmaxnreg works at warpgroup granularity, even though a single thread can issue TMA loads (Section 5), the producer role still has to occupy a full warpgroup of 128 threads, bringing the CTA to 384 threads in all.

Note the change of example here: this 3-warpgroup (384-thread) CTA comes from our heavy single-layer prefill and decode matrix-multiply kernel (tile column width 256, 213,040 B of dynamic SMEM), not the 16 KiB-slot qkv_gate ring from Sections 5–6. On the consumer side, threads must accumulate results across many tokens simultaneously: each consumer warpgroup (128 threads) computes a 64-token-row × 256-column FP32 output tile, so every thread has to hold 64×256÷128=128 partial sums in registers at the same time (Chapter 5, Section 4 shows how a matrix tile maps across threads), on top of addresses and temporaries. Accordingly, this kernel sets consumers to 232 registers and the producer—which only issues copy and arrival instructions—to 40 registers.

If every thread in the CTA had to take the same number of registers, the math would never work: giving 232 registers to all 384 threads requires 384×232=89,088 registers—23,552 more than the SM's 65,536 limit—so the CTA could not even launch on one SM. To fit 384 threads into an SM at launch, each thread can take at most ⌊65,536÷384⌋ rounded down to a multiple of 8, which is 168 registers. That leaves consumers with only 168 registers instead of the 232 set in the code (whether 168 registers would be enough or spill to local memory, we did not measure).

Reallocating registers by warpgroup right at kernel entry untangles this in four steps (Figure 3-6):

  • At kernel launch: All 384 threads start with 168 registers each, the largest multiple of 8 that fits in one SM (384×168=64,512≤65,536; the next step up, 176, would take 67,584).
  • Producer releases registers: The 1 producer warpgroup runs setmaxnreg to drop its quota to 40, returning 128×(168−40)=16,384 registers to the CTA pool.
  • Consumer claims registers: Each of the 2 consumer warpgroups runs setmaxnreg (increase form) to raise its quota to 232, requesting 128×(232−168)=8,192 registers each (16,38416{,}384 in total). By the PTX specification, each consumer's setmaxnreg increase waits in hardware until the CTA's own register pool holds enough registers to satisfy that warpgroup's request—so consumers wait until the producer's decrease has deposited those 16,384 registers into the CTA pool (all transfers stay inside the CTA's own pool, while the remaining 65,536−64,512=1,024 registers stay unallocated in the SM pool).
  • Result: The CTA uses 128×40+256×232=5,120+59,392=64,512 registers, matching the exact total allocated at launch.

Keep in mind that setmaxnreg only reallocates per-thread register quotas—it never makes registers shared across threads: after reallocation every register remains private to its own thread (Primer 3, Section 3), so one warp cannot read another warp's registers; exchanging values across warps still goes through SMEM (Sections 5–7), while threads inside the same warp exchange register values with the shuffle instruction in Chapter 4, Section 5.

With this handoff, consumers get all 232 registers they need to hold their 128 accumulators in registers. The tradeoff is that all 128 threads in each warpgroup have to execute the instruction together, and the producer warpgroup is left with just 40 registers per thread, so it cannot take on other work. Because 64,512 registers nearly fills the SM's register pool, each SM can hold only 1 such CTA at a time (see Section 1 for running such 1-CTA/SM kernels persistently, its unmeasured isolated savings, and the slower counterexample in Chapter 9, Section 6). How those 12 warps on one SM map onto its scheduler partitions and get served cycle by cycle is covered in Chapter 4, Section 1 (with the unit summary table in Chapter 10, Section 6).

When does reallocating registers fail to help? Lowering the producer's register quota alone does not automatically save time: step g1 → g2 in the multi-token qkv_gate GEMM of Chapter 6, Section 8 tested dropping the producer to 24 registers and measured a delta of +0.09 / +0.18 µs (T=128/256), inside measurement noise with zero gain (not adopted; why it saved no time was not measured). Going the other way and adding two more consumer warpgroups to this 232-register-per-thread CTA does not work either: 4 consumer warpgroups would need 4×128×232=118,784 registers, far beyond the SM's pool even after borrowing from the producer (Chapter 8, Section 9); other consumer-warpgroup counts (such as 1 or 3) on this heavy GEMM were not tested in this book (unknown). Also, in a dense matrix multiply these two consumer warpgroups simply compute their own output tiles independently; when a long stretch of non-matrix-multiply work sits inside the loop (such as attention softmax in Chapter 7), how the two consumer warpgroups stagger by half a beat to take turns on Tensor Core (ping-pong) is covered in Chapter 7, Section 7.

One compiler pragma ties back to register spilling from Section 1: starting in PTX 9.0 with CUDA 13, a kernel can write .pragma "enable_smem_spilling" to spill registers into SMEM first (about 23 cycles conflict-free; see next section's chart) before falling back to local memory; however, the specification disallows it in kernels that use dynamic SMEM (Section 6) or setmaxnreg (this section), so none of this book's kernels with over-48 KiB TMA rings or setmaxnreg can use it.

9Why Does One Warp Reading an SMEM Column Queue Up, and How Can We Stagger It with Zero Space Overhead?

Hardware organizes SMEM into 32 parallel 4-byte-wide banks, so requests in the same load that target different 4 B words within one bank must be served in serial order; bitwise-XORing the column chunk index with the row index spreads same-column data across distinct banks at zero extra byte cost.

Take the 16 KiB WW tile staged in SMEM in Section 5 right away to see why column reads queue up: each row is 128 B, divided into 8 chunks of 16 B indexed by c=0..7. For 16 B shared-memory loads per thread, hardware breaks a warp into 4 8-thread groups and processes them one phase at a time (see the second chart below); when one 8-thread group in a phase issues 16 B loads for the same column chunk cc across 8 consecutive rows (8 threads ×\times 16 B = 128 B; how wgmma in Chapter 5, Section 4 groups and orders its internal SMEM matrix-descriptor reads across those 8 rows is undocumented by NVIDIA and unknown), without swizzling, row rr, column chunk cc sits at byte offset offset(r,c)=128r+16c, spacing those 8 rows' column-cc chunks by exact multiples of 128 B.

Why does a 128 B row spacing make all 8 requests collide? Under the hood, SMEM is divided into 32 parallel shared-memory banks, each 4 B wide and able to serve one 4 B word per cycle. Consecutive 4 B words map to banks 0, 1, …, 31 in order, so every 128 B spans all 32 banks and SMEM as a whole can deliver at most 32×4=128 B per cycle. Serving all requests of a load instruction in one pass is called 1 wavefront; if threads in the same load request different 4 B words from the same bank, hardware cannot deliver them all in one pass and splits the instruction into multiple wavefronts served sequentially—a bank conflict, with DD requests targeting distinct 4 B words in one bank producing a DD-way bank conflict. Look back at those 8 column-cc chunks spaced 128 B apart: all 8 threads land on the exact same 4 banks—banks 4c..4c+3—causing an 8-way bank conflict that forces each load into 8 wavefronts and reading all 8 chunk columns into 64 wavefronts in total (Figure 3-7 Mode 1).

In our measurements, conflicts start slowing down back-to-back issue from 4-way onward: under an 8-way conflict, a single warp's SMEM read throughput drops to about a quarter (see the first chart below), while 16 B loads evaluate conflicts within each 8-thread group (see the second chart below). Two details round this out: when multiple threads read the exact same 4 B word, hardware performs a broadcast of that word to all requesting threads at once with no conflict; and while 1 wavefront takes 1 cycle at peak hardware rate, in the first microbenchmark below each extra wavefront adds about 2 cycles to dependent latency, and we did not measure why it is 2 rather than 1.

To fix this, we turn on XOR swizzle and change the on-chip byte offset to:

offset(r,c)=128r+16(c⊕(r mod 8))\mathrm{offset}(r, c) = 128r + 16\,(c \oplus (r \bmod 8))

Watch what happens now when you fix the column chunk index cc and step rr across 8 consecutive rows: c⊕(r mod 8) visits every number from 00 to 77 exactly once. Those 8 chunks of 16 B now land on 8 distinct groups of 4 banks, spreading cleanly across all 32 banks. The 8-way conflict drops to 0, each load finishes in 1 wavefront, reading all 8 columns takes just 8 wavefronts in total, and it costs zero extra bytes of SMEM (Figure 3-7 Mode 2). Keep in mind that 64 → 8 is a wavefront count, not an 8× speedup in time: every load has a fixed pipeline latency and an issue-interval floor—in the measured 4 B load chart above, 8-way conflict versus conflict-free (1-way) stretches dependent latency from 23.06 to 37.06 cycles (derived 1.6×) and back-to-back issue interval from 4.30 to 16.31 cycles (derived 3.8×), while the cycle time of reading this 8-row ×\times 128 B slab with 16 B loads (or matrix instructions) was not measured.

What XOR swizzle requires in return is that both the SMEM writer and the SMEM reader use the same address formula. With TMA transfers, enabling 128 B swizzle in the host-side tensor descriptor makes the TMA hardware permute bytes by this formula automatically as it writes into SMEM (Section 5, Path 4). Watch one alignment rule: TMA hardware only requires a 128 B-aligned SMEM base address, but because the 128 B swizzle pattern repeats every 1,024 B (8 rows), the formula above anchors row 0 cleanly only when the buffer base is 1,024 B-aligned—otherwise the pattern shifts by (address÷128) mod 8 rows. Every kernel in this book aligns to 1,024 B.

There is another classic way to stagger banks: row-stride padding. It fits small tables where 32 threads read the same column of 4 B words across 32 rows. When the row width is 32 words (128 B), the same column across all 32 rows lands on a single bank, causing a 32-way conflict. Pad each row with 1 extra word so the width becomes 33 words, and the same column shifts by 1 bank on each row, spreading all 32 rows across all 32 banks at the cost of 4 extra bytes per row.

Each method is built for its own access pattern. Because the 128 B XOR swizzle pattern repeats every 8 rows, if you use it when reading a column of 4 B words across 32 rows, rows rr, r+8, r+16, and r+24 still land on the same bank and leave a 4-way conflict—so that pattern needs row-stride padding instead. We will see XOR swizzle in action when reading the KV cache in Chapter 7, Section 5; narrower tiles with 64 B rows use a matching 64 B swizzle mode also covered in Chapter 7, Section 5 (PTX also defines a 32 B swizzle mode, unused in this book's kernels).

Across this chapter, six software execution and on-chip staging units have appeared; the table below maps all six to their hardware counterparts on one SM and what each holds:

Software unit Hardware unit on one SM What it holds
CTA (thread block) 1 CTA slot on one SM (cap 32; Section 1) Its allocated warp slots, per-CTA register pool, and SMEM share (plus 1 KiB driver reserve), held from dispatch until exit
warp (32 consecutive threads) 1 warp slot (cap 64) and registers allocated in 256-register chunks Per-thread private registers and the coalesced 32 B sector requests issued together to the LSU (Section 2)
warpgroup (4 consecutive warps starting at a multiple of 4; 128 threads) Unit of setmaxnreg reallocation (and of wgmma in Chapter 5, Section 4) Register quota released to or claimed from the CTA pool in lockstep (e.g., producer 128×40=5,120, each consumer 128×232=29,696)
Elected thread (1 leader chosen via elect.sync in the producer warp) SM's TMA unit and mbarrier expected-byte registration Registers expected bytes on full[s] and issues TMA bulk-copy commands for the ring (0 data-staging registers; Sections 5 and 7)
Ring slot slot[s] 16 KiB slice of SMEM (in our example) plus a pair of hardware barriers One tile in flight or in compute, paired with full[s] and empty[s] mbarrier objects (8 B each: arrival count, byte count, and 0/1 parity bit; Sections 6–7)
8-thread group (sub-warp conflict-evaluation group for 16 B SMEM loads) One 128 B bank phase across all 32 4 B SMEM banks (this section) 8 threads × 16 B = 128 B of shared-memory requests, served in 1 wavefront when conflict-free

Now recap the mechanisms from Sections 5–9 with each number kept on its own kernel (Section 8's heavy GEMM CTA is a separate example from Sections 5–7 and 9's 16 KiB qkv_gate ring): at kernel entry, the heavy GEMM CTA (384 threads, 213,040 B of dynamic SMEM) uses setmaxnreg to drop its producer warpgroup to 40 registers and raise its two consumer warpgroups to 232 registers (Section 8); on the W𝑡𝑖𝑙𝑒:[128,64]BF16\shape{W_{tile}}{128,\;64}{BF16} = 16 KiB ring of Sections 5–7 and 9, 1 leader thread elected via elect.sync in the producer warp waits on empty[s], records 16,384 B on full[s] of the 4-slot 64 KiB ring buffer (Section 6, keeping 3 slots = 48 KiB in flight on the plateau), and issues 1 multidimensional TMA command with 128 B XOR swizzle in its descriptor (Section 5 Path 4, 0 data registers, about 43-cycle startup); TMA writes all 16,384 B into slot ss permuted by c⊕(r mod 8) and decrements the byte counter to 0, flipping full[s] with its built-in cross-proxy fence (about 27 cycles per steady-state handshake, Section 7); consumer warps then read slot ss column-wise conflict-free (1 wavefront per 8-thread phase, 8 wavefronts across all 8 columns, Section 9), and arrive on empty[s] only after those shared-memory loads have returned to private registers so next-round TMA never causes a WAR overwrite (Section 7).

As for the shared-memory mechanisms assembled across Sections 5–9—TMA, ring buffers, mbarrier, setmaxnreg, and XOR swizzle—Chapter 6, Section 8 tallies how they stack up alongside cross-chapter changes from g0 to g5 and what measured payoff they deliver on multi-token qkv_gate (T≥8), after Chapter 5 connects them to asynchronous Tensor Core execution.

Takeaway: How quickly and safely an SM gets its data comes down to three things: how many contiguous useful bytes each load instruction brings back, how many bytes the warps actually resident on the SM keep in flight at once, and whether each SMEM buffer slot is handed back only after the data read from it has returned to registers.

Next chapter's question: In Section 4's v6 (1 warp per row, the whole grid fitting in a single wave), each SM has only about 17 resident warps and 8.7 KiB in flight; keeping that skeleton without adding resident warps per SM, how does each sub-partition inside the SM pick a warp to issue an instruction each cycle and what holds back or releases the next instruction, and how can a single thread issue multiple independent loads back to back without waiting for the previous load to return to lift recurring bytes in flight per SM from 8.7 KiB back into the 95%-knee band from Chapter 2, Section 3?

Single SMSP — When Each Cycle Can Issue Only 1 Instruction, How Do We Keep Waiting from Stretching Total Runtime?
