In Chapter 3, Section 4, we shrank each CTA in gemv's v6 down to a single warp computing 1 row so the whole grid fits in a single wave, and it actually ran slower than v5—because each SM received only about 17.45 resident warps on average and each thread kept only one 16 B load outstanding, dropping concurrent in-flight reads per SM to just ~8.7 KiB. Keeping that single-warp, single-wave skeleton without adding resident warps, how can one thread keep firing multiple independent loads without waiting for the previous load to return? To see that, we need to look one level deeper inside the SM: the SMSP (SM sub-partition, 4 per SM).

Chapter 3, Section 1 worked out that one SM holds at most 64 resident warps. Split them evenly across the 4 SMSPs, and each SMSP gets 1 warp scheduler and holds at most 16 resident warps. An SMSP scheduler can issue only 1 instruction per cycle, while a memory load waits tens to thousands of cycles (~23 cycles for on-chip shared memory in Chapter 3, Section 9; 600.2 measured cycles—about 600 cycles—for an unloaded HBM round trip, and longer under load in Chapter 2, Sections 2 and 3)—how do we keep that wait from turning straight into total runtime?

In this chapter we follow a single warp through one full pass: what it does while waiting for data, who waits for whom when its 32 threads split across branch paths, and why reducing 32 per-thread partial sums into one number leaves only 1 thread doing the work.

1Only 1 Issue Slot per Cycle: Which Waits Actually Count Toward Total Runtime?

An issue slot sits idle only on cycles when the SMSP has not a single eligible warp; whether those idle cycles add to total runtime depends on whether issue slots are the first resource to saturate (Section 3 shows which resource saturates first in gemv).

On every clock cycle (Chapter 2, Section 2), the SMSP's warp scheduler scans the warps resident in its sub-partition (Figure 4-1). Once a warp's next instruction has been fetched and decoded, all of its operands are ready, and the target execution unit is free, that warp is eligible.

Each SMSP has only 1 issue slot per cycle. The scheduler picks 1 eligible warp, issues 1 instruction from it, and marks that warp selected. Switching between warps takes zero time: every resident warp keeps its registers on-chip the whole time (Chapter 3, Section 1), so picking warp A on this cycle and warp B on the next never saves or restores any state. The table below puts what one SMSP owns alongside the two schematic assumptions we use in our figures and resource math:

Item Full SM (Chapter 3, Section 1) Single SMSP (1 of 4) Documented fact or schematic assumption
Scheduler & issue slot 4 independent schedulers 1 scheduler, 1 issue slot per cycle Documented hardware rule
Resident warp slots & lifetime 64 warp slots 16 warp slots Documented rule: a warp stays on its assigned SMSP from launch to exit
32-bit register pool 65,536 registers 16,384 registers (allocated per SMSP, 0-cycle switch) Documented rule: rounded up per thread in multiples of 8 registers
How CTA warps map to SMSPs Grid assigns CTAs across 132 SMs Schematic assumption: a 4-warp CTA places 1 warp on each SMSP; single-warp CTAs also spread evenly across the 4 SMSPs Real CTA-to-SM and warp-to-SMSP assignment rules are undocumented and not measured (whether software can choose the SMSP was not determined)
Tie-break among eligible warps Each of the 4 SMSPs picks independently Schematic assumption: Figures 4-1 and 4-2 pick the least-recently-issued (oldest) eligible warp Real hardware pick policy is undocumented (and not measured)

What about the other resident warps that don't issue on that cycle? They fall into two buckets. Some are not selected—ready to go, just not the warp chosen on this cycle. The rest are stalled, still waiting for data to return, for a barrier to release, or for a busy execution unit to free up. Only when the entire SMSP has zero eligible warps does the cycle count as no eligible, leaving the issue slot idle. Even if 15 warps sit not selected on a cycle, as long as 1 warp issues an instruction, that cycle's issue slot is full.

Using the even-split assumption in Row 4 of the table above, look at Mode 1 of Figure 4-1, which is v1 from Primer 3: each 128-thread (4-warp) CTA computes 1 row, and each thread loads one BF16 element (2 B) at a time. One SM holds 16 such CTAs, so each SMSP holds 16 warps—one from each CTA, each reading a different row of WW. On every iteration, each warp sends 2 loads to the Load/Store Unit (LSU; Chapter 3, Section 2), one BF16 of WW and one of xx, and then quickly stalls waiting for the data to return: because the input vector xx is only 16 KiB and hits mainly in the local SM's L1 cache (~94% hit rate measured on v3, which reads xx the same way; v1 was not profiled again, and misses hit in L2; Chapter 2, Section 2), Figure 4-1 draws only the WW load to HBM and the HBM bytes-in-flight numbers below count only WW; the figure plots each WW wait as a constant 600 cycles—the unloaded HBM round trip measured by pointer chasing in Chapter 2, Section 2 (600.2 cycles), used here as a constant schematic latency. Once all 16 warps are stuck waiting for WW, most cycles end up no eligible.

2Scoreboards and In-Order Issue: How Does a Warp Keep Moving After Firing a Load?

The scoreboard marks only the pending destination register as not ready, so the warp keeps going until the first instruction that uses it; the more independent instructions you pack in between, the fewer warps you need to keep the issue slot full.

Every GPU warp issues instructions strictly in program order (in-order issue), so it cannot jump ahead of a stalled instruction out of order. So how does it keep moving right after firing a load? With a scoreboard (Figure 4-2). When the warp issues a load, the hardware logs an entry on the scoreboard, and the warp keeps issuing the independent instructions that follow as long as they don't touch the pending result. Only when the warp hits the first instruction that actually uses that result does it wait for the scoreboard to clear, at which point the scheduler switches to another eligible warp. According to public reverse-engineering analyses, the compiler encodes ahead of time in each machine instruction's control bits which scoreboard to wait on and the minimum stall interval (NVIDIA's official documentation doesn't disclose this encoding; see Chapter 6, Section 6), while the hardware tracks at runtime when the data arrives and clears the scoreboard. Global memory loads and shared memory (SMEM) loads use this exact same mechanism; only the number of wait cycles differs.

Now apply Little's Law (Chapter 2, Section 3) to a single SMSP, where the resource we want to keep fed is the 1-instruction-per-cycle issue slot. (Here we count instructions in flight; Section 3 will count bytes in flight.) Suppose a load takes DD cycles to return, and a warp can issue nn instructions—including the load itself—between firing the load and first using its result. Since the issue slot wants 1 instruction every cycle, keeping it full takes about D/nD / n warps taking turns:

required resident warps≈⌈Dn⌉\mathrm{required\ resident\ warps} \approx \left\lceil \frac{D}{n} \right\rceil

Take a short-latency load first. A conflict-free SMEM load takes ~23 cycles (Chapter 3, Section 9). If each load is followed by 3 independent instructions (n=4), then ⌈23/4⌉=6 warps taking turns are enough to reach 0 no eligible cycles (Figure 4-2, Mode 4). With only 4 resident warps, they can't cover the whole wait window, and idle cycles show up on the timeline (Mode 3).

Now flip it around: what if the next load's address depends on the value returned by the previous load? Say three tables sit in SMEM and we chain lookups: idx = len[i]; p = table[idx]; v = data[p];. Right after each load issues, the very next instruction needs its result, pinning n=1 at every step. At about 23 cycles per load, 3 chained loads wait about 69 cycles in total, stalling a single warp on the scoreboard three times in a row (Figure 4-2, Mode 1). A single serial chain can't be split apart on its own. If an outer loop wraps it, though, len[i + 1] in iteration i+1 doesn't depend on iteration ii. While iteration ii is still waiting on data, the warp can fire off the next iteration's load early and stretch nn larger (v7 in the next section fires several independent WW loads ahead in just this way; Chapter 7, Section 6 walks through cross-iteration page-table prefetching in full). The catch is register pressure: every extra pending load ties up another set of destination registers, and using more registers may cut the number of resident warps (Chapter 3, Section 1). We check that trade-off in the next section when we run the numbers for v7.

3When Memory-Bound, Do You Feed the Issue Slot or HBM? (The Mechanism Behind gemv v6 → v7)

A memory-bandwidth-bound kernel needs to saturate SM-wide bytes in flight, not issue slots—and the way to do it is to have each thread fire several independent wide loads before using the first result.

Whether an under-filled issue slot hurts depends on the resource racing against it—HBM bandwidth: whichever resource hits its ceiling first sets total runtime through its own Little's Law equation. Because gemv streams 37.75 MB of weights and uses each weight for only a single multiply-add, HBM is the resource that hits its ceiling first. In our Chapter 2, Section 3 H200 measurement streaming 4 GiB across all 132 SMs, ordinary 16 B loads reach 95% of the bandwidth plateau at about 24–40 KiB/SM in flight in machine code depending on loads per thread, and at 64 KiB/SM every tested configuration reaches at least 98.3% (enough, not the minimum); once HBM is on that plateau, dividing in-flight bytes by bandwidth at 64 KiB/SM puts the estimated upper bound on mean round-trip latency at about 1.9 µs (about 3,400 cycles at about 1.8 GHz; v7's actual loaded round-trip time below was not measured), leaving the SMSP issue slot idle on roughly two-thirds to three-quarters of cycles.

What sets concurrent bytes in flight per SM? Because a warp stalls as soon as it hits an instruction that consumes a pending load, concurrent bytes in flight per SM at any point equal resident warps × 32 threads per warp × loads currently outstanding per thread × bytes per load. Why not raise the first factor—resident warps per SM—instead? Because keeping 1 single-warp CTA per row from v6 onward means 2,304 rows across 132 SMs supply only 17.45 resident warps per SM on average; packing in more warps would mean splitting a row across multiple warps as in v5, bringing back a cross-warp SMEM reduction and CTA barrier (Chapter 3, Section 4 and Section 5 below). So we turn the third factor—loads outstanding per thread—instead.

Look back at Figure 4-1: both modes spend over 80% of their cycles in no eligible, yet their runtimes are worlds apart because of how many bytes they keep in flight. In Mode 1 (v1 from Primer 3), each thread loads only 1 BF16 of WW per iteration, so 16 warps on an SMSP hold just 1 KiB in flight at once, or 4 KiB across the SM. In v6, each thread keeps only one 16 B load of WW outstanding per step, which still comes to only about 8.7 KiB per SM. Mode 2 is a constant-latency schematic model: it holds the ~600-cycle (600.2-cycle) unloaded HBM round trip from Chapter 2, Section 2 fixed and models 4 warps per SMSP with 56 schematic instructions per batch (eight 16 B WW loads plus 48 compute instructions waiting as a batch), giving 16 KiB of issued loads in flight on one SMSP (64 KiB across the 4 SMSPs, sitting in the >98% plateau region of Chapter 2, Section 3 inside Mode 2's recurring 8-load model) and 82% no eligible cycles. Mode 1 and v6 are slow because they keep too few bytes in flight, not because their issue slots sit empty.

Keep the schematic scale separate from real v7: in real v7 machine code, each batch executes 286 instructions (rather than the toy's compressed 56), hitting about 69.8 KiB/SM in a one-time opening burst and keeping 3–6 loads per thread, or about 26–52 KiB/SM, in flight afterward (see the next paragraph); and in real execution, both the plateau throughput calculation below (about 64%–67% non-issue cycles) and profiler measurements on v8 (71.6% non-active issue cycles, or about 28%–29% active—likewise just over 70% non-active—when scaled by instruction count and duration to v7) put non-issue cycles at about 64%–72%—fewer than the schematic's 82%, though roughly two-thirds to over 70% of cycles still issue nothing.

v6 → v7 raises that third factor by fully unrolling the loop so each thread fires multiple wide loads ahead of first use. In Chapter 3, Section 4, v6 took K as a runtime argument so its loop stayed un-unrolled: averaging about 17.45 resident warps per SM, each thread issued just one 16 B load of WW per step before immediately running multiply-adds, leaving only about 8.7 KiB/SM in flight throughout. In v7, we make K = 8192 a compile-time constant and fully unroll all 32 chunks (written in source as groups of BATCH = 8 that stage eight uint4 loads of WW and xx before the multiply-adds, together with __launch_bounds__(32), whose standalone effect was not measured). In the compiled machine instructions (SASS), the compiler places 8 loads of WW and 7 loads of xx back to back ahead of the very first multiply-add. Counting only WW, that opening burst lifts concurrent WW bytes in flight to a one-time peak of about 69.8 KiB/SM during the initial first-byte wait, while across the remaining 24 loads of WW each thread keeps 3–6 loads outstanding (about 26–52 KiB/SM, around the 95% knee region noted at the start of this section):

17.45×32×8×16 B≈69.8 KiB17.45 \times 32 \times 8 \times 16\ \mathrm{B} \approx 69.8\ \mathrm{KiB}

Even though the remaining 24 loads of WW step down to 3–6 per thread, two pieces of evidence show that v7 at 2,304 rows already comes within at most a few percent of the HBM plateau in steady state (inferred): first, scanning the SASS instructions linearly at each WW load's first register use (an instruction-schedule metric rather than a runtime time average), v7 averages 4.06 unconsumed WW loads across its 32 first-use points—above the 3.0 first-use average of a pure streaming control kernel that stages 4 × 16 B loads per thread (peak 32 KiB/SM, matching the K=4 point on Chapter 2, Section 3's curve) and already reaches a 4.43 TB/s large-size slope (about 97.6% of the plateau); second, doubling v7 itself from 2,304 to 4,608 rows (where residency rises to its 20-warp/SM cap) streams the extra 37.75 MB at a marginal rate of 4.54 TB/s (with a 4.59 TB/s slope up to 36,864 rows). We check both pieces of evidence because about 69.8 KiB/SM is only a one-time opening peak from the first 8 back-to-back loads, whereas the remaining 24 loads of WW sit interleaved with multiply-adds at 3–6 loads per thread (about 26–52 KiB/SM), keeping time-averaged bytes in flight below the opening peak (neither the runtime time average nor v7's actual loaded round-trip time was measured; see Section 6); with steady-state bandwidth already near the plateau, v7 at 2,304 rows is held back mainly by the fixed cost of a short 37.75 MB launch rather than in-flight starvation (the split between first-byte latency and CTA completion skew remains open; see Section 6).

To answer Section 1's question directly: in gemv, HBM bandwidth saturates first, so the issue slot neither needs to be full nor can be. Check the throughput first: in v7, each warp executes 1,231 machine instructions in total (1,144 in the main loop) to stream 32×512 B=16,384 B of weights WW, or about 0.075 instructions per byte of WW (about 0.070 in the main loop). Across all 132 SMs (132×4=528 SMSPs) running at about 1.8 GHz, even at the measured HBM plateau of about 4.54 TB/s (Chapter 2, Section 3), each SMSP receives at most about 4.8 B per cycle; multiplied by about 0.070–0.075 instructions per byte, that demands at most about 0.33–0.36 instructions per cycle—roughly a third of the 1-instruction-per-cycle issue slot (and when v8 reaches 67.1% of peak DRAM bandwidth below, the profiler measures an active issue-cycle share of 28.4%). Now cross-check Section 2's issue-slot formula ⌈D/n⌉\lceil D / n \rceil: at the unloaded HBM round trip of D≈600 measured cycles (Chapter 2, Section 2), a v7 warp keeps roughly 4 loads of WW in flight per round trip and pairs each load with about 36 unpack, multiply-add, and address instructions, giving n≈4×36=144 instructions per round trip (not n=4 from Section 2's SMEM toy), so ⌈600/144⌉=5 warps per SMSP—well within the 16-warp limit—could already fill the slot; what stops it is not warp count, but that HBM cannot deliver data fast enough to feed 1 instruction per cycle, leaving most cycles with nothing to issue.

What does v7 pay for those extra loads? Every outstanding 16 B (128-bit) load ties up four 32-bit destination registers (Chapter 3, Section 3), so the 8 loads of WW and 7 loads of xx held concurrently at the opening already occupy 15×4=60 registers; together with accumulators, addresses, and other unitemized state, per-thread register usage climbs from 30 in v6 to 83 in v7, rounding up to 88 under the 8-register allocation granularity (Chapter 3, Section 1). Under the per-SMSP pool and even-spread assumption in Section 1's table (16,384 registers allocated independently per SMSP, with single-warp CTAs spread evenly across the 4 SMSPs), each SMSP fits ⌊16,384/(32×88)⌋=5 warps, so each SM can still hold up to 20 single-warp CTAs—still above the 17.45 CTAs per SM assigned by the grid. So we don't lose a single resident warp: the one-time opening peak inside the initial first-byte wait scales by the full 8× over v6 (8.7→69.8 KiB/SM), while steady-state throughput is set by the recurring 3–6 loads of WW per thread kept outstanding afterward (about 26–52 KiB/SM, or 3–6× v6's 8.7 KiB/SM; see Section 6 for the 1.43× measured kernel speedup). If register pressure pushed the residency cap below the 17.45 warps assigned by the grid, resident warps would drop and the opening peak would no longer scale by 8× (we did not measure such a counterexample on gemv). Why hold those in-flight bytes in registers at all, when TMA in Chapter 3, Section 5 moves bytes using 0 data registers? Because at T=1 each byte of WW is used once by a single thread, so the register path is sufficient (opening of Chapter 3), and choosing ordinary loads versus TMA does not change the HBM bandwidth ceiling (1D TMA reaches 95% of its streaming plateau at about 36–40 KiB/SM, or about 32 KiB/SM with 2 KiB copies at 4 CTAs/SM; see Chapter 3, Section 6 and Chapter 10, Section 6). The table below puts the residency, bytes-in-flight, and register budgets of v1, v6, and v7 side by side:

Version Resident warps / SM WW loads in flight / thread (opening burst; later) WW bytes in flight / SM (KiB/SM) Registers / thread (used → allocated) Warps / SMSP allowed by registers
v1 64 (16 4-warp CTAs, capped by warp slots) 1 × 2 B load per iteration 4.0 (recurring) 22 → 24 (Ch. 3 §1) ⌊16,384/(32×24)⌋=21→ capped at 16 by warp slots
v6 ~17.45 (grid 2,304 rows ÷\div 132 SMs) 1 × 16 B load per step ~8.7 (recurring) 30 → 32 ⌊16,384/(32×32)⌋=16 (SM-wide capped at 8/SMSP by 32 CTA slots)
v7 ~17.45 (same grid, unclipped by registers) 8 × 16 B opening; 3–6 across later 24 issues ~69.8 opening peak; ~26–52 recurring (time avg. not measured) 83 → 88 (60 held by 8 WW + 7 xx loads) ⌊16,384/(32×88)⌋=5 (20 CTAs/SM >17.45> 17.45)

In source attribution, full loop unrolling—rather than the manual BATCH = 8 staging array—is what enables the compiler to hoist 7–8 loads of WW (inferred from a separate sweep on v9—the next kernel in Chapter 5, Section 2, which rewrites unpacking and uses 8 accumulators on top of v8—that kept full unrolling across BATCH = 1..16 and hoisted 7–8 loads at every setting, with BATCH = 1 hoisting 7 loads in 66 registers at 14.37 µs vs. 14.75 µs for v8 and default v9 in that campaign for reasons not determined; not expanded here).

With the main-loop memory wait pulled down, v6 and v7 still carry a one-lane epilogue after the main loop to sum the 32 per-thread partial sums of one warp into a single output. How long is that one-lane tail in machine code, and does it show up in total runtime (end of Section 4 and Section 5)? Answering that starts with what happens when the 32 threads of a warp take different branch paths.

4When a Warp Issues One Branch Path at a Time, Who Waits for Whom?

Short conditionals use predication to mask writeback at almost no cost; long divergent branches inside a warp have to run one path after the other, while branches split along whole-warp boundaries never hold each other up.

Pick up the question from the end of Section 3 right on v7's post-loop tail: once all 32 threads write their partial sums to shared memory and cross the CTA barrier, if (tid == 0) leaves thread 0 alone to sum 32 values serially—how many machine-code cycles does that one-lane tail cost, and how much of it shows up in total runtime? Inside a warp, those 32 threads are called 32 lanes. Starting with compute capability 7.0 (NVIDIA's version number for a GPU architecture; H200 is 9.0), GPUs use Independent Thread Scheduling: each lane keeps its own program counter tracking the next instruction it will run, yet on any cycle the warp scheduler still issues only 1 instruction from this warp, and the active lanes sitting at that instruction execute it together—an execution model called SIMT (Single Instruction, Multiple Threads; see Figure 4-3).

Before pricing v7's 32-value tail, we compare three post-barrier branching variants on Primer 3's v1 epilogue in Figure 4-3 (shown on v1 first because Figure 4-3 holds the work fixed at 128 additions to compare SASS instruction counts side by side):

  • Variant 1 (short conditional with predication): Every thread has a few 1-bit predicate registers, such as P0. On a short conditional when more code follows—such as if (tid == 0) y[row] = sum; (this variant omits additions to isolate predication itself)—the compiler emits no branch jump at all, attaching a predicate (such as @!P0) to the instruction instead. All 32 lanes issue the instruction together, and lanes where the condition is false simply suppress writeback: only lane 0 stores the value already in its register to y[row] (the compiler places kernel launch parameters such as y in constant memory, which the SM reads through its read-only constant cache with LDC instructions; its read latency was not measured—see Appendix B, Section 4, No. 27), finishing in one pass with zero jumps.
  • Variant 2 (one-sided long branch if (tid == 0), shown on v1's 128 additions in Figure 4-3 and then applied to v6/v7's 32 additions): Because no code follows if (tid == 0) at the end of the kernel, the compiler emits a predicated exit instruction @P0 EXIT right at the branch entry to terminate the other 31 lanes permanently, yet the warp cannot vacate its SMSP slot until lane 0 finishes its serial sum (the tail holds only this warp's own slot; while lane 0 waits on an addition or shared-memory read, other eligible warps on the same SMSP still issue normally, as in Section 1). A floating-point multiply-add takes about 4 measured cycles before the next dependent instruction can use its result (Chapter 5, Section 1), and we estimate a floating-point addition at the same value. For v1's 128 partial sums, walking v1's actual runtime-blockDim.x SASS (231 dynamic post-barrier instructions across 8 loop passes) with the compiler-encoded issue-stall intervals from Section 2 and the ~32-cycle full-warp 16 B SMEM read wait from Chapter 3, Section 9 puts this tail at about 970 cycles (about 923 cycles if 1-lane 16 B SMEM reads—not measured separately—are estimated at about 26 cycles from the 2-cycle-per-wavefront slope, with the upper bound not derived and standalone duration not measured; Figure 4-3 draws the ideal fully unrolled constant-128 bound of 128×4+32= 544 cycles, or about 538 cycles at ~26 cycles), with just 1 of the 32 lanes doing useful work (v2–v5 were not determined). Coming back to v6 and v7, each CTA is down to a single warp with only 32 partial sums, yet that same @P0 EXIT plus lane-0 serial loop still burns at least about 380 cycles in machine code (broken down in Section 5, with its end-to-end share examined in Section 6).
  • Variant 3 (two-sided long branch, illustrative code if (lane < 16) {…} else {…}, 128 additions per branch): Once a branch body is too long to predicate and both paths must later rejoin, you get branch divergence. Hardware tracks which lanes participate in the current instruction with a 32-bit active mask: the warp issues instructions for only one path at a time while lanes on the other path sit idle. In the SASS we inspect, the SMSP's convergence barrier unit (CBU) manages reconvergence: before a divergent branch, the compiler places a BSSY instruction that records the reconvergence PC and participating lane mask in the CBU, and at the reconvergence point it places a BSYNC where lanes finishing the first path wait until the other path arrives, restoring the lanes recorded at BSSY to run together again (all 32 if all 32 were active before the split, while lanes that already exited never return; see Chapter 10, Section 9 for a case study where BSSY counts change). If the warp finishes one path before starting the other, the 128 additions of the first 16 lanes and the 128 additions of the last 16 lanes add straight together (~2×512 cycles; we did not measure whether hardware interleaves the two paths to hide part of each wait).

As noted above, from compute capability 7.0 each lane has its own program counter. On GPUs below compute capability 7.0, the 32 lanes of a warp shared one program counter and one active mask: lanes of the same warp on different branch paths could not signal each other or exchange data, and algorithms that share data under locks could deadlock. With Independent Thread Scheduling, lanes of one warp can diverge and reconverge at a granularity smaller than the whole warp (Figure 4-3, Mode 4), so the assumption that all 32 lanes of a warp stay in lockstep at every instruction no longer holds. When code needs a group of lanes in one warp to align at a point and to make their earlier shared- or global-memory writes visible to one another, it calls __syncwarp(mask) explicitly: the non-exited lanes in mask continue only after all of them arrive there (mask defaults to 0xffffffff, all 32 lanes; Chapter 8, Section 11 uses it so each warp aligns before lane 0 issues a single release). We looked at its machine code in two cases: when we add __syncwarp() after Variant 2's if (tid == 0) block and more code follows, the compiler places BSSY / BSYNC around the branch and emits no WARPSYNC instruction; in the other SASS we sampled, a full-mask __syncwarp() compiles into one separate WARPSYNC.ALL (we did not measure the sync time in either case). Per-lane program counters also let one lane of a warp stay in a loop and poll for data that another thread writes while the other lanes move on; but these paths still take turns on the warp's one-path-at-a-time issue, and Chapter 8, Section 11 shows a case where this slows progress.

By contrast, if you split a branch along whole-warp boundaries—such as if (warp_id == 0)—all 32 lanes in a warp see the exact same condition, so the warp never diverges. That is how Chapter 3, Section 7 separates producer warps from consumer warps; the trade-off is that work can only be handed out in 32-thread chunks, and we did not measure the time cost of that coarser granularity separately. One more rule to keep in mind: __syncthreads() requires every thread in the CTA to reach the exact same barrier instruction, so you can't put it inside a branch taken by only some threads; when whole-warp branches for different roles do need to meet at a barrier, they use a named barrier (bar.sync) that specifies only the participating thread count (used in practice in Chapter 7, Section 7). Next, we break down v7's at-least-~380-cycle one-lane tail and replace it.

5Keeping the Reduction Inside One Warp: How Does Warp Shuffle Eliminate Shared Memory and CTA Barriers? (The Mechanism Behind gemv v7 → v8)

A reduction across at most 32 threads can read neighbor registers directly in 5 warp-shuffle steps, bypassing both shared memory and the CTA barrier.

Now replace v7's SMEM epilogue with a warp shuffle (Figure 4-4, Mode 2). In v8, the code calls __shfl_xor_sync(0xffffffff, acc, o), which lets each thread read acc from the register of thread lane XOR o. Why the _sync suffix and the 32-bit lane mask 0xffffffff in the first argument? As Section 4 explained, Independent Thread Scheduling no longer guarantees that all 32 lanes of a warp stay in lockstep by default, and a _sync shuffle folds __syncwarp(mask)-style alignment straight into the instruction: 0xffffffff means all 32 lanes take part, and the instruction waits for those lanes to align before reading neighbor registers. Compiled to the machine instruction SHFL.BFLY and issued through the Load/Store Unit (LSU; Chapter 3, Section 2), an XOR warp shuffle exchanges values between registers without reading or writing shared memory or global memory. Compared with the SMEM version (Figure 4-4, Mode 1)—which keeps a CTA barrier so all 32 threads finish writing shared memory before thread 0 reads their values—a warp shuffle never touches shared memory, so that barrier goes away too.

Before the shuffle begins, each lane has already summed the dot products of its own 32 chunks of 16 B (8 BF16 elements per chunk multiplied and accumulated against the matching entries of xx) into its private register acc during the main loop (the exact lane-to-column indexing formula is not expanded here and was not verified against source), so each of the 32 lanes starts with 1 initial partial sum. The reduction then runs log⁡232=5 halving steps with o = 16, 8, 4, 2, 1: in C++ source semantics, each step performs 1 warp shuffle plus 1 addition so all 32 lanes hold the full sum before lane 0 writes y[row], whereas in v8's compiled machine code all 32 lanes issue the 5th shuffle and lanes 1–31 immediately exit (@P0 EXIT, matching Variant 2 in Section 4) during its wait, leaving lane 0 alone to run the 5th addition and an unpredicated store. Each shuffle result is tracked by the same scoreboard mechanism from Section 2. The table below shows which lanes hold which partial sums after each step (matching Figure 4-4, Mode 2):

Shuffle step & stride o Partner lanes Initial partial sums combined in each active lane's acc Which lanes hold the exact same partial sum
Before shuffle (end of main loop) — 1 (sum of that lane's 32 chunks) All 32 lanes hold their own distinct partial sum
Step 1 (o = 16) lane and lane XOR 16 (e.g., 0 ↔ 16) 2 Each pair with equal lane % 16 (16 pairs of 2 lanes) shares one sum
Step 2 (o = 8) lane and lane XOR 8 (e.g., 0 ↔ 8) 4 Each group with equal lane % 8 (8 groups of 4 lanes) shares one sum
Step 3 (o = 4) lane and lane XOR 4 (e.g., 0 ↔ 4) 8 Each group with equal lane % 4 (4 groups of 8 lanes) shares one sum
Step 4 (o = 2) lane and lane XOR 2 (e.g., 0 ↔ 2) 16 All 16 even lanes share the even sum; all 16 odd lanes share the odd sum
Step 5 (o = 1) lane and lane XOR 1 (e.g., 0 ↔ 1) All 32 All 32 lanes in C++ semantics; in v8 SASS, lanes 1..31 @P0 EXIT after issuing the 5th shuffle, leaving lane 0 alone with the 32-lane total

Put the two cycle budgets side by side for summing those 32 values:

  • v8 warp shuffle: Each warp shuffle takes about 24 measured cycles before the next dependent instruction can use its result, paired with one about 4-cycle addition, giving a bare dependency chain of 5×(24+4)+1=141 cycles; walking v8's actual machine code using its compiler-encoded issue-stall intervals and 24-cycle shuffle scoreboards (with reading tid, comparing tid != 0, and loading parameter y overlapped inside the shuffle waits, followed by address calculation and store) comes to about 152 cycles, using 0 bytes of SMEM and 0 CTA barriers (standalone epilogue time was not measured).
  • v7 SMEM epilogue: Having all 32 threads write SMEM, cross the CTA barrier, read back the first 4 B value, and complete the 1st addition takes 44.3 measured cycles in our microbenchmark; on a simplified chain-only schematic that models only the addition dependency chain (omitting the 4.30-cycle scalar SMEM read issue interval), thread 0 finishes the remaining 31 serial additions in 31×4=124 cycles plus 1 final store, for about 169 cycles on the schematic axis. Walking v7's actual SASS under the exact same stall-field rule splits the epilogue into three parts: first, 118 cycles for writing SMEM (STS), the CTA barrier (BAR.SYNC), and 24 pre-loop runtime blockDim.x checks and branches (STS 1 + BAR.SYNC 1 + 24 pre-loop ops stalling 116) before the first SMEM load issues at cycle 118; second, 200 cycles across two loop passes (each pass issuing four 16 B LDS.128 loads and 16 serial additions at 100 cycles per pass using the 32-cycle full-warp LDS.128 latency, reaching cycle 318); and third, 66 cycles after the loop for remainder branch checks (54 cycles) plus loading parameter y, computing the address, and issuing the global store STG.E (12 cycles)—totaling at least about 380 cycles (118+200+66=384 cycles using the 32-cycle full-warp LDS.128 latency, or about 372 cycles if 1-lane LDS.128 is estimated at about 26 cycles; constant-cache and taken-branch costs were not measured, the upper bound was not derived, and standalone epilogue time was not measured). Notice that 118+54=172 of those cycles come from loop-control checks for a runtime blockDim.x trip count rather than from SMEM itself; a constant-trip SMEM epilogue hardcoded for 32 values was not built or tested.

The 4-row table below summarizes both totals alongside the one v7 split that creates the gap—runtime loop control:

v7 SMEM write, barrier & runtime loop control 32-lane STS + BAR.SYNC (1 cycle each), plus 24 pre-loop and post-loop remainder checks (stalling 116+54; schematic folds write, barrier, first 4 B load & 1st add into the 44.3 below) 128 B written to SMEM Included in 44.3 below 172 (Part 1's 118 + post-loop remainder checks 54)
v7 lane 0 readback, serial sum & store LSU SMEM loads → lane 0 serial FP32 adds, then y read, address ops & STG.E global store via L2 (lanes 1..31 already @P0 EXIT) 128 B read from SMEM (8 × LDS.128 in SASS) + 4 B global write ~169 (44.3 measured incl. 1st add + 124 for remaining 31 adds + 1 store; 4.30-cycle scalar load interval omitted) 212 (2 loop passes 200 + y read, address & STG.E 12; ~200 if 1-lane LDS.128 is ~26)
v7 total Uses 128 B SMEM, 1 CTA barrier (constant-32 SMEM tail not built) 128 B write + 128 B read SMEM + 4 B global write ~169 (44.3+124+1=169.3) at least ~380 (172+212=384, or ~372 at ~26-cycle LDS.128; ceiling & standalone time not measured)
v8 5-step shuffle total All 32 lanes issue 5 LSU SHFL.BFLY + FP32 adds (0 B SMEM, 0 CTA barriers); lanes 1..31 @P0 EXIT after 5th shuffle, lane 0 runs 5th add & STG.E 4 B/lane/step reg-to-reg (0 B SMEM) + 4 B global write 141 (5×(24+4)+1) ~152 (first 4 steps at 24+5=29 each for 4×29=116, plus Step 5 wait 24 + add/store 12=36; standalone time not measured)

Comparing the bottom two rows: the chain-only schematic differs by only about 28 cycles (169−141, or about 16 ns at about 1.8 GHz), whereas under the same machine-code walk v8 saves at least about 230 cycles per warp epilogue (384−152=232 cycles, of which about 172 cycles come from eliminating v7's runtime blockDim.x loop-control checks, or about 220 cycles if 1-lane LDS.128 is about 26 cycles—at least about 0.12 µs across 1.80–1.98 GHz, and about 0.13 µs at about 1.8 GHz, accounting for 0.12÷0.54≈22% to 0.13÷0.42≈31% of Section 6's 0.42–0.54 µs read-flush gain, with the upper bound not measured). Moreover, starting from v6, all 2,304 single-warp CTAs reside concurrently in a single wave (Chapter 3, Section 4; they do not all finish at the same instant, as Section 6 shows): each warp runs its epilogue once at its own end, so the whole kernel shortens by roughly one epilogue on whichever warp finishes last rather than multiplying across 2,304 rows.

Back in gemv, v8 drops v7's 128 B of SMEM and __syncthreads() and swaps in that 5-step warp shuffle. The immediate benefit is slightly fewer executed machine instructions (1,231 → 1,159) and slightly fewer registers per thread (83 → 78) than v7, while the grid still supplies 17.45 warps per SM on average (the profiler reports 4.38 warps/SMSP, or about 17.5 per SM, alongside 24.8% achieved active occupancy, or about 15.9 active warps/SM).

Two boundaries round out the picture: why warp shuffle cannot cross warps, and why we cannot collapse those 5 steps into 1 hardware reduction instruction. First, warp shuffle exchanges registers only within a single warp (the hardware reason two warps on the same SMSP cannot read each other's registers directly is undocumented and not determined here): a reduction across more than 32 threads (like v1) still shuffles within each warp first and then combines across warps through SMEM and a CTA barrier. Second, on Hopper a 32-bit integer warp sum really can use a single redux.sync instruction (compiled to machine instruction REDUX, which reduces 32-bit signed/unsigned integers across active lanes by sum, min/max, or bitwise ops across the uniform datapath into a warp-wide scalar uniform register UR shared by all 32 lanes (latency not measured; see Appendix B, Section 6)); Hopper (H200, compute capability 9.0), however, has no floating-point redux.sync at all (even the next generation adds only single-precision min/max, with no floating-point sum), so v8's FP32 sum must use this 5-step shuffle.

6The gemv Evolution v6 → v7 → v8: Why Does One Step Save So Much and the Next Save So Little?

v7 removes in-flight starvation across the entire 37.75 MB main loop, saving 6.48 µs (1.43×), whereas v8 in source replaces the epilogue reduction paid once on whichever warp finishes last in the single-wave grid: under the book's protocol of record—512 MiB clean read-flush CUDA event timing (chosen because it leaves L2 cold like production without dirty-line writebacks; Chapter 10, Section 2)—v8 beats v7 by 0.42–0.54 µs in all 4 paired runs (its machine-code epilogue saves at least about 230 cycles, or at least about 0.12 µs and about 0.13 µs at about 1.8 GHz—roughly 22%–31% of that 0.42–0.54 µs gain, with the epilogue upper bound not measured), while essentially tying in an earlier write-flush run, with the rest of the gain and the flush difference not determined.

In the evolution chart below, we use PyTorch's matrix-vector multiplication function torch.mv as our baseline; under the hood, it calls NVIDIA's matrix library cuBLAS.

Look at v6 → v7 first: v7 runs about 1.43× faster than v6 (saving 6.48 µs). Every step of the main loop across the 8,192 columns waits on HBM; once the opening burst climbs to about 69.8 KiB/SM and subsequent steps keep 3–6 loads of WW per thread outstanding (about 26–52 KiB/SM, around the 95% knee region noted at the start of Section 3; runtime time-averaged bytes in flight were not measured), steady-state HBM bandwidth is inferred (Section 3) to climb out of starvation to within at most a few percent of the plateau, shrinking the wait right away. That speedup also puts v7 back ahead of torch.mv (v5 was already faster before v6 slipped behind).

Now look at v7 → v8: under the book's protocol of record (512 MiB clean read flush + single-launch CUDA event timing), v8 is reproducibly faster than v7—beating it by 0.42–0.54 µs in every one of 4 paired runs (pooled medians 15.15 → 14.74 µs, 1.03×). How do we rule out run-to-run variation (measurement noise) inside that 0.42–0.54 µs? By two criteria: first, every paired run in the round has the same sign (Chapter 7, Section 1 and Chapter 10, Section 3 refine this into symmetric ABBA alternating runs inside one process to cancel linear temperature and clock drift, and Chapter 6, Section 8 gives the full-graph replay noise band); second, the paired difference (0.42–0.54 µs) exceeds each version's own median span across the 4 runs (two machines × forward and reverse orders: 0.32 µs on v7 and 0.29 µs on v8).

Why is 512 MiB read-flush event timing the protocol of record? Reading 512 MiB outside the timing events fills the 60 MiB L2 with clean lines so L2 starts cold as in 62-layer production rotation, without packing L2 full of dirty lines the way a 512 MiB write flush does—avoiding the dirty-line writebacks we infer perturb WW reads (a write flush even inverted v3 vs. v4 in Chapter 10, Section 2; meanwhile, the profiler replays kernels under altered clock and cache control to read internal counters, so wall-clock savings always come from CUDA events—see Chapter 10, Sections 1 and 2). All four measurement records for v7 and v8 sit side by side below:

Record L2 flush Timer SM clock v7 v8 Difference (v8 − v7) Verdict
Clean ladder (protocol of record) 512 MiB read flush CUDA events (2 machines × fwd/rev, 4 medians) Not recorded 15.15 µs (span 0.32) 14.74 µs (span 0.29) −0.42 to −0.54 µs paired (−0.41 µs pooled, 1.03×) Same sign in 4/4 pairs, beats both spans: reproducible gain under read flush
Earlier Run 1 events 512 MiB write flush CUDA events Not recorded 15.68 µs 15.62 µs −0.06 µs (−0.4%, 1.00×) Within run spread; no gain
Earlier Run 1 profiler Profiler cache clear NVIDIA Nsight Compute (NCU) profiler (single launch) Base clock locked 12.54 µs 13.47 µs +0.93 µs Single base-clock profiler pass; v8 slower
Follow-up profiler (used in chart below) Profiler cache clear NCU profiler (median of 2 launches) Unlocked (~1.96 GHz) Not run in pass 11.9 µs (11.87 µs) — Kernel-body reading on v8 only

Two sentences separate what is proven on v7 → v8 from what is not: what is proven is that v8 beats v7 by 0.42–0.54 µs in all 4 read-flush pairs and its machine-code epilogue saves at least about 230 cycles (about 0.12–0.13 µs, or 22%–31%) on the last-finishing warp; what is not proven is how that 0.42–0.54 µs splits across the epilogue, main-loop scheduling, and L2-flush effects. Checking the main loop and Section 5's hardware budget item by item: in a memory-bandwidth-bound main loop, executing about 5 fewer instructions (1,144 in v7 vs. 1,139 in v8; the 72-instruction drop per warp sits mainly in the epilogue) does not by itself cut total runtime. Also, in v8's compiled SASS the compiler places only 7 loads of WW ahead of the first multiply-add, moving the 8th load into the first multiply-add group (why the compiler chose this schedule was not determined); that lowers only the one-time opening burst inside the initial first-byte wait from 8 loads in v7 (about 69.8 KiB/SM) to 7 loads (112 B per thread, or about 17.45×32×7×16 B≈61.1 KiB per SM), whereas across the remaining 25 loads of WW, v8 keeps the same 3–6 loads per thread outstanding (about 26–52 KiB/SM, around the 95% knee region noted at the start of Section 3), and across all 32 loads of WW its static first-use average (4.12 vs. 4.06 in v7; 3.34 vs. 3.20 instruction-weighted) is no narrower than v7's. In the epilogue, the machine-code swap saves at least about 230 cycles on the last-finishing warp (at least about 0.12 µs across 1.80–1.98 GHz, or about 0.13 µs at about 1.8 GHz—roughly 22%–31% of the 0.42–0.54 µs read-flush gain, with the epilogue upper bound not measured); how the remaining share splits between main-loop scheduling and outside-kernel or L2-flush differences—and why the gain disappears under the 512 MiB write flush—was not determined.

Even though v8 fires an opening burst of 7 wide loads (about 61.1 KiB/SM) and keeps 3–6 loads per thread outstanding thereafter (about 26–52 KiB/SM, likewise around the 95% knee region noted at the start of Section 3), its runtime still sits well above the bandwidth floor: inside the GPU kernel body, subtracting the 8.3 µs needed to stream the weights at steady-state bandwidth leaves about 3.6 µs (see the chart above). Four candidates account for that about 3.6 µs: first, first-byte and drain round-trip latency on a short 37.75 MB launch; second, lower post-opening average WW bytes in flight once later loads sit interleaved with multiply-adds at 3–6 loads per thread (about 26–52 KiB/SM), keeping the time average below the opening peak (inferred from our steady-state comparisons in Section 3 and above to give up at most a few percent of plateau bandwidth; not measured separately); third, loading and unpacking the input vector xx (16 KiB, hitting L1 at about 94%: in an auxiliary v7 check that passed xx as a kernel argument—removing xx loads and per-thread xx unpacking while also letting the compiler hoist 12 loads of WW instead of 8 and keep 9–12 loads outstanding at later issues instead of 3–6—event time dropped by 0.61 µs and profiler body time by 0.83 µs, so the xx-only share was not measured and is inferred to apply qualitatively to v8); and fourth, per-CTA completion skew (measured on v7 across all 2,304 CTAs with the chip-wide global nanosecond timer %globaltimer (see Chapter 2, Sections 1 and 2): cross-SM start timestamps span about 0.16 µs—treated strictly as an estimate because sub-1 µs differences across SMs are uncalibrated; see Chapter 10, Section 5—whereas end timestamps spread from 7.71 µs at the 1st percentile to 12.64 µs at the max under the same cross-SM %globaltimer caveat in Chapter 10, Section 5, with the last 10% of CTAs taking 2.4 µs while DRAM sits under-used for reasons not determined; v8 was not timed per CTA, and how hardware assigns CTAs to SMs is undocumented and not measured). How much each of the four contributes inside v8 was not measured separately. Chapter 4 leaves all four candidates open without splitting their shares; looking ahead on T=1 gemv, v9 in Chapter 5, Section 2 streamlines unpacking and accumulation instructions (leaving runtime unchanged because T=1 is bound by HBM traffic and short-run overhead), and because pushing in-flight reads deeper has little room left on a short 37.75 MB launch, v10 in Chapter 6, Section 3 bypasses those four candidates by compressing weights to 12 bits so the kernel reads 25% fewer HBM bytes.

One last piece of bookkeeping: why is this gap about 2.8 µs when Primer 3, Section 5 quoted 4.6 µs? Because they measure two different things: 4.6 µs is the full event-timed duration of an empty kernel (including the empty kernel's own GPU execution), whereas about 2.8 µs here is v8's event timing minus its profiler kernel-body duration across two separate runs (mostly launch and event-recording overhead, plus an unseparated run-to-run machine and SM-clock difference; see Chapter 10, Section 1 for details).

Takeaway: An issue slot stays busy whenever at least 1 warp is eligible, while a memory-bandwidth-bound kernel must instead saturate SM-wide bytes in flight by firing multiple independent wide loads per thread; inside a warp, a divergent branch or a lane 0 serial tail holds the whole warp slot until the last lane finishes, whereas 5 dependent warp-shuffle rounds sum 32 values in registers without shared memory or a barrier.

Next chapter's question: Once loads are saturated, the weights landing in registers still run through a chain of unpack and multiply-add instructions: which hardware execution pipelines do those instructions enter after leaving the scheduler, can cutting roughly a quarter of v8's unpack and accumulation instructions (v9) shrink that ~3.6 µs in-kernel remainder, and as the token count TT grows from 1 to 8, 32, and 256, where do those ordinary arithmetic pipelines hit their ceiling and hand the baton to Tensor Cores?

Execution Pipelines and Tensor Core — As T Grows from 1 to 256, How Does Arithmetic Keep Up with Weight Loads?
