By v8 in Chapter 4, the profiler measures a kernel-average HBM bandwidth of only about 3.19 TB/s (Section 2 chart), still short of the steady-state plateau (for in-flight loads and the candidate causes of that gap, see Chapter 4, Section 6; how much each contributes was not measured). Once the data lands in registers, each BF16 pair still has to be unpacked and multiply-added—so which execution pipeline do those instructions enter?

As the token count TT grows from 1 to 256, how does arithmetic keep up with the weights we read in, and once we split KK, how do we add the partial sums back into a single output correctly? Primer 2, Section 1 splits Part I into two tracks: Chain 1 is T=1 single-token gemv (v0 → v10), and Chain 2 is multi-token qkv_gate GEMM (g0 → g5). In Sections 1–2 we first calculate and verify on hardware why gemv arithmetic at T=1 hides completely behind memory waits (wrapping up Chain 1), and starting in Section 3 we switch to the multi-token chain (Chain 2): seeing why the ordinary arithmetic pipelines bottleneck as soon as TT hits 8—forcing us onto the Tensor Core—and then building the multi-token main loop and writeback epilogue step by step.

1Which Pipeline Does an Issued Instruction Enter, and Which Bound Sets Loop Speed?

The minimum cycles per loop iteration is set by the largest of three lower bounds: issue slots, the busiest execution pipeline, and the dependency chain.

Look at Figure 5-1. Underneath each SMSP sit three baseline arithmetic pipelines (memory reads and writes go to the LSU from Chapter 3, left out of the arithmetic accounting below). Because they have different lane widths, the cycles needed to accept 1 warp instruction (issue interval (initiation interval)) follow directly from lane width, and microbenchmark measurements (including the dependent-instruction latency before a consumer instruction can issue; Chapter 3, Section 9) match them:

  • FMA pipeline: 32 lanes wide, accepting 1 warp instruction every 1 cycle for single-precision multiply-add FFMA, addition FADD, and multiplication FMUL (FFMA measures a 1.13-cycle issue interval and 4.10-cycle dependent latency). It consists of two halves, and integer multiply-add IMAD enters only one half at 1 instruction every 2 cycles (2.00-cycle measured interval).
  • ALU pipeline: 16 lanes wide, accepting 1 instruction every 2 cycles. Integer addition and subtraction (the compiler sometimes emits integer addition as IMAD on the integer-capable half of the FMA pipeline instead, doubling aggregate integer-add throughput per the official throughput table; standalone IADD3 integer add/subtract throughput was not measured), three-input bitwise logic LOP3, shift SHF, and byte permute PRMT run here (LOP3, SHF, and PRMT measure a 2.00-cycle interval and ~4.1–4.3-cycle dependent latency).
  • SFU (Special Function Unit): 4 lanes wide, accepting 1 instruction every 8 cycles. Exponential, reciprocal, and reciprocal square-root instructions run here (base-2 exponential MUFU.EX2 measures an 8.05-cycle interval and 17.0-cycle dependent latency).

What people usually call a CUDA Core is one of the 32 FP32 lanes of the FMA pipeline. A program that uses only the standard pipelines (FMA, ALU, and SFU) and no Tensor Core is what we call a CUDA Core kernel.

Put FMA, ALU, and SFU side by side, and their issue intervals stand in a 1:2:8 ratio. Combine those pipeline rates with the issue slot (Chapter 4, Section 1) and scoreboard dependencies (Chapter 4, Section 2), and the loop cycle lower bound (minimum cycles per iteration) is simply the maximum of three bounds. An out-of-order CPU can look past a stalled instruction and issue later independent instructions first, so only loop-carried dependency chains limit its speed. A GPU issues instructions in order (Chapter 4, Section 2), so even the longest dependency chain inside a single iteration stalls that warp; only other warps on the same SMSP can step in to fill those idle cycles, which is why we divide the third term by the number of resident warps:

min cycles per iteration=max⁡(Ninstr⏟issue slot, max⁡pNp⋅Ip, chain length×dependent-instruction latencyresident warps)\mathrm{min\ cycles\ per\ iteration} = \max\Big(\underbrace{N_{\mathrm{instr}}}_{\mathrm{issue\ slot}},\ \max_{p}\, N_p \cdot I_p,\ \frac{\mathrm{chain\ length} \times \mathrm{dependent\text{-}instruction\ latency}}{\mathrm{resident\ warps}}\Big)

Here, "one iteration" means one warp executing the loop body once, and all three terms count SMSP cycles amortized per warp:

  • NpN_p: the number of instructions routed to pipeline pp;
  • IpI_p: the issue interval of pipeline pp;
  • dependent-instruction latency: the number of cycles from issuing an instruction until the next instruction that consumes its result can issue;
  • chain length: the number of instructions along the longest dependency chain in one iteration; other independent chains in the same warp advance in parallel and do not lengthen this term;
  • resident warps: the number of warps taking turns issuing instructions on the same SMSP.

Let's do the math for unpacking first. In Chapter 4, v8 calls a library helper to convert a 32-bit word holding 2 BF16 values into 2 FP32 values, which costs 3 instructions per word: 1 PRMT to extract the high half-word, followed by 2 left shifts by 16 bits. Because BF16 has the exact same 1-bit sign and 8-bit exponent width and position as FP32—merely dropping the low 16 mantissa bits—it is already the upper 16 bits of an FP32 number, so placing those 16 bits in the upper half of a 32-bit register and zeroing the lower 16 bits gives an exact FP32 value: bitwise-AND the high half-word with 0xffff0000 (LOP3 on the ALU pipeline) and shift the low half-word left by 16 bits, and each word takes only 2 instructions. That is how v9 in the next section is written.

Now let's plug this 2-instruction-per-word unpacking loop into our three bounds. Splitting a row of 8,192 BF16 elements across 32 threads gives each thread 8,192÷32=256 BF16 elements, or 128 32-bit words. Both WW and xx need unpacking, so each thread issues (128+128)×2=512 unpacking instructions plus 256 FFMA instructions.

Average that per word pair (1 word of WW paired with 1 word of xx, or 4 BF16 elements in all): each word pair takes 4 unpacking instructions plus 2 FFMA instructions, or 6 instructions in total. Among the 4 unpacking instructions, 2 LOP3 instructions go to the ALU pipeline. For the 2 left shifts, the compiler emits some as SHF (on the ALU pipeline) and some as multiplication by 2162^{16} via IMAD (on half of the FMA pipeline). That averages about 3 ALU instructions per word pair, putting the ALU bound at about 6 cycles. Each 16 B uint4 holds 4 word pairs and costs about 24 ALU cycles. The FMA pipeline needs only about 12–16 cycles for it: 8 FFMA plus about 4 IMAD. It is a range because FFMA can go to either half of the FMA pipeline while IMAD uses only one half, and we did not measure how much the two overlap. Either way, the ALU pipeline hits its ceiling first.

Instruction ordering matters too (Figure 5-1, Modes 1 and 2). Within a single warp on its own (where the unrolled loop processes a batch of 8 uint4s side by side, each uint4 on its own multiply-add chain, so cross-uint4 interleaving within the batch hides operand latency and no other eligible warp steps in), alternating ALU and FMA instructions issues all 6 arithmetic instructions in 6 cycles with 0 idle cycles. Issue the 3 ALU instructions back-to-back instead—with neither an FMA instruction from this warp nor another eligible warp to fill the gap while the ALU accepts only 1 instruction every 2 cycles—and the scheduler has to wait, stretching the pair to about 8 cycles (assuming FFMA can use the other half of the FMA pipeline in overlap with IMAD; 9 cycles if they cannot overlap across the two halves; with about 4.4 resident warps in practice, other warps fill those idle slots).

Here the compiler turns 122 of the 256 left shifts into IMAD (IMAD.SHL), cutting the ALU unpacking instructions from 512 (if all used SHF) down to 390. That is a go-to move at this level: when one execution pipeline saturates while an adjacent one has headroom, rewrite with equivalent instructions to offload the work—moving left shifts onto the FMA pipeline is called left-shift FMA offloading. The trade-off: IMAD hands its result to the next LOP3 about 2 cycles later than an all-SHF sequence (measured in a microbenchmark; the cause was not determined), and if the adjacent pipeline is already full, offloading gains nothing. In Chapter 6, Section 5, we will apply this move by hand for 4-bit weight decoding.

Now check the third bound: the dependency chain. A single FFMA has a measured dependent-instruction latency of about 4.1 cycles, and we estimate FADD at the same value. One batch runs 8 independent chains of 8 multiply-adds each (one chain per uint4; see the next section for the v9 code), so the dependency-chain numerator is only 8×4.1≈33 cycles. Divided across about 17.45÷4≈4.4 warps taking turns per SMSP (Chapter 4, Section 3), that comes to about 8 cycles per batch—nowhere near the issue-slot bound of about 219 cycles per batch (192 arithmetic instructions alone, or about 219 measured instructions per batch once the 2 loads per uint4 and loop instructions are included).

Put all three together in a 3-row tally per uint4 (4 word pairs, or 512 B read across one warp):

Bound Instructions per uint4 Lower bound per uint4
ALU pipeline bound Unpacking instructions on ALU across 4 word pairs (~3 per pair, or ~12 per uint4 at a 2-cycle interval; whole-kernel measured ALU count amortizes to 24.6 cycles) 24.6 cycles (about 25 cycles)
FMA pipeline bound 8 FFMA plus ~4 offloaded IMAD (overlap across the two halves not measured) about 12–16 cycles
Issue-slot bound 24 arithmetic + 2 loads + loop instructions (27.4, or about 27, measured executed instructions amortized per uint4) 27.4 cycles (about 27 cycles, tightest)

The issue-slot bound is about 27 cycles (27.4 cycles) per uint4, slightly above the ALU bound of about 25 cycles (24.6 cycles, matching the profiler in Section 3 showing issue slots busier than the ALU at T=1). Digesting the 512 B read by one warp (1 uint4 per thread) every about 27 cycles at the sustained SM clock of about 1.8 GHz (1.7964 GHz; Chapter 2, Section 2) gives a chip-wide digestion rate of about 18 TB/s, still nearly 4× the 4.8 TB/s HBM peak. So at T=1, arithmetic is nowhere near the throughput bottleneck; it hides completely inside the time spent waiting on memory, as the v8 → v9 measurement in the next section confirms right away.

Conversely, if a loop contains an exponential, the tightest bound shifts straight to the SFU: with 1 exponential per element and the SFU accepting only 1 instruction every 8 cycles, the loop is locked at a minimum of 8 cycles per element (Figure 5-1, Mode 3). Attention softmax runs straight into this wall (see Chapter 7, Sections 8–9).

One integer path not used in this book: the profiler guide documents that the integer dot product dp4a (multiplying and accumulating 4 pairs of 8-bit integers into 32 bits per lane) runs on that same IMAD half of the FMA pipeline as well (issue interval not measured; see Appendix D, Section 3).

2gemv Evolution v8 → v9: A Quarter Fewer Instructions, So Why No Time Saved?

At T=1, runtime is limited by the 37.75 MB weight traffic from HBM and short-run startup/drain overhead: both versions read the same bytes with the same WW load schedule, so the saved arithmetic cycles were already hidden inside memory wait time.

Compare the inner loops of v8 and v9 (Figure 5-2), and v9 changes two things:

  • Unpacking implementation: It switches to the hand-written unpacking from Section 1, cutting each 32-bit word from 3 instructions down to 2.
  • Accumulation method: For every loaded uint4, v8 starts an 8-multiply-add chain from 0 and merges it into acc with 1 FADD; v9 instead assigns 1 cross-batch accumulator to each of the 8 uint4s in a batch and merges them only at the end of the loop, eliminating the per-uint4 zero reset and merge FADD.

Both versions fully unroll the loop and issue the exact same number of WW loads per batch; in the compiled SASS, both place 7 WW loads before the first multiply-add and interleave the later loads among the multiply-adds (Chapter 4, Section 3).

Look at the two charts above: across 4 paired runs, two tie and two leave v9 slightly slower; the difference does not keep the same sign, so by the criterion in Chapter 4, Section 6 it does not count as a speedup. Static SASS instructions drop from 1,160 to 879 (24% fewer) and dynamic executed instructions drop by about a quarter as well, yet v9 reads the exact same bytes from HBM as v8, with the same occupancy and the same WW reads in flight (Chapter 4, Section 6). Only the in-flight xx loads drop, from 7 to 5, and xx is just 16 KiB; HBM throughput is almost unchanged. At T=1, all three arithmetic bounds from Section 1 sit below the limit set by weight bytes read and short-run memory startup/drain overhead (Chapter 4, Section 6; in-flight depth is inferred from the matching peak curve's 24–40 KiB/SM 95% knee region measured when streaming 16 B loads across the full GPU in Chapter 2, Section 3 to sit near the plateau), so lowering the arithmetic bound leaves runtime unchanged—making this step a direct measured example of saving arithmetic without saving time.

Putting the accounting split of v8's 14.74 µs at T=1 directly on the table in three parts (Figure 5-3 cards in the next section and Chapter 4, Section 6):

  • Outside the kernel body (~2.8 µs): Subtracting the unlocked profiler kernel body (11.9 µs) from CUDA event timing across two separate runs (14.74 µs) leaves about 2.8 µs (2.84 µs measured across runs—mostly launch and start/end event-recording overhead plus unseparated machine and clock differences; Chapter 10, Section 1).
  • Peak weight-read floor inside the kernel body (7.86 µs): Inside the ~11.9 µs kernel body, streaming 37.75 MB of weights at the 4.8 TB/s nominal peak sets a 7.86 µs floor.
  • Overlapping remainder inside the kernel body (~4.0 µs): The derived remainder overlapping with that weight read is about 4.0 µs (4.04 µs), comprising the ~0.45 µs gap between the 4.8 TB/s peak and the 4.54 TB/s steady-state plateau measured in Chapter 2, Section 3, plus the four candidate causes from Chapter 4, Section 6—unamortized first/last-byte round trip, time-averaged in-flight depth, loading and unpacking the 16 KiB xx, and per-CTA completion skew (whose individual shares were not measured; steady-state in-flight depth is not shown to limit).

Since cutting arithmetic instructions inside a single kernel at T=1 cannot save time, Chain 1's verdict at this level is settled: to make T=1 faster still, the next step is to shrink the bytes each weight takes up (Chapter 6, Sections 1–3; see Chapter 9 for cross-kernel launch overhead). Where, then, does v9's leaner inner loop pay off? As soon as the token count TT grows: v9's inner loop is the starting point for the CUDA Core curve in Figure 5-3 (next section). Reasoning from the instruction counts in Section 1 and the next section, once T>1 so every token repeats unpacking and multiply-add against the issue-slot and ALU ceilings, the leaner inner loop delays when the ordinary arithmetic pipelines hit the wall—though at T>1 we did not run a standalone paired measurement comparing v8-style against v9-style unpacking and accumulation (the cost is writing hand-crafted bitwise unpacking code; no extra hardware-resource cost was measured). Starting in Section 3, we switch to the multi-token chain (Chain 2) and sweep TT from 1 to 256 to see where the ordinary pipelines give way.

3As T Grows Above 1: Where Does CUDA Core Lose to Tensor Core?

Paper peak throughput predicts a crossover at T≈14, but the measured crossover happens between T=4 and 88: extra unpacking, load, and address instructions saturate the issue slots and ALU pipeline first.

In multi-request decode, speculative decoding verification, and prefill (Primer 1, Sections 5–7), one forward pass processes TT tokens side by side: input x:[T,8192]BF16\shape{x}{T,\;8192}{BF16} times weights W:[2304,8192]BF16\shape{W}{2304,\;8192}{BF16} gives y=xW𝖳. Throughout this chapter, we write NN for the 2,304 rows of WW (Primer 3 called it MM). Counting all bytes read and written for WW, xx, and yy, the arithmetic intensity (Primer 2, Section 1) is:

I(T)=2TNK2NK+2TK+2TN,N=2304, K=8192I(T) = \frac{2TNK}{2NK + 2TK + 2TN},\quad N = 2304,\ K = 8192

When TT is much smaller than N,KN, K, I≈T FLOP/B; as TT grows, it crosses the 206 FLOP/B ridge point from Primer 2, Section 1 at T≈233. Let's estimate from paper peak throughput first. At the driver-reported maximum clock of 1.98 GHz, full-chip FP32 FMA peak throughput is 132×4×32×2×1.98 GHz≈67 TFLOP/s. Divide 67 TFLOP/s by 4.8 TB/s and you get ≈14\approx 14 FLOP/B: if each weight per token needed only 1 FFMA instruction, you would not hit the CUDA Core ridge point until T≈14.

Now let's put both implementations on H200 and measure them head-to-head: (a) the CUDA Core version, which extends the hand-unpacked inner loop from Section 1 so one warp computes several tokens at once, reading each uint4 of WW once and multiplying it across those tokens; and (b) the Tensor Core version, PyTorch's torch.matmul backed by cuBLAS (Chapter 4, Section 6), which runs on the Tensor Core at these TT values. Figure 5-3 plots the data from the two latency charts below on log-log axes.

Look at the two latency charts above: at T=1,2,4, (a) the CUDA Core version is still faster; starting at T=8, (b) the Tensor Core version overtakes it and is already about 1.45× faster at T=8.

Why does the CUDA Core version lose around 8 instead of 14—and how can it hit an issue wall when issue slots are only 70.7% busy at T=8? Direct answer first: T≈5.5 is an estimated full-issue ceiling assuming every SMSP issues 1 instruction every cycle while HBM runs at 4.8 TB/s; in practice the measured kernel stalls before reaching 100% issue-slot use, so by T=8 about 2.2 instructions issue per FMA-pipeline instruction, pushing issue slots to 70.7% busy (~70%; what the remaining 29.3% idle issue slots stall on was not measured) and the ALU pipeline to 61.9% busy (~60%) while HBM bandwidth has already dropped to 30.1% of peak—showing that the bottleneck has shifted from memory bandwidth to instruction issue and the ALU.

First, the table below lines up the three instruction-ratio definitions used in this section and on the Figure 5-3 cards so we can plug them directly into the math:

Ratio definition T=1 (tw=1) T=8,32 (tw=4) Source and scope
Total instructions ÷\div FFMA 3.47 2.54 Measured in profiler; denominator counts FLOP-bearing FFMA only (used for the T≈5.5 estimate)
Total instructions ÷\div FMA-pipeline instructions 2.24 2.21 (rounded to ~2.2 in text) Measured in profiler; denominator includes FFMA plus non-FLOP IMAD left shifts (gives the ~6.3 rough estimate)
Arithmetic instructions (unpack + multiply-add) ÷\div FMA-pipeline instructions ~1.9 ~2.0 Derived from compiled instruction counts; the remaining ~0.3 and ~0.25 to the row above come from loads, addressing, and final reduction (not broken down one by one)

Specifically, at T=8 (tw=4 tokens per warp), by Row 1 of the table above every FLOP-bearing FFMA requires 2.54 total instructions once the unpacking, loads, and address math from Section 1 are included; normalizing the paper ridge point by 1 instruction per cycle gives 14÷2.54≈5.5 (or about 6.3 by Row 2 if non-FLOP IMAD shifts are included in the denominator via the 2.21 "total ÷\div FMA-pipeline" ratio). The measured crossover lands between T=4 and 88 (T=5–77 were not measured).

Does having one warp compute several tokens at once (tw=1 at T=1, fastest tw=4 for T≥4; when T>tw, the grid splits tokens into groups and re-reads WW per group) bring that instruction ratio down? Barely: the twt_w tokens share the unpacking of WW, but each token brings its own xx that still has to be loaded and unpacked separately, and at tw=4 the compiler offloads only about 20% of left shifts to IMAD (versus about half at tw=1), putting fewer unpacking instructions on the FMA pipeline (compare the three rows in the table above).

Switching to the Tensor Core has a trade-off of its own: cuBLAS sits on a flat ~19 µs plateau all the way from T=1 to 32. For T≤4, the CUDA Core version finishes below that line, so calling cuBLAS is actually slower (see the latency chart). Between T=1 and 128, every cuBLAS torch.matmul call launches 2 kernels: one using Split-K (Chapter 2, Section 5) to compute partial matrix products, and a second to sum those partial results—paying for an extra kernel launch and an inter-kernel handoff gap (Chapter 1, Section 1). How much of that ~19 µs plateau comes from the extra launch and gap, and what makes up the rest, was not profiled item by item.

By the token count TT entering qkv_gate, single-layer execution splits into three regimes, whose names we will use throughout the chapters ahead:

  • Regime I: T<8 (measured at T=1,2,4). CUDA Cores are still faster here, so our T=1 gemv kernel stays on CUDA Cores. At T=1 the bottleneck is purely the weight bytes read; by T=2,4, even though WW is still read only once, latency has risen by 6% and 24%, showing unpacking and issue overhead starting to surface (profiler counters were not measured at these two points), while total latency still stays below cuBLAS's two-launch plateau of about 19 µs.
  • Regime II: 8≤T<233 (measured at T=8…128), where arithmetic intensity is still below the 206 FLOP/B ridge point. Here we have to switch to the Tensor Core, even though the full GPU remains memory-bandwidth-bound.
  • Regime III: T≥233, where arithmetic intensity reaches 206 FLOP/B or higher. Our sweep here only measured up to T=256; by the arithmetic-intensity formula, a chunked-prefill chunk of T=16,384 (Primer 2, Section 4) also lands in this regime (see Chapters 7–9 for larger TT).

4How Large a Tile Does One Tensor Core Instruction Compute, and Where Do Its Operands Come From?

Each SMSP is paired with a Tensor Core; across the whole SM, Tensor Core throughput is 16× that of the FP32 FMA pipeline and needs no unpacking, at the cost of a fixed instruction row height of 16 or 64.

A single Tensor Core delivers 1,024 dense (without 2:4 sparsity) FLOP per cycle (BF16 multiplication with FP32 accumulation; see Figure 5-4). With 4 per SM, a full SM delivers 4,096 dense FLOP per cycle, compared with 128×2=256 FLOP per cycle across the SM's FP32 FMA pipelines—a full 16× jump. Better yet, because the hardware takes BF16 directly, all 512 per-thread unpacking instructions from Section 1 vanish, and the ALU pipeline is no longer a bottleneck. One clock-accounting note when comparing the two ridge points from Section 3: the 989 TFLOP/s behind Primer 2's 206 FLOP/B is the dense peak from the datasheet (which prints 1,979 TFLOP/s with 2:4 sparsity), corresponding to ~1.83 GHz rather than the 1.98 GHz maximum clock used for 67 TFLOP/s; at the same clock, dense Tensor Core throughput is 16× FP32 FMA, so the two ridge points likewise differ by 16× rather than 206÷14.

The mMnNkK tag in the instruction name tells you the exact tile shape: one instruction multiplies an [m, k]×[k, n] tile and accumulates the product into an [m, n][m,\ n] tile. Hopper gives us two families of Tensor Core instructions:

The first family is mma.sync (m16n8k16), issued by a single warp on its own with a minimum row height of 16. Before issuing it, threads must load both the left matrix AA and the right matrix BB from SMEM into registers (spreading the AA, BB, and C/DC/D register fragments across all 32 lanes of the warp). On H200, back-to-back issue takes 1 instruction every 6 cycles (6.00 cycles measured), reaching only about 67% of Tensor Core peak throughput. It fits cases where valid rows do not fill 64 rows, or where registers are too tight to spread across 128 threads (Chapter 8, Section 3 uses it when each expert gets only a few tokens).

The second family is wgmma (m64nNk16), an architecture-specific instruction whose compilation target must be set to -arch=sm_90a (plain sm_90 is not enough; see the start of Appendix A for the full rule), and which 1 warpgroup must issue together (Chapter 3, Section 8: 4 consecutive warps whose first warp index is a multiple of 4, or 128 threads). Why all 4 warps? Because the instruction specification says so: every thread in the warpgroup must execute the same wgmma.

The result is split across the 4 warps too: under the specified accumulator layout, each warp's registers hold 16 rows, and the 4 pieces make up 64 rows. The common explanation is that the 4 warps sit on the 4 SMSPs and each SMSP's Tensor Core computes its own warp's 16 rows (Chapter 4, Section 1), but NVIDIA doesn't document this hardware detail.

So all 4 warps must reach this instruction: it can only sit inside a branch whose condition comes out the same for the whole warpgroup (Chapter 4, Section 4). That scope is the warpgroup, narrower than the whole CTA that __syncthreads() needs, so the producer warp and the consumer warpgroup can take different branches (Section 6). For the thread → warp → warpgroup → SMSP → SM conversion table, see Chapter 10, Section 6. Across the 4 warps of 1 warpgroup, those 64 accumulator rows divide up as follows (the per-lane row/column mapping formula for the n/2n / 2 registers is not expanded in the prose; see the Mode 1 card in Figure 5-7, Section 7):

Warp in warpgroup Rows held in the 64-row block FP32 accumulator registers per thread
warp 0 Rows 0–15 n/2n / 2 (32 at n=64)
warp 1 Rows 16–31 n/2n / 2 (32 at n=64)
warp 2 Rows 32–47 n/2n / 2 (32 at n=64)
warp 3 Rows 48–63 n/2n / 2 (32 at n=64)

Its row height mm is fixed at 64, while its column width nn can be any multiple of 8 from 8 to 256. In BF16, k=16, and once n≥64, the back-to-back issue interval comes right up to the ideal n/2n / 2 cycles (m64n64k16 measures about 32 cycles, or about 99.8% of dense peak).

Whenever the hardware reads a matrix operand directly out of SMEM, it uses a matrix descriptor: a 64-bit value encoding the starting address and layout of that matrix tile in SMEM. Depending on where the left operand AA lives, wgmma runs in one of two modes:

  • SS mode: Both AA and BB sit in SMEM. The hardware reads both directly through two matrix descriptors, using zero operand registers and keeping only the FP32 accumulators in registers.
  • RS mode: AA sits in registers across the 128 threads (4 32-bit registers holding 8 BF16 values per thread), while BB stays in SMEM.

Look at the issue-interval chart above: SS mode is slightly faster when n≥64, while RS mode actually pulls ahead when n≤32. Down at n=8, SS takes ~18 cycles and RS takes ~17 cycles; the interval stops shrinking as n/2n / 2 because we hit the per-instruction floor.

So when should you use RS mode? Only when the left matrix AA is already sitting in registers:

  • Intermediate result of chained matrix multiplications: Once attention computes P=softmax(QK𝖳), PP is already in registers, so the second matrix multiplication reads it straight from registers in RS mode (Chapter 7, Sections 9–10). Forcing SS mode here would mean writing PP out to SMEM first and adding the cross-proxy fence from Chapter 3, Section 7.
  • Compressed weights decoded to BF16 in registers and fed straight into the Tensor Core: This requires moving the weight matrix WW to the left-operand AA side (the next section shows how). It pays off only if decoding a weight tile takes less time than reading a 16-bit weight tile from HBM; otherwise it comes out slower (see Chapter 6, Sections 1–2 for the encoding and Chapter 6, Section 4 for measurements and counterexamples).

For standard dense BF16 matrix multiplication (such as our qkv_gate tiles at T≥128), we use SS mode.

Here is the price of switching to Tensor Core instructions: row height is locked at 16 or 64, which wastes work whenever valid rows do not fill the tile (next section); wgmma requires 4 warps to issue together, driving up register usage across all 128 threads at once, and RS mode takes extra operand registers on top. As a result, it loses in two places: first in Regime I (Section 3 latency chart), and second in MoE when each expert gets only a few tokens, where the extra registers and SMEM demanded by wgmma push occupancy down (see the measurements in Chapter 8, Section 4).

Other shapes and data types (unused in this book or used in later chapters):

  • mma four-lane (quad) fragment layout: In mma's register-fragment layout for the left matrix AA and the accumulators, every 4 consecutive lanes 4g..4g+3 in the warp form a four-lane quad (g = lane >> 2) that share rows g and g + 8 while lane & 3 selects the column pair, whereas for the right matrix BB the 4 lanes of a quad share column g (PTX ISA §9.7.16.5.8; see Chapter 7, Sections 3, 8, and 10 for hands-on use).
  • FP8 wgmma (used in Chapter 7): Switching to FP8 widens kk from 16 to 32 while the measured SS-mode back-to-back issue interval stays unchanged (still about 32 cycles at n=64), doubling dense peak throughput to about 1,979 TFLOP/s (PTX ISA §9.7.17.5.2 notes that FP8 into FP32 accumulators accumulates at higher than half precision but lower than single precision; see Chapter 7, Section 10 for hands-on use and precision discussion).
  • INT8 and TF32 wgmma (not used in this book): INT8 wgmma (AA and BB each independently .s8 or .u8, with mixed signedness supported since PTX ISA 8.4, accumulating into .s32) likewise uses k=32 with a 1,979 TOPS dense peak, whereas TF32 wgmma (FP32 exponent range with at least 10-bit precision) uses dense k=8 at a 494.7 TFLOP/s dense peak (about 7.4× FP32 FMA at datasheet clocks, or 8× per cycle; neither INT8 nor TF32 is used by our model, see Appendix D, Section 3).
  • 2:4 structured sparsity .sp (not used in this book): The .sp structured-sparsity variants (mma.sp / wgmma.mma_async.sp) require only the left matrix AA to be sparse—at most 2 nonzeros per 4 adjacent elements plus two 2-bit index metadata fields for 16-bit and 8-bit types—doubling kk once more to give the datasheet's 2× figures (Primer 2, Section 1; our weights are dense, so we do not use them).

5When T Is Only 8 to 32, How Do We Fill the 64-Row Left Matrix? (swap-AB: Swapping Operands A and B)

Using y𝖳=Wx𝖳 puts the thousands of rows of WW on the fixed 64-row operand-A side and the TT rows of xx on the variable-nn operand-B side so all 64 rows hold real data; at small batch sizes, the real saving is accumulator registers.

Look at the standard layout first: put the input x:[T,8192]BF16\shape{x}{T,\;8192}{BF16} on the left (m=64 rows) and the weights W:[2304,8192]BF16\shape{W}{2304,\;8192}{BF16} on the right (n=64). The fraction of those 64 rows that hold real data is the row fill ratio. At T=8, only 8 of the 64 rows hold real tokens and the other 56 rows are padded with zeros, wasting 87.5% of compute; T=16 and 3232 likewise waste 75% and 50% (Figure 5-5, Mode 1).

The fix is swap-AB (swapping operands A and B, Figure 5-5 Mode 2): flip the two sides so rows of WW sit on the mm side (filling all 64 rows at 100%) and xx moves to the variable-nn side with n=T. When TT is not a multiple of 8 (such as T=5), we pad nn up to 8. Once T=128, xx already fills two 64-row tiles on its own, so swapping operands saves no cycles (Figure 5-5, Mode 3).

Both instructions do the exact same amount of useful work (8 tokens × 64 rows of WW), and m64n8k16 runs about 1.76× faster per instruction than m64n64k16 (see the issue-interval chart in Section 4). Still, in the early part of Regime II (T=8–32), the full GPU is memory-bandwidth-bound, so those instruction cycles are already hidden behind the time spent reading weights. What swap-AB really buys us here is registers: per-thread FP32 accumulators drop from 32 right down to n/2n / 2, taking only 4 registers at n=8. The price you pay is that the accumulators now hold the transposed y𝖳y^{\mathsf T}, so you have to transpose the tile through SMEM once before writing it out to global memory—and once T≥64, swap-AB brings no gain at all. Neither the gain from saving registers nor the time spent on the SMEM transpose was measured on its own; in our multi-token GEMM evolution chain (Chapter 6, Section 8), swap-AB is measured together with another change in a single step. Once TT reaches 128 and 256 so the 64-row left matrix fills naturally, the next question is how to keep the Tensor Core busy alongside the instructions preparing the next input group as we step along KK.

6Asynchronous wgmma: How Do We Keep the Tensor Core Busy While Preparing the Next Input Group?

Using wait_group<1> keeps 1 commit group executing on the Tensor Core while waiting for the next buffer slot and issuing the next group, at the cost of releasing each SMEM slot one step later.

Across Sections 6–8, we use our hand-written multi-token qkv_gate kernel as the running example (Chapter 6, Section 8 walks through its full evolution), starting right away with the role split inside one CTA and the anatomy of one K-step (one step of fixed column width along the inner dimension KK in tiled matrix multiplication). At T=128, tile height BM\mathrm{BM} runs along token count TT and tile width BN\mathrm{BN} runs along output columns NN: each CTA computes a BM=128 row × BN=64 column output tile, stepping along KK by BK=64 each time while KK is partitioned three ways with Split-K = 3 (Chapter 2, Section 5). Inside each CTA, 1 producer warp (filling an SMEM ring buffer via TMA; Chapter 3, Sections 6–7) and 1 consumer warpgroup (expanding to 2 consumer warpgroups at T=256) share an 8-slot SMEM ring buffer (Figure 5-6 draws 4 slots schematically, and Figure 5-7 Mode 1 in the next section shows the full single-step anatomy). First, the table below pins down the tile partitioning, the two thread roles, and the on-chip ring buffer inside one CTA:

Role / on-chip unit Size (shapes / warps / slots) Main actions or instructions What it holds (registers, SMEM slots, barriers)
Tile & grid split T=128: BM=128, BN=64, BK=64, Split-K = 3 (108 CTAs); T=256: BM=256, BK=64, with BN=64 (Split-K = 3, 108 CTAs) or BN=128 (Split-K = 7, 126 CTAs) Each CTA computes one Split-K slice's partial sum for a BM×BN output tile, stepping across K=8,192 by BK=64 Partial sums stay in consumer registers and are written back and summed across slices after the main loop (Section 8)
Producer 1 warp (32 threads) Wait on empty barrier, set expected bytes, and issue two TMA copies (from 1 elect.sync-elected lane) 0 data registers; refills rotating free SMEM slots with xtilex_{\mathrm{tile}} and WtileW_{\mathrm{tile}}, whose arrival flips the slot's full mbarrier in hardware
Consumer T=128: 1 warpgroup (4 warps, 128 threads); T=256: 2 warpgroups (8 warps, 256 threads) Wait on full barrier, wgmma.fence, SS-mode wgmma sequence, commit_group, wait_group, consumer named barrier, and empty mbarrier.arrive (from 1 elected lane in consumer warp 0) 64 FP32 accumulator registers per thread (128 at T=256, BN=128); holds each active SMEM slot until its commit group finishes draining; waits on full mbarrier, joins at the consumer named barrier, and signals empty mbarrier
SMEM ring slots T=128: 8 slots (24,576 B/slot); T=256: 5 slots (BN=64, 40,960 B/slot) or 4 slots (BN=128, 49,152 B/slot) Rotate input and weight tiles between the TMA engine and the Tensor Core (Slot 0 is reused for writeback after the main loop; see Section 8) Holds xtilex_{\mathrm{tile}} and WtileW_{\mathrm{tile}} per slot, paired with full / empty mbarriers tracking fill and release

Walking through a single K-step from that table: at T=128, each slot in the ring holds an xx tile xtile:[128,64]BF16\shape{x_{\mathrm{tile}}}{128,\;64}{BF16} plus a WW tile Wtile:[64,64]BF16\shape{W_{\mathrm{tile}}}{64,\;64}{BF16}, or 24,576 B in total. The producer waits for an empty slot, sets the expected transaction bytes, and fires two TMA copies; once all 24,576 B land in SMEM, the full barrier flips phase (meaning hardware decrements the expected byte count to zero and toggles the barrier's 0/1 parity bit, signaling that this round's tile is ready to read; Chapter 3, Section 7). The consumer reads that xx tile and WW tile from the slot and does four things in order: wait for the slot to fill (full barrier), slice BK=64 into four k=16 pieces and issue 4 instructions on each of the upper and lower 64-row half-tiles for 8 SS-mode m64n64k16 instructions (~256 cycles), seal and wait on the commit group, and pass a named barrier gating only the consumer threads without blocking the producer warp (128 consumer threads at T=128, or 256 threads across the two consumer warpgroups at T=256) before 1 elected thread in consumer warp 0 returns the previous slot i−1 to the producer (empty barrier). Throughout the loop, each consumer thread holds 64 FP32 accumulators, each mapped to a fixed cell of the output tile (see the layout card in Figure 5-7 Mode 1 in the next section).

Issuing a group of wgmma instructions takes four steps: first issue wgmma.fence (so the accumulator registers are ready to hand over to the Tensor Core), then fire several wgmma instructions in a row (wgmma takes a scale-d predicate argument: 0 writes D=A⋅B directly and 1 accumulates D=A⋅B+D; our C++ implementation in this chapter zeros the accumulators once before the loop and passes 1 on every step), seal them into a commit group with commit_group, and finally call wait_group<N>—which waits until at most NN commit groups remain unfinished.

Compare the two wait strategies in Figure 5-6:

  • wait_group<0> (Mode 1: synchronous drain): Every step waits until the current group finishes completely and writes its results back to registers before waiting for the next slot and issuing the next group. As a result, every single step exposes an extra drain latency—measured at about 53 cycles (53.1 cycles) in 64-column SS mode from issuing the last instruction until all results write back.
  • wait_group<1> (Mode 2: 1-group in-flight overlap): After issuing group ii, the consumer waits only for group i−1 to finish and moves right on. While group ii is still running on the Tensor Core, the consumer is already waiting on slot i+1 and getting the next group ready. Drain latency is exposed only once, on the very last step (which internal hardware stage the drain latency waits on was not determined).

Watch the buffer-slot lifetime closely. In SS mode, both AA and BB sit in SMEM, and under either wait_group<0> or wait_group<1> the consumer holds the active slot while computing, so the producer has at most "slots − 1" in-flight slots to refill and rotate. With wait_group<1>, group i−1 is still draining when group ii starts, so the consumer can return slot i−1 only after wait_group<1> returns and confirms that group i−1 is completely done (holding two slots simultaneously across those about 53 overlapped drain cycles, leaving "slots − 2" slots rotatable on the producer side during that overlap before returning to "slots − 1" for the rest of the step once slot i−1 goes back). In RS mode, BB is still read from SMEM, so the SMEM slot likewise waits for wait_group<1> before going back. On top of that, the operand-AA registers need protecting: until the in-flight group retires, you cannot overwrite the AA registers it reads—either wait for it to retire before overwriting them (as the cross-iteration overlap of P⋅V in Chapter 7, Section 10 does), or alternate between two register sets. So what this overlap actually trades is holding slot i−1 for about 53 drain cycles (53.1 cycles) into step ii after group ii starts on the Tensor Core before returning it—each slot's total hold duration stays the same, so the shorter step makes two slots overlap (plus 1 extra set of operand-AA registers in RS mode when alternating between two sets)—in exchange for hiding those about 53 drain cycles when the next slot's data is already ready in SMEM (compute-bound). Conversely, whenever waiting on data or preparing the next group takes longer than the matrix multiplication itself—such as T=128 in Regime II (by Section 3, reading WW and xx at 4.8 TB/s alone sets an 8.30 µs floor, already exceeding the busiest slice's about 6.1 µs of MMA), BN=64 at T=256 in the next section, or the counterexample in Chapter 6, Section 4 where weight decoding runs longer than the matrix multiplication (which wait_group depth that experiment used was not recorded)—wait_group<1> cannot hide data waits and the Tensor Core stalls anyway. How much time this step saves on qkv_gate on its own was not measured.

7The K Loop of One Tile: How Deep Must the Ring Be and How Much Must Each Slot Hold So the Tensor Core Never Waits for Data?

The number of in-flight buffer slots times the MMA time per slot must cover the buffer-slot round-trip time. That round trip includes a fixed intercept that does not shrink when a slot gets smaller, so widening the tile to double the compute per slot covers it more easily than adding more slots.

Building on the K-step anatomy from Section 6 (Figure 5-7 Mode 1 draws the full single-step timeline at T=128), apply Little's Law (Chapter 2, Section 3) to this SMEM ring buffer: the in-flight slots held by the producer must cover the slots the consumer burns through during one buffer-slot round-trip time. For the Tensor Core not to wait for data, we need

(in-flight slots)×(per-slot MMA time)≥per-slot round trip(\mathrm{in\text{-}flight\ slots}) \times (\mathrm{per\text{-}slot\ MMA\ time}) \ge \mathrm{per\text{-}slot\ round\ trip}

Here per-slot MMA time depends on the work per slot, and in-flight slots = slots − 1 (Section 6); the per-slot interval is whichever of the two terms is larger:

per-slot interval=max⁡(per-slot MMA time, per-slot round tripin-flight slots)\mathrm{per\text{-}slot\ interval} = \max\Big(\mathrm{per\text{-}slot\ MMA\ time},\ \frac{\mathrm{per\text{-}slot\ round\ trip}}{\mathrm{in\text{-}flight\ slots}}\Big)

Here, the per-slot round trip starts when the consumer returns an empty slot at the empty barrier, runs while the producer fires TMA and the bytes land in SMEM, and ends once the full barrier flips phase so the consumer can use that slot again. A two-point linear fit to measured full-load main-loop durations at T=256 using BN=64 and a second probe configuration (how that fit run was timed and converted was not archived, so plugging BN=64 back in is a fit-point back-substitution rather than an independent check) gives the estimate ≈1.12 µs+slot bytes÷172 GB/s (the intercept was not measured separately). Next, we use this fitted model to check whether 3 in-flight slots cover one slot round trip at BN=128 (see the step chart in this section). The 1.12 µs intercept exceeds the unloaded round-trip latency; the excess may come from queueing delay along the memory path (where along the path it queues was not measured; see Chapter 2, Section 3). The 172 GB/s rate in the denominator is the arrival rate seen by a single CTA: because many CTAs share the xx tile and mostly hit in L2, multiplying the single-CTA rate by the total CTA count comes out higher than HBM bandwidth.

First, grouping every number in this section by its status—fitted, model, fit-point back-substitution, or measured—and naming its clock shows right away how firm each figure below is:

Quantity BN=64 (5 slots, 4 in flight, 43 steps) BN=128 (4 slots, 3 in flight, 19 steps) Epistemic status and clock
Slot round-trip formula 1.12 µs+Bslot÷172 GB/s ~1.36 µs (40,960 B) ~1.41 µs (49,152 B) Two-point linear fit (fit to BN=64 and a second probe; intercept not measured separately; timing and conversion details not archived)
In-flight MMA cover (in-flight slots ×\times per-slot MMA) 4×0.285≈1.14 µs<1.36 µs (uncovered) 3×0.57≈1.71 µs≥1.41 µs (covered) Model (µs values converted at 1.7964 ≈ 1.8 GHz; inside the fitted model, both inequalities hold across the full 1.8–1.98 GHz range)

Compare two tile widths at T=256 (BM=256, BK=64). Derived from the accumulator count, each of the two consumer warpgroups (256 consumer threads in all) holds 128 of the 256 rows (256×BN÷256 threads equals BN\mathrm{BN} FP32 accumulators per thread; why T=256 uses two consumer warpgroups rather than another count, and whether the two consumer warpgroups stagger their steps, were not recorded), and their 8 warps share the SM's 4 SMSPs and 4 Tensor Cores (the cards in Figure 5-7 Modes 2 and 3 list the bytes and cycles per slot):

  • BN=64 (Figure 5-7 Mode 2): At 40,960 B per slot and a 227 KiB usable SMEM cap per CTA (228 KiB minus 1 KiB reserved by the driver; Chapter 3, Section 1), SMEM fits at most 5 slots (200 KiB), leaving 4 slots in flight, and the slot round-trip time is ~1.36 µs. Each slot runs 16 wgmma instructions in ~513 cycles (converting cycles to µs across this section at ~1.8 GHz gives ~0.285 µs). Those 4 in-flight slots cover only ~1.14 µs in total, which cannot hide the ~1.36 µs slot round-trip time.
  • BN=128 (Figure 5-7 Mode 3): Per-slot MMA compute (1,025 cycles) doubles to ~0.57 µs, while the formula above predicts that the slot round-trip time rises only slightly to ~1.41 µs. At 49,152 B per slot, 227 KiB of usable SMEM fits 4 slots (192 KiB), leaving 3 slots in flight that cover 3×0.57=1.71 µs≥1.41 µs, which hides the round trip. We need 2.5 in-flight slots, so 3 in-flight slots are enough with about half a slot of headroom.

Widening the tile from BN=64 to BN=128 halves the number of output-column tiles from 2,304÷64=36 to 18. Because each CTA's ring takes 192–200 KiB of SMEM, at most 1 CTA fits per SM (Chapter 3, Section 1); to keep the total CTA count close to a full wave across the 132 SMs (Chapter 2, Section 1), we simultaneously raise Split-K from 3 (108 CTAs) to 7 (126 CTAs, so one wave of 126 CTAs computes 126 tile slices, 1 per SM)—note that this adjustment is to keep a full wave on the GPU, not to hide the slot round trip. The KK dimension spans 8,192÷64=128 K-steps in all; since 3 and 7 do not divide 128 evenly, the largest slice takes 43 steps and 19 steps respectively, and total duration tracks that heaviest slice (Chapter 2, Section 1).

Look at the chart above: widening the tile speeds up the main loop by 3.17 µs (about 1.28×), and Tensor active cycles on the busiest SM climb from 76% to 88% of main-loop cycles (on the full-graph multi-token evolution ladder g4b → g4 in Chapter 6, Section 8—where g4b is the BN=64 version with Section 8's new epilogue and g4 is the step that widens T=256 to BN=128—this transition saves 1.65 µs). Roughly half of that 3.17 µs comes from the busiest CTA doing ~12% less work (19 steps × 128 columns vs. 43 steps × 64 columns, or 2,432 vs. 2,752), and the other half comes from finishing that same work faster. Why does paired CUPTI timing in that same run show about 1.35 µs saved across the full kernel when the main loop gains 3.17 µs? Phase stamps from that exact same run measure two opposing costs: first, raising Split-K from 3 to 7 grows the partial sums to add from 3 to 7 (along with an SMEM ring-view staging change), lengthening the epilogue reduction from 1.03 µs to 2.11 µs (+1.08 µs; see Section 8); second, the initial slot-fill ramp rises from 1.05 µs to 1.34 µs (+0.29 µs; cause not isolated). Summing the three stamped phases gives 3.17−1.08−0.29=1.80 µs saved; the remaining ~0.45 µs gap to the 1.35 µs paired CUPTI whole-kernel improvement is undetermined (the cycle-to-µs conversion factor applied to the stamps was not archived). How much queueing adds to the intercept, how the main-loop savings split between the two halves, and how much each of the three parameter changes contributes were not measured separately.

Now check the right column of the status table earlier in this section: if the stamps were converted near about 1.8 GHz, the measured 11.16 µs sits only about 3% above the 10.8 µs MMA floor, supporting 3-slot cover (though without independently testing the 1.12 µs intercept or 172 GB/s slope); if converted at 1.96–1.98 GHz, it sits 12%–13% (about 1.2–1.3 µs) above the 9.94–9.84 µs MMA floor, matching the about 88% Tensor-active ratio in the chart note above. A separate side test removed the per-step 8-warp named barrier at T=256 and saw zero speedup as warps moved from the barrier to waiting on data (the surviving note did not record which BN\mathrm{BN} it tested); if it tested BN=128, that excess comes from residual data waits (non-barrier per-step loop overhead was not measured).

Here is the trade-off when you widen BN\mathrm{BN}: you double the MMA compute per slot and cut the total grid-wide bytes moved from L2 into SMEM by ~40%, in exchange for three costs:

  • Per-thread FP32 accumulators double from 64 to 128 (using 64 more registers per thread; Chapter 3, Section 1).
  • Each SMEM slot gets larger, so the ring shrinks from 5 slots to 4.
  • Split-K goes from 3 to 7, more than doubling the partial sums we have to add together at the end (Section 8; see Chapter 6, Section 8 for numerical accuracy).

Another hardware route for cutting repeated xx reads is a thread-block cluster (several CTAs co-scheduled as a group; see Chapter 7, Section 12) paired with TMA multicast: a cp.async.bulk (or tiled .tensor) copy with .multicast::cluster uses a 16-bit ctaMask to write the same block simultaneously to the same CTA-relative SMEM offset across multiple CTAs in the cluster while multicasting the mbarrier notification as well (PTX ISA §9.7.10.28.4.1; see Appendix B, Item 30b for the instruction reference). This chapter's kernels do not use it (the 96-CTA prefill pooler launch at T=753 in Chapter 9, Section 7 and the prefill router use 2-CTA .multicast::cluster, not unpacked in the text; see Appendix D, Section 1), and how many L2 reads it saves was not measured.

Push the slot size too far, though, and SMEM cannot even hold enough slots to cover the round-trip latency, slowing the kernel down instead (Chapter 9, Section 2 and Chapter 9, Section 7 show measured counterexamples).

8After One Tile Finishes: How Do We Add the Partial Sums from Multiple Slices Back into One Output Tile?

Partial sums are converted to BF16 and written to SMEM, and a single TMA tile reduction adds them to the output in global memory; before the addition, each slice first confirms through a release/acquire chain that Slice 0 has zeroed the output.

Split-K cuts the inner dimension KK into segments, handing each segment to one CTA; below we call one segment and its CTA a K-slice (split-K partition), with Slice 0 computing the first segment. Our new writeback takes three steps (Figure 5-8):

  • This kernel writes BF16 output, so each consumer thread first rounds and packs its 64 in-register FP32 accumulators pairwise into 32 BF16x2 words;
  • Next, 8 stmatrix instructions (each writing several 8×8 submatrices from warp registers into SMEM) write the ytile:[128,64]BF16\shape{y_{\mathrm{tile}}}{128,\;64}{BF16} tile (16,384 B) into Slot 0 of the ring buffer—all K-steps are finished by now, so the slot is free to reuse;
  • Finally, 1 thread issues 1 TMA 2D tile reduction (cp.reduce.async.bulk.tensor, SASS UTMAREDG.2D.ADD; see Appendix B, Item 32), which tells TMA to atomically add those 16,384 B element by element into the output in global memory. The instruction specification names only global memory as the target; we infer that the addition happens at L2. The tile as a whole is not one atomic operation, so additions from different slices can interleave. That thread waits until TMA finishes reading SMEM before exiting (see Hop 11 in the table below for the exact wait instructions), so no separate reduction kernel is needed.

Because TMA tile reduction (like the per-thread atomic adds compared below) adds onto the existing contents of output yy, this output tile (ytile:[128,64]BF16\shape{y_{\mathrm{tile}}}{128,\;64}{BF16} at T=128) must be zeroed first. By contrast, a regular non-Split-K tile writeback (only 1 slice) has nothing to add across slices, so a plain TMA tile store (cp.async.bulk.tensor...global.shared::cta, SASS UTMASTG; see Appendix B, Item 31) can overwrite the destination tile directly and logically needs no pre-zeroed output; our Split-K kernel here always uses the reduction form, plain TMA tile stores were not measured in this book, and a variant where Slice 0 overwrites the output directly while the remaining slices add onto it was not measured in this book either.

How do we guarantee across SMs that Slice 0 has zeroed the output tile before any slice adds to it? The chain relies on the cross-scope cumulativity from Chapter 2, Section 6: when a thread executes a release, it publishes not only its own writes, but also prior writes from other threads that it observed across an intra-CTA barrier or acquire. Here, Slice 0's consumers zero the tile, cross an intra-CTA named barrier, and hand the zero stores written by those 128 threads to their producer via Hop 4's CTA-scope release; after the producer observes that return via CTA acquire, its device-scope gpu release at Hop 5 carries those zero stores to the whole GPU so every slice's gpu acquire at Hop 6 is guaranteed to see them. Following the final T=128 CUDA C++ implementation (g5 in Chapter 6, Section 8), the table below lists every hop—who runs it, what operation executes, where the data sits, the synchronization scope, what the hop orders, and its verification label:

Hop Actor Operation / instruction Where the data sits Scope What this hop orders Label and verification status
1 Thread 0 (tid == 0) of each slice relaxed atomic add on cnt to claim ticket tt, computing call index n=⌊t/S⌋ L2 global counter cnt → registers t,nt, n gpu (relaxed, orders nothing) Gives all SS slices of this replay the same call index nn (counter and flag only increase) Spec rule; standalone latency not measured
2 128 consumer threads of Slice 0 Zero the output tile before the main loop (8 × 16 B stores per thread) Constant 0 → L2 global output tile out (16,384 B) Generic global stores Produces the zeroed tile to be published (other slices skip this hop) Standalone latency not measured
3 128 consumer threads of Slice 0 Pass named barrier bar.sync 1, 128 before returning the first slot in the main loop Intra-SM consumer barrier unit 128 consumer threads in CTA Ensures all 128 consumer threads have issued their zero stores before Hop 4's arrive (without blocking the producer warp) Spec rule; SASS not verified, cycle count not measured
4 1 thread elected via elect.sync in consumer warp 0 of Slice 0 Arrives alone on empty[0] (mbarrier.arrive) empty[0] mbarrier in SMEM CTA-scope release Publishes all 128 threads' zero stores (gathered at Hop 3) together with the freed slot to the producer warp Spec rule (elect.sync deterministically elects 1 active lane); chain not verified in SASS
5 Producer warp of Slice 0 (1 thread elected via elect.sync) After waiting on an empty slot return (CTA acquire) and issuing all TMA loads for Slice 0, increments flag with red.release.gpu L2 global "zeroing complete" flag gpu (device)-scope release Cross-scope cumulativity: publishes Slice 0's zeroed tile to the whole GPU (.gpu means device scope; Chapter 2, Sections 6 and 8) Measured placement trade-off: releasing right after entry zeroing stalls this CTA 2–3 µs as the device memory fence waits on zero stores; waiting until after the main loop makes other slices spin 0.96–1.44 µs (~1.0–1.4 µs) longer; writing flag inside the consumer wgmma sequence serializes wgmma and slows the main loop (Chapter 6, Section 7)
6 Thread 0 (tid == 0) of each slice (including Slice 0) After the post-loop 128-thread named barrier, polls ld.acquire.gpu(flag) until flag>n L2 flag → register gpu-scope acquire Observes Hop 5's release so Slice 0's zeroed tile is visible to this CTA's generic memory view Spec rule; 0 spins measured in paired Gluon run (producer released early); relies on single-wave co-residency
7 Thread 0 (tid == 0) of each slice fence.proxy.async.global L2 global output tile out Global generic proxy → async proxy (normal thread accesses and async TMA use separate proxies that hardware does not order automatically; Chapter 3, Section 7) Orders the newly acquired zero stores before the upcoming async TMA tile reduction Spec rule; standalone cycle count not measured
8 Consumer threads of each slice (warps 1..3 concurrent with Hops 6–7; warp 0 after spin) Round and pack 64 FP32 accumulators into 32 BF16x2 words and write 8 stmatrix ops into reused SMEM Slot 0 Registers (256 B/thread) → SMEM Slot 0 (16,384 B) Generic shared-memory stores Stages this slice's BF16 partial-sum tile into SMEM Slot 0 Spec rule
9 128 consumer threads of each slice fence.proxy.async.shared::cta SMEM Slot 0 (16,384 B) Shared generic proxy → async proxy (normal writes must cross a proxy fence before async TMA reading SMEM can see them; Chapter 3, Section 7) Makes generic stmatrix writes visible to TMA's subsequent async SMEM read Spec rule; ~19.8 cycles measured in microbenchmark
10 128 consumer threads of each slice Named barrier bar.sync 1, 128 Intra-SM consumer barrier unit 128 consumer threads in CTA Joins Hops 6–7 (tid == 0's zero-tile visibility and global proxy fence) with Hops 8–9 (all 128 threads' SMEM writes and shared proxy fence) Spec rule; cycle count not measured
11 Thread 0 of each slice (C++ writes tid == 0 here, not elect.sync) Issues 1 TMA tile reduction, seals it with cp.async.bulk.commit_group, and waits on cp.async.bulk.wait_group.read 0 until SMEM is read before exiting SMEM Slot 0 (16,384 B) → TMA unit → L2 out tile (later written back to HBM) Async tile reduction + per-thread .bulk_group Atomically adds this slice's partial sum element by element onto the zeroed out tile; outbound shared-to-global TMA has no mbarrier completion path, so only the single issuing thread can wait (PTX ISA §9.7.10.28.5.3, §9.7.10.28.6.2) L2 addition site inferred; whether tid == 0 triggered a compiler peeling loop not verified in SASS; standalone wait time not measured

Note: In the Gluon build (g4b in Chapter 6, Section 8) timed in the chart below, all consumer warps check the readiness flag first—observing 0 spins because the flag is already set—before storing to SMEM, so the epilogue speedup does not come from overlapping Hops 6–7 with Hops 8–9 in the table above.

Four validity conditions keep this chain sound:

  1. Only consumers polling the flag at Hop 6 spin-wait; Slice 0's producer never waits on another CTA. The grid has at most 132 CTAs (each CTA's ring takes 192–200 KiB of SMEM, so at most 1 CTA fits per SM; Chapter 3, Section 1), and no long-running kernel on another stream or in another process holds SMs. When both hold, Slice 0's CTA can get an SM and will not deadlock. This is an operating condition under single-layer deployment, not a specification guarantee like cooperative launch in Chapter 2, Section 6.
  2. Slice 0 must run more K-steps than there are slots in the ring buffer; otherwise the producer has not waited on Hop 4's slot return, and the zero-initialization writes are not on the chain.
  3. The counter and flag use 32-bit signed integers that only increase, so a continuously running service must reset them before wrap-around; switching to 64-bit counters removes this requirement. Our kernel here stays on 32-bit.
  4. Each (T,S)(T, S) configuration has its own counter and flag buffer, and a given buffer is used with only one SS. If two SS values shared a buffer, ⌊t/S⌋\lfloor t / S \rfloor would no longer be the call index; we do not use it that way. At any given moment, a buffer may also be used by only one call; replaying sequentially on a single stream satisfies this condition automatically.

Before looking at the latency numbers, keep two distinct comparison scopes separate:

  • Whole-epilogue comparison (the baseline in the chart below): The preceding version in our multi-token evolution chain (g4a in Chapter 6, Section 8) uses the parallel slice reduction from Chapter 2, Section 8—writing each slice's FP32 partial sum to a global workspace, claiming a synchronized ticket and waiting until all slices arrive, and then reading back and summing assigned row slices (with no pre-zeroing and no readiness flag). That full epilogue measures 3.19 µs and 5.06 µs at T=128 and 256256 (rounded to 3.2 and 5.1 µs in the chart), dropping to 0.99 µs and 1.58 µs (1.0 and 1.6 µs in the chart) with our new epilogue above.
  • Isolated add-phase comparison: Another direct atomic-add option is for each consumer thread to pack its accumulators in pairs (two adjacent BF16 values in one 32-bit word, BF16x2) and fire element-by-element global atomic adds at the output. Hopper hardware supports this instruction natively without the compare-and-swap retry loop of Chapter 2, yet 128 threads each firing 32 scattered atomic adds into L2 still eats registers and slows the add phase: measured in isolation on the reduction add phase alone, per-thread BF16x2 atomics take 1.00 µs and 2.62 µs at T=128 and 256256, versus 0.60 µs and 1.02 µs with the single TMA tile reduction.

Look at the epilogue chart above: at both TT values, the full epilogue shrinks to about one-third of what it took before.

Now let's weigh the trade-offs of this change. Compared with the preceding parallel slice reduction baseline, switching to SMEM plus 1 TMA tile reduction (keeping the ticket as a 1-thread entry relaxed atomic add without waiting for all slices, while adding Slice 0 pre-zeroing and the producer release / consumer acquire flag chain) eliminates writing and reading the FP32 workspace and waiting on sibling slices, shrinking the full epilogue to about one-third of its prior duration (and on the reduction add phase alone, 1 TMA tile reduction drops add-phase time from 1.00 / 2.62 µs to 0.60 / 1.02 µs versus per-thread BF16x2 atomic adds). Relative to parallel slice reduction, we pay three new costs:

  • Zero-initialization and cross-slice flag chain: Adding Slice 0's zero-init stores and the cross-slice release / acquire flag chain (standalone time not measured; because the producer releases the flag early, other slices observed 0 spins).
  • Pre-add rounding: Rounding each slice's partial sum to BF16 before adding.
  • No bitwise determinism: Addition order depends on arrival order at L2, so results are not guaranteed to be bitwise deterministic (see Chapter 2, Section 8 on floating-point non-associativity; after this change, relative output L2 error rises from 1.6e-3 to 2.7e-3, with the cause not verified; see Chapter 6, Section 8).

The gap between the epilogue time saved and the full-kernel time saved was not measured separately.

Expanding on Hop 5's timing trade-off: if Slice 0 issues red.release.gpu right after zeroing at kernel entry, even though release semantics only order prior reads and writes before the flag without blocking later reads, the instruction compiles to a device-scope memory fence (see Chapter 2, Section 6 for its cost) that stalls waiting for the freshly issued zero stores, keeping consumer warpgroup 0 from issuing wgmma and slowing Slice 0's CTA by 2–3 µs; conversely, holding the release until the whole main loop finishes forces the other slices to spin an extra 0.96–1.44 µs during the epilogue; and if consumers write the flag inside the wgmma issue sequence, the compiler stops overlapping those wgmma instructions and slows the main loop as well (measured in Chapter 6, Section 7).

Takeaway: At T=1, arithmetic hides inside memory wait time, so cutting static instructions by a quarter saves zero time (v8 → v9); between T=4 and 88, the issue slots and ALU pipeline saturate first, forcing a switch to the 16× higher-throughput Tensor Core. Once on the Tensor Core, small batches use swap-AB to save registers, larger batches combine wait_group<1> asynchronous overlap with a wider tile (BN = 128) so it never stalls on data, and after splitting KK, stmatrix paired with a single TMA tile reduction adds the partial sums back into a single output.

Next chapter's question: Both chains now hit the bottom-level wall of bits and machine instructions: first, since T=1 (and small-batch Regime II) ultimately comes down to weight bytes read, how can we store each weight in fewer bits and decode it in registers with a handful of integer instructions—and up to what TT does that pay off before slowing the Tensor Core down at a loss? Second, we wrote an asynchronous wait_group<1> region in source code, so did the 128-bit machine instructions (SASS) emitted by ptxas actually preserve that overlap?
