In Chapter 5, Section 2, v9 cut the instruction count by about one quarter, yet runtime did not budge — because at T=1, execution time tracks the bytes read in from HBM. At this 37.75 MB size, even pure streaming-read microbenchmarks reach only 3.1–3.3 TB/s in profiler kernel-body rate (with the 4-warp stream carrying a 4-versus-5-tile tail imbalance), in the same band as v8/v9 at about 3.1–3.2 TB/s across the whole kernel (see Chapter 4, Section 6 and the v9 section for short-run startup and tail costs); pushing in-flight reads deeper alone has little room left to trim runtime, so the most direct path forward is to read fewer bytes.

Level 6 zooms all the way in to a single machine instruction and the individual bits inside a 32-bit register. Sections 1–3 first wrap up the single-token gemv main line (Chain 1; see Primer 2, Section 1) in one pass, and Sections 4–8 then concentrate on the multi-token branch (Chain 2; see Primer 2, Section 1) and machine-code verification. Following weight compression first, we work out three things: first, how many bits we can shave off each weight (either losslessly down to 12 bits, or using the model's native 4-bit format; Sections 1 and 5); second, how many integer instructions it takes inside 32-bit registers to unpack those weights back (Sections 2 and 5); and third, whether those extra decoding instructions eat back the time we saved on memory (the T=1 cycle verdict closes Section 2, while Sections 3 and 4 break down the measured T=1 latency and the crossover across TT). Next comes a separate Level 6 question: how do we inspect the machine code emitted by ptxas to verify that it actually kept the overlap we wrote? (Sections 6 and 7, where Section 7 examines a flag-store bug inside our 16-bit T=128 GEMM.) Finally, Section 8 closes Chain 2 by walking through the complete multi-token GEMM progression from g0 to g5, pointing each step back to the chapter that introduced its underlying mechanism.

1Which of the 16 Bits in BF16 Can We Skip Storing? (C12 Lossless Weight Format)

The low byte of BF16 must be kept intact; when the top 7 exponent bits fall within a window of 8 adjacent values, the high byte needs only 1 sign bit plus a 3-bit offset, compressing each weight to 12 bits.

Before we touch any bits, we need to know what the accuracy rules allow. Expert weights ship in a lossy 4-bit format from the start (Section 5; Chapter 8, Section 1), whereas dense projection weights have to enter the math at their exact published BF16 values. Our correctness test enforces this with two checks (for the second check on general inputs, see g4b in Section 8): the first leaves only one non-zero element in xx, so the output pulls out a single column of WW, and each column's relative error must stay within 0.001. Quantizing the weights down to 8 bits produces an error far above that limit, and the benchmark rules permit only lossless compression in any case.

If we cannot lose precision, where can we save bits? Look at how the floating-point bit fields line up in Figure 6-1. An FP32 number has a 1-bit sign ss, an 8-bit exponent ee (with bias 127), and a 23-bit mantissa mm. BF16 keeps only 7 mantissa bits — it is literally the top 16 bits of FP32, with the exact same exponent width and bias — so it represents

w=(−1)s2e−127(1+m/27)w = (-1)^s\,2^{e-127}\,(1 + m/2^7)

That bit-field alignment is why, back in Chapter 5, Section 1, shifting a BF16 value left by 16 bits gave us a valid FP32 number right away.

Now split a 16-bit BF16 weight right down the middle into two bytes:

  • high byte: the 1-bit sign ss plus the top 7 bits of the exponent (e≫1).
  • low byte: the lowest 1 bit of the exponent plus the 7-bit mantissa mm.

Let's trace a concrete weight w=0.02 from qkv_gate (the weight matrix WW from our main gemv running example; see Primer 2, Section 1 for its tensor shape). Its BF16 encoding is 0x3CA4, or 0 01111001 0100100 in binary: the sign bit is s=0, the 8-bit exponent is e=121, and the top 7 exponent bits give e≫1=60. The low byte is 0xA4, where the top bit 1 is the lowest bit of the exponent and the other 7 bits are the mantissa.

Across those two bytes, both the NyoomFloat12 paper (Together AI, 2026) and nf12 (an open-source 12-bit weight library following the same idea) rest on the same premise: the low byte is distributed randomly across weights and cannot be compressed losslessly (not measured in this book), whereas the regularity sits in the 7 bits of the high byte—in trained large-model weights, e≫1 concentrates in 8 adjacent integers [base, base+7] (corresponding to the 16 adjacent BF16 exponents [2base, 2base+15]). We call the smallest integer of this 8-bin window the exponent window base (base), and we pick one base per matrix offline so that the fewest weights fall outside the window.

We tested this distribution only on normal random weights with mean 0 and standard deviation 1/K1/\sqrt{K} — all timings in this chapter use those same random weights, and real model weights were not measured. For these weights, the chosen window starts at base=54, which covers magnitudes in [2−19, 2−3)[2^{-19},\ 2^{-3}), or roughly 1.9×10−6 to 0.1250.125, so typical weights like 0.020.02 land squarely inside the window.

With that 8-bin window in place, we can define our own 12-bit weight format, C12 (12-bit lossless weight format):

  • For a weight that lands inside the window, the high byte keeps only the 1-bit sign plus the 3-bit window offset d=(e≫1)−base (4 bits in total). Together with the 8-bit low byte kept as-is, each weight takes 12 bits. For w=0.02 above, base=54 gives d=60−54=6, so its 4-bit code is 0 110.
  • For an escaped weight (outlier) whose e≫1 falls outside the window, open-source nf12 uses whole-group escape: as soon as 1 weight in a group of 8 escapes, it marks the entire group as escaped and reads back all 8 original BF16 values from a separate escape table, keeping the decoded weights bit-exact. C12 does not do this (why C12 chose a side table over whole-group escape is not recorded): an escaped weight still stores an in-window approximation in the main table (our gemv sets its offset dd to 0), and its position and true value go into a separate side table; in gemv, we add the difference back into the output (Section 2; for how multi-token kernels patch escapes, see Sections 4 and 8).

Let's run the byte math for qkv_gate. Packing every 8 weights into 12 B instead of 16 B cuts the footprint to 75% of the original size: the main table for W:[2304,8192]BF16\shape{W}{2304,\;8192}{BF16} drops from 37.75 MB to 28.31 MB, and in gemv the side table allocates a fixed capacity of 16 slots × 8 B per 4-row CTA across 576 CTAs, totaling 576×16×8 B=73,728 B≈0.07 MB (which fits the random weights above; the exact escaped-weight count was not measured, and if any tile exceeds the fixed side-table limit during offline packing, the entire (operator, T) dispatch cell falls back to the 16-bit kernel at prepare time; see Section 4). At H200's 4.8 TB/s peak HBM bandwidth (see Primer 2, Section 1), the lower bound for reading WW once from HBM drops from 7.86 µs to (28.31+0.07) MB÷4.8 TB/s≈5.91 µs. Keep in mind that this ~1.95 µs difference is only the gap between two theoretical lower bounds, not a measured speedup; we will look at the measured numbers in Section 3.

In HBM, we pack every 8 C12 weights into three 32-bit words: two low-byte words la (the low bytes of weights 0–3) and lb (the low bytes of weights 4–7), plus one codeword (cd) holding the 4-bit codes for all 8 weights. We do this packing once offline before running the model. Of course, if a matrix had widely scattered exponents, more weights would escape and the side table would grow accordingly; we have not measured such matrices. Over the next three sections, we will count the extra instructions needed to unpack these weights at runtime and see where the trade-off flips as TT grows.

2How Do 9 Integer Instructions Decode 8 C12 Weights into BF16?

Eight weights unpack back into four BF16x2 registers in 9 integer instructions (7 on the ALU pipeline, plus 2 integer additions that are mostly VIADD on the FMA pipeline): shift to align, mask, add the exponent window base, and permute bytes.

In a 32-bit register, two BF16 values sit side by side as a single BF16x2 (as we saw in Chapter 5, Section 8, with one weight in the low 16 bits and one in the high 16 bits). Our job is to turn the three 32-bit words la, lb, and cd back into four BF16x2 registers. The trick is how we lay out the bits inside cd offline: in byte ii of cd (i=0..3), bits 2..02..0 hold the 3-bit offset of weight ii, and bit 7 holds the sign of weight ii. That leaves the middle bits free, so we pack the 3-bit offset of weight 4+i (from the second half of the 8-weight group) into bits 6..46..4, and we tuck the sign of weight 4+i into bit 3 of the next byte (with byte 3 wrapping around to byte 0).

Once cd is packed in this layout, walking through the four steps in Figure 6-2 (9 instructions in total) reconstructs all 8 BF16 weights. We write those 9 instructions directly in the C++ source using PTX (Parallel Thread Execution ISA), NVIDIA's virtual instruction set — a style known as inline PTX (asm). When CUDA C++ compiles, it first lowers to PTX, and the backend assembler ptxas (PTX optimizing assembler) then compiles that PTX into SASS (Streaming Assembler machine code), the actual machine instructions executed by the GPU. We count pipeline cycles on the compiled SASS (Section 6):

  1. 1 funnel right shift (SHF) (rotating cd right by 4 bits to get rt): SHF concatenates two 32-bit inputs into a 64-bit value and slices out 32 bits, so passing cd as both inputs gives us a 32-bit rotate. Rotating right by 4 bits drops the 3-bit offset of weight 4+i right into bits 2..02..0 of each byte in rt, while pulling its sign bit from bit 3 of the next byte down into bit 7 of the same byte — now aligned with the exact bit positions that weight ii occupies in cd.
  2. 2 three-input logic instructions (LOP3) bitwise-ANDed with 0x87878787 (one on cd, one on rt): the single-byte mask 0x87 = 1000 0111b keeps only the sign at bit 7 and the 3-bit offset in the low 3 bits, clearing the middle 4 bits to zero.
  3. 2 integer additions (VIADD or IADD3 in SASS) adding EXP_BASE: the constant EXP_BASE=base×0x01010101 packs one copy of the exponent window base base\text{base} into each of the 4 bytes. After masking, each byte looks like s|0000|d; adding base\text{base} turns it into s|(base + d), which is the exact high byte of BF16. Call the resulting word ha for the first 4 weights and hb for the last 4 weights. Because base+7≤127, adding the low 7 bits never carries into the sign bit at bit 7, so a single 32-bit addition sums all 4 bytes in parallel without byte-to-byte interference.
  4. 4 byte permutes (PRMT): PRMT takes two 32-bit source registers (8 bytes total: source bytes 0..3 from the first register, 4..7 from the second) and picks 4 bytes using a 4-digit hexadecimal byte-permute selector mask to build a new 32-bit word, where the lowest hex digit (low 4 bits) selects byte 0 of the result. Reading from low byte to high byte, selector mask 0x5140 grabs source bytes 0, 4, 1, 5 — that is la byte 0, ha byte 0, la byte 1, and ha byte 1 — zipping low and high bytes together into the two BF16 values for weight 0 and weight 1; selector mask 0x7362 grabs bytes 2 and 3 to build weight 2 and weight 3. Running the same pair of PRMT instructions on lb and hb produces weights 4–7.

Follow w0=0.02 (0x3CA4) from Section 1 along weight 0 (0x3CA4) in Figure 6-2 to see this in action: in byte 0 of cd, the low 3 bits are 110 and bit 7 is 0; bitwise-ANDing with 0x87878787 leaves byte 0 as 0x06; adding base=54 (0x36) reconstructs the high byte 0x3C; and finally, the low 16 bits of PRMT(la, ha, 0x5140) stitch byte 0 of ha (0x3C) onto byte 0 of la (0xA4) to produce 0x3CA4, giving us back the exact BF16 weight.

How much does this 9-instruction sequence cost on the execution pipelines? Among the 9 SASS instructions, 1 SHF, 2 LOP3, 4 PRMT, and some of the IADD3 instructions run on the 16-lane ALU pipeline, whereas VIADD—emitted by ptxas for most of the integer additions (46 of the 64 decode additions in v10, including both in the first decode group)—runs on the integer-capable half of the FMA pipeline at 2 cycles per instruction, just like IMAD in Chapter 5, Section 1. Because both sub-pipelines take 2 cycles per instruction, unpacking 8 weights occupies 18 pipeline cycles in total (14 ALU cycles plus 4 FMA cycles in the first decode group, and about 15 ALU cycles plus 3 FMA cycles averaged across the kernel). In terms of registers, the sequence reads 3 input registers and writes 4 output registers; although the C++ source declares 3 extra temporary registers, in the disassembled SASS the first decode group touches only 7 physical registers (see Figure 6-5).

Note that those 18 cycles only unpack C12 into BF16x2: widening the BF16 values of WW and xx to FP32 before FFMA is separate work on top (needed by uncompressed BF16 too, as in Chapter 5, Section 1; in v10, across the 515 widen instructions per thread before the main-loop barrier, 296 run on the ALU pipeline and 219 left shifts compile to IMAD.U32 on the integer-capable half of the FMA pipeline).

Placing that single-thread sequence back inside v10's full gemv CTA shows who holds what across lanes and registers:

Scope / stage Actor Slice held and processed Capacity and reduction
Row assignment 1 warp (32 lanes; 4 warps per CTA cover 4 rows) Computes 1 row of WW (K=8,192 columns) 16 fixed side-table slots per CTA (8 B per slot)
Lane chunk offset lane (0..310..31) at word offset 128 * h + 4 * lane (4 B words) Reads 4 contiguous 32-bit words from each of la, lb, and cd per triple (16 B per plane = 32 weights = 4 decode groups) Adjacent lanes sit 16 B apart, filling 16 full 32 B sectors
Unrolled decode Each thread Runs 32 unrolled decode groups (8 triples × 4 groups = 256 weights per thread) 53 × 32-bit registers per thread overall (7 touched in group 0)
Escape fix Lanes 0..15 + full-warp reduction Before the K-loop, each of lanes 0..15 checks 1 side-table slot and accumulates matched row terms in private registers; the K-loop has 0 branches After the K-loop, SHFL.BFLY warp reductions (Chapter 4, Section 5) sum the main-loop partial sums and escape terms across all 32 lanes

How do we handle escaped weights that fall outside the window? In our gemv kernel, the 9-instruction sequence above has zero branches. It blindly decodes the d=0 placeholder stored in the main table and feeds the resulting wrong weight w^\hat{w} straight into the FFMA multiply-add (Chapter 5, Section 1). (The T=32 Tensor Core kernel instead XOR-patches the decoded register from the side table before the matrix multiplication.) gemv fixes the result afterward by adding an escaped-weight correction term to the output:

yr=∑kw^𝑟𝑘xk+∑k∈Er(w𝑟𝑘−w^𝑟𝑘)xky_r = \sum_k \hat{w}_{rk}\,x_k + \sum_{k \in E_r} (w_{rk} - \hat{w}_{rk})\,x_k

Here ErE_r is the set of escaped column indices in row rr. In our C12 gemv kernel (where each warp computes 1 row; see Section 3), lanes 0..15 check the side table before entering the main K-loop, read xkx_k at the escaped indices for their row, and accumulate the correction terms; once the main loop finishes, SHFL.BFLY warp reductions fold that correction into the output yry_r. That way, every weight inside the window is decoded bitwise-exact, and every escaped weight has its exact difference added back at the end. Mathematically, the result equals direct BF16 multiplication, though the lowest bits can differ slightly because the floating-point additions happen in a different rounding order (this error was not measured separately). On top of the 18 decoding pipeline cycles and temporary registers we counted above, the price you pay is reading the side table before the main loop and reducing the correction afterward.

As for the third question posed in the chapter opening—whether those 18 pipeline cycles eat back the saved HBM time at T=1—the answer up front is no: across the 4 SMSPs of one SM, unpacking 1,024 C12 weights (1,536 B) takes 18 pipeline cycles (about 15 on ALU) against about 76 cycles to deliver those 1,536 B from HBM even at the 4.8 TB/s peak split across 132 SMs, and in measured v10n C12 decode ALU work accounts for only about 10% of whole-kernel elapsed cycles, hiding completely behind HBM waits (Section 3 right below breaks down the measured T=1 latency, and Section 4 maps the crossover across TT).

3The Final gemv Step v9 → v10: Why Do 25% Fewer Bytes Yield Only a 7% Speedup?

The control variant v10cn bundles four changes — a 4-warp CTA shape, a 64 B-strided WW (and xx) lane layout, just-before-use xx loads, and shallower recurring WW loads in flight from 3–7 down to 1–3 — dropping HBM throughput from 3.08 TB/s to 2.61/2.59 TB/s (down 15.3% on the control variant, dominant cause not determined); combined with launch and event-recording overhead in event timing (see Chapter 4, Section 6 and below), the net speedup is only about 7%.

In v9, scanned in machine code by loads outstanding before first use, each thread fires a one-time opening burst of seven 16 B loads of WW (about 61.1 KiB/SM) and keeps 3–7 loads per thread in flight afterward (about 26–61 KiB/SM, staying around the 24–40 KiB/SM 95% knee band of the long-stream machine-code curve in Chapter 2, Section 3; see Chapter 4, Section 6 and Chapter 5, Section 2; at this 37.75 MB size, pure streaming microbenchmarks likewise reach only 3.1–3.3 TB/s in profiler kernel-body rate, in the same band as v8's about 3.2 TB/s in Chapter 4, Section 6 and v9n's 3.08 TB/s in the throughput chart below). For v10 (Figure 6-2 in Section 2), we launch 576 CTAs with 4 warps per CTA, reading the three words la, lb, and cd for every 8 weights and unpacking them in 9 instructions; in machine code, each thread keeps 1–3 loads of WW in flight (loads of xx excluded, for a recurring peak of about 26.2 KiB/SM). We took this grid and CTA shape from the final qkv_gate kernel of the Chapter 9 decode layer (the standalone dense-projection problem uses a different 12-bit gemv kernel: 1,152 CTAs of 288 threads each).

Because v10 changes both the grid configuration and the weight format at the same time, the charts below include a control variant v10cn (from Primer 3 through Chapter 5, v0 → v9 wrote FP32 outputs, whereas all three versions in the first chart below write BF16 outputs, which we mark by adding an n suffix to their names) to separate the two: it uses v10's grid configuration while keeping BF16 weights. Strictly speaking, v10cn changes four things relative to v9n:

  1. CTA shape: grows from 1 warp to 4 warps (576 CTAs × 4 warps).
  2. Lane layout of WW (and xx): changes from adjacent lanes reading adjacent 16 B chunks (filling 16 full 32 B sectors per load) to each lane taking 4 chunks while adjacent lanes sit 64 B apart (touching half of each of 32 32 B sectors per load, before reverting to adjacent-lane 16 B reads on the 12-bit main table in v10n).
  3. Load timing of xx: switches from hoisted bursts to just-before-use loads.
  4. WW in-flight depth in machine code: reaches 4 loads only at the opening burst (about 34.9 KiB/SM), staying at 1–3 afterward just like v10n (recurring peak about 26.2 KiB/SM).

Before looking at the measured bars, let's work out the best-case speedup we could hope for: using the about 2.8 µs gap by which event timing exceeds the profiler kernel body in Chapter 4, Section 6 (exact methodology and per-build gaps are in the chart note below), subtracting about 2.8 µs from v9n's latency below and scaling all of the remaining time down to 75% in proportion to bytes read saves at most about 20%. And because part of that remaining time does not scale with bytes read (Chapter 4, Section 6), the real saving has to be smaller than 20%.

Our paper ceiling says about 20%, yet the measured speedup is only about 7% (see the chart above). Where did the rest of the speedup go? Look at the HBM throughput reported by the profiler in the chart below: v10cn and v10n sit at almost the same lower bandwidth, well below v9n. If we compare v10n against the control variant v10cn at that nearly matching about 2.6 TB/s bandwidth (noting that besides switching to 12-bit weights and decoding, this step also reverts WW back to adjacent-lane 16 B reads), v10n reads about one quarter fewer bytes and its kernel body runs about one quarter shorter (see the chart note below); once we compare against high-throughput v9n, however, the loss from the 15.3% HBM throughput drop under the new configuration (3.08 → 2.61 TB/s; candidate causes below) eats back most of the byte-saving advantage.

There is also an instruction-count cost: unpacking C12 weights makes v10n execute about 40% more dynamic instructions than v9n. Meanwhile, the grid supplies an average of 17.45 warps per SM, and on the two kernels the profiler reports 4.06 and 4.20 resident warps per SMSP (about 16–17 resident warps per SM) alongside 25.6% and 25.1% achieved active occupancy (about 16 active warps per SM, roughly one quarter of the 64-warp hardware limit, capped by grid size). Taken together, HBM throughput drops 15.3% on v9n → v10cn (3.08 → 2.61 TB/s, and 2.59 TB/s on v10n) across the four bundled changes listed above (v10n reverts WW to contiguous 16 B reads while adding about 40% more dynamic decoding instructions). With those changes intertwined, the dominant cause was not determined, and time-averaged bytes in flight were not measured.

One more detail stands out in the control variant v10cn: the gap between its CUDA event time and its profiler kernel-body duration (about 4.9 µs) exceeds v9n's gap (about 2.6 µs) by about 2.3 µs; because the two come from separate runs where the profiler ran with unlocked clocks and its own cache flush (see the chart note above), where that extra gap occurs and what causes it were both not determined. Looking strictly at the profiler kernel body, applying v10cn's four changes above costs about 2.2 µs (12.3 → 14.5 µs), and switching to 12-bit weights while reverting WW to contiguous 16 B reads (v10n) wins back about 3.5 µs (14.5 → 11.0 µs), leaving a net saving of about 1.3 µs (applying 12-bit weights directly to v9's single-warp configuration was not measured).

Stepping back to look at the entire gemv progression: from v0 → v9 (with FP32 output), we sped the kernel up by ~45× across the evolution charts in Primer 3 through Chapter 5; v10n switches to BF16 output and adds the final step against v9n, which also writes BF16 output.

4When Does Compressing Weights Pay Off, and When Does It Lose?

12-bit weights win at T=1, flip into a loss on the 1-warpgroup RS kernel at T=128, and never win once compute-bound at T≥233; on qkv_gate, choosing 12-bit for T≤32 and returning to 16-bit for T≥128 rests on the full-graph measurement in Section 8 (g4 → g5, bundled with the C++ rewrite).

To see when weight compression helps and when it hurts, break a single K-step into three times (Figure 6-4): the time HH to read one weight tile from HBM (which depends only on the byte count, not on TT), the time DD that the decoding threads spend, and the matrix multiplication time MM (which grows with TT). When those three stages run on separate hardware units with buffering in between, the step time is simply the maximum of the three; when the same group of threads runs two stages back-to-back, their times add together (Mode 2 of Figure 6-4). Now, the number of pure decoding instructions depends only on the number of weights and is independent of TT. But in an RS mode (see Chapter 5, Section 4) kernel that feeds wgmma directly from registers, the same consumer threads have to both decode the weights and issue the wgmma instructions one by one, so DD changes with both the number of consumer warpgroups and TT. (This book built no kernel that decodes weights in separate warps into SMEM for SS-mode wgmma, so its cost is unknown.)

That gives us a clean comparison. A 16-bit kernel does zero decoding, so one K-step takes max⁡(H16,M)\max(H_{16}, M); a 12-bit kernel takes max⁡(H12,D,M)\max(H_{12}, D, M). For T≤128, both MM and H12H_{12} are smaller than H16H_{16}, which means the 12-bit kernel wins only when D<H16.

Let's compute the per-active-CTA read time H16H_{16} for a 64-row × 128-column weight tile (8,192 weights: 16,384 B in 16-bit BF16, 12,288 B in 12-bit C12). Because DD is one CTA's step duration, chip-wide bandwidth splits across the NCTAN_{\mathrm{CTA}} active CTAs (at 1 CTA per SM, leaving 132−NCTA SMs idle; see Primer 3, Section 1 for the 132 SMs): on unpooler at T=128 below (NCTA=128), the 16-bit MMA loop runs at a measured about 4.15 TB/s (about 18.0 B per active CTA per cycle at about 1.8 GHz), giving H16≈908 cycles (or about 785 cycles at the 4.8 TB/s peak); on qkv_gate at T=32 (NCTA=108, with 24 SMs idle), scaling at that same 4.15 TB/s gives H16H_{16} of about 766–844 cycles across 1.80–1.98 GHz.

How fast can the execution pipelines unpack those 8,192 weights at peak? By pure pipeline throughput alone, the 4 SMSPs on one SM unpack 4×32×8=1,024 C12 weights (1,536 B) every 18 pipeline cycles (about 14–15 of them on the ALU pipeline), so 8,192 weights take at most 144 pipeline cycles. Inside a real 12-bit RS wgmma kernel, the picture is very different. The comparison below spans experimental kernels written in two high-level Python GPU kernel languages (Triton and Gluon, whose compilers emit the matrix descriptors and barrier code; g1a–g4 in Section 8) alongside shipped handwritten CUDA C++ kernels. Before reading the numbers, here is a short legend of the four 12-bit RS kernels that appear in this section so their measurements stay distinct:

  • g5 (T=32, shipped C++ on qkv_gate): 2 consumer warpgroups alternating K-steps; owns the 2.65 µs full-graph g4 → g5 saving and the ~0.44 µs (~786–867 cycles) per-step upper bound (Section 8).
  • Early Gluon T=32 (qkv_gate experiment): 2 consumer warpgroups alternating K-steps; owns the ~1,730 cycles per two-step turn and ~865 cycles per K-step average.
  • Gluon T=128 (unpooler / o experiment, wider m64n128k16 MMAs, wait_group depth not recorded): owns ~1,393 cycles/step with 1 consumer warpgroup (512 Tensor Core busy, 881 idle) and ~1,260 cycles/step (46% barrier wait) with 2 warpgroups; whole-kernel unpooler 27.44 µs, o 10.03 µs (which variant is not recorded).
  • Shipped row-split T=128 (shipped C++ on pooler / unpooler): 2 consumer warpgroups each owning 64 rows of WW with intra-warpgroup a0/a1 double buffering (paired timings not listed).

The table below traces g5 (T=32 shipped C++) across one K-step (Gluon T=128's non-Tensor-Core span is inferred along the same in-register chain):

Stage Actor and instructions Who holds what (size and ownership) Ordering and wait constraint
1. HBM → SMEM ring Dedicated TMA producer warp issues async bulk tile loads HBM streams through L2 into one SMEM ring slot holding the 3 C12 planes of WW (12,288 B), escape descriptors (128 B), and the xx tile Producer flips the slot's full mbarrier once bytes arrive
2. SMEM → registers 128 threads of 1 consumer warpgroup issue bank-conflict-free LDS.128 loads Each consumer thread loads the la, lb, and cd plane words (24 × 32-bit words) for its assigned 64 weights plus its warp's escape entries into registers Must wait on the slot's full mbarrier before issuing LDS.128
3. In-register decode & patch The same 128 consumer threads run C12 decode + side-table XOR escape patch on ALU and fmaheavy (main-table escape placeholder is d=0 at T=32, or dd clamped to 00 or 77 in some other kernels) Each thread unpacks its 64 weights (owning its wgmma operand-A row slice of the 64-row tile across all eight k=16 chunks) into 8 operand-A fragments (32 × 32-bit registers per thread) Depends serially on LDS.128 completion within the same thread
4. RS wgmma & accumulate The same 128 consumer threads issue 8 RS wgmma instructions to the 4 Tensor Cores Operand A^\hat{A} is read from those 32 registers per thread, operand xx from SMEM, accumulating into FP32 accumulator registers Must wait for A^\hat{A} registers to be written; in g5 (T=32), wgmma.commit_group is followed immediately by wgmma.wait_group 0 and a named barrier so the next decode never overwrites in-flight A^\hat{A} registers before freeing the ring slot (which wait_group depth the Gluon T=128 experiment used was not recorded)

Because Stages 2, 3, and 4 all run back-to-back on the same 128 consumer threads while only 1 to 2 consumer warps reside on each SMSP, the formula in Chapter 4, Section 2 leaves too few warps to hide the dependent-instruction chain LDS → SHF → LOP3 → VIADD/IADD3 → PRMT → XOR (inferred; per-reason warp stalls on the Gluon T=128 experiment were not measured separately), pushing per-step duration far above the 144-cycle pipeline throughput floor.

When T=8..32, because the 16-bit loop rate was not measured and the ~865-cycle record from the early Gluon T=32 experiment was not verified, single-step cycle counts leave the per-step sign at T=32 open, while on the full graph in Section 8 g4 → g5 saves a measured 2.65 µs (about nine-tenths of the about 3.0 µs byte-scaled estimate after subtracting the 4.96 µs empty graph, bundled with the handwritten CUDA C++ rewrite; see the g5 unit-mapping table in Section 8 for the grid, warp roles, and waits of the shipped T=8 and T=32 12-bit kernels). To see those single-step bounds: here the operator sits in the first half of Regime II (Chapter 5, Section 3), where cutting 25% of the weight bytes can save at most 25% of H16H_{16}. In the early Gluon T=32 12-bit Tensor Core kernel, 2 consumer warpgroups took turns on adjacent K-steps (this is K-step alternation without cross-warpgroup named barriers locking MMA windows, distinct from the two-consumer half-step stagger [ping-pong] in Chapter 7, Section 7): each warpgroup took about 1,730 cycles from the start of one of its steps to the start of its next, averaging about 865 cycles per K-step under ideal alternation (the exact build, measurement method, and SM clock of that record were not verified). If the 16-bit T=32 loop actually ran at T=128's 4.15 TB/s rate (H16H_{16} of about 766–844 cycles across 1.80–1.98 GHz on 108 active CTAs), 865 cycles would be slightly longer than H16H_{16} across the entire clock range; however, the steady-state loop rate of the 16-bit T=32 version (g4 in Section 8) was not measured, and subtracting the 4.96 µs empty-graph overhead from its full-graph time bounds each step at about 0.56 µs (about 1,010–1,113 cycles, above 865), whereas the corresponding upper bound for the shipped handwritten C++ 12-bit g5 (T=32) is about 0.44 µs (about 786–867 cycles). Why T=1 gemv speeds up by only about 7% in measurement has a different cause, which Section 3 already unpacked.

At T=128, the operator is still in Regime II (arithmetic intensity about 120120 FLOP/B, below the 206206 FLOP/B ridge point), yet the 12-bit kernel actually runs slower. Why? Not because we ran out of Tensor Core FLOPS, but because the longest bar in each K-step shifts from HBM reads to the decoding threads. When decoded weights feed wgmma directly from registers (RS mode; see Chapter 5, Section 4), the same 128 consumer threads have to walk through all stages in the table above—LDS.128 loads from SMEM, in-register decode and patch, and issuing 8 wider (n=128) RS-mode MMA instructions one after another (Mode 2 of Figure 6-4). On the 1-consumer-warpgroup Gluon T=128 unpooler kernel, those 128 decoding threads take a measured about 1,393 cycles per K-step (leaving the Tensor Core busy for 512 cycles and idle for about 881 cycles waiting on decode and synchronization). Even with 2 alternating warpgroups in that Gluon T=128 experiment, the average drops only to about 1,260 cycles per K-step: nearly half the time (46%) stalls on barrier synchronization, and the two warpgroups almost never overlap (how these two cycle counts were measured was not verified, and why the two warpgroups almost never overlap was not determined). Since 1,393>908, each K-step of that 1-warpgroup Gluon T=128 12-bit kernel takes about 1.5× as long as in the 16-bit kernel. We did not build a 12-bit RS version of qkv_gate for T=128, but we ran paired measurements on unpooler and o in the same layer: the full unpooler kernel ran about 40% slower (see the chart below). On pooler and unpooler at T=128, the final submission instead installs the shipped row-split T=128 C++ 12-bit RS kernel: 2 consumer warpgroups each own their own 64 rows of WW and share the same xx tile, while inside each warpgroup two register sets a0 and a1 double-buffer the first-half and second-half decoded operand-A fragments (using wait_group<1> to overlap the second-half decode with the first-half wgmma within the same warpgroup; although the source code calls this ping-pong, it is intra-warpgroup register-A double buffering rather than the cross-consumer named-barrier ping-pong of Chapter 7, Section 7). Because the side table has a fixed capacity, if any tile of WW exceeds the side-table limit during offline packing, the entire (operator, T) dispatch cell refuses the 12-bit route at prepare time and falls back as a whole to the 16-bit kernel—never branching block by block at runtime (why this row-split kernel ships on pooler and unpooler is not recorded, and paired timings comparing it against the 16-bit version are not listed in this book).

Once T≥233 and the operator crosses into Regime III, the 16-bit kernel's matrix multiplication time MM already exceeds H16H_{16}. At that point the kernel is compute-bound, so reading fewer bytes saves zero time and decoding only adds work. For larger TT, the 12-bit format never wins again.

Our practical fix is dispatching the kernel by (operator, TT): on the host side, we index a lookup table by operator and TT to pick which kernel to launch, adding zero runtime branching. On qkv_gate, we launch the 12-bit weight kernel for T≤32. At T≥128, we switch to the 16-bit weight SS mode kernel, which reads both operands straight from shared memory (Mode 3 of Figure 6-4) and runs 0 decoding instructions. The other dense projections likewise select kernels cell by cell from whole-kernel evaluation: like qkv_gate, o uses 12-bit weights only for T≤32 (on qkv_gate in Section 8, the T=8,32 gains are bundled with the C++ rewrite) and returns to 16-bit SS mode for T≥128, whereas pooler and unpooler at T=128 use the shipped row-split T=128 2-warpgroup 12-bit RS C++ kernel above whenever its side table fits (paired timings against the 16-bit version are not listed in this book).

5How Do We Decode 4-Bit Weights (NVFP4) into BF16 in Registers?

Shifting the 4-bit code's sign to BF16 bit 15 and its magnitude to bits 8..68..6 yields the exact value times 2−1262^{-126}; after offline nibble permutation, decoding 8 weights takes only 8 instructions.

With dense projections settled, we turn to expert weights: in Chapter 8, Section 1, the model's expert weights ship in the 4-bit NVFP4 format, where every 16 weights share 1 scale factor (see Primer 2, Section 2). Here is how those bits are laid out:

  • Each 4-bit weight uses E2M1 bit fields: a 1-bit sign ss, a 2-bit exponent ee (exponent bias 1), and a 1-bit mantissa mm. Across the 8 possible values of the 3-bit magnitude code cc, the non-negative numbers v[c]v[c] are {0,0.5,1,1.5,2,3,4,6}\{0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 3, 4, 6\}.
  • The block scale sblocks_{\text{block}} shared by every 16 weights uses FP8 E4M3 bit fields (1-bit sign, 4-bit exponent with bias 7, and 3-bit mantissa), and the entire tensor then multiplies by one FP32 scale stensors_{\text{tensor}}. Put together, a weight's numerical value is

w=±v[c]⋅sblock⋅stensorw = \pm\,v[c]\cdot s_{\text{block}}\cdot s_{\text{tensor}}

Inside each byte, the low 4 bits hold the even-indexed weight w2iw_{2i} and the high 4 bits hold the odd-indexed weight w2i+1w_{2i+1} — get those two nibbles backward and your matrix columns will be scrambled.

Hopper has no hardware instruction that converts 4-bit values straight into BF16, so we have to assemble them with bitwise operations in registers. Although Hopper's mma.sync accepts 4-bit integer .s4/.u4 operands (PTX requires both multiplicands to be 4-bit integers accumulating into .s32), it neither accepts E2M1 floats nor carries block scales, whereas this model's activations are BF16—and wgmma has no 4-bit type at all. NVIDIA publishes no INT4 Tensor Core peak rate for H100, and what SASS this mma.sync compiles to on sm_90a was not disassembled in this book. Look at the bit alignment in Step 0 of Figure 6-3: if we drop the E2M1 sign bit into BF16 bit 15, the 2 exponent bits into bits 8..78..7, and the 1 mantissa bit into bit 6, and fill every other bit with 0, what BF16 number did we just build? By the formula from Section 1, that BF16 bit pattern evaluates to 2e−127(1+m/2), while the true E2M1 value is 2e−1(1+m/2). The two differ by the exact constant factor 2−1262^{-126}.

Wait — does that still hold when the exponent bits are 0? A BF16 number whose 8 exponent bits are all 0 is a subnormal number, where values sit at uniform steps around 0 with magnitude 2−126⋅m/27. When you take the E2M1 code for 0.50.5 (0 00 1, so e=0 and m=1) and shift it into those same bit positions, you get 0x0040. That lands right in the BF16 subnormal range with value 2−126⋅0.5 — the exact same 2−1262^{-126} factor (you can check the remaining magnitude codes in the Step 0 readout of Figure 6-3). That means we need zero special cases when the exponent is 0: for every weight, each BF16 halfword just keeps the 4 bits selected by mask 0x81C0 (bit 15 plus bits 8..68..6).

If we unpack weights directly from the published raw layout (where the low 4 bits of each byte hold the even index), the low nibble of byte jj (j=0..3) goes into the low halfword of BF16x2 and the high nibble goes into the high halfword. Each nibble's sign and 3-bit magnitude need their own shift-and-mask step:

uint32_t b  = x >> (8 * j);
uint32_t lo = ((b & 0x7u) << 6)  | ((b & 0x8u) << 12);   // w[2j]
uint32_t hi = ((b & 0x70u) << 18) | ((b & 0x80u) << 24); // w[2j+1]
D[j] = lo | hi;                                           // = BF16x2 × 2^-126

Why is that so instruction-heavy? Each BF16x2 has 4 separate fields — the sign and magnitude of both the low and high halfwords — and in the raw byte layout, all 4 fields sit at different bit distances from where they need to go, forcing a separate shift per field. When you compile that loop to SASS (Section 6), unpacking 8 weights (j=0..3) balloons to 31 integer instructions: 16 three-input logic instructions (LOP3), 9 integer multiply-add left shifts (IMAD.SHL), and 6 funnel right shifts (SHF), or about 8 instructions per BF16x2.

We can cut that down dramatically by rearranging and XOR-precoding the nibbles offline when we pack the weights. In the expert kernels of Chapter 8, offline packing XOR-precodes the source word RR so that 4 shifts (rotates left by 8 and 12 bits plus left shifts by 2 and 6 bits, producing s1..s4) line up multiple fields at once, shrinking the SASS sequence to 8 instructions per 8 weights: 4 shifts plus 4 three-input logic instructions (LOP3). Because a single LOP3 evaluates any 3-input Boolean truth table, the first LOP3 masks RR with 0x81C081C0 while each of the other three XORs either RR and a shifted word or two shifted words to cancel the precoding and masks with 0x81C081C0 in one instruction ((R ^ s2), (s1 ^ s3), and (s1 ^ s4) masked with 0x81C081C0), emitting a finished BF16x2 each time (we skip the bit-by-bit permutation table here; the bottom of Figure 6-3 shows a schematic view). The chart below compares the instruction counts before and after offline permutation.

Inside those 8 instructions, the two left shifts s3 and s4 (left shifts by 2 and 6 bits) are written as IMAD.SHL on the FMA pipeline while the two rotates s1 and s2 stay as SHF on the ALU pipeline—giving the right-hand group of the chart above (ALU 2+4=6 instructions, FMA 22 instructions; bottom timeline of Figure 6-3). That is the same left-shift offloading we saw in Chapter 5, Section 1: it cuts the ALU cost per 8 weights from 8×2=16 cycles down to (2+4)×2=12 cycles. Comparing the all-ALU schedule against this offloaded schedule here is a static pipeline accounting (Chapter 8, Section 3 isolated the measured gains and counterexamples of moving left shifts to IMAD.SHL on an earlier expert decoder, and in the profiler ALU remains the busiest pipeline across all batch sizes after offloading).

Once we have the four decoded BF16x2 registers, we multiply them by the block scale using paired BF16 multiplies HMUL2 (on H200, HMUL2.BF16_V2 occupies both halves of the FMA pipeline for a measured 2 cycles per instruction, so 4 instructions take 8 FMA cycles, or 12 FMA cycles together with the 2 preceding IMAD.SHL instructions), producing the 4 registers that serve as a slice of left matrix AA—an operand-A register fragment—for mma.sync (T≤32) or RS-mode wgmma (T≥128; see Chapter 5, Section 4). There is one catch: we still have to cancel the 2−1262^{-126} factor from our bit alignment, and multiplying the block scale by 21262^{126} all at once would overflow the BF16 maximum (about 21282^{128}). So we split that compensation across two steps:

  1. pre-multiplying the block scale by 2642^{64}: when we unpack the FP8 block scale into BF16, we add an offset to its exponent that multiplies the block scale by 2642^{64}. Because HMUL2 handles subnormal numbers normally without flushing them to 0, multiplying by 2642^{64} lifts the subnormal BF16 values for code ±0.5\pm 0.5 back into the normal BF16 range, leaving each scaled weight at "exact value ⋅sblock×2−62".
  2. multiplying by 2622^{62} in the epilogue: after the matrix multiplication accumulates in FP32, the epilogue already has to multiply by the per-tensor FP32 scale stensors_{\text{tensor}}, so we fold an extra 2622^{62} into that FP32 multiply to cancel the remaining 2−622^{-62}.

6How Does Our Code Become 128-Bit Machine Instructions, and Why Do We Need to Read SASS?

ptxas reorders instructions, emits SASS and allocates physical registers, and writes control bits inside each 16 B instruction word; according to public reverse-engineering studies, hardware mainly waits on prior results using the stall counts and scoreboard wait masks that the compiler encodes into SASS (NVIDIA does not publicly document this encoding), which is why we must inspect SASS.

All the instruction counts we used in Sections 2 and 5 — 9, 31, and 8 instructions — are compiled SASS counts, not lines of C++ or PTX. As we saw in Section 2, CUDA C++ compiles to PTX first and then ptxas assembles that PTX into SASS; let's look at what ptxas actually does under the hood and what sits inside a single SASS instruction word.

At the PTX level, your code is still written against an unlimited supply of virtual registers (%r1, %r2, …), with no physical register numbers and no final instruction order. When ptxas takes over, it does three jobs (unpacked in teaching order in Figure 6-5; ptxas's internal pass order and interleaving are not publicly documented):

  1. instruction scheduling: it interleaves independent instructions (such as the other half of decoding or surrounding widen and multiply-add work) between dependent steps to hide latency, while ordering the last read of a value ahead of in-place register reuse (for instance, in v10's first decode group it schedules the LOP3 that reads cd before SHF overwrites that same register in place with rt).
  2. emitting SASS and allocating registers: on that scheduled sequence, it emits SASS machine instructions and maps virtual registers onto physical registers, and the thread's whole-kernel physical register count sets the register cap on resident warps per SM (see Chapter 3, Section 1; for example, v10 uses 53 registers per thread overall, with the 9 instructions of the first decode group touching 7 of them).
  3. writing control bits inside each 16 B word: according to public reverse-engineering studies, it encodes pre-issue scoreboard wait masks and post-issue stall counts into the control bits of each 16 B instruction word (NVIDIA does not publicly document this encoding).

When generating SASS, ptxas lowers each PTX instruction into 0, 1, or several SASS machine instructions. Sometimes that lowering is one-to-one. Our 9 lines of inline PTX for C12 decoding in Section 2 compile through ptxas into 9 SASS instructions (main panel of Figure 6-5).

Other instructions, however, do not map one-to-one (see the side panel of Figure 6-5). The first is cvt.f32.bf16, which converts BF16 to FP32. In SASS it turns into a PRMT or a shift instruction. This ties back to Section 1: BF16 is the top 16 bits of FP32, so converting the type is just moving bytes. The second is wgmma. For BF16 (as well as half-precision FP16; see Chapter 7, Section 2 for its bit fields), its SASS mnemonic is HGMMA (for FP8 it is QGMMA), and wgmma.commit_group, which commits a group of matrix multiplications, has no SASS instruction of its own at all. It is only a group tag on the last HGMMA of the group, so that a later wait_group can wait by group (Section 7).

Every SASS instruction that comes out of ptxas is 128 bits (16 B) wide (this holds from compute capability 7.0, Volta, onward, including our Hopper GPU). According to public reverse-engineering studies, those 16 bytes carry a control word (stall count and scoreboard wait mask) written by ptxas, right next to the opcode and physical register numbers: it specifies which earlier results must finish before this instruction may issue, and how many cycles at minimum must pass after it issues before the next instruction can go. NVIDIA does not publicly document the bit encoding of this control word. Multi-source instructions like the 3-input LOP3 and 2-source PRMT in v10's decode block (Figure 6-5) read several source registers at once: per Section 10.2.7 of the NVIDIA CUDA C++ Best Practices Guide, physical registers are banked, and when multiple source operands of one instruction hit the same bank, bank conflicts add delay that the compiler and hardware thread scheduler schedule around automatically, with no direct application control; in disassembled SASS, .reuse tags on source operands let hardware reuse a just-read operand according to public reverse-engineering studies (Volta/Turing)—in v10's disassembled SASS, none of group 1's 9 decode instructions carry .reuse, whereas adjacent widens (0x4c0 / 0x4f0 IMAD.U32) and group 2's 0x590 PRMT R8, R9, 0x5140, R20.reuse do—while Hopper's register bank count and .reuse bit encoding are not publicly documented by NVIDIA.

Back in Chapter 4, Section 2, we noted that the compiler decides ahead of time which scoreboard to wait on, and before which instruction, and writes that into the machine instructions. This 16 B control word is where it goes. In this reverse-engineered model, the warp scheduler (Chapter 4, Section 1) mainly reads the scoreboard mask and stall count from the control word at runtime to decide when the instruction can issue (public documentation does not state whether the hardware also runs other internal dependency checks). If ptxas stamps a wait onto an instruction, the execution pipeline stalls right there (ptxas will even reshuffle the instruction order you wrote by hand if it thinks that saves registers; see Chapter 8, Section 8). So to check that your machine code really overlaps the way you intended, you have to run disassembly (turning the compiled binary back into readable SASS text) and check the SASS yourself.

7Why Does One Extra Normal Instruction Inside an Async MMA Region Slow the Main Loop by More Than 2×?

When predicated normal instructions are mixed into an async wgmma region, ptxas inserts a drain barrier after every HGMMA, slowing the main loop by 2.35×.

Let's call the instruction bracket from Chapter 5, Section 6 the async wgmma region: you open with wgmma.fence (compiled to the warpgroup collective SASS instruction WARPGROUP.ARRIVE), fire off several wgmma.mma_async instructions back to back, and close with commit_group and wait_group. Inside this async wgmma region, the accumulator registers belong to the Tensor Core, and multiple HGMMA instructions can overlap in flight.

What happens if you slip a normal instruction into the middle of that region? Look at a real bug we hit in Figure 6-6. In our T=128 GEMM kernel for qkv_gate (one of the kernels on the multi-token GEMM evolution chain in Section 8; see Chapter 5, Section 7 for its tiling), each K-step issues 8 HGMMA.64x64x16 instructions. In an early version of the cross-slice readiness flag from Chapter 5, Section 8, we put the release-ordered global store st.release (Chapter 2, Section 6) right inside the async wgmma region. Only consumer thread 0 ran that store on one specific iteration (in the final version, we moved the release flag write outside the region to the producer warp).

When we compiled that early version, ptxas printed a serialization hint, saying that a non-wgmma instruction defined an accumulator register inside the async region. This is a performance hint (printed at the ptxas info level), not a compile error; we saw it with verbose ptxas output enabled (-Xptxas -v). Now, a global store does not write to registers at all. Yet dropping that conditional-branch flag write into the async wgmma region tripped ptxas's conservative serialization rule, and the wgmma instructions stopped overlapping (NVIDIA does not publicly document the internal heuristic ptxas uses for this check).

Look at what changes in the SASS. In the normal case (Mode 1 of Figure 6-6), each K-step contains only 1 WARPGROUP.DEPBAR.LE gsb0, 0x1 (the wait instruction compiled from wait_group<1> in Chapter 5, Section 6). Reverse-engineering analysis identifies gsb0 as the scoreboard that tracks unfinished wgmma groups; 0x1 allows the newest 1 wgmma group to keep running, so the pipeline does not drain. Once serialized (Mode 2 of Figure 6-6), every HGMMA is followed by 1 drain barrier WARPGROUP.DEPBAR.LE gsb0, 0x0 (corresponding to wait_group<0>). Each one waits until no group is running and costs about 53 cycles (Chapter 5, Section 6). We saw this in a 4-HGMMA reproducer of this pattern and extrapolate it to the 8-HGMMA kernel. Reconciling those per-instruction numbers with the measured main-loop times (over 128/3≈42.7 K-steps at about 1.80 GHz): the normal 8.84 µs loop averages about 372 cycles per K-step, where the 8 back-to-back HGMMA instructions keep the Tensor Core busy for about 8×32.1≈257 cycles (about 69% busy) and the remaining about 115 cycles (about 31%) wait on the next SMEM ring slot's full mbarrier—streaming 37.75 MB of WW in 8.84 µs already reaches about 4.27 TB/s (about 4.5 TB/s with xx, right at the measured HBM plateau in Chapter 2, Section 3), so the normal loop is HBM/TMA-bound rather than 100% Tensor-Core-bound. Once serialized, draining every HGMMA stretches the consumer step enough that those ~115 cycles of TMA wait hide underneath instead of adding on top: the serial model gives 8×(32.1+53.1)≈681 cycles per step (about 16.2 µs across the loop) against the measured 20.74 µs (about 873 cycles per step, or about 501 extra cycles per step over the normal loop), so the 8 drains explain about 309 of the 501 extra cycles per step, while the remaining about 192 cycles per step (about 4.5 µs) stay undetermined (the SM clock of that run was not recorded, the 4-HGMMA reproducer also emits a WARPGROUP.ARRIVE per HGMMA, and the 8-DEPBAR count is extrapolated). The chart below shows the main-loop runtime.

The takeaway is simple: put only the matrix multiplication instructions themselves inside the async wgmma region. Move any flag stores and branches outside the region and hand them to the producer warp (Chapter 3, Sections 6–7) — that out-of-region pattern is what we showed in Chapter 5, Section 8, and it corresponds to the step in Section 8 of this chapter that switches to TMA tile reduction. Watch out for thread divergence too: any branch that diverges across threads inside the same warpgroup will also make ptxas serialize HGMMA instructions one by one (see Chapter 8, Section 9).

Our routine check comes down to two steps: turn on verbose ptxas output to see whether the serialization hint appears, and count how many DEPBAR instructions show up per K-step in the disassembled SASS.

8Multi-Token GEMM g0 → g5 (T = 8..256): How Do the Mechanisms from Five of Levels 1–6 Stack Up Step by Step?

From g0 to g5, mechanisms from Levels 1, 2, 3, 5, and 6 combine to beat cuBLAS across all four TT values: ~1.41× faster at T=8 and ~1.07× faster at T=256.

This progression was measured only on qkv_gate across four settings: T=8,32,128,256 (T=16 was not measured; see Chapter 5, Section 3 for the tensor shapes). Each reading in the first four charts below averages the medians of 4 full CUDA Graph replay runs and includes about 4.964.96 µs of empty-graph replay overhead. Several steps along the chain modify only some TT values while leaving the remaining TT values unchanged, and those unchanged pairs differ by at most 0.160.16 µs between versions, whereas a single version's own 4 medians span up to 0.540.54 µs. Between those two bounds, this section sets the noise band at 0.350.35 µs and labels any delta inside the band as noise.

The step names below keep our original experiment version IDs rather than mapping one-to-one to hardware levels. You will notice g3 is missing — that is because the Level 4 mechanisms from Chapter 4 are already superseded here by TMA and Tensor Core instructions rather than forming a separate step:

  1. g0: cuBLAS baseline (see Chapter 4, Section 6). At T=8/32/128, cuBLAS uses Split-K (see Chapter 2, Section 5) and launches two back-to-back kernels — a main kernel that writes partial sums, followed by a second reduction kernel that adds them up — while at T=256, cuBLAS runs a single kernel.
  2. g1a (fusing two kernels into one): launches only a single kernel where the last arriving CTA of each output tile sums that tile's partial sums in its epilogue (Chapter 1, Section 3 and Chapter 2, Section 6):
    • T=8/32: uses wgmma with swap-AB (putting WW on the 64-row operand-A side; see Chapter 5, Section 5) and launches 288 CTAs. This step both saves one launch and changes the MMA shape, so it runs faster (how much each change contributed was not measured).
    • T=128/256: launches only 72 CTAs (36 output tiles × Split-K 2), which runs 0.25 µs slower than g0 at T=128 (within the noise band) and ~46% slower at T=256. Two reasons explain the slowdown: first, 72 CTAs leave 60 SMs sitting idle (Chapter 2, Section 1); second, the single last-arriving CTA of each of the 36 output tiles has to read back and sum the FP32 partial sums of both split-K slices on its own, reading back 64 KiB per output tile at T=128 and 128 KiB per output tile at T=256 (Chapter 2, Section 8).
  3. g1 (Chapter 2 + Chapter 3): at T=128/256, raises Split-K to 3 and expands the grid to 108 CTAs, cutting idle SMs from 60 down to 24. We also switch the epilogue to parallel slice reduction (Chapter 2, Section 8) so each CTA claims 1/31/3 of the tile rows to sum in parallel, and upgrade data movement to a dedicated TMA producer warp, an mbarrier ring buffer (8 buffer slots at T=128 and 5 buffer slots at T=256; see Chapter 3, Sections 6–7), and 128 B XOR swizzle (Chapter 3, Section 9). All three changes went in together in the same version and were not measured separately. With g1, T=128 beats cuBLAS for the first time, while T=256 still trails cuBLAS (the cause was not measured). Here is a counterexample: Why not have each split-K slice atomically add its partial sum directly into the BF16 output? Under how this kernel is written, the compiler lowers scalar BF16 atomic adds into the compare-and-swap retry loop from Chapter 2, Section 8: because two adjacent BF16 columns share one 32-bit word, atomic adds to neighboring columns fight over the same 32-bit word, and the more threads contend, the more retries pile up. On the 12-bit weight qkv_gate kernel (T=16/32), a scalar BF16 atomic-add epilogue makes the entire kernel about 2–3× slower than a tile-reduction epilogue (see the final chart in this section). To avoid that contention trap, split-K reduction has to use either parallel slice reduction, paired BF16x2 atomic adds, or TMA tile reduction (see Chapter 5, Section 8).
  4. g2 (Chapter 3, Section 8, setmaxnreg): a controlled experiment that drops the register cap of the producer warpgroup to 24 registers per thread (setmaxnreg applies at warpgroup granularity). That change yielded no speedup (landing inside the noise band), so we did not adopt it; we collected no profiler counters on this version, and why it yielded no gain was not measured.
  5. g4a (waves from Chapter 2, Section 1 + ring buffer from Chapter 3, Section 6): mainly changes T=32 (relative to g2, at T=128/256 it only removes g2's register cap and returns to g1's code). At T=32, it replaces the old 3-slot cp.async ring buffer (which waits by batch via commit_group / wait_group for copies to land in a slot; see Chapter 3, Section 5) with 1 TMA producer warp plus a 9-slot ring buffer, dials Split-K down from 8 to 3, and shrinks the grid from 288 CTAs to 108. By the source code's SMEM footprint, the old kernel fits up to 2 CTAs per SM, so 288 CTAs come to about 1.1 waves: one full wave of 264 plus a 24-CTA tail (actual resident CTAs per SM were not measured). The new kernel's SMEM ring buffer fits only 1 CTA per SM, so all 108 CTAs run in a single wave. (Swap-AB was already in place back in g1a; this step did not add it.)
  6. g4b (Chapter 5, Section 8 + Section 7 of this chapter): at T=128/256, replaces the reduction with TMA tile reduction (Chapter 5, Section 8), which adds element-wise and atomically in place in global memory. Following the rule from Section 7, we hand the readiness flag writes to the producer warp outside the async wgmma region. That shaves about 1.3 µs off T=128 and about 1.5 µs off T=256 (see the charts below). The paired comparison in Chapter 5, Section 8 measures this exact same transition from the same parallel slice reduction baseline (saving about 1.24 / 1.84 µs on the full kernel; because the two timing methods differ, the savings differ slightly, while per-thread BF16x2 atomic adds appear in Chapter 5, Section 8 only as a standalone comparison of the reduction phase itself). Our second correctness check on general inputs leaves room for the rounding differences of parallel accumulation: against the exact FP64 product, the full output's relative L2 error (the square root of the sum of squared errors divided by the square root of the sum of squared exact values) must not exceed 0.01 (1e-2), each row must stay within 0.05, and the output must contain no NaN or Inf. In measurement, the full output's relative L2 error creeps up from 1.6e-3 to 2.7e-3, still well under that 1e-2 limit; this bump matches what we expect from rounding each split-K slice to BF16 before accumulation (Chapter 5, Section 8), though whether this rounding is the sole cause was not verified.
  7. g4 (Chapter 5, Section 7): at T=256, widens the tile column width BN from 64 to 128 (with Split-K = 7, a 4-slot ring buffer, and 126 CTAs), doubling how much Tensor Core work each buffer slot feeds. On this chain, that shaves 1.65 µs off T=256 (23.78 → 22.13 µs, see the chart below; when Chapter 5, Section 7 measured this same change in paired runs, the full kernel saved about 1.35 µs, and because the two measurement methods differ, the time saved need not match). With g4, all four TT values now beat cuBLAS. The output relative L2 error rises to 3.65e-3 (for the same reason as g4b; not determined separately).
  8. g5 (this chapter): brings in three changes together:
    • kernel rewrite: g1a through g4 were written in the two Python GPU kernel languages introduced in Section 4 (Triton and Gluon), whose compilers emitted the descriptors and barrier code; g5 rewrites the kernels straight in CUDA C++ with inline PTX (Section 6), building the matrix descriptors, TMA tensor descriptors, and barrier phases explicitly in source code.
    • switching to 12-bit weights (C12) for T=8/32: switches to the 12-bit weight kernel (with one offline weight permutation pass before execution), reading 25% fewer bytes and sharing the unpacked weights on chip across all 8 or 32 tokens. At T=8, if we run the same upper-bound estimate from Section 3 on g4 → g5 (subtracting the 4.96 µs empty-graph replay overhead and scaling the rest of the time to 75% in proportion to bytes read), it predicts about a 2.7 µs saving, and we measure 2.95 µs (see the chart below; at T=32, the same estimate predicts about 3.0 µs against 2.65 µs measured). At T=8, the about 0.2 µs gap between those two numbers sits inside our 0.35 µs noise band, so it does not count as an extra saving; on top of that, this step also rewrote the kernel in CUDA C++ (see the bullet above), and the two changes were not measured separately. Here at T=8, the 16-bit baseline g4 is still g1a's 3-slot cp.async ring (288 CTAs) while g5 is a non-Split-K mma.sync kernel, so neither is the wgmma loop analyzed in Section 4 (which also does not pin down a single-step saving at T=32). The unit mapping of the two shipped 12-bit kernels in g5 is:
TT setting Shipped kernel and grid Threads and warp roles per CTA MMA instruction and SMEM ring Synchronization and waits
T=8 p4_qkv_proj_w12a16_m8_kstream, 96 CTAs (24 rows per CTA, walking all of KK sequentially with no Split-K) 288 threads = 9 warps: 4 k-warps (decode C12 stream and run MMA) + 4 escape warps (accumulate side-table corrections; why 4 dedicated escape warps are used is not recorded) + 1 TMA producer warp Warp-level mma.sync.m16n8k16, 5-slot ring (why mma.sync without Split-K is used at T=8 is not recorded) mbarrier slot handoff; synchronous warp-level mma.sync with no cross-CTA Split-K reduction
T=32 p4_qkv_proj_c12a16_m32_splitk, 108 CTAs (grid 36 × 1 × 3, 64 rows per tile, Split-K = 3) 384 threads = 12 warps: 2 alternating consumer warpgroups (warps 0–3 and 4–7 taking even/odd K-steps) + 1 TMA producer warp (warp 8) + 3 idle padding warps (warps 9–11; why 3 idle padding warps are kept is not recorded) Warpgroup RS wgmma.m64n32k16 (8 per K-step, swap-AB), 10-slot ring Consumer waits on full mbarrier, loads/decodes and XOR-patches escapes in registers from the side table (d=0 placeholder in the main table, or dd clamped to 00 or 77 in some other kernels), issues 8 RS wgmmas, runs wgmma.wait_group 0 right after commit (so the next decode never overwrites in-flight operand-A registers), then hits its own warpgroup's 128-thread named bar.sync (not a cross-consumer turn barrier) before freeing its prior ring slot; epilogue merges via TMA tile reduction
  • keeping 16-bit weights (BF16) for T=128/256: following the crossover boundary from Section 4, T=128 stays on 16-bit weights and matches g4's latency; T=256 also stays on 16-bit weights while switching to a BM = 128, BN = 192, 5-slot ring-buffer tiling with Split-K = 5 and 120 CTAs total. Those 120 CTAs fit into a single wave across the 132 SMs (leaving 12 SMs idle) and shave off a bit more time. The tiling change and the CUDA C++ kernel rewrite were not measured separately.

Takeaway: Compressing weights by a few bits saves HBM bytes at the cost of integer instructions in registers; the trade pays off only when decoding outruns HBM delivery without stalling the Tensor Core. How those instructions are actually scheduled in the end can only be seen by reading the SASS.

Next chapter's question: Part I dissected a dense linear projection all the way from the full GPU down to individual bits — its weight addresses are contiguous and regular, and its math is pure multiply-accumulate. In the next chapter, we return to the 8-stage single-layer map, where Stage 2 paged attention must read historical KV cache at every step while hitting three new constraints at once: historical KV rows sit scattered across HBM in 128 B paged rows indexed through a page table, so multi-dimensional TMA tile copies cannot gather them in one shot; an exponent-and-row-sum softmax sits right between the two matrix multiplications (QK⊤Q K^\top and PVP V); and from token-by-token decode (L=1) to 8-token verify (L=8) to 16,384-token prefill, arithmetic intensity spans four orders of magnitude. Across those three regimes, which of our six hardware levels bottlenecks it first, and how does a single operator shed whichever bottleneck is slowest at each step?

Position in the 8-stage single-layer pipeline: Stage 1 qkv_gate → [Stage 2: Paged Attention] → Stage 3 o and gated residual → Stage 4 router ∥ Stage 5 pooler → Stage 6 routed experts → Stage 7 unpooler → Stage 8 second gated residual

In Part I, we followed a single operator — gemv (qkv_gate in Stage 1 at T=1) — down through all 6 hardware levels, and at the end of Chapter 6 we scaled that same projection up to T=256 with multi-token GEMM (g0 → g5). Now Part II puts those same hardware mechanisms to work across the rest of the layer. Stage 1 hands off the qkv tensor (which packs query, key, value, and gate together) as the input to Stage 2. Where are the bottlenecks of Stage 2 paged attention under single-token decode, 8-token verification, and long-sequence prefill, and how does the kernel remove the slowest bottleneck step by step?

1What Does Stage 2 Compute, and What Quantity Governs Its Bottleneck?

Stage 2 turns qkv into the gated attention output; its bottleneck is governed by how many query rows share each key-value row.

Before we trace the math, let's get the basic numbers on the board. BB is the number of concurrent requests, LL is the number of new tokens per request in this forward pass, and T=B×L is the total number of tokens in this forward pass (see Primer 2, Section 4). In token-by-token decode, L=1; in verify, L=8, where we stack 1 committed token and 7 draft tokens from the drafting mechanism into 8 rows and run them together (see Primer 1, Section 7); in prefill, LL runs into the thousands. Each GPU holds 16 query heads and 2 KV heads (denoted g=0,1), with 64 dimensions per head. Because every 8 query heads share 1 KV head (GQA; see Primer 2, Section 2), each key-value row of a given KV head is shared across nq=8L query rows.

Stage 2 takes qkv:[T,2304]BF16\shape{\mathrm{qkv}}{T,\;2304}{BF16} as input and slices it by column into q:[T,16,64]BF16\shape{q}{T,\;16,\;64}{BF16}, k:[T,2,64]BF16\shape{k}{T,\;2,\;64}{BF16}, v:[T,2,64]BF16\shape{v}{T,\;2,\;64}{BF16}, and gate:[T,16,64]BF16\shape{\mathrm{gate}}{T,\;16,\;64}{BF16}, with column widths 1024+128+128+1024=2304.

Request lengths keep changing, and allocating contiguous device memory leaves fragments and forces data copies. So we store each request's historical keys and values in a paged KV cache, where each page can live anywhere in device memory. A page table page_table:[B,max_pages]int32\shape{\mathrm{page\_table}}{B,\;max\_pages}{int32} maps each request to its pages: each row corresponds to one request, and max_pages is the number of columns in the page table (no less than the page count of the longest request in the batch). Row b, column i records which physical page slot holds request b's page i; a new token can be appended to any free slot. Our workload sets each page to 1 token (page_size = 1), so reading every historical token takes a page-table lookup first. Section 6 deals with that wait. This page table shares its name with the page table of an operating system, but it is only a plain int32 array in device memory: software fills it in ahead of time, and the kernel reads it like any other data. The page table that the operating system and the hardware use to translate addresses is a different thing; see Appendix D, Section 1.

In memory, the cache tensors have shape K_cache, V_cache:[pages,1,2,64]FP8 E4M3\shape{K\_cache,\ V\_cache}{pages,\;1,\;2,\;64}{FP8\ E4M3} (page slots, tokens per page, KV heads, head dimension), paired with sequence lengths seq_lens:[B]int32\shape{\mathrm{seq\_lens}}{B}{int32}. Every historical token takes 2×2×64×1 B=256 B per layer on each GPU. A single token's K row packs 64 B from each of the two KV heads into 128 B total (and the same goes for the V row); a kernel that computes only one KV head reads only 64 B of that row, which we call a half-row (64 elements) below. Turning qkv into o_attn takes five steps:

  1. per-head RMSNorm (unweighted, computed in FP32; see Primer 1, Section 1 for the formula): q^=rmsnorm(q), k^=rmsnorm(k); v is not normalized.
  2. RoPE (rotary position embedding): applied only in the 46 sliding-window layers and skipped in the 16 full-attention layers (for RoPE, see Primer 2, Section 2): rotate adjacent dimensions (2i,2i+1) in FP32 by an angle determined by the token position.
  3. FP8 cast and KV cache write: cast q to E4M3; first divide new k and v by the cache's per-tensor scale factors given as external inputs (1 in scored cases — NVIDIA's Transformer Engine splits into a hardware half providing FP8 Tensor Cores that accept E4M3 and E5M2 inputs plus saturating FP8 conversion, and a software half selecting scale factors from tensor statistics, i.e., amax history / delayed scaling; our kernel uses only the hardware half), then cast them to E4M3 with saturation, clamped within the E4M3 maximum ±448\pm 448 (see Chapter 6, Section 5 for the bit layout), and write them into the cache by page slot index.
  4. GQA attention: for a token at position pp, a full-attention layer attends to all keys in 0..p0..p, whereas a sliding-window layer attends only to the most recent 2,048 keys (max⁡(0,p−2047)..p); the LL new tokens of the same request use a lower-triangular causal mask among themselves: o𝑟𝑎𝑤=softmax(5.4738qfp8K⊤)Vo_{raw} = \mathrm{softmax}\!\left(\frac{5.473}{8}\, q_{fp8} K^{\top}\right) V Here the model also multiplies the dot product by 5.4735.473 (an attention scaling factor fixed in the model configuration); combined with 1/64=1/8, this folds into a single multiplier 0.6840.684 applied to the dot product rather than to q.
  5. gated attention output: o𝑎𝑡𝑡𝑛=rmsnorm(o𝑟𝑎𝑤)⊙σ(gate)o_{attn} = \mathrm{rmsnorm}(o_{raw}) \odot \sigma(gate) producing o_attn:[T,1024]BF16\shape{\mathrm{o\_attn}}{T,\;1024}{BF16} for Stage 3.

Read one KV head of one historical token (K 64 B + V 64 B = 128 B), and nq=8L query rows use it; each query row does one 64-dimensional dot product and one 64-dimensional weighted sum, for 2×64+2×64=256 FLOPs in total. Divide that by the 128 B read, and you get the operations per byte read (arithmetic intensity; see Primer 2, Section 1): arithmetic intensity≈256nq128=2nq=16L FLOP/B\text{arithmetic intensity} \approx \frac{256 n_q}{128} = 2 n_q = 16L\ \mathrm{FLOP/B} In decode, L=1 (nq=8), so the arithmetic intensity is 16 FLOP/B. That 16 already sits above the ~14 FLOP/B ridge point of CUDA Cores (Chapter 5, Section 3), so CUDA Cores cannot keep up. On the Tensor Core, FP8 runs at twice the throughput of BF16 (Chapter 5, Section 4), which puts the ridge point at about 2×206=412 FLOP/B (for 206, see Primer 2, Section 1), so the Tensor Core is still waiting on data. When we run decode on the Tensor Core, its lower bound is therefore the time to read KV. Move to 8-token verify (L=8, nq=64), and the arithmetic intensity rises to about 128 FLOP/B: CUDA Cores still cannot keep up, and on the Tensor Core the kernel remains bandwidth-bound. Move further to long-sequence prefill (LL in the thousands), and the intensity shoots far past the ridge point into the compute-bound regime. As LL grows, the bottleneck shifts the same way qkv_gate did with TT in Chapter 5, except the horizontal axis here is nq=8L rather than TT: the same T=32 can be 32 decode requests (nq=8) or 4 verify requests (nq=64).

Two lower bounds anchor the two ends of this spectrum. Take decode first: for 1 request in a full-attention layer with 80,000 historical tokens, reading 20.5 MB of keys and values at 4.8 TB/s gives a bandwidth lower bound of about 4.3 µs. Decode has only 8 query rows, so the Tensor Core spends most of its time waiting on three things: at CTA entry, reading seq_lens first and then the page table, after which each page waits only for the page-table load to return (Section 6); fixed prologue and epilogue work per CTA (Section 4); and merging after splitting across segments (Section 3). Even after we tune the split count, the profiler clocks the attention kernel at about 13.8 µs on this shape, more than 3× the bandwidth lower bound: decode is latency-bound and cannot reach the pure bandwidth lower bound (how the ~9.5 µs gap between ~4.3 µs and ~13.8 µs splits across those three waits was not measured separately).

Now look at the other end, prefill: on a full-attention layer that appends 16,384 new tokens after 65,536 cached tokens, under the causal mask each new token attends to an average of n¯𝑘𝑒𝑦≈65,536+16,384/2=73,728 keys. Each query-key pair performs 4×64 FLOPs, which adds up to 16 heads×16,384×n¯𝑘𝑒𝑦×64×4 FLOP≈4,948 GFLOP. In the final version of this chapter, both QK⊤Q K^{\top} and PVP V run in FP8; the FP8 dense peak is twice the BF16 dense peak of 989 TFLOP/s, or about 1,979 TFLOP/s (see Chapter 5, Section 4), which puts the compute lower bound at about 2.50 ms. Reading the KV cache for those 65,536 tokens once from HBM takes only about 3.5 µs, but every query tile has to re-read the keys it attends to from L2; we will calculate that L2 traffic in Section 4 once we have the tile count.

In production, we run this model on the open-source inference framework SGLang, and our baseline for this chapter is SGLang's stock attention implementation. It runs the five steps above as 7 separate kernels, one after another: the first 5 perform Steps 1–3 — per-head RMSNorm (on sliding-window layers, RoPE runs inside the same kernel), a cast of k to FP8, a cast of v to FP8, and a cache write (3 kernels), plus a cast of q to FP8 (we call the kernel for Steps 1–3 before main attention the prologue kernel below; see the end of Section 3 and Section 11); next comes paged attention (which may launch an extra merge kernel when split); and finally the gated output. The evolution versions in this chapter launch them as a PDL chain instead, where each kernel reads the output of the preceding kernel only after the wait call (see Chapter 1, Section 4).

Sections 2–3 first build the shared starting point a0 (GQA query-row stacking, FP8 Q⋅K⊤, single-pass online softmax, and Split-KV); a0 → a6 then removes the slowest bottleneck in each of the three regimes in turn:

Regime nq=8L & arithmetic intensity Sequence of bottlenecks Sections
Decode (L=1) nq=8, ~16 FLOP/B Fill all 132 SMs, hide the page-table round trip, then fold prologue/merge boundaries Sections 4, 6, 11–12
Verify (L=8) nq=64, ~128 FLOP/B Scattered row gather first, then intra-CTA registers, consumer stagger, issue slots, and boundary merges Sections 5, 7–10, 11–12
Prefill (LL in the thousands) Far above the ~412 FLOP/B ridge Light-tile tail imbalance and the SFU exponential pipe, then issue slots and conversions Section 4 tail, Section 9, Sections 11–12

In the final standalone operator of this chapter, each shape lands on its corresponding kernel:

  • decode 1/16-request sliding window and verify 1-request sliding window: the 3-in-1 mma.sync cluster kernel fusing prologue, split-KV main loop, and intra-cluster DSMEM merge (Path 3 in Section 12; no separate merge kernel; decode 1 uses one 16-CTA cluster per KV head for 32 segments, decode 16 uses one 8-CTA cluster per request and KV head, and verify 1 uses two 16-CTA clusters per KV head covering 4 new tokens each).
  • verify 16/32-request sliding window: sliding-window single-KV-head wgmma cluster kernel (up to 3 CTAs per SM, with intra-cluster DSMEM direct-write merge; Path 3 in Section 12).
  • verify 16/32-request full attention: two-KV-head fusion wgmma kernel (2 CTAs per SM, with in-kernel L2 atomic-add merge; Path 1 in Section 12).
  • decode 1/16/32-request full attention, decode 32-request sliding window, and verify 1-request full attention: prologue fused into each split-KV CTA, followed by a separate merge kernel in this chapter's standalone operator.
  • prefill: a 1-CTA-per-token prologue kernel followed by the 1-CTA-per-SM, 3-consumer-warpgroup main kernel (full-attention layers also stage paged FP8 KV into contiguous 128-key tiles on a side stream and after the prologue; the 40 lightest query tiles split into 4 segments each and merge in-kernel via last-arriver tickets; Path 2 in Section 12).

When assembled into Chapter 9's single-layer chain, decode 1-, 16-, and 32-request full attention and decode 32-request sliding window in the fourth bullet switch to Path 2's last-arriver merge in Section 12 (see Chapter 9).

We evaluate every version in this chapter across 12 shapes: decode and verify with 1, 16, and 32 requests each (single-request history is 80,000 tokens, while 16- and 32-request histories are distributed within 80,000±7.5%), with each workload split between sliding-window layers and full-attention layers. Shape labels below follow the pattern "decode / verify + request count + full-attention / sliding-window"; for example, "verify 32-request full attention" means 32 requests with 8 new tokens each (T=256) on the 16 full-attention layers; across the sections that follow, one primary reference shape anchors each regime — decode 16-request full attention for decode, verify 32-request full attention for verify, and prefill 65K-history full attention for prefill (single-request-only mechanisms name their 1-request shape explicitly). The latency of each workload equals 46×46 \times sliding-window layer latency +16×+ 16 \times full-attention layer latency, giving the 62-layer attention total for one step; we then take the geometric mean (the 6th root of the product of the 6 numbers) across the 6 workloads as the representative latency for the entire suite.

Every single-shape latency for decode and verify comes from a paired ABBA benchmarking comparison of the standalone attention operator: within the same process, each shape is captured as a CUDA Graph and replayed in full after an L2 flush, alternating old and new versions in symmetric A, B, B, A order and subtracting their medians so both share identical inputs and cancel slow thermal and clock-frequency drift (for noise-band rules, see Chapter 4, Section 6); the two standalone paired criteria (60-round V1c and high-round S series) are stated where each is first used — in the first chart note of Section 4 and at the 1-request experiment in Section 6. Prefill figures come from single-layer or standalone-kernel prefill timings. Each chart note below names its exact harness (and notes whenever round counts or timing methods were not recorded), marking deltas that fall inside that run's own noise band as "within the noise band."

2a0 (Part 1): Why Stack the 8 Query Heads of the Same KV Head as Matrix Rows?

Each CTA handles one KV head and stacks all query rows sharing that head into operand A, so each key-value tile is loaded into the SM once to multiply against all query rows.

Suppose you launch one CTA for each query head: then 8 separate CTAs all have to read the exact same KV row.
