Because many of those 8 reads hit the 60 MiB L2 cache (see Chapter 2, Section 2), the bytes read from HBM are not necessarily 8× higher (how many HBM bytes query-row stacking saves, and on which shapes it would lose, were not measured separately) — what you definitely cut is the number of transfers into the SM and the number of load instructions, which by tile count drop from 8 copies down to 1.

So for a given KV head gg, we stack all nq=8L query rows that share it into Qg:[8L,64]FP8\shape{Q_g}{8L,\;64}{FP8}; in verify, each query head has 8 new tokens, giving 64 rows in total. Each time a 64-token KV tile is loaded (K takes 4 KiB, and K plus V takes 8 KiB in total), we multiply QgQ_g by the transpose of K𝑡𝑖𝑙𝑒:[64,64]FP8\shape{K_{tile}}{64,\;64}{FP8} to compute the entire score tile S:[8L,64]FP32\shape{S}{8L,\;64}{FP32} in one pass.

Who holds which query rows (for register-fragment layouts, see Chapter 5, Section 4)? In a 64-row wgmma at L=8, the 4 warps of a consumer warpgroup take 16 rows each; in the two-head decode split kernel (swap-AB mma.sync below), each of the 4 warps holds all 8 query rows in registers and splits the 64-key tile into 4 disjoint 16-key slices (see the table in Section 4).

That row count nq=8L also decides which Tensor Core instruction family we use (see Chapter 5, Section 4 for the two instruction families). In token-by-token decode (L=1), there are only 8 rows. The kernel for decode 1- and 16-request sliding window places them into the 16 rows of mma.sync (m16n8k32), so half the rows are padding. The split kernel for decode full attention and decode 32-request sliding window swaps operands A and B instead (see Chapter 5, Section 5) and computes S⊤=KQ⊤: 16 keys sit on m=16 and the 8 query rows fill n=8 exactly, with zero padding. In exchange, it first converts FP8 K losslessly to half-precision FP16 (1 sign bit, 5 exponent bits, and 10 mantissa bits, with a maximum of 65,504 — able to represent every E4M3 value exactly) and issues FP16 mma.sync (m16n8k16). Because decode arithmetic intensity (16 FLOP/B) sits far below the ~412 FLOP/B FP8 Tensor Core ridge point and is bottlenecked on reading the KV cache (Section 1: latency-bound), the Tensor Core has plenty of idle cycles, from which we infer that neither the 8 padded rows nor the FP16 conversion sits on the critical path (not measured separately). In verify, 64 rows fill m=64 of wgmma to the brim. Verify full attention adopts wgmma from the early versions onward, whereas verify 16- and 32-request sliding window initially process 16-row groups with mma.sync before moving to wgmma in Section 5 (a2).

While we are at it, we also run the first matrix multiplication Q⋅K⊤ directly in FP8: K in the cache is already FP8 E4M3 (see Chapter 6, Section 5 for the bit layout), so once q is cast to E4M3 as well, the multiplication can consume the bytes of K directly and skip unpacking K to 16-bit first (except in the decode split kernel above that losslessly converts K to FP16 for KQ⊤K Q^{\top}). The trade-off is that casting q to FP8 introduces rounding error (accounted for in Section 8); how much time this step saves on its own was not measured separately. Once each KV tile streams into the SM and produces a score tile SS, the full row of keys has not been read yet — how do we build the softmax denominator on the fly in a single pass?

3a0 (Part 2): Before All Keys and Values Are Read, How Is the Softmax Denominator Computed on the Fly, and How Are Split Segments Merged Exactly?

Online softmax tracks only the running maximum, denominator, and unnormalized output, rescaling prior values by the exponential difference as each new key tile arrives and merging split-KV segments via log-sum-exp weights.

First, let's switch the exponential base to 2: the hardware transcendental instruction ex2 computes 2x2^x directly on the SFU (the machine instruction is MUFU.EX2; see Chapter 5, Section 1 for the SFU pipeline). If we multiply the dot product by 0.684×log⁡2e (log⁡2e≈1.4427) before taking 2x2^x, we get the exact same math as base ee. Every score ss below already bakes in this factor.

The naive way to compute softmax makes two passes over memory: pass one finds the full-row maximum m=max⁡ksk and the denominator l=∑k2sk−m (subtracting mm prevents exponent overflow), and pass two computes ∑k2sk−mvk/l\sum_k 2^{s_k-m} v_k / l. Doing that forces us to read the keys and values twice. The single-pass method (online softmax) fuses both passes into one sweep: whenever a new key tile arrives, we find the tile maximum m𝑡𝑖𝑙𝑒m_{tile} and update m𝑛𝑒𝑤=max⁡(m𝑜𝑙𝑑,m𝑡𝑖𝑙𝑒). Because our running ll and OO were scaled against m𝑜𝑙𝑑m_{old}, multiplying both by the rescaling factor α=2m𝑜𝑙𝑑−m𝑛𝑒𝑤 shifts them onto m𝑛𝑒𝑤m_{new}: l←αl+∑k∈tile2sk−m𝑛𝑒𝑤,O←αO+∑k∈tile2sk−m𝑛𝑒𝑤vkl \leftarrow \alpha\, l + \sum_{k\in tile} 2^{s_k-m_{new}},\qquad O \leftarrow \alpha\, O + \sum_{k\in tile} 2^{s_k-m_{new}}\, v_k Once all tiles have streamed through, a final division gives o=O/l. Packing the 2sk−m𝑛𝑒𝑤2^{s_k-m_{new}} values within a tile into a matrix gives the attention score weight matrix P, which turns the two recurrences into l←αl+P𝟏 and O←αO+PV. Once m𝑛𝑒𝑤m_{new} is known, computing P and its row sum P𝟏P\mathbf{1} does not wait on αO\alpha O, whereas the second MMA P⋅V takes the rescaled αO\alpha O directly as its accumulator in place and therefore waits for both P and αO\alpha O. Both "P · V" and "BF16 P" below refer to this matrix.

In hardware, mm, ll, and the accumulator OO stay in per-thread private registers throughout: the MMA accumulator fragment spreads each row across a quad of 4 consecutive lanes (in both mma.sync and wgmma, each thread owns 2 rows within its warp's slice; see Chapter 5, Section 4). To agree on a row's new maximum, each thread first takes a local maximum over its own scores (FMNMX) and then runs 2 butterfly XOR-shuffle steps (SHFL.BFLY) with comparisons inside the 4-lane quad so all 4 threads sharing that row obtain the same m𝑡𝑖𝑙𝑒m_{tile}.

Let's trace a small example you can check by hand (and play tile by tile in Figure 7-3): take one query row, 3 key tiles with 2 keys per tile, and base-2 pre-scaled scores Tile 1 =[1,3]= [1, 3], Tile 2 =[2,5]= [2, 5], Tile 3 =[0,4]= [0, 4], where each key has a 1-dimensional value v: Tile 1 =[4,2]= [4, 2], Tile 2 =[0,8]= [0, 8], Tile 3 =[6,2]= [6, 2].

After Tile 1 arrives: m=3, l=2−2+20=1.25, O=2−2⋅4+1⋅2=3.

When Tile 2 arrives: m𝑡𝑖𝑙𝑒=5 updates m𝑛𝑒𝑤=5, giving α=23−5=0.25; rescaling and adding the new tile yields l=1.25×0.25+2−3+20=1.4375, and O=0.25×3+2−3⋅0+1⋅8=8.75.

When Tile 3 arrives: m𝑡𝑖𝑙𝑒=4<5, so α=1 (no rescaling needed); we get l=1.4375+2−5+2−1=1.96875, O=8.75+2−5⋅6+2−1⋅2=9.9375, and finally o=9.9375/1.96875≈5.048. Compare that with the two-pass method: ∑2s−5=2−4+2−2+2−3+1+2−5+2−1=1.96875 and ∑2s−5v=9.9375, which lands on the exact same result.

With the intra-tile recurrence in place, keys and values are read only once, yet without splitting along keys — launching just 1 CTA per request and KV head — at B=1 only 2 of the 132 SMs on the GPU do any work (about 1.5%, leaving 130 SMs idle while each CTA sweeps all 80,000 keys, or 1,250 tiles, serially; how much slower unsplit execution runs was not measured separately). To fill the GPU, we add Split-KV (partitioning along the key dimension): slice the visible keys of a request into SS segments assigned to SS CTAs across the 132 SMs. Each segment writes its partial results into a global-memory region called the workspace buffer, which typically stays hot in L2 right after being written (for the general pattern of merging partial sums across CTAs, see Chapter 2, Sections 6 and 8). Segment ii runs the recurrence above on its own slice and outputs oi=Oi/li along with the log-sum-exp (lse) lsei=mi+log⁡2li. Because 2lsei=2mili is segment ii's exact unshifted denominator relative to 0, the total log-denominator across all keys is lse=log⁡2∑i2lsei, and the merge step accumulates o=∑i2lsei−lseoio = \sum_i 2^{\mathrm{lse}_i-\mathrm{lse}}\; o_i Multiplying by 2lsei−lse2^{\mathrm{lse}_i-\mathrm{lse}} swaps out segment ii's own denominator and replaces it with the denominator across all keys. Now split the example above into two segments (Figure 7-3 Mode 2). Segment A holds Tiles 1–2: mA=5, lA=1.4375, 2lseA=32×1.4375=46, oA=8.75/1.4375≈6.087. Segment B holds Tile 3: mB=4, lB=1.0625, 2lseB=16×1.0625=17, oB≈2.235. The total denominator is 46+17=63=25×1.96875, the merge weights are 46/6346/63 and 17/6317/63, and the weighted sum is 4663oA+1763oB=280+3863≈5.048, which is mathematically identical to no splitting; when the floating-point summation order differs, the last bit of the result may differ, and this only becomes important in Section 12.

Together, online softmax and Split-KV let us read the keys and values only once while spreading work across multiple CTAs. In exchange, we pay two costs: each tile adds one maximum reduction, one ex2, and an elementwise multiplication on OO (Section 8 removes most of this); and splitting across segments writes an extra (oi,lsei)(o_i, \mathrm{lse}_i) per segment and runs an extra merge step. Meanwhile, Steps 1–3 of Section 1 (per-head RMSNorm, RoPE, and FP8 cast plus KV cache write) run in a separate kernel launched before the main kernel, called the prologue kernel. Put all of these together and we get our starting point a0: separate prologue kernel + GQA query-row stacking + FP8 Q⋅K⊤ + fixed-split Split-KV + separate merge kernel, where the split count in a0 is fixed — for example, decode 1-request full attention is fixed at 128 segments.

4a0 → a1: Into How Many Segments Should One Request's Keys Be Split, and How Should They Be Balanced?

Split more finely at low concurrency to keep enough reads in flight, and less finely at high concurrency to avoid multi-wave CTA launch/exit overhead, while balancing work by actual sequence lengths.

Every split segment launches one CTA. Fitting the profiler readings on the decode 16- and 32-request shapes (fitting method not recorded) shows that each CTA spends about 2.04 µs per 64-key tile, plus about 6.6 µs of entry/exit overhead to read the page-table start offset, load Q, and write back (oi,lsei)(o_i, \mathrm{lse}_i) (distinct from the kernel launch gap in Chapter 1). Because most of this 6.6 µs is spent waiting on memory rather than saturating issue slots, CTAs within the same wave (see Chapter 2, Section 1) wait in parallel across the chip, and critical-path launch/exit overhead is bounded by approximately "waves × 6.6 µs" rather than "CTAs × 6.6 µs". On top of that, the merge step reads back one partial result per segment, which we account for separately.

So whether to raise or lower the split count SS comes down to whether all CTAs already fit inside 1 wave. When they fit, splitting further adds no wave entry/exit overhead; once they spill past 1 wave, each additional wave pays the fixed per-CTA entry/exit overhead (about 6.6 µs) one more time. At this stage, the split kernel for decode full attention computes both KV heads in each CTA. For each 64-key tile, it uses the page table to randomly read 16 KiB of K and V for the two heads, or 8 KiB per KV head; we call this gather below. It places 4 CTAs per SM, so 1 wave holds 132×4=528 CTAs (see Chapter 3, Section 1 for how residency is calculated). Until Section 5 switches it to full-row gather, it gathers only a 64 B half-row per head at a time; in the isolated gather-only microbenchmark in Section 5 below, such 64 B half-row gather reaches 2.6–3.1 TB/s. Below 1 full wave, there are not enough bytes in flight to saturate HBM (see Chapter 2, Section 3): at low concurrency (decode 1-request full attention), 128 segments launch 128 CTAs — just 0.24 waves — and measured gather bandwidth crawls at about 1.3 TB/s; splitting into 256 segments (256 CTAs, 0.48 waves) keeps all CTAs within 1 wave while doubling in-flight reads, which makes execution faster.

Kernel Threads & warpgroups Registers / thread (compile → post-setmaxnreg) Shared memory / CTA CTAs / SM & 1-wave capacity (132 SMs) What each role holds in registers and shared memory
Two-head decode split kernel (decode full; also decode 32 sliding from Section 5) 128 threads = 4 warps (4 disjoint 16-key slices per 64-key tile; Head 0 then Head 1 serially per warp) 127–128 (unsplit) 48 KiB (3 slots × 8 KiB each for K and V after Section 5 full-row gather) 4 CTAs / 528 CTAs Registers hold two-head Q (swap-AB FP16 mma.sync), in-flight int32 page-entry vectors, and FP32 (m,l,O)(m, l, O) (per-variable register split not measured); shared memory holds the 3-slot KV ring
Single-head mma.sync split kernel (a1 decode & verify sliding) 1 CTA per KV head (exact thread count not listed separately) Residency set by register usage (exact count not listed separately) Single-head 64 B half-row KV ring (shrunk to 1 stage on verify 1 sliding before replacement in Section 12) 3–4 CTAs / 396–528 CTAs Registers hold 1 KV head's query rows (8 rows at L=1, 16-row groups at L=8) and FP32 (m,l,O)(m, l, O); shared memory holds single-head 64 B half-row KV tiles
Prefill full-attention wgmma main kernel (T=16,384, etc.) 512 threads = 1 producer warpgroup + 3 consumer warpgroups Compile 128 (65,536 / CTA) → producer 56, 3 consumer groups 152 each, plus warp-shared UR (see Section 7) ~78 KiB (79,952 B: Q_0..Q_2 12 KiB + 4-slot × 16 KiB K and V⊤V^{\top} ring) 1 CTA / 132 CTAs Producer streams staged 128-key tiles into the ring; 3 consumer groups compute 64 query rows each (192 rows = 24 tokens), holding S,P,O,m,lS, P, O, m, l in 152 regs and warp-uniform scalars in UR (per-variable split not measured); shared memory holds Q_0..Q_2 and the 4-slot ring

For the auxiliary and fused kernels in Sections 11–12: the fused prefill prologue launches 1 CTA per token (96 threads = 3 warps, 0 shared memory; register usage and residency not measured separately); the standalone merge kernel launches 4 warps (dropping to 2 warps when segments ≤16\le 16); and exact thread, register, and shared-memory counts for the 1-request sliding-window 3-in-1 mma.sync 16-CTA cluster kernel (Path 3 in Section 12) are not listed separately (for the three verify wgmma kernels, see the table in Section 5).

At high concurrency, the math flips and we must split into fewer segments instead. Take our primary decode reference shape, decode 16-request full attention: keeping 128 segments launches 2,048 CTAs, or 3.88 waves; consolidating to 32 segments (512 CTAs, 0.97 waves; with segments still above 16, the merge kernel stays at 4 warps) pulls the grid inside 1 wave, saving about 3 waves of entry/exit overhead and cutting the partial results read by the merge step to 1/4. Multiplying 3 waves × 6.6 µs predicts a maximum saving of about 20 µs, and the measured saving is 12.10 µs (about 12 µs); the source of the difference was not measured separately (the other three cells that drop to 16 segments bundled with a narrower merge launch appear in the chart note below).

Conversely, full-attention verify at this stage uses the single-KV-head split kernel (one CTA computes one KV head, likewise placing 4 CTAs per SM, or 528 CTAs per wave): once verify 16-request full attention already fits inside 1 wave (16 segments, 512 CTAs, 0.97 waves), cutting it further from 16 segments down to 8 segments (256 CTAs, 0.48 waves) slows execution by 101 µs instead (see the note in the chart below). Our explanation (unverified): once all CTAs already fit within 1 wave, cutting further saves zero waves and only drops co-resident CTAs per SM from about 4 to about 2 — halving in-flight reads — while doubling the number of tiles each CTA processes serially.

Verify 1-request sliding window has a neat boundary quirk of its own: the latest of the 8 new tokens attends to 7 more keys than the earliest, so at most 2,048+7=2,055 keys are visible, requiring ⌈2,055/64⌉=33 tiles of 64 keys — 1 more than 32. Originally, each KV head was split into 32 segments, forcing 17 CTAs to process 2 tiles serially each. We first switch to 64 segments per KV head: 33 segments process 1 tile each and the remaining 31 empty segments write only lsei=−∞\mathrm{lse}_i = -\infty, eliminating the serial wait for a second tile and saving about 1.10 µs (see the chart below). Later steps drop the empty segments to launch 33 single-tile CTAs per KV head (66 in total) and shrink the ring buffer here (see Chapter 3, Section 6) to 1 stage; those two steps were measured separately. The cost is that the merge step reads 33 (oi,lsei)(o_i, \mathrm{lse}_i) pairs.

Requests in the same batch often have different lengths: in this workload suite, historical lengths lie within ±7.5%\pm 7.5\% of the mean, so the longest request is about 16% longer than the shortest (1.075/0.925≈1.16). When segments are divided equally per request, CTAs for the longest request run about 16% longer than those for the shortest, holding up the last SMs at the tail. To fix this, we concatenate the keys of all requests into a single logical strip and partition it evenly across all CTAs by actual key count; the trade-off is that one segment may span two requests, requiring extra work in the merge step.

In the two-KV-head fusion wgmma kernel introduced in Sections 5 and 7 for full-attention verify, register usage places 2 CTAs per SM, so 1 wave is 2×132=264 CTAs. On our primary verify reference shape, verify 32-request full attention, before this change the grid launched 256 CTAs, occupying 0.97 waves (leaving 8 CTA slots empty across the GPU) with unequal key counts per CTA; after this change, it launches all 264 CTAs (1.00 wave) directly, concatenates the key tiles of all 32 requests into one logical strip, inserts 5 virtual tiles at each of the 31 boundaries between adjacent requests (155 virtual tiles total, standing for the cost of crossing a request boundary), and splits the strip evenly across the 264 CTAs by tile count to fill 1 wave exactly, saving about 3.7 µs (see the chart in Section 7; with the same trade-off that a segment may span two requests and add work in the merge step).

Prefill also needs to balance its tail, using the 512-thread kernel in the last row of the table above: each CTA has 1 producer warpgroup and 3 consumer warpgroups (512 threads in total; Chapter 3, Sections 6 and 8; why 3 consumer warpgroups were chosen rather than 2 or 4 was not measured). Each consumer warpgroup computes 64 query rows, so one CTA handles 24 tokens × 8\times\ 8 query heads =192= 192 query rows for one KV head; its register usage (512×128=65,536) allows only 1 CTA per SM, making 1 wave equal to 132 CTAs. At T=16,384, the grid launches ⌈16,384/24⌉×2=683×2=1,366 query-tile CTAs in total.

Each of those 1,366 query-tile CTAs streams all KV entries visible to it from L2: 1,366 CTAs ×\times an average of about 73,728 visible keys ×\times 128 B per key per KV head, totaling about 12.9 GB. H200's L2 peak bandwidth is unpublished: at the 7.33 TB/s re-read rate measured in the residency-hint microbenchmark of Chapter 2, Section 4, streaming through once takes about 1.76 ms; using the 16-bit MMA loop of unpooler at T=128 from Chapter 6 (where 128 CTAs read about 67.11 MB of weights in 16.17 µs at about 4.15 TB/s while re-reading twice that volume of input tiles from L2 into shared memory, for an estimated total of about 12.4 TB/s), it takes about 1.0 ms. Either figure is shorter than the 2.50 ms dense FP8 compute lower bound from Section 1, so prefill remains compute-bound.

We launch the 683 CTAs of each KV head in descending order of work from heaviest to lightest. As explained in Chapter 2, Section 1, CTAs do not switch in lockstep waves — as soon as an SM frees a slot, the next CTA is dispatched; under the causal mask, earlier query tiles attend to fewer keys and do less work, so the last CTAs dispatched onto SMs are the lightest 40 query tiles (40 CTAs). Once the dispatch queue drains, SMs that finish early sit idle waiting for this last batch of CTAs to complete. Splitting each KV head's lightest 40 query tiles into 4 segments along the key dimension (40 and 4 were tuned empirically) expands the grid to (683−40+40×4)×2=1,606 CTAs. We pay the entry/exit and merge overhead of 240 extra CTAs, and in return the final batch of CTAs takes only 1/4 of the original time, letting the tail SMs finish earlier and saving 345 µs on our primary prefill reference shape, 65K-history full attention (see the chart below).

What if we replace static key-count balancing with dynamic claiming, where each CTA claims its next tile from a global counter? In measured runs, that is actually slower (about 23 µs slower on verify 32-request full attention). Every claimed 64-key tile adds a metadata handoff and a 128-thread intra-CTA barrier, raising the measured per-tile cost by about 10% while breaking the pipeline that prefetches the next tile's page-table entries (see Section 6). At the same time, static imbalance is at most about 16% to begin with and is already tiny once we split evenly by key count, so dynamic claiming has very little ceiling left to recover.

With a fixed segment count, short requests or sliding-window boundaries can also produce empty segments (start ≥\ge end). On shapes that enable empty-segment skipping, an empty segment writes only lsei=−∞\mathrm{lse}_i = -\infty and skips writing an all-zero output. Because 2−∞=0, the formula in Section 3 still holds, and when the merge step sees −∞-\infty, it skips that segment directly. We did not measure the time saved by skipping empty segments separately.

No single combination of kernel and split count wins across all shapes, so a1 looks up a per-shape table. At this stage, decode sliding window and verify sliding window both use the single-KV-head mma.sync split kernel (one CTA computes one KV head; register usage sets 3–4 CTAs per SM). Decode full attention uses the two-KV-head split kernel described earlier in this section. Per-shape table lookup cuts the 6-workload geometric mean defined in Section 1 by about 8%; because this version also switched several kernels at the same time, not all 8% comes from table lookup alone (the final kernel assignment for each shape is listed at the end of Section 1).

5a1 → a2 (Part 1): When Two KV Heads Share the Same 128 B K Row, How Should the Two Halves Be Read?

Gathering the full 128 B row in one shot reads the exact same HBM bytes while cutting global memory requests in half and widening each request from 64 B (2 sectors of 32 B) to a full 128 B cache line (4 sectors).

Start with the broad picture: when we turn off the consumers' matrix multiplies and softmax inside the real verify kernel and leave only the producer gathering KV (which we call the producer-only microbenchmark below), runtime is still 92%–94% of the full kernel — so verify really is gather-bound.

Because the page table scatters each token into an arbitrary page slot, the kernel sees a stream of random addresses. TMA multidimensional tensor copies cannot follow a page table. That leaves two options: each thread issues 16 B cp.async instructions, or each row gets one 128 B 1D bulk copy, cp.async.bulk (see Chapter 3, Section 5 for the four paths). The decode and verify kernels in this chapter gather row by row with 16 B cp.async. One token's K row is 128 B wide — exactly 1 full 128 B cache line of 4 sectors of 32 B each (for sectors and cache lines, see Chapter 3, Section 2): 8 threads issuing one 16 B cp.async each coalesce into 1 four-sector request for the full 128 B row, whereas gathering two 64 B half-rows separately (4 threads × 16 B each time) reads the same total bytes across twice as many global requests of 2 sectors (half a cache line) each (whether a 64 B read also fills the untouched 2 sectors into L2 is unpublished and not measured). In an isolated gather-only microbenchmark, gathering the full 128 B row at once hits 4.0–4.1 TB/s of random-row gather bandwidth — about 30% to 50%+ faster than gathering two 64 B half-rows separately at 2.6–3.1 TB/s (see the chart below).

The lightest fix is to reorder the grid dimensions so that two CTAs with adjacent blockIdx values handle the two KV heads of the same token segment: launching them back-to-back places the reads of the two halves of the same row right next to each other in time (see Chapter 2, Section 2; whether the second read hits L2 was not measured, only the latency). This relies on the measured behavior from Chapter 2, Section 1 — H200 dispatches CTAs in increasing blockIdx order. It takes zero registers and zero shared memory, at the cost of depending on an unspecified dispatch order; even if that dispatch order changes, the numerical result is still right. On our primary verify reference shape, verify 32-request full attention, this saves about 12 µs (and leaves verify 16-request full attention unchanged).

In the decode (L=1) kernel, the two KV heads of one token together have only 2×8=16 query rows, so a small 4-warp (128-thread) CTA using mma.sync can compute both heads together (Row 1 of the Section 4 table: the 4 warps split each 64-key tile into 4 disjoint 16-key slices, and each warp computes Head 0 then Head 1 serially). In Section 4 this two-head CTA still gathered two separate 64 B half-rows; switching to 8 threads coalescing the full 128 B row into shared memory in one shot — applying a 128 B XOR swizzle on write to avoid bank conflicts (see Chapter 3, Section 9) — lets both heads read from the same buffer. Capping each CTA at 128 registers per thread and 48 KiB of shared memory (3 buffer slots ×\times 8 KiB each for K and V) keeps residency at 4 CTAs per SM across the same 512-CTA grid. Profiler measurements on decode 32-request full attention confirm that DRAM bytes read did not change (~665 MB before and after, i.e., 1× KV), while achieved bandwidth rose from 3.32 TB/s to 3.62 TB/s: halving the request count and fetching 4-sector full cache lines saves 15.58 µs (about 16 µs; at the cost of a shared full-row buffer in shared memory).

In verify (L=8), a single KV head already has 64 query rows and must use wgmma. So full-attention verify switches to a 3-warpgroup (384-thread) two-KV-head fusion (merging 2 KV heads per CTA) kernel: 1 producer warpgroup gathers one full K row and one full V row (256 B in total) per token and feeds 2 consumer warpgroups, one per KV head (for warp specialization, see Chapter 3, Section 6; even though the producer only issues copies, it occupies a full 128-thread warpgroup because setmaxnreg reallocates registers per warpgroup in Section 7 — see Chapter 3, Section 8). That saves about 5 µs on verify 32-request full attention (see the chart below). Sliding-window verify uses a sliding-window single-KV-head wgmma kernel, where each CTA computes one KV head with 1 producer warpgroup and 1 consumer warpgroup. Replacing the single-KV-head mma.sync split kernel with it makes verify 16- and 32-request sliding window faster (see the note in the chart below). In both wgmma verify kernels, each consumer warpgroup feeds one head at a time to wgmma (K-extent D=64 FP8 bytes =64= 64 B; the two-KV-head fusion kernel stores each 128 B row as two 64 B per-head blocks), so Q and K in shared memory use Hopper's 64 B swizzle mode per head (XORing 16 B chunks by (row÷2) mod 4, repeating every 512 B; see Chapter 3, Section 9) and set the matching wgmma descriptor mode, whereas only V converted to 16-bit (128 B per row) keeps the 128 B swizzle. The table below summarizes the three verify wgmma kernels:

Kernel Threads & warpgroups Registers / thread (compile → post-setmaxnreg) Shared memory / CTA CTAs / SM & 1-wave capacity (132 SMs) What each role holds in registers and shared memory
Single-head wgmma full-verify kernel (a0–a1 verify 16/32 full; final verify 1 full) 256 threads = 1 producer warpgroup + 1 consumer warpgroup (128 threads each) Compile 64 (16,384 / CTA) → producer 32, consumer 96 ~53 KiB (54,500 B: includes Q_0 4 KiB + 4-slot × 8 KiB single-head KV ring; rest not itemized) 4 CTAs / 528 CTAs Producer holds page slots and addresses in 32 regs; consumer holds S,P,O,m,lS, P, O, m, l in 96 regs (per-variable split not measured); shared memory holds resident Q_0 and the 4-slot single-head KV ring
Sliding-window single-head wgmma kernel (verify 16/32 sliding from Section 5) 256 threads = 1 producer warpgroup + 1 consumer warpgroup 72 ~53–56 KiB (54,400–57,296 B; drops to 46,208 B ≈ 45 KiB after Section 10 FP8 P⋅V, saving 8 KiB) Up to 3 CTAs / up to 396 slots (grouped into single-GPC clusters in Section 12) Producer gathers single-head 64 B K, V into the ring; consumer holds S,P,O,m,lS, P, O, m, l in regs (per-variable split not measured); shared memory holds Q_0 (4 KiB), KV ring (64 B swizzle), and Section 12 cluster-merge staging
Two-KV-head fusion wgmma verify kernel (verify 16/32 full from Section 5) 384 threads = 1 producer warpgroup + 2 consumer warpgroups Compile 80 (30,720 / CTA) → unpeeled base 24 / 112 / 104, Section 7 default-producer build 32 / 104 / 104 ~105 KiB → ~89 KiB (107,584 B → 91,200 B after Section 10 FP8 P⋅V, saving 16 KiB; final m64n72k32 adds 1 KiB/head of all-ones rows, Section 10) 2 CTAs / 264 CTAs Producer holds segment bounds, base addresses, and next-tile page slots in 32 regs; 2 consumer groups hold S,P,O,m,lS, P, O, m, l in 104 regs each (plus 8 in-flight P regs in Section 10; per-variable split not measured); shared memory holds resident Q_0, Q_1 (8 KiB total, 64 B swizzle) and 4-slot × 16 KiB two-head KV ring (64 KiB)

The trade-off of two-KV-head fusion is that the total CTA count is cut in half and each SM holds only 2 CTAs. What if we copy this heavy 384-thread two-KV-head fusion structure over to token-by-token decode (L=1)? Decode 16- and 32-request full attention run about twice as slow (see the note in the chart below). Our explanation (unverified): the 128-thread small CTA places 4 CTAs per SM whereas the 384-thread heavy structure places only 2, cutting in-flight gather reads per SM in half; at L=1, 56 of the 64 rows in wgmma are also padding.

The first half-row versus full-row bandwidth chart above came from a standalone microbenchmark that only does gather. The gather microbenchmark below copies the structure of the two-KV-head fusion kernel: 2 CTAs per SM, 1 producer warpgroup gathering into a shared-memory ring buffer, and consumer warpgroups that simply return ring slots without doing any compute. When we measure its gather bandwidth with a real page table, even laying out all addresses completely contiguously saves only a little over 10% of the gather time (see the chart below), matching the producer-only finding above (92%–94% of the full kernel). This two-KV-head fusion gather microbenchmark achieves lower bandwidth than the standalone microbenchmark; how much of that drop comes from having fewer bytes in flight was not measured separately.

6a1 → a2 (Part 2): When Reading Each KV Page Requires a Three-Hop Pointer Chain First, How Do We Hide That Wait?

Preloading the first 4 page-table tiles before the loop and prefetching 2 iterations ahead with even/odd register pairs to avoid copying pending loads aims to hide the page-table lookup round trip inside the pipeline; issuing sequence-length and page-table loads concurrently at batch size 1 saves a measured ~0.26 µs on decode 1-request full attention.

When each page holds only 1 token, reading a single KV row has to walk a three-hop pointer chain first: Hop 1 reads seq_lens[b], Hop 2 uses the resulting logical page index to read page_table[b, i], and Hop 3 uses the physical page slot to compute addr=base+slot×128, fire the first cp.async, and wait for the KV data to land. On the lightly loaded verify 1-request full-attention shape, the measured time from launch until the first tile's data lands is about 2.4 µs (see Figure 7-6 Mode 1 for the duration of each hop); this 2.4 µs is entry latency, distinct from the 6.6 µs full-load overhead in Section 4. Where does that wait land? Right on the integer multiply-add instruction that first computes a memory address from the physical page slot: the profiler shows that warps at this instruction stall mostly on the scoreboard waiting for the page-table load to return — a hardware warp-state sampler inside each SM periodically checks why an active warp did not issue an instruction, and a reason's fraction of all non-issuing samples is its stall sampling share, reaching 37%–42% here (for the full sampling mechanism, see Chapter 10, Section 7; for the scoreboard, see Chapter 4, Section 2). The multi-slot ring buffer from Chapter 3, Section 6 can hide data transfer latency, but it cannot hide address latency — cp.async cannot issue until the address is known.

To pull that per-tile page-table round trip off the critical path, we prefetch page-table entries ahead and widen the gap between issuing a page-table load and using its slot to form an address. In the two-head decode full-attention kernel, page_table in global memory is int32 across every build (64 entries = 256 B per tile; none of these edits cut global bytes), and the shared-memory ring always holds 3 slots of 16 KiB (48 KiB; small decode CTAs track cp.async completion by group via commit_group / wait_group, whereas producer-consumer verify rings signal slot readiness via cp.async.mbarrier.arrive, see Chapter 3, Sections 5 and 7). Before entering the loop, the pre-change code issues cp.async for Tiles 0, 1, loads Tile 2 page_table, and immediately forms the int64 slot offset slots_pf and mask in registers; both rewrites instead preload int32 page entries for Tiles 0..3 (256 entries = 1 KiB, with ld.global.L1::evict_last hint) before the PDL wait call and pre-issue cp.async for Tiles 0, 1. At iteration jj of the main loop, the three code states hold and wait on the following:

Page-table registers at iteration jj Page-table LDG in flight at iteration jj KV cp.async in flight Who waits for whom
Before (1-iteration lookahead, 3-way unroll): 1 int64 slots_pf + mask (Tile j+2, issued at j-1) Issue Tile j+3 page_table (256 B) into slots_pf wait_group(1) lands Tile j; Tile j+1 stays in flight while slots_pf issues cp.async(j+2) Only 1 iteration overlaps j+3, so the integer multiply-add forming slots_pf stalls on the scoreboard waiting for page_table (top stall on decode 1 full)
Rewrite 1 (still 3-way unroll): 2 int32 page vectors pg_a (j+2) and pg_b (j+3), forming int64 slots only at cp.async issue (0 spills) Issue Tile j+4 page_table (256 B) into pg_n; copy (pg_a, pg_b) ← (pg_b, pg_n) at loop latch wait_group(1) lands Tile j; Tile j+1 stays in flight while pg_a issues cp.async(j+2) 3-way latch copies read pending pg_n (right before Rewrite 2, NCU on decode 32 full measured 20 of 36 latch copies reading pending LDGs, top 3 stall PCs taking 20.0% of all stalls, ≥20.0%\ge 20.0\% across all 20 uncounted; Rewrite 1's own stall share not measured)
Rewrite 2 (6-way even/odd in place): pg_a and pg_b alternate in place by parity — even jj consumes pg_a (j+2, issued at j-2), odd j+1 consumes pg_b (j+3, issued at j-1), 0 pending-load copies Even jj refills pg_a in place with page_table[j+4] (pg_b untouched in flight); odd j+1 refills pg_b with page_table[j+5] Same (Tile j lands for compute; Tiles j+1, j+2 stream in the 3-slot ring) Gives page_table[j+4] a full 2-iteration code distance before iteration j+2 consumes it (post-change stall share not measured)

In 60-round V1c paired runs, Rewrite 1 (three-part page-table bundle, shares not measured separately; the same commit also raised the decode 16/32 sliding ring to 3 stages, unrelated to page prefetch; holding 3 page vectors hit 128 registers with 2 spills, and the register saving of 2 int32 vectors versus int64 was not measured) saves 0.99–1.58 µs on our primary decode reference shape, decode 16-request full attention (while 0.18–0.26 µs on decode 1 full and decode 32 full sit within V1c noise); Rewrite 2 passes the standalone 60-round V1c paired gate (V1C_PASS), saving 0.34–0.48 µs and 0.70–0.86 µs on decode 16- and 32-request full attention (clearing the V1c gate at margins comparable to identical-code file-copy bias, while decode 1 full shifts 0.08–0.16 µs inside the 0.4 µs noise band). Other lookahead depths were not measured separately.

For a single request, we can also avoid waiting on the sequence length. The kernel launch parameters already include the page-table column count max_pages (Section 1); at B=1, this usually equals the request's own page count, though the page table may also be pre-allocated to a larger cap, so seq_lens[0] must still be read. For 1-request decode, the kernel computes the segment range from max_pages first and issues the page-table loads for the first 4 tiles concurrently with seq_lens[0]; once seq_lens[0] returns, it verifies before actual use whether the true range matches (re-reading only on a mismatch; the check itself has zero measured cost). Turning three hops into two saves a measured ~0.26 µs on decode 1-request full attention in high-round S-series paired runs (600–18,000 rounds, including an identical-code replica control whose recorded spread across shapes and runs is 0–0.16 µs plus a 95% confidence interval, counting a change as resolved whenever its 95% confidence interval excludes 0 and clears that run's replica spread; here 95% CI [−0.272,−0.240][-0.272, -0.240] µs, clearing the identical-code replica spread and winning across two independent paired runs; see the chart below), and applies only to B=1. On verify 1-request full attention there is no gain: starting at Tile 3, the producer must wait for the consumer to free a ring-buffer slot, so the small head start won at entry is absorbed by Tile 3.

Push prefetching past the register limit, however, and it turns into a loss. In the two-KV-head fusion verify kernel of Section 7, the producer has only 32 registers at runtime (setmaxnreg cuts it to 32 in Section 7; see Chapter 3, Section 8 for the mechanism), so it prefetches only the page slots of the next tile (Tile j+1). Increase that prefetch distance, and the extra in-flight page slots no longer fit in registers and spill to local memory (see Chapter 3, Section 1): verify 32-request full attention gets about 2.4%–2.6% slower instead (raw log not verified).

Prefetching across the memory-queue boundary brings no gain either. The preceding prologue kernel writes only q and K/V for the new tokens of this pass. The old historical pages were written earlier and are already ready before the wait call, so we could kick off main-loop prefetching early — yet measured runs show no gain (0.13–0.56 µs slower, paired round count not recorded; see the chart below). The reason is probably queueing delay: those non-critical requests enter the memory request queue first (where along the memory path the bottleneck sits was not measured), ahead of the critical Tile 0 requests, making Tile 0 wait longer.

Prefetching across the L2 residency boundary brings no gain either. Hardware L2 prefetch instructions (cp.async.bulk.prefetch.L2 for a single-thread contiguous byte span, or per-thread cache-line prefetch.global.L2; see Appendix B, Quick Reference 2) only pull data from HBM into L2 without bringing it into the SM. If we issue one before the wait call to prefetch the page table, those prefetched lines may be evicted by KV data streaming through L2 before they are used, forcing a second read from HBM; in 60-round V1c paired runs, this is 0.03–0.53 µs slower (with the 0.03 µs lower end inside the 0.4 µs noise band; see the chart below).

7a2 → a3: Once Multi-Token Attention Enters wgmma, How Do the Producer and Two Consumer Warpgroups Split Registers and Stagger the Pipeline?

One producer warpgroup hands its spare registers to two consumer warpgroups (one per KV head), two named barriers stagger the consumers by half a step so they take turns on the Tensor Cores, and computing addresses after role splitting keeps unmasked loop peeling at zero spills.

Inside the "two-KV-head fusion" kernel used for verify (summarized in Row 3 of the Section 5 table; for how software units map onto SM hardware units, see Chapter 3, Section 8 and the opening of Chapter 4), one CTA packs 3 warpgroups totaling 384 threads — 1 producer warpgroup plus 2 four-warp consumer warpgroups; the query tiles Q0, Q1:[64,64]FP8\shape{Q_0,\ Q_1}{64,\;64}{FP8} (8 KiB total) stay resident in shared memory, and the producer gathers 256 B per token into the 4-slot × 16 KiB ring buffer (see Section 5). At compile time, we allocate 80 registers per thread, so one CTA uses 384×80=30,720 registers and the 65,536 registers of one SM can hold at most 2 CTAs (for residency, see Chapter 3, Section 1); at runtime, setmaxnreg trims the producer to 32 registers per thread and hands the freed registers to the two consumer warpgroups, raising each consumer thread to 104 registers (128×32+256×104=30,720; see Chapter 3, Section 8; the producer's 32 registers hold segment bounds, base addresses, and next-tile page slots while each consumer's 104 registers hold S,P,O,m,lS, P, O, m, l, with the per-variable register split not measured).

Warpgroup Role Warps Query rows owned Registers / thread after setmaxnreg Tensor Cores used
Warpgroup 0 Producer (gathers two-head K, V into 4-slot ring) 4 (128 threads) 0 rows (addresses & cp.async only) 32 0 Tensor Cores
Warpgroup 1 Consumer 0 (KV Head 0) 4 (128 threads) 64 rows of Head 0 (4 warps ×\times 16 rows) 104 Uses all 4 SM Tensor Cores (1 per SMSP) together per wgmma
Warpgroup 2 Consumer 1 (KV Head 1) 4 (128 threads) 64 rows of Head 1 (4 warps ×\times 16 rows) 104 Same 4 SM Tensor Cores, alternating half a step out of phase with Consumer 0

Note: Following Chapter 4, Section 1, this book assumes that the 4 warps of each warpgroup sit across the 4 SMSPs (NVIDIA documentation does not state how warps map to SMSPs), so the 4 producer warps and 8 consumer warps share each SMSP's 1-instruction-per-cycle issue slot.

Now look at what happens inside each loop iteration: a consumer warpgroup first issues the wgmma for Q⋅K⊤, then runs the elementwise softmax operations (on the ALU/FMA and SFU pipelines), and then issues P⋅V (for P, see Section 3). Because every KV tile starts a fresh score tile from scratch, the first Q⋅K⊤ wgmma passes predicate scale-d = 0 to write D=A⋅B directly without reading old accumulator values (wgmma.fence is still required before the first issue; see Chapter 5, Section 6). If both consumer warpgroups execute the same phase at the same time, they fight over the Tensor Core simultaneously and then leave it idle simultaneously. Building on warp specialization from Chapter 3, Section 6, we stagger them with two named barriers (see Chapter 5, Section 8): each barrier synchronizes the 256 threads of the two consumer warpgroups, while the producer warpgroup in the same CTA does not participate. A named barrier provides two instructions: bar.arrive adds 128 to the arrival count without blocking so the calling warpgroup keeps running, whereas bar.sync adds 128 to the arrival count and blocks until the count reaches 256. Using PTX barrier IDs 4 and 5 (referred to as Barrier 0 and Barrier 1 below and in Figure 7-7), three moves stagger the two consumer warpgroups by half a step — having two consumer warpgroups take turns entering their Tensor Core MMA windows so one runs softmax while the other issues wgmma is commonly called warpgroup ping-pong (across all delivered code in this book, only this two-KV-head fusion verify kernel uses named-barrier consumer ping-pong; moreover, our two consumers split work by KV head rather than splitting query rows as in FlashAttention-3, and we did not try splitting them by stage — one group running Q⋅K⊤ and softmax while the other runs P⋅V — so its cost was not measured):

  1. Before entering the loop, the 128 threads of Group 1 issue a non-blocking bar.arrive on Barrier 0. Next, the 128 threads of Group 0 execute bar.sync on Barrier 0, bringing the arrival count to 128+128=256 so Group 0 passes immediately and starts the first MMA stage [Q⋅K(0)]; meanwhile, the 128 threads of Group 1 execute bar.sync on Barrier 1, where only 128 threads have arrived so far, causing Group 1 to wait at Barrier 1.
  2. Once Group 0 issues its MMA window and waits with wait_group<0> until all matrix multiplications in that window complete, its 128 threads issue a non-blocking bar.arrive on Barrier 1, bringing Barrier 1's arrival count to 256 to release Group 1 before Group 0 moves on to compute softmax.
  3. From then on, the two groups alternate: once the matrix multiplications in its combined MMA window [P⋅V(j), Q⋅K(j+1)] complete, each group issues bar.arrive on the other group's barrier to release it and moves on to softmax; before its next MMA window, it executes bar.sync on its own barrier to wait until the other group arrives and brings the count to 256.

We pay one extra 256-thread barrier synchronization per iteration and serialize the MMA issue windows of the two groups. On the single task where this change was ever measured (verify 32-request full attention, c18k 60-round V1c pairing), forward/reverse paired runs measured −2.32/−1.65 μs (about 0.94%/0.67%0.94\% / 0.67\%; see the chart below) — the same size as the identical-code file-copy bias in that same run (LIVECP +1.17/+0.98 μs), with serialized NCU differing by only −0.4%-0.4\% (249.41→248.38 μs; in the immediately following zero-spill loop-peel build below, NCU barrier stall samples summed across all barriers without per-barrier breakdown rose from 3,8203{,}820 to 4,2404{,}240, whose attribution to the ping-pong barriers is inferred), and true Tensor Core idle share with versus without these barriers was not measured in NCU — making it a directionally plausible candidate gain that existing measurements cannot separate from replica bias, rather than an established net win (its effect on L=1 decode or small-TT projections was not measured either). Conversely, the variant that locks only the [Q⋅K(j)] segment instead of combining [P⋅V(j), Q⋅K(j+1)] into a single window slows verify 32-request full attention by a measured ~4.5–4.8 µs (why the window must be [P⋅V(j), Q⋅K(j+1)] was not determined at the microarchitectural level).

Remember from Section 5 that the producer-only microbenchmark accounts for 92%–94% of total runtime, so any slowdown in the producer directly drags down the entire kernel. To avoid register spills in the producer, one invariant has to hold: every value still live when setmaxnreg.dec executes must fit inside the reduced register budget. At this stage the kernel is written in Gluon (see Chapter 6, Section 8), and gl.warp_specialize assigns the warpgroup roles. The default partition runs directly on the 4 launch warps, outside the worker dispatch loop, and takes the remainder of the CTA register pool. The worker partitions sit inside a worker dispatch loop that the compiler generates, each with an explicit register target. Before splitting out the unmasked loop, the shipped baseline made the producer a worker partition (trimmed to 24 registers at runtime by setmaxnreg.dec 24, with 112 and 104 for the two consumers) at 0 spills; yet whenever unmasked loop peeling was added onto that worker-producer layout, the compiler hoisted a loop-invariant producer KV-row address above the worker dispatch loop so it stayed live across setmaxnreg.dec 24, overflowed 24 registers, and spilled 8 B to local memory (see Chapter 3, Section 1), adding a local-memory load wait on each use — so those candidates were rejected. The fix makes the producer the default partition and the two consumer warpgroups worker partitions (104 registers each). The producer now runs outside the dispatch loop and gets the remainder of the register pool: 384×80/128−2×104=32 registers, i.e., setmaxnreg.dec 32. Segment bounds and addresses are built after role splitting, so no live variable crosses setmaxnreg.dec and the peeled unmasked loop compiles with 0 spills (the later CUDA C++ rewrite likewise keeps this setup inside each role branch):

// Unshipped loop-peel candidate (illustrative): producer is a worker partition (dec 24; unpeeled base has 0 spills), peeling hoists address above dispatch loop, crossing dec 24 and spilling 8 B
if (wg_id > 0) { /* the two warpgroups get 112 and 104 */ consumer_loop(); }
else           { setmaxnreg_dec<24>();  producer_loop(); }

// Shipped fix: producer is the default partition (32 remaining registers, outside the dispatch loop); bounds and addresses are built after role splitting, peeled loop keeps 0 spills
if (wg_id == 0) { setmaxnreg_dec<32>();  producer_loop(); }
else            { setmaxnreg_inc<104>(); consumer_loop(); }

On our primary verify reference shape, verify 32-request full attention, comparing this combined "producer as default partition + unmasked loop peel" build against the 0-spill unpeeled baseline keeps local-memory spills at 0 and saves about 15.8 µs (we did not measure the two changes separately). Splitting out the unmasked loop means that key tiles that fall completely inside the visible range run a tight main loop without mask checks, and only the last few tiles run a masked tail loop. We measured that split alone on verify 16-request full attention, in the single-KV-head verify kernel, where it saves about 3.4 µs (see the chart below). The catch: whether the producer spills depends on the compiler's dispatch structure and on which variables stay live across setmaxnreg.dec. Change the partition order or the compiler version, and you must recheck the disassembly.

Inside that same CTA loop, scalars that are identical across all 32 threads of a warp — such as the ring-buffer slot index, phase bit, and matrix descriptor — can live in a uniform register (UR), a scalar register shared across the entire warp (see Figure 7-7 Mode 4, shown on the prefill kernel). A general-purpose vector register stores one copy of the same value per thread, which takes 32 register slots across the warp. A uniform register stores a single copy for the whole warp, and uniform-datapath instructions compute on it. Both forms issue once per instruction; what UR saves is vector register capacity and vector pipeline occupancy. ptxas decides which variables go into UR; source code cannot specify this directly. The limitation is that uniform registers hold only values identical across all 32 lanes of a warp, and the per-warp uniform-register limit bounds them. The latency gain was not measured separately on this kernel.

8a3 → a4: When the Softmax Between the Two Matrix Multiplications Accounts for Over Half the Instructions, How Do We Lighten It?

After RMSNorm, the base-2 attention scores have a bounded upper limit so BF16 weights cannot overflow, allowing per-tile rescaling to be skipped entirely and row sums to be offloaded onto the idle Tensor Core.

An SMSP can issue only 1 instruction per cycle (see Chapter 4, Section 1). Look at the compiled 64-key loop of the verify kernel: it takes 288 machine instructions in total, and softmax accounts for 58% of them — the intra-tile maximum reduction, ex2 to compute α\alpha, multiplying every element of OO by α\alpha, and the row-sum reduction (from disassembly counts at the time; raw disassembly not kept and not verified). Under the warp-to-SMSP assumption noted in the Section 7 table, the producer warps share each SMSP's 1-instruction-per-cycle issue slot with the warps of the two consumer warpgroups, so every instruction a consumer avoids issuing is one fewer cycle in which a producer cp.async can be blocked from issuing. In Section 5, the producer-only microbenchmark accounted for 92%–94% of total runtime; part of the remaining about 6%–8% is the cost of consumers occupying issue slots and delaying producer cp.async instructions.

Rescaling on every tile in Section 3 existed solely to prevent 2s−m2^{s-m} from overflowing. After unweighted RMSNorm, each row has a root mean square of 1, so a 64-dimensional vector has Euclidean length 64=8; RoPE is a rotation and preserves length. Across all versions in this chapter, the prologue kernel finishes RMSNorm and RoPE in FP32 before casting q and k directly to FP8 E4M3, and historical keys in the cache were written the same way: with a 3-bit mantissa, round-to-nearest has a relative error of at most 2−42^{-4}, which stretches vector length by at most a factor of 1.06251.0625. Because the dot product of two vectors cannot exceed the product of their lengths (the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality), ∣q⋅k∣≤8×8×1.06252=72.25; multiplying by 0.6840.684 and then by log⁡2e\log_2 e gives: ∣s∣≤72.25×0.684×1.4427≈71.3|s| \le 72.25 \times 0.684 \times 1.4427 \approx 71.3 That is a worst-case upper bound, not a statistical estimate. It requires every historical key to have been written by this chapter's prologue, so that each key has a root mean square of exactly 1. FP8 subnormal components with ∣x∣<2−6 round with an absolute error of at most 2−102^{-10}, which raises the worst-case bound by about another 0.1. The standalone operator benchmark synthesizes historical keys directly from standard normal random numbers, with no per-key normalization. So on those synthetic inputs the bound is not a strict guarantee, though actual dot products stay far below it.

Like FP32, BF16 has an 8-bit exponent with an upper limit of about 21282^{128}. When the weights P are stored in BF16 and we compute p=2min⁡(s, 72) directly, the largest value is only 2722^{72}. Since 80,000≈216.3, summing across all 80,000 keys reaches at most about 2882^{88}, which fits in the FP32 denominator; the smallest value, 2−71.32^{-71.3}, also sits well above the smallest normal BF16 number (about 2−1262^{-126}). So we do not need a reference maximum at all: the per-tile max reduction, α\alpha, and the rescaling of OO all disappear. That saves about 6.7 µs on our primary reference shape, verify 32-request full attention (see the chart below). The trade-off is that we now depend on the upper bound above: it holds only along the "unweighted RMSNorm + FP8 rounding" path, and must be re-derived if the model or data type changes. Because that bound sits below 72, the clamp at 72 never triggers and acts only as a safety guard. The baseline runs RMSNorm and RoPE inside one prologue kernel, writes BF16 out, and then converts to FP8 in subsequent kernels. What if we used this no-rescaling scheme on that baseline numerical path? On the 46 sliding-window layers that run RoPE, q and k are rounded to BF16 once in registers after RMSNorm and rounded to BF16 a second time when written out after RoPE, adding two extra BF16 roundings that push the upper bound up to about 72.4. At that point, the clamp at 72 may trigger; once it does, the output changes silently. Full-attention layers skip RoPE, so they add only one extra BF16 rounding on writeback, with an upper bound of about 71.9.

Next, we move the row-sum reduction onto the Tensor Core. We first did this in the single-KV-head full-attention verify kernel, where it shipped in one commit with two other changes to save about 2.6 µs on verify 16-request full attention (no standalone number was recorded in the changelog); the sliding-window single-KV-head wgmma kernel copied from it carried this over, whereas the two-KV-head fusion verify kernel still summed in registers at this stage until folding the row sum into a single FP8 wgmma.m64n72k32 instruction in Section 10. Each tile's contribution to the denominator ll is the row sum of P, which equals P×𝟏. Doing that sum on the ALU/FMA pipeline takes 38 additions plus 4 warp shuffles (from disassembly counts at the time; raw disassembly not kept and not verified). Why 4 shuffles? As explained in Section 3, each row sits across a 4-lane quad with 2 rows held per thread (see Chapter 5, Section 4), so summing within each quad likewise takes 2 XOR shuffles per row, or 4 shuffles in total. Instead, we place a constant [64, 8] FP16 all-ones matrix in shared memory (1 KB; 256 B per instruction) and issue 4 wgmma.m64n8k16 instructions after P⋅V (64 keys =4×k16, FP16 input; see Chapter 5, Section 4): the row sum itself drops from 42 instructions to 4 (not verified), while because this earlier single-head kernel still rescales by α\alpha, holding the 8-column l accumulator grows per-thread α\alpha multiplies on ll from 2 per tile to 4 FMULs — giving a derived net saving of about 34–38 instructions per tile (raw disassembly not archived; exact count not measured), alongside the cost of extra Tensor Core cycles and 1 KB of shared memory. This only works if the Tensor Core has idle cycles: this kernel is bottlenecked on gather and issue slots. Section 9 covers how the FP8 version uses it.

The final version removes the Tensor Core row-sum reduction from both single-KV-head wgmma verify kernels (verify 1-request full attention and verify sliding window, Section 5) and goes back to in-register accumulation. Measured inside the same build as a module-consolidation rewrite, the delta is about 0.26 µs on verify 32-request sliding window and about 0.13 µs on verify 1-request full attention (paired round count and noise band not recorded, and the standalone net gain was not measured separately; see the chart below); on which workloads it would become a loss was not measured. Inferring from the pipeline rules of Chapters 4 and 5, offloading row sums onto the Tensor Core pays off only when the ALU/FMA pipeline saturates first while the Tensor Core still has idle capacity.

One more attempt brings zero gain: using the half-precision paired instruction ex2.approx.f16x2 in hopes of halving SFU time. Because the Hopper SFU executes scalar operations one lane at a time (see Chapter 5, Section 1), the compiler expands this instruction into 2 MUFU.EX2.F16 instructions plus 1 byte-permute PRMT (we read this from the disassembly at the time and did not keep the record; for PTX-to-SASS translation, see Chapter 6, Section 6). That saves zero SFU time and adds 1 extra instruction: zero gain.

9a4 → a5 (Part 1): After Compressing the Weight Matrix P to 1-Byte FP8, How Do We Compute Exponentials Quickly Without Overflowing?

Leaving exponent headroom triggers rescaling via a warp-vote instruction only when a tile exceeds the threshold, and computes E4M3 bytes directly on the FMA/ALU pipelines via the linear approximation 8(y+7).

Verify: How Do We Keep FP8 P in Range?

To run the P⋅V multiplication in the next section on the FP8 Tensor Core, we first have to store P in E4M3. The catch is that the upper bound of E4M3 is only 448 (see Section 1), and when the exponent field is all zeros its value is (j/8)⋅21−7 (where jj is the 3-bit mantissa value) with a minimum positive subnormal value of 2−92^{-9} (for subnormal numbers, see Chapter 6, Section 5) — so P must be scaled into this narrow range.

Rescaling historical accumulators only when a tile threatens to overflow is called lazy rescaling. Keeping the row maximum of Tile 0 as the reference m𝑟𝑒𝑓m_{ref}, we write the weights as P′=28−τ⋅2s−m𝑟𝑒𝑓P' = 2^{\,8-\tau}\cdot 2^{\,s-m_{ref}} where τ\tau is the headroom reserved for lazy rescaling (a base-2 exponent). As long as a new tile's maximum satisfies m𝑡𝑖𝑙𝑒≤m𝑟𝑒𝑓+τ, we have P′≤28−τ⋅2τ=256<448, so it cannot overflow and m𝑟𝑒𝑓m_{ref}, OO, and ll remain untouched. On each iteration, the entire warp executes just one vote instruction: __any_sync(…, m_tile > m_ref + τ). Here __any_sync asks all 32 threads (lanes) of a warp whether the condition holds for any lane; if even one lane is true, every lane receives true. Only when some row exceeds the threshold does the warp update m𝑟𝑒𝑓m_{ref} and multiply by α\alpha. Because E4M3 has a narrow range and every tile must check whether m𝑡𝑖𝑙𝑒m_{tile} exceeds the threshold, each thread again has to find the maximum of its own scores on every tile; the cross-thread quad-shuffle reduction (Section 3) runs only on Tile 0 and when the vote is true. The other costs are one vote instruction and the occasional rescaling (when no row exceeds the threshold, computing α\alpha and rescaling OO are still skipped). At τ=4, the per-tile trigger rate is only 7%–18%; relaxing it to τ=6 saves another ~1.4 µs on our primary reference shape, verify 32-request full attention.

However, the headroom τ\tau also has a bound at the other end: the larger τ\tau is, the smaller 28−τ2^{8-\tau} becomes, and the sooner small weights drop below 2−102^{-10} (half of the smallest subnormal 2−92^{-9}) and round to 0. In the two-KV-head fusion verify kernel, before adopting τ=6 we tried pushing τ\tau directly from 4 to 8: that caused too many small weights to underflow, pushing the output error beyond the numerical tolerance (the maximum error allowed relative to the reference implementation; see Chapter 10, Section 4), so it was rejected (even though it ran about 3.7 µs faster). Yet the same τ=8 passes inside the sliding-window single-KV-head wgmma kernel (Section 5) and saves about 0.83 µs (see the chart below). One possible explanation is that full-attention layers attend to about 80,000 visible keys (versus at most 2,055 in sliding-window layers), so more small weights get flushed to 0; why one kernel exceeds the tolerance while the other passes was not determined.

Prefill: Why Is the SFU the Bottleneck, and How Do We Take exp Off It?

Execution pipeline (Chapter 5, Section 1) Lanes per SMSP (full SM across 4 SMSPs) Issue interval per 32-lane warp instruction
FMA (FP32 FFMA / FADD / FMUL) 32 lanes (128 per SM) 1 cycle
ALU (bitwise logic, shifts, PRMT, etc.) 16 lanes (64 per SM) 2 cycles
SFU (MUFU.EX2 transcendentals & scalar F2F) 4 lanes (16 per SM) 8 cycles

In Section 5 we saw that verify is gather-bound (producer-only takes 92%–94% of runtime), hiding the SFU behind memory; only compute-bound prefill exposes the SFU on the critical path. As the table shows, the SFU accepts only 1 warp instruction every 8 cycles — an issue interval 8×\times that of FMA (see Chapter 5, Section 1); in the 128-key loop, each consumer warp issues 66 MUFU.EX2 instructions per tile, driving SFU pipeline utilization to 77.3%. Because softmax sits right between the two matrix multiplications, any slowdown on the SFU directly delays the start of the subsequent P⋅V stage.

How can we offload the exponential from the SFU? Look at the E4M3 byte code of the target weight 2y2^{y}: it is approximately a linear function of yy (see Chapter 6, Section 5 for the bit fields). Write the base-2 exponent yy as an integer part plus a fractional part, y=n+f (0≤f<1): the 4-bit exponent field holds n+7, which shifted left by 3 bits gives 8(n+7); the 3-bit mantissa field uses the linear approximation 2f≈1+f to hold 8f8f. Combined, the byte code is c≈8(y+7). Let's check one byte by hand: take y=2.5 (n=2, f=0.5), which gives 8(2.5+7)=76, or 0100 1100 in binary. Here the exponent field is 1001 =9=2+7 and the mantissa field is 100 =4=8×0.5; decoding gives 22×(1+4/8)=6, compared with the exact value 22.5≈5.66. For normal weights 2y≥2−6, the pre-rounding continuous approximation 2f≈1+f has a worst-case relative error of about 6.1% (at f≈0.44, 1.441.44 versus 1.361.36, derived), and after rounding to the stored integer byte round(8(y+7)) the worst-case normal relative error rises to about 10.8% (1.51.5 decoded versus 1.3541.354 exact at f=0.4375, derived; compared with E4M3's own round-to-nearest worst error of about 5.9%, derived, half-step bound 6.25%); below 2−62^{-6} the error grows larger, and below 2−72^{-7} the byte code goes negative and is clamped to 0.

Because c=8(y+7) is a linear function, there is no need to queue on the SFU — we can compute the byte directly on the FMA and ALU pipelines. To encode every 4 values, we first use a saturating multiply-add FFMA.SAT (where .SAT clamps the result to [0,1][0, 1], clamping negative byte codes to 0 right here) to compute the normalized value u=(y+7)/15∈[0,1]. Next, cvt.rn.f16x2.f32 converts into a half-precision pair (f16x2), and a half-precision multiply-add computes 1024+120u=1024+c. Because half-precision FP16 (bit layout in Section 2) has an exact unit step size of 1 on the interval [1024,2048)[1024, 2048), the integer c∈[0,120] lands directly in the low 8 mantissa bits of the FP16 value. After register moves (MOV), PRMT packs the 4 low bytes into a 32-bit word: counting the original multiply-adds and saturating FP8 pack as well, disassembly at the time recorded 9 versus 10 issue slots per 4 exponentials before and after (the original report did not keep which side was 9, and the exact breakdown by instruction type was not measured), while measured static SASS instructions in the unmasked loop drop from 344 to 330 — giving a derived count across the 16 groups per tile of about 10 issue slots before and about 9 after. This step cuts measured MUFU.EX2 instructions per tile from 66 down to 2 (which 2 MUFU.EX2 instructions per tile remain was not recorded; see the Figure 7-9 readout for the change in SFU utilization), and the profiler measures about an 18% latency reduction on our primary prefill reference shape, 65K-history full attention (see the third chart at the end of the chapter): the kernel no longer stalls on the SFU, leaving the remaining runtime governed jointly by issue slots (measured profiler issue-active cycles rise from 46.1% to 53.9%, unsaturated) and the intra-warpgroup byte-pack dependence chain (a delete-pack control experiment runs a measured 24.5% faster), with the shares of the two not measured separately, at the cost of the piecewise-linear and rounding error above. Because the denominator ll multiplies those exact same bytes by the all-ones matrix (the method from Section 8), the numerator and denominator use the exact same approximated values, so the error does not appear on only one side.

Next, we use the subnormal range of FP16 to drop that half-precision multiply-add step. FP16 has an exponent bias of 15, and its all-zero-exponent subnormal range is evenly spaced: its values are 21−15⋅m/210=m×2−24 (where mm is the 10-bit integer mantissa), with a minimum step size of 2−242^{-24}. We multiply the byte code c=8(y+7) by 2−242^{-24}, folding the factor 8×2−24=2−21 straight into FFMA.SAT. The lower bound 0 of .SAT handles the negative-bytecode clamp from above (E4M3 could represent down to 2−92^{-9}, but this small range of tiny weights is flushed to 0); meanwhile, the maximum cc of 120 times 2−242^{-24} stays far below the upper bound 1. Next, calling cvt.rn.f16x2.f32 converts two values to FP16 at once with round-to-nearest, so the hardware rounds cc directly into the low 8 mantissa bits of FP16; PRMT then packs the 4 bytes into a 32-bit register. That cuts 4 instructions per 4 values (2 half-precision multiply-adds and 2 MOV instructions) and saves about another 78 µs on the 65K-history full-attention kernel (see the third chart at the end of the chapter).

In the final prefill version of a5, an all-f16x2 formulation replaces the 2−212^{-21} scaling above: before finding the intra-tile maximum, cvt.rn.f16x2.f32 converts the raw FP32 scores in pairs to f16x2. Because FP16 has a step size of 1 on [1024,2048)[1024, 2048) and the low 8 mantissa bits of 1024+c equal cc directly, both the intra-tile maximum reduction and the linear encoding 1024+c (clamping negative values to 1024) execute on f16x2 at two half-precision values per instruction (for paired 16-bit floating-point arithmetic, see Chapter 6, Section 5). This saves a net 28 instructions per tile (from disassembly counts at the time; raw disassembly not kept and not verified), at the cost of rounding the scores to FP16 once before finding the maximum. The standalone latency change of this step on the 65K single operator was not measured separately (and is not plotted in the third chart at the end of the chapter); Right below, we eliminate that initial batch of conversions as well. By contrast, approximating exp2 with an FMA polynomial issues about 7.5 extra instructions for every MUFU instruction it replaces, which runs slower in a loop where issue slots are already tight.

In prefill, Q⋅K⊤ can also switch to half-precision (f16x2) accumulation. Because the accumulator holds raw unscaled E4M3 dot products before multiplying by the attention scale (test cache keys are not necessarily normalized per key, and the scale factor can be 1/641/64, so Section 8's post-scale 72.25 bound does not apply here), we bound the raw dot product directly: RMS-normalized and E4M3-rounded q has length at most 8×1.0625=8.5, and any E4M3 key has components within [−448,448][-448, 448] for a length of at most 448×64=3,584, so Cauchy-Schwarz bounds the raw accumulator at 8.5×3,584=30,464, below the FP16 maximum of 65,504; FP16's 11 significand bits also give enough precision for softmax scores (keeping results within the numerical tolerance). The all-f16x2 approach above still wrote 32 cvt.rn.f16x2.f32 calls per tile in source to pack 64 FP32 scores per thread into f16x2; now the accumulator of wgmma.m64n128k32.f16.e4m3.e4m3 produces f16x2 directly, eliminating 32 cvt.rn.f16x2.f32 calls in source (34 conversion instructions in disassembly) and freeing 32 accumulator registers. Applying this only on unmasked full tiles cuts the full-attention prefill kernel runtime by 14.5% at T=753 and by 16.8% at T=16,384 with 65K history (see the chart below). We also tested splitting softmax and P⋅V into a two-stage pipeline or splitting 128 keys into 64-key subtile pipelines, but neither yielded a gain because the compiler scheduled more instructions.

10a4 → a5 (Part 2): How Do the Two Matrix Multiplications Consume Narrower Inputs and Hide the Transpose of V Inside the First Stage's Background Execution Window?

Compute P⋅V directly with native FP8 wgmma, hiding the 18 byte-transpose instructions for V inside the asynchronous wait window of the first MMA stage.

Originally, we had to convert V to 16-bit in shared memory before running 16-bit wgmma for P⋅V — which both added a chain of conversion instructions and consumed twice as much shared memory. Once both P and V are in E4M3, P stays in registers as E4M3 instead of going back to shared memory and feeds P⋅V directly as operand A (RS mode; see Chapter 5, Section 4) while V⊤V^{\top} comes from shared memory, issuing the native FP8 instruction wgmma.m64n64k32.f32.e4m3.e4m3 (a 64×64 tile with inner dimension k=32 per step, E4M3 inputs, and FP32 accumulation) — which is also why only V in shared memory needs the byte transpose below. Per the PTX specification note, internal summation order and intermediate rounding inside Tensor Core matrix multiplies are unspecified, and FP8 wgmma with .f32 accumulators accumulates internally at higher than half precision but lower than single precision (published papers measure about 13–14 mantissa bits on Hopper and often pair it with two-level accumulation to curb error; a5 in this book passes the numerical tolerance with direct accumulation, and how much further two-level accumulation would reduce error was not measured). In the two-KV-head fusion verify kernel, switching to FP8 P (τ=4; see Section 9) and FP8 P⋅V together saves about 8.8 µs on our primary reference shape, verify 32-request full attention; the sliding-window single-KV-head wgmma kernel (Section 5) switches to FP8 P⋅V in the same way (see the chart below). Each CTA also saves 8–16 KiB of shared memory (16 KiB in the two-KV-head fusion kernel, from 107,584 B down to 91,200 B; 8 KiB in the sliding-window single-KV-head wgmma kernel, from 54,400 B down to 46,208 B); the trade-off is that FP8 P introduces the approximation error discussed in Section 9. The final two-KV-head fusion kernel also appends 8 all-ones rows to V⊤V^{\top} and issues wgmma.m64n72k32 to compute P⋅V and the row sum in a single instruction; the cost is 1 KiB more shared memory per KV head for the all-ones rows and 4 more accumulator registers per thread, and its standalone gain was not measured.

Sixteen-bit wgmma can pass the instruction immediate argument imm-trans-b = 1 to read N-major V directly, whereas FP8 wgmma requires the right-hand matrix in shared memory to be contiguous along the inner-product dimension — bytes from the same feature dimension at different key positions sitting next to each other, called K-major layout (inner-dimension major) (where K is the matrix-multiply inner-product dimension, which in P⋅V is the key position). In the KV cache, however, V packs the 64 features of a single key contiguously, so every tile needs a software byte transpose. For this we use the shared-memory matrix load instruction ldmatrix: for each 8×8 sub-tile, 8 consecutive lanes supply the 8 row addresses and each 4-lane quad (see Chapter 5, Section 4) receives one 16 B row. Each tile's transpose takes 2 ldmatrix.x4.trans instructions (transposing 8×8 sub-tiles of 16-bit elements), 8 byte-permute PRMT instructions (see Chapter 6, Section 2), and 8 shared-memory stores STS, for 18 instructions in total (PTX also offers the in-register transpose movmatrix.m8n8.trans.b16, SASS MOVM, likewise at 16-bit granularity — see Appendix B, Quick Reference 3 — but because V starts in shared memory and must be written back to shared memory for wgmma, ldmatrix.trans combines the shared-memory load and 16-bit transpose in one instruction, so movmatrix is unused). After writing to shared memory, the warpgroup also issues a fence.proxy.async and waits on the named barrier from Section 7 for its turn. Those two steps order the generic shared-memory writes from the warpgroup's 4 warps ahead of the asynchronous reads of wgmma (see Chapter 3, Section 7). Both steps are present before and after the change below, so they do not affect the comparison.

Once issued, wgmma executes asynchronously in the background, and its results are not needed until wait_group (for commit and wait, see Chapter 5, Section 6). Inserting these 18 transpose instructions between the commit point of Q⋅K⊤ and wait_group<0> runs them concurrently with the matrix multiplication. The transpose still issues all 18 instructions, but they hide inside the background execution window of Q⋅K⊤ and no longer sit on the critical path, saving about 1.8 µs on verify 32-request full attention.

In the final two-KV-head fusion kernels for verify 16- and 32-request full attention, we go one step further with cross-iteration overlap: we also remove the wait for P⋅V at the end of each tile, so Tile jj's P⋅V is committed without waiting, crosses the loop back-edge, and stays in flight alongside Tile j+1's Q⋅K⊤ (no wait_group in between); after transposing V on the next tile, a single wait_group<0> retires both together. Each consumer thread still uses 104 registers with zero spills (at the cost of keeping one extra set of 8 in-flight P fragment registers). On verify 16-request full attention, overlapping the transpose with Q⋅K⊤ plus cross-iteration overlap saves about 1.7 µs in total (see the chart below).

11a5 → a6 (Part 1): Should the Prologue and the Gating Epilogue Each Take a Separate Kernel?

Prefill fuses the prologue into a one-CTA-per-token kernel; decode and single-request verify fuse the prologue into each split-KV CTA and fuse the gating epilogue into the final kernel that writes o_attn.

Remember from Section 1 that our original baseline runs the five steps as about 7 separate kernels, where each additional kernel adds one launch and one "write back to HBM or L2 and read it out again" round trip (see Chapter 1, Section 3): across its 5 prologue kernels, each token reads 5,120 B and writes 3,840 B for 8,960 B moved in total, whereas collapsing them into a single prologue kernel reads q, k, v once (2,560 B) and writes q_fp8 plus new K/V (1,280 B) for 3,840 B per token — 43% of the 5-kernel total (derived from tensor sizes; the standalone latency delta of 5-kernel versus 1-kernel prologue was not measured separately). An early fused prologue for prefill split the 20 heads of each token (16 q, 2 k, and 2 v) across 5 CTAs per token (from notes at the time; early source not kept and not verified); a6 consolidates this into 1 CTA per token (3 warps totaling 96 threads): RMSNorm, RoPE, casting q to FP8, and writing the new K/V entries all happen inside this single CTA, with each head's sum of squares reduced in registers via warp shuffles without using shared memory or a CTA barrier. With 4 threads per head, 96 threads cover 24 head slots; because there are only 20 actual heads, the extra 4 head slots leave 16 threads idle (register usage and residency were not measured separately). At T=16,384, prologue latency drops from about 53 µs to about 31 µs (see the chart below).

For decode and single-request verify, launching a separate prologue kernel just for a few rows of q and the new tokens' K/V isn't worth the boundary cost. Because one KV head has only 8 rows × 64\times\ 64 dimensions per token, each split-KV CTA can read qkv directly to recompute the q rows it needs; each segment whose key range contains the new token positions computes and writes only the K/V entries for the new positions falling inside its own range, crosses a CTA barrier, and then reads them back. Why does this work without any cross-CTA synchronization? Because each segment reads only the keys and values in its own key range: the segment covering the new positions uses the values it just computed, and all other segments read only older historical cache entries that were already written in prior passes. Dropping the prologue kernel eliminates one launch and one dependency edge, saving about 1.8 µs on decode 1-request full attention and 1.30 µs on our primary reference shape, decode 16-request full attention (see the chart below).

At the other end of the pipeline, the gating epilogue rmsnorm(o𝑟𝑎𝑤)⊙σ(gate) cannot run until the complete o𝑟𝑎𝑤o_{raw} is ready, and it no longer launches as a separate kernel either. In prefill, unsplit query tiles compute it directly, while for the 40 light query tiles split into 4 segments in Section 4, whichever of the 4 CTAs finishes last merges the segments inside the main kernel and then computes the gating epilogue (using ticket numbers; see the second path in Section 12). Shapes that merge inside the main kernel in Section 12 likewise compute the gating epilogue inside the main kernel before writing out, while shapes that still keep a separate merge kernel compute the gating epilogue at the end of the merge kernel after summing the partial results. The trade-off of fusing the prologue and epilogue is that every split segment recomputes q and the code becomes tightly coupled; the time saved by fusing the epilogue alone and any extra register or shared-memory usage were not measured separately.

Where a separate merge kernel remains (such as decode 1-request full attention), the main kernel hands off to the merge kernel via PDL (see Chapter 1, Section 4 for the mechanism). Comparing the three modes — "no PDL", "trigger after the main loop", and "trigger at function entry" (see the chart below) — shows that placing the trigger at function entry is actually the slowest: the merge-kernel CTAs enter too early, occupy SMs while sitting idle at the wait call for about 7.5 µs, and slow down the main kernel as well, probably because CTAs from both kernels co-reside on the same SMs and contend for slots (unverified). Because every shape with a separate merge kernel behaves this way, this chapter places the trigger after the main loop and before writeback.

12a5 → a6 (Part 2): Without a Separate Merge Kernel, How Are the Partial Results of Each Segment Summed Inside the Main Kernel?

In-kernel merging splits into three paths by whether the grid fits inside 1 wave or a single-GPC cluster: 1-wave full-GPU grids use L2 vector atomic adds with a grid barrier, multi-wave grids use last-arriver ticket merge, and sliding-window shapes with up to 8 (or non-portable 16) segments push partials across intra-GPC cluster shared memory.
