Why did the merge in Section 3 need lse\mathrm{lse}? Because each segment's Oi,liO_i, l_i were scaled by its own mim_i. If each segment outputs Oi2miO_i 2^{m_i} and li2mil_i 2^{m_i} instead (the true numerator and denominator referenced to 0), segments can accumulate directly with atomic adds without waiting for the global denominator, summing to ∑iOi2mi\sum_i O_i 2^{m_i} and ∑ili2mi\sum_i l_i 2^{m_i} before a single division o=O𝑡𝑜𝑡𝑎𝑙/l𝑡𝑜𝑡𝑎𝑙. In Section 8 we derived ∣mi∣≤71.3, so 2mi2^{m_i} stays far below the FP32 upper limit of about 21282^{128}. Path 1 and the decode shapes on Path 2 use this zero-referenced atomic sum; light prefill tiles and Path 3 still merge with per-segment maxima or lse\mathrm{lse} weights as in Section 3. The table below puts all three paths in this chapter's standalone operator side by side — shapes, residency vs. 1-wave capacity, who waits, who divides and gates, bitwise determinism, and the cost of the alternative (decode 1-, 16-, and 32-request full attention, decode 32-request sliding window, and verify 1-request full attention keep a standalone merge kernel in this chapter; see the end of Section 1):

Path Standalone shapes in Ch. 7 Grid vs. 1-wave capacity & co-residency guarantee Who waits for whom Who divides & runs gating epilogue Bitwise deterministic? Cost of the alternative or wrong regime
1. L2 vector atomic add + grid barrier Verify 16- and 32-request full attention 264 CTAs =2×132=1.00 wave; skips cooperative launch, relying on 1-wave occupancy check + exclusive SM access + post-barrier PDL trigger + observed dispatch (not guaranteed by CUDA spec; hangs silently if violated) All 264 CTAs wait on the L2 arrival counter (1 polling warp/CTA calls __nanosleep(64), while the other 7 consumer warps wait at a named barrier) All 264 CTAs partition output rows, read the L2 sum, divide, apply RMSNorm + σ(gate)\sigma(gate), and zero their workspace slice No: cross-CTA FP32 atomic order varies with scheduling (relative diff <10−4< 10^{-4}, within tolerance; effect on draft acceptance rate not measured) Keeping the standalone merge kernel takes 5.2 / 7.2 µs (Path 1 saves net 1.73 / 2.98 µs); cooperative launch adds ~1.2–1.8 µs launch overhead (raw log not archived); using Path 1 on 1-request full attention slows decode 1 / verify 1 full by 2.96 / 0.62 µs (inferred from 256 segments serializing atomic adds on 1 row)
2. Last-arriver ticket merge 40 light prefill tiles split ×4\times 4 Works on multi-wave grids (e.g., prefill 1,606 CTAs >132> 132) and sub-wave grids alike; requires zero co-residency Earlier CTAs (ticket < G - 1) draw a ticket and exit immediately — no CTA ever waits on another CTA, so multi-wave grids cannot deadlock Only the CTA drawing the final ticket (ticket == G - 1) merges segments 0..3 in fixed lse order, divides, applies gating, and zeroes the counter with an ordinary store Yes: fixed 0..3 order, with zero FP atomics Standalone merge kernel costs an extra launch, PDL boundary, and per-segment readback; applying Path 1's grid spin-wait on a multi-wave grid would deadlock

Intra-GPC cluster DSMEM direct write (st.async + mbarrier) Verify 1-, 16-, and 32-request sliding window & decode 1- and 16-request sliding window Each request's segments form 1 cluster co-scheduled inside 1 GPC by hardware (portable cap 8 CTAs: verify 16/32 sliding use 7/4; 1-request sliding opts in to non-portable 16 CTAs) Senders push row partials into receivers' SMEM via st.async (0 L2 traffic); each merging CTA waits on its local mbarrier byte count Merging CTAs in the cluster partition output rows, merge by lse or shared-reference weights in SMEM, apply gating, and write o_attn Yes: fixed segment summation order per cluster, with zero cross-CTA FP atomics Separate split + merge kernels cost 2 launches + L2 round trip (1-request 3-in-1 saves 0.86 / 0.56 µs; verify 16 sliding 8→7 saves 1.31 µs, and pull →\to st.async push saves 0.49 / 0.25 µs); >16>16 segments cannot form a cluster, and dropping verify 32 sliding to 2 CTAs/SM fits only 62/64 clusters, spilling 2 clusters to wave 2 (+11.7 µs slower)

In Chapter 9's single-layer chain, routing differs in two places (see Chapter 9): decode 1-, 16-, and 32-request full attention and decode 32-request sliding window switch from a standalone merge kernel to Path 2 (accumulating via schedule-dependent cross-CTA FP32 atomic adds, with decode 1 full sharding across s mod 8s \bmod 8 workspace copies whose standalone gain was not measured), whereas decode 1- and 16-request sliding window there use a different split kernel followed by a standalone merge kernel: it swaps operands A and B and puts the 8 query rows plus 8 padding rows on the n=16 side of wgmma (FP8 m64n16k32 for S⊤S^{\top}, with 64 keys on m=64; BF16 m64n16k16 for P⋅V, with the 64-wide head dimension on m=64).

The first path is L2 atomic add + grid barrier + per-row normalization epilogue, used only on the verify 16- and 32-request full-attention shapes (264 CTAs). All CTAs atomically add their partial sums into the L2 workspace buffer defined in Section 3, then increment the same arrival counter in L2 and wait until it reaches the total count — this device-wide wait across all CTAs is a grid barrier. Its causal chain has three steps:

  1. Each consumer thread atomically adds its numerator into the L2 workspace buffer using non-fetching vector atomic adds, and likewise for the denominator: verify 32-request full attention uses red.global.add.v4.f32 (adding 4 FP32 values at once) and verify 16-request full attention uses .v2.f32 (adding 2 FP32 values at once); red means write-only without fetching the old value (see Chapter 2, Section 8). Next, the 256 threads of the two consumer warpgroups cross a named barrier; in the memory model, that barrier orders the atomic adds of all threads in both consumer warpgroups before the representative thread's release (without requiring the atomic adds to have already landed in L2).
  2. A single representative thread for the CTA (thread 0 of consumer warpgroup 0) executes one atom.acq_rel.gpu addition on the global arrival counter and then polls it with ld.acquire.gpu until all CTAs have arrived. In CTAs still waiting, that 1 polling warp calls __nanosleep(64) (PTX nanosleep.u32, SASS NANOSLEEP) between polls to sleep briefly and yield issue slots — which the profiler's stall taxonomy (see Chapter 10, Section 7) records under sleeping — while the other 7 consumer warps wait at the next named barrier (the standalone gain of this backoff was not measured).
  3. Once the representative thread observes that all CTAs have arrived, the 256 threads of the two consumer warpgroups cross a second named barrier so that all consumer threads are ordered after that acquire.gpu; the 264 CTAs then partition the rows among themselves: read the accumulated numerators and denominators, divide, apply RMSNorm, multiply by σ(gate)\sigma(gate), write out o_attn, and zero their own slice of the workspace buffer for the next launch. Normal global loads after acquire.gpu observe the results published to L2 by every CTA's release without reading stale L1 lines on the local SM (Chapter 2, Section 6).

Why can a single thread's release represent the entire CTA? Because a release operation publishes all prior writes that the releasing thread has already observed (for cumulativity, see Chapter 2, Section 6) — without that first named barrier, the representative thread's release would not cover the atomic adds issued by the other consumer threads.

Who zeroes the arrival counter for the next launch? Nobody does. The 32-bit counter only ever increments, and the total increment per launch must divide 2322^{32} evenly so that launch boundaries stay aligned across wrap-around; because 264 does not divide 2322^{32}, we set the per-launch total to 65,536 and partition it across the 264 CTAs: 64 CTAs add 249 and 200 CTAs add 248, so the weights sum to 65,536 per launch. Each CTA adds its own weight to the old value returned by its atom and rounds up to the next multiple of 65,536 as the target value to wait for on this launch; using a signed difference for the comparison avoids any need to zero the counter across graph replays.

Why does reusing the same counter across launches never mix two launches? Because the PDL chain enforces a strict handoff invariant: every PDL kernel executes its own wait call before finishing (see Chapter 1, Section 4), and the next kernel that uses this counter touches it only after its own wait call — which guarantees that the previous launch has completely finished and all its writes are visible.

What keeps this spin-wait from deadlocking? Every CTA is guaranteed to see the counter complete only if all 264 CTAs achieve co-residency (simultaneous residency). By resource usage, each SM holds 2 CTAs, and 264=2×132 equals the exact capacity of 1 wave. Formally, CUDA guarantees full-grid co-residency only under cooperative launch (see Chapter 2, Section 6). Here we skip cooperative launch and rely on three prerequisites plus the empirical dispatch behavior observed on hardware (the CUDA specification does not promise to dispatch all 264 CTAs onto SMs at once):

  1. The grid does not exceed the capacity of 1 wave. The host verifies this before launch via an occupancy query and falls back to a separate merge kernel if the grid does not fit.
  2. No other work occupies the SMs for an extended period, including kernels on other streams in the same process (such as cross-GPU communication kernels) and other processes; the preceding PDL kernel does not count — because the current kernel enters only after every CTA of its predecessor has either triggered or exited (Chapter 1, Section 4), all predecessor CTAs are already on SMs, do not wait on us, and will exit.
  3. The main kernel waits until the entire grid has arrived at the barrier before issuing the PDL trigger call to release the next kernel, preventing CTAs of the next kernel from entering SMs early and taking slots.

Within this chapter's isolated Stage 2 benchmark, no other kernel competes for SMs while Stage 2 executes, so Prerequisite 2 is satisfied; when multiple streams or processes share the SMs, you must switch to cooperative launch (see Chapter 2, Section 6). In single-request trials on this operator, cooperative launch added about 1.2–1.8 µs of launch overhead (we did not keep the raw record). Avoiding cooperative launch saves that overhead in exchange for accepting a risk: if Prerequisite 2 or the dispatch behavior above fails to hold, the kernel will hang silently without reporting an error (Chapter 2, Section 6).

Folding this merge step in eliminates the separate merge kernel, saving a net ~3.0 µs on verify 32-request full attention (see the chart and note below).

Because the arrival order of cross-CTA floating-point atomic adds in the first path varies with scheduling, two runs on the exact same input can differ in the last few bits (with a relative difference below 10−410^{-4}, within the numerical tolerance), whereas a separate merge kernel produces bitwise-identical results every run. How this last-bit difference affects the draft acceptance rate (see Primer 1, Section 7) was not measured.

The second path is last-arriver merge, which handles decode 1-, 16-, and 32-request full attention and decode 32-request sliding window in Chapter 9's single-layer pipeline, along with the 40 split light prefill tiles in this chapter. Earlier CTAs never stay behind to spin-wait in place. Across those decode shapes, each segment still adds its 2mi2^{m_i}-scaled numerator and denominator into the workspace buffer with floating-point atomic adds (for decode 1-request full attention, which has 256 segments, segment ss accumulates into replica s mod 8s \bmod 8 of 8 workspace copies, spreading writes across 8 addresses to sidestep the single-address contention discussed at the end of this section; the standalone gain of that sharding was not measured). All threads in the CTA then cross a first CTA barrier before thread 0 draws a ticket with atom.acq_rel.gpu (using the mechanism from Chapter 2, Sections 6 and 8): earlier CTAs exit right after drawing their ticket, while the CTA that draws the final ticket crosses a second CTA barrier, reads the accumulated numerator and denominator for the row, resets that row's workspace and ticket counter to 0 with ordinary stores, and runs the division and gating epilogue. Those two CTA barriers play the exact same role as the two named barriers on the first path: the first orders all atomic adds in the CTA before thread 0's release, and the second orders all reads in the CTA after thread 0's acquire. Ordinary stores are enough to zero the state because nothing touches that row again until the next launch, and the PDL invariant above ensures the two launches run strictly one after the other. Because no CTA ever waits on another CTA, this path is deadlock-free even when the grid spans multiple waves; in exchange, cross-CTA floating-point atomic adds execute in schedule-dependent order, so bitwise-identical outputs are not guaranteed by construction. Eliminating the standalone merge kernel means the finishing CTA reads back only the summed numerator and denominator rather than fetching every segment's partial output one by one.

The 40 split light prefill tiles also merge in the last-arriving CTA via ticket numbers (where the final ticket writes 0 back to the counter), but without floating-point atomic adds: the 4 segments each write their own (oi,lsei)(o_i, \mathrm{lse}_i), and the CTA that receives the final ticket merges them in the fixed segment order 0–3 using the lse\mathrm{lse} weights from Section 3 before computing the gating epilogue; that leaves no accumulation workspace buffer to zero and keeps the result bitwise deterministic.

Verify 1-, 16-, and 32-request sliding window and decode 1- and 16-request sliding window take the third path: direct cross-CTA write to remote shared memory (DSMEM) within the same cluster. Take verify 16-request sliding window as our example (both 16- and 32-request sliding window use the sliding-window single-KV-head wgmma kernel from Section 5, with 72 registers per thread and 256 threads per CTA so each SM holds at most 3 CTAs, unlike the 3–4-CTA-per-SM mma.sync split kernel in Section 4): 16 requests × 2\times\ 2 KV heads =32= 32 groups, each containing NS split-KV CTAs. Declaring the NS segments of the same request as a thread block cluster guarantees in hardware that the group stays co-resident simultaneously. Physically, a GPC (Graphics Processing Cluster) is a group of adjacent SMs on the die wired together by its own inter-SM interconnect, and all CTAs of a cluster must fit inside the same GPC (scattered slots across different GPCs cannot form a cluster; beyond outbound st.async on-chip merging below, clusters can also pair with TMA multicast from Chapter 5, Section 7). Each GPC is built from TPCs (Texture Processing Clusters, with 2 SMs per TPC): a full GH100 die has 8 GPCs ×\times 9 TPCs =144= 144 SMs, whereas the 132-SM H200 enables 66 TPCs, and how many are enabled in each GPC is not publicly documented. The portable cluster-size limit is 8 CTAs; at 3 CTAs per SM, the full chip can hold at most 132×3/8≈49 clusters of 8 CTAs, and because a cluster cannot span GPC boundaries, 49 is only an upper bound — how many 8-CTA clusters the chip can actually hold is neither publicly documented nor measured here.

Under the sliding window, each request sees 2,055 keys, or 33 tiles, and those 32 clusters at NS = 8 total 256 CTAs, which fit in one wave; yet assigning ⌈33/8⌉=5 tiles per segment means the first 7 segments already cover all 33 tiles, leaving the 8th segment with 0 tiles while still occupying a CTA slot. When NS = 8, measured runs place 3 CTAs on 16 of the SMs, and those SMs finish last and drag out the tail. Changing to NS = 7 drops the empty segment and shrinks each cluster to 7 CTAs, for 32×7=224 CTAs in total. Each cluster fits inside a single GPC more easily, no SM has to hold a 3rd CTA in measured runs, and latency drops by about 1.3 µs (measured when the sliding-window wgmma cluster merge still used its earlier pull form, before switching to st.async direct-write push below saved about another 0.49 and 0.25 µs on verify 16- and 32-request sliding window; see the chart below); the trade-off is that with 7 segments, merging must partition 64 output rows across 7 segments, which no longer divides evenly.

Once each segment finishes its slice, how does it push partial results to its peers? Through DSMEM (Distributed Shared Memory), which lets one CTA in a cluster directly read and write a peer CTA's shared memory: when sender and receiver sit on different SMs, traffic crosses the intra-GPC SM-to-SM interconnect without going through L2, whereas the hardware path when two CTAs of one cluster co-reside on the same SM or when a CTA writes to itself is undocumented. In both cluster-kernel families, the grid dimension spanned by the cluster equals the cluster width, so that block index is already the intra-cluster rank (blockIdx.x in the 1-request sliding-window clusters and blockIdx.z in the sliding-window wgmma merge, whereas general grids read the special register %cluster_ctarank for the cross-dimensional CTA rank within the cluster; see Chapter 9, Section 3). The sender first uses mapa.shared::cluster.u32 ra, la, r to map a local shared-memory address la to the address ra of the same variable in CTA r, mapping the receiver's mbarrier (see Chapter 3, Section 7) address the same way; it then issues st.async to asynchronously write a 4–16 B register value into the shared memory of a target CTA in the same cluster (including the executing CTA itself), pushing each row's partial result into the shared memory of the CTA responsible for that row (each merging CTA in the cluster owns a subset of rows) and recording the arrived byte count on the receiver's mbarrier so the receiver knows all segments have arrived as soon as the expected byte count is reached.

The 16-CTA clusters used on 1-request sliding window (end of Section 1) exceed the 8-CTA portable cap and require opting in to a non-portable cluster size (CU_FUNC_ATTRIBUTE_NON_PORTABLE_CLUSTER_SIZE_ALLOWED = 1, or cudaFuncAttributeNonPortableClusterSizeAllowed in the runtime API, set before launch). On 1-request sliding window, the prologue was already fused into the split-KV kernel; fusing the split-KV main loop and the cluster merge into that same kernel gives a single 3-in-1 kernel (prologue, split-KV, and cluster merge), turns 2 launches into 1, and saves about 0.6 µs on verify 1-request sliding window (see the chart below). We measured this 3-in-1 kernel in the standalone attention benchmark of this chapter. In the full-layer chain of Chapter 9, verify 1-request sliding window likewise merges inside the cluster; there the QKV projection kernel handles the prologue, so it is a 2-in-1 split-KV and merge kernel. Decode 1- and 16-request sliding window there instead use a wgmma split kernel followed by a separate merge kernel (see earlier in this section).

Why not replace st.async at the push step with intra-cluster bulk copy or asynchronous reduction? TMA can bulk-copy a block directly from local shared memory into a peer CTA's shared memory (cp.async.bulk.shared::cluster.shared::cta, likewise decrementing the peer's mbarrier), which fits forwarding large blocks already sitting in shared memory, but it requires a byte size that is a multiple of 16 B, 16 B-aligned source and destination addresses, and a strictly remote target CTA; PTX's peer-SMEM reduction red.async likewise forbids targeting the executing CTA itself and supports integer operations only (see Chapter 9, Section 3 and Appendix B, Quick Reference 3). Across both cluster-merge families in this chapter, every CTA that merges rows also pushes its own assigned rows to itself (bulk copy forbids self-writes while st.async allows them, and Chapter 9's 4 B floating-point exchange likewise includes 1 self-write): the 1-request 3-in-1 merge sums 264 B floating-point rows in registers (so bulk copy would first have to stage them into shared memory and add fence.proxy.async.shared::cta), while the sliding-window wgmma merge already stages 16 B-aligned row partials and lse values in shared memory, though whether remote bulk copy plus that proxy fence would beat st.async for its remote peers was not measured.

Applying in-kernel merge in the wrong regime causes a loss (see the chart below). On single-request full attention, the in-kernel merge tail is more than twice as slow as a standalone merge kernel, making decode 1-request full attention about 3.0 µs slower — inferred from same-address atomic adds serializing one by one in L2 when all 256 segment CTAs target the exact same output row (the second path above spreads writes across 8 workspace copies, whose standalone gain was not measured). On verify 32-request sliding window (64 clusters of 4 CTAs, totaling 256 CTAs), each SM originally holds up to 3 CTAs, fitting all 64 clusters in 1 wave. Expanding each CTA to 2 consumer warpgroups or increasing shared memory drops residency to at most 2 CTAs per SM; querying cluster occupancy shows that at 2 CTAs per SM the GPU co-resides at most 62 clusters of 4 CTAs (with 2 SMs per TPC, even per-GPC SM counts still sum to 132÷2=66 rather than 62, so which hardware or scheduling limit caps this at 62 was not determined), pushing the last 2 clusters into a 2nd wave and stretching the tail. In addition, inlining the epilogue reduction code directly into the function containing the main loop disrupts compiler scheduling of the main loop and slows execution down.

By this point, both the head and the tail have been pulled into the main kernel, landing each shape on the final kernel assignment listed at the end of Section 1.

Stage 2 Paged Attention Evolution Chain (a0 → a6)

Across this chapter, a0 → a6 groups our optimizations by the bottleneck each mechanism removes (for the three-regime roadmap and final shape-to-kernel map, see the end of Section 1). The three charts below follow the chronological order in which versions were developed; because a single version often bundles several steps together, the a labels in the second chart interleave. In same-session paired ABBA runs against original SGLang, the final version runs about 2.7–2.8× as fast as the baseline (with the final step inside the noise band; see the second chart). Closing the ledger on the three decode waits beyond the bandwidth floor in Section 1: Section 6 hid the entry and per-page page-table round trips via preloading and even/odd lookahead (plus concurrent seq_lens and page-table loads at batch size 1), Sections 4 and 11 trimmed per-CTA entry/exit and boundary launch overhead by pulling grids inside 1 wave and folding the prologue into each split CTA, and Section 3, the end of Section 11, and Section 12 carried split merging from standalone lse merge to post-loop PDL handoff and in-kernel merge (how the ~9.5 µs gap between the ~4.3 µs floor and ~13.8 µs measured on 1-request decode splits across those three waits remains not measured separately).

  • a0 (Sections 2–3): launch a separate prologue kernel, stack 8 query heads as matrix rows, and run Q⋅K⊤ in FP8, with fixed-split Split-KV followed by a separate merge kernel (corresponding to Bar 1 of the first chart).
  • a1 (Section 4): tune split count to the concurrent request count, balance segments by key and tile count, and look up configurations per shape, cutting the 6-workload geometric mean by about 8% (corresponding to Bar 2 of the first chart and Bars 1–4 of the second chart).
  • a2 (Sections 5–6): reshape how the two halves of the same K row are read, preload page-table tiles before the loop and prefetch 2 iterations ahead with even/odd register pairs to hide the three-hop wait in the pipeline, and issue sequence-length and page-table loads concurrently at batch size 1; bundled with other changes, these land in Bars 2, 3, 4, and 10 of the second chart (Bar 2 cuts time by about 33% across its bundle, while Bar 10's whole-version gain stays within cross-session run-to-run variation).
  • a3 (Section 7): size residency by register allocation, apply verify full-attention split scheduling and insert virtual tiles to balance 264 CTAs evenly by tile count (see Section 4), make the producer the default partition to split out the unmasked loop at zero spills, and stagger the two consumer warpgroups by half a step (ping-pong) via named barriers (landing in Bars 3, 4, 5, and 8 of the second chart).
  • a4 (Section 8): skip per-tile rescaling altogether for BF16 P using the score upper bound, and offload row sums onto the Tensor Core when it has spare capacity. Single-KV-head Tensor Core row sum already shipped inside Bar 2 of the second chart, whereas Bar 4 ships BF16 skip-rescaling along with rewriting the main kernels to emit inline PTX inside CUDA C++ (for explicit control over registers, barriers, and instruction scheduling), removes row sum from the single-KV-head kernels, and bundles sliding-window cluster merges to cut time by about 17% (individual shares cannot be separated).
  • a5 (Sections 9–10): compress P to FP8 with lazy rescaling, move exponential encoding onto the FMA/ALU pipelines, overlap FP8 P⋅V with the transpose, and use half-precision accumulation in prefill; this cuts prefill kernel time by about 19% in the third chart and lands in Bars 5–7 and 9–10 of the second chart.
  • a6 (Sections 11–12): fold the prologue and the gating epilogue into neighboring kernels, and for some shapes fold the segment merge into the main kernel (landing in Bars 2, 4, 5, 8, and 10 of the second chart).

Takeaway: The bottleneck of paged attention is governed by how many query rows share each KV row (nq=8L). When nqn_q is small, the job is filling all 132 SMs and hiding the page-table round trip; when nqn_q is large, the challenge shifts inside each CTA to registers, the SFU, and issue slots. Each step of a0 → a6 removes only whichever bottleneck is slowest at that point.

Next chapter's question: After passing through the o projection in Stage 3 and the fork of Stages 4 and 5, the attention output arrives at Stage 6, the stage with the largest byte volume in a single layer: 32 local 4-bit (NVFP4) routed experts per GPU under 8-GPU expert parallelism (28.3 MB per expert). Every weight is a 4-bit float that H200 Tensor Cores cannot consume directly, and routing scatters tokens dynamically across experts — as the total token count TT grows from 1 to 16,384, the token count MeM_e landing on a single expert crosses the ~58 compute threshold from 1 into the hundreds, with wide load skew between hot and cold experts. Why is the expert-by-expert dequantizing starter implementation slow, and why can no single expert kernel cover the whole range — forcing five generations (m0 → m5) that split into three branches by MeM_e?

Position in the 8-stage single-layer pipeline: Stage 1 qkv_gate → Stage 2 paged attention → Stage 3 o and gated residual → Stage 4 router ∥ Stage 5 pooler → [Stage 6: Routed Experts] → Stage 7 unpooler → Stage 8 second gated residual

Stage 6's 32 local NVFP4 experts hold the largest share of weights in a single layer. Why is the starter implementation that dequantizes one expert at a time so slow? And as the total token count TT grows from 1 to 16,384, why does Stage 6 ultimately split into three distinct kernels by TT, and how does each generation evolve from the last?

1What Five Steps Does Stage 6 Compute for Each Hit Pair, and How Does MeM_e Split Stage 6 into Two Regimes?

When the token count MeM_e routed to an expert is less than about 58, reading weights is slower than matrix multiplication: decode, verify, and T=753 prefill fall below this threshold, whereas T≥3,012 prefill lies above it.

Stage 6 takes p:[T,4096]BF16\shape{p}{T,\;4096}{BF16} from Stage 5, along with the routing indices topk_ids:[T,8]int32\shape{\mathrm{topk\_ids}}{T,\;8}{int32} and routing weights topk_weights:[T,8]FP32\shape{\mathrm{topk\_weights}}{T,\;8}{FP32} from Stage 4. In each row, the 8 routing weights sum to 1 (see Primer 2, Section 2). All 256 experts in the model are split across 8 GPUs, and this GPU's 32 local experts stay resident in HBM (see Primer 1, Section 2). Once Stage 6 finishes, it outputs m:[T,4096]BF16\shape{m}{T,\;4096}{BF16} to Stage 7. A token toktok has 8 slots slotslot, and only a slot that lands on a local expert ee on this GPU counts as a hit pair (tok,slot,e)(tok, slot, e); if all 8 slots miss this GPU, that token's output row is all zeros.

For the MeM_e tokens that hit local expert ee on this GPU (one row per hit pair (tok,slot,e)(tok, slot, e)), Stage 6 runs five steps in order:

  1. gate/up projection (W13): [gu𝑔𝑎𝑡𝑒∣gu𝑢𝑝]=p𝑡𝑜𝑘dequant(W13[e])⊤, producing the gate and up halves gu:[Me,8192]FP32\shape{\mathrm{gu}}{M_e,\;8192}{FP32}. The first 4096 columns are the gate gu𝑔𝑎𝑡𝑒gu_{gate}, and the last 4096 columns are the up projection gu𝑢𝑝gu_{up}. These are the FP32 accumulator values of the matrix multiply; the kernels below usually keep them in registers and pass them straight to Step 2.
  2. SwiGLU: inter=silu(gu𝑔𝑎𝑡𝑒)⊙gu𝑢𝑝, producing inter:[Me,4096]BF16\shape{\mathrm{inter}}{M_e,\;4096}{BF16} (see Primer 2, Section 2).
  3. down projection (W2): y=interdequant(W2[e])⊤, producing y:[Me,4096]BF16\shape{y}{M_e,\;4096}{BF16}.
  4. post-expert RMSNorm: y𝑛𝑜𝑟𝑚=rmsnorm(y⊙(1+w𝑝𝑜𝑠𝑡)), producing y𝑛𝑜𝑟𝑚:[Me,4096]FP32\shape{y_{norm}}{M_e,\;4096}{FP32}. Here w𝑝𝑜𝑠𝑡:[4096]BF16\shape{w_{post}}{4096}{BF16} (written as wpost_expertw_{post\_expert} in Primer 2, Section 2) is the post-expert RMSNorm weight shared across all experts, and a tiny constant ϵ\epsilon sits inside the root mean square to prevent division by zero.
  5. weighted accumulation by routing weights: m𝑡𝑜𝑘+=topk_weights[tok,slot]⋅y𝑛𝑜𝑟𝑚, writing out m:[T,4096]BF16\shape{m}{T,\;4096}{BF16}.

H200 Tensor Cores do not accept 4-bit floating-point (E2M1) inputs. After NVFP4 codewords are loaded onto the chip, the kernel must decode them to BF16 before feeding them into the matrix multiply. Each weight is w=c⋅s𝑏𝑙𝑜𝑐𝑘⋅s𝑡𝑒𝑛𝑠𝑜𝑟: a 4-bit codeword cc multiplied by a block scale and then by a tensor scale (see Chapter 6, Section 5 for the bit layout and decoding instructions). Counting the bytes, each codeword takes 0.5 B0.5\text{ B}, every 16 weights share a 1 B1\text{ B} block scale (0.0625 B0.0625\text{ B} per weight), and each projection matrix (W13W_{13}, W2W_2) of each expert carries one FP32 tensor scale, totaling 0.5625 B0.5625\text{ B} per weight. Within each expert, the gate half and the up-projection half share a single FP32 tensor scale (Step 4's per-expert RMSNorm cancels out any positive constant factor; see Section 13 for the derivation).

Why split by TT at all? Because the row count of an expert's matrix multiplication is simply the number of tokens MeM_e routed to that expert. At 2 FLOP2\text{ FLOP} per weight ÷0.5625 B\div 0.5625\text{ B} per weight =3.56 FLOP/B= 3.56\text{ FLOP/B} per token against the H200 ridge point of 206 FLOP/B206\text{ FLOP/B}, an expert needs Me≈58 tokens before matrix-multiply compute time catches up with the time to read its weights once from HBM (Primer 2, Section 4). Which 8 experts each token picks is the routing distribution: spreading tokens evenly across experts is uniform routing, clustering them onto a few experts is skewed routing, and our single-operator benchmarks generate multiple random routing distributions. That Me≈58 line splits the workload into two regimes:

  • decode and verify (T=1..256): Under uniform routing at T=256, almost all 32 local experts on this GPU get hit, leaving each expert with an average of only 8 tokens. Under skewed routing, tokens pile onto fewer experts, so fewer experts get hit than under uniform routing. By the task router means of this chapter's single-operator benchmark, at T=256 the busiest GPU receives about 390 hit pairs and hits about 24 local experts on average (the measured busiest-GPU mean across 20 random routing distributions is 393.6393.6 hit pairs and 24.824.8 experts; see the table below), leaving each hit expert with an average of about 16 tokens—still far below 58. Only a few hot experts at T=128..256 receive several dozen to over a hundred tokens, which we handle in Section 9. Throughout this regime, weight reads set the physical lower bound.
  • prefill (T=753,3,012,16,384): Under uniform routing, each local expert receives an average of 8T/256=T/32 tokens—about 24, 94, and 512 tokens across the three points. T=753 still sits below the ridge point, but T≥3,012 crosses 58, shifting the bottleneck of our fifth-generation kernel (m5) onto the Tensor Cores and instruction pipelines.

This chapter first measures single-GPU Stage 6 latency under the busiest GPU's routing load (excluding cross-GPU waiting and reduction in an 8-GPU deployment; the three latency accounting terms are defined at the first measured number in Section 2), while the prefill workloads at T=753,3,012,16,384 are treated separately in Sections 14–16.

Along the evolution chain, decode and verify start out sharing two kernel generations (m1 and m2), before the final deployment splits into three branches by TT: m3 for T≤32, m4 for T=128..256, and m5 for prefill.

Putting the physical lower bounds at both ends—verify and prefill—side by side in one table makes this read-versus-compute crossover clear at a glance (compute lower bounds convert against the 989 TFLOP/s989\text{ TFLOP/s} BF16 dense peak without 2:4 sparsity, since 4-bit weights unpack to BF16 on chip before the multiply; read lower bounds convert against 4.8 TB/s4.8\text{ TB/s}):

2Why Does the Starter m0 Take Tens of Milliseconds, and Why Is the First Grouped-GEMM Step m1a ~80× Faster?

m0 loops over experts one by one, launching small kernels and decompressing weights to FP32 in HBM; m1 switches to a single grouped-GEMM launch per projection with on-the-fly in-register decompression.

m0 is the plain-PyTorch starter implementation, not the kernel that baseline SGLang runs in production. On every call, it steps through all 32 local experts one by one in a Python loop—whether hit or not, running every token through each expert with routing weight 0 where not routed: for each expert, it decompresses that expert's entire weight set into a 201.3 MB201.3\text{ MB} FP32 dense matrix in HBM, converts it to BF16, and runs the matrix multiplies. Look at the HBM byte accounting for a single expert: the useful weights are only 28.3 MB28.3\text{ MB}, yet even counting only reading the 4-bit weights, writing out the dense FP32 matrix, and reading it back moves at least 28.3+201.3+201.3=431.0 MB—about 15× the useful bytes.

First, let us fix the three latency terms used throughout the chapter. Stage 6 latency measures Stage 6 in isolation: within the same benchmark run, we alternate A/B paired comparisons before and after a change (see Chapter 7, Section 1 for the paired protocol and Chapter 4, Section 6 for the variation criterion). Single-layer latency, by contrast, covers all eight stages of a full layer in Chapter 9. Take the geometric mean of Stage 6 latency across the 6 decode (T=1,16,32, with 1 new token per request) and verify (T=8,128,256, with 8 new tokens per request) workloads and multiply by 60 (the middle 60 layers use 4-bit experts; see Primer 1, Section 2): that gives the 60-layer total, which we compare against the baseline SGLang implementation (invoking a 4-bit grouped-GEMM library routine once per projection; see the first chart at the end of the chapter).

Across the 6 benchmark cases, the measured geometric-mean Stage 6 latency is about 37.8 ms37.8\text{ ms}. Across all 32 local experts, that HBM round trip alone costs at least about 2.9 ms2.9\text{ ms} even at full HBM bandwidth; its actual share was not measured separately (see the chart below). Beyond that round trip, each expert in the per-expert loop also runs two dequantizations (producing temporary FP32 and BF16 tensors), two BF16 matrix multiplications, SwiGLU, normalization, and a small launch that adds the weighted result across all output rows. The share of each item was not measured. m1a drops the HBM round trip, the per-expert loop, the temporary tensors, and the repeated small launches all at once, running about 80× faster than m0.

m1 removes that extra round trip in two steps. First (m1a in the first chart at the end of the chapter), we run token bucketing (grouping tokens that hit the same expert together) and then launch a single grouped GEMM grid per projection instead of launching once per expert. A grouped GEMM is a single launch where each CTA processes one token tile for one expert. Stage 6 now runs in four parts: "token bucketing → gate/up grouped GEMM (with SwiGLU) → down-projection grouped GEMM → post-expert RMSNorm and weighted accumulation." Once an expert's 4-bit codewords and block scales arrive on chip, we decode them to BF16 right in registers and feed them straight into the matrix multiply without writing back any dense weights; HBM reads the 4-bit weights only once. This step is faster on all 6 benchmark cases (see the first chart at the end of the chapter).

Second (m1 in the first chart at the end of the chapter), we interleave the gate and up projections in 32+32 rows so the gate and up outputs for the same row land in the same tile and can run SwiGLU directly. At the same time, we switch weight decoding to branchless bitwise unpacking (see Chapter 6, Section 5) and turn on Programmatic Dependent Launch (PDL; see Chapter 1, Section 4) so the next kernel launches early to prefetch static weights. Even with those improvements, m1 still takes about 1.6× the latency of baseline SGLang, and only overtakes the baseline with m2 in the next section. What we pay for m1 is maintaining a fixed-shape token-bucketing index table (sorted_pair_ids; see Section 5) ahead of the matrix multiplications; the overhead of that table and the individual shares of the three items in Step 2 were not measured separately.

3When MeM_e Is Only a Handful to a Dozen Tokens, How Does m2 Keep the Tensor Cores Fed?

m2 first rewrites the whole kernel around pipelined wgmma tiling (accounting for ~2.69× of the ~3.18× m1 → m2 speedup), then adds the remaining ~1.18× via small-batch Split-K, multi-slot weight rings, left-shift offloading, and tail-tile trimming.

Step 1 replaces the kernel: m2 switches to Hopper's asynchronous wgmma instruction, placing the in-register decoded weights in operand A and the tokens on the operand-B side (swap-AB; see Chapter 5, Sections 4–6: m64nNk16 fixes m=64 on weights and lets nn on tokens take any multiple of 8, so tile height can shrink to 8, 16, or 32; for the operand-A fragment layout of decoded weights, see Chapter 5, Section 4 and Chapter 6, Sections 4–5—the per-thread mapping inside m2 is not listed separately here). m2 selects the matrix-multiply instruction according to tile height: 8-row tiles keep warp-level mma.sync, while taller tiles use wgmma—at T=8, switching to wgmma drops per-SM occupancy from 9→8 and pushes A=9 routing distributions into a second wave (Section 4). Running wgmma with operand A in registers (RS mode; Chapter 5, Section 4) comes with a catch: weight decoding consumes ALU cycles and registers. If ALU decoding cycles exceed Tensor Core cycles, operand supply cannot keep up (see Chapter 6, Section 4 for a counterexample). In the Me<58 regime, once we compress the decoding instructions tightly enough, the ALU is no longer the bottleneck.

Two bundled whole-kernel rewrites (dropping the 60-layer total from 21,369.20 μs21{,}369.20\ \mu\text{s} to 17,362.60 μs17{,}362.60\ \mu\text{s} and then 7,944.29 μs7{,}944.29\ \mu\text{s}, or ~2.69×, with individual sub-changes not isolated) carry most of the m1 → m2 gain, while roughly 20 incremental rounds (the sub-steps below and Sections 4–5) trim it to 6,718.85 μs6{,}718.85\ \mu\text{s} (~1.18×).

Step 2 raises the tile count: each expert's down projection has only 64 column tiles (4096 columns ÷ 64\div\ 64, half of the 8192 columns of the gate/up projection), which sometimes fails to fill all 132 SMs at T=1 and falls short of one 924-slot residency wave at T=16. Specifically, at T=1 (about 2.6 hit experts on the busiest GPU on average, leaving only 128 column tiles on 2-expert cases) total tiles can fall below the 132 SMs, whereas at T=8,16 the grid already exceeds 132 CTAs yet still sits inside a partial residency wave (about 570–760 CTAs at T=16, below one 924-slot wave at 7 CTAs per SM; T=8 runs at 9 CTAs per SM, 1,188 slots per wave; T=32 uses no Split-K on the down projection). Following Split-K from Chapter 2, Section 5, at T=1,8,16 the down projection is sliced 2-way or 4-way along K (pushing the grid past one full wave at T=8,16; we infer that keeping more concurrent warps and memory requests per SM outweighs the wave tail, though this was not profiled), storing partial sums into a temporary BF16 matrix that the subsequent post-expert RMSNorm kernel reduces; at T=1, even the gate/up projection lacks enough tiles and is sliced along K too. What Split-K costs us is writing and reading an extra buffer of partial sums and running the reduction additions, plus the lower precision of BF16 partial sums compared to FP32. Splitting too finely loses performance—cutting the T=16 down projection into 4 slices makes it slower (see the second chart below).

Step 3 keeps weight loads continuously in flight. Prior to this step, weight unpacking had already moved to paired 4-bit nibble decoding (where each instruction unpacks two 4-bit codes into a packed BF16x2 pair at once; see Chapter 6, Section 5). Next, we build a multi-slot weight ring buffer in shared memory driven by cp.async (Chapter 3, Section 5, rather than TMA), which we infer keeps enough bytes in flight across K-steps to hide HBM latency (Chapter 2, Section 3; Chapter 5, Section 7). Because the ring-removal ablation simultaneously shifted per-SM occupancy from 8 to 7 CTAs without separating the two effects, the 5–6 µs below is not the ring's standalone contribution: removing that 3-slot cp.async ring buffer slows Stage 6 down by 5–6 µs at T=16 and T=32.

At T=128 and T=256, we likewise introduce a weight-only 2-slot cp.async ring buffer: at T=128, per-SM occupancy stays unchanged at 7 CTAs, cleanly isolating a 4.64 μs4.64\ \mu\text{s} saving from the 2-slot ring; at T=256, Stage 6 latency drops by about 19 μs19\ \mu\text{s} alongside fewer registers lifting occupancy from 5 to 6 CTAs per SM (again bundling an occupancy shift; see the chart and note below).

Opening too many ring slots consumes extra shared memory and drops occupancy (see Section 4; for the TMA ring counterexample where too few slots leave insufficient bytes in flight, see Section 9). We also tried refilling ring slots early inside the loop, but the compiler inserted an intra-CTA barrier (bar.sync) between refilling and dequantization, serializing the two steps and slowing Stage 6 by 2.102.10 and 4.51 μs4.51\ \mu\text{s} at T=16,32 (see the second chart below).

Step 4 relieves the busiest integer pipe: profiler runs during register dequantization measured the 16-lane ALU pipeline per SMSP as the busiest pipe at 44%–59%44\%\text{–}59\% utilization, with math_pipe_throttle as the top stall reason. Offloading the decoding left shift via IMAD.SHL onto the 32-lane FMA pipeline (left-shift FMA offloading, cutting 12 ALU instructions per step; see Chapter 5, Section 1 and Chapter 6, Section 5) relieves that ALU contention and speeds up 5 of the 6 benchmark workloads—saving up to about 9.4 μs9.4\ \mu\text{s} in Stage 6 at T=128—with only T=8 coming out slightly slower by 0.46 μs0.46\ \mu\text{s} (cause not measured separately).

Here is who holds what in m2:

4Why Does the Same Occupancy Change Turn from Faster to Slower Under a Different Routing Distribution?

As the number of active experts varies with routing, the total tile count varies too; changing per-SM occupancy alters the wave count only for routing distributions that cross a full-wave capacity step.

Back in Chapter 2, Section 1, we calculated wave counts: when each SM holds kk resident CTAs at once (where kk is set jointly by each SM's 65,536 registers and 228 KiB228\text{ KiB} of shared memory; see Chapter 3, Section 1), a single wave fits 132k132k CTAs, and total runtime is approximately ⌈Ac/(132k)⌉×\lceil A c / (132 k) \rceil \times the duration of one wave. The expert kernel adds a moving variable: the number of active experts AA is not constant, because different routing distributions hit different numbers of local experts, so the device-wide tile count AcA c (where cc is the CTAs per expert) fluctuates with the routing distribution. Any change whose register or shared-memory footprint alters kk shifts the capacity step 132k132k. Routing distributions whose tile counts land between the old and new steps run one wave more or one wave fewer, shifting latency by several to over ten microseconds; distributions that do not cross a step see only the small intrinsic cost or benefit of the change itself.

This is the measured basis for keeping mma.sync on 8-row tiles in Section 3 (from which we infer why m2 does not switch 8-row tiles to wgmma): when we replace mma.sync with wgmma at T=8 (see Chapter 5, Section 4), each expert launches c=128 CTAs (gate/up projection 8,192 columns÷64 columns/CTA), per-SM occupancy drops from k=9 to k=8, and a single wave shrinks from 1,1881{,}188 CTAs to 1,0561{,}056. The two routing distributions with A=9 have 9×128=1,152 CTAs, so they drop right across the boundary from 1 wave into 2 waves and slow Stage 6 down by over 10 μs10\ \mu\text{s}. The other three routing distributions (A=8, 1,0241{,}024 CTAs still within 1 wave) run slightly faster instead (see the chart below). The same thing happens at T=16 and T=32 when we expand the weight ring buffer from the previous section from 3 slots to 4 slots and per-SM occupancy drops from 8 to 7: across multiple routing distributions it averages about 1.9 μs1.9\ \mu\text{s} faster, yet under each of the two workloads one routing distribution regresses.

That directly sets a rule: every occupancy or register change to an expert kernel must be benchmarked across multiple routing distributions simultaneously; a change that wins on only one distribution is rejected. To stop a change from moving the wave step 132k132k, we pin each CTA's register and shared-memory usage to the exact quota that fits kk CTAs per SM (Chapter 3, Section 1), isolating the change's own gain or loss. For instance, pinning the T=16 down projection at 7 CTAs per SM turns its new weight-only 2-slot ring buffer from a loss of about 2.1 μs2.1\ \mu\text{s} into a gain of about 1.8 μs1.8\ \mu\text{s}.

The cost of pinning occupancy is a tighter per-thread register cap. Push the compiler attribute __maxnreg__(N) too low and the compiler spills excess values to local memory (see Chapter 3, Section 1). Switching to wgmma at T=8 and capping registers at 56 spills 8 registers per thread and slows Stage 6 by about 62 μs62\ \mu\text{s}; capping at 80 or 72 registers at T=256 also causes slowdowns from register spilling (see the chart below). The same common pools of 65,536 registers and 228 KiB228\text{ KiB} of shared memory per SM govern every later generation in Sections 6, 8, 9, and 15 (each kernel's budget sits in its own section).

5How Do Narrower Shapes Skip Blank Padding Rows in the Tail Tiles of Light Experts?

Tail tiles with v≤16 valid rows issue 16-row or 8-row narrow wgmma, while tail tiles with 17..3117..31 valid rows keep height 32.

Because token bucketing in Section 2 requires all tokens in a tile to belong to the same expert, we have to pad each expert's token count up to a multiple of the tile height BMBM (BMBM is the number of tokens per tile, which maps to nn of wgmma after swap-AB). Under skewed routing, many light experts receive only a few tokens, and the last tile of a heavy expert (its tail tile, a partially filled M-tile) often holds only a few valid rows as well; the extra rows padded at the bottom are called padding rows. If we do nothing, every matrix multiplication issues at the full tile height.

Tail-tile M-dimension trimming never reads or computes a tile's valid row count vv. Bucketing places valid entries (<R< R) first in the index table sorted_pair_ids and fills the trailing padding rows with the sentinel RR; at tile entry (for M-tile blk), the kernel compares sorted_pair_ids[blk * 32 + 16] with RR and loads +8 only when +16 is ≥R\ge R, learning only whether vv falls in v≤8, 9..169..16, or ≥17\ge 17: a tail tile with 17..3117..31 valid rows keeps height 32, and only v≤16 gets the narrower 16- or 8-row shape. As explained in Section 3, swap-AB puts tokens on the nn side of m64nNk16, so tile height can step down through 32→16→8 across 3 heights (see Chapter 5, Sections 4–5).

How much tail-tile trimming saves varies with MeM_e. On verify workloads (MeM_e around a dozen), tail tiles make up a large share of all tiles: clipping tail tiles down to 16 rows at T=256 cuts Stage 6 time by 25.68 μs25.68\ \mu\text{s} (about 26 μs26\ \mu\text{s}) in one step (even though the prior solver model already counted skipped activation loads and epilogue work, it predicted only 10.05 μs10.05\ \mu\text{s} saved, and standalone RS wgmma microbenchmark issue intervals drop only from 20.3820.38 to 17.6717.67 cycles—a 2.712.71-cycle cut—so Tensor Core issue cycles alone explain only a small fraction; the runtime shares of activation loads, MMA, and the epilogue, and why the measured gain is about 2.5×2.5\times the 10.05 μs10.05\ \mu\text{s} model, were not profiled with NCU), and adding the 8-row tier (17.2917.29-cycle issue interval) saves another 7.12 μs7.12\ \mu\text{s} at T=256. As MeM_e grows larger, on the other hand, the tail tile is only a small fraction at the end of a long queue, so the gain from trimming shrinks (the prefill kernel applies the same trimming; see Section 15).

What you pay for tail-tile trimming is generating extra narrow-tile code branches in the kernel, and having every CTA of every M-tile execute the +16 load at entry (adding 1 load when v≥17 and 2 dependent loads when v≤16); at what workload size it loses performance was not measured.

6At T = 1..32, How Are Multi-Launch Round Trips Folded into a Persistent Kernel?

Fold bucketing, gate/up projection, and down projection into a persistent kernel with 132 resident CTAs—switching from m2 to m3 saves 5.795.79, 11.3111.31, 13.7113.71, and 7.70 μs7.70\ \mu\text{s} at T=1,8,16,32 (dropping the 60-layer total from 6,718.856{,}718.85 to 6,123.21 μs6{,}123.21\ \mu\text{s})—and for T=8..32, split back into two PDL-chained kernels to avoid the grid barrier.

In Stage 6, m2 launches token bucketing, the gate/up projection, the down projection, and post-expert RMSNorm one after another, paying a tail wave on every launch.

In the third generation (m3), Stage 6 moves to a persistent kernel (see Chapter 3, Section 1): 132 CTAs stay resident on the SMs (1 CTA of 8 warps per SM; see the resource table below for register budgets and the 3-slot TMA weight ring at 35,840 B35{,}840\text{ B} per slot). At entry, each CTA works out which tiles it owns; it then steps through them one after another without exiting between tiles. Inside the kernel, Phase 0 runs token bucketing, followed by the gate/up projection with SwiGLU and then the down projection, streaming weights through a TMA ring buffer (see Chapter 3, Sections 5 and 6). Matrix multiplication inside m3 uses warp-level mma.sync (see Chapter 5, Section 4) rather than wgmma. Because m3 keeps 132 CTAs resident, it has no wave capacity steps (the Section 4 example, where occupancy dropped from 9 to 8 and crossed a wave step, was measured on m2's non-persistent grid); why mma.sync was still chosen was not determined. Here is m3's resource budget:

Kernel (sections) Threads / CTA and warp roles Registers / thread (→ allocated / CTA) SMEM rings and bytes / slot CTAs / SM MMA instruction
m3 persistent kernel (T≤32, §§6–7) 256 threads = 8 warps (all compute; Phase 0 bucketing uses 1 warp at T=1 and final T=8, 8 warps at T=16,32; thread 0 issues TMA) T=1 coop cap 144 (36,864); T=8 down 136 (34,816); T=16,32 down 206–210 (53,248–55,296) TMA 3-slot weight ring at 35,840 B35{,}840\text{ B} (35 KiB35\text{ KiB}) per slot; CTA SMEM 115–129 KiB115\text{–}129\text{ KiB} across T=8..32 (129 KiB129\text{ KiB} at T=16,32), plus bucketing table and preloaded tensor scales Resident 1 (132 CTAs across GPU; at T=8..32 both gate/up and down exceed 114 KiB114\text{ KiB}, preventing co-residency) mma.sync.m16n8k16

Once the gate/up projection and the down projection are merged into a single persistent kernel, the down projection has to wait until the entire GPU finishes writing inter. Because CUDA guarantees full-grid co-residency only under cooperative launch (see Chapter 2, Section 6; see Chapter 7, Section 12 for the grid-barrier conditions required without cooperative launch), the T=1 persistent kernel uses cooperative launch; synchronizing all 132 resident CTAs across the grid barrier once costs 1.42 μs1.42\ \mu\text{s} (about 1.4 μs1.4\ \mu\text{s}) in a standalone microbenchmark. In this chapter's single-operator benchmark, T=1 retains this single cooperatively launched persistent kernel.

For T=8..32 in this chapter's single-operator benchmark, splitting the gate/up projection and the down projection into two kernels chained back-to-back with PDL pays off (Chapter 9's single-layer pipeline instead shares a single persistent expert kernel with an internal grid barrier across T=1 and T=8, and replaces cooperative launch with PDL in Chapter 9, Section 4). Because each kernel uses 115–129 KiB115\text{–}129\text{ KiB} of shared memory (129 KiB129\text{ KiB} at T=16,32; see the resource table above), the two kernels do not fit together inside the 228 KiB228\text{ KiB} per SM. Still, as soon as a gate/up CTA exits an SM, that SM immediately accepts a down-projection CTA, preloads its 3-slot down-projection weight ring buffer into shared memory while the other SMs are finishing, and then pauses at griddepcontrol.wait until the entire GPU finishes writing inter (the cooperative build likewise preloads the first 3 down-projection weight slots before the full-grid barrier). Splitting into two kernels costs one extra PDL edge of about 0.64 μs0.64\ \mu\text{s} (see Chapter 1, Section 4; if the predecessor executes no GPU-scope release fence before triggering, the successor still cannot read inter before the wait returns, see Section 8) and nets under 1 μs1\ \mu\text{s} in Stage 6 (which factor produces the gain was not measured separately; see the chart below).

Can we stay in a single kernel and avoid the grid barrier? We tested fine-grained tile counters (where each finished inter tile increments its own counter so the down projection waits only for the tiles it needs) and in-band payload readiness flags (encoding the readiness flag and the inter payload in the same word). Every fine-grained counter handoff requires a device-wide memory barrier—the device-scope acq_rel memory fence from Chapter 2, Section 6: the issuing warp stalls until all prior writes reach L2, while other warps and SMs keep running. That slowed down several benchmark cases, and in-band payload readiness flags also slowed T=1 by about 1 μs1\ \mu\text{s} (the exact causes of the slowdown in both approaches were not measured separately).

The post-expert RMSNorm kernel reads back y, skips non-local slots, and completes Steps 4 and 5 of Section 1; it already overlaps with the main kernel via PDL, and fusing it into the tail of the main kernel ran slower in single-operator tests. Separating the m2 → m3 kernel switch per TT from the subsequent inside-m3 parallel bucketing bundle (alongside the final kernel-and-barrier layout) gives:

On m3's 1-CTA-per-SM persistent grid, adding warps per CTA does not necessarily pay off either: expanding each CTA from 8 warps to 16 warps at T=32 (from 2 to 4 warps per SMSP) saves only about 0.85 μs0.85\ \mu\text{s}, sitting inside the control variation envelope (about 0.78 μs0.78\ \mu\text{s}) with no clear gain while costing an extra 8 warps of registers per CTA. With tokens on the nn side of mma.sync.m16n8k16 (n=8), one mma.sync tile holds at most 8 tokens; experts with more than 8 tokens are handled next.

Now consider hot experts where tokens pile up. Because a single mma.sync tile holds up to 8 tokens, that parallel-bucketing build (detailed next) still split experts with more than 8 tokens into multiple 8-token passes that re-read weights; a later m3 version merges 9–16 tokens routed to one expert into a 16-token segment that feeds two 8-token tiles from the same decoded weight registers so weights are read once, while an expert routed 17–32 tokens is broken into two segments. Once T≥128, hot experts accumulate still more tokens, prompting the switch to a new kernel in Section 9.

The inside-m3 update in the right-hand column above replaced the single-thread serial scan over 256 slots at T=8..32 (for example, 32 tokens×8 slots at T=32) with 8 warps scanning 32 slots each in parallel, bundled in the same build with 8-token virtual passes and 8-warp epilogue rotation (not measured separately). __ballot_sync collects a yes/no predicate from each of a warp's 32 lanes into a 32-bit integer where bit ii holds lane ii's answer, and __popc counts the set bits in that integer to tell us how many lanes in this warp hit. Each warp writes its hit count n to shared memory; after an intra-CTA barrier, summing n across the preceding warps gives this warp's write offset base (the snippet below shows that build's parallel-ballot step, still used for active-expert compaction, whereas the frozen final build upgrades per-expert lane grouping to a single __match_any_sync instruction—SASS MATCH.ANY, returning in one step the mask of lanes in the warp holding the same expert ID—paired with __popc):

hit  = (topk_id[slot] == e);              // each lane tests whether its slot hits expert e
mask = __ballot_sync(FULL, hit);          // FULL = 0xffffffff (all 32 lanes participate)
n    = __popc(mask);                      // number of hits in this warp
pos  = base + __popc(mask & lanes_below); // lanes_below = (1u << lane) - 1 (mask of lower-numbered lanes)

7At Persistent Kernel Startup, Why Does Activation p Wait in Line Behind Weights?

At kernel entry, all 132 SMs issuing 3 weight slots (35,840 B35{,}840\text{ B} per slot, 132×3×35,840 B=14.19 MB total) simultaneously send about 14 MB of requests into the memory path; the first MMA waits on both shared-memory Slot 0 (full[0], Slot 0's full mbarrier; see Chapter 3, Section 7) and p in registers (see Chapter 4, Section 2 for scoreboards), so issuing p and Slot 0 first while delaying Slots 1–2 by a few hundred nanoseconds is intended to reduce contention from Slots 1–2 against Slot 0 and p (arrival order after staggering was not measured).

On the T=1 cooperative persistent kernel, activation p is only a few kilobytes and loads via LDG (through LSU → L1 → the on-chip crossbar XBAR) directly into registers, whereas weights load via TMA (bypassing L1) into shared-memory Slots 0–2 (35,840 B35{,}840\text{ B} per slot, 14.19 MB14.19\text{ MB} across 132 SMs; see the Section 6 resource table), sharing the path from the L2 slices to HBM (see Chapter 3, Section 5). Entry timestamps taken with the GPU's 64-bit global nanosecond timer register %globaltimer (see Chapter 10, Section 5 for the stamping method; here elapsed time is measured within a single CTA) show that after Slot 0 weights (full[0]) arrive, warp 0 still waits about 0.96 μs0.96\ \mu\text{s} on p's register scoreboard, whereas warps 1–7 wait about 0.06 μs0.06\ \mu\text{s}: thread 0 of warp 0 issued all 3 weight TMA commands for its SM before warp 0 issued its own p loads, placing warp 0's p requests behind about 14 MB14\text{ MB} of weights, while warps 1–7 issued no TMA. A likely reason is that normal global loads (LDG) and TMA requests contend for queues along the memory path (queueing could sit at the SM exit port, XBAR, L2 slice, or memory controller—the exact site was not measured, and other causes are not ruled out). That is queueing delay (see Chapter 7, Section 6): a small request of a few kilobytes gets stuck in line behind the bulk weight requests.

To fix it, we flip the issue order: issue the load of p and Slot 0 weights first, spin-wait on %globaltimer within the same CTA for a few hundred nanoseconds, and only then issue Slots 1 and 2. We do not call __nanosleep(500) here: the PTX specification guarantees only that nanosleep.u32 t sleeps for an interval in [0,2t][0, 2t], so holding a fixed delay requires spinning on %globaltimer. Using a fixed delay without checking whether data has arrived is called open-loop staggering (intended to reduce contention from Slots 1–2 against Slot 0 and p; arrival order after staggering was not measured). At T=1 (a single cooperative kernel), a 4-arm part sweep breaks down the three entry changes: preloading tensor scales into shared memory alone saves 0.41 μs0.41\ \mu\text{s} (and 0.82,0.40,0.48 μs0.82, 0.40, 0.48\ \mu\text{s} at T=8,16,32), scale preload plus hoisting p saves 0.71 μs0.71\ \mu\text{s}, scale preload plus the 500 ns500\text{ ns} stagger saves 0.65 μs0.65\ \mu\text{s}, and all three together save 1.05 μs1.05\ \mu\text{s} (the individual increments of hoisting p and staggering—0.300.30 and 0.24 μs0.24\ \mu\text{s}—do not simply add to their joint 0.64 μs0.64\ \mu\text{s} increment). After splitting T=8..32 into two PDL kernels (with tensor-scale preload already active; per-warp timestamps were not retaken at T=8, so the queueing mechanism there is inferred from T=1), the gate/up kernel isolates hoisting p plus the delay: T=8 waits 600 ns600\text{ ns}, while T=16 and 3232 simply issue p first with the delay set to 0 ns0\text{ ns}.

Because this is an open-loop wait, we cannot stretch the delay too far—waiting too long just artificially delays the weights. Sweeping the delay at T=8 (see the chart below) shows the tradeoff: 0 ns0\text{ ns} (only issuing p first) captures only about half the gain, the three settings across 300–800 ns300\text{–}800\text{ ns} perform similarly (with 600 ns600\text{ ns} chosen in the end), and by 1,200 ns1{,}200\text{ ns} the saving drops back again.

The catch with open-loop staggering is that the best delay shifts with TT, so each TT needs its own sweep; a closed-loop alternative ("wait until p arrives, then issue Slots 1 and 2") was not measured. On the T=128..256 kernel (Section 9), delaying Weight Slots 1 and 2 moves the first MMA instruction earlier by only about 0.4 μs0.4\ \mu\text{s}, and the upper bound on remaining savings at kernel entry is less than 1 μs1\ \mu\text{s}, so we stopped here.

8In the SASS of the Post-Expert RMSNorm Kernel, What Did the Compiler Schedule Poorly, and What Can Be Loaded Before Waiting?

Issuing loads via asm volatile blocks instruction sinking, and an empty asm volatile statement blocks rematerialization; both are only effects observed with the current compiler, not guarantees of the specification.

The post-expert RMSNorm kernel launches 1 CTA of 256 threads (8 warps) per token after the main kernel via PDL, reading y to run the RMS reduction and the routing-weighted sum (only the 2×8 reduction loop shape is recorded; the exact cross-thread shuffle steps are not listed separately); here is its resource budget:

Kernel (sections) Threads / CTA and warp roles Registers / thread (→ allocated / CTA) SMEM rings and bytes / slot CTAs / SM MMA instruction
Post-norm kernel (§8) 256 threads = 8 warps (1 CTA per token: RMS reduction and weighted sum) Small-batch (T≤32): 110 (28,672) →\to final 114 (30,720); T>32: 110 →\to 112 On-chip reduction buffer (no weight ring) 110-reg build co-resides at T=1,8; final 114-reg build co-resides only at T=8 (34,816+30,720=65,536), entering freed SMs elsewhere None (vector reduction and weighted sum)

The first compiler rewrite we run into is instruction sinking (code sinking), where the compiler moves instructions to a later point in the schedule. In Chapter 1, Section 4, the call cudaGridDependencySynchronize() that waits for the predecessor kernel compiles to griddepcontrol.wait in PTX and ACQBULK in SASS. Before that wait, the kernel can issue loads for data that the predecessor kernel does not write (such as this kernel's own static weights), overlapping those loads with the wait:

uint4 w0 = w_ptr[idx];              // load issued early
cudaGridDependencySynchronize();    // PTX: griddepcontrol.wait / SASS: ACQBULK
use(w0);                            // consumed only after the wait

griddepcontrol.wait acts like an acquire barrier (Chapter 2, Section 6). The PTX specification promises only one thing: it waits until all prerequisite grids have completed and their memory operations are visible to the current grid. So accesses after the wait cannot move ahead of it. But nothing in the specification stops normal loads that sit before the wait from moving down past it. Once those loads sink past ACQBULK, the overlap between loading and waiting is gone. When we issue those loads with asm volatile, the SASS from our build shows that the loads stay ahead of the wait. Still, the PTX specification makes no such promise, so you need to inspect the SASS again after changing compiler versions.

There is a strict correctness boundary here: data written by the predecessor kernel (its output tensors and the routing results it computed) is guaranteed to be visible only after griddepcontrol.wait. Loading predecessor outputs early is valid only when both grids belong to the same memory synchronization domain (Hopper lets different streams be assigned to separate domains to narrow cross-stream fence scope; all kernels share the default domain unless configured otherwise) and the predecessor kernel finishes writing and executes a GPU-scope release fence before triggering the successor (see Chapter 9, Section 5 for the complete rules and measured data-race violations). Instruction sinking itself affects only speed, not correctness.

The second compiler rewrite is rematerialization: instead of keeping a value that has already been computed, the compiler throws it away and recomputes it every time it is needed. Take this 4-line example: outside the loop, the kernel unpacks 16 BF16 weights w[i] to FP32 (Chapter 6, Section 1), adds 1.0f, and stores them into nw[i], then reuses nw[i] repeatedly inside the loop:

float nw[16];
for (int i = 0; i < 16; ++i) nw[i] = 1.0f + float(w[i]);
for (int step = 0; step < steps; ++step)
    for (int i = 0; i < 16; ++i) acc[i] += x[step][i] * nw[i];

To save those 16 registers, ptxas may throw nw[i] away and unpack the BF16 w[i] to FP32 and add 1.0f again on every loop iteration. The numerical result stays identical, but every iteration runs 16 extra unpacks and 16 extra additions.

To stop ptxas from doing that, we place an empty inline-assembly barrier (asm volatile) asm volatile("" : "+f"(nw[i])); right after the precomputation:

for (int i = 0; i < 16; ++i) {
    nw[i] = 1.0f + float(w[i]);
    asm volatile("" : "+f"(nw[i]));
}

Because this empty assembly statement declares that it "reads and writes nw[i]," the compiler must treat nw[i] as the output of an opaque instruction that cannot be rematerialized from w[i]. At runtime it emits 0 instructions, at the cost of holding 16 FP32 registers (64 B per thread) live throughout the loop; after merging this barrier, the small-batch post-norm variant (256 threads = 8 warps per CTA; see the resource table at the start of this section) grew from 110 (28,672 allocated) to 114 registers per thread (30,720 allocated registers per CTA), pushing its sum with the 144-register T=1 cooperative main kernel (36,864 registers) past 65,536 and ending co-residency on the same SM at T=1 (the cost of losing that co-residency was not measured separately).

Stage 6's post-expert RMSNorm kernel ran into both compiler rewrites at once. The first was instruction sinking. In the single-operator benchmark, the kernel entry originally issued 4 pre-wait 16 B16\text{ B} loads (w_post and topk_weights, 2 each) with ld.global.nc, which routes loads through the SM's read-only cache path. ptxas sank them past ACQBULK. We made two changes: we issued normal global loads via asm volatile, and we replaced the post-wait local[] loads with pre-wait topk_ids loads (2 each; local[] is the per-slot local expert index written by the main kernel, with −1 for a slot that is not on this GPU). Now all 6 LDG.E.128 instructions stay ahead of ACQBULK. The PDL overlap window comes from two sources: co-residency where the register budget fits, or entering SMs freed as early-finishing primary CTAs exit while remaining primary CTAs finish (primary CTA exit-time spread was not measured). Because four distinct builds participate here, the table below separates each build's registers, co-resident shapes, pre-wait loads, and measured gains:

Post-norm build Registers / thread (allocated / 256-thread CTA) Co-resident TT shapes (non-co-resident shapes) Pre-wait loads ahead of ACQBULK Stage 6 paired delta and notes
Standalone final build (deployed across all TT) (after adding the empty-asm anti-rematerialization barrier: T≤32 runs the prefetch variant, T>32 runs the unprefetched variant) T≤32: 114 (30,720); T>32: 112 Co-resident at T=8 only (34,816+30,720=65,536); enters freed SMs at T=1 (67,584>65,536) and T=16,32,128 6 loads (w_post ×2\times 2, topk_weights ×2\times 2, topk_ids ×2\times 2) only for T≤32; 0 loads for T>32 (reads local[] after wait) Keeps the T≤32 prefetch gate; isolated prefetch delta at T=1 was not re-measured under 114 non-co-resident registers
