Earlier ungated prefetch arm (inferred experimental build before the T≤32 gate, not deployed) 110 (28,672) Co-resident at T=1,8 (enters freed SMs at T=16,32,128) 6 LDG.E.128 loads at all TT T=128 slows by 0.45 μs0.45\ \mu\text{s} (0.4 μs0.4\ \mu\text{s} rounded in code comment; inferred cause: cold HBM read of topk_ids replacing an L2 hit on post-wait local[] outweighs overlap across m4's unmeasured CTA exit spread)
T≤32-gated 110-register experimental build (source of T≤32 bars in series 1 below, superseded by row 1) T≤32: 110 (28,672); T>32: unprefetched variant Co-resident at T=1,8; enters freed SMs at T=16,32 Same as row 1: 6 loads only for T≤32, 0 loads for T>32 Saves 0.45,0.27,0.67,0.41 μs0.45, 0.27, 0.67, 0.41\ \mu\text{s} at T=1,8,16,32 (up to ~0.7 μs0.7\ \mu\text{s} at T=16)

Keep one caveat in mind: issuing all 6 prefetches is safe only in the standalone operator benchmark, where none of the 3 inputs is produced by a preceding kernel. Inside Chapter 9's full-layer pipeline, the Stage 4 kernel writes both topk_weights and topk_ids; without a preceding release fence, reading them ahead of the wait triggers the data race explained under the correctness boundary above. Consequently, the standalone post-expert RMSNorm kernel in the final full-layer build issues no loads ahead of the wait, deferring w_post, topk_weights, and the per-slot local expert index (which the Stage 4 kernel also writes in the full layer) until after the wait returns (Chapter 9, Section 5 states the rule for what may be read before wait).

Second was rematerialization: the 16 values nwi=1+wpost,i that the post-expert RMSNorm kernel precomputed outside the loop were pulled back into the inner loop to re-unpack and re-run FADD (only ALU and FADD / FFMA / FMUL instruction counts change; a separate 1,596-instruction listing counted 321 recomputed FADD instructions). Adding the empty inline-assembly barrier cut static SASS on the small-batch variant (T≤32) from 1,615 instructions down to 1,133 (482 fewer; the T>32 variant drops from 1,603 to 1,120, or 483 fewer); in a 1,000-block paired run across T=1,16,32, Stage 6 saves 0.21–0.30 μs0.21\text{–}0.30\ \mu\text{s} with all 95% confidence intervals strictly above 0 (see the chart below).

9At T = 128..256, Why Switch to a Persistent wgmma Kernel?

A persistent wgmma kernel with 132 resident CTAs lets up to 64 tokens routed to a hot expert share a single tile so weights are read only once, while eliminating full-kernel handoff waits between bucketing, gate/up projection, and down projection.

m3 suffices for T≤32, but by T=128,256, hot experts receive several dozen tokens each. In the design space, continuing with 8 tokens per pass in m3 would re-read a hot expert's weights on every pass (m3 was not measured at T≥128), while staying on m2's 4-kernel tiled scheme pays 4 tail waves and forces the down projection to wait for the entire gate/up kernel to finish before reading inter.

The fourth generation (m4) switches to a single persistent kernel (see Chapter 3, Section 1), completing in-kernel bucketing, the gate/up projection with SwiGLU, and the down projection in one launch. All 132 CTAs take work in the order of one shared subtask table: during in-kernel bucketing, each CTA builds an identical copy of that table in its own shared memory. At first, work is assigned statically across the CTAs; in the next section, CTAs claim it by atomic increments of one global counter. One subtask covers at most 64 token rows × 256 output columns of one expert (which of the 256 output columns each of the 4 consumer warpgroups owns, and why 4 consumer warpgroups were chosen over 2, are not recorded). An expert with at most 64 tokens fits into a single tile, so its weights are read from HBM only once. A hot expert with more than 64 tokens splits into several 64-row token tiles; its first tile tags the weight loads with the L2 residency hint (evict_last; see Chapter 2, Section 4), so later tiles hit in the 60 MiB L2 cache as much as possible. After SwiGLU, the output inter goes to a global intermediate matrix, and the down-projection phase reads it directly (one down-projection subtask needs a full 4096-wide inter row, and 32 gate/up subtasks produce that row, usually across different CTAs [Section 10], so inter cannot stay in the registers of one warpgroup; Section 11 explains how the down projection knows that the inter tiles it needs are written). Meanwhile, the instruction family switches back from mma.sync in m3 to wgmma: once token counts reach several dozen rows, only wgmma, issued collectively by 4 warps, can keep the Tensor Cores fed (see Chapter 5, Sections 4 and 6). At T=256, replacing m2's 4-kernel tiled scheme with this persistent wgmma kernel for the first time cuts Stage 6 latency by 22.54 μs22.54\ \mu\text{s} in paired testing (about 22 μs22\ \mu\text{s}, measured with the two fixes below and Row 4 of Section 11's ladder table already included). Its costs are three: only 96 registers per thread (see the resource table below for the full warp-and-ring budget), 2 extra producer warps per CTA, and building that subtask table redundantly in every CTA.

In the initial version, each CTA has 18 warps (576 threads). During the kernel entry phase, 4 consumer warpgroups (512 threads) gather the activations of tokens hitting this GPU and write them into a global buffer; once the main loop begins, they dedicate themselves to matrix multiplication, while the other 2 warps serve exclusively as producers. Warp 16 uses TMA to feed the 3-slot shared-memory weight ring buffer. Warp 17 uses TMA to feed activations from the global buffer into the shared-memory activation ring buffer: the gate/up projection reads the gathered p, and the down projection reads the inter written by the gate/up projection. Slots in both ring buffers synchronize via full and empty mbarrier signals (see Chapter 3, Sections 5–7). Here is the SM resource budget of the initial m4 build:

Kernel (sections) Threads / CTA and warp roles Registers / thread (→ allocated / CTA) SMEM rings and bytes / slot CTAs / SM MMA instruction
m4 persistent wgmma kernel (T=128..256, initial build, §9) 576 threads = 18 warps (4 consumer warpgroups = 512 threads + warp 16 weight TMA + warp 17 activation TMA) Cap 96 (18 warps place 5 warps = 160 threads on two SMSPs, billed as 640 threads = 61,440) TMA 3-slot weight ring (35 KiB/slot=32 KiB codes +3 KiB+ 3\text{ KiB} block scales =35,840 B= 35{,}840\text{ B}, derived 2×35 KiB=70 KiB across 2 slots in flight in steady state) + TMA activation ring + subtask table Resident 1 (132 CTAs across GPU) RS wgmma

Only 96 registers per thread: in the Chapter 3, Section 8 example (1 CTA per SM, 2 consumer warpgroups), each consumer thread got 232 registers; here we have 4 consumer warpgroups, and 4×128×232=118,784>65,536 does not fit. As Chapter 4, Section 3 explained, an SM's 65,536 registers are partitioned equally across its 4 SMSPs at 16,384 registers per SMSP: spreading 18 warps across 4 SMSPs places ⌈18/4⌉=5 warps (160 threads, billed as 4×160=640 threads across the 4 SMSPs) on two SMSPs, capping every thread at 16,384/160=65,536/640=102.4, rounded down to a multiple of 8 to land on 96. That differs from dividing the whole-SM pool in Chapter 3, Section 1 by 576 threads alone, which would give 112 registers (which SMSP receives each specific warp is not documented by NVIDIA; the count rule alone determines the 96-register cap). Here are the roles of those initial 18 warps:

CTA warp / lane role Hardware units used What it holds and writes What it waits on (and who waits on it)
Consumer warps 0–15 (4 warpgroups = 512 threads) Registers, ALU / FMA / SFU, Tensor Cores, LSU Decoded weight fragments and accumulators (96 regs/thread); writes gathered p, inter, y, and publishes gate/up subtask completion flags Waits on weight and activation full mbarriers, and arrives on the matching empty mbarriers once a slot is consumed
Warp 16 lane 0 TMA unit Issues W13 / W2 TMA loads into the 3-slot SMEM weight ring following the SMEM subtask table Waits on weight-ring empty mbarrier; consumers wait on the weight full mbarrier it fills
Warp 17 (activation TMA) LSU, TMA unit Polls L2 readiness flags (gather-ready or gate/up completion) and issues TMA loads of p or inter into the SMEM activation ring Waits on activation-ring empty mbarrier and the L2 readiness flag before issuing TMA; consumers wait on the activation full mbarrier it fills

Profiling the initial build of this kernel turned up two problems. First, a runtime branch inside the wgmma pipeline region caused ptxas to serialize wgmma (placing a wait after every HGMMA; see Chapter 6, Section 7 for the mechanism), which we fixed by hoisting that branch out of the region. Second, the entry activation gather originally used scalar writes before we switched it to 16 B16\text{ B} coalesced wide stores (see Chapter 3, Section 2). Prior to those two fixes, the kernel lagged behind the 4-kernel tiled scheme (both fixes were already inside the initial build that saved 22.54 μs22.54\ \mu\text{s} above).

Now look at the byte budget of the weight ring buffer. All 4 consumer warpgroups step through one shared 3-slot weight ring together without cross-warpgroup ping-pong between one group's epilogue and another's MMA (see Chapter 7, Section 7; an experiment on m4 that had two consumer groups alternate epilogue and MMA had to shrink each pair's weight ring from 3 slots to 2 to fit shared memory, ran 1.85 μs1.85\ \mu\text{s} and 2.47 μs2.47\ \mu\text{s} slower at T=128 and T=256—slower on 155–160 of 160 random routing distributions—and was rejected, while whether ping-pong was tested with a 3-slot ring kept intact is not recorded). Each slot holds 256 columns×inner dimension 256 elements: 32 KiB32\text{ KiB} of codewords plus 3 KiB3\text{ KiB} of block scales packed to 6 bits, for 35 KiB35\text{ KiB} (35,840 B35{,}840\text{ B}) in total (see the resource table above). By the rule in Chapter 3, Section 6, while 1 slot is being computed, the remaining N−1 slots are in flight: a 3-slot ring keeps a derived 2×35 KiB=70 KiB across 2 slots in flight, whereas shrinking to 2 slots leaves only 1 slot (35 KiB35\text{ KiB}) in flight—below the roughly 36–40 KiB36\text{–}40\text{ KiB} per SM 95%95\% knee of Chapter 3, Section 6's streaming TMA curve (40 KiB40\text{ KiB} at 1 CTA per SM, with 48 KiB48\text{ KiB} as the 3-slot plateau step at about 98%–99%98\%\text{–}99\%; though 35 KiB35\text{ KiB} already sits above that curve's 32 KiB32\text{ KiB} point at about 92%–95%92\%\text{–}95\%, and here it also overlaps consumer decode/MMA and warp 17's activation TMA; how much each masks the bandwidth dip was not measured). Shrinking the ring to 2 slots alone therefore slows Stage 6 by about 1.2–1.3 μs1.2\text{–}1.3\ \mu\text{s} (1.171.17 and 1.31 μs1.31\ \mu\text{s}) at T=128 and T=256 (see the chart below).

10How Do All 132 Resident CTAs Finish Together?

All four optimizations target tail latency: longest-processing-time-first ordering, atomic producer work claiming, reverse-order down-projection assignment, and tail K-halves splitting.

The duration of a persistent kernel equals the duration of its last-exiting CTA. When full heavy subtasks and light 8-row tail tiles (which still read an entire weight tile, taking about 17 μs17\ \mu\text{s}) are mixed together, whichever CTA lands a heavy task near the end stalls the entire GPU. Each of the four changes below pays off only when there is a tail skew to trim:

First is LPT (Longest Processing Time first scheduling), which we already used in prefill attention in Chapter 7, Section 4: we sort subtasks in descending order of padded token count so heavy subtasks run first and short 8-row subtasks fill the remaining gaps across SMs at the end. The cost is that every CTA runs the sort at entry (reusing Section 6's __ballot_sync + __popc warp-vote code); by T=3,012 and 16,38416{,}384, the speedup disappears (at T=16,384, nearly every tile is already a full tile, so there are no short tail tiles left to pack; see the fourth chart below).

Second is dynamic work claiming (atomic ticket). Take a T=128 routing distribution from the full-layer benchmark: 16 token tiles, each with 32 gate/up subtasks and 16 down-projection subtasks, for 768 subtasks in total. With static assignment, 108 CTAs get 6 subtasks and 24 CTAs get 5. That one-subtask gap comes from integer division and cannot be eliminated. The real saving comes from uneven subtask durations: gate/up and down-projection subtasks take different amounts of time, and so do full tiles versus short 8-row tail tiles. Under static assignment, a CTA that happens to be assigned several slow subtasks in a row drags out the tail, while SMs assigned only 5 subtasks finish early and sit idle. Instead, 3 stages before the current subtask ends, lane 0 of each CTA's weight-producer warp 16 executes one L2 atomic add on a global counter and writes the next subtask into the shared-memory subtask ring. Dynamic work claiming pays off only when single-subtask duration far exceeds claiming overhead and claiming introduces no extra intra-CTA barrier: here a single subtask runs for over ten microseconds, and the claimed subtask is handed to consumers through shared memory without adding a barrier. In Chapter 7, Section 4, by contrast, every claimed 64-key attention tile adds a metadata handoff and a 128-thread intra-CTA barrier, raising per-tile cost by about 10% while breaking the page-table prefetch pipeline, which loses performance.

Third is reverse load-rank assignment, used on Chapter 9's full-layer T=256 static back-and-forth variant (not used in the standalone Stage 6 m4). Under static dealing, the gate/up projection and the down projection originally claimed subtasks in the same alternating sweep order, so the heaviest down-projection subtasks landed on the exact CTAs that had just finished the heaviest gate/up subtasks, stacking two heavy phases onto the same SMs. Recording each CTA's load rank in Phase 0 (which itself adds 1.6–1.8 μs1.6\text{–}1.8\ \mu\text{s} to Phase 0; its initial version lost slightly on T=128 sliding-window at 0.995×0.995\times) lets the down projection assign work in reverse order: the CTAs with the lightest gate/up load claim the heaviest down-projection subtasks first. Per-CTA exit timestamps at T=256 compress the latest CTA exit from 189.4 μs189.4\ \mu\text{s} to 176.3 μs176.3\ \mu\text{s} on sliding-window layers (and from 215.0 μs215.0\ \mu\text{s} to 195.0 μs195.0\ \mu\text{s} on full-attention layers), with the project changelog recording single-layer speedups of 4.2%4.2\% (about 4%4\%) and 0.82%0.82\% (see the third chart and note below).

Fourth is tail K-halves splitting, used in the standalone cooperative m4 at T=128,256 (see Chapter 2, Section 5 for the K-halves mechanism). Two conditions trigger it. First, the final wave of the subtask table has at most 66 subtasks left (no more than half of 132). Second, after sorting by row count in descending order, the fifth-from-last token tile has only 8 rows. Because each token tile produces 16 down-projection subtasks, the last 5 token tiles cover 80 subtasks, which guarantees that all 66 split subtasks at the end of the table are short 8-row tiles. When both conditions hold, we split each of the last 66 subtasks in the table in half along K, creating 2 × 66 half-K tasks that divide evenly across all 132 SMs. Chapter 2, Section 5 splits only the subtasks left over in the final wave; here we also split subtasks from the end of the second-to-last wave to fill out a full set of 66. The first half writes out an FP32 partial sum and sets a readiness flag (release), and the second half waits on that flag (acquire) and adds its half in (see Chapter 2, Section 6 for the ordering rules of cross-SM partial-sum merging). That wait always finishes, for three reasons: all 132 CTAs are resident at once (the single-operator version guarantees this with cooperative launch; see Section 6), every first half sits ahead of its second half in the table, and the CTAs claim subtasks in table order. So the earliest unfinished subtask in the table only ever waits on subtasks that have already finished, never on a later subtask. With the split, the other half of the SMs, which would otherwise sit idle, get work too. The cost is an extra partial-sum matrix and a set of flags; on routing distributions where the guard keeps splitting off, Stage 6 still slows down by 0.75 μs0.75\ \mu\text{s} and 0.52 μs0.52\ \mu\text{s} (exact cause not measured; see the second chart below), so we enable splitting only when both conditions above hold.

The two shipped builds select from these four changes as follows:

  • Standalone Stage 6 m4 (this chapter): Both T=128 and T=256 enable LPT, dynamic atomic claiming, and tail K-halves splitting (without reverse load-rank assignment).
  • Chapter 9 full-layer m4: Splits into two variants—T=128 enables dynamic atomic claiming, while T=256 keeps static back-and-forth dealing with reverse load-rank assignment (neither uses tail K-halves splitting; whether either variant enables LPT is not recorded here).

11Why Do Consumers Stall on Synchronization, and How Do We Move GPU-Scope Releases Off the Critical Path?

When every consumer thread pays its own GPU-scope release, Stage 6 is measured about 93 µs slower; the fix has only one thread per warp issue the release once, and then hands the GPU-scope release to a dedicated warp.

In the persistent wgmma kernel, every time the consumer warpgroups finish a gate/up subtask, they set a completion flag to tell the down-projection phase that this inter tile has been written. Why does a GPU-scope release stall consumers? Because every GPU-scope release (fence.acq_rel.gpu or red.release.gpu) compiles to an instruction sequence containing the device-wide memory barrier MEMBAR.ALL.GPU. L1 caches across SMs are not automatically coherent. On the writer side, each device-wide memory barrier waits for prior global writes to drain to L2: per-CTA timestamps on Chapter 9's full-layer expert kernel measured 0.6–1.3 μs0.6\text{–}1.3\ \mu\text{s} per barrier under load (inside standalone m4, the per-subtask stall was not stamped, and design notes estimated about 400–700 cycles), and multiple threads firing atomic releases at the same L2 counter also queue at one address. On the reader side, once a thread reads the flag with acquire.gpu, subsequent normal loads from that same thread see all prior writes published by the release (Chapter 2, Section 6).

First, here is the single five-step ordered timeline in the final 608-thread build (with exclusive release warp 18) from writing a gate/up inter tile to reading it back via TMA in the down projection:

  1. Consumers write inter: consumer warps 0–15 finish SwiGLU and store inter to the global intermediate matrix.
  2. On-chip CTA-scope release: consumer threads issue only red.release.cta on their warpgroup's shared-memory counter (0 MEMBAR.ALL.GPU).
  3. Dedicated warp polls SMEM counters: lane 0 of dedicated release warp 18 waits via ld.acquire.cta until all 4 warpgroups' SMEM counters reach target.
  4. Single delegated GPU-scope release: warp 18 issues 1 red.release.gpu on the L2 completion flag (isolating the MEMBAR.ALL.GPU stall to warp 18).
  5. Down-projection acquire and proxy-fenced TMA: warp 17 of the down-projection CTA spins on ld.acquire.gpu until that L2 flag reaches target, executes a reader-side fence.proxy.async.global, and issues the TMA load of inter.

The table below traces the six-rung ladder that cuts per-subtask completion releases from 512 down to 1 and arrives at that five-step chain (for __syncwarp alignment in rung 2, see Chapter 4, Section 4):

To publish entry activation readiness and carry out rungs 5–6 above (removing even the last 4 GPU-scope releases from the consumers), m4 makes three changes. Step 1: publishing activation-gather readiness at kernel entry switches to a cross-proxy fence. Normal thread loads and stores travel through the generic proxy, whereas asynchronous TMA and wgmma reads travel through the async proxy; bridging the two takes fence.proxy.async (see Chapter 3, Section 7). On the reader side, the thread issuing TMA executes fence.proxy.async.global after ld.acquire.gpu and before issuing TMA (both when the gate/up projection reads gathered activations and when the down projection reads inter). On the writer side, 16 consumer warps write gathered activations into the global buffer at kernel entry, where previously every thread executed fence.acq_rel.gpu (5 SASS instructions). Now each thread executes only a single-instruction fence.proxy.async.global, and after a CTA barrier, thread 0 issues a single red.release.gpu; by cumulativity (Chapter 2, Section 6), this suffices (see the chart below for the speedup). For safety, we placed this cross-proxy fence on both the writer and reader sides; what happens if the writer-side fence is removed was not measured.

Step 2: consumers perform only an on-chip CTA-scope release and delegate the GPU-scope release to a dedicated release thread. Why did just 4 warpgroup leaders wt == 0 issuing MEMBAR.ALL.GPU still stall all 512 consumers? Because wgmma is warpgroup-wide (sync.aligned; see Chapter 5, Section 4) and all 4 warpgroups step through the shared weight ring together (without cross-warpgroup alternation; see Section 9): stalling wt == 0's warp on MEMBAR.ALL.GPU stalls its entire 128-thread warpgroup and holds back the CTA's Tensor Core pipeline. Instead, each time a consumer thread finishes a subtask, it issues only an on-chip red.release.cta on its warpgroup's shared-memory counter. A dedicated thread waits with ld.acquire.cta until all 4 warpgroup counters reach the target, and then issues a single red.release.gpu on behalf of the CTA for each subtask that needs a flag, in subtask order. Every gate/up subtask needs this flag; among down-projection subtasks, only the first half of a K-halves split from Section 10 needs a readiness flag (which this dedicated thread also publishes), while the remaining down-projection subtasks publish none. When the dedicated thread observes the counters via acquire, it also observes all writes performed by the consumers before their release. When it then issues a GPU-scope release, it publishes all writes it has observed—cumulativity holds across scopes as well (see Chapter 2, Section 6). After warp 17 in the down projection observes the flag via ld.acquire.gpu, it likewise executes a reader-side fence.proxy.async.global before issuing TMA (see Step 1; inter has no writer-side proxy fence). Because all gate/up subtasks precede all down-projection subtasks in the subtask table, by the ordering invariant of Section 10 this wait cannot deadlock either.

Step 3: give the dedicated release thread its own dedicated release warp. Initially, the release thread lived on lane 1 of weight-producer warp 16. Although lane 0 and lane 1 of warp 16 each have their own program counter, the warp issues instructions for only one of their paths at a time (see Chapter 4, Section 4). While lane 1 polls and issues releases, lane 0's path waits for the warp to switch back, so lane 0 cannot issue the next round of weight TMA loads on time (how long each switch takes was not measured separately). We therefore add 1 extra warp per CTA (warp 18, expanding the CTA from 576 to 608 threads) and move the release thread there. At T=256, deleting MEMBAR in place without moving the thread to a separate warp saves much less time (see the chart below), showing that most of the gain comes from no longer blocking lane 0. The cost is 32 extra threads per CTA (608 threads are still billed as 640 threads at the same 96-register per-thread cap from Section 9). Conversely, having this dedicated thread also emit per-phase signals to wake the post-expert RMSNorm kernel early does not pay off: the upper bound of tail latency that could be hidden is only 1.06–2.21 μs1.06\text{–}2.21\ \mu\text{s}, while emitting the signal itself costs 2.2–3.2 μs2.2\text{–}3.2\ \mu\text{s}, so every signaling variant tested ran slower. Here is the before-and-after role split for moving the release thread from warp 16 lane 1 to warp 18 (warps 0–15, warp 16 lane 0, and warp 17 are in Section 9):

CTA warp / lane role Hardware units used What it holds and writes What it waits on (and who waits on it)
Warp 16 lane 1 (before →\to after split) Before: LSU / L2 atomic unit (sharing warp 16's single SIMT stream with lane 0); After: idle in main loop (joins lanes 1–31 zeroing in Section 12) Before: polled SMEM counters and issued red.release.gpu; After: holds no release state Before: stalled lane 0's TMA issue because divergent lanes in one warp issue one branch at a time
Warp 18 lane 0 (608-thread final release warp) Dedicated warp stream, LSU, L2 atomic unit Polls the 4 warpgroups' SMEM counters and issues 1 red.release.gpu per flagged subtask (gate/up and K-halves first half) to the L2 flag Waits via ld.acquire.cta on all 4 SMEM counters; isolates the MEMBAR.ALL.GPU stall to warp 18 alone while warp 17 and K-halves second halves wait on its L2 flag

Why Must Consumers Delay Their Arrival on the Empty Barrier?

Consumers must not arrive on the weight ring's empty barrier before the shared-memory loads from the slot have returned to registers; otherwise the producer's next TMA transfer can overwrite a slot that is still being read (see Chapter 3, Section 7 for the arrival rule). This correctness fix was measured across two distinct builds in the standalone operator benchmark and Chapter 9's full-layer benchmark. In the code, mbarrier.arrive.shared::cta uses the default .release.cta semantics. By the PTX specification, that orders prior shared-memory reads before the arrival only within the generic proxy; it does not cover the next round's TMA write, which goes through the async proxy (Chapter 3, Section 7). On top of that, the compiled arrival instruction did not wait for the scoreboard of preceding shared-memory reads (see Chapter 4, Section 2 for scoreboards). In the isolated standalone Stage 6 build, moving only the weight-ring empty-barrier arrival after the wait on the activation ring's full barrier (Section 9)—with no intra-CTA fence and no change to activation-ring arrivals—reduced observed corruptions from 551 events in about 4.58 million calls down to 0 events in about 4.40 million calls, at a measured cost of slowing Stage 6 by 0.4–1.6 μs0.4\text{–}1.6\ \mu\text{s} (this is a correctness requirement, not an optional optimization).

Waiting on the activation ring's full barrier, however, has no data dependency on the weight reads. In the compiled T=256 full-layer version of Chapter 9, even when the source code placed the decoding instructions that consume the weight registers before the arrival instruction, the compiler still sank them past it. Reordering the source alone was no longer enough at T=256, so Chapter 9's full-layer fix bundled three changes: deferring the weight-ring empty arrival, adding a gated explicit fence.acq_rel.cta before that arrival (always active at T=256; at T=128, unreturned shared-memory loads at arrival sites drop from 16 of 34 down to 0 of 34), and having lane 0 of each consumer warp arrive once on the activation ring's empty barrier. In the T=256 SASS, that fence lowers to an instruction that waits until pending shared-memory loads land in registers, pairing with the deferred arrival to clear unreturned shared-memory loads at arrival sites from 24 of 50 down to 0 of 50; the 3-part bundle slows the 12-case full-layer geometric mean by 0.55%0.55\% (2.0%2.0\% and 1.1%1.1\% on T=256 sliding-window and full-attention layers). Why the default release did not emit that wait instruction was not determined; this is only what the current compiler does (Section 8). Neither the latency delta of the fence alone nor the race count of this merged full-layer build was measured separately.

Empty-barrier WAR-fix build Changes included (isolation) Measured "x of y" count and build owner Measured latency cost
Standalone Stage 6 isolated fix Isolated: moves only weight-ring empty arrive after activation-ring full wait (no fence.acq_rel.cta, no xempty change) Runtime WAR corruptions drop from 551 in 4,580,400 calls on the racy standalone baseline to 0 in 4,395,600 calls on the fixed build (later fence/version-gate builds had no measured failing case) Stage 6 slows by 0.4–1.6 μs0.4\text{–}1.6\ \mu\text{s}

12Before Each CUDA Graph Replay, Who Zeros the Completion Counters?

Maintain even and odd counter arrays alternated by launch index; once a launch gets its ledger index, idle producer threads zero the opposite array for the next launch.

The completion flags in Section 11 are an array of global counters; on every CUDA Graph replay (see Chapter 1, Section 2), the next launch has to see all zeros. Previously, before each launch finished, every CTA ran an exit sequence (one device-wide memory barrier, two CTA barriers, one atomic increment, and several zeroing stores) so the last-exiting CTA could zero the counters. That exit sequence sat right on the critical path of the last-exiting CTA.

To get that cleanup off the tail, we switch to an even-odd ledger (alternating counter array): the counter buffer in device memory is doubled and split into an even ledger and an odd ledger (see Figure 8-11 for indices and buffer sizes). At kernel entry, thread 0 of each CTA runs atom.inc on a global counter to claim a ticket tt (see Chapter 2, Section 8 for atomic ticket numbers). Because that instruction carries the upper limit 2G−1 (where GG is the number of CTAs per launch), hardware wraps the counter back to 0 once it hits the limit, keeping every ticket tt between 00 and 2G−1. Taking ⌊t/G⌋\lfloor t / G \rfloor gives 0 or 1 to pick which ledger this launch uses: each launch claims GG tickets that all land on the same ledger, and the next launch switches to the opposite ledger. Lanes 1–31 of the weight-producer warp are otherwise idle; once Phase 0 bucketing ends and the CTA barrier hands them this launch's ledger index, they zero the inactive ledger for the next launch. The K-halves readiness flags and dynamic work-claiming counter from Section 10 are zeroed together inside the same even-odd ledger.

Why do tickets from two consecutive launches not interleave, and why does zeroing the opposite ledger never collide with the previous or next launch? Two preconditions guarantee this. First, every launch uses the same GG, and all launches execute in order on the same CUDA stream. Second, every expert kernel launch is followed by the post-expert RMSNorm kernel; when that kernel's griddepcontrol.wait returns (see Chapter 1, Section 4; Section 8 of this chapter), the expert kernel before it has finished. The single-operator final expert kernel launches without PDL, so it enters only after the preceding post-expert RMSNorm kernel finishes. By the time it enters, claims tickets, and zeroes the idle ledger, the prior expert kernel launch has exited completely and will not claim another ticket or touch that ledger. Likewise, the next expert kernel launch enters only after the current launch's post-expert RMSNorm kernel finishes, by which time the current launch (zeroing stores included) has already finished.

Deleting the exit sequence from the tail of the kernel removes one device-wide memory barrier and two CTA barriers on the tail path, saving about 0.3 μs0.3\ \mu\text{s} in Stage 6 at T=256 (see the chart below). The cost of the even-odd ledger is 4 KiB4\text{ KiB} of extra device memory while shifting the zeroing stores onto the idle threads of the producer warp; zeroing the counters via a memset node in the CUDA Graph was not measured, and whether any workload loses performance was not measured either.

13What Bottlenecks the Gap Between Subtasks, and Why Does Folding the Scale into the Exponent Save Instructions?

Inside the gate/up subtask-switch gap, the SwiGLU epilogue is issue-slot bound (the down-projection switch has no SwiGLU and its cause was not determined); folding the tensor scale into the exponent argument and denominator cuts instructions from 9 to 7 per element, and the final version switches to a tanh⁡\tanh form to cut them to 6.

Per-CTA timestamps split subtask switches (including the tile epilogue; see Chapter 1, Section 3) into about 1.26 μs1.26\ \mu\text{s} (about 1.3 μs1.3\ \mu\text{s}) per gate/up switch and 1.75 μs1.75\ \mu\text{s} (about 1.8 μs1.8\ \mu\text{s}) per down-projection switch, totaling about 12.7 μs12.7\ \mu\text{s} per CTA (6.1%6.1\% of total kernel runtime). Look first at the gate/up (1.26 μs1.26\ \mu\text{s}) pre-fold 9-instruction (ex2 plus reciprocal) SwiGLU epilogue: a derived SMSP cycle tally gives 4×233=932 issue cycles across the 4 consumer warps on one SMSP (16 consumer warps over 4 SMSPs; Section 9) versus 768 SFU (MUFU) cycles (the per-thread element breakdown behind 233 cycles is not retained on disk, so 932 versus 768 is a derived cycle tally rather than a direct measurement); combined with recompiled source-edit variants on this 9-instruction form—where trading the 2 MUFU ops for roughly 14 extra issue slots per element was flat or slower on every arm—and with the measured speedup from scale folding below, these pieces of evidence support the conclusion that the gate/up epilogue is limited by the issue slot (at most one instruction per cycle; see Chapter 4, Section 1) rather than by SFU throughput (see Chapter 5, Section 1). As for the 1.75 μs1.75\ \mu\text{s} down-projection switch gap: the down projection has no SwiGLU, timestamps show neither stores nor stage-0 data are exposed, and expanding m4's main loop from 2 decoded-weight register buffers (operand A) to a third (wait_group<2>; see Chapter 5, Section 6) moves warpgroup_arrive stalls only from 14.6%14.6\% to 14.3%14.3\% for zero gain—data supply is not the bottleneck, and its cause was not determined.

Here we also answer the question left open in Section 1: why do the gate half and the up-projection half of each expert share a single tensor scale ss? In the original model, the two halves have separate tensor scales sgs_g and sus_u; let r=su/sg. Because SwiGLU is linear in the up projection uu, changing uu's scale from sus_u to the gate scale sgs_g only multiplies the down-projection output yy by a positive constant 1/r=sg/su. And in Step 4 of Section 1, each expert runs its own RMSNorm right after the down projection and before the weighted accumulation across experts. Because RMSNorm divides a vector by its own root mean square, any positive constant c>0 cancels out between numerator and denominator: ignoring the tiny constant ϵ\epsilon, rmsnorm(cz)=rmsnorm(z). Each expert's gate/up projection therefore stores only a single tensor scale s=sg.

Because instruction count is the bottleneck, we use that shared scale ss to fold instructions algebraically. Let dg,dud_g, d_u be the unscaled accumulator values in registers before multiplying by ss (g=sdg, u=sdu), and substitute them into SwiGLU:

silu(g)u=sdg1+e−sdgsdu=dgduk+k⋅2dg⋅(−slog⁡2e),k=1/s2.\mathrm{silu}(g)\,u = \frac{s\,d_g}{1 + e^{-s\,d_g}}\, s\,d_u = \frac{d_g\, d_u}{k + k \cdot 2^{\,d_g \cdot (-s \log_2 e)}},\qquad k = 1/s^2 .

Here both −slog⁡2e-s \log_2 e and kk are constants per expert: multiplying once when computing the exponent argument and evaluating the denominator with a single FFMA(e, k, k) absorbs both multiplications by ss. That cuts the gate/up epilogue from 9 instructions per element down to 7; the build introducing this fold saves about 0.6 μs0.6\ \mu\text{s} in Stage 6 at T=256 (see the chart below). The final version goes one step further and rewrites SwiGLU as silu(g)=g2(1+tanh⁡(g/2)). With K=s2/2 and A=Kdg, each element computes A(1+tanh⁡(dg⋅s/2))⋅du. A single tanh.approx (MUFU.TANH) replaces ex2 plus the reciprocal, dropping the gate/up epilogue to 6 instructions, with only 1 of them on the SFU. This chapter does not list the standalone gain of this step (Chapter 10, Section 8 separately reports recompiled source-edit checks on this later 6-instruction tanh⁡\tanh form: removing MUFU.TANH changed whole-kernel latency by 0.0%0.0\%—with exact build, cell, and replacement unrecorded, which does not by itself separate SFU from issue slots, cause not determined—whereas replacing it with a longer polynomial slowed the kernel by 0.4%0.4\%).

What epilogue scale folding costs is computing two scale constants before each subtask's epilogue (−slog⁡2e-s\log_2 e and kk, or s/2s/2 and K=s2/2 in the tanh⁡\tanh form). This folding pays off only when the epilogue is issue-slot bound: porting it to Chapter 9's full-layer expert kernels (m3 and m4) trims 22%–41%22\%\text{–}41\% of the epilogue instructions yet leaves single-layer latency unchanged (0.999×0.999\times), from which we infer that the epilogue inside the full layer is not issue-slot bound.

14When All 32 Experts Are Busy in Prefill, How Large Should the Grid Be and Who Dispatches Tiles to SMs?

m5 caps the main grid at twice the per-GPU average hit-pair count (~TT) plus alignment padding (with 2 separate overflow kernels in the measured builds, later folded into the main kernels' tail loops), while launching 9,216 ordinary CTAs for the down projection under the hardware block distributor.

Across the workloads in the earlier sections, the mean token count per expert remains under 58; in prefill, T=3,012 and 16,38416{,}384 step past 58 (while T=753 stays below the threshold). The fifth generation (m5) is the grouped GEMM built for prefill, and every optimization below is measured in paired ABBA runs against the immediately preceding version of m5 itself (m4 and m5 were not benchmarked against each other on the same shape). Three names appear throughout this section. The route-alignment kernel reorders hit pairs by expert, pads each expert up to a multiple of the tile height BMBM, and outputs the reordered token table and per-tile expert IDs. gemm1 is the gate and up projection (Step 1 of Section 1, computing SwiGLU in its epilogue). gemm2 is the down projection (Step 3 of Section 1).

Step 1 keeps only tiles belonging to this GPU: the route-alignment kernel outputs tiles only for the 32 local experts on this GPU, filtering out non-local slots at the source. The cost is pre-allocating a fixed-size worst-case buffer in device memory that CUDA Graph reuses on every replay (Chapter 1, Section 2). How much extra memory that buffer takes and when it would lose performance were not measured separately.

Step 2 sets the grid size. Each CUDA Graph replay uses the grid size fixed at capture (or at the last graph update; see Chapter 1, Section 2), while the actual number of local hits is only computed on the GPU during that replay. Originally, the grid was sized for the worst case: all 8 slots of every token landing on this GPU, plus one padding tile for each of the 32 local experts (1,056 tiles in total at T=16,384). Counted under the busiest-GPU benchmark workload at T=16,384, 77% of the tile CTAs exit empty upon entry, implying that only about 1,056×0.23≈243 tiles do actual work (see Figure 8-13). Because every one of the TT tokens picks exactly 8 experts, the total across all 8 GPUs is fixed at 8T8T hit pairs, so the per-GPU mean is always 8T/8=T hit pairs regardless of routing skew (skew raises the busiest GPU above TT and lowers quieter GPUs below TT, without changing the 8-GPU sum or mean). m5 takes twice the average as routing-skew headroom, adds at most 127 padding rows per expert (truncation is enabled only for T>3,012, where m5 uses 128-row tiles; see Section 15), and truncates the grid at ⌈(2T+32×127)/128⌉ tiles: plugging in T=16,384 gives 2×16,384+32×127=36,832, and 36,832/128=287.75, rounding up to 288 tiles—about 20% above the derived ~243 active tiles (Figure 8-13). This factor of 2 is a design choice and was not calibrated against measured worst-case skew.

Should the active tile count ever exceed that cap, the two builds in which the truncation gain was measured handed excess tiles to two separate persistent overflow kernels for gemm1 and gemm2 (costing about 1.25 μs1.25\ \mu\text{s} each when empty, already included in the measured net gain; folding overflow into the tail loops of the two main kernels was a later final-code cleanup whose delta was not measured separately); under the benchmark routing distributions, overflow never occurs, and runtime when overflow actually happens was not measured.

Step 3 decides who dispatches down-projection tiles. Earlier, gemm2 was written as a 264-CTA (2×132) persistent kernel (see Chapter 3, Section 1) that claimed tiles at a fixed stride. At T=16,384, tile completion times vary widely, fixed-stride claiming cannot shift work from slow SMs to fast SMs, and the small successor post-norm kernel sits blocked at griddepcontrol.wait (ACQBULK) until the last gemm2 CTA finishes: the profiler recorded 60.3 μs60.3\ \mu\text{s} of intra-kernel SM idle time. Reverting to a non-persistent grid launches 288×32=9,216 standard CTAs (288 row tiles × 32 column tiles) so the hardware block distributor (see Chapter 2, Section 1) dispatches the next tile to whichever SM frees up first, cutting intra-kernel SM idle time from 60.3 μs60.3\ \mu\text{s} down to 18.6 μs18.6\ \mu\text{s} (by contrast, gemm1 in the next section stays a 264-CTA persistent kernel because it carries ring state across tiles and triggers launch_dependents early once resident, letting gemm2's ordinary CTAs immediately backfill freed SMs as early gemm1 CTAs exit). That wins at T=16,384, where tiles are numerous and completion times vary. It is the exact flip side of the rule in Section 10: when tasks are long and numerous, the hardware block distributor acts as zero-barrier dynamic work claiming. On next-generation Blackwell (sm_100), a CTA already on an SM can ask the hardware block distributor to cancel an unstarted block and take over its block index, combining persistence with hardware load balancing (absent on H200; see Appendix A, Section 5).

15Why Does the Main Loop Split into Two Paths Between T = 753 and T ≥ 3,012?

At T=753, m5 selects 64-row tiles, and per-SM occupancy rises from 2 to 3 CTAs—and 4 CTAs after single-grid fusion; at T≥3,012, it takes the 128-row tile path and sets aside 4 gather warps to gather activations.

What the two paths share is only the outer setup (dispatched in code between T≤1,024 and T>1,024): 4-bit weights are decoded to BF16 in registers and fed directly as operand A of wgmma (RS mode; Section 3), while tokens sit on the operand-B side in shared memory.

At T=753, the tile height is set to 64 (see Section 5 for how tile height relates to MeM_e), and each CTA has 128 threads (1 consumer warpgroup). Instead of threads issuing cp.async to load weights, the consumer warpgroup issues TMA loads directly. Dropping the copy-address registers lowers measured registers per thread from 180 to 151 / 150, allocated as 152 (registers are allocated in multiples of 8; 3×128×152=58,368≤65,536; see Chapter 3, Section 1 and the resource table below), raising per-SM occupancy from 2 to 3 CTAs. A single weight decode is shared across up to 64 hit pairs (any unfilled rows are padding rows from Section 5; see Figure 8-14), speeding up single-layer latency by about 4%4\%. The tradeoff is that consumers issue extra memory-transfer instructions: applying this scheme to 128-row tiles at T=3,012 makes execution slower, and conversely, using 128-row tiles with two consumer warpgroups at T=753—where an expert averages only a few dozen tokens and leaves most of a 128-row tile empty—also runs slower.

Next, for T≤1,024, we apply single-grid fusion: folding gemm1, SwiGLU, and gemm2 into the same 64-row-tiled grid eliminates the tail drain and launch boundary between the two kernels. Registers per thread are capped at 128, fitting 4 resident CTAs per SM (4×128×128=65,536), and the main loop uses only 2 rotating operand-A register buffers with wait_group<1> (see Chapter 5, Section 6). Work assignment uses ticket numbers: each CTA claims a ticket upon entry (see Chapter 2, Section 8), where lower-numbered tickets execute gemm1 tiles first and higher-numbered tickets execute gemm2 tiles. A gemm2 tile acquires the completion counters of the specific gemm1 tiles it needs and starts as soon as they arrive, without waiting for the entire gemm1 phase to finish (see Chapter 2, Section 6 for acquire). Because each CTA claims its ticket via atomic add only after being scheduled onto an SM (see Chapter 2, Sections 6 and 8), the lower-numbered gemm1 tiles are guaranteed to be running already, so higher-numbered gemm2 tiles waiting on those completion counters cannot deadlock.

At T≥3,012, we step the tile height up to 128 (with a K-step of 128), sharing a single weight decode across up to 128 hit pairs. Those 128 token rows are scattered across the original sequence: the reordered token table stores each hit pair's pairpair index (hit-pair index) pair=tok×8+slot, which maps back to token index ⌊pair/8⌋\lfloor pair / 8 \rfloor. Because Hopper's TMA cannot gather rows through an index table (see Chapter 3, Section 5; a row-gather mode is introduced only in the next architecture generation, see Appendix A, Section 4), gemm1 carves out 4 gather warps (128 threads in total, using setmaxnreg to trim the gather warps to 40 registers and raise the consumer warpgroup to 216; see Chapter 3, Section 8) to gather activations row by row with cp.async, calling cp.async.mbarrier.arrive (cp.async.mbarrier.arrive.noinc) to tie cp.async completion onto the same slot full mbarrier as TMA (see Chapter 3, Section 7), while TMA streams contiguous weights into shared memory (see Chapter 3, Section 6 for producer/consumer specialization); after waiting on that full barrier and before wgmma reads X0 and X1, the consumer warpgroup executes a reader-side fence.proxy.async.shared::cta (the gather warps execute no writer-side proxy fence, and whether a reader-side fence alone suffices under the PTX specification was not determined). Shared memory holds three rings—first-half activations X0 (2 slots, K=0..63), second-half activations X1 (3 slots, K=64..127), and weights W (3 slots, packing codewords and block scales into the same TMA slot; see the resource table below for both paths).

Tile startup primes Slots 0..2 of W and 0-based Steps 0 and 1 of activations, filling both slots of the 2-slot X0 ring; starting at the third step (0-based it = 2), every activation gather for it >= 2 must therefore wait first on empty barrier e2[it & 1]—specifically, the third step it = 2 waits on e2[0] until Slot 0 is consumed before overwriting Slot 0, maintaining 2-step lookahead in the main loop. Meanwhile, on full tiles, the two GEMM kernels for T>1,024 pair 4 rotating operand-A register buffers (whereas m4 in Section 13 uses 2) with wait_group<2> so that 2 wgmma commit groups stay in flight concurrently (see Chapter 5, Section 6; partial tiles still use 2 operand-A buffers and wait_group<1>), speeding up single-layer latency by about 5%5\% at T=16,384. What the gather warps cost us is 128 threads and their registers. Skipping the dedicated gather warps and gathering activations in-kernel across wider token tiles disrupts the register budget and ring pipeline, buying zero gain at T=753 and slowing execution at T=3,012. Here is the resource budget for both prefill paths:

Kernel (sections) Threads / CTA and warp roles Registers / thread (→ allocated / CTA) SMEM rings and bytes / slot CTAs / SM MMA instruction
m5 prefill 64-row path (T=753, §15) 128 threads = 4 warps (1 consumer warpgroup, also issuing weight TMA and activation cp.async) Consumer-TMA build: 151 / 150 (allocated as 152 at 8-reg granularity; 3 CTAs = 58,368); fused single-grid final: 128 (4 CTAs = 65,536) Consumer-TMA build: 3-slot TMA weight ring + cp.async activations/scales; fused single-grid final: 2-slot TMA weight ring + 2-slot cp.async activation ring + 2-slot scale ring (bytes/slot not listed) Consumer-TMA build: 2→2 \to 3; fused single-grid final: 4 RS wgmma (2 rotating A-buffers, wait_group<1>)
m5 prefill 128-row path (T≥3,012, §§14–16) gemm1: 1 consumer warpgroup (128 threads) + 4 gather warps (128 threads, row-by-row cp.async activation gather + weight TMA) setmaxnreg rebalanced: gather warps 40, consumer warpgroup 216 3 rings: first-half activations X0 (2 slots, K=0..63) + second-half activations X1 (3 slots, K=64..127) + TMA weight ring W (3 slots, codes + block scales together; bytes/slot not listed) gemm1: 264 persistent CTAs (2 per SM); gemm2: 9,216 ordinary CTAs RS wgmma (4 rotating A-buffers on full tiles, wait_group<2>)

A few other ~1%–2% refinements—merging the per-K-step CTA barriers, keeping gemm1 as a 264-CTA persistent kernel (carrying ring state across tiles and triggering launch_dependents early so gemm2's 9,216 ordinary CTAs backfill freed SMs, pairing with Section 14's non-persistent gemm2), and applying producer/consumer specialization to full gemm2 tiles—are left out here.

Both the 64-row and 128-row paths also apply the tail-tile trimming from Section 5. We measure waste as the average number of rows issued per valid hit pair, where 1.0 means zero wasted rows. The larger MeM_e gets, the smaller the gain: a single layer runs about 4%4\% faster at T=3,012, but only about 1%1\% faster at T=16,384 (see the chart below). In the implementation, a single scalar load plus a uniform branch (a conditional jump where all 32 lanes of the warp take the same path) checks whether every row from row rr onward is padding; that keeps the ring-slot counters in uniform registers (UR; see Chapter 7, Section 7). Switching to an intra-CTA reduction forces those counters back into per-thread general-purpose registers and adds 34 instructions per K-step.

16Why Is the Prefill gemm1 Epilogue Slowed Down by Type Conversion?

Scalar FP32-to-BF16 conversion (F2F) shares the SFU pipeline with MUFU.EX2; replacing it with paired packed rounding (F2FP) moves the conversion off the SFU and nearly halves kernel-wide SFU utilization.

For T>1,024, SwiGLU in gemm1's epilogue (see Chapter 1, Section 3) computes exponentials (MUFU.EX2). Before SwiGLU, the gate and up accumulator values are rounded to BF16 and converted back to FP32. That intermediate rounding carries over the numerical convention of the preceding kernel version, whereas the reference implementation stays in FP32 throughout without rounding (removing this BF16 round trip directly was not measured). Originally, each value took one scalar conversion (F2F). On Hopper, F2F and MUFU.EX2 queue on the same SFU pipeline (the SFU accepts only 1 warp instruction every 8 cycles; see Chapter 5, Section 1 for pipeline definitions), stretching out the epilogue window.

To fix this, we call cvt.rn.bf16x2.f32, reshaping the in-register dataflow to "two FP32 accumulators →\to F2FP rounds and packs them into one BF16x2 pair in a 32-bit register →\to shift and bitwise-AND instructions unpack them back into two FP32 values →\to feed into SwiGLU": cvt.rn.bf16x2.f32 compiles to F2FP (paired packed conversion) off the SFU, at the cost of a few extra shift and bitwise-AND ALU instructions to unpack the pair back to two FP32 values. Replacing most of the scalar conversions in the epilogue with paired packed conversions cuts the profiler's kernel-wide average SFU utilization on gemm1 (T=16,384 sliding-window) from 5.74%5.74\% down to 3.08%3.08\%, while whole-kernel SM cycles drop by only 0.6%0.6\% (from 4.506 M4.506\text{ M} to 4.479 M4.479\text{ M}, leaving the epilogue latency-bound afterward); the build combining F2FP with a barrier merge improves the overall 8-case prefill score by 0.33%0.33\% (0.23%–0.44%0.23\%\text{–}0.44\%, see the chart below), about 3× the profiler's SM-cycle drop (we infer that higher unlocked SM boost clocks at lower instruction power also contribute, though this was not measured separately; see Chapter 10, Section 1 for NCU clock locking versus unlocked event-timed SM clocks). Kernel-wide average SFU utilization is only a few percent because the main matrix-multiplication loop does not use the SFU, so the SFU is busy only during the epilogue; when the SFU is not the bottleneck in the epilogue, this change buys no speedup (it was not measured on the decode and verify kernels).

Stage 6 Routed-Expert Evolution Chain (m0 → m5)

Section 1 laid out how we dispatch across the three kernel families by TT; here is the complete evolution chain from start to finish (see the charts below for step-by-step latency):

  • m0: Per-expert loop that decompresses weights to FP32 in HBM and reads them back (Section 2; m0 in the 60-layer total chart).
  • m1: Single grouped-GEMM launch per projection that decodes 4-bit weights in registers and reads them only once (m1a, ~80× faster), followed by gate/up row interleaving, branchless decoding, and PDL (Section 2; m1 in the 60-layer total chart).
  • m2: Two bundled whole-kernel rewrites around pipelined wgmma tiling (dropping the 60-layer total from 21,369.2021{,}369.20 through 17,362.6017{,}362.60 to 7,944.29 μs7{,}944.29\ \mu\text{s}, not isolated, accounting for ~2.69× of the ~3.18× m1 → m2 speedup), followed by Split-K, multi-slot weight rings, left-shift offloading, pinned occupancy, and tail-tile trimming adding the last ~1.18× down to 6,718.85 μs6{,}718.85\ \mu\text{s}—running ~2.0× faster than the baseline SGLang implementation (Sections 3–5; m2 in the 60-layer total chart).
  • m3 (for T≤32): Combines the persistent kernel, 16-token segments, two PDL-chained kernels, and entry staggering (see Sections 6–7; the two compiler fixes in Section 8 were measured only on the standalone Stage 6 operator).
  • m4 (for T=128..256): Combines the persistent wgmma kernel (saving about 22 μs22\ \mu\text{s} in Stage 6 at T=256), tail balancing, the even-odd ledger, and epilogue scale folding, making the 60-layer total of the m3 + m4 version ~2.5× faster than the baseline (see Sections 9–13; this factor excludes the dedicated release thread and exclusive release warp).
  • m5 (for prefill T=753,3,012,16,384): Grouped GEMM for prefill; at the grid-truncation step, the two GEMMs total 4,207 μs4{,}207\ \mu\text{s} (about 2.4%2.4\% faster than before truncation; see Sections 14–16 for the other changes).

Takeaway: An expert kernel has to adapt to the number of tokens MeM_e routed to each expert: below about 58, strip away HBM round trips, synchronization waits, and launch overhead; above it, keep the Tensor Cores and instruction pipelines fed.

Next chapter's question: Taken one by one, the dense projections of Stages 1, 3, 5, and 7 (Chapter 6), paged attention in Stage 2 (Chapter 7), and routed experts in Stage 6 (this chapter) have all been pushed fast. Yet when we wire all 12 kernels of the 8 stages back into a single layer on one GPU and replay them inside one CUDA Graph (starting point l0), the T=1 sliding-window layer measures 71.4 μs71.4\ \mu\text{s}—still about 26 μs26\ \mu\text{s} above the 40.0 μs40.0\ \mu\text{s} reference floor after subtracting about 5.4 μs5.4\ \mu\text{s} of graph-replay overhead. Where inside the layer does that time leak away? How much can dual-stream scheduling, cross-kernel and cluster reductions, and end-to-end PDL handoffs claw back—and what if we fused the entire layer into one persistent megakernel? → Chapter 9

Chapter 9

When Scheduling a Single Layer's Kernels Across 132 SMs, Where Does the Time Above the Lower Bound Go, and How Much Can Scheduling and Kernel Handoffs Recover?
