The previous chapter left us with one question: how do we connect dense projections, normalizations, and gated residuals with attention and experts into a single-layer pipeline? Back in Primer 2, we drew all eight stages on a single GPU as a directed acyclic graph (DAG; see Primer 2, Section 3 and Figure P2-3) and worked out the layer's lower bound (counting dense weights in BF16; see Primer 2, Sections 1, 3, and 4). Here we call the task-specified single-layer lower bound for each scenario the reference bound: 40.0 µs for the T=1 sliding-window layer, 44.2 µs for the T=1 full-attention layer, and 62.3 µs and 66.4 µs for the T=8 sliding-window and full-attention layers. Note that this reference bound is not a lower bound on the bytes that any variant actually reads. The first eight chapters already made each stage's kernel fast on its own; yet when we string those kernels together along the DAG and replay them as a CUDA Graph (see Chapter 1, Section 2), the baseline l0 still takes 71.4 µs on the T=1 sliding-window layer. In this chapter we chase a single question: where does the time above the reference bound go, and how much of it can scheduling and handoffs win back?

Direct answer up front: after subtracting ~5.4 µs of graph replay, baseline l0 (71.39 µs) sits ~26 µs above the 40.0 µs reference bound; intra-layer scheduling, cross-kernel reductions, and safe PDL handoffs recover ~3.6 µs to bring the T=1 sliding-window layer down to the race-free final 67.79 µs, still ~22 µs above the reference bound. At most about 12.5 µs of that ~22 µs is in handoff gaps and the tail, and the remaining ~10 µs is the kernel bodies' excess over the bound (50.02 − 40.0 µs, derived): on an earlier build (68.22 µs; the final build was not decomposed), per-CTA timestamps cap handoff gaps (6.41 µs) plus tails (6.12 µs) at ~12.5 µs while over 70% (50.02/68.22≈73%) of the layer sits in the sum of kernel main bodies (50.02 µs), and neither model estimates nor synthetic experiments support a whole-layer persistent megakernel (no complete whole-layer megakernel was built; see Section 6).

1Baseline l0: How Does a Single Layer's DAG Map to a Sequence of Kernels and Two CUDA Streams, and Where Does the Time Go?

l0 lowers the 8-stage DAG onto 12 kernels—10 on the main stream and 2 on the side stream (using the 68 idle SMs left while pooler occupies 64 SMs); after subtracting ~5.4 µs of CUDA Graph replay overhead, its ~26 µs excess above the 40.0 µs reference bound leaks out inside the kernels and their handoffs (brought down to 67.79 µs in the final version, with main bodies summing to 50.02 µs on the earlier 68.22 µs build; three-part definition in Section 6).

First, let's be clear about scope: when we say a single layer in this chapter, we mean the eight stages running on a single GPU. A real 8-GPU run also performs three cross-GPU collectives inside every layer: an all-reduce after Stage 3 o, an all-reduce after Stage 6, and—when T≤8—an all-gather of columns across GPUs after Stage 7 (see Primer 2, Section 2). None of the single-layer measurements in this chapter include those cross-GPU collectives.

To see where a single layer spends its time, we first need the critical path: the longest chain of "must wait for the previous step to finish" dependency edges from layer entry to layer exit. Single-layer latency is just the length of that critical path plus one CUDA Graph replay overhead (~5.4 µs, as we will see shortly). As long as side-stream kernels use only the SMs and bandwidth left idle by the main chain and finish before the join point, they add nothing to single-layer latency. Keep in mind, though, that all 132 SMs and HBM bandwidth are shared across the entire GPU—the moment a side-stream kernel competes with the main chain for SMs or bandwidth, it stretches the critical path instead (see Section 7).

Each step below is measured by switching later sections' changes off one section at a time; throughout this chapter, final (Fixed) means l3 plus Section 5's Fix (a), measured on a patched copy, whereas the submitted file in the repository remains l3 (see the evolution chain at the end of the chapter for full variant details).

On the T=1 sliding-window layer, the baseline l0 already fuses adjacent small steps and turns on PDL (see Chapter 1, Section 4; we complete the remaining edges in Section 4) across part of the chain. Running the layer launches 12 kernels in total: 10 on the main CUDA stream and 2 on a second stream, in the order shown in Figure 9-1 below. Stage 3 and Stage 8 each end with a boundary kernel that updates the FP32 residual stream stream and runs the next stage's RMSNorm across all 8,192 columns (see Primer 2, Section 2 for the formula). Stage 5 normalization also sits in its own standalone kernel in l0 (we split it away in Section 3). Also, attention merge remains a separate kernel in this chain rather than using the fused version from Chapter 7, Section 12.

Laying out all 12 kernels that l0 launches on the T=1 sliding-window layer shows each kernel's stream, grid size, shared memory per CTA, and main bytes read:

# Stage and kernel CUDA stream CTAs launched SMEM / CTA Main weight / KV bytes read
1 Stage 1 qkv_gate Main CUDA stream 576 0 B (dynamic) 28.4 MB (12-bit W_qkv_gate, plus 16 KiB input)
2 Stage 2 attention split-KV Main CUDA stream 64 not recorded 0.52 MB (FP8 KV cache for 2,048 sliding-window tokens)
3 Stage 2 attention merge Main CUDA stream 16 not recorded L2 workspace partial outputs (no large weight matrix)
4 Stage 3 o projection Main CUDA stream 1,024 not recorded 16.8 MB (16-bit W_o)
5 Stage 3 boundary kernel Main CUDA stream (records fork event) 8 (1 GPC cluster; thread block clusters in Chapter 7, Section 12) not recorded stream_in 32 KiB + 4 parameter vectors 96 KiB (plus a 16 KiB)
6 Stage 5 pooler Main CUDA stream 64 (1 per SM) 207,720 B (~203 KiB) 50.4 MB (12-bit W_pooler)
7 Stage 5 standalone pre_expert_norm Main CUDA stream 1 (8 warps) not recorded Activation x_pool 8 KiB + parameter vector 8 KiB
8 Stage 6 experts Main CUDA stream (waits on join event) 132 (1 per SM) 120,896 B (~118 KiB) ~2 local experts in 4-bit format, ~56.6 MB (~53 MB for ~1.87 experts in reference bound)
9 Stage 7 unpooler slice Main CUDA stream 128 (1 per SM) not recorded 8.4 MB (16-bit W_unpooler 1,024-row slice on this GPU)
10 Stage 8 boundary kernel Main CUDA stream 8 (1 GPC cluster; thread block clusters in Chapter 7, Section 12) not recorded Intra-layer activations 34 KiB + 4 parameter vectors 96 KiB (writes 48 KiB)
11 Stage 4 router Side stream (waits on fork event) 256 (256 threads / CTA) not recorded (CTAs / SM not measured) 8.4 MB (8.39 MB FP32 W_router)
12 Stage 4 Top-8 Side stream (records join event) 1 (1 warp) not recorded router scores and bias (writes topk_ids 32 B, topk_weights 32 B)

Stage 3's output h forks into two branches here. Whereas a single CUDA stream runs its kernels in launch order (see Primer 3, Section 4 and Chapter 1, Section 1), the GPU front end maintains multiple independent hardware work queues (historically called Hyper-Q) feeding the hardware block dispatcher so independent kernels on different streams can dispatch onto free SMs concurrently. We call the second CUDA stream the side stream, and use it to launch kernels that do not depend on the current step of the main CUDA stream. The two streams synchronize across streams through CUDA event (inter-stream event) markers (single-stream event timing was introduced in Primer 3, Section 5)—an event recorded on one stream that the other stream waits for. After the Stage 3 boundary kernel finishes, the main stream records an event. Once the side stream sees that event, it runs router to score all 256 experts, then runs the Top-8 kernel: it picks the top 8 experts by their biased scores, normalizes their weights using those 8 experts' unbiased scores, writes out topk_ids and topk_weights, and records a second event. Back on the main stream, the experts kernel waits for that side-stream event before reading the routing results.

Why does this pay off at T=1? At T=1, pooler on the main stream partitions its 4,096 output columns at 64 columns per CTA to launch only 4,096/64=64 CTAs, and each CTA takes 207,720 B (about 203 KiB) of shared memory so only 1 CTA can reside per SM (see Chapter 3, Section 1), leaving 68 of the 132 SMs (see Primer 3, Section 1) idle. While pooler streams its weights (~50 MB in 12-bit format), router (256 CTAs) and Top-8 (1 CTA) on the side stream can use those 68 idle SMs (how many CTAs reside per SM, whether they fit all at once, and which SMs they actually land on were not measured).

Of course, the side stream has a price: each layer records two extra events, and kernels from both streams must be able to co-reside on the chip (see Chapter 3, Section 1); once the main kernel fills all 132 SMs, side-stream kernels can only steal SMs from it (see Section 7). Section 4 presents the measured timeline in which the side branch completes ahead of pooler; how much time we would lose by disabling the side stream was not measured.

One measurement boundary first: we did not measure a per-CTA breakdown of how many microseconds each of the four places below holds in l0 (Section 6's breakdown of main bodies, gaps, and tails comes from a separate, earlier 68.22 µs build with PDL enabled). Trace the evolution chain and that extra ~26 µs leaks out in four places: first, projections that read too many bytes or launch grids too small to fill a wave (Section 2); second, a standalone kernel that exists only to sum across a full row, plus a device-wide memory barrier that waits for all of a thread's prior writes to reach L2 (see Chapter 8, Section 11 and Section 3 of this chapter); third, the handoffs between kernels (Sections 4–5); and fourth, each kernel's main body together with its slowest-CTA tail duration (Section 6).

Every step in this chapter's evolution chain is measured the same way (see Primer 3, Section 5): we record the single layer into a CUDA Graph, flush L2 before each replay, time a full-graph replay with CUDA events, and take the median. The sliding-window layer attends over 2,048 historical tokens and the full-attention layer over 80,000 historical tokens, matching the reference bounds in Primer 2, Section 4. Note that every measured number includes ~5.4 µs of CUDA Graph replay overhead—even a graph with just 1 empty kernel takes that long to replay. Production serving records all 62 layers into a single graph so the whole model amortizes that cost, whereas the reference bound leaves it out. By the way, the 4.96 µs figure cited in Chapter 6 came from a separate batch of empty-graph replay measurements of the same class of overhead; the two numbers come from different experiments, and the cause of the difference was not determined.

The noise band for the single-layer evolution chain is ~0.5 µs, and the paired ABBA noise band for multi-token and prefill runs is ~0.5%; whenever a delta is smaller than the noise band, we report it as "within the noise band" (defined in Chapter 4, Section 6 and Chapter 7, Section 4).

Following the four leak sites listed at the start of this section, let's plug the leaks inside the projections first.

2l0 → l1: Once Projection Kernels Are Placed Inside a Single Layer, How Can They Read the Fewest Bytes and Fill All 132 SMs?

Because projections are bandwidth-bound, latency equals bytes read divided by achieved bandwidth; l1 reduces bytes read and sizes small-batch grids to fill a full wave.

Let's start with the 12-bit weight layout and decoding at T=1. To read fewer bytes, we use 12-bit weights, which take 3/43/4 the bytes of 16-bit weights (see Chapter 6, Section 1); to saturate bandwidth, we put enough SMs to work and keep enough bytes in flight on each SM (see Chapter 2, Section 3). At T=1 in l0, qkv_gate and pooler already read 12-bit weights (while the unpooler slice stays at 16-bit), yet three things in the old version hold them back: a 13-instruction decoder, a non-step-major pooler weight-plane layout without evict_first L2 residency hints, and late preparation of escaped-weight corrections. Variant l1 fixes all three: first, it switches to the 9-instruction decoder from Chapter 6, Section 2; second, it reorders the pooler weight planes to step-major layout so all 64 CTAs read a contiguous address range at every KK-step, while tagging streaming weight loads with the evict_first L2 residency hint (see Chapter 2, Section 4); and third, it prepares the escaped-weight correction operands ahead of the final KK-step. The bytes read stay the same, and the time drops (the share of each of the three changes was not measured separately).

Now look at SM occupancy and 12-bit weights at T=8. When T≤8, each GPU computes only its own 1,024 output columns of unpooler, a [1024, 4096][1024,\ 4096] weight slice that takes 8.4 MB in 16-bit format (see Primer 2, Section 2). At T=8, l0 still leaves this unpooler slice in 16-bit format: it cuts the 1,024 rows into 16 tiles of 64 rows each and splits KK into 4 segments, launching only 16×4=64 CTAs in total (Figure 9-2), so 68 SMs sit idle (the exact bottleneck of this about 4–6 µs short kernel was not measured; dividing weight bytes by the 6.11 µs profiler time gives about 1.4 TB/s, with the profiling mode—whether it includes pre-wait residency—not retained on disk). In l1, we compress this weight slice to 12-bit format (shrinking it from 8.4 MB to 6.3 MB) and split KK into 8 segments instead, so 128 CTAs fill 128 SMs; the Stage 8 boundary kernel then sums the 8 FP32 partial sums for each output directly, without needing an extra reduction kernel launch (for Split-K, see Chapter 2, Section 5).

On qkv_gate at T=8, baseline l0 launches 144 CTAs at 2 CTAs per SM and already fits in a single wave; l1's 12-bit kernel fits only 1 CTA per SM, so 144 CTAs would spill into two waves and l1 launches 108 CTAs instead to stay in one wave. Specifically, l0 uses 16-bit weights (37.75 MB) across 36 row tiles and 4 KK-splits (36×1×4=144 CTAs) at 81,936 B (about 80 KiB) of shared memory per CTA, allowing 2 resident CTAs per SM; l1 compresses to 12-bit weights (28.4 MB, with the same grid and register math as Chapter 6, Section 8), slicing the 2,304 output rows into 36 tiles of 64 rows each and 3 KK-splits to launch 36×3=108 CTAs (leaving 24 SMs idle) rather than spilling 144>132 into a 12-CTA tail wave (see Chapter 2, Section 1).

In single-GPU benchmarks, Stage 8 at T=8 also ships bundled in the same switch as the 128-CTA 12-bit unpooler with a zero-column shortcut: Stage 3 precomputes and saves the sum of squares of the 7,168 zero columns so Stage 8 runs 8×8=64 non-cluster CTAs (8 per row, without forming an 8-CTA cluster or waiting across peer CTAs), whose isolated gain is ~0 and which does not apply on 8 GPUs. In the Stage 8 boundary kernel, the residual stream update is stream_out=α2⊙stream_mid+β2⊙RMSNorm(f⊙(1+wpost_ffn)) (see Primer 2, Section 2 for the formula). In a single-GPU benchmark, the 7,168 output columns of ff owned by the other 7 GPUs are identically 0, so on those columns stream_out\mathrm{stream\_out} is just α2⊙stream_mid and does not depend on the experts or unpooler. Because α2\alpha_2 is a fixed vector, the Stage 3 boundary kernel can compute and store the sum of squares for those columns on the spot while writing stream_mid\mathrm{stream\_mid}; the Stage 8 boundary kernel then sums the squares across only this GPU's 1,024 columns and adds the value stored at Stage 3 to finish the RMSNorm without forming an 8-CTA cluster. In an ablation on another baseline, enabling only the zero-column shortcut plus the cluster-free Stage 8 kernel gave paired ratios of 0.9995×0.9995\times and 1.0021×1.0021\times (the two items in that switch were not re-ablated apart inside l0 → l1), showing that the T=8 gain comes mainly from the 128-CTA 12-bit unpooler; in a real 8-GPU run, an all-gather after Stage 7 first assembles all 8 GPUs' columns into 8,192 non-zero columns, so you cannot take this shortcut.

Across all four scenarios, we get the biggest saving at T=8 (about 3.5 µs); looking at the sliced unpooler kernel on its own, switching to 12-bit weights and expanding the grid to 128 CTAs makes it about 1.7 µs faster (the separate contributions of cutting 2.1 MB with 12-bit weights versus expanding from 64 to 128 CTAs were not measured separately; see the two charts below).

What is the price of these changes? Unpacking every 8 weights costs each thread 9 integer instructions, occupying about 18 pipeline cycles (14 ALU cycles plus 4 FMA cycles in group 0, and about 15 ALU plus about 3 FMA cycles on average across the kernel), plus a side-table lookup to patch escaped weights (see Chapter 6, Section 2). At T=8, the 8-way Split-K first writes out 8×8×1,024×4 B=262,144 B≈0.26 MB of FP32 partial sums once, and in the cluster-free Stage 8 boundary kernel all 8 CTAs of each row re-read all 8 partials of their row to compute the row normalization factor, reading 8×0.26 MB≈2.1 MB (2 MiB) in total—because 0.26 MB is tiny next to the 60 MiB L2 cache, we infer that the re-reads hit in L2, so compared with l0's 4-way split (about 0.13 MB written and read), HBM sees only about 0.13 MB of extra writes, far less than the 2.1 MB of weights saved. Once T≥128, 12-bit weights decoded by 1 warpgroup start to lose. Every projection then falls back to 16-bit weights, except the 2-warpgroup 12-bit unpooler at T=128 (see Chapter 6, Section 4). The 1,024-column slice is used only for T≤8 (see Primer 2, Section 2). (For how TMA ring-buffer depth trades off at larger batch sizes, see Section 7.)

Now that we have plugged the leaks inside the projections, the next piece of overhead sits right between two projections: every cross-CTA full-row reduction for RMSNorm.

3l1 → l2: How Can a Cross-CTA Full-Row Reduction Avoid Paying for an Extra Kernel or a Device-Wide Memory Barrier?

When a row is split across multiple CTAs, no single CTA sees the full-row sum: we either use the linearity of matrix multiplication to split the normalization across the preceding and succeeding kernels (Modes 1–2), or write partial sums directly into peer shared memory inside an 8-CTA GPC cluster — where l1's release cluster barrier also drains prior global stream writes to L2 across incoherent per-SM L1s, while l2 switches to st.async plus a local mbarrier waiting only for 32 B in shared memory (see "Boundary Kernels" below for Mode 3's two row reductions and instruction details).

Pre-Expert RMSNorm: Cross-Kernel Full-Row Reduction

Setting aside the full-row normalizations in the Stage 3 and Stage 8 boundary kernels, every other normalization in the layer has already been folded into a neighboring kernel—except Stage 5 pre-expert RMSNorm (pre_expert_norm) (see Primer 2, Section 2; for Q/K and gated-output normalizations see Chapter 7, Sections 11–12, and for intra-expert normalizations see Chapter 8, Section 1). At T=1, it still sits in a standalone kernel in l0 and l1. At T=8, all versions already use the split we are about to describe: the pooler epilogue multiplies by the column gain and accumulates the sum of squares, leaving the per-row scale factor to be multiplied later without launching a standalone kernel.

Let xpool=hWpooler⊤ be the result before Stage 5 normalization, with shape xpool:[T,4096]BF16\shape{x_{\mathrm{pool}}}{T,\;4096}{BF16}; the reciprocal root mean square of row mm is

rm=114096∑kxpool[m,k]2+10−5r_m = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\tfrac{1}{4096}\sum_k x_{\mathrm{pool}}[m,k]^2 + 10^{-5}}}

and the normalized output is

p[m,k]=rm⋅xpool[m,k]⋅(1+wk)p[m,k] = r_m \cdot x_{\mathrm{pool}}[m,k] \cdot (1 + w_k)

The model stores normalization weights as offsets relative to 1, so the applied gain is 1+wk; the 10−510^{-5} term in the denominator prevents division by zero.

Why can't pooler finish computing p[m,k]p[m,k] directly inside its own epilogue? Because pooler partitions the 4,096 output columns across different CTAs: each CTA holds only its own column segment of row mm, and no single CTA can see the full-row sum of squares ∑kxpool[m,k]2\sum_k x_{\mathrm{pool}}[m,k]^2 across all 4,096 columns.

The way out comes from the linearity of matrix multiplication under row scaling: (rmxm)W⊤=rm(xmW⊤): scaling a row before matrix multiplication is equivalent to multiplying by the matrix first and scaling the resulting row afterward. Here xmx_m is row mm of xpoolx_{\mathrm{pool}} after multiplying by the column gain 1+w, and WW is the experts up-projection weight matrix before SwiGLU. Look at the two factors in p[m,k]p[m,k]. The gain 1+wk depends only on the column index kk, and each pooler CTA already has the finished values for the columns it computes, so pooler can multiply by 1+wk right in its output epilogue (see Chapter 1, Section 3). Meanwhile, rmr_m depends only on the row index mm, so the experts kernel can run its entire KK loop first and then multiply its full-row FP32 accumulators (see Chapter 5, Section 7) by rmr_m.

We have to do this scaling before SwiGLU, because silu(ra)≠rsilu(a) (for SwiGLU, see Primer 2, Section 2). In exact arithmetic the two orders give the exact same result; in BF16 the rounding point moves from pp to xpool⋅(1+wk), and the single-layer output still passes verification.

At T=1 (Figure 9-3 Mode 1), each pooler CTA writes out xpool⋅(1+w) and at the same time uses one atomic add (see Chapter 2, Section 6) to add its column segment's partial sum of squares into a single shared FP32 slot in global memory; once the PDL wait call returns, the experts kernel reads that slot and multiplies by rmr_m. We keep that slot in FP32 both because scalar BF16 atomic adds compile down to a slow compare-and-swap retry loop as written in Chapter 6, Section 8's kernel, and because summing squares in FP32 preserves more precision. We zero the slot after the wait call of the Stage 3 boundary kernel (by which time the previous round's experts has already finished), and we place the atomic add after the wait call of pooler, so the order is always: previous read complete → zero → current accumulation (see Chapter 1, Section 4). That takes one kernel and the handoff in front of it off the critical path, cutting single-layer kernel launches from 12 down to 11.

What this split saves changes with the token count TT. At T=1, it saves one kernel handoff. By T=3,012 (Figure 9-3 Mode 2), what it saves is an HBM round trip: a standalone normalization kernel has to read 24.7 MB of xpoolx_{\mathrm{pool}} and write it back out (a 49.3 MB round trip, with a 10.3 µs lower bound at 4.8 TB/s) and measures about 14 µs (see the chart below), from which we infer that those bytes went to HBM. Once we split the normalization, pooler divides the 4,096 columns into 16 column segments and each segment writes one partial sum of squares per row—producing a small partial-sum table rs:[T,16]FP32\shape{\mathrm{rs}}{T,\;16}{FP32} that totals just 0.39 MB across the write and the read; isolated on the prefill baseline, this makes the T=3,012 sliding-window and full-attention single layers 0.34% and 0.19% faster.

At intermediate token counts, the benefit is tiny or even negative: the standalone kernel already runs in just ~3.7 µs at T=753, while splitting at T=128 and 256 runs 0.5%–1.0% slower, so both of those settings retain the standalone kernel.

The price of splitting is that the pooler epilogue does one extra atomic add (or writes a 0.19 MB partial-sum table), and the experts kernel does one extra load plus a full-row scaling step. And because atomic-add arrival order is not fixed, the least significant bits of the output may change from run to run (see Chapter 2, Section 8).

Boundary Kernels: Intra-Cluster Full-Row Reduction

Now look at the Stage 3 and Stage 8 boundary kernels. Every boundary kernel runs two consecutive full-row RMSNorm reductions: the first normalizes the branch output just produced (a at Stage 3, or f multiplied by 1+wpost_ffn at Stage 8) to update the FP32 residual stream stream, and the second normalizes the updated stream across the full row to produce the next stage's input (h at Stage 3, or the next layer's xl+1x_{l+1} at Stage 8). In both boundary kernels at T=1 and the Stage 3 boundary kernel at T=8 (plus Stage 8 at T=8 in l0; from l1 onward, Stage 8 at T=8 already takes Section 2's single-GPU zero-column shortcut across 64 non-cluster CTAs), the 8,192 columns of each row are split across the 8 CTAs of one thread block cluster, 1,024 columns per CTA (see Chapter 7, Section 12), and every CTA needs the partial sums of squares from the other 7. Both l1 and l2 (Figure 9-3 Mode 3) write those partial sums straight into peer shared memory; they differ only in what primitive waits for them:

Step Who writes what where, and what each CTA waits for Synchronization scope and measured cost
Per-rank slot write (same in l1 and l2) Rank r (0..7) writes its 4 B FP32 partial sum of squares into slot r of all 8 CTAs (7 peers + 1 self = 32 B received per CTA), then sums slots 0..7 in fixed 0..7 order Direct intra-cluster shared-memory writes; the rank read, first address translation, and 8-slot ordered sum are identical in both variants, and their standalone cost was not measured
How l1 waits Plain cluster-shared store followed by a release/acquire cluster barrier on the GPC's hardware cluster barrier unit Hardware cluster barrier, also waiting for global writes to reach L2
How l2 waits Writes via st.async (see Chapter 7, Section 12), while each receiver waits on a local mbarrier (see Chapter 3, Section 7) for 8 partial sums = 32 B Waits only for the 32 B in shared memory without waiting for global stream writes to reach L2 (the next kernel sees stream through the inter-kernel handoff); saves 0.86–0.99 µs per call in an isolated boundary microbenchmark (whose timed shape, source text, and WAR-fix state were not recorded, so which edits it timed was not verified, the device-wide fence share was not measured, and it cannot be multiplied by 2 to account for the 1.84 µs layer step)

Why does l1's cluster barrier (PTX barrier.cluster.arrive / .wait, SASS UCGABAR_ARV / UCGABAR_WAIT; full SASS sequence in Appendix B, Quick Reference 3, Item 39) also wait for global writes to reach L2? Because the 8 CTAs sit in the same GPC but may land on different SMs (CUDA guarantees only the same GPC, see Chapter 7, Section 12; per-SM L1 caches are incoherent and global data becomes coherent only at L2, see Chapter 2, Section 6), so this release barrier waits for all 8 peers and for earlier global stream writes to reach L2 (switching Stage 8 at T=8 to Section 2's cluster-free zero-column shortcut removed Stage 8's cluster barrier as well). On H200, it compiles the device-wide memory-barrier sequence MEMBAR.ALL.GPU + ERRBAR + CGAERRBAR before arrival (the execution units and hardware details of the hardware error-barrier instructions ERRBAR and CGAERRBAR are unpublished); when the profiler samples warp stall reasons at fixed cycle intervals (see Chapter 10, Section 7), 36%–46% of non-issued samples on the T=16 2-CTA boundary kernels stall on this ERRBAR wait (the 8-CTA cluster at T≤8 was not sampled separately).

At the instruction level, the four steps compare across l1 and l2 as follows:

Step (purpose) l1 l2
Rank read (find my peer number) Find this CTA's peer number 0..7 in the 8-CTA cluster: mov.u32 r, %cluster_ctarank (unlike Chapter 7, Section 12 where the grid width matched the cluster width so blockIdx gave the rank directly, Stage 3 at T=8 launches 64 CTAs across 8 clusters and must read this cluster-identity special register for its intra-cluster peer rank; see Appendix B, Quick Reference 4, Item 64) Same as l1 (keeps per-rank 0..7 slots and fixed-order sum)
Address map (find the peer's slot) Find slot r's address in each target CTA: 1 × mapa.shared::cluster.u32 (translating a local CTA shared-memory address into the corresponding shared address in a specified peer CTA of the cluster; see Chapter 7, Section 12) Find both slot r and the peer mbarrier address: keeps the slot mapa and adds a 2nd mapa.shared::cluster.u32 for the mbarrier
Write (send 4 B partial sum) Send 4 B into slot r of all 8 CTAs: plain cluster-shared store Send 4 B and notify arrival: st.async store into slot r, updating the target mbarrier byte count
Wait (wait until all 8 slots = 32 B arrive) Wait for all 8 peers (and global writes at L2): release/acquire barrier.cluster.arrive / .wait Wait until all 8 slots (32 B) are full: waits on the local mbarrier by byte count (kernel entry still pairs a fence publishing only shared-memory mbarrier initialization—ignoring global-memory writes—with a cluster barrier without device-wide release to confirm peers' mbarriers are initialized, without compiling to a device-wide memory barrier)

red.async (SASS REDAS; see Appendix B, Quick Reference 3, Item 38) cannot be used here: its cluster-shared .add form supports .u32, .s32, and .u64 integers only (no .f32) and forbids writing to the executing CTA itself, whereas we exchange FP32 partial sums—including 1 self-write—and sum all 8 slots in fixed 0..7 order.

The catch with dropping the cluster barrier between the two row reductions in favor of st.async plus a local mbarrier is that it is easier to get wrong: without that cluster barrier separating the second reduction's CTA-local shared-memory writes from the first reduction's reads, our first implementation reused the same shared-memory buffer and the shared-memory read/write hazard checker (see Chapter 10, Section 4) caught 8 write-after-read hazards (WAR; see Chapter 3, Section 7), which we fixed by giving each reduction its own buffer. Where this approach would start to lose was not measured.

Putting both changes together gives l1 → l2, saving 1.84 µs (about 1.8 µs) on the T=1 sliding-window layer (see the chart below for all four scenarios): because this step bundles splitting pre-expert RMSNorm with switching the boundary kernels to st.async, the separate share of each change inside that 1.84 µs was not measured. Earlier single-switch paired runs on their own baselines do show that both matter differently: enabling the T=1 pre-expert RMSNorm split alone saved 0.82 µs on the T=1 sliding-window layer (and 1.47 µs on T=1 full attention), whereas enabling the boundary-kernel st.async swap alone won on T=1 full attention and several larger-TT shapes without winning on T=1 sliding window or T=8 sliding window—confirming that the 0.86–0.99 µs microbenchmark figure cannot be doubled to explain the 1.84 µs step. At T=8, pre-expert RMSNorm was already split (see the start of this section); once placed back into this evolution chain's single layer, only the T=1 sliding-window delta clears the noise band, and in the other three scenarios the expected savings do not show up: the T=1 full-attention layer likewise drops one pre-expert RMSNorm kernel and the handoff in front of it, and switches both boundary kernels' wait to st.async plus a local mbarrier; at T=8, only the Stage 3 boundary kernel changes. The cause was not determined.

With the standalone row-normalization kernel and the boundary device-wide memory barriers out of the way, the remaining inter-stage cost sits in the handoffs between back-to-back kernels.

4l2 → l3: How Can Every Inter-Kernel Handoff Be Hidden Inside the Preceding Kernel's Epilogue?

l3 completes the PDL edges along the main chain so successor kernels enter early to prefetch weights; using PDL safely requires two rules: pair predecessor and successor calls, and place the trigger point based on measurements, successor placement, and HBM bandwidth.

PDL lets a successor kernel enter SMs early while the preceding kernel is wrapping up, and then pause at wait until the preceding kernel finishes and its writes become visible (see Chapter 1, Section 4).

Without overlap, a single serial handoff costs 0.64 µs to 0.93 µs in our earlier reference measurements. Specifically, 0.64 µs comes from Chapter 1, Section 4's 1-CTA microbenchmark for a serial PDL edge that calls wait right at entry (Chapter 1, Section 2 also cites a ~1.0 µs per-node median calibrated on real SGLang inference graphs in a separate test, so the two cannot be subtracted directly), and 0.93 µs comes from Chapter 7, Section 11's paired test on decode 1-request full attention (main attention → merge), where disabling PDL ran 0.93 µs slower than triggering after the main loop. Inside a layer, dense projection weights are already fixed before the layer starts and do not depend on the previous step's activations, so the next dense projection kernel can start reading its own weights without waiting for the previous kernel to finish. Routed experts are the one exception: which expert weights to read depends on Top-8's output (see Section 5).

Listing every edge of this chapter's single layer across l2 and l3 (Figure 9-4 Mode 1)—whether PDL is enabled and what each successor does before wait returns—shows what l3 completes:

Dependency edge (scenario) PDL in l2 PDL in l3 Successor's pre-wait work
qkv_gate → attention (both layer types) No (waits for full predecessor exit) Yes Enters SMs early (for T=1 full attention, merge runs inside the split-KV kernel with no separate merge kernel; see below)
Attention split-KV → merge → o (T=1 sliding window) Yes Yes o loads its CTA's entire weight tile directly into registers before wait
Attention → o (T=1 full attention) No No (ordinary launch) None before wait
Attention → o (T=8, and 16, 32) No Yes Issues hardware L2 prefetch prefetch.global.L2 (per-thread cache-line prefetch; for single-thread contiguous bulk prefetch cp.async.bulk.prefetch.L2, see Chapter 7, Section 6 and Appendix B, Quick Reference 2, Item 25) to move weights from HBM into L2 using zero thread registers; after wait returns, TMA loads them from L2 into shared memory
Stage 3 boundary kernel → pooler Yes Yes pooler prefetches weights into its shared-memory ring buffer before wait
Stage 3 boundary event → side-stream router No No (ordinary launch) None (launches after fork event)
pooler (and side-stream Top-8) → experts (T=1,8,16) No (COOPERATIVE launch in l0–l2; see Chapter 2, Section 6) Yes The expert kernels load their opening batch of weights into the shared-memory ring buffer before wait
experts → unpooler → Stage 8 boundary kernel Yes Yes unpooler preloads weights before wait

To get PDL right across a full layer, we have to follow two rules.

Rule 1: PDL must be paired across predecessor and successor kernels. Along a multi-kernel chain, every middle kernel is both the successor of the previous step and the predecessor of the next step: the predecessor has to fire its trigger call on time, and the successor has to launch with the PDL attribute and call wait before reading dependent data. Leave out either half, and the successor waits until the predecessor exits completely before launching—so by the time it hits wait, there is nothing left to overlap. In an earlier baseline, attention on the T=1 full-attention layer ran as a split-KV kernel plus a separate merge kernel, and both lacked the launch attribute and the trigger call, so neither edge overlapped; adding the missing halves makes the T=1 full-attention layer ~1.2 µs faster (paired ABBA measurement; see the chart below; l3 and the final build take the second path of Chapter 7, Section 12 instead, merging via the last arriver inside the split-KV kernel). You can only see this cross-kernel overlap in a full-layer replay (see Chapter 10, Section 1).

Rule 2: Placing the trigger call after the main loop versus at kernel entry must be judged from measurements together with successor placement and HBM bandwidth. On the attention-to-merge chains in Chapter 7, Section 11 (see Chapter 1, Section 4), triggering at function entry slowed the predecessor by 0.07–1.65 µs, likely because early-entering successor CTAs co-scheduled onto the same SM contended with still-running predecessor CTAs (mechanism not verified). Here, as we saw in Section 1, pooler at T=1 uses only 64 of the 132 SMs and leaves 68 SMs idle, and pooler (207,720 B ≈ 203 KiB shared memory per CTA, rounded to ~200 KiB in prose) plus experts (120,896 B ≈ 118 KiB shared memory per CTA) exceed the 228 KiB per-SM shared-memory limit (see Chapter 3, Section 1) and cannot co-reside on the same SM—so triggering at pooler entry places early-entering successor CTAs only onto those 68 completely idle SMs (whether the entry trigger slows pooler was not measured separately—only the joint l2 → l3 gain below was measured). Laying out the 132 SMs at the T=1 join shows who holds what:

SM range (schematic) Late pooler window (after side-stream Top-8 exits) SMEM per CTA Pre-wait work and bytes After pooler exits
SMs 0–63 (64 SMs) Run pooler's 64 CTAs 207,720 B (about 203 KiB) pooler streams 50.4 MB of weights and writes its output SMs free up; the remaining 64 late experts CTAs dispatch onto these freed SMs and run their prologue and Phase A from scratch
SMs 64–131 (68 idle SMs) Run the first 68 early-entering experts CTAs (inferred to enter ~2.65 µs before pooler ends on Figure 9-4's earlier build) 120,896 B (about 118 KiB) Inferred from the final kernel code (that earlier build's frozen source was not retained): compact local expert IDs, initialize barriers, and issue TMA loads for all 3 weight-ring slots (68×3×36,864 B≈7.52 MB, sharing HBM bandwidth with pooler; how much arrives before pooler exits was not measured), then block at wait Enter the main loop as soon as wait returns, then meet the 64 late CTAs at the 132-CTA software grid barrier

In this chapter's single-layer pipeline, both T=1 and T=8 share one 132-CTA persistent experts kernel with an internal grid barrier (unlike Chapter 8, Section 6's standalone benchmark, which splits T=8 into two PDL kernels; here T=8 appends a separate post-norm combine kernel). Variant l3 (Figure 9-4 Mode 2) replaces its cooperative launch from l0–l2 with the PDL attribute, setting it as pooler's successor with pooler triggering right at entry—giving up the CUDA specification's guarantee of co-residency and dispatch order (see Chapter 2, Section 6). Furthermore, because Top-8 on the side stream never calls an explicit trigger, experts can launch only after Top-8's CTA exits (see Section 5 for how this cross-stream join behaves).

Progress across its 132-CTA software grid barriers relies instead on Chapter 7, Section 12's three prerequisites (at most 1 wave; router and Top-8 on the side stream have already exited before experts launches while pooler exits unconditionally; experts triggers its own successor only after its combine barrier at T=1 and omits early trigger at T=8) plus the observed hardware dispatch of the 64 waiting CTAs onto freed SMs 0–63.

If hardware dispatch violated that observed behavior and failed to place those 64 late CTAs onto the freed SMs, the 68 early CTAs would spin forever at the software grid barrier and the kernel would hang without an error.

Why the cooperative launch attribute was dropped rather than kept alongside PDL is not recorded.

We measured the added PDL edges and early entry of the experts kernel together: l2 → l3 saves the most on the T=1 full-attention layer (~3.6 µs), with all four scenarios shown in the chart below.

The price of this handoff optimization is that early-entering successor CTAs hold onto their registers and shared memory the whole time they wait. Even after every CTA of the preceding kernel exits, the hardware still has to confirm that all prior writes are visible to the successor before it lets the successor's wait call return; Section 6 measures how long that handoff gap takes. And if a successor enters too early and fights the predecessor kernel for SM resources, the whole pair runs slower instead—see Chapter 1, Section 4 and Chapter 7, Section 11 for counterexamples.

There is a catch, though: that prologue setup work reads topk_ids—written by Top-8 on the side stream—before wait, and that cross-stream read steps across a memory-visibility boundary.

5l3 → Fixed: What Can an Early-Entering Kernel Read Before wait?

Before wait, a kernel may in general read only data unmodified during the current graph replay (i.e., static weights); reading the predecessor's output before wait requires the predecessor to execute a gpu-scope release fence before issuing the trigger call.

A data race is when two threads (in the same kernel or in different kernels) access overlapping addresses, at least one of them writes, no causal order links them, and they are not both strong operations such as atomics. In PTX, the trigger call is written griddepcontrol.launch_dependents and the wait call griddepcontrol.wait (see Chapter 1, Section 4 and Chapter 8, Section 8).

By the PTX specification, the PDL mechanism itself gives two visibility paths that guarantee a predecessor kernel's writes are visible to its successor. Path 1: every writing thread in the predecessor first runs fence.release.gpu (a gpu-scope release fence; or the threads can pass an intra-CTA barrier and let one thread run the fence for the whole CTA, as in Chapter 2, Section 6), then calls launch_dependents in program order. If both grids sit in the same memory synchronization domain, the spec says this release fence synchronizes with the start of the successor grid, so the successor sees those writes the moment it launches. A memory synchronization domain is a tag CUDA attaches to each kernel launch; we use the default setting throughout, which puts all kernels in the same domain. Path 2: in every other case, writes are guaranteed visible only after the successor's griddepcontrol.wait returns (for release, acquire, and memory scope, see Chapter 2, Section 6). Every kernel along the chain finishes only after its own wait returns, so waiting for the previous kernel also waits for every earlier one. Under these two paths, unless you take Path 1, code before wait may read only data that nobody writes during the current replay—that is, static weights. Code before wait must also never write a buffer that any earlier kernel, the previous one included, might still be reading. That is why Section 3 zeroes the FP32 accumulation slot only after wait; otherwise the previous round's experts might still be reading it, and a release fence in the predecessor does not change that rule. (A third route is not part of PDL: polling a release/acquire flag under the memory model, as in Chapter 2, Section 6. This chapter's PDL chain does not use it; only the T=128 merged launch in Section 7 does, so the side stream can wait for the router scores.)

Note: Static tensor-map descriptor prefetch (prefetch.tensormap; see Appendix B, Quick Reference 2, Item 25). A host-built 128 B __grid_constant__ tensor-map descriptor may likewise be prefetched before wait via prefetch.tensormap (opcode table UTMACCTL, not recorded in this book's disassemblies); this book's single-layer chain gets no overlap gain from it (only the first-in-layer T=8,16 qkv_gate kernel includes it with no predecessor ahead, and its cache level and latency effect were not measured).

Why did reading topk_ids before wait in l3 look safe at first? The main stream that carries experts first waits on the completion event recorded after Top-8 on the side stream, and an event join normally waits for the whole Top-8 grid to finish. In eager mode—where the CPU launches kernels one by one without capturing a graph—that is exactly what happens. Capture the chain into a CUDA Graph, though, and as soon as experts carries the PDL launch attribute, this cross-stream event-join edge behaves differently. We infer that it runs as a programmatic dependent edge: the successor may launch before the predecessor's writes are visible (even before the predecessor finishes, if it triggers early), and it waits only at wait. So experts can enter SMs before Top-8's writes are visible. Public CUDA documentation says only that, after stream capture, a kernel with the PDL launch attribute gets a programmatic dependent edge; it does not say whether a cross-stream event-join edge does the same. This is inferred from a controlled test: in that test (original report not retained), a predecessor kernel on the side stream triggers at kernel entry and a PDL successor on the main stream reads its output before wait, giving 0 failures in 50 runs in eager mode versus 50 failures in 50 runs (wrong outputs) in graph mode, from which we infer that the captured cross-stream join acts as a programmatic dependent edge.

A CUDA Graph reuses the same topk_ids buffer on every replay. When Top-8 triggers at kernel entry (Figure 9-5 below, Mode ①), experts gets to the buffer first every time and reads the previous replay's expert IDs, which look completely valid. Our surviving records show the single-layer output completely wrong: the update this layer adds to the residual stream has a relative error of 0.7–1.09 against the reference implementation (the original report was not kept). Turn off Top-8's entry trigger so that it triggers implicitly at kernel exit (Figure 9-5 below, Mode ②, i.e., l3), and 240 standard replay tests show 0 errors (0 errors gives only an upper bound on the failure rate—240 error-free runs statistically rule out only common bugs above ~1% and cannot catch intermittent races around 1 in 10,000; see Chapter 10, Section 4 for the derivation). But 0 errors is not a guarantee. Top-8 in l3 never calls launch_dependents, so the trigger happens implicitly after all its CTAs exit. The CUDA Programming Guide states that the successor's CTAs may still launch before the predecessor's writes are visible. Only a returned wait guarantees that experts sees topk_ids. So l3 is still outside both guaranteed visibility paths; it just fails less often (see Chapter 2, Section 6).

Scale the replay count past 550,000 per shape and per version, spread across multiple H200 GPUs (see the chart below), and the race shows up. We call a single-layer output a severe numerical corruption when its relative L2 error exceeds 0.01 against a verified-correct output for the same input—one that the same version produced earlier and that passed the numerical-tolerance check. We re-checked 36 such outputs against the numerical tolerance (0.119–0.150; see Chapter 10, Section 4), and all 36 failed it. One GPU slot in our test pool failed far more often than the rest (163 failures in total), so we left it out of the tally. Without that outlier, l3 on the T=1 full-attention layer still hits 75 severe numerical corruptions across 816,528 replays (91.9 per million, or 1 about every 11,000 replays); the chart below shows the other three scenarios. The failure rate stays flat during steady-state execution, so it is not a warm-up effect. We also had CTA 0 of experts log the expert IDs it read before wait (see Chapter 10, Section 5 for the logging method). It repeatedly read IDs that did not match the current replay, and every mismatch we checked was exactly the previous replay's IDs.

As Section 4 noted, Top-8 decides which experts experts reads, so its whole prologue setup depends on topk_ids: compacting the local indices that land in this GPU's 32 local experts, initializing barriers, and issuing TMA loads for all 3 weight-ring slots (7.52 MB across the first 68 CTAs). The two visibility paths at the start of this section give two fixes. Fix (a) moves the topk_ids read, and all prologue setup that depends on it, to after wait (Figure 9-5 Mode ③). Fix (b) has every Top-8 CTA pass an intra-CTA barrier after writing, let one thread run fence.release.gpu, and then call launch_dependents explicitly. Fix (b) is correct under both edge types. But whether it lets the prologue overlap with Top-8 depends on the graph-capture behavior that the docs do not spell out for cross-stream edges. This book's final build (Fixed) is l3 plus Fix (a), measured on a patched copy; the submitted file is still l3 and retains this data race.

Comparing all three modes of Figure 9-5 side by side lines up each mode's trigger point, read point, visibility guarantee, and observed result:

Mode Top-8 trigger point Where experts reads topk_ids Guaranteed by Path 1 or Path 2? Observed result
Mode ① (entry-trigger control) Kernel entry (before writing topk_ids) Before wait No 50/50 failures in graph mode vs. 0/50 in eager mode in the control test; residual-update relative error 0.7–1.09 in surviving records
Mode ② (l3) Implicitly after all CTAs exit (no fence.release.gpu) Before wait No 0 errors in 240 test runs; at scale, 23.0 (T=1 sliding), 91.9 (T=1 full, outlier GPU excluded), and 1.2 / 1.2 (T=8 sliding / full) severe corruptions per million replays
Mode ③ (Fixed, Fix (a)) Implicitly after all CTAs exit After wait returns Yes (Path 2) 0 severe corruptions across ~2.26 million total replays (~1.35 µs slower on T=1 sliding window)

With Fix (a) in place, about 2.26 million total replays across all four shapes ran with 0 severe numerical corruptions. Aside from severe numerical corruptions, a separate class of small deviations (relative error about 0.003) that still pass single-layer verification shows up just as often before and after the fix, so it does not come from the topk_ids race (its cause was not determined). The fix in this chapter modifies the persistent expert kernel shared by T=1 and T=8 (as noted in Section 4, this chapter's single-layer pipeline runs that same internal-grid-barrier persistent kernel at T=8 as well, followed by a separate post-norm combine kernel). At T=16, the layer dispatches a separate early-entering expert kernel that likewise reads topk_ids ahead of wait. We did not modify that kernel; the same fix should apply there too, though neither the fix nor its failure rate was measured.

At T=8, l3 originally failed only once every ~840,000 runs, so running ~560,000 error-free replays on the fixed version cannot prove the fix by count alone (see Chapter 10, Section 4 for the derivation). Instead, safety at T=8 comes straight from the spec: whether that cross-stream edge runs as a regular event edge or as a programmatic dependent edge, Top-8 is done and its writes are visible once wait returns, so reading after wait is always safe.

Fix (a) moves the prologue setup of the 68 early-entering expert CTAs after wait (the remaining 64 CTAs already started their prologue after pooler exited in l3), making the T=1 sliding-window layer about 1.35 µs slower (see the chart below for all four scenarios; the exact breakdown of that 1.35 µs behind the grid barrier was not measured separately, while the 3.2 µs prologue time was stamped on an earlier cooperative-launch build). After this fix, when the experts kernel enters SMs early, it no longer runs its prologue setup ahead of time. Variant l2 and the fixed version were not timed in the same experiment, and how much the PDL edges vs. early expert entry each contributed—as well as how fast Fix (b) runs—was not measured.

Take the ~5.4 µs CUDA graph replay overhead off the fixed version's 67.8 µs, and the single layer still sits ~22 µs above the 40.0 µs reference bound. Is that remaining time sitting in the handoffs between kernels, or inside the kernels themselves?

6How Much Time Can Fusing a Single Layer into a Megakernel Recover?

Very little: handoff gaps plus tail durations total at most about 12.5 µs, device-wide counter handoffs save zero tail time, and measured multi-stage fusion runs slower instead; most of the excess time sits inside kernel main bodies.

Start by recording per-CTA timestamps along the critical path of an earlier 68.2 µs PDL-enabled build of the T=1 sliding-window layer (each CTA logs entry, wait return, and exit, see Chapter 10, Section 5), splitting each kernel's time into three parts: the handoff gap, from the last CTA exit of the preceding kernel to the first wait return in the next kernel; the kernel main body, within a single kernel from wait return to the median CTA exit; and the tail duration (CTA exit skew), within a single kernel from the median CTA exit to the last CTA exit. Even if you fused multiple stages into a persistent full-chip megakernel, at most you could ever win back the handoff gaps and tail durations—totaling ~12.5 µs.

This section dissects the same slightly earlier PDL-enabled, race-unfixed T=1 sliding-window build as Figure 9-4 in Section 4 (a different build from l3 in Section 4's evolution chain, so their totals cannot be compared directly, and no per-CTA timeline was recorded for the final build); the three bases align as follows, and the chart and table below use the 62.57 µs rescaled-probe base:

Base Measurement method Span and o example
Full-layer total (no probes) Single-layer CUDA Graph replay 68.22 µs (~68.2 µs, incl. 5.65 µs outside CTA timestamps)
Figure 9-4 (nsys whole-kernel) Unprobed nsys start-to-exit across all 11 kernels (side stream included) 63.86 µs (e.g., o spans 8.10 µs: ~6.18 µs pre-wait preload/wait, 18.21 → 20.19 µs after wait)
Figure 9-6 & table (per-CTA probes) Probed 9 critical-path kernels rescaled by × 0.959, starting at wait return 62.57 µs (e.g., o has a 1.31 µs post-wait body and 0.58 µs tail)

Break that 68.2 µs total apart (see the chart above and the table below, with probe overhead factored out) and the bulk sits in the ~50 µs (50.02 µs) of kernel main bodies—roughly 1.25× the 40.0 µs reference bound. Inferred for this earlier build from the shipped kernel code, o and unpooler issue all of their weight loads before wait returns, and pooler and experts issue part of theirs; because those pre-wait reads fall in the predecessor's body, tail, or handoff-gap window, a kernel's post-wait body can sit below its own byte floor (per-kernel megabytes are in the last column below). Handoff gaps and tail durations each take only ~6 µs, where each handoff gap includes acknowledging that every CTA of the previous grid has exited and flushing its writes. In this build, the experts stage (Chapter 8) has a byte lower bound of ~11.8 µs (reading 2 full local experts, ~56.6 MB); its main body (18.35 µs) runs ~6.6 µs above that bound, and its tail duration (3.28 µs) makes up more than half of the layer's tail duration.

Now let's do the math on what fusing into a megakernel actually costs. Within a single layer, every output of y=Wx depends on the entire input vector xx written in segments across all CTAs of the previous stage; thus every CTA of the next stage must wait for all CTAs of the previous stage to finish writing. If you marked individual tiles ready so the next stage could consume each tile as soon as it arrived, you could in theory hide part of the tail duration, at the price of per-tile acquire polling and finer-grained synchronization (this approach was not measured). When a megakernel hands off stages through a device-wide counter (working the same way as the grid barrier in Chapter 8, Section 6), the next stage still has to wait for the slowest producer CTA to finish writing xx, so the tail duration does not go away; and the SMs that free up during the tail are already busy prefetching weights, so there is no extra work left to pack into them. To shrink each kernel's tail duration, you have to balance the load inside the heavy kernels themselves (see Chapter 7 for attention and Chapter 8 for experts).

To put numbers on the handoffs, we built a synthetic memory-streaming chain: for each of the six weight-reading stages in a single layer, it reads one segment of that stage's byte count (qkv_gate and pooler at 12-bit, o and the unpooler slice at 16-bit, router at FP32, and experts at 4-bit), about 169 MB in total. Because this chain reads 2 full local experts (56.62 MB, giving 169.23 MB total and a 35.26 µs byte lower bound at 4.8 TB/s) instead of the about 1.87 local experts (~53 MB) counted in the reference bound (75% of the mean distinct local experts touched on the busiest GPU; see Primer 2, Sections 2 and 4—subtracting Section 2's 26.0 MB of 12-bit savings from Primer 2, Section 4's 40.0 µs sliding-window reference bound (~53 MB for ~1.87 experts) sits slightly below this chain in bytes, whereas counting 2 experts matches this chain), its byte lower bound is slightly higher than that 1.87-expert count. On this synthetic chain, adding each device-wide counter handoff increases whole-chain runtime by 1.08 µs on average (5.41 µs across 5 handoffs, without separating pure counter wait from synthetic stage tail skew). Substituting either 1.08 µs per handoff or Chapter 8, Section 6's about 1.4 µs (1.42 µs) 132-CTA grid-barrier microbenchmark into the 8 stamped gaps above gives the following model estimates (not upper bounds; no complete whole-layer megakernel was built):

Cost per counter handoff Replace only the 2 long gaps (entering attention merge and pooler, ~1.41 µs each; keep separate PDL kernels on the other 6 boundaries totaling 3.59 µs) Replace all 8 boundaries (inside one whole-layer persistent megakernel, vs. 6.41 µs across all 8 stamped gaps)
Synthetic chain 1.08 µs Estimates ~0.66 µs saved (~1% of the layer; see the chart below) Grows the 6 short gaps to 6.48 µs, estimating 8×1.08−6.41≈2.23 µs slower on handoffs alone
Chapter 8, Section 6 microbenchmark ~1.4 µs (1.42 µs) Estimates ~0 µs saved Estimates ~4.9 µs slower across all 8 boundaries

That same 6-stage synthetic memory-streaming chain also isolates the cost of the persistent kernel structure itself: when we write those exact same 6 stages as a persistent kernel that does zero waiting between stages (see Chapter 3, Section 1), it still runs 8.3 µs slower than a standard launch reading the same bytes (see the chart below). The cause was not determined, and the overhead when scaled up to the full single layer was not measured. Because this control kernel does no inter-stage synchronization, its numerical results are wrong—it is only there to measure the structural cost of persistence itself. On top of that, every stage fused into a single kernel has to share one compile-time register and shared-memory budget, which forces lightweight stages to run under the occupancy cap of the heaviest stage (see Chapter 3, Section 1).

We also explored a family of multi-stage cluster and cooperative fusions across adjacent stages (spanning Stages 6–8, Stages 2–3, and QKV projection plus attention): most variants remained unpromoted estimates, while the one measured head4 lineage (whose exact fused-stage subset and raw changelog were not retained on disk) ran 1.05 ms slower across the 6 decode and verify shapes (see Chapter 8, Section 1) weighted 46 sliding-window to 16 full-attention layers—where the live score (total score) is the 62-layer full-model weighted latency across those 6 shapes in milliseconds (not a single-layer time in microseconds), so +1.05 ms against the ~10.4–10.9 ms live score is about 10%—with surviving notes attributing the loss to longer in-kernel serial tails than separate PDL-overlapped kernels (alongside the compile-time occupancy cap above; separate shares were not measured).

Packing a small kernel into the epilogue of the preceding kernel (see Chapter 1, Section 3) is also slower. With PDL, that small kernel has already entered early on other SMs; once you pack it into the epilogue, it gives up that early entry, and—unlike the per-row last arriver at T=1 in Section 4—this folds all rows onto a single last-arriving CTA. Per surviving records, on the T=256 sliding-window layer (called verify 32-request sliding window in Chapter 7), folding the attention merge step into the last CTA of the split-KV kernel made the single layer 6.75 µs slower (original report not retained). On this shape, our single layer keeps the split-KV kernel plus a separate PDL merge kernel (whereas the standalone operator in Chapter 7, Section 12 takes the third path, with CTAs in the same cluster writing partial results directly into one another's shared memory). Chapter 7's second path (last-arriver merge) is used for 1-, 16-, and 32-request full-attention decode and 32-request sliding-window decode: each row is wrapped up by that row's own last-arriving CTA, spreading the epilogue work across different CTAs.

At this point, the T=1 layer is scheduled around its own shape. Once the batch size changes, the number of SMs occupied by pooler changes with it, and the trade-offs of the two earlier techniques flip as well.

7At Larger Batch Sizes: How Does the Number of Idle SMs Reshape the Schedule?

A side stream generally pays off only when the main kernel does not saturate HBM bandwidth and either leaves idle SMs or allows SM co-residency; the stream schedule must switch per TT.

Once the main kernel saturates HBM bandwidth or fills all SMs, every extra byte read and every SM occupied by a side-stream kernel stretches the main kernel. As the token count TT changes, both conditions shift together (Figure 9-7; for residency limits, see Chapter 3, Section 1). Gathering the grids, per-SM residency, shared memory, busy/idle SMs, and wave counts of the heavy kernels across TT in one view (where Fixed at T=1,8 has the same grids as the submitted l3 file except that experts's first 68 CTAs run their prologue after wait, while the T≥128 rows come from the submitted decode/prefill schedules for each TT) shows directly why the schedule flips:
