At T=1, pooler launches 64 CTAs and leaves 68 SMs idle, so router and Top-8 run on the side stream (Section 1) and the first 68 CTAs of experts enter SMs early (Section 4).

At T=32 (standalone ring-depth sweep), pooler launches only 64 CTAs (1 per SM) and streams weights from HBM into shared memory through a TMA ring buffer: each slot holds 16 KiB of weights plus a small activation tile read from L2, the producer waits for an empty slot to launch TMA and the consumer waits for a full slot to compute, leaving the remaining slots in flight while 1 slot is held by the consumer (see Chapter 3, Sections 6–7). By Chapter 3, Section 6, when all 132 SMs stream via TMA, the 95% bandwidth knee sits at about 36–40 KiB per SM (40 KiB at 1 CTA/SM); when only 64 SMs read, scaling by 132/64132 / 64 under Little's Law (see Chapter 2, Section 3) raises the per-SM 95% knee to about 74–83 KiB:

Ring-buffer depth Slot split (16 KiB weights/slot) In-flight weights per reading SM (vs. 74–83 KiB knee) Isolated-kernel latency
6 slots 1 held by consumer + 5 in flight 80 KiB (right inside the knee band) 18.14 µs
7 slots 1 held by consumer + 6 in flight (SMEM still within 228 KiB) 96 KiB (past the knee) 17.59 µs (~0.55 µs faster)

Expanding from 6 slots to 7 makes the standalone kernel about 0.55 µs faster (see the chart below; why it still falls short of the byte lower bound was not measured), at the cost of one extra slot of shared memory per CTA while occupancy stays at 1 CTA per SM. The very next stop at T=128 shows the counterexample when we cut the ring shallower.

At T=128, both router and pooler launch 128 CTAs: router's 4-slot ring buffer takes ~128 KiB of shared memory, and pooler's 8-slot ring buffer takes ~193 KiB of shared memory (for ring buffer slots, see Chapter 3, Section 6). Together they need 128+193>228 KiB, exceeding the per-SM shared-memory limit (see Chapter 3, Section 1), so the two kernels cannot co-reside on the same SM; pooler can only enter after router runs on its own and exits, and router's standalone run plus the handoff takes ~8.5 µs in total. Cutting pooler's and router's ring buffers shallower and swapping their order to force both onto the same SM starves in-flight bytes under Little's Law—the exact mechanism just seen at T=32—making the sliding-window layer 8.4 µs (T=128) and 5.0 µs (T=256) slower instead.

What actually works here is a merged launch. router and pooler read the same input h, so we put the router projection and pooler into one kernel: each CTA first computes its slice of router scores through the same shared-memory ring buffer, then goes straight into the pooler main loop. The layer reads the same total bytes as before, with router's 8.4 MB of weights streaming through pooler's ring buffer. The side stream keeps only a 1-CTA wait kernel, which polls the completion counter written by the merged kernel and launches Top-8 once all 128 slices of router scores are in. Why does closing an ~8.5 µs hole net only ~3.0 µs? Per-CTA timestamps show the merged kernel entering ~9.8 µs earlier and running ~7.2 µs longer, with experts measured entering ~3.0 µs earlier (the small difference was not determined): the merged kernel enters ~9.8 µs (~10 µs) earlier than standalone pooler to close the inter-kernel hole, while streaming 8.4 MB of router weights (12.5% more weight bytes on top of pooler's 67.1 MB) grows its own duration by ~7.2 µs (why it grows by 7.2 µs was not determined), making the sliding-window single layer 1.30% faster (paired ABBA median; see the chart below). At T=256 (where pooler's grid size was not recorded), the change falls inside the ~0.5% paired noise band and shows no measurable gain, so we keep the two kernels separate there.

At T=753, prefill pooler slices its output into 128×256 tiles to launch 96 CTAs, leaving 36 SMs idle. Putting router, Top-8, and the route-alignment kernel—which sorts token indices by expert and pads each bucket to the tile size (see Chapter 8, Section 14)—on the side stream to run in parallel across those 36 idle SMs makes the single layer ~3.2% faster (see the chart below).

Step up to T=3,012, and pooler's persistent two-CTA cluster grid is derived from H200's 66 two-SM TPCs to fill all 132 SMs (runtime return count not recorded separately). If we keep running pooler first with router on the side stream, the T=3,012 whole workload runs 0.76% slower; launching router on the side stream right after the Stage 3 boundary kernel (without waiting for pooler) also makes the whole scored workload 1.01% slower (about 2.0% slower on the T=3,012 sliding-window layer; exact slowdown mechanism not measured). So at T=3,012, we finish router first on the main stream, then have the host issue pooler on the main stream before issuing the lightweight Top-8 and route-alignment kernels on the side stream (actual overlap amount not measured).

At T=16,384, the shipped pooler runs 132 persistent CTAs looping over 2,048 output tiles (0 queued CTAs), keeping all 132 SMs busy from start to finish. Even with zero idle SMs, an earlier trial that placed router, Top-8, and route-alignment all on the side stream alongside pooler still beat serial execution by 0.93% (0.72% in another run; no timeline was kept, and the source of the gain was not determined); however, a code comment (whose pooler grid size was not recorded separately, though the comment writes "behind the pool's 2048 CTAs") notes that the side-stream router started only near pooler's end. The submitted prefill schedule therefore finishes router first on the main stream, after which the host issues the lightweight Top-8 and route-alignment kernels on the side stream before issuing pooler on the main stream (which kernel dispatches first, how much they overlap or help/hurt, and the delta over side-stream router were not separately recorded or measured).

The same idle-SM check applies inside Stage 1 qkv_gate at T=3,012 (for tail-wave splitting, see Chapter 2, Section 5). There qkv_gate has 216 output tiles across 132 SMs: Wave 1 runs 132 tiles across the full chip, leaving 216−132=84 tiles in Wave 2 and 132−84=48 SMs idle. Having those 48 idle SMs (CTAs 84..131) inside the same qkv_gate kernel split the 84 Wave-2 tiles 2-way along KK makes qkv_gate finish 8.7 µs earlier on in-layer per-CTA timestamps (167.6 → 158.9 µs; standalone kernel latency was not measured). Across the whole layer, the sliding-window layer runs ~0.47% faster (+0.471%, or +0.177% on the 8-shape score), whereas the full-attention layer runs 0.10% slower because its KV preparation kernel (stage_kv on the side stream; for the prefill prologue see Chapter 7, Section 11) competes for those SMs (~3 µs loss)—so the submitted prefill code enables this split on sliding-window layers only.

Now that we know how a single layer is scheduled across batch sizes on one GPU, how does this one layer add up across all 62 layers of a full decode step—and what do our single-layer numbers leave out?

8Placing This Layer Back into All 62 Layers: Which Part of One Decode Step Do This Book's Measurements Cover?

Summing the 62 final single-layer latencies at T=1 gives 4,329.2 µs, which overcounts 62 single-layer graph replay overheads and omits 186 cross-GPU collectives over NVLink (H200's inter-GPU high-speed interconnect, 900 GB/s bidirectional and 450 GB/s unidirectional; see Section 9 for the three per-layer data paths and isolated timings), token embedding, lm_head, and sampling.

The solid bars in Figure 9-8 are the 62-layer single-GPU body that this book measures (46 sliding-window layers and 16 full-attention layers), and the cross-GPU wire-time figures in the Step 2 card use that unidirectional NVLink bandwidth.

Add up all 62 single-layer reference bounds and you get ~2.55 ms, which is higher than the ~1.87 ms number from Primer 1. The 2.55 ms sum adds the expert weights counted in the reference bound plus the KV cache and activations, and leaves out lm_head (the chart below breaks out the three pieces).

How does the measured 4,329.2 µs sum (46×67.79+16×75.68) differ from a real one-step decode? On one hand, it counts the ~5.4 µs single-layer graph replay overhead from Section 1 62 times (an overcount derived as 62×5.4 µs≈335 µs), whereas real serving amortizes graph replay across one 62-layer graph (how much replay overhead remains after amortization was not measured). Layers 0 and 61 also store their experts in BF16 (see Primer 1, Section 2), while this sum treats every layer as 4-bit experts, biasing the total low (the difference was not measured separately).

On the other hand, the four unmeasured parts in Figure 9-8 (the three light-gray dashed stage bars and the dashed-amber intra-layer exchange blocks) lie outside single-layer, single-GPU benchmarking, and we measured none of them inside a full decode step. Before Layer 0, the vocabulary embedding table is split by rows across all 8 GPUs, so the token lookup is followed by an all-reduce across GPUs (see Primer 1, Section 1). Each layer has 3 cross-GPU collectives (see Section 1). At T=1, the all-reduce after o moves a:[1,8192]BF16\shape{a}{1,\;8192}{BF16} (16 KiB), the all-reduce after Stage 6 moves m:[1,4096]BF16\shape{m}{1,\;4096}{BF16} (8 KiB), and the all-gather after Stage 7 takes 1,024 BF16 elements from each GPU (2 KiB) to gather f:[1,8192]BF16\shape{f}{1,\;8192}{BF16} (16 KiB). At that unidirectional NVLink rate, one 16 KiB copy takes ~36 ns on the wire (16,384 B÷450 GB/s). Even in the all-reduce, where each GPU sends its 16 KiB to each of the other 7 (112 KiB in total), the bytes take only ~255 ns. So bytes are not the cost: the cost is that all 186 collectives across the 62 layers sit on the critical path, and we did not measure their latency inside a full step; Section 9 times the three per-layer collectives in isolation on an 8-GPU node. After Layer 61 and the final RMSNorm, this GPU's slice of lm_head reads 413.8 MB (an 86.2 µs byte lower bound at 4.8 TB/s; see Primer 1, Sections 3–4), followed by an all-gather of logits across GPUs and token sampling. If the serving engine uses speculative decoding, each step also adds the draft model plus a T=8 verification pass (see Primer 1, Section 7; we did not measure the draft model's latency).

9Three Cross-GPU Collectives per Layer: Which Path Do Bytes Take, and What Does Each Cost in Isolation?

At T=1, each of the three cross-GPU collectives per layer sends only 2–16 KiB per GPU, and Section 8 showed that these bytes need at most ~255 ns on the wire. Yet even the fastest path measures ~10 µs per single-collective graph replay on 8 H200 GPUs. Wire bytes are a small part of that time; this section did not split the rest into its parts.

Start with the physical wires on the node (top of Figure 9-9). Our measured node houses 8 H200 SXM GPUs that connect through NVSwitch chips (high-speed inter-GPU switch ASICs): all 18 NVLink links of every GPU (bandwidth in Section 8) feed into the switches, so any GPU pair can use all 18 links through them, whereas PCIe Gen5 (128 GB/s) connects only to the host CPU and carries none of our GPU-to-GPU exchanges. Third-generation NVSwitch does more than forward loads and stores between GPUs—it also supports hardware multicast objects (Virtual Memory Management maps one multicast virtual address to one physical HBM replica on each of the 8 GPUs; this is not the TMA cluster multicast of Chapter 5), and NVIDIA calls the broadcast and reduction done inside the switches NVLink SHARP: when an SM issues one multimem.st to a multicast address, the switches broadcast that store to all 8 GPUs at once; when it issues one multimem.ld_reduce, the switches read all 8 replicas, sum them inside the switch fabric, and return only the reduced sum to registers. Each GPU also has dedicated DMA copy engines separate from the SMs, which can copy bytes peer-to-peer with zero SMs, but CUDA's copy calls only copy and never add—every all-reduce and all-gather measured below runs as an SM kernel. Note also why all-to-all token dispatch (where every GPU sends a distinct slice of tokens to every peer and gathers them back) never appears in our decode or verify layer: under TP8 attention and EP8 experts without sequence parallelism, every GPU already holds all TT token activations, runs whichever of its 32 local experts were selected, and finishes with one all-reduce; cross-GPU all-to-all dispatch and combine enter only if sequence-parallel prefill shards tokens across GPUs ahead of the MoE block (disabled in this configuration and not measured).

To sum each GPU's partial a:[1,8192]BF16\shape{a}{1,\;8192}{BF16} (16 KiB per GPU) across all 8 GPUs, bytes can travel five ways (Cards 1–5 in Figure 9-9; exact CTA counts and byte tallies sit on the figure's step cards):

  • 1-shot push (1shot_push, peer-to-peer remote stores): Every GPU stores its full row directly into push slots in symmetric memory (a buffer at the same offset on every GPU that all 7 peers can load and store directly) on all 8 GPUs (7 copies cross NVLink in a single one-way hop; before storing, every all-zero 4-byte word (two BF16 +0.0 values) is rewritten to a -0.0 bit pattern, which is numerically identical, so an all-zero word can mark "not arrived yet"), polls its own 8 local slots until no all-zero word remains, sums all 8 rows on its SMs, resets the slots to all zeros, and flips its even/odd epoch counter.
  • 1-shot pull (1shot_pull, peer-to-peer remote loads): After a cross-GPU barrier (each GPU adds 1 to a counter on every GPU, then waits until its own counter has 8 arrivals) confirms all inputs are ready, each GPU loads the full row from all 8 GPUs over NVLink (reading directly from the callers' buffers via a pointer table, written after CUDA Graph capture, that holds the callers' buffer addresses on all 8 GPUs, with no staging copy, though each remote load costs a request-plus-reply round trip), sums the 8 copies on its SMs, and closes with a second cross-GPU barrier.
  • 2-shot pull (2shot_pull, fused reduce-scatter + all-gather): After the opening barrier, each GPU owns 1/81/8 of the row, pulls that 1/81/8 shard from all 8 GPUs, sums it on its SMs, stores the reduced 1/81/8 shard back to all 8 GPUs, and finishes with a release/acquire cross-GPU barrier—adding a second link phase, while per-GPU link bytes in each direction drop from 7 full rows (112 KiB) to 7/8 of a row (14 KiB), 1/8 of 1-shot push in total.
  • NVSwitch multicast sum (2shot_pull + multimem): Keeps the same two 1/81/8-shard phases, except one multimem.ld_reduce lets NVSwitch read and sum the 8 copies in the switch fabric and one multimem.st broadcasts the reduced shard back to all 8 GPUs; because multimem instructions must target a dedicated symmetric multicast workspace rather than arbitrary caller buffers in the graph pointer table, each call is bracketed by two small same-GPU SM copy kernels that stage the tensor in and out.
  • General-purpose NCCL: Fuses communication and reduction into a single library kernel on the SMs. It ships several algorithms, such as Ring, Tree, and NVLS (reduction on NVSwitch), and NCCL_ALGO selects one (which one it chose under default settings was not recorded).

The third exchange after Stage 7—the all-gather stitching each GPU's 1,024-column slice (2 KiB at T=1) into f:[1,8192]BF16\shape{f}{1,\;8192}{BF16} (16 KiB; Card 6 in Figure 9-9)—moves data like the second phase of the multicast sum (one multimem.st writes into all 8 GPUs), but it ends with local slot polling, as 1-shot push does, instead of a cross-GPU barrier: each GPU issues multimem.st so NVSwitch broadcasts its 2 KiB slice into all 8 GPUs' push workspaces, and work CTAs poll locally until all 8 slices arrive, write out the full row, and zero the slots with no cross-GPU addition.

We time these paths with the same kind of method as Section 1: each path is captured alone in a CUDA Graph, L2 is flushed before every replay, and CUDA events time the replay. Unlike Section 1, all 8 GPUs time themselves, and each replay follows one cross-GPU sync so that the GPUs start as close together as possible; the remaining difference in start times (start skew below) stays inside the timing. A layer waits for the slowest GPU, so we report the slowest of the 8 per-GPU medians in the chart below and in the size curves of Figure 9-9:

The measurements show two regimes. First, across the 2–16 KiB decode range, no path's latency changes much with message size, and the fastest path sits at about 10 µs: 1-shot push sends 7 extra row copies per GPU, yet it leads at 16 KiB at about 1/2.8 of NCCL's time (1-shot push has no explicit cross-GPU barrier and no staging kernels; how much each difference is worth was not measured separately). Second, when Figure 9-9 sweeps the message size up to 16 MiB, the leader changes twice: at 256 KiB, 2-shot pull, with 1/8 of the link bytes, overtakes 1-shot push; at 2 MiB, the NVSwitch multicast sum overtakes 2-shot pull. The serving stack's Hopper configuration also stops using 1-shot push above 128 KiB.

This small-message fast path has costs. First, collective kernels hold SMs while they run: 1-shot push always launches a fixed grid of 132 CTAs, even for 2–16 KiB (at 16 KiB only 32 CTAs have 1 warp each that moves data, and the other 100 only sync and flip the phase; which SMs they land on was not recorded). Chapter 7, Section 12's second precondition counts "kernels on other streams in the same process (such as cross-GPU communication kernels)"; kernels of this kind are among them. Second, stock serving on H200 runs only 2 all-reduces per layer and keeps a full unpooler copy on every GPU; the sliced projection plus multicast gather is a fast path behind chip and token-count gates. Third, multiplying the fastest isolated medians by 62 layers puts the 186 exchanges at about 1.9 ms with single-op replays, or about 0.5 ms with 32-op chains. Neither number is a server time: each single-op replay value contains one graph replay overhead (about 5.4 µs on one GPU in Section 1, not measured on these nodes), and inside a real 62-layer 8-GPU graph, how much start skew PDL hides, how much load imbalance stretches the waits, and whether collectives contend with compute for SMs were not measured end to end.

Chapter Evolution Chain (l0 → l1 → l2 → l3 → Fixed)

  • l0 (Section 1): baseline obtained by turning off the changes from Sections 2–4 in l3, with the main chain on one CUDA stream and router plus Top-8 on the side stream.
  • l0 → l1 (Section 2): projections switch to the 9-instruction decoder from Chapter 6; we reorder the pooler weight layout, add the evict_first L2 residency hint, and prepare escaped-weight corrections before the final KK-step. For 8-token verify, both qkv_gate and unpooler switch to 12-bit weights with launch grids sized to fit in a single wave. At T=1, qkv_gate and pooler already use 12-bit weights in l0.
  • l1 → l2 (Section 3): we split pre-expert RMSNorm across the pooler epilogue and expert accumulators, and boundary kernels keep peer-SMEM writes while replacing the release cluster barrier with st.async plus a local mbarrier.
  • l2 → l3 (Section 4): we complete the PDL edges along the main chain, and the first 68 CTAs of the experts kernel enter early on the SMs left idle by pooler (containing the data race analyzed in Section 5).
  • l3 → Fixed (Section 5): we move the topk_ids read in the T≤8 experts kernel after wait, eliminating that cross-stream data race. This book's final build (Fixed) is l3 plus Fix (a), measured on a patched copy; the submitted file is still l3 (and retains the race).

Takeaway: Most of a single layer's time sits inside the kernel main bodies themselves (50.02 µs in per-CTA timestamps on an earlier 68.22 µs build; the final build was not decomposed): intra-layer scheduling, cross-kernel reductions, and safe PDL handoffs bring the T=1 sliding-window layer down from 71.39 µs to the race-free final 67.79 µs, while neither model estimates nor synthetic experiments support a whole-layer megakernel (no complete whole-layer megakernel was built).

Next chapter's question: Since most of the latency still sits inside individual kernels—and across the first nine chapters we have seen false speedups from cache state, thermal/clock drift, and intermittent data races—given a brand-new slow kernel, how do you measure its runtime accurately, rule out false speedups, and walk the Level 1–6 diagnostic tree down to the four hardware limits fixed in H200 silicon? → Chapter 10

Chapter 10

Given a Slow Kernel, How Do We Measure It Accurately and Diagnose Its Bottleneck Level by Level?

  • Preface
  • Primer 1

  • Chapter 1 [Level 1]
  • Chapter 2 [Level 2]
