The previous chapter ended with a question: when you get a brand-new slow kernel, how do you pin down where it stalls level by level without guessing? Only two things can fool you on a slow kernel: measuring the time wrong, or looking at the wrong level. So this chapter organizes diagnosis into a four-step closed loop you can follow on your own kernel (continuing with single-request gemv at each level, and bringing in operators from Part II only when a phenomenon does not show up in gemv):

  1. Measure right first (Sections 1–5): pick the right timer (Section 1), read-flush L2 before timing (Section 2), cancel drift and jitter with same-process ABBA pairing and a noise band (Section 3), verify outputs and bound intermittent races before timing (Section 4), and keep probes and allocations from perturbing the kernel (Section 5).
  2. Walk the profiler from the outside in (Sections 6–7): check the outer three levels first (Levels 1–3: timeline, full chip, single SM; Section 6), and once they are clean, check the inner three levels (Levels 4–6: SMSP scheduler, execution pipelines, SASS machine code; Section 7).
  3. Bound the gain before rewriting and gate the win (Sections 8–9): run a runtime-skip perturbation test to cap the maximum possible saving (Section 8), and accept a change only when it clears the noise band, keeps the same sign on re-runs, and causes no regression across all shapes in the full layer (Section 9).
  4. Stop at a hardware limit and route around it (Section 10): recognize the four H200 hardware limits that software cannot eliminate and can only work around (see Appendix A for the hardware fixes).

1Why Do CUDA Event Timing and the Profiler Report Two Different Latencies, and What Should Each Be Used to Read?

CUDA event timing includes launch and event-recording overhead, while the profiler times only the kernel itself. Use event timing to report microsecond savings, and use the profiler to see where the kernel is bottlenecked.

For kernel-level profiling in this book, we use Nsight Compute (NCU). It focuses on one kernel at a time and replays that kernel across multiple passes, collecting one set of hardware counters per pass (the GPU's hardware performance counters can collect only a limited number of signals at once, so requesting many metrics splits profiling across multiple passes; see NCU Profiling Guide §2.2.3). Because NCU flushes all GPU caches between passes by default (controlled by --cache-control), those counters give you cold-cache readings. Its gpu__time_duration.sum metric is the gap between two timestamps written by the GPU front end—the hardware that processes the command stream before the grid goes out to the SMs. It records the start timestamp after launch setup, right before dispatching the grid to the SMs, and records the end timestamp after the GPU finishes waiting for all work to complete (WaitForIdle). So this number leaves out CPU-side launch and event-recording overhead, but it is longer than the pure execution span from the first CTA starting to the last CTA exiting; by how much, we did not measure.

Take gemv v8 from Chapter 4, Section 6 and measure it both ways: the CUDA event timing from Primer 3, Section 5 comes out ~2.8 µs longer than the gpu__time_duration.sum reported by NCU, as shown in the chart below.

Where does that extra ~2.8 µs (2.84 µs from rounded 11.9 µs, or 2.87 µs from unrounded 11.87 µs) in CUDA event timing go? We infer that most of it is the launch command and event-recording overhead sitting between the two timing events (which NCU does not measure): across the follow-up 1-warp v8 / v9 variants and C12 (the 12-bit lossless weight packing from Chapter 6, Sections 1–2) 4-warp v10 variants, the cross-run event − NCU difference consistently falls in 2.6–3.4 µs (4.06–4.91 µs on the BF16 4-warp controls, cause not determined). Also, the two runs did not use the exact same machines and their SM clock frequencies may differ, and v8 has no single-launch record of both event and on-chip spans, so we did not measure how much went to launch/event overhead versus cross-run machine and clock differences. Do not compare this 2.8 µs directly with the 4.6 µs from Primer 3, Section 5: the two numbers do not measure the same thing, because 4.6 µs also includes the GPU execution of the empty kernel itself.

NCU 2025.1, the version used in this book, locks the SM and memory clocks to their lower base clock by default; newer NCU releases lock them to boost frequency instead, so check --clock-control before you profile. In this run, we turned clock locking off and the SM ran at ~1.96 GHz. We did not record the SM frequency during CUDA event timing, and we did not measure the effect of clock frequency on v8 latency separately.

So when you report how many microseconds an optimization saves, always use CUDA event timing, not NCU duration. To time a single kernel, wrap a single launch in CUDA events; to time a single layer, wrap one CUDA Graph replay in events. If you want to time one specific kernel inside a CUDA Graph replay, use the Activity API of NVIDIA's profiling interface CUPTI (CUDA Profiling Tools Interface): instead of replaying that kernel in isolation, it records the GPU start and end timestamps of every kernel during graph replay. Conversely, when you want to know why a kernel is slow, switch to NCU to read the bandwidth share, stall sampling share, and instruction counts.

The table below summarizes the start point, end point, and use of each tool:

Tool Start point End point When to use
CUDA event timing Start event recorded before launch End event recorded after the kernel or CUDA Graph finishes (includes launch and event-recording overhead) Report microsecond savings on a single kernel launch or a single-layer CUDA Graph replay
NCU gpu__time_duration.sum GPU front-end timestamp after launch setup, right before dispatching the grid to SMs GPU front-end timestamp after waiting for all work to finish (WaitForIdle) Diagnose why one kernel is slow (read bandwidth share, stall sampling share, and instruction counts; check --cache-control and --clock-control)
CUPTI Activity API Per-kernel GPU start timestamp during normal graph replay Per-kernel GPU end timestamp during normal graph replay (no isolated replay) Time one specific kernel inside a CUDA Graph replay

2Why Must We Read 512 MiB to Flush L2 Before Every Timed Run—and Why Only Read, Not Write?

A single operator's weights fit inside the 60 MiB L2 cache, so without a flush you measure warm-cache latency; if you flush L2 with writes, you can even invert the speed ranking of two versions.

Before every timed run, do a 512 MiB read flush outside the start and end timing events: read a buffer much larger than L2 once so all the old data in L2 gets replaced with clean cache lines.

Why flush L2 at all? Compare Mode 1 and Mode 3 in Figure 10-1. The weights W:[2304,8192]BF16\shape{W}{2304,\;8192}{BF16} of qkv_gate take up only 37.75 MB, which easily fits inside the H200's 60 MiB L2 cache. If you run the same kernel back-to-back in a loop without flushing, most of WW is already sitting in L2 from the second iteration onward; in production, though, 62 layers take turns running and L2 is cold whenever a layer reads its weights (see Chapter 2, Section 2).

Warm L2 and cold L2 give wildly different numbers. Take gemv v1 from Primer 3, Section 6: on the same H200 GPU and in the same process, timing without an L2 flush (38.24 µs) comes out ~30% (29.6%) shorter than timing after a 512 MiB read flush (54.30 µs), as shown in the first chart below; if you choose a kernel design from warm-cache timings, the winning variant may not hold up in production. Worse yet, flushing L2 by writing a 512 MiB buffer (Figure 10-1 Mode 2) can flip the measured speed ranking of two versions—which is why we withdrew v4 from the gemv evolution chain. Starting from v3 (Chapter 2, Section 7), v4 added cache hints to the loads of WW and xx: the L2 residency policies from Chapter 2, Section 4, plus matching L1 eviction hints—evict_first on WW and evict_last on xx (see Appendix B, Quick Reference 2, Item 24 for the code). With a 512 MiB write flush, v4 looked ~10% faster than v3 (see the second chart below); once we switched to a 512 MiB read flush and tested in both forward and reverse orders across two H200 GPUs, all 4 medians of v4 came out above v3, averaging ~1 µs slower (see the third chart below).

First see why the warm and cold timings of v1 in the first chart differ by so much: gemv v1 keeps only 4.0 KiB / SM in flight, and its 2,304 CTAs split into wave 1 (2,112 CTAs) plus a 192-CTA tail wave that walk 2 × 64 = 128 serial dependent rounds back to back (see Chapter 2, Sections 1–2). Plugging 4.0 KiB / SM and the ~0.33 µs unloaded round trip into Little's Law (bytes in flight == bandwidth ×\times round-trip latency; see Chapter 2, Section 3) over 37.75 MB gives only wave 1's ~23 µs and misses the second 64-round tail wave—at the 0.334 µs unloaded cold HBM round trip, 128 rounds spend 42.75 µs waiting on loads alone, plus the ~4.6 µs empty-launch floor, while the remaining SMEM reduction and tail residual inside 54.30 µs were not split; without a flush, most loads hit L2 at ~0.18 µs per round and shrink the chain to 38.24 µs.

Now see why write flushing flipped the v3 and v4 ranking in the next two charts: writing a 512 MiB buffer leaves the 60 MiB L2 cache packed with modified dirty cache lines that have not been written back to HBM yet. We infer that when the tested kernel then goes to read WW, L2 has to write each evicted dirty line back to HBM before pulling in a new line, tying up the HBM path and lengthening each miss's round-trip time (and competing for bandwidth on bandwidth-saturated operators). Those two charts come from two runs on different machines; put them side by side and you see that after switching to a read flush, v3 got ~5 µs faster while v4 barely moved. Although those two charts' original binaries were not re-run on the same machine changing only the flush method, we ran a same-machine, same-round control on template-equivalent kernels varying only the flush: write flushing did slow v3 by 6.18 µs (49.06 vs. 42.88 µs), while v4 shifted by only 0.64 µs (44.13 vs. 43.49 µs); an ablation further showed that every WW load qualifier that also keeps WW from staying in L2 (L2 evict_first alone, L1 and L2 evict_first together, or L1::no_allocate) recovers that about 5 µs, whereas hints on xx alone or .cg on WW do not (why .cg has no effect while L1::no_allocate does was not determined). Whether dirty-line writebacks are the underlying mechanism lengthening miss reads remains inferred, because we cannot read HBM writeback counters directly without first disturbing the cache state. So we do not count v4 as a step, and the evolution chain jumps straight from v3 to v5; for why v4 saves no time under a read flush, see Chapter 2, Section 4.

After a read flush, L2 is just as cold as when 62 layers rotate in production, and the interference from dirty cache line writebacks is gone. The cost is an extra 512 MiB read outside the timing events on every iteration, which stretches the total wall-clock time of the experiment (by how much, we did not measure). Keep in mind, though, that if an input is naturally warm in production—like the activations just written by the preceding kernel inside the same layer—cold-flushing an isolated single kernel will make it look artificially slow. When you time a single layer, wrap the whole layer in one CUDA Graph replay so warm intra-layer data stays in cache naturally (see Chapter 9, Section 1). Also, if an earlier kernel used a host-side L2 persisting window (cudaAccessPolicyWindow; see Chapter 2, Section 4), normal or streaming accesses can use the set-aside portion of L2 only while persisting accesses leave it unused (CUDA Programming Guide §4.15.1)—so we infer that a plain 512 MiB read flush may not evict persisting lines, and you should reset them first with cudaCtxResetPersistingL2Cache() before timing (not measured in this book).

3How Much Must Two Versions Differ Before One Is Truly Faster?

Run the two versions alternately in A, B, B, A order inside the same process to cancel linear drift; then run an A/A null-hypothesis control to measure the operator's noise band, and count a delta only when it clears that band.

When you have a new kernel of your own, calibrate its noise band in two steps before benchmarking any change:

  1. Run an A / A paired control: feed two identical copies of the kernel as A and B into the same in-process ABBA harness (no formula sets the group count—campaigns in this book used 14 runs, 20 groups, or 60 rounds).
  2. Set the gate above the observed spread: place the winning threshold above the observed A / A spread so only paired deltas that clear it count (on a multi-step evolution chain without a dedicated A / A run, use the span of same-version medians across rounds or machines as the resolution floor instead).

Why does the alternating A, B, B, A order from Chapter 7, Section 1 cancel drift? Even on a single machine, back-to-back runs experience slow latency drift driven by temperature, clock frequency, and other factors (whose individual contributions we did not measure). If you run NN back-to-back iterations of A followed by NN back-to-back iterations of B as in Figure 10-2 Mode 1, the later B runs execute in a consistently slower state, mixing that drift straight into the difference. Switch to the A, B, B, A order in Figure 10-2 Mode 2 and label the four runs in a group as timestamps 1,2,3,41, 2, 3, 4: the mean timestamp of A is (1+4)/2=2.5, and the mean timestamp of B is (2+3)/2=2.5. As long as drift across those four runs is roughly linear, A and B see the exact same average drift, which cancels out when you subtract them. Run multiple groups in a row and take the median of the per-group deltas, and you also iron out random jitter within individual groups.

Once linear drift is canceled, we run the A/A null-hypothesis control above from Chapter 7, Section 4. On the dense projection kernels, the largest observed difference is 0.13 µs, so we set the winning threshold at 0.15 µs; note that this threshold is simply the maximum observed A/A delta, not a statistical confidence interval.

Now see why you cannot time two versions on different machines and subtract the numbers directly, as shown in the chart below. Take the exact same version of gemv and run it on two different H200 GPUs with the same cold-L2 CUDA event timing: setting aside v0 (which takes nearly 700 µs), the medians on the two machines differ by up to 0.32 µs. Now look at v8 → v9 in Chapter 5, Section 2: across 4 paired comparison rounds, two rounds tied and two rounds came out slightly slower for v9, with every delta smaller than the span of v8's own 4-round medians. That puts the change in v9 squarely inside measurement noise (see Chapter 4, Section 6 for the multi-round span criterion).

The table below shows the noise bands, units, calibration methods, and recorded run counts that this book used across six campaigns; the five µs bands are plotted in the chart below (the sixth band, long-sequence prefill at ~0.5%, is in relative percent rather than microseconds and is therefore omitted from the chart):

Operator or chain Noise band & unit Calibration method (A/A replica vs. multi-run span) Recorded run count & chapter
Dense projection threshold 0.15 µs Gate set above the 0.13 µs max same-process A / A paired diff 14-run alternating ABBA (this section)
Single-request gemv 0.29 µs 4-median span (14.59–14.88 µs) of v8 across 2 GPUs × 2 orders (not an A / A replica) 4 rounds × 500 launches per median (Chapter 4, Section 6)
Multi-token GEMM 0.35 µs Threshold chosen between the 0.16 µs untouched-TT shift and the 0.54 µs 4-round median span 4 rounds of graph-replay medians (Chapter 6, Section 8)
Persistent expert kernel ±0.40 µs Same-process paired A / A replica spread Run count not recorded (Chapter 8, Section 9; Section 9 below)
Single-layer evolution chain 0.50 µs Cross-GPU arm resolution floor of the single layer (0.1–0.7 µs at T=1; note the unit is µs, not 0.5%) 500 graph replays per median (Chapter 9, Section 1)
Long-sequence prefill (not plotted below) ~0.5% Same-process paired A / A replica relative spread (in percent) Run count not recorded (Chapter 9, Section 1)

What is the catch with paired ABBA benchmarking? Each group takes 4 runs, and both A and B have to stay loaded in the same process at the same time (see Section 5 for how to keep their device memory allocations from crowding each other and skewing the numbers). Also, if a non-linear jump like a sudden clock drop hits mid-run, the symmetric order cannot cancel it out (we did not measure behavior under such sudden jumps). And if one side computes wrong outputs, paired ABBA timing cannot make the delta meaningful either—so always check outputs before timing (see Section 4).

4Before Timing, How Do We Verify That a Version's Output Is Correct—and Stays Correct Every Time?

A version that computes wrong outputs can look faster because it skips work or changes power draw, so always check outputs before timing. Intermittent data races take large replay counts: seeing 0 errors in NN runs shows only, with ~95% confidence, that the failure rate is below 3/N3/N.

Always feed your tests non-zero random inputs rather than all-zero tensors: all-zero inputs can give you artificially fast readings (we did not measure the exact cause separately).

Timing a version that produces wrong outputs is pointless. In one full-layer comparison, we ran A several times in a row and then B several times in a row, and B came out ~8.55% faster than A—only for us to check the outputs and find that B was wrong. Two things were tangled up in that gap: B computed corrupted values (which can change chip power draw), and running A then B mixed in drift (see Section 3); we did not measure how much each contributed. Once we fixed the bug and re-tested with 20 groups of paired ABBA benchmarking, the speedup vanished completely.

Outputs must be checked against a numerical tolerance (the maximum error allowed relative to the reference implementation) rather than bitwise equality: the PTX specification leaves Tensor Core internal accumulation order, rounding, and subnormal handling unspecified (and FP8 wgmma with .f32 accumulators accumulates at lower than single precision), so valid rewrites can shift low-order rounding bits (this chapter records no single tolerance value; the tolerance is set per kernel against its reference implementation). Even after a single-run output check passes, you still have to watch out for intermittent concurrency data races. You can catch shared-memory read/write hazards and CTA barrier misuse with racecheck and synccheck in NVIDIA's runtime checking tool compute-sanitizer—but neither tool can see cross-kernel global-memory data races.

To catch an intermittent cross-kernel data race, your only option is counting errors across a huge number of replays (isolated gemv is a single kernel with no cross-kernel race, so take the topk_ids data race from Chapter 9, Section 5 instead): the Top-8 kernel on the side stream writes the 8 selected expert indices to the global buffer topk_ids (made visible across SMs through the shared L2 cache), while early-dispatched CTAs of the experts kernel on the main stream—launched early via PDL (which lets the next kernel start before the previous one finishes, provided it stops at griddepcontrol.wait before reading the previous kernel's output; see Chapter 1, Section 4)—read topk_ids before their griddepcontrol.wait returned—whenever they beat Top-8's write arrival at L2, they read stale indices left from the previous graph replay, and the fix moves griddepcontrol.wait ahead of the first topk_ids read. On a T=1 full-attention layer, that race showed up only about once every 11,000 CUDA Graph replays, and at T=8 it took about 840,000 replays to trigger once.

So how many error-free replays does it take before you can say a data race is fixed? That comes down to the rule of three. If the true per-run failure rate is pp, the probability of seeing zero errors across NN consecutive runs is:

(1−p)N≈e−pN(1 - p)^N \approx e^{-pN}

Set that probability to 5%5\% and take the natural log: since ln⁡0.05≈−3\ln 0.05 \approx -3, you get pN≈3. In other words, seeing 0 errors across NN consecutive replays does not prove the bug is gone—it only tells you with ~95%95\% confidence that the true failure rate pp sits below 3/N3/N. This bound assumes independent replays and an equal failure rate across GPUs; in Chapter 9, Section 5 one GPU failed far more often than the others, so the bound constrains the average failure rate across those GPUs.

Let's plug the numbers from Chapter 9, Section 5 into that formula. After the fix, 567,200 consecutive replays on the T=1 full-attention layer (including the outlier GPU) produced 0 severe numerical corruptions. By the rule of three, that pushes the upper bound on the severe numerical corruption rate down to 3/567,200≈5.3×10−6. Before the fix, the failure rate was ~9.2×10−5: if the data race were still there, 567,200 replays should have hit it ~52 times, so seeing 0 proves the fix worked. Now look at T=8: the original race triggered only about once every 840,000 runs. After the fix, we ran 556,000 replays and saw 0 errors—but even if the bug were completely unfixed, 556,000 runs would be expected to hit it only ~0.7 times, so that 0 proves nothing. Moving griddepcontrol.wait earlier cost +1.35, +1.24, +0.16 (inside the ~0.5 µs noise band), and +1.19 µs in latency across the 4 layer shapes (T=1 sliding, T=1 full, T=8 sliding, and T=8 full; see Chapter 9, Section 5).

The catch with this check is that replay counting takes a lot of time: bounding the failure rate below pp takes at least ~3/p3/p runs, and turning on compute-sanitizer slows the kernel down heavily too (we did not measure the slowdown factor). When an intermittent race has an ultra-low trigger rate like the T=8 case above, the replay count NN you can practically run is too small to push 3/N3/N below the original failure rate. At that point, only a proof from the memory-model specification itself can settle it (see Chapter 9, Section 5).

5How Do We Keep the Measurement Harness from Altering the Tested Kernel?

When probing timestamps inside a kernel, hold readings in registers and write them out at exit; when comparing two versions, keep the device memory allocation layout unchanged.

CUDA event timing gives you only the end-to-end duration of the whole kernel. If you want to know how long one slice inside a kernel takes—say, the prologue or the reduction tail step—you have to drop a timestamp probe into the kernel: a snippet of code that reads the clock and logs stage-by-stage elapsed time. That probe reads %globaltimer, a 64-bit global nanosecond timer register predefined by the PTX specification: whereas clock64() (%clock64) counts clock cycles on one SM, %globaltimer reads nanoseconds from one timer for the whole GPU (see Chapter 2, Section 2 and Appendix B, Item 62). The specification notes that this register is meant for NVIDIA tools and behaves in a target-specific way, without promising that readings across different SMs are strictly synchronized. On H200, we measured its smallest non-zero step at 32 ns, only 1/25 of the ~0.8 µs gaps in Chapter 9, Section 6. We did not measure whether readings skew across SMs, so whenever a sub-1 µs gap comes from subtracting timestamps across CTAs, this book treats it as an estimate only.

Write the probe the wrong way and it will directly stretch the code you are trying to measure. Recorded timestamps eventually have to go out to a global memory buffer; if every probe point first loads that buffer's output address from global memory, each probe adds a global memory load, and the store has to wait for that load to come back. We measured the elapsed time from function entry to the first useful compute instruction on a dense projection kernel, with the result shown in the chart below: a probe that loads the output pointer from global memory at every timestamp takes 0.576 µs longer than a probe that holds timestamps in registers and writes them out at exit—as large as the entire prologue the experiment was trying to measure (~0.1–0.6 µs), and larger than the reorderable portion inside it (0.06–0.4 µs). Holding timestamps in registers and writing them out at the end adds only a few register moves inside the measured interval.

Next, look at how device memory allocation affects neighboring operators. When we allocated an extra 84.9 MB buffer for new weights during setup, we measured a ±0.5%–1% latency shift on subsequent neighboring operators whose code we had not touched at all—for instance, unpooler at T=32 slowed down by ~0.5%, enough to drown out small real wins. Pointers inside a kernel hold virtual addresses that get converted to physical addresses during memory access (PTX §8.2; see Appendix D, Section 1); we did not measure the underlying physical-page placement or address-mapping mechanism, and we infer that allocating an extra buffer alters the virtual and physical addresses the device memory allocator assigns to subsequent tensors, shifting which HBM partitions they map to (see Chapter 2, Section 2).

So when you compare two versions, do not change the order or total byte count of device memory allocations. You can keep the layout fixed in two ways: either build the new-format weights in place inside an old buffer that is no longer used, or use a fixed device memory pool where all tensors are carved at fixed offsets out of one pre-allocated block of device memory. In that C12 (the 12-bit lossless packing of WW from Chapter 6, Sections 1–2) experiment, once we built the packed weights in place inside unused existing buffers (keeping total allocated bytes unchanged), 0 of 27 untouched neighbor cells shifted outside the gate, cleanly exposing the real T=1 C12 wins (−0.968, −0.867, and −0.500 µs on pooler, qkv_gate, and unpooler). Also, a CUDA Graph saves each kernel's parameters—every address included—at capture time, and every replay reuses those exact addresses. To change an address, you first update the graph with Graph Update (for example cudaGraphExecKernelNodeSetParams) and only then replay it (see Chapter 1, Section 2). So any temporary workspace buffer used for timing must also be allocated and warmed up before you capture the graph.

These precautions have their own costs. Because registers are allocated per thread (in 256-register warp units; see Chapter 3, Section 1), holding one 64-bit timestamp costs 2 32-bit registers per thread across every thread that holds it (so the SM's 65,536-register pool pays that cost multiplied by the resident threads), which in a kernel already near its register cap can lower occupancy or trigger register spilling (we did not measure the actual impact; see Chapter 3, Section 1). A fixed device memory layout is also more tedious to maintain, and it only keeps neighboring operators steady rather than making anything faster. Finally, when a single execution of the candidate code is shorter than 32 ns, in-kernel timestamp probing cannot resolve it; as long as that code runs enough times for its total cost to clear the noise band, you can measure it from the outside with the perturbation test in Section 8.

6The Outer Three Levels (Levels 1–3): Which Metric Do We Check on the Timeline, the Full Chip, and a Single SM, and What Fix Does Each Point To?

Diagnose from the outside in: check first whether the timeline has gaps, then how many bytes the full chip reads and whether it has a tail wave, and finally whether a single SM spills registers or falls short on bytes in flight.

Until you rule out outer-level bottlenecks, do not rush to tune inner-level code—the code you optimize may not even sit on the critical path (see Section 8, and the gemv v9 lesson at Level 5 in Section 7 where cutting ~24% of instructions gave zero speedup).

Before stepping into Level 1, the table below maps all six levels walked across Sections 6 and 7 from the outside in:

Level Hardware unit Tool or panel First reading to check Where the fix is taught
Level 1: Timeline Host launch queue & GPU front-end handoffs Nsight Systems timeline CPU launch gaps and inter-node hardware handoff gaps between adjacent kernels Section 6 (Level 1); Chapter 1, Sections 1, 2, 4; Chapter 9, Sections 4–6
Level 2: Full Chip HBM, 60 MiB L2, and all 132 SMs NCU SOL + Memory Workload Analysis; %globaltimer + %smid Achieved HBM bandwidth % of peak, dram__bytes_read.sum, and whether a few SMs drag out a tail wave Section 6 (Level 2); Chapter 2, Sections 1–7
Level 3: Single SM Register file, SMEM (32 banks), and L1 coalescing sectors ptxas -v / cuobjdump -res-usage; NCU Memory Workload, Launch Statistics, Occupancy Zero register spills, per-SM bytes in flight, sector efficiency & SMEM bank conflicts, resident CTAs/occupancy Section 6 (Level 3); Chapter 3, Sections 1–9
Level 4: SMSP Scheduler 4 SMSP warp schedulers per SM & scoreboards NCU Scheduler Statistics, Warp State, Source Counters (-lineinfo) Active issue-slot share (issue_active), no eligible cycle share, and top stall sampling reasons Section 7 (Level 4); Chapter 4, Sections 1–6
Level 5: Execution Pipelines FMA, ALU, 4-lane SFU, LSU, Tensor Core & 1-inst/cycle issue slot NCU Compute Workload Analysis Per-pipeline utilization and total executed instructions (one saturated pipe vs. saturated issue slots) Section 7 (Level 5); Chapter 5, Sections 1–8; Chapter 7, Sections 8–9; Chapter 8, Section 13
Level 6: SASS 128-bit machine instruction stream & in-register ops cuobjdump --dump-sass Drain waits after HGMMA, sunk prefetches or rematerialized invariants, pending LDS before empty[s] arrive, in-register bit decode Section 7 (Level 6); Chapter 6, Sections 1–7; Chapter 8, Section 8

Start at Level 1: Timeline (see Chapter 1, Section 1). Open the system-wide timeline profiler Nsight Systems: it plots CPU launches and the start and end of every GPU kernel on the same timeline, so you can see at a glance whether idle gaps sit between adjacent kernels. If tensor shapes are fixed and CPU launch gaps show up on the timeline, capture the chain into a CUDA Graph (see Chapter 1, Section 2). If hardware handoff gaps from the predecessor's tail still remain between adjacent graph nodes after capture, turn on PDL so the dependent kernel enters early (see Chapter 1, Section 4). Only small kernels whose gaps even PDL cannot hide are worth fusing.

Chapter 9, Section 6 showed what happens when you ignore that rule: fusing kernels that were already hidden—or merging stages into a megakernel—made execution slower instead. On the gemv chain, the step at this level is v2 (see Chapter 1, Section 5): capturing the 3-kernel Stage 1 chain into one CUDA Graph cut the pre-queued chain from 61.6 µs to 60.0 µs (2-GPU mean, saving ~1.6 µs, exact source not determined; the ~41.0 µs drop from the 102.6 µs unpaced stream came from harness queue pre-filling rather than v2, the 2 intra-graph hardware handoffs remain, and standalone gemv itself sits unchanged at 54.19 µs vs. v1's 54.08 µs).

Once the timeline is packed tight, zoom in to Level 2: Full Chip (see Chapter 2, Sections 1–3). First put your measured latency next to the theoretical lower bound: for gemv, reading WW once has a bandwidth lower bound of 7.86 µs (see Primer 2, Section 1). Next check two numbers in NCU: achieved HBM bandwidth as a percentage of peak in the Speed Of Light (SOL) panel, and measured HBM bytes read (dram__bytes_read.sum) in the Memory Workload Analysis panel (or collected directly as a raw counter, where prefixes lts__t, lts__m, and lts__d denote the Tag, Miss, and Data stages of L2 cache slices LTS, see Appendix D, Section 1: checking lts__t_sector_hit_rate shows overall cold-L2 hit rate—for example, 3.07% measured on gemv v7, within which L1TEX read sectors hit at 1.68% from the reused 16 KiB input xx alone (20,204 hits out of 1,200,296 sectors, while the dominant 37.75 MB weight matrix WW never hits) and the rest of the 3.07% is not split (the xx-removed control v7nox has 0 L1TEX read-sector hits yet still shows 2.03%, source not determined), matching why v3 → v4's L2 hints in Chapter 2, Section 7 and Section 2 above barely move hit rates under a clean flush). Those two numbers put you in one of three cases:

  • measured bytes read significantly exceed algorithmically required bytes: global loads are uncoalesced or cache thrashing re-reads the same bytes; drop to Level 3 to check coalescing and cache behavior.
  • measured bytes read equal required bytes, but achieved bandwidth is a low share of peak: either per-SM in-flight reads are too shallow (check Level 3), or fixed ramp-up and tail costs on a short kernel dilute the whole-kernel average (so only reading fewer bytes helps).
  • measured bytes read equal required bytes and achieved bandwidth is near peak: ramp and tail are amortized and the kernel sits against HBM's physical ceiling, so schedule tweaks cannot buy large wins and the only lever left is reading fewer bytes—compressing bit-width (Chapter 6, Section 4) or keeping shared inputs in L2 (Chapter 2, Section 4).

A classic case-2 kernel is gemv v9: NCU measures 37.78 MB read (almost identical to the 37.75 MB of WW), yet whole-kernel bandwidth over its 12.03 µs NCU span averages only ~66% of the 4.8 TB/s peak (3.14 TB/s). In-flight depth is not the culprit: counted in SASS before first use, v9 fires an opening burst of 7 16 B loads of WW (61.1 KiB / SM) and sustains 3–7 loads per thread (~26–61 KiB / SM), already reaching or exceeding the full-load 95% knee band given in Level 3, Step 2 below (see Chapter 2, Section 3 and Chapter 4, Section 3). Why only 66% on average, then? A measured row-count sweep on v7 showed marginal weights already streaming at the 4.54–4.59 TB/s plateau (8.32 µs per extra 37.75 MB = 4.54 TB/s; v9's own steady state was not measured separately); transferring that measured rate to v9 estimates its 12.03 µs NCU span as ~8.3 µs streaming at the plateau plus ~3.7 µs of fixed ramp-up and tail that do not scale with bytes (see Chapter 4, Section 6; ~6.5 µs fixed including launch/events inside the 14.83 µs event span). Because steady-state streaming is already at the plateau and 37.75 MB is too small to amortize the fixed ends, deeper prefetch or fewer math ops cannot shorten runtime—the next lever is reading fewer bytes, as v10 does in Chapter 6, Section 3.

For case 3 (which, as inferred from the 8.3 + 3.7 µs estimate above, single-request gemv cannot show because moving tens of MB does not amortize the fixed ends), the Stage 6 small-batch cooperative expert kernel at T=32 (see Chapter 8, Section 6; already streaming 4-bit NVFP4 weights at 28.3 MB per touched expert, see Chapter 8, Sections 1–2) runs in 96.8 µs at 83.6% of the 4.8 TB/s nominal peak (near the 94.6% measured streaming plateau), leaving byte reduction as the only lever there as well.

While you are at the full-chip level, also check whether all 132 SMs finish together. Probe %globaltimer and %smid (the current SM ID) at kernel entry and exit using the pattern from Section 5. If you see the final batch of CTAs dragging on across only a few SMs, you have a tail wave. In gemv v1, for example, launching one CTA per row fills 2,112 CTA slots in the first wave and leaves the remaining 192 CTAs as a tail wave (see Chapter 2, Section 1); v3 splits each of those 192 rows into two half-row CTAs to flatten that tail wave (see Chapter 2, Section 7).

Once you rule out the full-chip lower bound and tail waves, step into Level 3: Single SM (see Chapter 3) and check four readings in order:

  1. ptxas -v prints each kernel's register count and register-spill byte counts (spill stores / loads). Check first that spilling is 0; the moment it is non-zero, register accesses degrade into round trips to local memory in device memory (see Chapter 3, Sections 1 and 8). That same line also reports bytes stack frame, and STACK and LOCAL in cuobjdump -res-usage should likewise be 0: a non-zero count signals non-inlined function calls, dynamically indexed local arrays, or spills, all stored in local memory (Binary Utilities §2.1.3; PTX §5.1.5). Inside NCU, you can also read sass__inst_executed_register_spilling_mem_local and _mem_shared (NCU §2.4.14) to count how many spill load and store instructions actually ran to local memory versus shared memory (see Chapter 3, Sections 1 and 8).
  2. Next, check whether each SM keeps enough bytes in flight. In our H200 in-flight measurement streaming 4 GiB concurrently across all 132 SMs, reaching 95% of the bandwidth plateau takes about 24–40 KiB / SM in flight in machine code with ordinary 16 B ld.global loads (depending on loads per thread; at 1–4 loads per thread, 32 KiB / SM already reaches about 95%–98% of the plateau) and about 36–40 KiB / SM with TMA (32 KiB with 2 KiB copies at 4 CTAs / SM), while 64 KiB / SM is enough (reaching at least 98.3% across all tested configurations) but not the minimum; by Little's Law, if only half the SMs are reading, the bytes in flight each SM must keep outstanding double. These numbers are bandwidth knee points measured at full load; because round-trip latency is shorter under lighter load, falling slightly short of the threshold gives up very little bandwidth. In Chapter 3, Section 4, however, v6 shrank each CTA to 1 warp, dropping machine-code bytes in flight to 8.7 KiB / SM (1 16 B load per thread—far below 24, 32, and 64 KiB / SM) and slowing the kernel right down.
  3. Third, open NCU's Memory Workload Analysis panel (the small colored squares along unit edges in the Memory Chart show data-port utilization, while raw counter prefixes lsuin, l1tex__t, l1tex__m, and l1tex__d denote the input, Tag, Miss, and Data stages of L1TEX, see Appendix D, Section 2: checking l1tex__t_sector_hit_rate verifies whether data reused across CTAs on one SM stays in L1 instead of getting evicted by streaming weights—for example, gemv reads equal sector counts of streaming WW and the 16 KiB input xx (2,359,296 global load sectors on v7 = 2×W sectors, with 1,111,976 hits ≈\approx 94.3% of xx sectors vs. 0% on v7nox), so the measured 47.08% L1 sector hit rate confirms that xx reused across CTAs on the same SM already hits in L1, which is why adding v3 → v4's L1 eviction hints in Chapter 2, Section 7 barely moved the L1 hit rate) to also check what fraction of bytes in each global memory request is actually used (see Chapter 3, Section 2) and whether shared memory hits bank conflicts (see Chapter 3, Section 9).
  4. Fourth, in the Launch Statistics and Occupancy panels, check the resident CTAs per SM and the achieved occupancy (see Chapter 3, Section 1).

Putting the thread → warp → warpgroup → SMSP → SM mapping for Levels 2–3 into one table ties together slot counts, bytes in flight, role-based register rebalancing, and the pigeonhole bound where 18 warps across 4 SMSPs put at least ⌈18/4⌉=5 warps on one SMSP to cap registers per thread (Hardware Limit 1 in Section 10; for the hardware pool sizes, see Chapter 3, Section 1 and Chapter 4, Section 1):

Case Threads / warps / warpgroups per CTA Per-SM residency & limiting pool How wave capacity, bytes in flight, or registers/thread follow
gemv v1 (Level 2 tail wave) 128 threads = 4 warps 16 CTAs / SM (capped by the 64-warp = 2,048-thread SM limit: 64÷4=16) Wave 1 holds 132×16= 2,112 CTAs, leaving 2,304−2,112= 192 tail CTAs; 1 × 2 B load/thread ⟹16×128×2 B= 4.0 KiB / SM
gemv v6 vs. v7 (Levels 3–4 bytes in flight) 32 threads = 1 warp 2,304 CTAs across 132 SMs average 17.45 warps / SM (below the 32-CTA/SM slot cap) v6 keeps 1 × 16 B load/thread: 17.45×32×16 B= 8.7 KiB / SM; v7 hoists 8 opening loads: 8×8.73= 69.8 KiB / SM (v8 / v9 hoist 7 = 61.1 KiB / SM)
2-consumer-WG heavy GEMM (Chapter 3, Section 8) 384 threads = 12 warps = 3 warpgroups (1 producer + 2 consumer) 1 CTA / SM (3 warps on each of the 4 SMSPs, balanced) setmaxnreg gives producers 40 and consumers 232 regs/thread: 128×40+2×128×232=64,512≤65,536, fitting inside one SM's register file
4-consumer-WG persistent expert m4 (Chapter 8, Section 9; Section 10 Limit 1) 576 initial threads (18 warps: 4 consumer WGs + 2 producer warps), 608 final (19 warps) 1 CTA / SM (65,536 regs/SM split across 4 SMSPs at 16,384 each) Giving 4 consumer WGs 232 regs needs 512×232=118,784>65,536; under any placement, the busiest SMSP holds at least ⌈18/4⌉=5 warps (160 threads, billed as 4×160= 640 threads per SM), capping each thread at ⌊16,384/160⌋8=⌊65,536/640⌋8= 96 registers (640×96=61,440≤65,536)

7The Inner Three Levels (Levels 4–6): Which Metric Do We Check on the Scheduler, Execution Pipelines, and SASS?

Check first whether the scheduler has an eligible warp every cycle and what stall reasons dominate; then check which execution pipeline or issue slot is saturated; finally, read the SASS machine code to see whether the compiler inserted drain waits or reordered instructions.

Follow the lower half of Figure 10-3 into Level 4: SMSP Scheduler (see Chapter 4). At a fixed cycle interval, the profiler samples a warp and logs whether it issued an instruction on that cycle or why it could not issue. A hardware sampler inside each SM performs this check: without modifying the code, every fixed number of cycles it picks a random active warp and outputs its program counter and scheduler state, while on that same cycle the scheduler may issue a different warp. The interval can be set to 25+n2^{5+n} cycles (n=0..31), and by default NCU picks the minimum interval for the chip (for example, every 32 cycles on small devices or 2,048 cycles on larger chips in the documentation); our H200 runs did not record this value. The share of non-issuing samples attributed to a given reason is its stall sampling share (note that the profiler counts not selected as one of the reasons). In the Scheduler Statistics panel, check the active issue-slot share and the share of cycles with no eligible warp; for the breakdown of stall reasons, check the Warp State panel; and to map stalls back to exact source lines, compile with -lineinfo and open the Source Counters page.

If issue slots are busy and the top warp state is not selected, your warps are already eligible and simply yielded that cycle's issue slot to another warp on the same scheduler (see Chapter 4, Section 1). On the early Gluon gate/up kernel in Stage 6 at T=16, for instance, NCU measures issue_active = 75.8% (~3/4 of cycles issuing an instruction) with not_selected = 33.6% as the top warp state. When you see that reading, skip straight to Level 5. If the no eligible share is high instead, match the top stall reason against the list below—check first the five reasons measured on our kernels (long_scoreboard, mio_throttle / short_scoreboard, barrier, wait, and cold-start no_instructions); the other three (lg_throttle, sleeping, and drain) did not appear in this book's recorded profiles and are listed for reference:

  • long_scoreboard: warps are waiting for global memory loads to come back, either because per-thread in-flight reads are too shallow or because address math has serial dependencies (see Chapter 4, Section 2). On gemv, the number to watch is average stall cycles per issued instruction: v6 stalls for 12.9 cycles, and v7 drops to 8.1 once we expand per-thread in-flight WW loads to 8.
  • lg_throttle: the SM's LG instruction queue for global and local memory accesses is full, keeping the warp from even issuing its memory instruction (whereas long_scoreboard means the instruction already issued and is waiting for data to return). Per the NCU documentation, this usually shows up only when global or local memory instructions fire at extreme density, and register spills to local memory (Section 6, Step 1) can trigger it as well; fix it by dropping redundant global accesses, eliminating spills, combining narrow memory ops into wider ones, and interleaving memory ops with math. NVIDIA does not publish the queue depth; none of this book's recorded profiles reports this stall.
  • mio_throttle / short_scoreboard: MIO is the SM's memory input/output instruction queue. It carries shared-memory instructions, special math instructions such as MUFU, and dynamic branches; once it fills up, later instructions have to wait. short_scoreboard means a warp is waiting for the result of an MIO operation—most often a shared-memory load sitting too close to the instruction that uses it, though frequent MUFU or dynamic branches can cause it too. The fix is to separate the producer and consumer instructions (see Chapter 4, Section 2). mio_throttle means the MIO queue itself is full; the fix is to send fewer instructions into that queue or offload work to another pipeline. In our prefill attention experiments (see Chapter 7), for example, cutting mio_throttle from 22.7% to 13.5% saved 22.7% of runtime.
  • barrier: warps arrive at the CTA barrier __syncthreads at uneven times (see Primer 3, Section 3). Fix it by balancing the work across warps or switching to a named barrier that waits on only a subset of threads (see Chapter 5, Section 8 and Chapter 7, Section 7). In our prefill attention experiments (see Chapter 7), cutting barrier stalls from 46.7% to 13.7% saved 21.6% of runtime.
  • wait: NCU defines this as a warp waiting on a fixed-latency execution dependency. Based on public reverse-engineering analyses, the compiler encodes this stall count directly in the instruction's control bits—a format NVIDIA does not document (see Chapter 6, Section 6). The fix is more instruction-level parallelism or a better instruction order. For waits on the asynchronous matrix multiply wgmma.wait_group, see Chapter 5, Section 6. The NCU documentation files stalls on warpgroup wait instructions under warpgroup_arrive; whether WARPGROUP.DEPBAR.LE is the wait instruction it means was not verified by measurement.
  • no_instructions: the warp is waiting to fetch its next instruction or waiting on an instruction-cache miss (NCU §2.4.7). Each SMSP fetches from its own L0 instruction cache, and NCU also lists an instruction constant cache (ICC) shared across each Texture Processing Cluster, TPC (2 SMs). This is typical for very short kernels smaller than one full wave or code that jumps across large blocks of assembly. NVIDIA does not publish the cache capacities; on Chapter 7's earlier 1-request sliding-window split-KV kernel (Chapter 7, Sections 4 and 12), replaying right after an L2 flush put 23.6% of that kernel's samples in this stall, concentrated at kernel start (our profiling summary inferred a cold instruction cache as the cause; isolated time cost not measured).
  • sleeping: all threads in the warp are in a blocked, yielded, or sleep (nanosleep.u32 / SASS NANOSLEEP, whose actual sleep duration lies in [0,2t][0, 2t]; see Appendix B, Quick Reference 4) state (NCU §2.4.7). Spin-poll backoff uses this deliberately to yield issue slots to sibling warps on the same scheduler; if its share is high unintentionally, execute fewer NANOSLEEP instructions or shorten the delay. None of this book's recorded profiles reports this stall.
  • drain: after executing EXIT, the warp is still waiting for all of its outstanding memory operations to finish before its hardware resources can be freed (NCU §2.4.7). This commonly appears when a kernel writes out a large volume of data near the end, and can also reflect a tail wave; fix it by coalescing end-of-kernel stores or parallelizing reductions. None of this book's recorded profiles reports this stall.

Once you confirm that the scheduler is issuing instructions every cycle, step into Level 5: Execution Pipelines (see Chapter 5). Open NCU's Compute Workload Analysis panel and read the utilization of each physical execution pipeline along with the total executed instruction count:

  • one execution pipeline is near saturation while neighboring pipelines sit idle: rewrite the math on the crowded pipeline into equivalent instructions that run on an idle neighbor (see Chapter 5, Section 1). In the 128-key prefill loop of Chapter 7, for example, online softmax pushed the 4-lane SFU to 77.3%; offloading row sums and exponentials onto other pipelines dropped SFU utilization to 0.58% and cut runtime on the 65K full-attention prefill kernel by ~18% (see Chapter 7, Sections 8–9).
  • no single execution pipeline is saturated, yet issue slots are already busy: now the bottleneck is the issue slots themselves, because each SMSP can issue at most 1 instruction per cycle. Shuffling work between pipelines will not help; you have to cut the total instruction count directly through algebraic folding and packed instructions. That is how we caught the expert epilogue bottleneck in Chapter 8, Section 13: in the pre-fold 9-instruction gate/up epilogue, 4 warps on 1 SMSP needed 4×233=932 issue cycles versus 768 SFU cycles; folding the tensor scale into the exponent and denominator (9 → 7 instructions per element) saved 0.54–0.60 µs on Stage 6 at T=128/256 (bundled with a wide shared-memory job read, not split separately).

The classic cautionary tale at this level is gemv v9 from Chapter 5, Section 2: v9 applied a textbook Level 5 fix—breaking the accumulator dependency chain and switching to shift-and-mask unpacking to cut total executed instructions by ~24% (2.67 M → 2.02 M)—yet event latency went from 14.74 µs to 14.83 µs, not budging at all. The Level 2 reading from Section 6 tells you why: v9's runtime was pinned by both halves of its memory-side span—steady-state HBM weight streaming at the plateau (~8.3 µs estimated) plus fixed ramp-up and tail (~3.7 µs estimated inside the NCU span)—so issuing fewer math instructions only brought warps to the scoreboard wait earlier for the exact same 37.78 MB transfer. Level 5 fixes pay off only after you have cleared Levels 2–4.

Finally, drop down to Level 6: SASS (see Chapter 6, Section 6). Run cuobjdump --dump-sass to read the generated machine code directly, and check three things in particular:

  • Check whether the compiler inserted WARPGROUP.DEPBAR.LE gsb0, 0x0 (a drain wait) after every HGMMA (the SASS instruction for half-precision wgmma; see Chapter 5, Section 4). If it did, your async region has collapsed into one-by-one synchronous execution; see Chapter 6, Section 7 for the cause and the ptxas performance warning.
  • Check whether the compiler sank your early read-only prefetch ld.global.nc instructions past the PDL wait instruction from Chapter 1, Section 4, or repeatedly recomputed loop invariants inside the inner loop. Reading SASS is how we caught both rematerialization and instruction sinking in Chapter 8, Section 8.
  • Check whether the consumer of an on-chip ring buffer still has shared-memory loads in flight when it arrives on empty[s] (the barrier telling the producer that slot ss is free to refill; see Chapter 3, Section 7): if so, you have the write-after-read hazard (WAR) from Chapter 3, Section 7. After fixing it, scan the machine code to confirm that every shared-memory load (LDS in SASS) has returned before each arrival.

On the gemv chain, the Level 6 step is v10's in-register 12-bit lossless weight decoding in Chapter 6, Section 3 (9-instruction integer decode sequence in Chapter 6, Section 2): packing WW from 37.75 MB down to 28.4 MB (−24.8% bytes read, lowering the bandwidth floor from 7.86 µs to 5.92 µs) cuts matched BF16-output, no-epilogue latency from 14.91 µs (v9n) to 13.92 µs (v10n)—a measured saving of 0.99 µs (6.6%, ~7%; production v10 with fused epilogue is 15.09 µs). Why does cutting bytes by ~25% cut runtime by only ~7%? Apply the Level 2 split from Section 6: inside 14.91 µs, only the ~8.3 µs steady-state streaming portion scales with bytes (the other ~6.6 µs is fixed launch, event, and tail cost), so a 24.8% byte cut predicts ~2.1 µs (8.3×0.248≈2.06 μs, ~14% of 14.91 µs, estimated), never 25%; the remaining ~1.1 µs shortfall against the measured 0.99 µs (alongside the simultaneous 4-warp CTA reshape, +40% decode instructions, and shallower ~26.2 KiB / SM steady in-flight peak; see Chapter 6, Section 3) was not isolated.

8Is a Code Segment Truly on the Critical Path, and How Much Can Optimizing It Save at Most?

Skip the candidate code at runtime while keeping the machine code unchanged, and measure the latency delta with paired ABBA benchmarking: if latency stays flat, the main track hides that code; if latency drops, the drop is the maximum speedup you can get from fixing it.

On a GPU, HBM / TMA transfers, Tensor Cores, and ordinary arithmetic pipelines run in parallel along separate tracks (see Chapter 5, Section 1). Whenever a shorter arithmetic or synchronization branch sits completely hidden behind a slower main track, reducing that branch to 0 cycles leaves total runtime completely unchanged (see Chapter 4, Section 1).

How do you test whether a branch is hidden before you spend time rewriting it? Run the perturbation test (ablation test) shown in Figure 10-4: keep the non-zero random inputs unchanged, pass an extra runtime kernel parameter int run_seg, and guard the suspect code with if (run_seg) { /* candidate segment */ }—because run_seg is passed from the host at launch time (1 to execute in the baseline arm, 0 to skip in the test arm), ptxas cannot see its value at compile time, dead-code elimination and loop unrolling leave it intact, and cuobjdump --dump-sass confirms that both arms run the exact same 100% identical SASS binary; then measure the CUDA event timing delta with paired ABBA benchmarking. Despite the "ablation" name, it is strictly a runtime skip: the skipped instructions stay right where they are in the machine code, and you do not delete a single line of source.

A perturbation test gives you one of two outcomes:

The first outcome is total latency unchanged: the candidate branch is completely hidden behind a slower main track, so optimizing it buys you nothing. Single-request gemv runs its intra-CTA or intra-warp reduction sequentially after the streaming load-and-FMA loop (with no skip test recorded) and has no separate parallel side branch to test, so this section switches to Stage 5–6 operators. This book has no example of a runtime skip leaving latency unchanged; the MUFU.TANH experiment below modifies source code and serves only as corroborating evidence. In one version of the Stage 6 expert kernel (Figure 10-4 Mode 1), the activation epilogue used the hardware hyperbolic tangent instruction MUFU.TANH to compute sigmoid(x)=0.5(1+tanh⁡(x/2)). Deleting MUFU.TANH in source code changed total latency by 0.0%, whereas replacing it with a multi-instruction polynomial approximation slowed execution by 0.4%—corroborating indirectly that a single MUFU.TANH likely did not block the critical path. Assuming the ~125 non-SwiGLU epilogue issue slots per warp derived from the pre-fold ex2 epilogue stay unchanged, one gate/up subtask epilogue on 1 SMSP (4 consumer warps × 12 elements) needs 4×(6×12+125)≈ 788 cycles on the issue-slot main track (estimated; baseline tanh⁡\tanh-build cycles were not measured directly) versus 4×12×8= 384 cycles (derived, at 8 cycles per warp instruction) for the MUFU.TANH branch on the 4-lane SFU, putting the SFU branch shorter than the main track (see Chapter 8, Section 13 for the 932-vs.-768 cycle tally on the pre-fold 9-instruction form).

The second outcome is total latency decreases, as shown in Figure 10-4 Mode 2 and the chart below. For Stage 5 pooler at T=256, skipping the final cross-CTA reduction tail step (each split writes its partial sum and exits; whether this used a runtime switch with unchanged machine code was not recorded) cut latency by about 4.9 µs, from which we estimate the speedup upper bound for fixing that step. Only after confirming that upper bound did we rewrite the tail step as a TMA tile reduction following Chapter 5, Section 8; paired benchmarking measured a 2.66 µs net saving, well within the upper bound.

Why not just delete the code in the source file? Because the moment you delete source lines, ptxas sees a different control-flow graph (see Chapter 6, Section 6) and re-decides loop unrolling and register allocation across the whole kernel—so the compiled binary is no longer the same kernel. Take the persistent expert kernel in Chapter 8, Section 9 (where dedicated producer warps move data while consumer warpgroups stay resident on the SM running the wgmma main loop): we wanted to know the maximum possible savings from the entry step where consumers gather activations xx. Deleting that code in source bloated the machine code by ~12% and made the kernel run 23–26 µs slower instead (see Figure 10-4 Mode 3). Once we switched to a runtime skip, the machine-code size stayed identical. At T=256, even though we derived that the first HGMMA started 5–7 µs earlier, the whole kernel sped up by only a measured 3.11 µs (why a derived 5–7 µs earlier first HGMMA yields only 3.11 µs whole-kernel speedup was not determined)—and that measured 3.11 µs is the speedup upper bound for optimizing this section (see the chart below for each TT).

Here are the trade-offs of a perturbation test:

  • What you gain: you find out whether a code segment is worth optimizing before you spend time rewriting it.
  • What it costs: each suspect code segment requires compiling a separate binary with a runtime conditional switch and running a round of paired ABBA benchmarking; the runtime branch itself adds a few instructions, which sit in both the baseline and test arms and cancel out.
  • When it can mislead: if the skipped code produces data that later steps consume, the resulting corrupted values may steer subsequent code down a different control-flow path or alter power draw and clock frequency (see Section 4). Then the measured delta reflects more than just omitting that segment, and the upper bound is only a rough estimate.

9What Does It Take for a Change to Count as a Real Win?

For a change to count as a real win, it must clear three bars: exceed the noise band under paired ABBA timing, keep the same sign on re-runs, and cause no regressions across all input shapes inside the full layer.

The first rule combines Bars 1 and 2 (Bar 1: clear the noise band under paired ABBA timing; Bar 2: keep the same sign on re-runs, as in the 4-round sign check of Chapter 4, Section 6): fewer static instructions do not guarantee a speedup; the delta must clear the operator's A/A noise band and keep the same sign on re-runs (throughout this section we write latency change as Δt=tnew−told, so negative = faster, positive = slower). Single-request gemv has no large divergent branches (Section 3 already showed v8 → v9's instruction cut falling inside its noise band), so look at the Stage 6 persistent wgmma expert kernel of Chapter 8, Section 9: rewriting the second-stage writeback to use predicated execution cut the compiler-inserted branch reconvergence instruction BSSY (see Chapter 4, Section 4) from 123 instructions down to 58—more than a 50% reduction. Now look at paired ABBA benchmarking (chart below). At T=256, the change moved latency by −0.29 µs, while the A/A control arm of two identical copies in the same job differed by +0.25 µs on its own; at T=128, the change moved latency by +0.05 µs, against +0.14 µs on the control arm. Measured once per shape, both deltas fail Bar 1 right away (falling inside this kernel's ~±0.4 µs noise band), so we record zero speedup for the change. If you look only at static instruction counts or run only a single pass, you will mistake random jitter for a real speedup.

The second rule enforces Bar 3 (no regression on any shape in the full layer): after winning in an isolated kernel benchmark, a change must be re-tested inside the full layer across all input shapes. A change that wins when you benchmark the kernel in isolation does not necessarily win inside the full layer: SMs that sat idle in isolation may be busy running other kernels on parallel branches, occupancy can shift, and cross-kernel handoffs can slip out of alignment. Chapter 9, Section 7 gives two examples. At T=3,012, splitting the 84 second-wave tail tiles of qkv_gate along KK across the 48 SMs sitting idle in wave 2 inside the same kernel made qkv_gate finish 8.7 µs earlier by in-layer timestamps (167.6 → 158.9 µs; standalone single-kernel latency was not measured separately); under the same latency-change sign convention (negative = faster), total layer time got faster on sliding-window layers (−0.47% latency change, i.e., a +0.47% net speedup) but ran slightly slower on full-attention layers (+0.10% latency change, a 0.10% regression) where stage_kv on the side stream competed for SMs, so the final version enables it on sliding-window layers only. Likewise, whether concurrent stream scheduling wins or loses flips across token counts.

Whenever you report a speedup, state the measurement baseline explicitly: whether it is the isolated single-kernel cold benchmark from Section 2 of this chapter, or the single-layer CUDA Graph replay from Chapter 9, Section 1. Never mix numbers from the two measurement baselines in the same evolution chain.

What does enforcing these two rules cost? Verification time: every change takes at least two rounds of paired ABBA benchmarking plus a full-layer re-run across all input shapes. Small changes whose true gain is smaller than the noise band get filtered out by these rules; whether stacking multiple rejected small changes would clear the noise band was not measured.

10At the End of the Diagnostic Tree: Which Bottlenecks Cannot Be Fixed in Software?

After you walk all six levels of the diagnostic tree, four hardware limits on H200 remain that software can only work around, never eliminate.

  1. Hardware Limit 1: Register file capacity (Level 3). Single-request gemv does not use large-tile wgmma, 4-bit NVFP4, or paged row gathers, so the four limits below draw on multi-token GEMM, expert, and attention kernels. Large-tile matrix-multiplication accumulators sit directly in the vector registers of the 4 warps, sharing each SM's pool of 65,536 32-bit registers with ordinary thread variables (see Chapter 3, Section 1 and the Section 6 mapping table above). Because each SMSP owns and allocates from its own slice of 16,384 registers, the SMSP holding the most warps sets the per-thread register cap for the CTA; under any warp-to-SMSP placement (the exact placement rule is undocumented; see Chapter 4, Sections 1 and 3), placing 18 (or 19) warps across 4 SMSPs puts at least ⌈18/4⌉=5 warps on one SMSP. On H200, software works around this by rebalancing registers across roles or shrinking each subtask's accumulator tile: in Chapter 3, Section 8, setmaxnreg squeezed the producer warpgroup down to 40 registers per thread and gave the 2 consumer warpgroups 232 registers per thread (128×40+2×128×232=64,512≤65,536); in Chapter 8, Section 9, with 4 consumer warpgroups in the persistent expert m4, 232 registers per consumer is impossible, forcing at most 64 token rows per subtask to run spill-free within the hard cap of 96 registers per thread (for the full arithmetic, see Row 4 of the Section 6 mapping table above; see Appendix A, Section 1 for the hardware fix).
  2. Hardware Limit 2: 4-warp warpgroup issue (Levels 4–5). Asynchronous matrix multiplication wgmma carries .sync.aligned: all 4 warps in the same warpgroup must execute the same instruction, or behavior is undefined (see Chapter 5, Section 4 and Appendix A, Section 2). On H200, software can only move data movement and slow releases onto dedicated producer or release warps (Chapter 8, Sections 9 and 11), never drop the 4-warp wgmma requirement itself (single-thread issue arrives in the next architecture; see Appendix A, Section 2). When we profile that Stage 6 persistent wgmma expert kernel here (see Chapter 8, Section 9 for the kernel structure), 84%–94% of the measured non-issuing stall samples at each HGMMA land on warpgroup_arrive. According to NCU's Profiling Guide, this means a warp is stalled on WARPGROUP.ARRIVE or a warpgroup wait instruction (NCU's manual describes warpgroup MMA as acting like a barrier across the 4 schedulers, whereas PTX .sync specifies only that the 32 threads within one warp wait for each other and leaves unspecified whether the 4 warps wait for each other; see Appendix A, Section 2 and Appendix B, Item 44). That reading alone cannot tell whether a warp is waiting for peer warps in its warpgroup or waiting for operands or completion.
  3. Hardware Limit 3: 4-bit weight conversion (Level 6). Hopper has no hardware instruction to convert 4-bit floating-point NVFP4 directly into BF16. Software on H200 works around this by overlapping branchless in-register integer unpacking with loads and matrix math (for hardware conversion and block-scaled MMA, see Appendix A, Section 3): unpacking every 8 four-bit weights takes 8 integer instructions, and you still have to multiply the unpacked values by the block scale before feeding them to a Tensor Core instruction (mma.sync in the small-batch kernel, or left operand AA of RS-mode wgmma in the large-batch persistent kernel; see Chapter 6, Section 5). Those 8 unpacking instructions are 2 SHF + 2 IMAD.SHL + 4 LOP3: SHF and LOP3 are the 6 instructions on the ALU pipeline, and IMAD.SHL is the 2 instructions on the FMA pipeline (offloading two left shifts onto FMA so ALU stalls less; see Chapter 6, Section 5). Whenever decoding takes longer than loading weights and multiplying matrices, operand supply cannot keep up (see Chapter 6, Section 4 and Chapter 8, Section 3).
  4. Hardware Limit 4: Non-contiguous row gather (Level 3). On Hopper, TMA tensor copies come in two modes only: rectangular tiles (tile) and im2col for convolutions (which rearranges elements from each convolution window into columns in SMEM; see Appendix D, Section 4), plus cp.async.bulk for 1D contiguous byte copies (see Chapter 3, Section 5 and Appendix B, Item 33). None of them can gather scattered rows by arbitrary row indices in one command. So when Chapter 7, Sections 5–6 read non-contiguous KV rows through a page table, tensor TMA is off the table, and each row has to move on its own: either every thread issues 16 B cp.async copies, or one 1D cp.async.bulk goes out per row. This book's decode and verify kernels do the former (see Chapter 7, Section 5).

Those four limits are the exact four lines inside the endpoint box at the bottom of the diagnostic tree in Figure 10-3 (Readings point to hardware itself → Appendix A).

Takeaway: Get the timing right first, walk the profiler level by level from the outside in, and bound the maximum speedup with a perturbation test before rewriting any code; only a change that clears the noise band and causes no regression inside the full layer counts as a real win.

Next question: Which of these four limits does the next-generation Blackwell (B200) architecture change in hardware, and how? → Appendix A.
