Appendix A

From H200 to B200: What Changes in Hardware, and Which Kernels in This Book Benefit?

  • Preface
  • Primer 1
  • Primer 2
  • Primer 3
  • Chapter 1 [Level 1]
  • Chapter 2 [Level 2]
  • Chapter 3 [Level 3]
  • Chapter 4 [Level 4]
  • Chapter 5 [Level 5]
  • Chapter 6 [Level 6]
  • Chapters 7–9
  • Chapter 10
  • Appendix A: From H200 to B200

Chapter 10, Section 10 left us with four hardware limits on H200 that software cannot change, and Chapter 8, Section 14 left a dispatch trade-off between persistent kernels and ordinary grids. Sections 1–4 below walk through how the next-generation Blackwell architecture (B200, target architecture sm_100a) changes the hardware at those four limits, and Section 5 covers one block-scheduling change outside those four limits that Chapter 8, Section 14 can use. For comparison, H200's compute capability 9.0 (see Chapter 4, Section 4) maps to targets sm_90 and sm_90a: TMA, thread block clusters, elect.sync, and griddepcontrol need only the forward-compatible sm_90 target, whereas an a-suffixed target enables architecture-specific features that run only on that exact generation and are neither backward nor forward compatible—on Hopper (which has no family target), wgmma and setmaxnreg require sm_90a, while on Blackwell tcgen05 (except .kind::i8) is supported on sm_100a and, from PTX 8.8, on the family-specific target sm_100f that also runs on later sm_10x chips.

For this book's code, any binary compiled for the architecture-specific sm_90a target runs only on compute capability 9.0 GPUs, so moving to B200 requires at least recompiling every kernel for sm_100a. A kernel that does not use wgmma needs only that recompilation: the mma.sync, setmaxnreg, and baseline sm_90 features it uses (TMA, clusters, elect.sync, and griddepcontrol) all still exist on sm_100a; examples are the gemv chain in Chapters 1–6 (v0 → v10), the g5 T=8 projection in Chapter 6, Section 8, and the m3 persistent kernel in Chapter 8 (none of these kernels was run on B200). A kernel that uses wgmma must also replace its matrix-multiply instructions, because wgmma exists only on sm_90a; to check a kernel, look for HGMMA or QGMMA in its SASS (Appendix B, Items 42–46). In this book, such kernels are the m64n256k16 heavy GEMM in Chapter 3, Section 8; the multi-token projections in Chapter 5, Sections 5–8 and Chapter 6, Section 8 (except g5 at T=8); the verify and prefill wgmma attention kernels in Chapter 7, Sections 5 and 7–10; and m2 (tiles taller than 8 rows), m4, and m5 in Chapter 8. The replacement instructions are TMEM and single-thread tcgen05.mma in Sections 1–2 below; Chapter 8's paths that unpack 4-bit weights in registers also need Section 3.

First, let's be clear about one thing: B200 speeds up single-request decode through wider HBM, not through the on-chip changes below. Dividing the public 8-GPU node spec by 8 gives a single B200 about 8 TB/s of HBM bandwidth. Counting only the fixed ~9.0 GB of dense and lm_head weights that each GPU reads on every forward pass (see Primer 1, Section 4), the weight-read lower bound drops from ~1.87 ms on H200 to ~1.12 ms. Note that this ratio compares weight-read lower bounds, not full decode latency (the lower bound leaves out the busiest GPU's expert weights and the KV cache; for handoff gaps and tail duration, see Chapter 9, Section 6; for CUDA Graph replay and the 186 cross-GPU collectives, see Chapter 9, Sections 8–9).

The first four changes live inside a single SM and Section 5 acts at the chip-wide block distributor; where they really help is prefill, large-batch verify, large-batch expert computation, and attention loads of non-contiguous KV rows. Every measurement in this book was taken on H200; we did not measure any latencies on B200, so the trade-offs in each section below are derived directly from the PTX specification and the CUDA Programming Guide.

1Can Accumulators Avoid Occupying Vector Registers?

Blackwell adds a dedicated 256 KiB Tensor Memory (TMEM) separate from vector registers, where fifth-generation Tensor Core instructions write their accumulators directly.

Recall the H200 register file capacity limit from Chapter 10, Section 10: with the wgmma tile shape from Chapter 5, Section 4, splitting a 64×256 FP32 accumulator (m64n256k16) evenly across 128 threads takes 64×256/128= 128 registers per thread—eating roughly half of the 255-register per-thread cap for the accumulator alone (Figure A-1, Mode 1, left).

Blackwell solves this by adding a dedicated on-chip TMEM (Tensor Memory), separate from the vector register file (see Figure A-1, Mode 1, right). In the PTX specification, each CTA on sm_100a sees a TMEM of 128 rows × 512 columns of 32-bit cells, so its capacity is:

128×512×4 B=256 KiB128 \times 512 \times 4\ \mathrm{B} = 256\ \mathrm{KiB}

At runtime, a CTA asks the hardware for TMEM columns with tcgen05.alloc (which blocks if not enough columns are free) and returns them with tcgen05.dealloc when done. The fifth-generation Tensor Core MMA instruction tcgen05.mma places accumulator DD directly in TMEM: left matrix AA can come from SMEM or TMEM, and right matrix BB comes from SMEM. Accumulator DD no longer occupies the vector register file from Chapter 3, Section 1. This change most directly helps large-tile prefill dense matrix multiplications whose operands already sit in SMEM (such as Chapter 3, Section 8's m64n256k16, which uses 128 accumulator registers per thread and caps each SM at 2 consumer warpgroups, whose time cost was not measured; note that at M=64 without .ws, single-CTA tcgen05.mma claims 256 columns while using only 16 of each warp's 32 rows at half Tensor Core datapath width, whereas M=128 uses all 32 rows at full width). Although Chapter 8, Section 15's T>1,024 expert path also holds 128 accumulator registers per thread (2 × m64n128k16), its 2-CTA-per-SM residency is simultaneously capped by shared memory (232,768 / 233,472 B on gemm1, about 227.3 / 228 KiB) and its RS-mode register weights require Section 3's staging or block-scaled route for tcgen05.mma, so moving the accumulator to TMEM alone does not raise residency; likewise, Chapter 8, Section 9's persistent wgmma expert kernel is capped at 96 registers per thread across 4 consumer warpgroups, runs RS m64n8k16..m64n64k16 (≤32\le 32 accumulator registers per thread, zero spills) because each subtask has at most 64 tokens, and also feeds weights from registers—whether TMEM makes either expert path faster was not measured.

Once the accumulator moves into TMEM, you can spend the freed vector registers on address calculation, prefetching, or higher occupancy. In return, you pay three costs: first, the kernel must explicitly call tcgen05.alloc / tcgen05.dealloc to claim and release TMEM; second, before the epilogue runs, it must pull the results back into general-purpose registers via tcgen05.ld; third, hardware restricts each warp in a warpgroup to accessing only its own 32 rows of TMEM (128 rows split across 4 warps). At small shapes like T=8, where the accumulator is already small and vector registers are plenty, that extra round trip between TMEM and registers adds overhead for zero gain.

2Can Matrix Multiplication Avoid Requiring 4 Warps to Issue Together?

wgmma requires 4 warps to issue together; tcgen05.mma is issued by a single thread.

Chapter 10, Section 10 showed the 4-warp warpgroup issue limit on H200: on Hopper, the accumulator is spread across the registers of all 4 warps (128 threads) in one warpgroup (Figure A-1, Mode 2, left). The wgmma.mma_async instruction carries the .sync.aligned suffix: under the PTX ISA specification, .aligned defines a thread group for each instruction and requires every thread in that group to execute the same instruction, or behavior is undefined (for wgmma and setmaxnreg, all 4 warps in the warpgroup; for bar.sync, which defaults to .aligned, the literal specification text says all threads in the CTA, and how partial-warp bar.sync id, n in Chapter 7, Section 7 corresponds to that literal wording was not determined in this book); meanwhile, .sync synchronizes the participating threads at the instruction (for wgmma.fence.sync.aligned, .sync synchronizes the 32 threads within one warp, while PTX does not state whether the 4 warps wait for one another there). Before issue, wgmma.fence orders register accesses; after issue, all 4 warps can run independent instructions while the Tensor Core executes in the background, and before reading or reusing the accumulator they call wgmma.wait_group so each thread waits for its own committed groups (PTX does not state whether the 4 warps wait for one another; see Chapter 5, Section 6).

Now that the accumulator lives in TMEM (Section 1), Blackwell's tcgen05.mma switches to single-thread issue just like TMA in Chapter 3, Section 5 (Figure A-1, Mode 2, right): launching a matrix multiplication takes only 1 thread in 1 warp issuing 1 instruction. That thread waits on an mbarrier until the data is ready (see Chapter 3, Section 7), while the remaining warps do not have to execute the MMA instruction and can go compute addresses, run activation functions, or move data on their own. This change is cleanest in pure SS matrix multiplications whose operands stay in SMEM across the whole K-loop and whose accumulator is read back only once in the epilogue (such as prefill dense projections, where the other 3 warps touch neither AA staging nor MMA issue throughout the K-loop). In Chapter 7, Section 7's verify two-heads attention and Sections 4 and 9–10's multi-warpgroup prefill attention, Q⋅K⊤ writes QQ to SMEM once in the prologue so 1 thread waits on KK and issues tcgen05.mma without per-tile AA staging, but because online softmax runs on every KV tile, all 4 warps still wait on the completion mbarrier and call tcgen05.ld every tile to read back scores SS. For RS-mode paths that today feed left operand AA from registers (such as decoded weights in Chapter 8, Section 9's persistent expert kernel and in-register softmax PP in attention's P⋅V), tcgen05.mma cannot read general-purpose registers: except in the expert-weight case when switching to Section 3's block-scaled route (with weights in AA read from SMEM via a-desc and tokens in BB), the 4 warps producing AA must first write their 32-row quarters into TMEM (tcgen05.st with wait and tcgen05.fence) or SMEM (with fence.proxy.async) and join on an mbarrier before that 1 thread issues tcgen05.mma—removing 4-warp lockstep at issue while moving peer-warp synchronization to that staging mbarrier (how much arrival skew ring buffering hides was not measured); in the epilogue, all 4 warps calling tcgen05.ld to read back the output likewise wait on the completion mbarrier signaled by tcgen05.commit.

The trade-off is that the single issuing thread has to manage mbarrier waits and completion notifications itself, and you have to repartition work in your kernel code to keep the freed warps busy. Also remember that the warpgroup_arrive stall does not tell you whether warps are waiting for peer warps in the warpgroup or waiting for data; if they are mainly waiting for data, switching to single-thread issue will not remove that wait either. How much each cause contributes was not measured on either H200 or B200.

3Can 4-Bit Weights Avoid Unpacking in Registers?

Blackwell adds both hardware 4-bit float conversion instructions and a zero-unpacking-instruction block-scaled MMA inside the Tensor Core; the former still requires multiplying E4M3 block scales separately and writing registers into TMEM or SMEM to feed tcgen05.mma, while the latter requires both inputs to be low-bitwidth floats and thus quantizing BF16 activations first.

We saw the 4-bit weight decompression limit on H200 in Chapter 10, Section 10: on Hopper (where 4-bit sub-byte mma.sync accepts only integer multiplicands on both sides and wgmma has no 4-bit type; see Chapter 6, Section 5), every 8 NVFP4 weights must first be unpacked in general-purpose registers into four BF16x2 registers with 8 SASS integer instructions and multiplied by their E4M3 block scale via HMUL2 before feeding small-batch mma.sync or RS-mode wgmma in the large-batch persistent kernel from registers (see Figure A-1, Mode 3, left, and Chapter 6, Section 5).

Blackwell offers two routes (see Figure A-1, Mode 3, right). Route A keeps activations unquantized to 4-bit and uses the new PTX hardware conversion instructions (4 PTX instructions per 8 weights): from PTX ISA 9.2 on, cvt.rn.bf16x2.e2m1x2 (added for the sm_100f family and usable on sm_100a under the .target family rule) converts directly to bf16x2; below PTX 9.2, only cvt.rn.f16x2.e2m1x2 (from PTX 8.6) is available, which also requires converting BF16 activations to narrower-exponent FP16 because tcgen05.mma.kind::f16 requires both operands to be FP16 or both BF16 (its numerical effect was not measured). How many machine instructions cvt compiles to and which pipeline it uses on sm_100a were not measured; the f16x2 form has no scale operand and the bf16x2 form's optional .scaled::n2::ue8m0 modifier accepts only UE8M0, so this model's E4M3 block scales still multiply separately in registers under both forms; and because sm_100a has no wgmma and tcgen05.mma reads left operand AA only from SMEM or TMEM, all 4 warps must then write the scaled registers to TMEM via tcgen05.st (with wait and mbarrier join) or to SMEM (with fence.proxy.async and mbarrier). Route B uses the fifth-generation Tensor Core's block-scaled MMA instruction tcgen05.mma...kind::mxf4nvf4.block_scale.scale_vec::4X (aliased as .block16 on sm_100f): under the PTX specification, single-CTA mode fixes M=128, both AA and BB must be 4-bit E2M1 floats, and pairing .scale_vec::4X with UE4M3 (7-bit unsigned E4M3 with MSB 0, matching this model's non-negative block scales; UE8M0 is also supported) applies one block scale per 16 elements and multiply-accumulates directly inside the Tensor Core (0 register unpacking or block-scaling instructions). That fits Chapter 8's Stage 6 expert computation, except that this model's expert activations are BF16 (see Primer 2, Section 2), so using Route B requires quantizing activations to NVFP4 first; although the alternative kind::mxf8f6f4 accepts FP8 activations with 4-bit E2M1 weights, it requires both AA and BB block scales to be one 8-bit exponent-only power-of-2 UE8M0 per 32 elements, so even this model's per-16 E4M3 weight scales cannot be fed as-is. Quantizing activations (or re-scaling weights) changes numerical results, which was not measured.

Hardware block-scaled MMA cuts out the in-register integer decoding instructions, so the ALU and FMA pipelines spend zero cycles decoding weights. Beyond the activation quantization above, you pay two costs: first, both low-bitwidth inputs (AA in SMEM or TMEM, BB in SMEM) and both operands' block scale factors (staged into TMEM first) must follow the exact block size and memory layout the hardware expects, or else loading requires an extra layout permutation; second, this model's NVFP4 weights also carry one tensor scale per tensor (see Chapter 8, Section 1) that this instruction does not apply, so you still have to multiply by it separately in the epilogue. Whether this model's existing weight layout can feed this instruction directly was not measured.

In the T=1 decode regime on H200, by the same mechanism measured on 12-bit gemv in Chapter 6, Section 4, software decoding instructions can hide behind the wait for weight bytes returning from HBM. Because B200's derived HBM bandwidth is about 1.67× that of H200, that latency-hiding window shrinks; whether software decoding still stays hidden on B200 was not measured.

4Can TMA Gather Non-Contiguous Rows by Row Index?

Blackwell TMA adds .tile::gather4 mode: a single command specifies 4 row indices, and hardware gathers all 4 rows directly into one SMEM tile.

We saw the non-contiguous row gather limit on H200 in Chapter 10, Section 10: here, one row means a 128 B K row or V row. When each page holds only 1 token, those KV rows sit scattered across device memory, so Hopper has to move each row on its own (per-thread cp.async copies, or one 1D cp.async.bulk per row); this book's kernels use per-thread cp.async (see Figure A-1, Mode 4, left, and Chapter 7, Section 5).

On Blackwell, TMA adds .tile::gather4 mode (Figure A-1, Mode 4, right): one TMA command gives the hardware 4 non-contiguous row indices, and TMA gathers all 4 rows and packs them into the same SMEM tile, cutting out the per-thread address math and the string of cp.async instructions. This change targets Stage 2 attention in Chapter 7, Section 5, where decode and verify gather non-contiguous KV rows one row at a time.

With .tile::gather4, gathering non-contiguous rows by row index can also run through single-thread-issued TMA. The catch is that .tile::gather4 supports only 2D tensors, taking a fixed 4 row indices and 1 starting column index each time. Those 4 row indices still have to be read from the page table first: the first two hops of Chapter 7, Section 6's three-hop entry chain (reading seq_lens and page_table to get the physical page slots, about 1.24 µs cold at CTA entry and hidden by lookahead in steady state) are unchanged, while the third hop is the gather4 transfer itself, so gather4 saves the per-lane address math and cp.async issue after the row indices return (whose runtime share on H200 was not measured). Moreover, even if consumers read a joint 128 B-row tile across both KV heads, each command moves only 4×128 B=512 B: by Little's Law (Chapter 2, Section 3), TMA on H200 needs about 36–40 KiB/SM in flight (95% knee; see Chapter 3, Section 6), or 48–60 KiB/SM for 98%; at 48 KiB that works out to about 96 commands (conversely, in the two-heads verify kernel implementation—sketched only as 256 B per token in Chapter 7, Sections 5 and 7, Figure 7-5 Mode 4—the source splits each 128 B row into two 64 B halves across two 64-byte-swizzled per-head SMEM blocks 4 KiB apart, with each consumer group's descriptor pointing to its own head's block; keeping that split per-head layout requires 2 commands of 4×64 B=256 B per 4 rows, or about 192 commands at 48 KiB; which layout B200 prefers was not measured). B200 has higher bandwidth and needs even more bytes in flight; whether 1 thread can issue commands that fast was not measured.

There are also cases where gather4 does not help: if the number of rows you need to gather is not a multiple of 4, the final request leaves some slots unused; and if each page holds multiple contiguous tokens, the rows within a page are already stored contiguously, so ordinary rectangular-tile TMA per page is all you need.

5Can Resident CTAs Take Over Blocks That Have Not Started?

Blackwell lets a CTA already running on an SM cancel an unstarted CTA and take over its block index in place—so each tile no longer needs a fresh CTA start, while hardware load balancing and preemption stay.

Sections 1–4 targeted the four H200 hardware limits from Chapter 10, Section 10 that software cannot change; this section turns to the dispatch dilemma we hit on prefill down-projection gemm2 in Chapter 8, Section 14. On H200, running gemm2 as a fixed-stride persistent kernel left SMs idle about 3 times as long on average as launching an ordinary grid under the hardware block distributor (see Figure A-2, Modes 1 and 2, and Chapter 8, Section 14); yet reverting to an ordinary grid pays a fresh CTA start and prologue on every tile, giving back what persistence buys (Chapter 3, Section 1: one start per resident slot, one prologue); that cost was not measured separately on gemm2. The software middle ground is claiming tiles from a global atomic counter (Chapter 8, Section 10), which wins only when each tile is much longer than the claim overhead and adds no intra-CTA barrier; when tiles are short and each claim adds an intra-CTA barrier while breaking the page-table prefetch pipeline, dynamic claiming loses instead (Chapter 7, Section 4).

Blackwell (compute capability 10.0, sm_100 and higher) introduces cluster launch control (Figure A-2, Mode 3). The caller still launches the full ordinary grid; while the first wave of CTAs runs on the SMs, 1 thread in a resident CTA issues an asynchronous cancellation request asking the hardware block distributor to atomically cancel a CTA in the grid that has not started executing yet (or an entire unstarted cluster when launched as clusters). The request is an async-proxy operation (Chapter 3, Section 7): hardware writes a 16 B opaque response into shared memory and subtracts those 16 B from the byte count of an 8 B mbarrier to signal completion; the core loop takes just a few cuda::ptx calls (CUDA's C++ wrappers for PTX instructions):

__shared__ uint4 result;     // 16 B cancellation response
__shared__ uint64_t bar;     // 8 B completion mbarrier
int phase = 0, bx = blockIdx.x;
if (threadIdx.x == 0) ptx::mbarrier_init(&bar, 1);
while (true) {
  __syncthreads();           // prevent next round from overwriting result before all threads finish reading
  if (threadIdx.x == 0) {
    ptx::fence_proxy_async_generic_sync_restrict(
        ptx::sem_acquire, ptx::space_cluster, ptx::scope_cluster);
    cg::invoke_one(cg::coalesced_threads(), [&]() {  // issued by exactly 1 thread; lets the compiler drop the per-lane peeling loop
      ptx::clusterlaunchcontrol_try_cancel(&result, &bar);
    });
    ptx::mbarrier_arrive_expect_tx(
        ptx::sem_relaxed, ptx::scope_cta, ptx::space_shared, &bar, sizeof(uint4));
  }
  compute_tile(bx);          // cancellation runs in the background while computing tile bx
  while (!ptx::mbarrier_try_wait_parity(ptx::sem_acquire, ptx::scope_cta, &bar, phase)) {}
  phase ^= 1;
  if (!ptx::clusterlaunchcontrol_query_cancel_is_canceled(result)) break;
  bx = ptx::clusterlaunchcontrol_query_cancel_get_first_ctaid_x<int>(result);
  ptx::fence_proxy_async_generic_sync_restrict(
      ptx::sem_release, ptx::space_shared, ptx::scope_cluster);
}

If the cancellation succeeds, the response carries the cancelled block's index (no other successful response in the grid carries the same index), and the resident CTA computes tile bx in place on the next iteration without a new CTA launch or repeated prologue. If the cancellation fails—because no unstarted blocks remain, or for another reason such as a higher-priority kernel being scheduled—the CTA breaks out and exits; in the latter case, the freed SM slot can run the higher-priority kernel first, after which hardware resumes dispatching the remaining blocks of this grid.

Cluster launch control avoids a fresh CTA start and prologue per tile while regaining hardware load balancing and preemption. Its costs and limits are equally concrete: each CTA permanently holds 16 B + 8 B = 24 B of shared memory (reused every turn), and each stolen tile executes 1 async cancellation request, 1 mbarrier wait, cross-proxy fences, and 1 intra-CTA barrier per loop turn to keep the next request from overwriting result early; moreover, once a CTA observes a failed cancellation response, issuing another try_cancel (or reading the block index of a failed response) is undefined behavior, so the loop exits right after the first failure. Because the kernel still launches with the full ordinary grid, the grid size remains fixed when recording a CUDA Graph, so Step 2's grid truncation in Chapter 8, Section 14 does not go away. How long a try_cancel round trip takes on B200, and whether per-turn intra-CTA barriers make it lose on microsecond-scale short tiles just as the software atomic queue did, were not measured in this book.

Takeaway: B200 addresses in hardware the four H200 limits that software can only work around, not remove, and lets resident CTAs take over unstarted blocks from the hardware block distributor—mainly helping prefill, large batches, and non-contiguous row gather in attention, while faster single-request decode still comes from wider HBM.

At the end of Appendix A, we asked: when you run into an unfamiliar SASS instruction, where does it come from, which hardware pipeline does it use, and which level does it belong to? This appendix covers the PTX and source-code forms discussed in the main text, figures, and Appendix D; the SASS column lists the mnemonics seen in this book's disassembly, with only Items 3, 23, 29, and 31 taken from earlier disassembly records records (marked "raw sample not retained" or "mapping from an earlier disassembly records"); entries without a retained disassembly sample are marked "Not recorded in this book's disassembly" (meaning no sample was retained, not that the opcode never appeared), and selected rows also note the corresponding opcode from the opcode table. We group them by function into four quick-reference tables, followed by an alphabetical mnemonic index at the end.

We assign each entry to a level by the hardware it uses, and the "Where used in this book" column points to the section that explains or uses it:

  • Level 1: Grid launch and handoff (see Chapter 1), and grid-wide synchronization (see Chapter 2, Section 6; Chapter 7, Section 12; and Chapter 8, Section 6).
  • Level 2: Operations that act directly on the central L2 cache or across SMs, including L2 residency hints, L2 atomics and reductions, and device-wide memory barriers and release/acquire operations (see Chapter 2), as well as L2 and tensor-descriptor prefetching (see Chapter 7, Section 6 and Chapter 9, Section 5) and thread block clusters and DSMEM (see Chapter 7, Section 12 and Chapter 9, Section 3).
  • Level 3: Data paths and resources inside a single SM, including normal global loads and stores through the local SM L1 cache, SMEM, TMA, cp.async, mbarrier, setmaxnreg, and intra-CTA memory fences (see Chapter 3; for intra-CTA memory fences, see also Chapter 8, Section 11), as well as the constant cache (see Chapter 4, Section 4).
  • Level 4: SMSP scheduling, including CTA and warp barriers, warp shuffles and integer reductions, leader-thread election, branches, and scoreboard waits (see Chapters 3–4 and Chapter 7), warp sleep (see Chapter 7, Section 12; Chapter 8, Section 7; and Chapter 10, Section 7), and warp votes (see Chapter 7, Section 9 and Chapter 8, Section 6), along with special-register reads such as thread and cluster indices (see Primer 3, Section 2 and Chapter 9, Section 3) and clock counters (see Chapter 10, Section 5).
  • Level 5: Execution pipelines and Tensor Core, including FMA, ALU, and SFU arithmetic and transcendental instructions, as well as matrix-multiply instructions (see Chapter 5 for the mechanism, and Chapter 6, Section 5 plus this appendix for the SASS mnemonics HMMA, HGMMA, and QGMMA).
  • Level 6: Bits and machine code, including bit permutation and packed type conversion, SASS encoding, and group flags encoded in the control bits; see Chapter 6.

1How Do We Dissect and Read a Single SASS Instruction?

A SASS mnemonic combines an opcode with modifier suffixes, followed by operands for the destination register, memory descriptor, and 64-bit address.

Getting from source code to machine code goes through three layers: CUDA C++ → PTX → the 128-bit (16 B) SASS instruction words emitted by ptxas (loaded at runtime into the SM's instruction cache, with the program counter advancing by 0x10 = 16 B per instruction; see Chapter 6, Section 5). Let's take Mode 1 in Figure B-1, LDG.E.EF.128 R8, desc[UR12][R8.64], and break it apart. This instruction is a 16 B-wide streaming global load with an L2 residency hint (see Chapter 2, Section 4 and Chapter 3, Section 3):

  • LDG: the opcode for a global memory load;
  • .E: an instruction modifier suffix that selects a 64-bit extended address;
  • .EF: a suffix carrying the evict_first eviction priority hint; NVIDIA does not document whether it acts on L1 or L2 (in this book's samples, the PTX specifies both L1::evict_first and an L2 residency policy, while the disassembly shows only one .EF suffix and one desc[URn] operand);
  • .128: each thread loads 128 bits (16 B) at once into four consecutive 32-bit vector registers R8..R11;
  • desc[UR12]: a 64-bit memory descriptor held in uniform register UR. We infer, but have not determined, that it encodes the L2 residency hint from Chapter 2, Section 4 (created with createpolicy in PTX). UR is shared across the entire warp (see Chapter 7, Section 7), and instructions whose mnemonics start with U read and write it;
  • [R8.64]: a 64-bit byte address formed by the register pair R8:R9;
  • .reuse (often seen on source registers of multi-source arithmetic instructions, such as R20.reuse): the official Best Practices Guide notes that the register file is banked and that the compiler and hardware scheduler avoid bank conflicts with no direct programmer control; public reverse-engineering studies (Volta / Turing) show that .reuse is encoded in the 16 B instruction control bits to hint operand reuse, while Hopper's register-bank count and bit encoding are not documented by NVIDIA.

2Why Does One PTX Instruction Not Always Become One SASS Instruction with the Same Name?

ptxas may compile a single PTX instruction into zero standalone instructions, expand it into a multi-instruction sequence, or map it to a different mnemonic and operands.

  • Category 1: No standalone SASS instruction. Take wgmma.commit_group (see Chapter 5, Section 6 and Chapter 6, Section 5): it takes up no separate instruction word in SASS, and is encoded directly as the group flag at the end of the last HGMMA / QGMMA in that batch (see Quick Reference 3, Item 45; by contrast, cp.async.bulk.commit_group for TMA writeback or reduction emits a standalone UTMACMDFLUSH "TMA Command Flush" instruction—see Quick Reference 2, Item 31).
  • Category 2: Expanded into a multi-instruction SASS sequence. A single-warp FP8 matrix multiplication mma.sync … e4m3 on sm_90a first uses F2FP to unpack FP8 into FP16 and then issues 2 back-to-back HMMA instructions (see Quick Reference 3, Item 41). Likewise, the cluster barrier (barrier.cluster.arrive/wait) in Chapter 9, Section 3 compiles into UCGABAR_ARV / UCGABAR_WAIT, and its default form also prepends a device-wide memory barrier (MEMBAR.ALL.GPU + ERRBAR + CGAERRBAR) before the arrival and appends CCTL.IVALL after the wait (see Quick Reference 3, Item 39).
  • Category 3: Renamed mnemonic or encoded as an operand/modifier. Cache modifiers on global loads become suffixes in SASS, and we infer that some go into a descriptor operand. For instance, the load with createpolicy in Chapter 2, Section 4 gets the .EF / .EL suffix in SASS, and we infer, but have not determined, that its L2 policy sits in the desc[URn] operand of LDG (plain loads without hints carry desc[URn] too); see Quick Reference 2, Item 24.

Why the mismatch? Because the PTX specification defines only semantics, not a fixed SASS instruction sequence. NVIDIA has not published hardware details for ERRBAR and CGAERRBAR inside the device-wide memory barrier; this book records only the sequence seen in sm_90a disassembly, so re-check the disassembly whenever you switch compiler versions.

When you look up an instruction in this group, check first which pipeline it runs on—FMA, ALU, or SFU (see Chapter 5, Section 1). Arithmetic and transcendental functions sit at Level 5, while bit permutation and packed type conversions sit at Level 6.

4Quick Reference 2: Global and On-Chip Memory Access and Asynchronous Copy

Here the first question to ask is which path the data takes: LDG / STG moving data in and out of registers through the Load/Store Unit (LSU), LDGSTS writing directly into SMEM while bypassing registers, or TMA initiated by a single thread (for the differences among the three paths, see Chapter 3, Section 5).

Accesses that act directly on L2 sit at Level 2: loads and stores that bypass L1, L2 residency policies, and L2 atomic reductions. Normal global loads and stores through the local SM's L1, along with SMEM, TMA, and cp.async, sit at Level 3.

No. PTX SASS Pipeline · Level Where used in this book Source form and notes
20 ld.global.b32; ld.global.v4.b32; st.global.v4.b32 LDG.E, LDG.E.64, LDG.E.128, LDG.E.U16, STG.E, STG.E.64, STG.E.128 LSU → L1 → L2 · Level 3 Chapter 3, Section 2; Chapter 3, Section 3 *p, p[i], reinterpret_cast<uint4*>(p)[i] (16 B); bit width appears directly as a suffix (.64 / .128 / .U16), and all forms carry a desc[URn] operand (for generic address-space windows, see Item 59); if you use only some components of a 16 B vector, ptxas splits the load into scalar LDG.E instructions
21 ld.global.nc.u32; ld.global.nc.v4.f32 LDG.E.CONSTANT, LDG.E.128.CONSTANT, LDG.E.64.CONSTANT LSU → L1 read-only path → L2 · Level 3 Chapter 8, Section 8 __ldg(p), const __restrict__ T* p, or inline ld.global.nc; .nc compiles into the .CONSTANT suffix; use only for data that nothing modifies while this kernel runs. The documented condition is "read-only for the entire lifetime of the kernel": .nc goes through a non-coherent read-only cache, so modified data can come back stale. With PDL enabled, this book infers that the preceding and dependent kernels that overlap with this kernel count too (see Chapter 9, Section 5)

6Quick Reference 4: Warp Operations, Memory Fences, Atomic Operations, Grid Handoff, and Control Flow

The intra-warp collectives SHFL (see Chapter 4, Section 5) and VOTE (see Chapter 7, Section 9 and Chapter 8, Section 6) sit at Level 4; per the profiler guide, the LSU pipeline issues SHFL to the local SM's unified L1 data cache / texture / shared-memory unit (denoted L1TEX; its internal shuffle datapath is undocumented). Device-wide memory barriers, L2 atomics, and release/acquire handoffs sit at Level 2 (see Chapter 2, Section 6), while PDL grid handoffs and grid-wide synchronization sit at Level 1 (see Chapter 1, Section 4, Chapter 7, Section 12, and Chapter 8, Section 6).

55 fence.acq_rel.cta; fence.acq_rel.gpu; fence.sc.cta; fence.sc.gpu MEMBAR.ALL.CTA, MEMBAR.ALL.GPU, MEMBAR.SC.GPU, ERRBAR, CGAERRBAR, CCTL.IVALL LSU / memory-system acknowledgment · Level 2 (.cta belongs to Level 3) Chapter 2, Section 6; Chapter 3, Section 7; Chapter 8, Section 11 __threadfence_block() (fence.sc.cta), __threadfence() (same semantics as fence.sc.gpu; in this book's nvcc sample, inline fence.sc.gpu expands into 4 instructions, MEMBAR.SC.GPU + ERRBAR + CGAERRBAR + CCTL.IVALL, whereas a separate NVRTC [version not recorded] build of __threadfence() prepends 1 MEMBAR.ALL.CTA for 5 instructions in total, without retained PTX, and why that extra instruction appears was not determined); when you need only acq_rel semantics, write inline fence.acq_rel.cta (a single MEMBAR.ALL.CTA) or fence.acq_rel.gpu (nvcc sample expands into 4 instructions, MEMBAR.ALL.GPU + ERRBAR + CGAERRBAR + CCTL.IVALL, while Chapter 8, Section 11's NVRTC [version not recorded] sample likewise prepends 1 MEMBAR.ALL.CTA for 5 in total, cause not determined). A device-wide memory barrier waits for prior writes to be acknowledged by L2 and invalidates the local SM L1. For one-way producer-consumer handoffs, acq_rel is sufficient; acq_rel does not prevent a store in this thread from reordering with a subsequent load from a different address, whereas when both sides first write their own flag and then read the other side's flag (the Dekker pattern), you need fence.sc to forbid that reordering
56 fence.release.gpu Not recorded in this book's disassembly LSU / memory-system acknowledgment · Level 2 Chapter 2, Section 6; Chapter 9, Section 5 Inline PTX; it defines ordering only: it orders this thread's prior reads and writes before subsequent strong writes or griddepcontrol.launch_dependents. A strong write is a store with a memory-ordering qualifier such as st.relaxed; a plain st is a weak write. Making prior writes visible to another thread requires pairing with one of two patterns: a subsequent strong write (such as st.relaxed to a flag paired with an acquire load on the receiving side; see Chapter 2, Section 6), or a griddepcontrol.launch_dependents ordered after it in program order (within the same memory synchronization domain, which is the default setting; see Chapter 9, Section 5). Supported starting from sm_90
57 atom.global.add.u32; atom.global.add.f32; atom.global.exch; atom.global.inc ATOMG.E.ADD.STRONG.GPU, ATOMG.E.ADD.S32.STRONG.GPU, ATOMG.E.EXCH.STRONG.GPU, ATOMG.E.INC.STRONG.GPU LSU → L2 atomic unit · Level 2 Chapter 2, Section 6; Chapter 6, Section 8 atomicAdd, atomicExch, atomicCAS, atomicInc, and fetch_add when you use the return value; performs a read-modify-write at L2 and waits for the old value to return, incurring one extra L2 round trip compared to fire-and-forget REDG; as written in Chapter 6, Section 8's kernel, scalar BF16 atomic add compiles down to a compare-and-swap retry loop (Chapter 5, Section 8 covers the paired .bf16x2 form)
58 red.global.add.f32; red.global.add.v4.f32; red.global.add.s32; red.global.min.u64 REDG.E.ADD.S32.STRONG.GPU, REDG.E.ADD.F32.FTZ.RN.STRONG.GPU, REDG.E.ADD.F32x4.FTZ.RN.STRONG.GPU LSU → L2 reduction unit · Level 2 Chapter 2, Section 8; Chapter 7, Section 12; Chapter 9, Section 3 atomicAdd(p,v) when you ignore the return value, and vector atomicAdd(float2* / float4*); the compiler automatically lowers these into fire-and-forget REDG (at the cost of not returning the old value)
59 ld.acquire.gpu.global.u32 [a]; red.release.gpu.global.add.s32 [a],v; atom.acq_rel.gpu LDG.E.STRONG.GPU, CCTL.IVALL, MEMBAR.ALL.GPU, ERRBAR, CGAERRBAR, REDG, ATOMG, ATOM LSU + L2 · Level 2 Chapter 2, Section 6; Chapter 7, Section 12; Chapter 8, Section 11 cuda::atomic_ref<int, thread_scope_device> (store / load / fetch_add) or inline ld.acquire.gpu, red.release.gpu; PTX guarantees ordering only; invalidating L1 and waiting for L2 acknowledgment is how the local SM implements it (for coherence at L2 while L1 is non-coherent, see Chapter 2, Section 6): ld.acquire.gpu expands into LDG.E.STRONG.GPU + CCTL.IVALL, and red.release.gpu expands into MEMBAR.ALL.GPU + ERRBAR + CGAERRBAR + REDG; C++ pointers are generic addresses: .shared, .local, and .const are windows inside the generic address space, and the .param window sits inside .global (cvta converts spaces, such as cvta.to.shared in inline PTX—see Chapter 3, Section 5; isspacep and QSPC in the SASS opcode table query spaces); when the compiler can prove the state space it emits state-specific LDS / LDG / ATOMG, and otherwise emits generic LD / ST / ATOM (such as cuda::atomic_ref on a plain pointer emitting ATOM.E.ADD.S32.STRONG.GPU bracketed by MEMBAR.ALL.GPU + ERRBAR + CGAERRBAR and CCTL.IVALL), with hardware resolving the window at runtime
60 griddepcontrol.wait; griddepcontrol.launch_dependents ACQBULK, PREEXIT Hardware grid distributor and SM · Level 1 Chapter 1, Section 4; Chapter 8, Section 8; Chapter 9, Section 5 cudaGridDependencySynchronize(), cudaTriggerProgrammaticLaunchCompletion(), or inline griddepcontrol (see Chapter 8, Section 8). wait → ACQBULK: blocks until the predecessor grid finishes and its writes are visible. launch_dependents → PREEXIT: once all CTAs issue it or exit, the hardware can schedule the dependent grid. Under the PTX specification, if a predecessor thread executes fence.release.gpu before launch_dependents (with both grids in the same memory synchronization domain, which is the default setting), its prior writes are visible from the start of the dependent grid; otherwise they are guaranteed to be visible only after the dependent grid executes griddepcontrol.wait (see Chapter 9, Section 5). Triggering too early makes the dependent grid occupy SMs while it waits idle (see Chapter 1, Section 4; Chapter 7, Section 11)
61 Standard library implementation (undocumented; inferred in this book: global atomic counter + device-wide memory barrier + polling + bar.sync) Not recorded in this book's disassembly L2 atomic unit + per-SM polling · Level 1 Chapter 2, Section 6; Chapter 7, Section 12; Chapter 8, Section 6 cooperative_groups::this_grid().sync() (used with cudaLaunchCooperativeKernel); this book infers that the standard library builds it from a CTA barrier, a device-wide memory barrier, and L2 counter polling (which load form the polling uses was not verified); all CTAs of the grid must be co-resident (see Chapter 2, Section 6; Chapter 7, Section 12; Chapter 8, Section 6)
62 mov.u64 d, %clock64; mov.u64 d, %globaltimer CS2R Special-register read · Level 4 Chapter 2, Section 2; Chapter 10, Sections 5–6 clock64(), clock(), or inline read of %globaltimer and %clock64; in this book's disassembly, clock64() compiles into CS2R R2, SR_CLOCKLO and a %globaltimer read compiles into CS2R R4, SR_GLOBALTIMERLO, each reading 64 bits in 1 instruction; %clock64 reads the local SM's cycle counter (incrementing with the SM clock), whereas %globaltimer reads the nanosecond global timer (minimum step size measured at 32 ns, and the PTX specification does not guarantee cross-SM synchronization; see Chapter 10, Section 5); clock() reads only the 32-bit %clock and is not recorded in this book's disassembly
63 bra; bra.uni; exit BRA, EXIT, BSSY, BSYNC Branch and issue unit · Level 4 Chapter 4, Section 4; Chapter 10, Section 9 if / for, return; warp-uniform branches carry .U, whereas divergent branches are bracketed by BSSY ... BSYNC (for the cost of branch divergence, see Chapter 4, Section 4; Chapter 10, Section 9)
63a nanosleep.u32 t Not recorded in this book's disassembly (opcode table lists NANOSLEEP) Warp sleep / slot yield · Level 4 Chapter 7, Section 12; Chapter 8, Section 7 __nanosleep(t) or inline PTX (sm_70+); suspends threads for about t nanoseconds (the specification guarantees only [0,2t][0, 2t], up to 1 ms), counted by the profiler under sleeping stalls (which group suspended or yielded warps) while freeing issue slots for other warps on the same SMSP; suitable for spin-poll backoff (Chapter 7, Section 12; standalone benefit not measured), not as a fixed-delay timer (Chapter 8, Section 7)
64 mov.u32 %tid.x; %ctaid.x; %ntid.x; %nctaid.x; %cluster_ctarank; %cluster_nctarank S2R, S2UR, R2UR; LDC, ULDC for %ntid / %nctaid (cluster-rank registers not recorded in this book's disassembly) Special registers, uniform registers, and constant bank · Levels 3–4 Primer 3, Section 2; Chapter 7, Section 7; Chapter 9, Section 3 threadIdx.x and blockIdx.x live in each SM's read-only special registers SR_TID.X and SR_CTAID.X, read into per-thread vector registers R via S2R or directly into a warp-shared uniform register UR via S2UR (R2UR copies R into UR; see Chapter 7, Section 7); on sm_90a, blockDim.x (%ntid.x) and gridDim.x (%nctaid.x) are read from launch-parameter constant bank c[0x0][0x0 / 0xc] via LDC / ULDC (constant-cache reads count as Level 3, see Item 27; special and uniform registers count as Level 4); sm_90 intra-cluster CTA rank %cluster_ctarank (cluster.block_rank(), 0..%cluster_nctarank-1; see Chapter 9, Section 3) is not recorded in this book's disassembly

Takeaway: When you spot an unfamiliar SASS instruction, look up its mnemonic in this appendix to see what source pattern produced it, which pipeline it runs on, which level it belongs to, and which section of this book uses it. To trace an instruction back to a specific source line, compile with -lineinfo and check the source view in NCU (see Chapter 10, Section 7).
