This appendix collects the terms, instruction families, and symbols that appear more than once in this book. Each term gets one row, and "Where Covered" points to the section that defines it.

Sorting rule: all terms sit in one A–Z list by the English term, ignoring backticks, $, periods, %, and underscores, with terms that start with a digit placed before A. To look up a SASS instruction by its mnemonic, see Appendix B.

Term One-Sentence Explanation Where Covered
128-bit SASS instruction word On Volta and newer architectures (including Hopper), every SASS instruction is 16 B wide; based on public reverse-engineering analyses, it packs the opcode, register operands, and control-bit scoreboard wait masks and stall counts (an encoding NVIDIA does not document) Chapter 6, Section 5
1.87 ms lower bound 9.0 GB of fixed weights divided by 4.8 TB/s, not a timing measurement Primer 1, Section 4
2:4 structured sparsity Sparse 16-bit and 8-bit Tensor Core instructions (mma.sp / wgmma.mma_async.sp) require at most 2 non-zeros per 4 adjacent elements in matrix A plus 2-bit index metadata, doubling kk and datasheet peak throughput; unused on this book's dense weights Primer 2, Section 1; Chapter 5, Section 4
A/A null-hypothesis control Runs the exact same code as both A and B through the same paired benchmark and uses the maximum difference as the winning threshold Chapter 7, Section 4; Chapter 10, Section 3
accept / reject draft tokens Accepts draft tokens before the first mismatch and replaces the mismatch position with the target model's prediction Primer 1, Section 7
activation The intermediate result just computed by the preceding stage; it does not exist until the preceding step finishes Primer 2, Section 3
.aligned suffix The PTX specification defines a thread group for each instruction, and all threads in that group must execute the exact same instruction or behavior is undefined (the warp for barrier.cluster, the entire warpgroup for wgmma and setmaxnreg, and the entire CTA for bar.sync) Appendix A, Section 2
all-gather Concatenates the slices from all 8 GPUs into the full output Primer 2, Section 2; Chapter 9, Sections 1 and 9
all-reduce Sums the results from all 8 GPUs elementwise Primer 2, Section 2; Chapter 9, Sections 1 and 9
all-to-all Exchanges distinct data slices between every pair of GPUs; unused in this book's TP8/EP8 decode and verify, entering only in sequence-parallel prefill (disabled and not measured) Chapter 9, Section 9
arithmetic intensity II FLOPs performed per byte moved, in FLOP/B Primer 2, Section 1
async region and serialization hint Mix normal instructions into an async region and ptxas drains and waits after each instruction one by one Chapter 6, Section 6
asynchronous launch Once a command enters the queue, the CPU keeps running without waiting for the GPU to finish Primer 3, Section 4
ATOMG / REDG Global atomic with a return value; ignore the return value and it compiles to a fire-and-forget reduction Appendix B, Section 6
atomic add An indivisible read-modify-write addition that returns the old value Chapter 2, Section 6
attention Compares queries Q against keys K for similarity, then takes a weighted sum of values V Primer 1, Section 2
autoregressive generation Each new token comes from the tokens before it, so you can only generate tokens one by one Primer 1, Section 6
BB (batch size), LL (sequence length per request), T=B×L (total tokens) Number of requests, number of new tokens per request, and total number of tokens Primer 2, Section 4
__ballot_sync warp-vote bucketing Computes prefix positions via warp voting Chapter 8, Section 6
bandwidth Bytes transferred per second; device memory bandwidth is measured in TB/s Primer 1, Section 4
bank conflict Lanes in the same warp access different words in the same shared-memory bank, splitting the access into multiple transactions Chapter 3, Section 9
base clock The lower rated clock frequency in the GPU specification; under default settings, NCU may pin the SM and memory clocks to this frequency (see Chapter 10, Section 1) Chapter 10, Section 1
BF16 (bfloat16) 16-bit floating point formed by the upper 16 bits of FP32 Primer 1, Section 1; Chapter 6, Section 1
BF16x2 (__nv_bfloat162) Packs two BF16 values side by side into one 32-bit register Chapter 5, Section 8; Chapter 6, Section 2
bitwise determinism (deterministic) Floating-point addition is not associative, so a non-deterministic reduction order may alter the least significant bits Chapter 2, Section 8
Blackwell (B200) Compilation target sm_100a, with ~8 TB/s bandwidth Appendix A, opening
block-scaled MMA Tensor Core instruction where both A and B are low-bitwidth floats, scaled per block before multiply-accumulate (one factor per 16 elements for 4-bit NVFP4, per 32 for FP8) Appendix A, Section 3
boundary kernel At the end of Stages 3 and 8, updates the residual and computes the normalization for the next input Chapter 9, Section 1
branch divergence When threads in the same warp take different branches, execution time equals the sum of both branches Chapter 4, Section 4
bucketing and grouped GEMM First groups tokens routed to the same expert together, then launches one grid per projection Chapter 8, Section 2
busiest GPU (straggler rank) The GPU whose local experts receive the most (token, expert) hit pairs in a layer (at T=1, also the GPU that touches the most distinct local experts); this GPU sets the latency of the whole layer Primer 2, Section 2
bytes in flight Bytes whose read requests have gone out while the data has not yet returned to the SM Chapter 2, Section 3
C12 (12-bit lossless weight format) Retains the BF16 low byte, sign bit, and a 3-bit window offset, for 12 bits in total Chapter 6, Section 1
cache hit / cache miss A hit when the requested data is already in the cache level being checked (such as L1 or L2); a miss when it is not and must be fetched from the next level or HBM Chapter 2, Section 2
causal attention Each token attends only to itself and earlier tokens, never to later tokens Primer 1, Section 2
chunked prefill Splits a long prompt into chunks and runs them one after another (16,384 tokens per chunk in this book's examples) Primer 2, Section 4
clock cycle One tick of the SM clock; about 0.56 ns at 1.8 GHz Chapter 2, Section 2
cluster launch control Blackwell (sm_100+) mechanism where a CTA already on an SM asynchronously cancels an unstarted CTA and takes over its block index Appendix A, Section 5
coalesced access (coalescing) Addresses falling into the same sector merge into a single request Chapter 3, Section 2
commit group (commit_group / wait_group<N>) Waits until no more than N committed groups (per-thread cp.async copy groups or warpgroup wgmma matrix-multiply groups) are still incomplete before continuing Chapter 5, Section 6
completion flag Set after a subtask finishes writing to notify consumers waiting on it Chapter 8, Section 11
compute-sanitizer Checks intra-kernel data races and CTA barrier misuse, but cannot see cross-kernel races Chapter 10, Section 4
cooperative launch The driver guarantees that the whole grid is resident at one time; if the grid does not fit, the driver rejects the launch Chapter 2, Section 6
copy engine Dedicated asynchronous DMA hardware unit separate from the SMs that copies bytes without SMs, while CUDA's copy calls only copy and never sum Chapter 9, Section 9
cp.async Asynchronous copy that moves data directly from global memory into SMEM without passing through registers Chapter 3, Section 5
CPU launch gap The command queue drains empty, leaving the GPU waiting for the CPU to issue the next command Chapter 1, Section 1
critical path The longest chain of dependency edges; single-layer latency equals the critical path plus CUDA graph replay overhead Chapter 9, Section 1
CTA barrier __syncthreads() Holds until all threads in the CTA arrive and makes prior writes visible across the whole CTA Primer 3, Section 3
cuBLAS / torch.mv The NVIDIA matrix library and the PyTorch baseline Chapter 4, Section 6
CUDA Core One FP32 lane of the FMA pipeline (32 per SMSP) Chapter 5, Section 1
CUDA event (inter-stream event) A marker recorded on one stream that another stream can wait on Chapter 9, Section 1
CUDA Graph A pre-recorded dependency graph of GPU commands that replays in a single launch at runtime Chapter 1, Section 2
CUDA graph replay overhead The latency of replaying a CUDA Graph containing only 1 empty kernel once Chapter 9, Section 1
CUDA stream A queue of GPU commands executed in enqueue order Primer 3, Section 4
cumulativity A release operation publishes both its own prior writes and writes from other threads that it has already observed Chapter 2, Section 6
CUPTI (CUDA Profiling Tools Interface) NVIDIA's profiling and tracing interface; this book uses its Activity API to record the start and end timestamps of every kernel in a graph replay without replaying kernels in isolation Chapter 10, Section 1
data race Two threads (in the same kernel or different kernels) access overlapping addresses with at least one write, no causality order between them, and not both morally strong (such as atomic operations) Chapter 9, Section 5
decode (token-by-token decoding) Each forward pass takes only the 1 token just produced, and the next token must wait for this pass to finish Primer 1, Section 6
dedicated release thread Each consumer performs only a CTA-scope release; a single dedicated thread then issues one GPU-scope release to notify other SMs Chapter 8, Section 11
dependent-instruction latency The number of clock cycles from when an instruction issues until a dependent instruction can use its result Chapter 3, Section 9; Chapter 5, Section 1
desc[URn] (uniform-register memory descriptor) A 64-bit memory descriptor held in a uniform register Appendix B, Section 1
device-wide memory barrier A gpu-scope memory barrier sequence (MEMBAR.ALL.GPU, etc.) that waits for this thread's prior writes to reach L2 and invalidates L1 on this SM Chapter 2, Section 6; Chapter 8, Section 11; Appendix B, Section 2
diagnostic tree (six-level) Timeline, full GPU, single SM, scheduler, pipelines, and SASS Chapter 10, Section 6
directed acyclic graph (DAG) Arrows mean "must wait for its result"; each layer has one main chain Primer 2, Section 3
disassembly Recovering SASS text from binary machine instructions Chapter 6, Section 5
drafting mechanism (draft model) A mechanism that guesses the next 7 candidate tokens first, such as a small draft model Primer 1, Section 7
drain latency The extra wait exposed from issuing the last wgmma until all results are written back to registers Chapter 5, Section 6
E2M1 / E4M3 Bit layouts for 4-bit floating point and 8-bit floating point (FP8) Chapter 6, Section 5
eager mode The CPU launches kernels one by one without recording a computation graph Chapter 9, Section 5
embedding table A table indexed by token ID to look up rows, of shape [202,048, 8,192] Primer 1, Section 1
EP8 (8-way expert parallelism) Assigns different experts to different GPUs, with 32 local experts per GPU Primer 2, Section 2
escaped weight (outlier) and side table Any weight whose exponent falls outside the window keeps an in-window placeholder code in the main table while its true value is logged in a side table, to be corrected either by adding the delta to the output or by patching registers Chapter 6, Section 1
even-odd ledger (ping-pong counter array) Two counter arrays that alternate by launch index; while one is in use, the other is zeroed Chapter 8, Section 12
F2F and F2FP Scalar floating-point conversion F2F runs on the SFU, while paired FP32-to-BF16/FP16 packing F2FP does not use the SFU (which pipeline FP8 pack/unpack F2FP uses was not measured) Chapter 7, Section 9; Chapter 8, Section 16; Appendix B, Sections 2, 3, and 5
feed-forward network (FFN) Multiplies the input by the gate matrix and by the up-projection matrix, multiplies the two results elementwise, and then applies the down projection Primer 1, Section 2
fence.sc (sequentially consistent fence) Sequentially consistent fence you need when threads wait on each other's flags or when multiple flags must follow a single total order Appendix B, Section 6
fixed overhead Timing a single empty kernel with events takes about 4.6 µs, which covers launch, event recording, and running the empty kernel itself Primer 3, Section 5
fixed weights Dense weights that every token uses with no routing selection, plus lm_head; each GPU must read them on every forward pass (~9.0 GB for at most 8 tokens) Primer 1, Section 4
FLOP (floating-point operation) Floating-point operation count; one multiply-add counts as 2 FLOPs Primer 1, Section 4
FMA / ALU / SFU pipelines Execution pipelines with instruction issue intervals of 1, 2, and 8 cycles Chapter 5, Section 1
four hardware limits Four limits such as the register file pool and 4-warp warpgroup issue that software cannot change and can only work around Chapter 10, Section 10
FP8 (8-bit floating point) 8-bit floating point; E4M3 uses 1 sign bit, 4 exponent bits, and 3 mantissa bits Primer 1, Section 2; Chapter 6, Section 5
gemv (matrix-vector multiplication) Matrix-vector multiplication y=Wx — matrix multiplication at T=1 Primer 2, Section 1
%globaltimer A predefined 64-bit global nanosecond timer register in PTX used for timestamp probes (cross-SM synchronization is not guaranteed by the specification) Chapter 10, Section 5
GQA (grouped-query attention) Divides the 16 query heads per GPU into 2 groups of 8, where each group shares 1 KV head (16 KV heads across the full layer) Primer 2, Section 2
grid barrier All CTAs increment the same L2 counter by 1 and wait until it reaches the total CTA count (waiting for all CTAs to arrive) Chapter 7, Section 12; Chapter 8, Section 6
grid truncation and tail loop Bounds the main grid's tile count at twice the per-GPU average hit-pair count (~T pairs), leaving any excess tiles to the tail loops inside the main kernels Chapter 8, Section 14
griddepcontrol.wait / griddepcontrol.launch_dependents The PDL wait and trigger calls; see Appendix B for SASS Chapter 8, Section 8
H200 An NVIDIA data-center GPU; this book examines a single H200 Preface, Section 1
handoff gap A successor kernel must wait for all CTAs of the preceding kernel to exit; Chapter 9 measures the time from when the preceding kernel's last CTA exits until the successor kernel's first wait returns Chapter 1, Section 1; Chapter 9, Section 6
happens-before Without PDL: a later command in the same stream sees all writes of an earlier command; with PDL, see "two visibility paths of PDL" in this table (Chapter 9, Section 5) Primer 3, Section 4
HBM (High Bandwidth Memory) Main GPU device memory; H200 has a nominal peak bandwidth of 4.8 TB/s Primer 1, Section 4
HGMMA The SASS mnemonic for BF16 / FP16 wgmma (QGMMA for FP8) Chapter 6, Section 5
hidden size 8,192 numbers represent each token; that is its width Primer 1, Section 1
hit pair (tok,slot,e)(tok, slot, e) A (token, slot) pair routed to local expert ee on this GPU Chapter 8, Section 1
Hopper The GPU architecture of H200, with compilation target sm_90a Chapter 1, Section 4; Appendix A, opening
in-order issue / scoreboard Warps issue in program order; the scoreboard marks registers whose loads have not returned, and a warp stalls only when an instruction uses one of them Chapter 4, Section 2
issue slot 1 per SMSP per clock cycle; switching warps takes zero cycles Chapter 4, Section 1
K-halves When the tail-wave remainder does not exceed half a wave's capacity, splits each row across two half-row CTAs Chapter 2, Section 5
kernel A program launched once on the GPU and executed together by many threads Primer 3, Section 1
kernel fusion Merges adjacent kernels so intermediate results stay on-chip Chapter 1, Section 3
key-value head (KV head) Segments of K and V of width 64: 16 per layer, 2 per GPU Primer 1, Section 2
KV cache Stores already computed K and V in each layer for later tokens to read Primer 1, Section 2
L2 cache The 60 MiB level-2 cache shared across all 132 SMs Chapter 2, Section 2
L2 partitions / LTC Fabric H200's 60 MiB L2 cache is split across a partitioned crossbar into two partitions (one near and one far relative to each SM) joined by the L2 communication fabric (ltcfabric in NCU) Chapter 2, Section 2
L2 residency hint (cache policy) A policy attached to load instructions that controls eviction priority in L2 Chapter 2, Section 4
lane / SIMT The 32 lanes of a warp; each time the scheduler issues from the warp, it issues 1 instruction, and the active lanes sitting at that instruction execute it together (under Independent Thread Scheduling, each lane has its own program counter) Chapter 4, Section 4
__launch_bounds__ Tells the compiler the maximum threads per CTA and minimum CTAs per SM so it caps per-thread register usage Chapter 3, Section 1
lazy rescaling Reserves logarithmic headroom and rescales only when a warp vote triggers it Chapter 7, Section 9
ldmatrix (SASS LDSM) One warp loads 8 × 8 sub-matrices from SMEM into registers Chapter 7, Section 10
left-shift FMA offloading Moves left shifts onto the FMA pipeline to reduce ALU cycles Chapter 5, Section 1
Little's Law Bytes in flight equal bandwidth times round-trip latency, which tells you how many loads to keep in flight Chapter 2, Section 3
lm_head (vocabulary projection) The matrix that scores every candidate in the vocabulary; the 202,048-row vocabulary is evenly divisible by 8, so it is split across 8 GPUs at 25,256 rows per GPU without padding Primer 1, Section 3
local expert An expert stored on the local GPU; out of 256 experts per layer, each GPU stores 32 Primer 1, Section 2
logit softcap Multiplies logits by a fixed scale factor ss and compresses them into [−c, c][-c,\ c] via c⋅tanh⁡(⋅/c) to prevent individual logits from growing too large Primer 1, Section 3
logits Unnormalized FP32 candidate scores of shape R × 202,048 Primer 1, Section 3
lower bound (roofline floor) The fastest possible time for a stage: the maximum of bytes divided by bandwidth and FLOPs divided by compute throughput Primer 2, Section 1
matrix descriptor / SS and RS modes A 64-bit value describing an SMEM matrix; SS when operand A is in SMEM, RS when operand A is in registers Chapter 5, Section 4
mbarrier An 8-byte hardware object in SMEM that tracks pending thread arrivals and pending transaction bytes Chapter 3, Section 7
MeM_e (tokens routed to expert ee) The number of tokens routed to expert ee, used to partition hit pairs into two regimes Chapter 8, Section 1
megakernel Fuses an entire layer into a single large kernel Chapter 9, Section 6
memory fence Explicitly orders when reads and writes before and after the fence become visible; on the GPU you must insert it yourself Chapter 2, Section 6
memory ordering (relaxed / release / acquire) Three orderings that control when reads and writes become visible to other threads Chapter 2, Section 6
memory scope (scope) The visibility range where a release or acquire operation takes effect Chapter 2, Section 6
memory synchronization domain A label CUDA attaches to each launch; by default, all kernels belong to the same domain Chapter 8, Section 8; Chapter 9, Section 5
memory-bound (HBM-bound) / compute-bound (Tensor Core-bound) When II is below the ridge point, execution waits on HBM; when II is above it, execution waits on compute Primer 2, Section 1
merged launch Merges router and pooler, which read the same input, into a single kernel launch Chapter 9, Section 7
MIO (memory input/output instruction queue) The memory input/output instruction queue inside an SM for shared-memory instructions, special math functions (MUFU), and dynamic branches Chapter 10, Section 7
Mixture of Experts (MoE) Each layer has 256 experts, and each token uses only the 8 highest-scoring experts Primer 1, Section 2
mma.sync (m16n8k16) A Tensor Core instruction issued by a single warp Chapter 5, Section 4
multi-token GEMM g0 → g5 The evolution chain for T=8..256, stacking mechanisms across five levels Chapter 6, Section 8
multicast object (multimem) A virtual address range mapped by Virtual Memory Management to one physical HBM replica on each GPU for NVSwitch broadcast stores and in-fabric reductions Chapter 9, Section 9
named barrier A per-CTA hardware barrier numbered 0..15 that waits only for the specified count of threads Chapter 5, Section 8; Chapter 7, Section 7
NCCL NVIDIA Collective Communications Library, executing cross-GPU communication and reduction inside a single SM kernel (Ring, Tree, NVLS, etc.) Chapter 9, Section 9
noise band The threshold for judging whether a single change yields a real speedup: paired differences must have the same sign in every round and exceed the span of medians across several rounds of the same variant; see Chapter 10, Section 3 for the values and measurement methods per operator Chapter 4, Section 6; Chapter 6, Section 8; Chapter 10, Section 3
Nsight Compute (NCU) A kernel-level profiler that replays a kernel across multiple passes to collect hardware counters Chapter 10, Section 1
Nsight Systems A system-level profiler that plots CPU launches and GPU kernel start/end times on a single timeline Chapter 10, Section 6
NVFP4 (4-bit floating-point format) 4-bit floating point where every 16 weights share a 1-byte scale factor Primer 2, Section 2
NVLink H200's high-speed inter-GPU interconnect: 18 links per GPU, 900 GB/s bidirectional and 450 GB/s unidirectional Chapter 9, Sections 8–9
NVSwitch / NVLink SHARP High-speed switch ASICs connecting all 18 NVLink links of all 8 GPUs, with hardware multicast broadcast and in-fabric reduction (NVLink SHARP) Chapter 9, Section 9
occupancy The number of resident warps divided by the 64 warp slots per SM Chapter 3, Section 1
offline weight permutation Permutes weights offline in decoding order, reducing decoding instructions from 31 to 8 Chapter 6, Section 5
online softmax Tracks the running maximum, denominator, and accumulator in a single pass, rescaling when each new block arrives Chapter 7, Section 3
open-loop staggering Issues activation p and slot 0 weights first, while the remaining slots spin-wait a fixed delay on the nanosecond timer before issuing (500 ns at T=1, 600 ns at T=8, and 0 at T=16/32 in the final version) Chapter 8, Section 7
operator One computation step in a model, such as a single matrix multiplication Preface, Section 6
padding row Blank rows padded into a tail tile to reach the full tile row count Chapter 8, Section 5
paged KV cache Stores KV in page slots at arbitrary positions, while a page table maps logical pages to physical page slots Chapter 7, Section 1
paired ABBA benchmarking (A, B, B, A) Alternates runs in the order A, B, B, A to cancel linear drift and takes the median across multiple paired differences Chapter 7, Section 1
parallel slice reduction / ticket number S CTAs each reduce 1/S of the rows, claim a ticket via atomic add, and wait until all S CTAs arrive Chapter 2, Section 8
partial sum Each piece of a dot product split along K (one per thread, or one per CTA under Split-K), reduced into a single sum afterward Primer 3, Section 3; Chapter 2, Section 5
PCIe Gen5 Host-to-GPU interconnect (128 GB/s); GPU-to-GPU collectives on our node use NVLink rather than PCIe Chapter 9, Section 9
PDL (Programmatic Dependent Launch) Decouples "successor can be dispatched" from "predecessor writes are visible" Chapter 1, Section 4
per-K-step three-stage times HH / DD / MM (HBM read / decode / MMA) The three stages of HBM read, weight decode, and matrix multiply; when buffered, the longest stage dominates Chapter 6, Section 4
persistent kernel A grid that launches only one wave of CTAs, where each CTA stays resident and claims work items in a loop Chapter 3, Section 1
perturbation test (ablation test) Uses a runtime parameter switch to skip the code under test (keeping the machine code unchanged) and measures the upper bound via paired benchmarking Chapter 10, Section 8
pre-expert RMSNorm (pre_expert_norm) Applies RMSNorm to the 4,096-dimensional activation between Stage 5 and Stage 6 Chapter 9, Section 3
predicate Short conditions do not branch: the instruction carries a predicate, and lanes whose predicate is false do not write back Chapter 4, Section 4
prefill Processes the whole known prompt in parallel in one forward pass and keeps only the last row Primer 1, Section 5
PRMT (byte permute instruction) Selects bytes using 4 hexadecimal nibbles to assemble a new 32-bit word Chapter 6, Section 2
producer / consumer (warp specialization) Producer warps issue TMA transfers while consumer warps perform computation Chapter 3, Section 7
programmatic dependent edge Allows the successor to launch before the predecessor finishes and wait only at wait Chapter 9, Section 5
prologue / epilogue Setup before the main loop; elementwise computation after the main loop and before writeout Chapter 1, Section 3
proxy PTX label for memory-access methods: normal thread accesses use the generic proxy while TMA and wgmma use the async proxy, requiring a cross-proxy fence fence.proxy.async across proxies (for the instruction, see Chapter 5, Section 8 and Chapter 8, Section 11) Chapter 3, Section 7
PTX / ptxas / SASS Virtual instruction set; backend assembler; actual machine instructions executed by hardware Chapter 6, Section 2
quad A 4-lane group of consecutive lanes in a warp (g = lane >> 2, lane & 3 within the group): in mma register fragments for matrix AA and the accumulator, one row sits across the 4 lanes of a quad (quad g holds rows g and g + 8, whereas for matrix BB the 4 lanes hold column g), and ldmatrix likewise delivers one 16 B row per quad Chapter 5, Section 4
RR (number of rows to predict) Takes 1 row in prefill and decode; takes 8 rows in verify Primer 1, Section 3
read flush Reads a 512 MiB buffer once before timing so that L2 holds only clean lines Chapter 10, Section 2
reduction Combining many partial sums into one value, such as adding 128 partial sums together Primer 3, Section 3
reference bound The single-layer lower bound the task sets for each scenario (T=1 sliding-window layer 40.0 µs, T=1 full-attention layer 44.2 µs, T=8 sliding-window / full-attention layer 62.3 / 66.4 µs); it is not a lower bound on the bytes any version actually reads Chapter 9, Section 1
register / shared memory / global memory Thread-private; on-chip shared within one CTA; in HBM shared across all CTAs Primer 3, Section 3
register spilling (spill) Values that do not fit in registers spill to local memory in device memory Chapter 3, Section 1
rematerialization and sinking The compiler recomputes values instead of keeping them in registers; loads are sunk past wait points Chapter 8, Section 8
request / batch (BB) The number of requests batched together in one forward pass, denoted BB Primer 2, Section 4
residual stream (stream) The shared 32-bit main state that every layer merges its output into Primer 1, Section 1
ridge point The crossover point of arithmetic intensity; 206 FLOP/B for dense BF16 on H200 Primer 2, Section 1
ring buffer Divides SMEM into N slots reused in a ring to overlap data movement with computation Chapter 3, Section 6
RMSNorm (root mean square normalization) Divides a vector by the square root of the mean of its squared elements to stabilize numerical range Primer 1, Section 1
RoPE (rotary position embedding) Rotates each pair of elements by an angle determined by the token position Primer 2, Section 2
route-alignment kernel In prefill, sorts hit pairs by expert and pads each expert to an integer multiple of the tile height BMBM (64 or 128 rows) Chapter 8, Section 14
router / pooler / unpooler router scores the 256 experts; pooler projects 8,192 dimensions down to 4,096; unpooler projects expert outputs back to 8,192 dimensions (at T≤8, each GPU computes 1/8 of the columns) Primer 2, Section 2
row fill ratio The fraction of the 64 rows that hold useful data Chapter 5, Section 5
row-stride padding Adds 1 extra word to the row stride so the same column in adjacent rows shifts by 1 bank Chapter 3, Section 9
rule of three Observing 0 errors in NN runs shows only that the error rate is below 3/N3/N (95%) Chapter 10, Section 4
sector 32 B, the minimum request unit for global loads; 4 sectors form one cache line Chapter 3, Section 2
setmaxnreg A warpgroup-wide hint to change the per-thread register cap: dec returns registers to the CTA pool and inc claims them from the pool (blocking if the pool runs short); called at kernel entry in this book Chapter 3, Section 8
severe numerical corruption An output result whose relative L2 error against a verified-correct output for the same input exceeds 0.01 Chapter 9, Section 5
side stream A second CUDA stream that lets kernels independent of the main chain run in parallel Chapter 9, Section 1
single layer / full model Single layer means one decoder layer on one GPU (µs); full model means all 62 layers (ms) Preface, Section 6; Chapter 9, Section 8
single tile / 16-token segment Experts with up to 8 tokens fit into a single mma.sync tile; experts with 9–16 tokens run as one 16-token segment to share a single weight read, while those with 17–32 tokens are divided into two segments Chapter 8, Section 6
skewed routing A routing distribution where tokens pile onto a small number of experts Chapter 8, Section 1
sliding-window layer / full-attention layer A sliding-window layer attends only to the most recent 2,048 positions; a full-attention layer attends to the entire history Primer 1, Section 2
SM (Streaming Multiprocessor) The compute unit that executes instructions; H200 has 132 SMs Primer 3, Section 1
sm_90a (architecture-specific target) Compilation target carrying the architecture-specific a suffix for compute capability 9.0: required for wgmma and setmaxnreg (binaries run only on CC 9.0 GPUs), whereas TMA, clusters, elect.sync, and griddepcontrol need only sm_90 Chapter 5, Section 4; Appendix A, opening
SMEM/L1 carveout Per-kernel partitioning of each SM's 256 KiB unified storage into discrete shared-memory steps up to 228 KiB (at most 227 KiB per CTA after the 1 KiB system reserve; > 48 KiB requires dynamic shared-memory opt-in), with the remainder serving as L1 Chapter 3, Sections 1 and 6
SMSP (SM sub-partition) 4 per SM, each with its own warp scheduler Chapter 4, Section 1
softmax Turns a vector of logits into weights that sum to 1, where the denominator sums over all candidates Primer 2, Section 2
speculative verification break-even condition The average number of tokens produced per round must exceed the ratio of (verify + drafting) latency to a single decode latency Primer 1, Section 7
Speed Of Light (SOL) The percentage of peak bandwidth or peak compute throughput reported by NCU Chapter 10, Section 6
speedup upper bound How much latency drops when a perturbation test skips the code under test — the most time you can save Chapter 10, Section 8
spin-wait Repeatedly reads a flag until its condition holds; requires both CTAs to be co-resident Chapter 2, Section 6
Split-K Splits K into S segments so S CTAs jointly compute one output Chapter 2, Section 5
Split-KV / lse (log-sum-exp) / merge step Splits keys into S segments, records lse per segment, and merges them exactly Chapter 7, Section 3
stall sampling share The profiler samples warps at a fixed cycle interval; this is the share of non-issuing samples that a given stall reason accounts for Chapter 10, Section 7
st.async Writes directly to remote shared memory across CTAs and tracks byte completion via mbarrier Chapter 7, Section 12
stmatrix Writes 8 × 8 sub-matrices from warp registers into SMEM Chapter 5, Section 8
subnormal number Floating-point numbers whose exponent bits are all 0; they are evenly spaced and fill the smallest range Chapter 6, Section 5
subtask table In the persistent wgmma kernel, each CTA builds the same subtask order in shared memory and dynamically claims subtasks via a global counter Chapter 8, Section 9
swap-AB (swapping operands A and B) Computes yT=WxT by placing 64 rows of WW as the left operand Chapter 5, Section 5
SwiGLU Passes gate gg through silu and multiplies elementwise by up-projection uu Primer 2, Section 2
SwiGLU scale folding Folds the scale factors into the exponent argument and denominator, reducing per-element instructions from 9 to 7 (and to 6 in the final tanh form) Chapter 8, Section 13
TT (tokens per forward pass) The number of tokens processed concurrently in one forward pass; the token-ID array has shape [T][T] Primer 1, Section 1
tail duration (CTA exit skew) The time within the same kernel from when the median CTA exits until the last CTA exits Chapter 9, Section 6
tail wave The final batch of CTAs that does not fill a full wave, leaving most SM slots idle Chapter 2, Section 1
tcgen05.mma Fifth-generation Tensor Core instruction whose accumulator resides in TMEM Appendix A, Section 1
Tensor Core The dedicated on-chip compute unit for matrix multiply-accumulate Primer 2, Section 1
tensor scale / block scale One FP32 tensor scale per projection matrix (W13W_{13}, W2W_2) of each expert, and one E4M3 block scale per 16 weights Chapter 8, Section 1
tensor shape Notation that gives the tensor name and the length of each dimension, with the data type as a lower-right subscript Preface, Section 6
thread / grid A single execution thread; all CTAs in one kernel launch together form a grid Primer 3, Section 1
thread block (CTA) A group of threads that process a block of work together and run on a single SM Primer 3, Section 1
thread block cluster / GPC / DSMEM A group of guaranteed co-resident CTAs (up to 8 portably, or 16 with explicit opt-in); a cluster of adjacent SMs; cross-CTA shared-memory reads Chapter 7, Section 12
three-hop pointer chain Reading one KV page traverses three pointer hops through seq_lens, the page table, and the physical page index Chapter 7, Section 6
tile A small block of WW staged in SMEM for repeated reads across the whole CTA Chapter 3, Section 5
.tile::gather4 A single TMA command takes 4 row indices and gathers them into one tile Appendix A, Section 4
timestamp probe In-kernel code that reads %globaltimer to record per-stage elapsed time Chapter 10, Section 5
TMA (Tensor Memory Accelerator) Hardware unit where a single thread initiates asynchronous bulk copies (on Hopper sm_90a, tensor copies support rectangular tiles and plain convolution im2col, plus 1D contiguous copies) Chapter 3, Section 5
TMA tile reduction (cp.reduce.async.bulk) TMA atomically adds an SMEM tile elementwise into the output in global memory (inferred to happen at L2; not determined) Chapter 5, Section 8
TMEM (Tensor Memory) Dedicated on-chip Tensor Memory separate from vector registers; 128 rows × 512 columns (256 KiB) per CTA in the PTX specification Appendix A, Section 1
token The basic unit processed by the model, never abbreviated to "word" in this book Preface, Section 6
Top-8 kernel Selects the top 8 out of 256 experts using scores plus router_bias, normalizes their unbiased scores into weights, and writes topk_ids and topk_weights Chapter 9, Section 1
TP8 (8-way tensor parallelism) Partitions the same matrix by head across 8 GPUs, with each GPU computing one slice Primer 2, Section 2
trigger call / wait call After the preceding kernel issues a trigger call, its successor can enter SMs early; the successor's wait call returns only after the preceding kernel finishes and its writes are visible Chapter 1, Section 4
two visibility paths of PDL Issuing fence.release.gpu before launch_dependents makes writes visible as soon as the successor launches; otherwise writes become visible only after wait returns Chapter 9, Section 5
uniform register (UR) A scalar register shared across all lanes of a warp Chapter 7, Section 7
verify (speculative decoding verification) Checks all 8 draft positions in one forward pass, with R = 8 Primer 1, Section 7
vocabulary The table that maps tokens to integer IDs, with 202,048 entries in total Primer 1, Section 1
warp A group of 32 consecutive threads that issue the same instruction together when they have not diverged (see Chapter 4, Section 4) Primer 3, Section 2; Chapter 3, Section 1
warp shuffle (__shfl_xor_sync) Directly reads a neighbor lane's register within the same warp Chapter 4, Section 5
warpgroup 4 consecutive warps whose first warp index is a multiple of 4, or 128 threads in total Chapter 3, Section 8
WARPGROUP.DEPBAR.LE Drain wait for wgmma: waits until at most N groups remain incomplete (for bare DEPBAR.LE, see Appendix B, Quick Reference 2, Item 31) Chapter 6, Section 7
wave The number of CTAs the whole GPU can keep resident at once; 2,112 in v1 Chapter 2, Section 1
weight Fixed parameters in the model; every inference reads the same copy Preface, Section 1
wgmma (m64nNk16; k32 for FP8) Must be issued collectively by an entire warpgroup, with row height 64 Chapter 5, Section 4
write-after-read hazard (WAR) Marking a slot empty before its data enters registers lets the next TMA round overwrite it silently without raising an error Chapter 3, Section 7
XOR swizzle Permutes column indices by XOR to stagger shared-memory banks without extra space overhead Chapter 3, Section 9
zero-column shortcut In single-GPU benchmarks, the 7,168 columns owned by the other 7 GPUs are identically 0, so Stage 3 precomputes the sum of squares Chapter 9, Section 2

Hopper (H200) inference hardware at a glance

Chapters 1–9 open up only the hardware units directly hit by this book's kernel evolution chains; Appendix B covers the machine instructions discussed across the main text, figures, and this appendix; and Appendix C indexes terms that recur across the book alphabetically. When you read NVIDIA architecture whitepapers, the PTX and CUDA manuals, or Nsight Compute (NCU) panels, you also run into single-GPU inference hardware units and modes that our Muse Spark Open workload either never expands on or mentions only once in passing—this appendix organizes them into four quick-reference tables, moving from off-chip to intra-SM and from arithmetic to data movement.

Scope and epistemic labels: This appendix covers model-inference hardware on a single Hopper (sm_90a, H200 SXM) GPU only; graphics rasterization and ray tracing, texture sampling and filtering, video and image codecs (NVDEC / NVENC / OFA / NVJPG), confidential computing and virtualization administration (TEE / MIG setup / SR-IOV), power/thermal governors and ECC scrubbing, double-precision-only (FP64) pipelines, dynamic-programming DPX instructions, and multi-GPU or host interconnects (NVLink / NVSwitch / PCIe / GPUDirect RDMA / multimem) lie outside this book's scope. Every entry distinguishes what is Documented in official NVIDIA manuals/datasheets, what is Measured via device attribute on H200 or on sibling GH100 GPUs in public papers, what is Derived from documented or measured constants, what is Inferred, and what remains Unknown (not published / not measured / not disassembled) in public documentation and in this book.

1Chip Physical Topology and Global Memory Path

On the compute side, the chip groups hardware across four levels—Die → GPC → TPC → SM—while on the global-memory side traffic travels from SMs through the partitioned crossbar (XBAR) and the L2 Request Coalescer (LRC) into two-partition L2 slices (LTS) and out through FrameBuffer Partitions (FBPA) to HBM3e; internal arbitration orders, exact attachment points of the MMU and LRC, and H200's active slice and controller counts are not published.

Unit / NCU Name Location on Chip What It Does, Limits, and Epistemic Status Book kernel and Chapter Pointer
Die → GPC → TPC → SM hierarchy (tpc, launch__tpc_count) Full GH100 die → GPC → TPC (2 SMs plus 1 shared ICC per TPC; 1 IDC inside each SM) Documented (H100 whitepaper p18, p29; NCU §2.3.4, §2.4.2): a GPC is a group of physically close SMs; TPCs sit inside a GPC, with 1 Instruction Constant Cache (ICC) per TPC servicing all SM sub-partitions in that TPC, whereas the Indexed Constant Cache (IDC, accessed by LDC) is a per-SM cache; full GH100 has 8 GPC × 9 TPC × 2 SM = 144 SM (72 TPCs) and H100 SXM5 has 8 GPC / 66 TPC / 132 SM (the H200 datasheet prints no SM count). Measured via device attribute on H200: querying multi_processor_count on our H200 returns 132 SMs. Derived: combining full GH100's 2 SMs per TPC and at most 9 TPCs (18 SMs) per GPC with 132 active SMs shows that H200 enables 132 ÷ 2 = 66 TPCs, and because 132 > 7 × 18 = 126, all 8 GPCs are active. Unknown: how many TPCs / SMs each individual GPC enables on H200 is not published (even TPC pairs also do not explain the measured 4-CTA cluster residency cap at 2 CTAs per SM in Chapter 7, Section 12, whose cause is not determined); instruction and constant cache byte capacities, and whether NCU's ICC is the same unit as the whitepaper's L1 instruction cache, are not published. Every kernel in this book runs across these 132 SMs (Primer 3, Section 1; Chapter 2, Section 1); CTAs of the same thread block cluster co-reside inside one GPC (Chapter 7, Section 12; Chapter 9, Section 3)
Virtual-to-physical address translation (GPU MMU) Along the memory path between the SM and physical-address L2 (exact hardware site of translation not published) Documented (PTX §8.2; CUDA Guide §4.18; NCU §2.3.1): kernel pointers and tensor descriptors hold virtual addresses that the OS/driver and hardware Memory Management Unit (MMU) translate into physical device addresses during memory access, and L2 operates in physical-address space. Unknown: where between the SM and L2 translation physically happens, how many on-chip TLB levels exist and their capacities, the miss penalty, and the default allocation page size are not published by NVIDIA and not measured in this book. Every global access and TMA transfer passes virtual addresses; buffer allocation order shifting the physical-page and partition placement of later tensors is inferred (Chapter 10, Section 5)
Partitioned crossbar (XBAR; L1-to-XBAR / XBAR-to-L1) Between the 132 SMs (GPCs) and the two L2 partitions Documented (H100 whitepaper p37, p43; NCU §2.3.5, §2.11.2): the partitioned crossbar carries packets from source units to destination units; NCU's L1/TEX table separately reports peak-utilization percentages for the L1-to-XBAR request interface and the XBAR-to-L1 return path. Measured on other GPUs in public papers (MICRO 2024 abstract): core-to-partition on-chip latency can differ by about 70% depending on core position. Unknown: whether TMA and L1TEX share one per-SM XBAR injection port, along with XBAR peak bandwidth and internal arbitration order, is not published and not measured in this book. Every global load, store, atomic, and TMA transfer crossing L2 / HBM traverses it (Chapter 2, Section 2); also one candidate queueing site at kernel startup in Chapter 8, Section 7 (exact queueing site not measured)
L2 Request Coalescer (LRC / VIDLRC) Inferred to sit in front of L2 (VIDLRC for global device memory; which side of XBAR it sits on and unit count not published) Documented (NCU §2.3.4, §2.3.5): LRC receives incoming requests headed for L2, tries to coalesce read requests before forwarding them to L2, serves programmatic multicast requests from SMs, and supports write compression (the Inline Compressor ILC is part of LRC, compressing writes before L2 when possible and decompressing read responses). Inferred: sits on the L2 ingress side from that functional description, and "programmatic multicast requests" corresponds to thread-block-cluster TMA .multicast::cluster (PTX §9.7.10.28.4.1 / .5.3). Unknown: whether it sits before or after XBAR, how many LRC units exist across the chip, its coalescing window, and its service order are not published, and not measured in isolation in this book. No standalone step in this book isolates LRC (vector x reuse in Chapter 2, Section 2 is explained by L1/L2 cache hits; the cluster merges unpacked in the main text—Chapter 7, Section 12 and Chapter 9, Section 3—use distributed shared memory st.async rather than TMA multicast, whereas the shipped prefill pooler [T = 753, see Chapter 9, Section 7, and 3,012] and router use 2-CTA cluster .multicast::cluster, not unpacked in the text, with LRC effect not measured)
Per-allocation inline compression (ILC, GXC, XCOMP; scope note) GPC-to-L2 write path (GXC), inside LRC (ILC), and L2 / HBM (XCOMP hardware position not published) Documented (Hopper Tuning Guide §1.4.2.3; CUDA Guide §4.18.5.2; H100 whitepaper p37; NCU §2.3.4–§2.3.5): explicitly opted into per allocation via the CUDA Driver virtual-memory API with CU_MEM_ALLOCATION_COMP_GENERIC (GXC attempts to compress fully covered 128 B writes coming from GPCs to L2, the Inline Compressor ILC lives inside LRC, and XCOMP is the crossbar compressor); depending on the data, it saves DRAM bandwidth, L2 read bandwidth and L2 capacity (CUDA Guide §4.18.5.2), while the allocated memory footprint does not shrink. Inferred: off by default on ordinary cudaMalloc allocations. Unknown: the exact hardware position of XCOMP is not published; how many bytes it would save if enabled on BF16 or quantized weights was not measured. None of this book's kernels allocates compressible memory; weight and KV byte reductions use explicit narrow formats instead (C12 / NVFP4 in Chapter 6, Sections 1–3; FP8 in Chapter 7, Section 1)
Shared L2 cache and two-partition interconnect (LTC, ltcfabric) Central cache layer between on-chip memory clients and FBPA Documented (NCU §2.3.1, §2.3.4, §2.11.3; H100 whitepaper p18, p37): LTC is the chip-wide physical-address Level 2 cache, physically split into two L2 partitions connected by the partition communication fabric LTC Fabric (ltcfabric) (documented as 60 MB on full GH100 and 50 MB on H100 SXM5; the H200 datasheet states no L2 size). Measured via device attribute on H200: querying cudaDevAttrL2CacheSize (and NCU device attributes) on our H200 gives 60 MiB (62,914,560 B). Unknown: H200's hardware peak L2 read bandwidth is not published. Unloaded round-trip latency and the two partitions are in Chapter 2, Section 2, residency policy hints in Chapter 2, Section 4, and read-only versus write-flush comparison in Chapter 10, Section 2
L2 cache slices and three-stage pipeline (LTS: lts__t / lts__m / lts__d) Parallel sub-partitions inside the two L2 partitions Documented (NCU §2.3.4; H100 whitepaper p43): each L2 Cache Slice (LTS) is a sub-partition of L2, and counter prefixes lts__t, lts__m, and lts__d denote its Tag, Miss, and Data stages. Measured on sibling GH100 H20 (preprint) (arXiv:2611.13860): 96 slices grouped into 12 FBPs across the two partitions, selected by a physical-address XOR hash. Unknown: H200's active slice count, address hash function, and intra-slice hit/miss service order are not published and not measured in this book. Encountered when inspecting low-level NCU L2 counters (Chapter 10, Section 6); serialization when many CTAs atomically add into the same L2 address is inferred and does not depend on total slice count (Chapter 7, Section 12)
Memory controllers / FrameBuffer Partitions (FBPA; i.e., HBM partitions) Between L2 (LTC) and the 6 off-chip HBM3e stacks Documented (NCU §2.3.4; H100 whitepaper p18; H200 datasheet): FBPAs are the memory controllers sitting between LTC (L2) and off-chip DRAM, and their count varies by GPU; full GH100 pairs 6 stacks with 12 512-bit controllers, H100 SXM5 pairs 5 stacks with 10 512-bit controllers, and H200's nominal total bandwidth is 4.8 TB/s. Derived / Inferred: combining full GH100's 6 stacks with the 6,016-bit (> 5 × 1,024-bit) memory bus listed in the H200 NVL brief gives 6 HBM3e stacks. Unknown: H200 SXM's exact active FBPA count, address hash, and DRAM row-scheduling policy are not published and not measured in this book; mcc in NCU §2.3.4 belongs to the SoC Memory Subsystem (MSS), and whether data-center H200 has such a unit is unknown. Every HBM weight, activation, and KV stream in this book enters and leaves device memory through it (Chapter 2, Sections 2–3; startup queueing candidates and the "HBM partition" mapping-shift inference are in Chapter 8, Section 7 and Chapter 10, Section 5)

2Intra-SM Cache Sub-Stages, Shared Data Ports, Address Generation, and Warp-Stall Index

NCU breaks each SM's unified L1TEX unit into an input stage plus Tag, Miss, and Data stages, and explains how a shared bidirectional unit data port can saturate before any single directional link hits its own peak; warp-stall reasons and the on-chip hardware warp sampler are consolidated in Chapter 10, Section 7.

Sub-Stage / NCU Name Location on Chip What It Does, Limits, and Epistemic Status Book kernel and Chapter Pointer
L1TEX input and three internal stages (lsuin, l1tex__t, l1tex__m, l1tex__d) Each SM's unified L1 data cache / texture / shared-memory unit (L1TEX, managing 256 KiB of on-chip SRAM) Documented (NCU §2.3.4, §2.3.5, §2.11.2): lsuin is the Load/Store input stage; l1tex__t, l1tex__m, and l1tex__d denote the Tag, Miss, and Data stages of L1TEX; requests, serialized cycle-by-cycle wavefronts, and 32 B sectors are defined in NCU §2.11.2 (note that the global-load pipeline diagram in that section is drawn for Ampere GA100, not GH100). Measured on sibling GH100 H800 PCIe (paper) (arXiv:2501.12084): TMA transfers bypass the L1 cache. Unknown: internal queue depths, detailed stage division of labor, and per-stage peak bandwidths on GH100 are not published, and not measured in isolation in this book. Ordinary global loads/stores, cp.async, shared-memory accesses (including ldmatrix / stmatrix), and SHFL all pass through L1TEX (Chapter 3, Sections 2 and 9; Appendix B, Section 6); consult this row when reading raw l1tex__* metrics in NCU (Chapter 10, Section 6, Step 3)
Shared bidirectional unit data ports (NCU Memory Chart Ports) Ports on cache and memory unit boundaries in NCU's Memory Chart Documented (NCU §2.10.1 Ports): incoming and outgoing traffic of a memory or cache unit often share a single common data port; even when every individual directional link sharing that port operates well below its own peak, the unit's shared data port can already reach saturation. Unknown: which specific hardware units on GH100 share one bidirectional port versus split separate ports is not itemized by NVIDIA and not measured in isolation in this book. Encountered when opening NCU's Memory Workload Analysis panel to inspect the memory chart (Chapter 10, Section 6, Step 3)
Address Generation Unit and interleaved .local layout (AGU) Along the SM memory path (specific parent hardware block not published) Documented (NCU §2.3.1 Memory): thread-private local memory (.local, backed by global device memory) has its addresses translated into global virtual addresses by the AGU; local memory is interleaved so consecutive thread IDs access consecutive 32-bit words, making accesses to the same relative offset across a warp fully coalesced. Unknown: which hardware block inside GH100 houses the AGU, and whether it also computes shared-memory or ordinary register-offset addresses, is not published by NVIDIA. Touched only when register spills, uninlined function stack frames (STACK), or dynamically indexed local arrays land in .local (Chapter 3, Section 1; Chapter 7, Section 7; Chapter 8, Section 4; Chapter 10, Section 6, Step 1; Appendix B, Item 26); compare multi-dimensional tile hardware address generation in TMA (Chapter 3, Section 5)
Warp-stall reasons and hardware warp sampler (lg_throttle, no_instructions, sleeping, drain, etc.) Per SMSP (smsp__pcsamp_* stall counters; L0 instruction cache: H100 whitepaper p21 Fig. 7 (figure label only)), per SM (hardware warp sampler), per TPC (ICC); exact hardware location of the LG queue not published The four stalls lg_throttle, no_instructions, sleeping, and drain, together with each SM's hardware warp sampler (alongside long_scoreboard, mio_throttle / short_scoreboard, barrier, and wait), are not defined a second time in this table (per-TPC ICC containment is in Section 1, Row 1 above; queue depths and instruction-cache byte capacities are not published). See Chapter 10, Section 7

3Tensor Core and Integer Datapath Quick Reference

Beyond the BF16 / FP16 and FP8 paths used directly in our operators, Hopper Tensor Cores also support TF32, INT8, and 2:4 structured sparsity; 4-bit integers remain only in single-warp mma.sync and are absent from wgmma, while CUDA-core integer dot product dp4a runs on the heavy half of the FMA pipeline.

Datapath / Feature On-Chip Execution Unit Shapes, Precision Rules, Nominal Peaks, and Epistemic Status Book kernel and Chapter Pointer
FP16 / BF16 Tensor Core (mma.sync, wgmma) 4 Tensor Cores per SM (1 per SMSP) Primary 16-bit floating-point matrix-multiply path in this book (instruction shapes, SS / RS operand modes, dense compute peak, and SASS mnemonics are not restated here). See Primer 2, Section 1; Chapter 5, Section 4; and Appendix B, Quick Reference 3 (Items 40 and 42)
FP8 (E4M3 / E5M2) Tensor Core and accumulator precision 4 Tensor Cores per SM (single-warp mma.sync expands on sm_90a into unpack plus HMMA) Primary 8-bit floating-point matrix-multiply path in this book (2× throughput at k = 32, direct .f16 f16x2 or .f32 accumulators, PTX's documented .f32 accumulation "at higher than half precision but lower than single precision" alongside about 13–14 mantissa bits measured in external papers, and single-warp expansion are not restated here). See Chapter 5, Section 4; Chapter 7, Section 10 (.f32 and f16x2 accumulators); and Appendix B, Quick Reference 3 (Items 41 and 43)
TF32 Tensor Core path (mma.sync m16n8k4/k8, wgmma m64nNk8) 4 Tensor Cores per SM Documented (PTX §5.2.3, §9.7.17.2, §9.7.17.5.2; H100 whitepaper Table 1 p20, Table 3 p39; H200 datasheet Footnote 2): same dynamic range as .f32 with >= 10-bit precision (internal bit layout implementation-defined; wgmma truncates the lower 13 bits of 32-bit inputs before multiplying), accumulates into .f32 with dense k = 8; nominal peak 494.7 / 989.4 TFLOP/s (dense / sparse). Derived from documented constants: about 7.4× the datasheet FP32 FMA peak (66.9 TFLOP/s) at rated boost clocks, and 8× per clock at equal frequency (2,048 vs 256 FLOP/cycle/SM). Unknown: sm_90a SASS mnemonics and modifiers are not disassembled; accuracy impact on Muse Spark Open was not measured. Unused in this book's kernels; in the baseline inference code, Stage 4 router runs in FP32 at T <= 8 and splits weights into high/low BF16 halves summed in FP32 at T > 8 (see Primer 2, Section 2), whereas this book's shipped kernels use FP32 CUDA cores at T = 1 and split high/low BF16 halves into FP32 on Tensor Cores at T >= 8
Transformer Engine (hardware FP8 vs software amax scaling) Hardware half in Tensor Cores and conversion pipelines; software half in host framework libraries Documented (H100 whitepaper p11, p23, p46; Transformer Engine 2.0 User Guide FP8 Primer; PTX §5.2.3, §9.7.17.5.2): the hardware half supplies dual-format FP8 Tensor Core inputs—E4M3 (4 exponent + 3 mantissa bits, finite range ±448, finer precision) and E5M2 (5 exponent + 2 mantissa bits, finite range ±57,344 plus ±inf, wider dynamic range, with mixed E4M3 × E5M2 operands supported in wgmma)—plus saturating conversion instructions; the software half tracks historical maximum absolute values (amax, delayed scaling) across steps to compute per-tensor scale factors. Unknown: which execution pipeline runs FP8 pack/unpack F2FP on H200 was not measured (see Appendix B, Items 19 and 41). This book uses only the hardware half: the Stage 2 prologue divides by the supplied input scale factor (1 on benchmark shapes) and saturates into ±448 E4M3 (Chapter 7, Section 1; native FP8 attention MMA is in Chapter 7, Sections 9–10)
INT8 Tensor Core path (.s8 / .u8 → .s32, opcodes IMMA / IGMMA) 4 Tensor Cores per SM Documented (H100 whitepaper Table 1 p20, Table 3 p39; H200 datasheet Footnote 2; PTX 9.5 §9.7.16.5.14, §9.7.17.5.2, §13.11; Binary Utilities §4.3 Table 8): inner dimension k = 32, accumulating into .s32 (optional .satfinite clamping, wrapping otherwise); both single-warp mma.sync (m16n8k32) and sm_90a wgmma (m64nNk32, from PTX 8.4 onward) let A and B choose .s8 or .u8 independently (supporting mixed .s8 × .u8 and .u8 × .s8; the stale same-signedness summary line in PTX §9.7.17.3 is superseded by the instruction section and §13.11 release notes); nominal peak 1,978.9 / 3,957.8 TOPS (dense / 2:4 sparse); Hopper instruction-set opcodes are IMMA and IGMMA. Unknown: full sm_90a shape suffixes and whether single-warp integer mma.sync expands into multiple instructions on sm_90a are not disassembled in this book (compare single-warp FP8 expansion in Appendix B, Item 41). Unused in this book's model (used in W8A8 integer quantized inference; for the k = 32 FP8 Tensor Core path, see Chapter 5, Section 4 and Appendix B, Quick Reference 3, Items 42–43)
Sub-byte INT4 single-warp MMA (mma.sync .s4 / .u4 → .s32; absent from wgmma) Single-warp mma.sync target ISA (sm_90a lowering unknown) Documented (PTX §9.7.16.2, §9.7.16.5.4, §9.7.16.5.14, §9.7.17.3; H100 whitepaper and H200 datasheet): PTX single-warp mma.sync accepts m8n8k32 (sm_75+) and m16n8k32 / m16n8k64 (sm_80+), but requires both A and B to be 4-bit integers (.u4 or .s4, mixed .u4 × .s4 allowed per §9.7.16.5.14 example) accumulating into .s32; Hopper wgmma has no .s4 / .u4 type at all, and NVIDIA publishes no INT4 Tensor Core peak on H100 or H200. Unknown: what SASS sm_90a emits for this mma.sync and its actual throughput are not disassembled and not measured in this book. Unused in this book, and directly explains why Hopper NVFP4 must unpack weights in registers with 8 integer instructions: expert weights are block-scaled E2M1 floats, activations are BF16, and large batches require wgmma (Chapter 6, Section 5; Chapter 8, Section 1; Appendix A, Section 3)
Tensor Core 2:4 structured sparsity (mma.sp, wgmma.mma_async.sp) 4 Tensor Cores per SM (left-operand A path) Documented (PTX §9.7.16.6.1, §9.7.17.6; H100 whitepaper p20 Table 1, p22; H200 datasheet Footnote 2): sparsity applies only to left matrix A; 16-bit and 8-bit types store at most 2 nonzeros per 4 consecutive elements at 2:4 granularity (1:2 granularity for .tf32) alongside a .b32 metadata operand holding 2-bit nonzero indices, doubling the instruction k dimension (BF16/FP16 16→32, TF32 8→16, FP8/INT8 32→64) and doubling nominal peak throughput (e.g., BF16 989 → 1,979, FP8 1,979 → 3,958 TFLOP/s). Unknown: Hopper's internal zero-skipping mux hardware details are not published; our model weights are unpruned, and sparse accuracy and speedup were not measured. Unused because our model weights are dense; explains how the datasheet's 2× "with sparsity" footnote numbers relate to this book's dense lower bounds (989 / 1,979 TFLOP/s) (Primer 2, Section 1; Chapter 5, Section 4; Chapter 7, Section 1)
CUDA-core 4-way byte integer dot product (dp4a / dp2a, opcodes IDP / IDP4A) Heavy half of the FMA pipeline (FMA Heavy) in each SMSP Documented (PTX §9.7.1.24–25; Binary Utilities §4.3 Table 8; NCU §2.3.6 Pipelines): dp4a computes a per-thread dot product of 4 pairs of packed 8-bit integers (.s8 / .u8) from two 32-bit registers and accumulates into a 32-bit integer register (dp2a is the 2-way form), mapping to Hopper SASS opcodes IDP / IDP4A; per the NCU manual, integer dot products run on the FMA Heavy half of the FMA pipeline alongside IMAD, not on the ALU pipeline. Unknown: full SASS modifiers and H200 issue intervals are not published, and not disassembled or measured in this book. Unused in this book's model (single-token gemv uses floating-point FFMA; for the FMA pipeline and its IMAD half, see Chapter 5, Section 1 and Appendix B, Item 12a)

4Extended TMA Modes, Descriptor Updates, and Cluster Bulk Copy

Beyond the rectangular .tile loads/reductions and static host descriptors used in the main text, Hopper's TMA also supports convolution im2col, narrow-channel interleaved global layouts, in-kernel descriptor updates through the tensormap proxy, and intra-cluster peer-CTA shared-memory bulk copies.

TMA Mode / Mechanism On-Chip Unit and Proxy Syntax Rules, Hardware Limits, and Epistemic Status Book kernel and Chapter Pointer
TMA im2col convolution unrolling mode (.im2col) Each SM's TMA unit (async proxy) Documented (PTX §5.5.2, §5.5.4, §5.5.5, §9.7.10.28.5.3): supports 3D (NWC), 4D (NHWC), and 5D (NDHWC) tensors, extracting elements from a convolution window bounding box plus offsets in DHW space and rearranging them directly into columns in shared memory; H200 (sm_90a) supports only plain .im2col, while .im2col::w, .im2col::w::128, and .im2col_no_offs::w require sm_100 or higher. Because it still steps across regular sliding-window geometry, it cannot accept an arbitrary page-table row-index array. Unknown: .im2col throughput and SASS modifiers on H200 were not measured in this book. Unused in this book's kernels; explains why neither multi-dimensional TMA mode on Hopper can gather scattered KV rows from a page table in one command (Chapter 10, Section 10; Appendix C, TMA (Tensor Memory Accelerator) entry; for Blackwell's .tile::gather4, see Appendix A, Section 4)
Tensor-descriptor channel interleave and allocation class (.alloc_class) Fields in the 128 B CUtensorMap descriptor, parsed in hardware by TMA Documented (PTX §5.5.3.3, §5.5.6, §9.7.10.29 Table 36, §9.7.10.30; CUDA Guide §4.13.2.2): interleave applies only to 3D–5D tensors and groups channel dimension C in global memory into 16 B (NC/8DHWC8) or 32 B (NC/16HWC16) interleaved slices to speed up loads of elements narrower than 4 B—it alters global-memory layout, unlike on-chip bank-conflict XOR swizzle; .alloc_class (.alloc_small / .alloc_large / .alloc_same, introduced in PTX 9.5 and supported on sm_90a) tags the underlying tensor allocation size class to bound out-of-bounds access safety. Unknown: latency differences from either attribute on H200 were not measured in this book. Every kernel in this book uses INTERLEAVE_NONE and never sets .alloc_class; for the tiled descriptor fields built on the host, see Chapter 3, Section 5
In-kernel descriptor updates and the tensormap proxy (tensormap.replace, tensormap.cp_fenceproxy, fence.proxy.tensormap::generic) SMEM → global memory → TMA tensormap proxy Documented (PTX §8.6, §9.7.10.29, §9.7.15.4, §9.7.15.17; CUDA Guide §4.13.2.2.2–§4.13.2.2.3): TMA reads tensor descriptors through a separate tensormap proxy; when patching a 128 B (1024-bit) descriptor on the device, in tensormap.replace (requires sm_90a) the .ss operand may be .global or .shared::cta; the shared-memory path is recommended (CUDA Guide §4.13.2.2.2): the modifying thread edits fields in shared memory first and then copies back to global memory with release via tensormap.cp_fenceproxy.global.shared::cta.tensormap::generic.release (sm_90+) (or releases with fence.proxy.tensormap::generic.release if editing directly in global memory); before using the descriptor, one thread in the same CTA must also run fence.proxy.tensormap::generic.acquire, after which it or other threads in that CTA following a block sync can issue TMA (read-only const __grid_constant__ descriptors built on the host—and prefetch.tensormap on them—require none of these proxy fences). Unknown: which cache level holds descriptors in hardware, the SASS lowering, and device-side update latency are not published by NVIDIA, and not disassembled or measured in this book. Every TMA kernel in this book builds static descriptors on the host ahead of launch, avoiding device-side proxy fences (see Chapter 3, Section 5 and Appendix B, Item 30a)
Intra-cluster peer-CTA shared-memory bulk copy (cp.async.bulk.shared::cluster.shared::cta) Source SM's TMA unit writing directly into peer CTA shared memory over the intra-GPC SM-to-SM interconnect Documented (PTX §9.7.10.28.4.1; Hopper Tuning Guide §1.4.1.2; CUDA Guide §4.13.2; H100 whitepaper p11, p22): issued by a single thread without staging payload through registers, copying contiguous bytes from local shared memory (.shared::cta) directly into another CTA's distributed shared memory (.shared::cluster) in the same cluster and decrementing the receiver CTA's mbarrier expected-byte count on arrival (if generic shared-memory stores just wrote the source buffer, fence.proxy.async.shared::cta is required before issuing). PTX imposes three hard rules: (1) byte count size must be a multiple of 16 B; (2) both source and destination addresses must be 16 B-aligned; and (3) the destination must lie in the shared memory of a different CTA in the cluster (self-copy is forbidden). Unknown: its speed crossover byte size against st.async on H200 was not measured, and cluster-direction SASS modifiers are not disassembled in this book. Both cluster merges in this book use st.async instead: in Chapter 7, Section 12, both cluster kernel families write their own CTA's slice (forbidden by the no-self-copy rule; the 3-in-1 mma.sync kernel also holds partial sums in registers and would need shared-memory staging plus a proxy fence, while the sliding-window wgmma kernel already stages output rows and LSE in two separate 16 B-aligned/sized shared-memory arrays but would still need a proxy fence and a separate self-write path, with which is faster not measured); in Chapter 9, Section 3, each partial sum of squares is only 4 B (one FP32, under 16 B) and likewise includes 1 self-write. For global → SMEM TMA forms, see Appendix B, Quick Reference 2, Items 30 and 33

Takeaway: Whenever an unfamiliar single-GPU Hopper hardware name shows up in whitepapers, PTX manuals, or NCU panels, check first which chip level it lives at, what specification rules bind it, and which details even official documentation leaves unpublished—then follow the rightmost column back to the operator step in this book.
